IDF Query Scaleout Design

## 1 Introduction
IDF Query offers a rich SQL-like interface capable of performing sophisticated queries on Entity Relationship Graph Database. Query follows a sequential processing pipeline which consists of broadly the following stages:
FROM
WHERE
SELECT

Arithmos Deep Dive
The doc is written for Arithmos developers to have code level understanding of Arithmos. This doc does not include container, storage pool and cluster usage calculations. The usage calculation details can be found here.

[Arithmos & Metric Collection | Arithmos Deep Dive]
## Entity Partition Cluster-level entities are entities that are owned by Arithmos master. Examples are container, storage pool and cluster entities. There should only be a few cluster-level entities and owning by Arithmos master should be fine. Having only Arithmos master own cluster-level entities simplify the up aggregation from node-level entities to cluster-level entities and also queries of cluster-level entities. Node-level entities are entities that are distributed among Arithmos agents. There are a number of partition schemes: Physical partition. The entities are partitioned based on the nodes that the entities belong to. Examples are disk, node, vm and virtual disk entities. AHV only binds power-on VMs and virtual disks to the nodes. For power-off VMs and virtual disks, AHV is responsible for distributing the entities among Arithmos agents. Random partition. These are entities that do not belong to any nodes and the number of the entities are high. Therefore we cannot make them cluster-level entities. Examples are volume group, snapshot and protection domain schedule entities. Periodically Arithmos master queries Cassandra partition information and remaps the partitions to healthy Arithmos agents. (BaseArithmosMaster::AggregateUsagesOp::FetchMedusaPartitionInfo). Using entity ids, Arithmos agents hash the entity ids and figure out the partitions that the entity ids fall into (ArithmosStatusManager::LookupOwner). Then Arithmos agents forward the data to the owning

[Arithmos & Metric Collection | Arithmos Deep Dive]
healthy Arithmos agents. (BaseArithmosMaster::AggregateUsagesOp::FetchMedusaPartitionInfo). Using entity ids, Arithmos agents hash the entity ids and figure out the partitions that the entity ids fall into (ArithmosStatusManager::LookupOwner). Then Arithmos agents forward the data to the owning Arithmos agents (SingleClusterArithmosAgent::ForwardPartitionedEntities). Parent partition. These are entities that follow their parent entities to simplify the up aggregation where up aggregation only requires local entities. Examples are virtual disks that contribute to volume groups. The virtual disks will be partitioned using “attach_volume_group_id” of the virtual disks (ArithmosStatusManager::GetEntityOwner). Therefore when up-aggregating from virtual disks to volume groups, Arithmos agents will have all the required virtual disks. Another example is vdisk entities. When virtual disks are created, Arithmos agents will resolve the nfs file paths in the virtual disks to vdisk names. Arithmos agents will publish the vdisk names to Pithos (QueueVDiskPartitionAddition) so that other Arithmos agents will forward the vdisks to the owning Arithmos agents. Above are two examples that use parent partition scheme with different methods of figuring out the parent locations. One more detail is there can be other publishers which do not know the parent of the entities like the volume group of the virtual disk. Therefore, Arithmos agents publish the virtual disks that belong to volume groups

[Arithmos & Metric Collection | Arithmos Deep Dive]
there can be other publishers which do not know the parent of the entities like the volume group of the virtual disk. Therefore, Arithmos agents publish the virtual disks that belong to volume groups that they own to Pithos (QueueVirtualDiskPartitionAddition) so that other publishers can publish the same virtual disks without specifying “attach_volume_group_id”. More information about partition can be found here.

[Arithmos & Metric Collection | Arithmos Deep Dive]
## Arithmos Status Manager Arithmos stores ArithmosStatus protobuf in Zookeeper to communicate with other Arithmos agents and also stats clients like Stargate. For example, done_copying_old_stat_proto in Arithmos status indicates to the stats cassandra backend clients that Arithmos has finished upgrading the data model in Cassandra. Refer to the usage doc “Upgrade” section for more information. Arithmos also stores the partition to Arithmos agent assignment in ArithmosStatus. This is used by the random partition scheme described in the previous section and also the usage computation which is in the usage doc. The partition to Arithmos agent is done as part of the heavyweight usage aggregation in BaseArithmosMaster::AggregateUsagesOp::FetchMedusaPartitionInfoDone and publish to Zookeeper in BaseArithmosMaster::AggregateUsagesOp::PublishPartitionInfo. Pithos: Arithmos also maintains the entity ids in each partition. The information is maintained for the parent partition scheme described above where the publishers do not know the parents of the entities. For example, Stargate does not know the virtual disks that the vdisks belong to and some publishers do not know the volume groups that the virtual disks belong to. Therefore Arithmos agents publish the entity ids that it owns for certain entity type and under certain conditions. Refer to the Queue... functions in ArithmosStatusManager. In Pithos, the key is arithmos agent, entity type pair and the value is the list of entity

[Arithmos & Metric Collection | Arithmos Deep Dive]
owns for certain entity type and under certain conditions. Refer to the Queue... functions in ArithmosStatusManager. In Pithos, the key is arithmos agent, entity type pair and the value is the list of entity ids. During startup, Arithmos scans all the key value pairs and populates the memory to expedite the lookup. When a node is removed, Arithmos gets the notification through Zeus config callback, the stale keys in Pithos will be removed (ArithmosStatusManager::DeleteStalePartitions).

## Stats Controller
Arithmos clients can send the stats to Arithmos using Arithmos rpcs. Older clients like Stargate still send stats to Arithmos through StatsController using Arithmos backend (StatsArithmosBackend). In this case, the clients usually also write the stats to Cassandra using Cassandra backend (StatsCassandraBackend). The reason to write the stats twice is Arithmos was a new service then and the reliability was not proven yet. Also we do not invest in the deprecation project because the benefit is minimal.
StatsArithmosBackend only allows clients to send stats to Arithmos. To read the stats, the clients have to use Arithmos rpcs. To reduce the number of AgentSendStats rpcs, the stats are staged and written to Arithmos every 10s and will be increased to 30s if Arithmos returns a timeout error, which means Arithmos is overloaded. Also we do not retry on error and drop new stats to avoid overloading Arithmos.
StatsCassandraBackend supports writing and reading the stats to Cassandra. More details about the backend can be found in this doc under “Stats Aggregator Internal Details” section.

[Arithmos & Metric Collection | Arithmos Deep Dive]
## Up Aggregation Up aggregation aggregates attributes and stats from an entity type to another entity type, for example, from virtual disks to VMs or from nodes to clusters. Every attribute or stat has a “entity_merge_operation” that specifies the up aggreatoin operator. If an attribute or stat should not have an up aggregation operator, kInvalid is used. There are two types of up aggregations - cross-node aggregation and local aggregation. Cross-node aggregation only happens on cluster-level entities like container, storage pool and cluster where Arithmos master periodically polls local summary from Arithmos agents and merges the local summary (CollectDataFromAgents). Arithmos agents compute the local summary in PartialAggregate class. Local aggregation is where most of the up aggregation happens. The partition schemes like physical partition and partition based on parents are optimized for local aggregation (ArithmosUtil::UpAggregate). Local up aggregation is a complex and time consuming function. We have seen Arithmos used 100% CPU mostly due to up aggregation. Therefore for some entity types, we have changed inline up aggregation to background up aggregation that runs periodically to reduce the number of up aggregation calls (SingleClusterArithmosAgent::UpAggregation). Clients can specify the attribute name to merge the entities and aggregate the data. For example, clients can up aggregate the virtual disks based on attach_vm_id. High level, up aggregate consists of The

[Arithmos & Metric Collection | Arithmos Deep Dive]
(SingleClusterArithmosAgent::UpAggregation). Clients can specify the attribute name to merge the entities and aggregate the data. For example, clients can up aggregate the virtual disks based on attach_vm_id. High level, up aggregate consists of The stats is normalized due to difference in timespans (NormalizeStats) The stats is merged using entity merge operation based on attribute value. Entity merge operation like kAverage requires two passes where the first pass performs summation and the second pass performs division (MergedEntity::FirstPassMerge and MergedEntity::SecondPassMerge). Local up aggregation has many other bells and whistles. One has to read the codes to understand all the functionalities.

## Data Properties
Arithmos supports creating attributes and stats during runtime through CreateGenericAttributesAndStats rpc. This is mostly used by health checks and kEntityBackup. Note that this is not the preferred way of creating attributes and stats because they can’t be discovered by developers when looking at the list of attributes and stats. Arithmos stores the attribute and stat properties across 23 Zookeeper nodes since each Zookeeper node can only store up to 1MB of data. Entity type is used to shard the properties among the Zookeeper node.
CreateGenericAttributesAndStats is supported by Arithmos agent. Whenever an Arithmos agent receives the rpc, it updates the Zookeeper by adding the new attribute/stat to the Zookeeper node. Once the Zookeeper update is done, the Arithmos agent will add the newly created attribute/stat to memory. Other Arithmos agents watch the data property Zookeeper nodes and will apply the diff whenever there are changes.

[Arithmos & Metric Collection | Arithmos Deep Dive]
## Data Persistence Arithmos persists data in Cassandra and local file system. Periodically every 0.5s to 1s depending on the number of stats (arithmos_cassandra_flusher.cc), Arithmos flushes a single stat to Cassandra. In newer versions, a single stat can translate 1 or 2 Cassandra columns if the stat values cross the Cassandra column boundaries. Each Cassandra column (ArithmosHistoricalProto) contains 12 hour of stats and is represented by a list of time slices (TimeSlice). The reason is to optimize for stat values which are not contiguous within a column since using -1 to represent no stats is expensive because -1 doesn’t benefit from protobuf variable length encoding. The Cassandra column is compressed before storing into Cassandra. Arithmos flushes single stat periodically in round robin fashion going through entity types, entities within an entity type and stat types within an entity. This cycle is only broken by deleted entities. Arithmos prioritizes flushing stats for deleted entities. This is to mitigate the workflow where VMs are vmotioned from source node to target node where the VM is deleted from source node and created on target node. In this workflow, the design is for the target node to pick up the historical stats as fast as possible. Therefore Arithmos on source node needs to flush the stats for the deleted VMs asap. Since Arithmos only flushes a single stat periodically, there are stats doesn’t get flushed to Cassaandra. Every 1 minute, Arithmos flushes the

[Arithmos & Metric Collection | Arithmos Deep Dive]
source node needs to flush the stats for the deleted VMs asap. Since Arithmos only flushes a single stat periodically, there are stats doesn’t get flushed to Cassaandra. Every 1 minute, Arithmos flushes the unflushed stats and attributes into persist files in the local file system (for Arithmos agent) and Cassandra (for Arithmos master). Arithmos agents flushes the data into a persist file directory that contains multiple persist files. Each persist file contains multiple PersistEntityType. The enables Arithmos to flush the data in pieces and doesn’t get blocked for a long time because of flushing the data.

## LUA
LUA is an efficient embedded language that can be modified during runtime without restarting the process. The goal of introducing lua in Arithmos is enabling clients to implement their own data processing logic like deriving a stat without compiling Arithmos. Two places where lua are used
Determine whether a hardcoded stat is a derived stat (EntityTypeData::LuaIsDerived)
Computing a derived stat. This is disabled since it causes memory issue with PowerPC (gflag arithmos_lua_stat_derive)
This feature doesn’t take off as in Arithmos clients do not use LUA to implement custom logic to derive the stat. I think the reason is Arithmos clients do not want to spend time learning a new language.

Arithmos aggregation for disaggregated storage and compute clusters

## Introduction:
Nutanix provides an option where storage can be provided from a separate CVM
to a cluster where compute is running. This enables a disaggregated
architecture that separates storage and compute resources into distinct
clusters for better resource optimization and flexibility.
In this architecture, we have two types of clusters:
• Cluster 1 (Storage Cluster): Runs Stargate service and publishes vdisks
• Cluster 2 (Compute Cluster): Runs AHV and publishes virtual_disks and VMs

## Current Behavior (HCI Clusters)
In traditional HCI (Hyperconverged Infrastructure) clusters, Arithmos performs
a hierarchical aggregation of storage statistics. The aggregation flow works
as follows:
1. vdisk stats → aggregated to → virtual_disk stats
2. virtual_disk stats → aggregated to → VM stats
3. virtual_disk stats and VM stats → synced to Prism Central (PC)
This aggregation pipeline works seamlessly in HCI environments because both
Storage and Compute metrics reside on a single cluster, allowing Arithmos to
perform the up-aggregation locally before syncing to the PC.

[Arithmos & Metric Collection | Arithmos aggregation for disaggregated storage and compute clusters]
## Problem Statement:
With disaggregated storage and compute architecture, the entities are
distributed across different clusters:
• vdisks exist on the storage cluster
• virtual_disks and VMs exist on the compute cluster
The current up-aggregation logic FAILS in this scenario because:
• vdisk → virtual_disk aggregation cannot happen since these entities are
on different clusters
• virtual_disk → VM aggregation cannot complete due to the missing underlying
vdisk data
• This results in incomplete or missing stats being synced to PC, leading
to inaccurate reporting and monitoring

[Arithmos & Metric Collection | Arithmos aggregation for disaggregated storage and compute clusters]
## Approach 1: Pull vdisk Data from Storage Cluster
In this approach, the compute cluster takes responsibility for gathering the
necessary vdisk data from the storage cluster. The compute cluster would
periodically pull vdisk stats from the storage cluster and use this data
to perform the up-aggregation at the virtual_disk level, followed by
aggregation to the VM level. This maintains the existing aggregation logic
but extends it across cluster boundaries.
Key characteristics:
• Compute cluster initiates periodic pulls of vdisk data from storage cluster
• Up-aggregation logic remains on the compute cluster (vdisk → virtual_disk → VM)
• Maintains existing Arithmos aggregation patterns with minimal architectural changes
Advantages:
• Aggregated data will be present on PE and can be consumed if required.
• Preserves existing aggregation logic on the compute cluster
Disadvantages:
• Creates a connectivity dependency between storage and compute clusters
• If connectivity issues persist for more than a minute, aggregate data
will not sync to PC

[Arithmos & Metric Collection | Arithmos aggregation for disaggregated storage and compute clusters]
## Approach  2: Sync vdisks to PC and Aggregate on PC
This approach shifts the aggregation responsibility from the PE cluster level to
Prism Central. Instead of aggregating stats at the PE cluster, we would sync
vdisk data from the storage cluster to the PC, along with virtual_disk and VM
data from the compute cluster. A background job on PC would then perform the
same hierarchical aggregation that Arithmos currently does, but in a
centralized manner.
Key characteristics:
• Storage cluster syncs vdisk data directly to PC
• Compute cluster syncs virtual_disk and VM data to PC (as it does today)
• Background job on PC performs up-aggregation:
- vdisk → virtual_disk
- virtual_disk → VM
• Mirrors Arithmos aggregation logic but executes centrally on PC
Advantages:
• Centralized aggregation logic on PC provides a single source of truth
• Eliminates dependency on inter-cluster connectivity for aggregation
Disadvantages:
• Significant scalability concerns: vdisk scale is very large and could
potentially overwhelm PC IDF storage and processing capacity
• Entity ID collision problem: Vdisk with the same ID can exist on different clusters.
Syncing to PC requires entity_id collision resolution logic

[Arithmos & Metric Collection | Arithmos aggregation for disaggregated storage and compute clusters]
## Approach 3: Sync vdisk Stats and Map to virtual_disk
This approach represents a hybrid solution that balances complexity,
scalability, and maintainability. Instead of syncing
entire vdisk entities, we sync only vdisk statistics from PE to PC, and
introduce a new operation in the Insights Proxy that maps these stats directly
to the corresponding virtual_disk entries.
Key characteristics:
• Storage cluster PE syncs vdisk stats (not full entities) to PC
• New Insights Proxy operation on PC:
- Receives vdisk stats from storage cluster
- Maps and copies vdisk stats directly to the virtual_disk table
• Background job on PC performs simplified aggregation:
- Only virtual_disk → VM aggregation needed
- vdisk → virtual_disk mapping already handled by Insights Proxy
Advantages:
• Reduces complexity compared to Approach 2 (no full entity sync)
• Avoids entity ID collision issues since mapping happens at the stats
level, not entity level
• Better scalability than full vdisk entity sync - only stats are transmitted
Disadvantages:
• Requires new functionality in Insights Proxy for stats mapping
• Need to benchmark if the proxy can handle the increased load in memory as well as CPU.

[Arithmos & Metric Collection | Arithmos aggregation for disaggregated storage and compute clusters]
## Approach 4: Marker Entities on Storage Cluster with Reverse Aggregation
This approach introduces a reverse-aggregation pattern in which lightweight "marker" entities (e.g., virtual_disk, vms)  are created in a storage cluster that mirrors the compute cluster's entity hierarchy. By establishing this entity linkage on the storage cluster, we enable local aggregation of vdisk stats into virtual_disk and VM aggregates, which can then be synced to PC alongside the raw stats from the compute cluster.
Key Characteristics:
On Storage Cluster (PE):
Create dummy/marker entities (virtual_disk and VM) with the same entity IDs as those on the compute cluster
These marker entities contain only entity linkage attributes:
Arithmos performs standard up-aggregation locally on the storage cluster
vdisk stats → aggregate to virtual_disk marker
virtual_disk marker stats → aggregate to VM marker
Sync aggregated stats (virtual_disk and VM aggregates) to PC
On Compute Cluster (PE):
Maintains actual virtual_disk and VM entities with full entity attributes
Syncs raw stats (non-aggregated) for virtual_disk and VM to PC

Arithmos notification for partition change
Arithmos notification for Cassandra partition change

## Problem Statement:
Arithmos maintains its partitioning in sync with Cassandra's partitions. When Cassandra's partitioning changes (e.g., due to node additions or deletions), Arithmos must update its partition information accordingly. This information is stored in a ZooKeeper node at /appliance/logical/arithmos_status.
Whenever Arithmos detects a partition change, it updates the ZooKeeper node and deletes entities that no longer belong to the current node’s partition. Additionally, Arithmos fetches the latest partition details from Cassandra every five minutes. This means there can be a delay where Cassandra has already changed its partitioning, but Arithmos continues operating with outdated partition information until the next update cycle.
Clients like Stargate monitor the Arithmos ZooKeeper node for partition change notifications. Once notified, they wait for a fixed period to ensure Arithmos has completed entity deletions before repopulating entities. However, since the repopulation happens after a longer delay to guarantee deletions are complete, there is a downtime during which users cannot access these entities. This results in a temporary gap where entities are unavailable between their deletion by Arithmos and their repopulation by the clients.

[Arithmos & Metric Collection | Arithmos notification for cassandra partition change]
## Solution:
To address the issue, we propose implementing a notification mechanism using a dedicated ZooKeeper node that clients can monitor. Once Arithmos detects a partition change and completes the deletion of stale partitioned entities, it updates the new ZooKeeper node to notify clients.
Upon receiving the notification, clients can assess whether repopulating data in Arithmos is necessary and take immediate action. This approach ensures a more dynamic and responsive update process, reducing downtime significantly. Since clients will now repopulate data as soon as Arithmos completes deletions, users will experience minimal data unavailability. Additionally, this solution is generic enough to be extended across all entity types in Arithmos

[Arithmos & Metric Collection | Arithmos notification for cassandra partition change]
## Workflow:
Client Registration & Initialization:
Arithmos clients will register a watch on a newly created ZooKeeper (ZK) node with a logical timestamp.
On startup, each client will:
Read the ZK node.
Set a watch on it.
Cache the logical timestamp.
Repopulate their entities.
Handling Partition Changes:
When a partition change occurs, Arithmos will:
Delete stale partitioned entities.
Update the ZK node with a new logical timestamp (incrementing the existing value by 1 if it already exists, or setting it to 1 if not).
Client Response to Partition Updates:
When Arithmos updates the ZK node, clients will receive a watch notification.
Upon receiving the notification, clients will:
Fetch the updated logical timestamp from the ZK node.
Compare it with their cached value.
If the new timestamp exceeds the cached value, they will repopulate their entities in Arithmos.
This approach ensures efficient synchronization between Arithmos and its clients while minimizing downtime.

[Arithmos & Metric Collection | Disk Usage]
Stargate periodically publishes disk usage to Cassandra and Arithmos through StatsController. The disk usage proto DiskUsageStatProto is defined in stats/stats.proto. The disk usage proto only captures the extent store usage. The only exception is statfs_usage in the disk usage proto. The disk usage proto has the total disk usage and per container usage. Untransformed means the sum of slice untransformed length and the transformed means the sum of slice transformed length (after compression).
Since the disk usage update is not a synchronous update, the disk usage can be wrong if Stargate crashes. Therefore, Stargate has a background job that recalculate disk usage. The background job can take a while (few days) if there are many extent groups. The source file is egroup_disk_usage_op.cc and estore_background_scan_disk_usage_op.h.
Common issues
The sum of per-container usages is different from total disk usage within the proto.
The extent store usages in disk usage is wrong.
The untransformed usage is wrong.

[Arithmos & Metric Collection | Downsampling interval based arithmos stat sync]
Downsampling interval-based arithmos stat sync
Kumar Gaurav
April 2022
In-progress
Introduction:
Currently as a part of Arithmos sync, we sync all the stats periodically with an interval of 30secs. As evident from the doc, many stats have downsampling intervals greater than 30secs so the same value is being synced to PC multiple times. This can be avoided by implementing a downsampling interval-based stat sync which decreases the sync payload as well as improves Arithmos performance.

Implementation:
We will create 3 buckets for ds intervals 30, 120, and 300 and create a map of stats that lies in the respective buckets. last_sent_timestamp will be maintained for each bucket which will be taken in consideration while creating MasterGetInMemoryTimeRangeStatsForEntitiesArg for fetching stats from Arithmos and synced to PC. 

NOTE: All the stats whose downsampling interval is greater than or equal 300sec will lie in the 300sec bucket.
Pros:
1. Sync payload will decrease
Cons:
1. Stats with downsampling intervals greater than 30secs will not be synced to PC till their respective buckets are synced which can cause unavailability of stats on PC for a maximum time of 300secs.
Note: This downsampling interval-based sync is not applicable for dynamically registered stats that sync to PC.

[Arithmos & Metric Collection | FEAT-3223_ Data Avoidance Stats]
FEAT-3223: Data Avoidance Stats The feat is to introduce more stats that showcases different space saving techniques like clone, snapshot, thin provisioning and etc. as our competitors have done so. There are 2 classes of space saving techniques. The first is data reduction techniques which are documented here. The second is data avoidance techniques. There is no clear rules for the classification. Currently dedup, compression and erasure coding are classified as data reduction where other techniques are classified as data avoidance. Same as data reduction stats, all data avoidance stats will and pre and post bytes,saved bytes and saving ratio as documented in the data reduction doc. Note: All data avoidance stats will have “data_reduction” namespace in Arithmos for simplicity sake. Modelv Let’s assume the following setup: Example1: (assuming the vDisk is only 1MB size with 1 extent) V1 (extent 3), chain id: x -- has 1MB data V2 (extent 3), chain id: x - empty vdisk V3 (extent 3), chain id: y - empty vdisk V4 (extent 3), chain id: z - empty vdisk V5 (extent 3), chain id: z - empty vdisk When curator goes through each chain, it sees reference to the extent_v1 in chain X, Y, Z respectively, So post snapshot of extent_v1 is counted as 1 in chain X, and 1 in chain Y, and 1 in chain Z and total post-snapshot usage is 3. For clone, the pre-clone usage is output of post-snapshot usage which is 3 (or you can also look at it as because extent_v1 is shared by 3 chains, without clone,

[Arithmos & Metric Collection | FEAT-3223_ Data Avoidance Stats]
post-snapshot usage is 3. For clone, the pre-clone usage is output of post-snapshot usage which is 3 (or you can also look at it as because extent_v1 is shared by 3 chains, without clone, it will be 3 extent). Post-clone usage is 1 as 1 extent of extent_v1. As summary: Snapshot and Clone: Pre - 5 extents, Post - 1 extent, Saved: 4 extents, Saving Ratio: 5 to 1 Snapshot: Pre - 5 extents, Post - 3 extents, Saved: 2 extents, Saving Ratio: 5/3 to 1 Clone: Pre - 3 extents, Post - 1 extents, Saved: 2 extents, Saving Ratio: 3 to 1 Note: In implementation, the non-zero region sizes of the vblocks that point to the extent will be used instead of the size of the extent. Dedup extents will not have clone savings since there isn’t a good way to differentiate between dedup savings vs clone savings. The order where snapshot saving comes before clone saving or vice versa is not important. Even though it affects the saving ratio, the saved bytes are the same. Curator will calculate the snapshot and clone saving. Thin Provisioning Saving: Thin provisioning is a hypervisor feature where hypervisor filesystem like VMFS only allocates the space that the virtual disk needs. For example, a virtual disk size can be 10 GB and only uses 1GB. The virtual disk size will come from hypervisor (Acropolis) and the virtual disk usage will come from Stargate (sum of inherited bytes and user bytes in vdisk usage proto).

Removing Stats Aggregator Overview: Stats Aggregator aggregates the stats in Cassandra. The stats are being used by Prism and Stargate. Most of the stats has already been replaced by the stats in Artihmos. The stats that has not been replaced is the cluster-wide usage stats like container, storage pool and cluster usages. The reason is Arithmos does not persist the stats right away and the stats can be inaccurate when an Arithmos agents are down. Reasons to Remove Stats Aggregator: 1. Stats Aggregator is designed during ISCSI vdisk time. Therefore, it is not efficient in handling the high number of vdisks in NFS world. The Cassandra data model only has a single row for the vdisk real time stats, which is not scalable. The limit for a single Cassandra row size is 16MB. Also, a row is owned by a single Cassandra node. When loading, Cassandra always load the whole row to memory even if a single column is requested. 2. All the aggregation work is done by a single node. Therefore, the resource usage like CPU and memory usages of the node will be higher. 3. Unify the Prism UI data sources. Currently, Prism UI gets most of the stats from Arithmos and some stats from Stats backend. It is easier if Prism UI just gets everything from Arithmos. Possible Solutions for ensuring entity uniqueness based on specified attribute
IDF only Internal Doc
March 18
In Progress

## Objective:
Aplos team has a schema requirement. Use case and ask is detailed in this doc here.
Goal is to ideate internally within the IDF team and put forward and discuss possible ideas in this doc itself. Then finalise on one of them before sharing the shortlisted options back to the Aplos team.

## Add a feature in IDF
Support unique attributes in IDF.

## Transaction implemented in IDF
Let's call the entity type we are working with etype.  Create an additional entity type called etype_unique_attr.  The entity ID for this entity type will be the stringified attribute that needs to be unique. etype has an ancestor link of type etype_unique_attr.  etype_unique_attr has an ancestor link of type etype.
Let the entity ID be eid and the unique attribute be attr.

## Creation protocol
First, create an etype_unique_attr with entity ID attr that has an ancestor link to eid. If there already exists an entity with entity ID attr then abort. Next, create an etype entity with entity ID eid that has an ancestor link to attr.

## Deletion protocol
First delete the etype entity then delete the etype_unique_attr entity.

[Customer Issues & Interactions | Brainstorm ideas for Unique entity use case]
## Recovery protocol
The etype_unique_attr entity is effectively a lock.  If one is created but the creator dies before creating a linked etype entity (or a similar process in deletion) then there will be a unique attribute value that can’t be chosen.  In order to rectify this, the user must grab a system level lock (i.e. stop creation/deletion of etype entities) and delete all orphaned etype_unique_attr entities.  This could be detected heuristically by finding etype_unique_attr entities that have no parent etype and that have been around for a long period of time. (A client that has internal transactional guarantees, (i.e. rollback capability) may be able to clean up on its own.)

## Transaction implemented in Zookeeper
Let the entity ID be eid and the value of the unique attribute be attr.

## Protocol to create entity:
Grab a ZK lock on a node named attr.
Do a query, select all entities that have the unique attribute attr.
If such an entity exists then abort.
Create the entity.
Release the ZK lock.

## Protocol to delete entity:
Just delete the entity.

## Recovery protocol:
Use standard ZK recovery protocols for orphaned locks.

## Open Questions:
How much data will be stored in entities using this feature?
How frequently will the data data stored in these entities be modified? (Specifically the unique attribute.)
Answer to the above question (copied and pasted from requester’s comments)
1. Categories will be updated less frequently and the max number of categories that we are expecting is close to 30-35k in the large PC.
2. Intent_spec and abac_entity_capability will be updated quite frequently and the scale numbers for these entities will be of the same order as number of entities on a cluster. E.g Cluster with 12.5k vms managed by v3 apis will have 12.5k abac_entity_capability and intent_spec entities.
3. Remote connection and Availability zone will not be updated that frequently and the number will also be in the range of 1-100 (100 will be extreme)

## Introduction
This is to address the DraaS requirement for FIQL string -> IDF query parser. This document discusses proposals  to support the converter functionality.

## Proposal 1:
The client gives an FIQL AST to IDF. IDF converts to the equivalent GetEntitiesWithMetricsArg -> Query -> Where clause.
Workflow
If client gives an FIQL AST of the form
FIQL Expression {
Repeated FIQL Expressions
OP
}
IDF can implement a C++ script to convert  FIQL AST to Boolean Expression(Where clause - C++ protobuf object) . The Boolean Expression can be used by client to generate the GetEntitiesWithMetricsArg and invoke queried.
Here the Lexer/Parser part is the responsibility of the client code. The AST->where clause conversion will be implemented as part of an IDF client library.

[Customer Issues & Interactions | FIQL -_IDF query converter]
## Proposal 2:
The client gives FIQL string. IDF converts to the equivalent GetEntitiesWithMetricsArg-> Query->Where clause.
Python has a standard parser and we have already developed FIQL parser and AST->IDF query converter on top of that, We can leverage that to generate a Where Clause Protobuf in string format which can be easily converted to C++ Protobuf object.
Workflow
The client gives FIQL string. IDF invokes the existing python parser/converter (via command:-  python run_fiql fiql_string) and returns the where clause in string format. This can be converted to Where clause protobuf and returned to user.
Here the  Lexer/Parser and AST->IDF where clause conversion  will be part of IDF client library. We need to write python script that does the functionalities of  fiql parser and idf_converter. And also package this as part of NOS tar.

Date: 02-Aug-2017 Author : Swagat Borah Attendees: IDF : Swagat Borah Uhura: Rahul Paul, Prathyush Thota, Shubham Agarwal Cerebro: Naveen Kumar, Simranjit Singh Part 0: Semantics of AttachEntity() and DetachEntity() AttachEntity() and DetachEntity() RPCs are essentially wrappers over UpdateEntity() and DeleteEntity() RPCs respectively which allows for preservation and reincarnation of entities state across different sources (PEs). DetachEntity() takes in the same argument as the DeleteEntity() RPC and also takes in the uuid of the target cluster. This RPC deletes the given entity like any normal DeleteEntity call and sets the moved_to_cluster_uuid metadata field as well. The delete operation will move the entity into a deleted state after removing all its existing attributes. Only the metadata is preserved. The deleted entity will not be part of any subsequent queries. AttachEntity() takes in the same argument as the UpdateEntity() RPC and also takes in the new incarnation id for this entity. The incarnation id is like a version number for the entity which is preserved across multiple reincarnations across different sources. The incarnation id has to be greater than the previous incarnation id of this entity. This RPC creates the given entity like any normal UpdateEntity() call and also updates its incarnation id. The create operation will create a brand new entity with all the given attributes and metadata if the entity with the same id did not exist earlier in a deleted

[Customer Issues & Interactions | Issue with Attach_Detach Entity behaviour wrt VM migration workflows]
updates its incarnation id. The create operation will create a brand new entity with all the given attributes and metadata if the entity with the same id did not exist earlier in a deleted state. If the entity was in a deleted state, then it would be reincarnated with the updated metadata and with all the attributes provided in the input argument. Part 1 : The issues and possible fixes Two issues were discussed regarding the existing AttachEntity() and DetachEntity() behaviour in Acropolis, Uhura and Cerebro VM migration workflows. The details of the existing workflows and the race conditions that has occurred are added in the later part of this document. 1. DetachEntity() issue After detach entity is called, the entity is deleted. Now Uhura / Acropolis has a race condition which wrongly re-incarnates the entity on that same PE after it was detached. This entity further complicates the migrate back workflows explained later. A possible fix for this from IDF side is to disallow this incarnation after a detach is called. Some metadata flag can be set on the entity specifying that the entity has been detached. Only an explicit attach entity call should clear this flag on the detached, deleted entity. Any other UpdateEntity() call should not be allowed to reincarnate this entity. 2. AttachEntity() issue Cerebro attaches the entity with only metadata but no attributes. This happens because the VM attributes are not known at the time of AttachEntity() currently. Now Uhura expects

[Customer Issues & Interactions | Issue with Attach_Detach Entity behaviour wrt VM migration workflows]
reincarnate this entity. 2. AttachEntity() issue Cerebro attaches the entity with only metadata but no attributes. This happens because the VM attributes are not known at the time of AttachEntity() currently. Now Uhura expects some attributes to be mandatorily present in all existing VMs. hypervisor_specific_id should be present on every live VM. Other clients such as Prism would want some other fields to be present, such as VM name , etc. Currently an entity reincarnated by AttachEntity() has no attributes which causes issues with these workflows. Until Uhura’s VM publisher restores the attributes, which can take a few minutes, this problem persists. A possible fix from IDF side, as suggested from the Uhura team, is for AttachEntity() to only update the incarnation id and clear its detached state metadata flag but keep the entity in the deleted state. An explicit UpdateEntity(cas=0) call by Uhura later on should re-incarnate the entity with the correct attributes. This new flow can be triggered by an explicit flag in the AttachEntityArg on whether to create the entity or to keep it in deleted state. This attached entity should however be synced to any remote IDF as usual. Part 2: Detailed Context on how Acropolis and Uhura handles VM data Acropolis Acropolis manages publishing VM entities from hypervisor to arithmos. In AHV, there is only one publisher for VM information from hypervisor. In EsX, there are two sources. 1. Periodic publisher -> Fetches data from hypervisor

[Customer Issues & Interactions | Issue with Attach_Detach Entity behaviour wrt VM migration workflows]
manages publishing VM entities from hypervisor to arithmos. In AHV, there is only one publisher for VM information from hypervisor. In EsX, there are two sources. 1. Periodic publisher -> Fetches data from hypervisor every 30 secs and this operation usually takes around 5-10 secs to complete. After that it fetches the list of existing VMs from Arithmos. It does then a diff between these two VM sets and writes the updated set back into Arithmos. For creates and updates, there is no difference in arithmos. However for deletes, it is a separate RPC call. 2. Property collector -> Receives callbacks whenever there is any change in VM attributes. During VM creation and deletion as well. Property collector takes a version id and then it returns all the updates that have happened since this version id for the given entity type. Property collector is reported to be flaky and sometimes does not send updates correctly all the time. Sometimes, updates go missing. Acropolis team has worked around this issue by using a combination of Periodic publisher and property collector. Otherwise, they could have simply used the Property collector as the single source for VM information. Uhura Uhura reads the VM entities from Arithmos every 30 secs and publishes it to IDF. In the first call, Uhura will read all the VMs from Arithmos Thereafter, every 30 secs it will do an incremental fetch of VM entities which has changed during the last 30 secs from Arithmos. using the API

Uhura will read all the VMs from Arithmos Thereafter, every 30 secs it will do an incremental fetch of VM entities which has changed during the last 30 secs from Arithmos. using the API MasterGetInMemoryStats(cur_time - 30, cur_time) VM entity fetched from ESX does not have any creation_timestamp, modified_timestamp, cas values; just the VM entity. Arithmos does not store any deleted entities, not even metadata like IDF does. This makes it difficult for client to do any version checks for entities stored in Arithmos. Part 3: Details of the race condition in Acropolis/ Uhura VM data workflows The scenario is the periodic publisher fetches VMs from EsX. During this time, a VM got deleted which the property collector sends as part of the callback and the same VM is deleted from Arithmos. Uhura does not do anything at this point since the VM is already deleted from IDF as part of the DetachEntity() workflow which Cerebro had called. Now when the periodic publisher completes its fetch and publishing, it ends up re-creating the VM on Arithmos. Uhura ends up picking this re-created VM from Arithmos and re-incarnates the VM on IDF PE from the detached (deleted state). Currently, IDF does not prevent the detached entity from being reincarnated using UpdateEntity(cas_value=0) workflow. This is because it does not differentiate between a detached entity and a deleted entity as of now. Uhura detects if a VM is deleted from Arithmos and then marks it as deleted, which is an UpdateEntity()

[Customer Issues & Interactions | Issue with Attach_Detach Entity behaviour wrt VM migration workflows]
it does not differentiate between a detached entity and a deleted entity as of now. Uhura detects if a VM is deleted from Arithmos and then marks it as deleted, which is an UpdateEntity() call which sets a given attribute. After 5 minutes, if it is still not found in Arithmos, then Uhura ends up calling DeleteEntity() call on it. So this race condition can cause the VM entity to be present in IDF for around 6 odd minutes even after it was detached from that PE. After 6 mins, Uhura ends up deleting this wrongly created entity. Part 4: Protection Domain Migrate operation details Uhura calls VM destroy on source This deletes the VM from the hypervisor but entity remains on IDF on PE Uhura updates the VM with a vm_state set to transient. The significance of this field is that the VM is in transient state so no operation will be done on it by Uhura. No other service understands this field. Cerebro calls DetachEntity() call for this VM on IDF on PE This will delete the entity from IDF on PE which also gets synced to IDF on PC. All attributes get dropped for this VM in IDF. Metadata is updated moved_to_cluster_uuid field is set to target PE cluster in IDF. On Target PE, cerebro calls AttachEntity() in IDF for this VM. This attach entity call does not send any attributes at this point in time because Cerebro or Uhura does not know the attributes of this VM at this stage. This reincarnates the VM on the new target PE, which will also get synced to the same PC with the new incarnation

[Customer Issues & Interactions | Issue with Attach_Detach Entity behaviour wrt VM migration workflows]
Uhura does not know the attributes of this VM at this stage. This reincarnates the VM on the new target PE, which will also get synced to the same PC with the new incarnation id and existing cas values. Cerebro calls Uhura VM register which Creates the VM on the hypervisor. Once the VM is created on the hypervisor, the periodic publisher / property collector will pick up the newly created VM and put the same in Arithmos. At this point the VM’s attributes are known and the same is put in Arithmos Uhura reads the newly created VM from Arithmos and puts it in IDF which now re-populates the VM attributes. In case of any issue during this migrate operation and Cerebro triggers a migrate back operation to the source PE cluster. Part 5: The error scenario Now both the above mentioned race condition happened along with the migrate back operation happened at the same time. This race condition can happen if 100s of VMs are migrated at the same time. The migrate back operation attempted to perform an AttachEntity() on the source PE for an entity which already existed due to the race condition where it got reincarnated wrongly, resulting in the kEntityAlreadyExists error. Part 6: Suggestion from Uhura team AttachEntity() and DetachEntity() should not delete or create entities; it should simply do metadata changes to satisfy the entity migration workflow. The clients should be allowed to delete and create the entity later on using explicit API calls. Moreover, DetachEntity() and

## Insights changes
Insights will remove the AttachEntity and DetachEntity RPCs and instead modify the existing UpdateEntity and DeleteEntity RPCs to facilitate the migration of entity from one PE to another:
UpdateEntityArg will include one more parameter: incarnation id. The client will set this field to indicate that the entity is being moved from some other cluster to the current one. This should be higher than the incarnation id of the entity(if already present in deleted state). If entity is already present in not deleted state, UpdateEntity should throw kEntityAlreadyPresentError.
DeleteEntityArg will include one more parameter: moved_to_cluster_uuid. Client will specify this field to indicate that the entity is being moved to some other cluster.
DeleteEntity(moved_to_cluster_uuid) on source PE will be invoked before UpdateEntity(incarnation_id) on target PE. However, Insights should handle the case when there could be network connectivity issues between source PE and PC which could result in the update from source PE(of DeleteEntity) reaching PC after update from target PE(of UpdateEntity). This case would only arise if source PE and target PE are registered to same PC.

[Customer Issues & Interactions | Issue with Attach_Detach Entity behaviour wrt VM migration workflows]
## Uhura changes
Uhura will invoke Insights DeleteEntity with moved_to_cluster_uuid and UpdateEntity with incarnation_id as a part of migrate workflow. Thus Uhura VmDestroy and VmRegister be as follows:
VmDestroy(vm_uuid, keep_deleted_entity, moved_to_cluster_uuid):
If keep_deleted is true, VM will be deleted from hypervisor, and vm_state in IDF entity will be set to transient.
If keep_deleted is false, VM will be deleted from hypervisor and VM entity should be deleted from IDF, irrespective of whether it was in transient state or not.
If moved_to_cluster_uuid is specified, Uhura will invoke Insights DeleteEntity(moved_to_cluster_uuid)
VmRegister(vm_uuid, hyperint::RegisterVmArg, …, incarnation_id):
If vm_uuid is specified, Uhura will assign the provided hypervisor agnostic uuid to the VM.
Uhura will register VM using hyperint::RegisterVmArg
If incarnation_id is specified, Uhura will invoke Insights UpdateEntity(incarnation_id)
vm_state in VM IDF entity should be set to normal after VmRegsiter.

[Customer Issues & Interactions | Issue with Attach_Detach Entity behaviour wrt VM migration workflows]
## Cerebro changes Cerebro will invoke only Uhura APIs for VM operations and not deal with Insights directly for VM entity. For INPLACE restore: Cerebro will invoke Uhura::VmDestroy(vm_uuid, keep_deleted=true). This will set the vm_state of VM entity in IDF to ‘transient’. If VmDestroy fails, cerebro will assign new uuid to the VM that will be registered. After recovering VM files, cerebro will issue Uhura::VmRegister(vm_uuid, hyperint::RegisterVmArg). This should register the VM on hypervisor and set the vm_state in IDF to normal. For PD MIGRATE operation: On source cerebro will GetEntities from IDF to get the incarnation ids of entities. Cerebro will invoke Uhura::VmDestroy(vm_uuid, keep_deleted=false, moved_to_cluster_uuid=c2). This API should delete the IDF entity on source immediately and set the moved_to_cluster_uuid field in metadata of entity which will be synced to PC. On failure of VmDestroy(either due to host or DB update error), cerebro will assign new uuid to VM on target. On target cerebro will invoke VmRegister(vm_uuid, hyperint::RegisterVmArg, incarnation_id). vm_uuid and incarnation_id may not be specified in case new uuid is being assigned to the VM. This should register VM on host and indicate IDF about the change of ownership of entity via incarnation id in UpdateEntityArg. For PD Activate or clone: Cerebro will issue VmRegister(_, hyperint::RegisterVmArg, _). This should be a normal VmRegister and the VM should get new uuid and incarnation_id 0. For PD

[Customer Issues & Interactions | Issue with Attach_Detach Entity behaviour wrt VM migration workflows]
via incarnation id in UpdateEntityArg. For PD Activate or clone: Cerebro will issue VmRegister(_, hyperint::RegisterVmArg, _). This should be a normal VmRegister and the VM should get new uuid and incarnation_id 0. For PD Deactivate: Cerebro will issue VmDestroy(vm_uuid, keep_deleted=false). This should simply delete VM from host and IDF.

## Some Key Points:
The detached state of an entity should be interpreted probably by Insights. An entity will be detached if the cluster with moved_to_cluster_uuid in entity metadata is registered to the same PC(?). Otherwise the entity should be shown as deleted.
The transient state of VM entity makes sense for inplace restore only. Inplace restore takes place on single cluster so no business of incarnation_id or moved_to_cluster uuid is involved.
The detached state of VM entity makes sense for Migrate operation only and should not be confused with transient state. Transient state is an application level state managed by Uhura. The detached state is an entity level state managed by Insights.

Problem Statement Number of concurrent users that can be served in AFS Spectre release (AOS 5.5) came down to 1400 from 2200 in AFS 2.2.1 release (AOS 5.1.2). This is seen as a performance regression. Hypotheses One hypothesis was that IDF was serving fewer number of queries in Spectre release compared to 2.2.1 minerva release. The observed throughput went down and the latency of IDF query latencies went up. Observations and Improvements CPU time taken to process the “share_dir_metadata” query in IDF has been reduced to ~95 ms in Spectre compared to 110 ms in 2.2.1. There is one more diff in the pipeline that brings down the latency from 95 ms to about 75 ms (this diff is yet to be checked into Spectre branch -- but we have tested this on AFS cluster and have confirmed that we are able to get a ~18% increase in throughput). Total number of IDF queries on the minerva platform increased from 2.2.1 to Spectre. Decreasing number of the newly added queries did alleviate the latency a bit, but we still weren’t able to reach 2200 concurrent users. In order to validate if this performance regression was specific to Spectre branch changes outside of IDF, we tried an experiment of compiling and deploying 2.2.1 IDF build on the Cluster that was running the Spectre release (i.e replacing only IDF bits from the previous release). Questions on publishing stats to PE by Containers. Point of contact : Akshay Khole Insights Data Fabric Dev (insightsdatafabric-dev@) Oct 16 Issues faced: 1) Container moves from 1 node to another . These become special cases in arithmos and have to be handled differently, some cases it causes data loss of couple of hours of stats Response to whether this is applicable in Insights case : For the leader only insights solution in asterix, I do not think that this is an issue since an entity moving from a node to another should not affect its corresponding data on IDF. However, on PE metric data logging is disabled, so we can lose about an hour of metric data on IDF crash. For a scale out solution, unless the entity is deleted and re-created with a different entity id when it moves from one node to another, I don’t think the shard owner would change and therefore, no shard would get unloaded and re-loaded. Moreover, even with any shard movement, data loss should not happen for stats. 2) During rolling upgrade , if arithmos agent goes down then local stats are gone, this has to be handled differently. Response to whether this is applicable in Insights case : Metric loss during server restarts, rolling upgrades etc is prevented in IDF by keeping a backup of the hourly stats on a local file which is stored in the distributed cassandra directory and used to reload the stats upon such restarts. This feature has been in place since 4.6.1 on PC. This is currently disabled on PE.

Enabling this is just a config setting for IDF, but we need get quota on the metadata disk. Expected retention period is around 90 days. Other questions: 3. What is lifecycle of stats in edb ? Response: Varies according to the customer requirement and on the downsampling granularity. They are controlled via gflags. For Example: The default metric data retention period is controlled via gflags, and can be overridden by metric type definition. For Asterix, the default raw metric data retention is 2 weeks, hourly downsampled data is 52 weeks. 4. How do we start publishing entity when its created, what change is expected when its moved around, how to handle delete of entity.? Response: Currently, entity doesn't "move". Stats cannot be published for a deleted entity, stats are not accessible for a deleted entity (even though they are present, so if the entity is re-created, old stats will become accessible). 5. How do you recommend batching , is there any expectation from edb side ? Response: The PutMetrics() API supports batching of metric data. Multiple entities of different entity types, containing multiple metrics with a time series data for each such metric is currently supported. The consumer should send a reasonable sized batch of metrics per RPC call . 5 MB for the total arg size is

Add node does not change anything on IDF PE side. If a current leader node is removed or is under-going restarts because of a rolling upgrade, then leader election will trigger another leader which would re-load the existing entities and the last one hour’s worth of metrics without any data loss. On PE, Scaled out solution - Metrics are forwarded to the corresponding shard owners once IDF is up on the node. So assuming that IDF will eventually restart, there would be no metric data loss, but metrics could be temporarily missing. [Customer Issues & Interactions | Raw retention in hours]
ENG-211065: Support raw retention in hours
Aiswarya S
07 March 2019
In review

## Introduction
Based on the calculation mentioned here . We need more than 1.5 TB to store OSS raw data for  a period of 1 week. The OSS needs the raw data to be retained only 1 day or so - amounting to 214 GB data. Here we investigate how to reduce the disk usage for OSS usecase  by supporting raw_retention_in_hours for raw data

## Present Metric Data Purging Logic :
Presently metric data purging is done once in 7(gflag) days. The raw_retention_in_weeks  is used to specify the number of weeks the raw data should be persisted.  When purging is initiated, We do the following:-
collect all the row keys from insights_metric_data_by_entity column family with timestamp  time_usecs such that time_usecs - now_time > raw_retention_in_weeks(in usecs) . One row in the raw stats column family consists of 1 week worth of data in insights_metric_data_by_entity.
Remove the rows with these row keys from insights_metric_data_by_entity column family.
For the row_keys removed from insights_metric_data_by_entity, remove the corresponding row keys from insights_metric_data_by_shard column family as well.
We also use cassandra per row/ per column ttl (based on raw retention per week/ hour retention_per_week)  for the compaction thread in cassandra to remove the expired values - there by freeing disk space.

[Customer Issues & Interactions | Raw retention in hours]
## Proposal:
Instead of 1 week per row- use a flag set parameter to specify the duration of raw data stored in a row. The flag should have a granularity of hours.
Support raw_retention_in_hours parameter in MetricType - So that we can delete rows that have timestamp greater than the raw_retention_in_hours.
In addition, Cassandra TTL calculation should first consider raw_retention_in_hours filled in metric Type. Only if it is not set, we use the raw_retention_in_weeks field.

[Customer Issues & Interactions | TH 952 - Jetblue Prism Central 3 Node cluster running out of disk space]
## Problem statement
On 10/2 customer reported malfunction of prism services, also reported one of the cassandra node went down.  The review of the logs and run time stats revealed that PC cluster ran out of disk spaces on all three nodes, because of which IDF and Cassandra stopped operating, all the existing services that depend on IDF or cassandra also stops functioning.

[Customer Issues & Interactions | TH 952 - Jetblue Prism Central 3 Node cluster running out of disk space]
## Observations
We examined the IDF/cassandra data set and found out of the 4 biggest IDF metric data column families, metric_data_by_shard (139GB) and metric_data_by_shard_ds (220GB) account for more than 60% the total disk usage, metric_data_by_entity and metric_data_by_entity_ds takes the rest of 40%.
Our first attempt to address the disk space usage issue is to scan the entire metric data CF and identified all the data files that are soon to be expired (auto deleted). Those files added up to around 60GB on each node. We managed to manually remove those Cassandra data files to free up the spaces and were able to bring up the prism central services.
However, shortly after the services were up and running, one of the cassandra node went into forwarding mode because it has accumulated too many small SSTables, as the result, the dynamic ring changer services had triggered the cassandra node to start flushing data from one node to the replica node, that behavior was observed in the way that even without IDF running, each cassandra node was flushing around 30MB of metric data every 5-10 seconds, that caused the disk space usage on all nodes to run out again.

[Customer Issues & Interactions | TH 952 - Jetblue Prism Central 3 Node cluster running out of disk space]
## RCA Following are some hypothesis that might lead to the many SSTables and rapid spike of the metric data column family sizes, luckily for most of them, we already identified fixes or had a plan to resolve: Since Capacity planning VMBL/right sizing feature was introduced, the amount of metric data that is ingested into IDF has significantly increased. As the VMBL plugin pushes 50 VM level metrics for 7 days worth at 5 mins granularity across all VMs to IDF on daily basis. Because those metrics are cross many hours, that causes huge write amplifications when IDF flushes the data on the cassandra disk, also cause big memory pressures on IDF. In fact, there were previous customer issues in which case IDF ran out of memory because it caches too much VMBL metrics before the scheduled flushing kicks in. Following are some of the references the relevant oncalls and THs: https://jira.nutanix.com/browse/ONCALL-3916 https://jira.nutanix.com/browse/ONCALL-3983 https://jira.nutanix.com/browse/ONCALL-3722 https://jira.nutanix.com/browse/TH-424 This issue had since been fixed by CPD-2105, which introduced a dynamic throttling algorithm where IDF accelerates the flushing of metric data to cassandra if it detects a memory pressure and unable to cache more data from the client. What might have been a side effect of this algorithm is that it might invoke a lot more frequent flushing cycle at times when VMBL plugin is running, pushing the pressure to Cassandra. With the memtable flushing

[Customer Issues & Interactions | TH 952 - Jetblue Prism Central 3 Node cluster running out of disk space]
been a side effect of this algorithm is that it might invoke a lot more frequent flushing cycle at times when VMBL plugin is running, pushing the pressure to Cassandra. With the memtable flushing threshold set only at 32MB in 5.8.2 code base, it doesn’t take too much time before the metric data filling up that buffer and write to a sstable, that is where the rapid increase of SStable might occur. Many of the rows that are written to cassandra as the result of this catchup algorithm might end up being written again at later time, resulting a different sstable for the duplicated data, that will amplify the disk space usage further. If cassandra background compaction process could not catch up, sstables will start accumulating, duplicated rows can’t be deleted effectively. In IDF 5.9.X we delivered an improved version of the algorithm which limit the premature catch up metric data flushing and prevent rewriting the metric data (https://jira.nutanix.com/browse/ENG-175558) In addition NCC 3.6.2 also had delivered an improved version of VMBL plugin where the metric data push rate is throttled. (This has already deployed on the customer cluster) [ JIRA number here] 2) Increased number of metrics in the new AOS releases From the IDF profiling page, we’ve found there are totally 4.5K metrics registered and almost ⅓ of which are NCC metrics synced from PE to PC which doesn’t have any client consuming those data, those metrics got auto registered from PC when it is first received by PC

almost ⅓ of which are NCC metrics synced from PE to PC which doesn’t have any client consuming those data, those metrics got auto registered from PC when it is first received by PC IDF with default retention period (raw data - 3 weeks , hourly data -1 year). That Will contribute to a significant amount of data which is never used. This is an known issue and a ticket has already been file to be addressed in future releases. ( CPD-2280 ) 3) As mentioned in point 1) Cassandra had a default 32MB memtable flushing threshold, this setting seems to be too small for large scaled data system. In release 5.9 this also had been addressed and default value has been increased to 128MB, this will allow cassandra to be able to absorb more repeated writes as in the case of 1). [JIRA number here]

[Customer Issues & Interactions | TH 952 - Jetblue Prism Central 3 Node cluster running out of disk space]
## Plan of actions
Manually compact the all metric data column families (done)
Apply IDF gflag insights_metric_data_snapshot_max_num_of_sets_in_catchup = 100
This will limit the IDF metric data flushing catch up algorithm to be the minimal since NCC throttled metric data has already been deployed on the cluster. (done)
Manually set the retention period of all NCC metric type (check.XXXX) synced from PE to be minimal value (raw - 0 week, hourly - 0 week) so that it won’t consume meaningful disk space to store the values. (done)
Apply skip commitlog and increase memtable size to be 128MB, this will allow memtable to absorb more repeated writes (if any) avoid writing into too many small sstables  (Action Item: Raghav)
ENG-175558 will be delivering in 5.9.0.1 and 5.9, so customer is encouraged to upgrade to this version when it becomes available, this basically will make the IDF gflag applied in step 2) unnecessary.
CPD-2280 is planned to delivered in 5.9.1 and 5.10

[Customer Issues & Interactions | Task as evictable entities - Discussion with Ergon Team]
## Write up on meeting with Ergon Team about converting ‘Task’ as evictable entities
Attendees :- Monica Jeyachandran, Bhuvnesh Jain, Aiswarya S
Date :- 26 Feb 2018

[Customer Issues & Interactions | Task as evictable entities - Discussion with Ergon Team]
## Generic Ergon Workflow
The task entities in IDF are created by Ergon when any NOS service invokes a TaskCreate RPC in ergon.
During the service life time, the services do a TaskPoll to see if any new tasks are created for that service.
Once the task is taken up by a service - it is marked `in progress` by the service - This involves a TaskGet and TaskUpdate RPCs - which results GetEntities and UpdateEntity calls to IDF.
Each NOS service can use the entire task entity for its processing - mainly the zprotobuf.
The task has a WAL field which services uses to store internal data corresponding to that task - This is inside zprotobuf. This can be modified throughout the task active time(create->status_complete).
Whenever a substage of a task is reached, again a TaskGet/TaskUpdate call is invoked
Whenever any subtask of the parent task is completed, the TaskGet/TaskUpdate call is invoked.
When the task is finished, the task is marked ‘completed’ again via a TaskGet/TaskUpdate call is invoked.
Once the task is completed, it will rarely be read/modified again.
After 1 hr and if the number of task entities are more than 4k, the tasks are deleted by Ergon. This is monitored by a periodic thread
There are other updations done by Ergon on uncompleted tasks - like task progress updation, modified time updates etc
The tasks synced from PE->PC, are mainly consumed via watches. The services are interested to know only their status and no frequent read calls are done on them after that.

[Customer Issues & Interactions | Task as evictable entities - Discussion with Ergon Team]
## Estimated Task Entities Processed at a time.
Ergon has done benchmarks in which they could create/update ~150 tasks per second.
Monica will get back on the estimated load in a real scenarios after checking the Nusights data.

## Observations on evictability
During the Task active time (create->status_complete), it can be accessed very frequently. Also the services receive the entire task entity from Ergon - not any predetermined field. This may not be the ideal scenario to convert them into evictable entities
The completed tasks on the other hand are ideal candidates for evictability - But that would mean IDF has to implement selective evictabitlity (Based on a metadata field).
The synced tasks are also suitable for eviction. Each PE will not delete any tasks unless the total task count reaches 4k. When all the tasks are synced from PE to PC- the number of tasks in PC can be very high  ~ 4k * number of PE’s attached to it + 4k(From PC). It will be good, if we can evict such synced tasks as well.

[IDF Design Documents | Reporting IDF Metrics through Pulse]
Jan 27, 2021
Collecting and reporting IDF metrics through Nusights (Pulse)
ali.dowair@nutanix.com

## Motivation
In an ongoing effort to improve the performance and scale of operation of IDF, we want to identify areas of improvement in our architecture by analyzing how IDF clients, and Nutanix customers, use IDF. Chiefly we want to analyze the queries being issued against IDF. To do this analysis, we need a representative set of such queries. This document gives the design for one proposal on how to obtain this data set.
In some of our previous experiments, we have had a hard time collecting queries from different clients - sometimes clients themselves may not know what queries they issued. And we have seen plenty of cases in production where IDF got choked by offending queries, which causes instability in the entire AOS. Hence the initial thought was to have some analytical data exported to pulse such that we can monitor what those queries may be, how often they came in, etc. Right now we have something in the 2027 page, but it’s very limited.

[IDF Design Documents | Reporting IDF Metrics through Pulse]
## Background: Pulse4k
Nusights is a cloud-hosted Nutanix service which collects diagnostic information from Nutanix clusters deployed in the field. This information is used by Nutanix support to perform preventative maintenance on our customers’ deployments.
Data us published from Nutanix clusters to the Nusights cloud service through Pulse. Today, Pulse is already integrated into IDF, and is used to collect entities (i.e. cluster). We can leverage this framework to collect not only entities/attributes, but also metrics on IDF’s performance.

## Information we’d like to collect:
IDF query profiles (done)
Number of entities [local + synced if required] for each type
Can be obtained from profile page or queries
Number of queries to IDF (hourly avg num) stats.
Perhaps also for other RPC types
Disk usage due to IDF CFs [maybe from profile page]
RSS usage is useful. [plus rss usage breakdown entities, evictable entities, stats, etc.]
Cassandra op queue size(if needed).
Sync related stats (CDS entities for Arithmos sync, number of RPCs for IDF sync can be collected in point 2 mentioned above)

[IDF Design Documents | Reporting IDF Metrics through Pulse]
## Queries
For each query, we would like to see:
Query expression
Latency
Time started
All of this information is already stored in QueryProfileRecord for each query, so no additional memory is needed on the client side. QueryProfileRecords are stored in a rotating buffer with a fixed size. We can batch and send information from this buffer every time it cycles over (the newest entry becomes the oldest).

## Push Model
Since this data is not cluster-specific (and indeed, we want to combine the information from all sources together), we will need to use the Push APIs provided by Pulse, as opposed to already built-in Insights Entity Collector.

## Data Model
Nusights’ data model does not differ too much from IDF. At the most basic level, we can store our data as follows:
Each data point is represented by a NusightsStats object.
Each NusightsStats object is initialized with a ‘stats_type_name’ (roughly corresponding to an entity_type_name), as well as a timestamp.
Each NusightsStats object can have multiple attributes and values. These attributes are not schema-driven, but there are some restrictions on changing/adding/removing attributes within one stats type.
Multiple NusightsStats objects can be added to a PutMetricDataArg RPC, to be all sent at once to Pulse.
Stats/data points with the same ‘stat_type_name’ can be aggregated and summarized on the server side using the FlexUI.
This model can be visualized as a table:
Table: “stat_type_name” (an example)

## Bandwidth Requirement
Assuming 500 bytes/query:
500 bytes / query, 10/s -> 500 * 10 * 60 / min = 300kB / min
300kB * 60 * 24 / day = 432000kB / day = 432MB / day from one node
From Peng’s observation:
Query Expression string: ~1600 bytes
Query Proto: ~600 bytes

## Use a “Query Shape” instead of a query expression column To save space on the server side, we can borrow the concept of query shape from MongoDB. A query shape is a structure which abstracts away the specifics of a query (for example, the value in a $lt clause). Two queries with the same clauses, order of clauses, and operations, but perhaps with different operands, could have the same query shape. For example: Would be of the same shape. This shape can be stored as a proto, or hashed and stored as an int64 Benefits: Can have some meaningful aggregation of queries Less bandwidth and memory usage, since shapes/shape hashes will be smaller than full query expressions. Reduce “row” size by (1600-8) ~1500 bytes. We have full flexibility to define what makes query shapes distinct (i.e. entity_type, whether columns are indexed). Challenges: Given a query shape, or its hash, how to deduce the full query in the server side. How to transform a query into its shape. This will need some designing. In order to be able to deduce the shape of a query from its hash, we will have to also publish the <shape, hash(shape)> pairs in a separate table: Table: “idf_query_shapes” The process for publishing and consuming this data is as follows: For every query processed in IDF, compute the query’s shape and the shape’s hash If this shape has not been seen before on this client, send the <shape, hash(shape)> pair to Pulse in a separate table On the server side, perform a JOIN on hash(shape)

Instead of emitting raw information for every query, we can bucketize queries that have been fired within some time interval, and report the summarized statistics for that interval. In order be able to replace Arithmos on PE, we need to finish IDF scale-out work, so that we can distribute resource usage among the cluster nodes.

## Metric Data Replay
Right now, we don’t turn on metric data logging on PE to avoid dealing with metadata disk quotas.  To fully support metric data, we’ll need to turn it on, estimate the quotas that we need for keeping metric data logs and implement some quota management logic that would try to keep metric data within the quota (at the cost of potential data loss if we don’t manage to stay within the quota).

We now need to run Proxy on PE to support ingest (put) interfaces, so that we can take data from Stargate, etc.  The Proxy would also need to pull some config data from Pithos (e.g.. vdisk data).
Arithmos interfaces are fairly tightly coupled with specific entities, the Proxy will have to implement the logic that would translate from protobufs that represent specific entity data into the IDF entity model. ## Metric Data Sync: Bootstrapping of Metric Data As the metric data is going to be now stored in IDF, the data should go via IDF-IDF sync pipeline. The normal "push" flow is mostly functional (need to implement logic to properly group metric data by entity type / shard), but bootstrapping / catch-up logic is not implemented. To support bootstrapping of metric data we need to have sequencing logic so that we could track data that is replicated and request missing data from the master. For sequencing we can use timestamp oracle. Metric data is going to be a separate logical stream from entity data (i.e. timestamp oracle for metric data is going to be different from the timestamp oracle for entity data). When a PutMetricData request comes in, we get a time range from the timestamp oracle, that would be unique for that request. Most of the time, metrics would come in real time (i.e. the timestamps of the metrics are going to be close to the wallclock), in which case we can just use the timestamp oracle ranges to track the input ranges. For the cases when the metric data comes out of order, we'd need to have an index of changes (think of it as a log sequenced by timestamp oracle that stores input ranges). The metric timestamps are not going to be perfectly synchronized with timestamp oracle, so we need to have fuzzy match logic, that would work as the following: Get {ts_oracle_start, ts_oracle_end} value pair. Extend ts_oracle_start down by 90 seconds and align it down to 10

Extend ts_oracle_start down by 90 seconds and align it down to 10 seconds boundary: fuzzy_ts_oracle_start = (ts_oracle_start - 90) / 10 * 10. Extend ts_oracle_end up by 30 seconds and align it up to 10 seconds boundary: fuzzy_ts_oracle_end = (ts_oracle_end + 30 + 9) / 10 * 10. If the input metric range is fully included into (fuzzy_ts_oracle_start, fuzzy_ts_oracle_end] range, then we don't need to log the index record. When a missing range comes from the replica, we first check if there is an index record that exists for the corresponding missing range, if it does, then we use the input ranges from the record, otherwise we extend the missing range the same way (90 seconds down, 30 seconds up, aligned to 10), so that we can cover the input ranges correctly. The query for metric data would also need to consider downsampling interval, e.g. if it's every 6 hours, then the changes for the range would actually affect the hour % 6. The index records are going to be per {shard, entity_type) pair (the same as timestamp oracle).
