Bootstrap update that doesn't include the latest incremental update may be applied after the latest update is applied, in which case the latest update is lost. Bootstrap update that includes the latest incremental update may be applied and then latest update is applied as well, in which case the latest update will double-count for kSum and kAvg. Older bootstrap update gets reordered on top of later bootstrap update, in which case the older would override the later. Also, for the same reason of minimizing double-counting for kSum and kAvg downsampled metrics we never retry push-based metric data flow and we don't push forwarded metrics (metric forwarding can happen as part of shard migration or server restart). If we fail to push metric data, we just rely on the bootstrapping to transfer metric data from master to replica. That's the high-level design for metric data replication and here is a list of things to be considered at the next level of design (most of these cases are solved for entities, but metrics may have slightly different solution): how to chunk up the requests, so that we send history in chunks how to handle case when the clock is set backwards, so the timestamp oracle is in the future (probably read latest index log) how to handle bootstrapping requests while metric log is being replayed (probably

[Arithmos & Metric Collection | Arithmos EoL Plan_]
to handle case when the clock is set backwards, so the timestamp oracle is in the future (probably read latest index log) how to handle bootstrapping requests while metric log is being replayed (probably just reject or delay) how to handle forwarded metrics (probably allocate timestamp oracle slot for them, but don't push data, so that bootstrapping will catch up) is time range bookkeeping granular enough? requesting a time range would get all metrics for an entity type for a shard (i.e. get by_shard rows for each metric of an entity type) For some metrics we may want to have an option to downsample at the source (probably beyond v1)

[Arithmos & Metric Collection | Arithmos EoL Plan_]
## Data Migration
When IDF replaced Arithmos on PC, we just lost the data that Arithmos had and bootstrap it from PE.  Now we cannot lose data and need to migrate it over from Arithmos.  The amount of data is fairly large, so if we tried to migrate it at the upgrade time it would cause potentially significant downtime.  So we need to implement some way of migrating data from Arithmos to IDF online.
One way to migrate data in quick and seamless manner would be to implement the logic to read data from Arithmos column families at the query time.  During upgrade time we would keep a "cutoff" timestamp.  Most likely the "cutoff" timestamp is going to be the upgrade time, but we need to check if Arithmos data can be in the future, in which case we would have to do more elaborate calculation.  If a query start time is below the "cutoff" time, we would also get data from Arithmos column families, otherwise we'd just get data from IDF column families.  The Arithmos metric data is going to age out after 3 months, so once the "cutoff" time is older than 3 months, we won't need to read Arithmos data any more.
For entities stored in Arithmos, we can read them from Arithmos column families on the first start and save them to IDF.

[Arithmos & Metric Collection | Arithmos EoL Plan_]
## Consumer App Migration
The Proxy on PE is only going to implement ingest interfaces (the same way it's done on PC), data retrieval requests will need to go through IDF interfaces.  All the application that consume data from Arithmos will need to be updated to use IDF instead.

[Arithmos & Metric Collection | Arithmos EoL Plan_]
## IDF-IDF Sync: Support Moving Entities from Arithmos to IDF
Currently, some entity updates (VM, task, virtual_disk, virtual_nic) are coming to PC through IDF-IDF sync and the rest of the entity updates are coming from Arithmos.  The problem is that the entities that came from the Proxy to IDF on PC are "local" entities (IDF doesn’t know that they came from Proxy, they just come via UpdateEntity RPC), so once we redirect all entities to be replicated via IDF-IDF sync, replication will fail because the entities are already created as “local” by the Proxy.
The easiest solution is probably to make IDF understand which entities came from Proxy and allow replicated entities to override those.  The entities that come from Proxy have _cluster_id_ attribute that has the cluster uuid of the master cluster, so we can reliably detect and handle the case.  This solution violates the IDF principle of being agnostic to the data attributes, but more generic alternatives seem to bring additional complexity without bringing much value just to handle one edge case scenario.
There are components such as Nusights which have recently added some fields to arithmos_entity_operation.proto and built some logic around it. We would need to see how to migrate such logic after we turn off arithmos PE to IDF PC sync. Eg: arithmos_golang_protobuf_method_name

[Arithmos & Metric Collection | Arithmos EoL Plan_]
## Backward Compatibility
Even when PC is upgraded to a version that would expect all entity+metric data to come via IDF-IDF sync, the PC would still have to support Arithmos data from older PEs.  This wouldn't require additional work, we just need to keep the Proxy running on PC.

## Introduction
This is the capture of the discussion that we had on 12/03/2014 and the plan that we agreed on w.r.t. data ingest logic.
This document is scoped to discussing data ingest on CVM (on-cluster).  The issues concerning data transport from PE to PC as well as Arithmos on PC are outside of the scope of this document.

## Current state
The current state of things can be represented by the following diagram:
There are several components (Stargate, etc.) that provide data to Arithmos and several components (NCC, etc.) that consume data from Arithmos.  The arrows represent the data flow.
Currently, the data is not flowing to Insights DB and here is the plan how to get there.

[Arithmos & Metric Collection | Arithmos transition plan - 12_03_2014]
## Phase 1 To keep the codebase stable and provide an early solution for our consumers (e.g. Acropolis) to integrate with, we agreed to first create a “proxy” solution that would get data from the sources and push it both to Arithmos and Insights DB. This intermediate solution will be on the path to the final solution and won’t require any non-trivial additional work. The intermediate solution can be represented by the following diagram: Here the Ingest proxy would support Arithmos ingest interfaces and would listen on the Arithmos port, so the data sources that pushed to Arithmos would push the the Ingest proxy (no change is required for the data sources). The Ingest proxy would also pull data from the sources that Arithmos pulls data from (e.g. Pithos), and implement vdisk ⇒ virtual disk business logic. The Ingest proxy would push the data to two places: the old Arithmos process and the Insights DB. The old Arithmos process will run on a different port and the current consumers of Arithmos data will get the data from the old Arithmos process (the consumers need to be updated to use a different port). At the end of phase 1 the codebase should satisfy the following quality criteria: Existing components (Arithmos clients) work, existing tests pass New components (Ingest proxy, Insights DB) have no build breaks, alpha-quality, ready for integration with early adopters With this quality, the feature is safe to push to the master, so that early adopters of Insights DB data (e.g.

[Arithmos & Metric Collection | Arithmos transition plan - 12_03_2014]
Insights DB) have no build breaks, alpha-quality, ready for integration with early adopters With this quality, the feature is safe to push to the master, so that early adopters of Insights DB data (e.g. Acropolis) can work with the new functionality as soon as possible.

## Phase 2
During phase 2, the current consumers of Arithmos data will migrate to use Insights DB interfaces.  The benefit of the phased strategy is that the consumers can do that at their pace and would require minimal involvement from our team (bug fix level).

## Phase 3
Once all consumers of Arithmos data are migrated to use Insights DB, we can remove Arithmos process and get to the final solution:
We believe that we’ll be able to implement most of the Ingest proxy functionality during phase 1, so the phase 3 works is going to be cleanup, fit & finish.

## Option 1: Arithmos reading/writing from/to IDF directly Highlights: Arithmos will remain as is; Instead of writing to Cassandra, it will write to IDF. Writes to Cassandra are batch mutate calls for stats. Reads from Cassandra are done on bootstrap or on stat queries - both are range queries to cassandra. Entity queries and latest queries are served from cache always. For writing to IDF, we already have the mapping from Arithmos protos to IDF protos for entities and stats in the insights proxy layer. The Control Plane DB is going to replace Arithmos by implementing Ingest proxy that would support Arithmos ingestion interfaces; thus the components that push data to Arithmos won’t need to change.  We expect that the current consumers of Arithmos data are going to be changed to consume data from the Insights DB.  The final state can be represented by the following diagram:

## Lifecycle of Virtual Disks
Virtual disks that belong to VMs are managed by the corresponding agent on the corresponding node.  I.e. virtual disks data is managed by the node where they are reported to by Acropolis.
The creation of a virtual disk entity entry is implicit.  Here is the corresponding code from AgentSendStats:
entity = entity_type_data->GetOrCreateMutableEntity(*entity_id);
This call will either create a new entity object a return a pointer to an existing one.  The stats and attributes are then stored in the entity object.
Update is the same as creation.
In newer software version, the virtual disks on all hypervisors are only deleted through AgentDeleteEntities RPC. Therefore the procedure below is no longer valid.
The deletion logic on other hypervisors works as the following:
entity ids of all virtual disk stats reported in AgentSendStats are added to valid_entity_id_set
all virtual disk objects are enumerated and if their id was not in the valid_entity_id_set, then it’s deleted (BaseArithmosAgent::ScanVirtualDisksAndMarkToDelete)

[Arithmos & Metric Collection | VDisk & Virtual Disk handling in Arithmos]
## Lifecycle of VDisks Lifecycle of VDisks is more complex. In Arithmos, VDisk entity objects only exist in the context of Virtual Disks they are attached to. VDisks that are not attached to Virtual Disks are not represented as entity objects. Due to such representation, VDisks are effectively considered node-scoped entities and managed by the agent on the corresponding nodes. Before VDisk entity can be considered by Arithmos, it needs to get Virtual Disks stats via AgentSendStats. The Virtual Disk stats will trigger nfs_path ⇒ vdisk_name resolution logic (each call of AgentSendStats for Virtual Disk stats calls BaseArithmosAgent::MaybeResolveVirtualDiskToVDisks). We’ll get into the detail of VDisk name resolution later, for now the important part is that in the end of the resolution logic there is an entry in the accepted_vdisk_name_resolver_map_, which defines which VDisks get to be accepted. Once the VDisk stat passes accepted_vdisk_name_resolver_map_ check, then the VDisk object is updated or created. It goes through the same update-or-create code: entity = entity_type_data->GetOrCreateMutableEntity(*entity_id); only here (and overall in Arithmos) the entity id for VDisks is vdisk_name, not vdisk_id. The deletion of VDisk happens as part of deleting the parent Virtual Disk. This happens in AgentDeleteEntities RPC. If a virtual disk is deleted in the function, CleanUpVirtualDiskData() will be called to remove the virtual disk from the vdisks. If the vdisks no longer has

## VDisk name resolution
Each Virtual Disk stat would have disk_extents_nutanix_nfs_file_path variable -- this is a list of NFS file paths the this Virtual Disk uses.  MaybeResolveVirtualDiskToVDisks iterates over disk_extents_nutanix_nfs_file_path list and checks if nfs_path_vdisk_name_map_ has an entry keyed by the path.  nfs_path_vdisk_name_map_ maps nfs_path ⇒ {vdisk_name, attach_virtual_disk_id_set}.  If there is no entry in nfs_path_vdisk_name_map_, then nfs_path ⇒ vdisk_name resolution is initiated.
Note that on KVM iSCSI is used, not NFS, so on KVM there are no VDisk entity objects.  That’s probably why there is no deletion logic on KVM.
The StargateRpcSvc::NfsFetchPathAttr is called (see stargate_interface.proto), and when it returns, it gives vdisk_name for the requested nfs_path.  We create an entry for the corresponding vdisk_name in the accepted_vdisk_name_resolver_map_ which maps vdisk_name ⇒ attach_virtual_disk_id_set.
Once the resolution is done, we set disk_extents_nutanix_vdisk_name attribute in the corresponding Virtual Disk entities, and we set attach_virtual_disk_id in the corresponding VDisk entities.

## Usage stat forwarding VDisks live double lives. They are represented as node-scoped Virtual Disk-attached entities, that’s what the users can see. They are also represented in usage_cache_, which is partitioned across all nodes by the Cassandra token range. The usage_cache_ is not visible to users, it’s used for aggregation and rolled into into container, pool and cluster usage. Each Arithmos agent “owns” a subset of VDisk usage information. When an Arithmos agent gets VDisk stat, it forwards it the stats to the “owning” Arithmos agents. This forwarding happens unconditionally, before the Virtual Disk - VDisk logic is invoked. The forwarding uses a partition_2_arithmos_handle_map that is computed from partition_info_list. partition_info_list is computed on the master from Medusa info and stored in Zookeeper in the /appliance/logical/arithmos_status node as part of ArithmosStatus proto. ## Update frequencies
Acropolis sends its stats (including Virtual Disk stats) every 20 sec.  Stargate sends its stats (including VDisk stats) every 10 seconds.
Every 10 seconds, the stats are forwarded by each agent to all “owning” agents.
Arithmos master sends no-scan aggregation operation to all agents every 30 seconds.  The no-scan aggregation just does aggregation from the usage_cache_. Non scan aggregation can be triggered by Zeus configuration update too. The reason is for thick provisioned virtual disks. When users create thick provisioned virtual disk, Stargate will create the corresponding vdisk configuration and update the Zeus configuration. Upon receiving a Zeus configuration update, Arithmos runs a no-scan aggregation. The goal is to reflect the thick provisioned virtual disks usage on the container usage as soon as possible.
Arithmos master sends do-scan aggregation operation to all agents every 5 minutes.  The do-scan aggregation scans Cassandra and updates usage_cache_ (removes stale cache entries as needed).

[IDF Design Documents | CPD-2072_ retry kTimeout for unit tests]
## Problem
https://jira.nutanix.com/browse/CPD-2072
The unit test insights_evictable_entities_test is failing 10-30% of the time in ptest.

## Root Cause
This test loads many entities that contain a lot of data.  During this process, cassandra is getting overwhelmed and throws a kTimeout error.
Fundamentally, IDF is not at fault for this issue.  This is either a cassandra problem (ticket has been filed) or an infrastructure/load problem.  Unfortunately, until this is resolved IDF unit tests will not consistently pass.

## Proposed Solution
insights_rpc_test.cc has a utility function that is used to update entities.  Allowing this utility function to retry the UpdateEntities RPC when it returns a kTimeout error allows our unit tests to pass even when cassandra/infrastructure is under too much load.  We already do something similar for errors like kRetry and errors in the 2xxx range (aka cassandra retry errors).
The following preview implements the retry logic:  http://codereview.nutanix.net/differential/diff/62654/

[IDF Design Documents | Deprecating cpdb_impl]
Deprecating cpdb_impl April 2017 Swagat Borah Introduction: Refer to this document for issues with using cpdb_impl. Solution: Two broad solutions for replacing cpdb_impl. 1. Use native IDF APIs. This is the least error prone and most efficient solution for both IDF and client side. However, some `of the existing clients may need to change a lot of code since they are used to using an ORM layer and dealing with protos only. Expecting some resistance for this approach. 2. Create a better ORM client. The source of all major problems with cpdb_impl is the asymmetric write and read flows, i.e, the write flow writes partial data into attributes and the complete data into zprotobuf while the read flow totally ignores the attributes and reads only __zprotobuf__. This asymmetry leads to data duplication, dependence on __zprotobuf__ and therefore, leads to all the other issues highlighted here. We need an ORM client which establishes a 1-1 mapping between the proto fields and the entity attributes and makes the reads and writes symmetrical. This will make __zprotobuf__ field completely redundant. More importantly, the ORM layer would adhere to the IDF schema making it totally compatible with any other client, whether that latter uses native APIs or any other ORM layer. New write flow: Similar to the cpdb_impl client, each proto field will be written as an attribute into the corresponding entity. The only two fields which were skipped by cpdb_impl can be handled as follows Repeated

[IDF Design Documents | Deprecating cpdb_impl]
flow: Similar to the cpdb_impl client, each proto field will be written as an attribute into the corresponding entity. The only two fields which were skipped by cpdb_impl can be handled as follows Repeated bytes fields -> This can be mapped into an attribute holding a bytes list. Nested messages -> Serialise the protobuf stored in this field and map it to an attribute holding a bytes value. Repeated nested messages -> Serialise each of the protobuf messages stored in this repeated field and map it to an attribute holding a bytes list. Existing Issues with using cpdb_impl April 2017 Swagat Borah Introduction: cpdb_impl.py is a python wrapper written on top of IDF native queries which provides ORMfunctionalities to the user; i.e, the user can store and retrieve protobuf objects to and from IDF without having to deal with the entity-attribute model that IDF provides. Cpdb_impl does the conversion from proto to entity and back under the covers, freeing the users from writing their own adapters to convert protobuf to entity and vice versa. Cpdb_impl.py was written originally for the ergon’s use cases and has been tailor made to suit ergon’s specific requirements. However, it was put into the util folder which led people to assume that it is a generic library, leading to its rapid adoption by majority of the python components such as Acropolis and Aplos. The ORM functionality is also a popular reason for its adoption. Write path: Cpdb_impl.py converts each field in the given proto to the corresponding attribute. It skips nested protos and repeated fields of bytes. It assumes that the attribute of the same name as the field is already registered (or the user can provide a custom field-attribute mapping) . It also stores the entire proto in its serialised format with zlib compression into a special attribute named __zprotobuf__. Read path: It simply reads the contents of __zprotobuf__ , decompresses it and deserializes it to retrieve the proto which is then returned to the user. The other attributes are ignored

[IDF Design Documents | Existing Issues with using Cpdb_impl]
attribute named __zprotobuf__. Read path: It simply reads the contents of __zprotobuf__ , decompresses it and deserializes it to retrieve the proto which is then returned to the user. The other attributes are ignored during the read path. The attributes are populated for the sake of queries; not in the case of direct entity reads. Issues with cpdb_impl: 1. No language interoperability, compatibility with other clients Cpdb_impl.py breaks the schema model (entity-attribute model) of IDF by essentially storing a blob of data and retrieving it directly. This makes it incompatible with any other languages such as C++, go, java, etc which rely on the native IDF APIs and schema. It is also incompatible with any other python client library because of the inherent dependency on the special attribute, __zprotobuf__. This is the biggest bottleneck of using cpdb_impl as it forces other clients to move away from IDF’s native schema to cpdb_impl’s specific schema. Uhura for example, does not rely on cpdb_impl for vm entities but since some of the readers of vm use cpdb_impl, it was forced to comply with that schema and write the redundant zprotobuf field as well. Similar problems are cropping up with each new user of cpdb_impl. 2. Correctness issues with maintaining integrity of duplicated data Data is duplicated between the attributes and within the serialised proto in zprotobuf. It becomes each client’s responsibility and an additional overhead to maintain integrity between these two

[IDF Design Documents | Existing Issues with using Cpdb_impl]
with maintaining integrity of duplicated data Data is duplicated between the attributes and within the serialised proto in zprotobuf. It becomes each client’s responsibility and an additional overhead to maintain integrity between these two data sources which is highly error prone. Any client can accidentally update the attribute without updating the zprotobuf or vice versa. 3. No support for partial updates, non-cas updates. Entities written via cpdb_impl have to always be cas updates and full updates by default. The workflow does a full update as far as the user is concerned since it always replaces the zprotobuf in each update. Users of these entities cannot do partial updates or non-cas updates which could be more efficient for their respective use cases. Cas updates and full updates also requires a read-modify-write workflow which is an overhead that can be avoided depending on the use case. 4. User has no access to or control over metadata Apart from entity id and cas value, the user does not have a way to specify or access the entity’s metadata such as creation time, modified time, etc. This has led users to resort to the following workarounds: Add the metadata as normal attributes to the entity. Examples generated_report, lcm_entity and abac_entity_capability. This is redundant info. Query for metadata and zprotobuf directly via queries and re-construct it all at the client side. The user could have simply used the entity object itself had they used the native APIs.

The user could have simply used the entity object itself had they used the native APIs. Moreover, it is a dangerous coding practise to have client side business logic rely on internal constructs such as zprotobuf. Example queries in nucalm use case. Alerts also queries for zprotobuf field directly to get the entire alerts proto based on given filter conditions. 5. Dependence on protobuf The user has to have a protobuf for the corresponding entity it wants to update. For a lot of use cases, the user may not need to have a protobuf defined or may want to read / write only a subset of attributes. Using cpdb_impl forces them to create a protobuf for each subset of attributes that they want to read or write. Example of such an issue was reported in one of the Draas use cases. 6. Overhead of serialising/ compressing protobufs by default Both IDF and the users of cpdb_impl have to bear the additional cpu cost of serialising/ deserialising and compressing/ decompressing of protobufs by default. GoLang Projects Dependency Links Devendra Shekhawat June 2018 Problem Statement- Fixing GoLang library dependency tree, currently a single call to build_go_binary ends up building/compiling almost the entire golang protos. This leads to unnecessarily increased build times even on incremental builds (because of swagger API version verifications, etc.). Current GoLang library dependency tree is in a very convoluted structure throughout the main codebase. There are a lot of implicit tertiary dependencies instead of direct dependencies which we have identified. Almost all the GoLang libraries currently depend on this tertiary dependency to bring needed libraries instead of explicitly adding only the needed ones. Biggest issue is that each GoLang binary gets util library added as a default dependency as part of the current overall framework, this is done by build_go_binary function in main/CMakeLists.txt, here. Now there are two utility libs in golang - first, a component specific util lib called util and second, a component agnostic core libraries called util-go. util lib has a dependency on util-go and for some reason util-go has a dependency on all_proto_go (which is a massive collection of all golang specific protos). None of the components add their specific proto dependencies explicitly and rely on this tertiary dependency to all_proto_go and util-go for most of their functionalities with the side effect of having almost the entire golang specific protos getting compiled.

[IDF Design Documents | Fixing GoLang Projects Dependency links]

Solution- As util-go is a component agnostic core library so it should not have a dependency on all_proto_go. If needed we can make util library depend on all_proto_go because it depends on many component specific libs. After all the components declare their own dependencies explicitly,we can make util lib depend only on required components only instead on all_proto_go. Adding explicit dependency for each component specific GoLang binaries. Currently, we are doing this for IDF specific protos and the protos that IDF depends upon. Eventually every component owners should declare their GoLang component’s dependencies explicitly and contribute in making this happen. Fixing build_go_binary function in main/CMakeLists.txt to not include util lib as a default dependency for everyone. Until all the components fix/declare needed dependencies explicitly rather than depending on tertiary dependencies, we are introducing a new optional flag (named skip_util_dependency) in build_go_binary to skip adding util as a dependency. ## Distributed Tracing Wrapper in Cpp
Mudit Wadhwa
May 2022

## Introduction
This document describes how distributed tracing will be added in cpp. A wrapper library encapsulating the tracing framework and configuration will be provided. Cpp application can adapt the library to onboard distributed tracing. Details regarding which framework (opentracing, open-telemetry, etc.) is used to generate spans from the service will be encapsulated by the wrapper. In future, if we want to change the tracing framework and collector endpoint, it can be done within the wrapper code and no changes need to be done by the service owners.
This document describes the functionalities the wrapper library provides and how distributed tracing can be enabled in cpp services.
Document regarding how to propagate trace context can be found here.

[IDF Design Documents | Distributed Tracing Wrapper in Cpp]
## Enable/Disable Distributed Tracing
Distributed Tracing requires all the services involved to contribute spans and stitch them together in order to form complete and meaningful traces. We have a global configuration file to enable/disable tracing. The global config file can be found at /home/nutanix/config/observability/config.json. The format of config file is:
This configuration will be loaded by the wrapper that the cpp application will use at InitNutanixObservability(). Applications simply use the interfaces provided by the libraries and won’t even know whether observability data is generated or not because the logic is handled by the wrapper libraries by reading the configuration.We can modify the “enabled” field to false in order to disable tracing on PCVM/CVM. The other fields present in the config file are beyond the scope of this document.

## Wrapper
A wrapper library is provided using which cpp services can generate distributed tracing spans. This wrapper hides the actual implementation of how spans are created, so if in future we modify the way to manage spans nothing will change for the services. Any service which has to onboard tracing needs to call InitNutanixObservability() to initialize the tracer.

Tracing Context Passing Mechanism
Mudit Wadhwa
May 2022

## Introduction
We are building a wrapper for cpp to work in distributed tracing. The goal is to encapsulate the framework and configuration being used. This document describes the changes to track the trace context in cpp applications.
Trace Context is the key information required to stitch spans to form a meaningful trace. Therefore, we need to make sure within a multi-threaded application, trace context is used correctly.
The wrapper will be provided for cpp services to use to create spans. Details regarding the wrapper are outside the scope of this document. In this document, we are more focussed on how trace context is being tracked. Details regarding cpp wrapper can be found here.

## Rpc Client Changes Every cpp service has to initialize the tracer as soon as the service starts in order to onboard tracing. Service might receive trace context (i.e. TraceId and parent SpanId) from the service one layer above it via rpc_server or the service can start its own span which is known as root span. Generally in microservice architecture, the top-most service generates the root span. In both the above cases whether root span is started by service or not, the service has to pass the trace context to the rpc_client. We have added a field trace_context in rpc.proto which will be used to inject and extract trace context into the rpc object. Currently we are autostamping spans in rpc_client and rpc_server side in order to make the onboarding process for different cpp services smoother. If trace_context is not present in RpcRequestContext, we start a new root span. Also we inject the trace context of the newly started span into the trace_context field of the rpc object. Now we need to end the span when the rpc is finished. We pass span object till RpcFinish() by adding extra argument to function signatures. [IDF Design Documents | Archivable Entities]
Archivable Entities

## Motivation
The entities data model was designed primarily for representing "inventory" objects and their operational state.  The algorithms and data structures are optimized for processing relatively small equally hot dataset, that should be the same in all replicas.  Not all data fit this access pattern and modelling such data as entities creates scalability problems.  In particular, we have data that exhibit "archived" pattern:
there is "active" state when state transitions are happening, and "archived" state that is read-only
for archived state, latest data is most important, older data is accessed less often and the user can tolerate higher access latencies
for archived state, replicas may want to have different retention period for archived data
Examples: alerts, events, tasks, audit records, etc.
Evictable entities provide some relief by reducing memory cost (only indexes need to be cached), but they don't fully solve the problem because the memory cost is still O(N) (albeit with significantly smaller factor), load time is O(N) (currently exactly the same as non-evictable), and retention period on replica cannot be decoupled (because IDF doesn't know the semantics).

[IDF Design Documents | Archivable Entities]
## Proposed Solution
The proposal makes the following assumptions about the access patterns [TODO: validate with the clients]:
most queries either have a time range or sorted by time desc with limit
queries on recent data are more frequent than on older data
it's ok if queries for older data take longer time
Archivable entities are going to have 2 components: "active" and "archived".  "active" component behaves just like normal evictable entity.  Tasks that are running or alerts that are not resolved are going to be "active".  Once the entity transitions into "archived" state, the entity is going to be handled by the new "archived" logic.  The UpdateEntity would have a special flag that would be set to indicate that the entity needs to be archived.  Once the entity is marked as archived it becomes read-only and cannot be modified further.  The retention of archived entity is going to be controlled by a config option on the entity type (the config option would be qualified with the cluster type, so PE and PC could use different values).  GetEntitiesWithMetrics would provide a flag that would hint whether the query should get "active", "archived" or both.  Some of the entities won't have "active" phase (e.g. events, audit records), those can be created in "archived" state.

## Entity Replication Design Replication of archivable entities is going to be mostly the same as the normal entities with a few notable differences: retention policy of "archived" entities is decoupled: replica can choose to keep "archived" entities longer than master LoadEntityTrail needs to use index to avoid scanning all "archived" entities we need to reverse LoadActiveEntities to make replica send a list of all ids it got from master Decoupling retention policy is trivial: the master just never replicates deletes of "archived" entities, expecting the replica would delete "archived" entities on its own, according to its retention policies. To support efficient retrieval of "archived" entities by the replication range, we use archived_entities_mod_ts as the index to look up entities. The logic is similar to what we do on startup. In fact, the startup recovery logic is designed so that replication can use it as well (at some point I thought we'd just keep a dirty flag index, but we'd need to keep archived_entities_mod_ts for replication, so we might as well do startup recovery logic using that). Currently, we send a list of active entities from master to replica, so that the replica could check if it has any entities that don't belong to the list and delete those. With archivable entities, we'd need to send both "active" and "archived" entities' ids, because if we just sent "active" entities, then the replica might delete entities if the archival operation hasn't replicated

If we reverse the flow and send "active" entities from replica, then the master can check if any of those entities don't exist on master and send the deletes to replica (if any). Fully Evictable Indexes in IDF

## Background
The current implementation of evictable entities in IDF still maintains in-memory indexes.  It reduces base memory footprint, but there is still some amount of memory that's consumed for every entity (even if the client never reads the entity), and the entities are still read from Cassandra to build the indexes.
To reduce startup times and memory footprint, we can implement fully evictable indexes in IDF.
To support fully evictable indexes in an efficient manner, we need to have an ability to do 2 things:
maintain materialized index in persistent store, so that it's possible to load relevant key range without full scan
cache and evict parts of index based on access patterns
Here is high-level overview of the approaches for each piece of logic.
This design assumes an ability to define multi-attribute indexes, e.g. an alert could have an index on {severity, create_time}.  So the logical index structure is an ordered list of entries {value_list, entity_id} that could be used to do range scans.  E.g. a {severity, create_time} index for alerts could have the following logical entries:
{{"ERROR", 8956}, "alert-1"}
{{"INFO", 1234}, "alert-6"}
{{"INFO", 1234}, "alert-25"}
{{"INFO", 4567}, "alert-4"}
Note, that this doc doesn't account for tenant_id, but tenant_id doesn't fundamentally change problem space and can be subsequently designed as we move forward.

[IDF Design Documents | Fully Evictable Indexes in IDF]
## Materialized Index At a high level, materialized index should satisfy the following fundamental requirements: efficient range scan in the index order (forward and reverse): O(logN + M) where N is the total entries and M is the number of scanned entries atomicity of index updates with the primary data updates The logical data for index entry is going to be {value_list, entity_id}, so each index entry is unique, and it's expected to be ordered as pairs (i.e. if value_list are different, then the entry with "smaller" value comes first, if values are the same, entity_ids are compared). For low cardinality attributes (e.g. when the value is an enum), we can have a lot of pairs where value is the same, so it would be beneficial if the underlying data structure supported some form of prefix compression. As we use ordered partitioner in our Cassandra, range scans are supported by Cassandra directly (not sure, if they are bi-directional, though). The only concern here is the number of rows is going to be significant: for every entity there would be a row for the entity itself plus a row for every indexed attribute. The index rows are not going to have any values, so it's just going to be pure row index. As far as atomicity is concerned, we could implement it in IDF using WAL, but it would be more efficient to implement it in persistence layer (Cassandra / RocksDB). IDF indexes are located together with entities, so they always go to the same token range as the entity and are

[IDF Design Documents | Fully Evictable Indexes in IDF]
would be more efficient to implement it in persistence layer (Cassandra / RocksDB). IDF indexes are located together with entities, so they always go to the same token range as the entity and are handled by a single Cassandra node, so we can just use the Cassandra transaction log as the WAL. Currently, at a high level, a row update would get to the log first, then it will go to a memtable, which will eventually materialize as an sstable. Writing a single entry to the log is atomic, so we just need to implement additional materialization for indexes. As a high level, each index would be a separate memtable which is sorted in the order of index, and then materialize as a separate sstable. ## Introduction
Looking at the etcd functionality (see https://docs.google.com/document/d/1mailkfcnaMHpuQmSSeugUXDXuk2WHDFGONdLPJK300M/edit#), it looks like the biggest gap in generally useful semantics would be the ability to support transactions.  Etcd has other features, such an ability to read snapshots of previous revisions and leases, but the former seems to be less commonly used and the latter could be easily implemented as a separate service on top of IDF.
We also have some internal use cases for multi-entity transactions in Acropolis (which currently uses Pithos).  From that perspective, implementing multi-entity transaction is useful regardless of etcd.
Here is the high level design that defines the problems and outlines solutions.  Let’s iterate on that and align it with Acropolis use cases as well as a potential backend for etcd.

[IDF Design Documents | Multi-entity Transactions in IDF]
## Semantics
The transaction semantics generally assume the following properties:
Atomicity -- how to make an operation atomically commit multiple CUD operations.
Composite predicate checking -- how to express the conditional part of atomic read-modify-write operations for multiple entities (for a single entity it's just a CAS check).
Causal consistency -- how to make a read operation see data in the same order it's committed (i.e. if a transaction T1 got committed before T2, then the reader shouldn't see results of T2 without also seeing results for T1).
Isolation -- how to make a read operation sees only committed state.
Multi-phase queries -- how to run multiple queries over the same consistent view.
IDF supports these semantics for a single entity, but there are no guarantees when it comes to different entities.
The proposal keeps the following goals in mind:
no overhead for operations that don't use transactions
optimize for success case (minimal overhead for success case, failure cases can be expensive, but it's ok)
minimize overhead for transactions / queries that operate on a single shard (should be typical case with tenant-id-based sharding)

All entities that are created / updated / deleted as a part of the transaction, are marked with the transaction id. ## Single Logical Timeline
With some additional serialization, we can make global transaction ids form single logical timeline.  Etcd expects that, so we could provide an option for the client to specify if transaction serialization is needed.
If the client requests transaction serialization, the coordinator will broadcast later commits (step 4 of the atomicity protocol) only after the previous commits were broadcasted.  E.g. if transaction with id 100 got committed before transaction with id 95, we don’t let participants know about the commit decision for 100, until the outcome for 95-99 is known.  Rolled back transactions can be processed in any order.
With this approach, for all updates that use these serializable transactions, the transaction ids could be used a single logical timeline.  The timeline can have gaps, but it’s monotonically increasing.  The clients would obviously need to cooperate to set the flag for all transactions (or maybe it could be a config option on an entity type), otherwise, if some clients don’t set the flags or don’t use transactions, they will break this semantics.

## Composite Predicate Checking etcd has a nested if-then-else structure of predicate checking / operations, given that we already have BooleanExpression construct for query, it would probably make sense to build on top of that. E.g. we can use a list of pairs {entity_guid, BooleanExpression} as a precondition. When preconditions are specified, we collect all entity ids that are involved in the transaction (both in operations and in the precondition) and broadcast the requests to the participants that own corresponding shards. For entities that are specified in the predicates we take read locks (updates would bounce off them, but other condition checks won't) and return the entity value back to coordinator. For entities that are used in the operation, we set update-in-progress flag (updates and condition check would bounce off them). Once we checked all conditions and figured out which ops need to be executed, we send out ops to execute and release locks on the entities. When we send ops for final execution, we don't take any more locks, we can only release locks. If the participant crashed and doesn't hold read locks any more, it will vote 'no' on the transaction, so transaction would be aborted. This way we maintain S2PL (strict 2-phase locking) property that would guarantee that the transactions are serializable. Let's consider an example. ## Causal Consistency The guarantee that we want to provide is that if transaction T2 could use a result of previously committed transaction T1, then the reader cannot see results of transaction T2 without also seeing results of transaction T1. This property needs to be maintained for individual entity updates too, not just for multi-entity transactions. For example, if the client updates VM vm1 and then than marks task t1 as 'complete' and embeds some of vm1 properties in the task (e.g. vm1 cas_value), then it would be an anomaly to return task t1 after it's updated to 'complete', but vm1 that wasn't updated. To get consistent results on each node, we can use snapshot isolation (a form of MVCC), where we install a reader view hook, such that any modification would first send the previous state to the reader view hook. This way the reader can read current state and then overlay the previous version to get a consistent point-in-time snapshot, so the readers can run concurrently with writers. But this is not enough to get results that are causally consistent across nodes. The problem of causal consistency doesn't arise on a leader-only system, as all operations happen on one node and it's possible to get a consistent view of data either by using locks or using MVCC, but on a sharded system it's possible to have the following condition: Query coordinator sends a query to node1 and node2. Query reaches node1, reads its data. Transaction T1 completes on node1. Transaction T2

[IDF Design Documents | Multi-entity Transactions in IDF]
but on a sharded system it's possible to have the following condition: Query coordinator sends a query to node1 and node2. Query reaches node1, reads its data. Transaction T1 completes on node1. Transaction T2 completes on node2. Query reaches node2, reads its data. In this case, the query would read T2, without reading T1. It's possible that T2 used the result of T1 (e.g. if T1 updated a VM entity and T2 updated a task entity), thus this query could violate causal consistency. One way to avoid this anomaly is to use the following protocol: Query coordinator would first issue completion gate requests to all participating nodes. When a node receives completion gate request, it would prevent all transaction from completion (i.e. an entity still can be updated, but the result won't be visible until the gate is opened). Once query coordinator receives replies from all nodes, it issues queries to all nodes, they would remove the gates and get consistent results from all nodes. With this protocol, if a transaction T1 runs on a node that started participating in the query, it won't be able to complete, so any transaction T2 that happened after T1 would be guaranteed to not depend on T1. The overhead of this protocol is one extra roundtrip for the query (to set the completion gates) and slowdown of transaction completions, while they are gated. The gating time should be very short in a typical case -- it's just a matter of the coordinator to get replies from all the participating

[IDF Design Documents | Multi-entity Transactions in IDF]

The gating time should be very short in a typical case -- it's just a matter of the coordinator to get replies from all the participating nodes, which happens in parallel. The completion gates would have an expiration time, so that the transactions are not gated forever if the query coordinator crashes. Setting the completion gates could be batched on the coordinator: instead of issuing a completion gate requests immediately, the query could wait for 50ms to see if there are other queries that want to issue completion gate requests, and then all queries that happened in 50ms timeframe would issue one batch of completion gate requests. Each coordinator would use its own batching, though, so queries originated from different coordinators won't batch between each other. If one completion gate request is pending on shard processor, and it gets another one, the later completion gate request would only gate new completions, this way overlapping completion gate requests won't starve completions. If the query happens to run on a single node (should be a typical case with tenant-id-based sharding), there is no overhead. Making it work for the same shard is fairly straightforward (just need to take proper locking to make visibility + push to queue atomic). For the distributed case we need to make sure that the results are not visible until the results reach the watch coordinator, but at the same time the results shouldn't be pushed to the client, until the results are visible on the server. So for each fired event we need to make sure that the following order is preserved: Event needs to get to the watch coordinator queue before it's visible (otherwise a later update can be based on new state and race to coordinator queue). Update needs to be visible before event gets to the client (otherwise a client can see the event, but then read from IDF wouldn't show the new state). To achieve that, we can implement a protocol, where the shard processor would "reserve" a place in the coordinator queue (additional round trip to coordinator), then make the changes visible, then send the event to the watch coordinator (normal flow). All events that happen after the reserved placeholder, will get held until the placeholder is fulfilled.

[IDF Design Documents | Multi-entity Transactions in IDF]
## Isolation The guarantee that we want to provide is that a read won't see a partially committed transaction, it would either see all results of a transaction or none. On one node, it's fairly straightforward to implement isolation, if we make sure that installing reader view hook would properly synchronize with making transaction visible so that we'll either read all previous versions for the entities updated by the transaction or all new versions. But this is not enough for reads from multiple nodes, because for a committed global transaction, some nodes may not be aware that the transaction is committed and didn't make it visible. To get consistent results from all nodes, we need to get consensus on the committed transaction set. We get the global committed transaction sets from all participants in the same RPC we used to send completion gate requests, so it doesn't increase the number of roundtrips. We then take a union of committed transaction sets and use it in the further query processing. We can take a union, because if one participant saw a transaction as committed, the other participant must have voted "yes" to the coordinator, so it has its part of the transaction ready (just waiting for the coordinator's decision) and can make it available to the query. (Note that we cannot take an intersection, because we may not be able to go back in time to the version prior to the transaction). When a participant receives a query that has committed transaction id that the

[IDF Design Documents | Multi-entity Transactions in IDF]
take an intersection, because we may not be able to go back in time to the version prior to the transaction). When a participant receives a query that has committed transaction id that the participant hasn't seen yet, the participant treats it as if it just got the commit decision from the coordinator. This is so that we can maintain read-after-read consistency. The query would have to opt-in to read consistent view, otherwise, the queries are going to behave the same way as they are now -- read dirty results and have no extra overhead. For watches, if the client requires consistency, we need to provide full transaction results in proper order. One way to do it is to assemble transaction results on the watch coordinator and set a special watch on the leader, where the leader would send txn id once transaction is complete. So the protocol is going to be the following: Shard processor would send transaction results to the watch coordinator whenever the results are visible. They won't reply to leader until the results are in the queue. Watch coordinator would assemble all transaction results into one event. All events that happen after this transaction are held in the queue until the transaction is fully assembled. After all participants are successfully make transaction results visible, the leader would send txn id to the watch controller, so controller would release the transaction results to the client as one event.

## Multi-phase Queries Currently, IDF supports queries for one entity type (with the exception of ancestor joins). If the client runs multiple queries, the results would lose isolation property -- the result of each query could be self-consistent, but the overall results may be not. For etcd scenarios, we don’t have this problem because etcd only supports a very simple query over a range of keys, which can be expressed with an IDF query over one entity type, but for Acropolis we may want to retrieve a consistent data set over multiple queries operating on multiple entity types. To support running multiple queries over a globally consistent view, we can implement a notion of a consistent snapshot, when a query runs, the caller can optionally request a consistent snapshot handle and use it in subsequent queries. When a consistent snapshot is requested, the reader view hooks are left in (rather than being removed on query completion) so other queries can run on top of them. If reader views are not used for some time, they are removed (so that we don’t have to keep reader hooks forever if the client dies). So if a query is marked to return a consistent snapshot handle the protocol is the following: Query coordinator generates a unique id for the handle. Query coordinator broadcasts RPCs to all nodes to set completions gates and return committed transaction sets. Each node would note the handle id in the reader view hook that it installs, return committed transaction set. Query

[IDF Design Documents | Multi-entity Transactions in IDF]
broadcasts RPCs to all nodes to set completions gates and return committed transaction sets. Each node would note the handle id in the reader view hook that it installs, return committed transaction set. Query coordinator waits for all nodes to respond, calculates a union of committed transaction sets. Query coordinator broadcasts query committed transaction set to all nodes and gets globally consistent results from all nodes. Each node remembers the committed transaction set in the reader view, so reader views would represent globally consistent snapshot identified by a unique id generated at step The subsequent queries would specify the consistent snapshot handle and just need to get consistent snapshots from nodes.

[IDF Design Documents | On-disk Indexes in IDF on RocksDB]
On-disk Indexes in IDF on RocksDB

## Why
The current implementation of evictable entities in IDF still maintains full in-memory indexes.  It reduces base memory footprint, but there is still some amount of memory that's consumed for every entity (even if the client never reads the entity), and the entities are still read from Cassandra on startup to build the indexes.
To reduce startup times and memory footprint, we can implement fully evictable indexes in IDF.

## What
To support fully evictable indexes in an efficient manner, we need to have an ability to do 3 things:
atomically maintain materialized secondary index in persistent store
support efficient range scans in index order (forward and reverse)
cache and evict parts of index based on access patterns
RocksDB already provides provides range scans and atomic batch operations, so IDF can use those building blocks to implement fully evictable indexes.  RocksDB also provides some caching abilities that could be improved as needed to support read performance, so IDF wouldn't need to build a separate in-memory evictable index structure.  If LSM-trees don't provide good enough read performance, we can implement B-tree-based column families in the future, which would be transparent to IDF.
This work would depend on the project to move IDF to RocksDB: https://docs.google.com/document/d/1EqwgRXbJoxNTyZ_loK3grkOeOLKCtR-GnapsGoJ-Qsg/edit.

[IDF Design Documents | On-disk Indexes in IDF on RocksDB]
## How
To implement on-disk indexes, IDF would calculate the index updates that are needed and update indexes atomically in the same batch as the entity row.  To evaluate query expressions using on-disk indexes IDF would issue scans directly to RocksDB, it wouldn't maintain any cache for indexes and rely on RocksDB to provide caching.
Let's consider index operations in more detail.

## Index Definition
We can start with our current way of defining an index: the attribute has a Boolean flag is_index, if it's set, then there is an index on this attribute.  This doesn't allow defining multi-attribute indexes, but we can add it later, as we develop query capabilities to consume multi-attribute indexes.
For each indexed attribute, IDF would dynamically create a CF in RocksDB, with the name i_<entity_type>_<attribute_name>.  For each entity, there would be an index row in each index CF.  The row key of the index row would be the following: <attr_value><tenant_id><entity_id>.

[IDF Design Documents | On-disk Indexes in IDF on RocksDB]
## Index Update
To create a row that has indexes, IDF would do the following:
Get all values for the indexed attributes.
For every indexed attribute, generate updates for each index column family.
Add all index updates to the same batch as the primary row and send it to RocksDB.
To delete a row that has indexes, IDF would do the following:
Get all values for the indexed attributes.
For every indexed attribute, generate deletes for each index column family.
Add all index deletes to the same batch as the primary row and sent it to RocksDB.
To update a row that has indexes, IDF would do the following:
Get the previous primary row and check which index values are different in the new row.
Get all values for the changed attributes as well as the flag whether to delete or create the index value.
For every indexed attribute, generate either delete or put for each index column family.
Add all index operations to the same batch as the primary row and sent it to RocksDB.

[IDF Design Documents | On-disk Indexes in IDF on RocksDB]
## Index Scan
If the query determines that it needs to use an index, IDF would use the RocksDB Iterator to position and iterate over the index keys.  IDF would then extract entity_id and tenant_id from the index row key and use them in subsequent processing.  Currently, the only query plan that IDF supports is to read entity ids from all indexes in the filter expression and then do a set operation on the result set to get to the ids set that then can be used to access the entities.  We can start with that and gradually add more sophisticated query planning.
The locks will be taken the same way we do for currently implemented in-memory indexes.

[IDF Design Documents | On-disk Indexes in IDF on RocksDB]
## Index Creation / Deletion
To delete an index, each shard processor would do the following:
Tell new queries that they cannot use the index.
Wait until queries that use the index are done.
Drop the column family.
When a shard processor restarts, it would check if the shard has extra indexes (as compared to metric type definition), and drop them.  This is to handle crashes during the index drop process.
To create an index, each shard processor would start a scan and build index from the values.  To handle concurrent updates, the scan task would keep a set of all updated ids, so that when update happens, it would insert the entity id into the set, so that the scan would know that the index is updated by a concurrent update with potentially newer value.
To handle crashes during index creation each shard needs to keep track of indexes that it has fully built.  This could be done by keeping a special row with empty key -- if it's present, that means shard processor crashed while building the index, and needs to drop and rebuilt it on restart.  Once the index is fully built the special row is removed.

[IDF Design Documents | On-disk Indexes in IDF on RocksDB]
## Query Layer Changes The query layer changes are orthogonal to the on-disk indexes work (because they are as relevant for in-memory indexes that we currently have), but lack of sophisticated query planning is going to be more noticeable with on-disk indexes. The query planning is going to be designed separately, but here are just a couple points give a sense of the scope of work there. Currently, query layer doesn't do much of a query planning, the where clause just evaluates each leaf expression to get a set of entity ids, and then applies the corresponding set operations to evaluate the final set. E.g. if the filter clause is (foo > 1) AND (bar = "x"), the index on foo will get a set of entity ids that have foo > 1, then a set of entity ids that have bar = "x", and then do an intersection (because it's AND) of those sets to get a final set. Either index access could read an unknown number of entries, and depending on the selectivity, the access could be planned differently: use the current logic of getting ids from both indexes and intersecting them use index on foo, then get entities to evaluate the rest of the clause use index on bar, then get entities to evaluate the rest of the clause A similar logic needs to be done when sort / limit condition is evaluated: if the query filter condition is not very selective, then the query could be faster if we use index on the sorted attribute first, then get the entities and do filtering on them (doing another iteration if we

[IDF Design Documents | On-disk Indexes in IDF on RocksDB]
condition is not very selective, then the query could be faster if we use index on the sorted attribute first, then get the entities and do filtering on them (doing another iteration if we filtered out some entities and went under the limit). Currently, we always filter first. We don't currently support composite indexes (i.e. an index on multiple attributes), so query wouldn't be able to use them. E.g. if we had an index on {bar, foo}, then the query could get the results directly from the index, by positioning to {foo=1, bar="x"} and scanning while bar="x". Initially we can use the current query plan, so we don’t have dependencies between on-disk index support and sophisticated query planning support.

## Component dependencies related to zeus: (common for all components and not specific to IDF)
In current PC all the components keep a watch on zeus_config for a number of use_cases. Most of the information such as cluster_uuid, etc. will be static and be used as it is in the container world also. But there are also other fields like upgrade_in_progress, on which the components depend for checking whether rolling upgrade has finished or upgrade is ongoing in order to enable features only after upgrade. Fields like these will have to be changed on a per-component basis since each component could potentially have a separate upgrade cycle, if we are just moving to containers but will fallback to a single upgrade cycle then this particular point can be ignored.
Similarly, for LeadershipElection and for peer HealthMonitor and heartbeat to zk, components use server_handle_ as the zk node data and accordingly receive the LeadershipChanged and LeadershipAcquired callbacks. This ip is derived from node_list which is present in the zeus_config, so we need to have some way to not depend on node_list as all the components could have different number of instances. node_list should be replaced by components having a way to know their fqdn and use that for health monitoring and leadership election. High availability (HA) for IDF container VM level HA on XI cluster: If the VM goes down on XI cluster. The vm won’t come up itself. On Node Deletion: There we power-off the vm where our container is running. For Deployment controller: The pod scheduled on powered off vm goes to unknown state. A new pod is scheduled on another worker node. For statefulset controller: The pod scheduled on powered off vm goes to unknown state. However no new pod is scheduled here. When the node object is deleted from the kubernetes cluster the pod is rescheduled on another worker node. Reason: Good read here: This is by design. k8 master is not able to reach to worker node & determine its state. Worker can be unreachable because of the network partition. Difference between Deployment and Statefulset controller Kubernetes recommends statefulset controller for stateful apps. StatefulSet: Ordering and uniqueness of these Pods. Horizontal scaling: When scaling for application is required. Stateful application will want the new pod to use a separate(new volume). With deployment you will end up with same volume. With statefulset a new pod will get new volume. Ref:https://akomljen.com/kubernetes-persistent-volumes-with-deployment-and-statefulset/ Headless service with statefulset: The main benefit of using a headless service is to be able to reach each Pod directly. Internal IDF Service for Xi Management Services

## Why
Xi services (e.g. Xi networking) need to keep persistent data somewhere.  It's not a lot of data, but with data comes responsibility of providing data availability and continuity, which is a burden for service owners who want to focus on the business logic of the service.  The data availability and continuity strategy may be pushed down the priority list (e.g. Xi networking may need to focus on networking, not on creating a data continuity plan for Postgres where they currently store the data), which is not good for business.  To solve that problem, we will deploy and operate an IDF service, with IDF team responsible for data availability and continuity strategy.

## Plan
For the v1 of IDF service, we'll work closely with Xi networking team to get the service working for them.
To get IDF running as a service, we need to get the following work done:

[IDF Design Documents | Internal IDF Service for Xi Management Services]
## Service Deployment
The service is going to be deployed in a container on the management rack, using Canaveral.  [AI]: meet with Will to understand how it could be done.  For v1, we can deploy a single-node IDF stack and set up DR to the other rack.
We’ll need to build an image for the container to deploy.
We need to figure out a way to preserve persistent data and do save upgrade orchestration.  From what Will said, when a container-based service is upgraded, a new container is started then old container is shut down, which wouldn’t play well if they both point to the same storage.

## Service Endpoint Discovery
For v1 (which would be sufficient for Xi networking), we can run IDF in containers on the management rack at well-known static IP.  We can then embed the IP into the Xi networking configuration and that's how they are going to know how to reach IDF.

[IDF Design Documents | Internal IDF Service for Xi Management Services]
## Security
Before we mark this as a P0 for v1, we need to check if network-level security is good enough for v1.
For security we need to solve the following problems:
have an encrypted channel from Xi networking to IDF; this could be done as RPC-over-HTTPS
issue certificate for the service endpoint and do proper certificate renewal / rotation [AI]: meet with Bala to see what options we have here
integrate with IAM so that IDF can authenticate requests [AI]: meet with Bala to see what options we have here
If we go to 3 node setup, we'd also need to solve security problems for backplane communication, specifically ZK and Cassandra (IDF-IDF backplane traffic can leverage the same framework we'd use to communication with consumer services).
We also need to audit service access.  If we don’t run on Nutanix (unlikely) we may need to encrypt data at rest.

[IDF Design Documents | Internal IDF Service for Xi Management Services]
## Multi-node setup considerations
Beyond v1, we'd need to get to multi-node setup, that would provide HA for unplanned and planned (e.g. rolling upgrade) node downtime.
To do a multi-node setup, we need to solve the backplane security (if network level isolation is not good enough, this could be quite a sizeable project to implement for ZK and Cassandra).
The other consideration is we need to understand what kind of “shared fate” failures we want to tolerate and how.  We have 2 management racks, so if we want to tolerate one rack failure we don’t really have a way to do an automatic failover.
For manual failover, we can do DR, but sync DR is not supported for AHV, so we don’t have a way to achieve 0 RPO with DR. For non-0 RPO, we need to understand if the services have data dependencies with data in different data sources, if IDF is the only data source, then non-0 RPO shouldn’t break the consistency.
If we want 0 RPO, one trick we could do is to run a 3-node IDF with one node down.  The reason for keeping the 3rd node down is to make sure that the remaining 2 nodes (each node would reside on separate rack) have a sync copy of data.  In the case of a rack loss, we’d need a manual process to add a second node to the cluster and bring it up.

Providing Insights Interfaces to Clients on GHE
Devendra Singh Shekhawat, Swagat Borah
Oct 2018
In Review

## Problem Statement
IDF server and client library code is hosted in gerrit whereas there are potential clients of IDF such as IAM which are hosted in GHE (GitHub Enterprise). There is currently no infrastructure available to provide seamless access to client libraries across such different code repositories.
The BigBang project aims to solve this issue in the long term by providing a separate common repository for client interfaces (i.e, NTNX-DB-Client). However, this project is in-progress as of date and until that completes, an interim solution is required.
This problem is unique to IDF since it is the one of the first server components to move to container infrastructure from main (gerrit) which has clients in GHE which needs access to these client libraries.
This document scopes the problem to the IDF golang client libraries and the client in question is IAM.

## Possible Solutions
Over the past two weeks, the various options mentioned below were explored to provide access to the IDF golang client library for current client i.e. IAM.

[IDF Design Documents | Providing Insights Interfaces to clients on GHE]
## 1) Explore Cloning entire main to GHE
We explored the option of cloning entire main to GHE so that the client library and its various dependencies can be built on GHE itself. Clients can then access the relevant client libraries as a sub module.
Problem for this approach is lack of toolchain access for repos on GHE so building main on GHE is an issue. Moreover, keeping main in sync from gerrit to GHE is an additional overhead. Therefore, this solution was not opted for.

## 2) Explore golang equivalent of a jar/egg/shared_lib client library package
The second option that was evaluated involved providing a java jar or python egg equivalent of GoLang client libraries. This option also didn’t work out because GoLang is a compiled language similar to C/C++ and all the libraries are compiled and linked statically with client binary at compile time only and there is no provision of linking a library dynamically at run time in GoLang. This option was skipped as well.

[IDF Design Documents | Providing Insights Interfaces to clients on GHE]
## 3) Explore creating an artifactory for golang such as JFrog
The next option was to host an artifactory for GoLang such as JFrog and push golang packages and their dependencies with source code to it. Clients can then pull these packages from the artifactory and build their binaries with them. This option should work but the downside is that it requires a lot of work in hosting, maintaining the artifactory. This solution is only limited to GoLang clients as for other languages, we will have to fallback to the option of jar/eggs/shared_libs. Moreover, BigBang project is already working on this approach and they are aiming at developing a general artifactory independent of language.

[IDF Design Documents | Providing Insights Interfaces to clients on GHE]
## 4) Explore creating a separate GHE repo with only IDF golang client libraries and pre-compiled headers Another option was to create a separate GHE repo with only IDF golang client libraries along with its dependencies such as go-lang specific utils and compiled proto headers. Adding pre-compiled proto headers obviates the dependency on toolchain as faced by option 1. Moreover, a smaller repo focussed solely on IDF golang libraries is easier to maintain and keep in sync with master. For using IDF client repo, clients can just do a “go get <remote_package>” and get insights interface and all its dependencies cloned onto their repo and then build the library as part of their binary. This seemed like a viable option and we spent a good portion of the week experimenting with this approach. There were other non-technical challenges such as getting the appropriate permissions to create new repositories on GHE which took a bit of time to resolve. The issue that we found with this approach is that all the existing imports do not point to the right locations and needed to be updated specifically for this scenario. To explain, when we do “go get <package>”, under the covers it just clones the whole repo but in a different directory under “$GOPATH/src/package”. So all the packages’ absolute path have changed and therefore, we will have to change the existing import paths as well. The import paths would have to be changed to something like import (

[IDF Design Documents | Providing Insights Interfaces to clients on GHE]
So all the packages’ absolute path have changed and therefore, we will have to change the existing import paths as well. The import paths would have to be changed to something like import ( "drt-it-github-prod-1.eng.nutanix.com/data-fabric/idf-interfaces/main/insights/insights_interface") We can create custom build scripts to change the import statements for IAM client but that will not be compatible with the package management tool that IAM uses - Glide (meaning simply doing a “go get” won’t be enough, we will have to change the imports or directory structure after that). Moreover, if we change the import paths, then the util and IDF golang library code will no longer compatible with the versions in main. It is a much harder task to manage two variations of the same code across different repos, especially for an interim solution.

## 5) Copy over the IDF golang interface to client repo
The final option that we tried was copying over the IDF golang interface, its dependencies and compiled proto headers directly to client repo. This option works seamlessly and does not have the import issue mentioned in the previous approach. Keeping this copied code in sync with main(gerrit) will be fairly simple because we can directly copy the files from main. It will be similar to cherry-picking any changes to IDF golang libraries to another branch. We can easily schedule a daily/weekly sync job as well if required.

[IDF Design Documents | Providing Insights Interfaces to clients on GHE]
## Conclusion
After evaluating all the above mentioned options while keeping the requirements and timelines in consideration, we have decided to go with option 5 (copying over the IDF golang interface to client repo) as our interim solution till the BigBang project reaches completion. Moreover, option 5 is a production ready solution and provides easy migration to other solutions that BigBang will provide.
This approach requires minimal efforts for keeping the client libraries in sync with main(gerrit) and has no dependency either on toolchain or on various build systems. IDF team will be responsible for keeping this code in sync with the IAM repo.

Control Plane Database V2

## Scope and Requirements
For the time being the Control Plane Database improvements are scoped to PC only.  PE is going to run the current software stack.  IDF feature set on PC (e.g. joins) is going to diverge from IDF feature set on PE.
The scale target is to handle 1M VMs (this includes all satellite data: entities, alerts, events, metrics) coming from 1K clusters.  The amount of resources required to process that data is TBD, but we all agreed that it must not be limited by the current specs (8vCPUs / 32GB RAM / 2.5TB storage).
The database should support joins for config and alerts.
The rest of the requirements are the same as for IDF (entities + metrics integration, filter / sort / group on metrics, sync / federation, etc.).

[IDF Design Documents | Control Plane Database V2]
## Solutions In MongoDB, joins are only supported for non-sharded collections, so collections that need to be joined together need to scale up. If we want to scale out, then we need to shard data at the IDF (or application) level into multiple databases, which would become "join domains" (i.e. joins are only possible between collections in each database). "Join domain" boundaries should be chosen carefully, as they affect functionality that application can use. The proposed "join domain" boundary is cluster: all config and alerts data that comes from one cluster is going to be stored in the same database in non-sharded collections, so that it's possible to do joins between config and alerts of the same cluster. For queries that span clusters (or requests that don't have cluster context, e.g. looking up VM by UUID), IDF would implement fan-out / merge logic to stitch data from multiple clusters. Given that we're going to use scale-up for config data, we also considered using proper SQL (e.g. Postgres), but decided against it for the following reasons: MongoDB already has enough maturity and adoption, so SQL doesn't have much advantage there MongoDB has support for sharding and replication, so we can store unsharded and sharded data in the same system In an MVP, we can put all config and alerts data into non-sharded collection, so that we can just do query rewriting and don't have to handle fan-out / merge and dealing with cluster context (right now the notion of cluster is

[IDF Design Documents | Control Plane Database V2]
and alerts data into non-sharded collection, so that we can just do query rewriting and don't have to handle fan-out / merge and dealing with cluster context (right now the notion of cluster is opaque to IDF). Fan-out / merge implementation is probably equivalent of writing a new IDF query layer, making cluster context a first-class citizen is probably equivalent to implementing tenant awareness. In the LCM, we'd assign (or learn about) the primary shard that's going to host unsharded data (i.e. all config and alerts) and try to do most of IDF compute on other nodes (e.g. stitching config and metric data, watches, sync, etc.). For timeseries data we looked into potentially building a custom persistence layer so that we can save memory that we use to cache the latest data, but after doing some back of the envelope calculation, we concluded that the savings are not worth the investment, as the net data size to store 12 samples of data is ~100 bytes (one hour with 5 min downsampling).
