[IDF Design Documents | IDF Backend Upgrade]
IDF Backend Upgrade

## Introduction
Changing the backend means that data needs to be stored in a different format managed by a different backend store.  In theory, it's possible to make MongoDB understand Cassandra's data format and avoid migration, but it's practically super hard, so a practical solution would involve data migration.  PC has a lot of data, so we cannot hold upgrade, so the data migration has to happen online, after MongoDB cluster is up while the system still processing requests.

## Rolling Upgrade
This is similar to what we've done for leader-only -> scale-out upgrade: before we change any data into new format we need to make sure that the cluster has finished upgrading and all nodes will be able to understand the new format.  We also need to make sure that MongoDB has started and ready to handle data requests.
We should be able to use existing framework, where the leader would wait for cluster to upgrade to the new version and flip a flag in ZK, saying that all nodes are now upgraded to the version capable of working with MongoDB.  Then each node would start the data upgrade.
Leader can save metadata in MongoDB and create document collections for all entity types before marking rolling upgrade complete.

[IDF Design Documents | IDF Backend Upgrade]
## Entity Data Upgrade Given that for the leader-only -> scale-out entity data upgrade we just disabled entity modifications while entity update is running, we can do the same for the Cassandra -> MongoDB migration. Each node would migrate its shards, and then mark each shard as migrated in ZK. The upgrade state machine is the following: Disable entity updates. Read entities from Cassandra, store them in MongoDB. Mark shard is migrated in ZK. Enable entity updates (they will now flow to MongoDB). Delete entities from Cassandra. Mark shard migration as completed in ZK. Remove entities / indexes form IDF cache. If the shard changes owner, the new owner would check the state and roll forward to finish the migration. The queries are going to go through old logic (entity cache / indexes / read from Cassandra) until step 3, then queries that come to the shard processor after step 3 are going to read entities from MongoDD, we can see what's easier -- do query push down (i.e. translate node query into MongoDB query) or just read all entities from MongoDB and execute old logic in the query layer -- this is a transitional state anyway. Step 5 is going to wait until queries that started executed before step 3 are complete. The leader would wait until all shards are migrated, and then would flip a flag in ZK, indicating that the entity data is fully located in MongoDB. Once coordinators see that flag, they can start issuing queries directly to MongoDB, without doing fan-out at IDF level.

The behavior of watches during upgrade is TBD, depending on whether we use changestreams or not. Given for the IDF-IDF sync we'd going to route entity updates to shard owners anyway, we can keep the current watch framework, in which case there won't be changes required.

## Metric Data Upgrade
Metric data upgrade is going to be similar to leader-only -> scale-out upgrade: once the rolling upgrade completes we start writing metric data to MongoDB, then we calculate the last timestamp that could have data in Cassandra and the queries would go to Cassandra for older data.
We should investigate how expensive it is to keep Cassandra running and let the data age naturally.  If it's not too expensive to keep Cassandra up (there wouldn't be any writes, no compactions, just occasional read-only requests that become more rare as time goes), then maybe we'll just let it age out naturally (would take a year), this is the easiest solution.  If keeping Cassandra up is too expensive, then we need to physically migrate metric data, which could be tricky because data isn't physically removed when it's deleted, so we need to wait for compaction to happen, so that we don't overflow disk.

## Introduction
Currently, logical replication streams (timestamps of entities that belong to the same logical data stream are unique and increasing) are co-located with the data shards, so whenever an entity is updated, it can get the next timestamp on the same node (which is just an atomic integer operation).  With MongoDB-based implementation, we don't need to have data shards, so we need to figure out how to maintain the sequencing information.

[IDF Design Documents | IDF-IDF Sync on MongoDB]
## Requirements and Solutions To maintain proper sequencing we need to make sure that the timestamps that are generated for each logical replication stream are unique and monotonically increasing, so at any given point in time, the timestamps for each stream need to be owned by one node. Entity updates can come to any IDF node, so we either need to forward the entity updates to the node that owns timestamp generation, or send RPCs requests asking to generate the next sequence number and report completion. Let's consider the above options in more detail. If we forward entity to the node that own timestamp sequences, we would have 1 entity forward at IDF level, then 1 entity forward at the MongoDB level (from mongos to the primary for the shard), and then 2 forwards in parallel to replicas, but we'd piggy back on the infrastructure that we already have and all timestamp manipulation is going to be local. If we process update on the coordinator, then we need to do one roundtrip to get a new timestamp, then the forwards at the MongoDB level are the same, then we need to do another roundtrip to report completed timestamp. The last one is needed, so that when we get sync barrier information, we know what's completed, for that reason we cannot reply to client until we managed to report completed timestamp. Thus, in the latter case we have one extra roundtrip, plus we need to develop new logic. The former case can be optimized further if we achieve MongoDB shard locality (which we

[IDF Design Documents | IDF-IDF Sync on MongoDB]
completed timestamp. Thus, in the latter case we have one extra roundtrip, plus we need to develop new logic. The former case can be optimized further if we achieve MongoDB shard locality (which we likely need to do anyway), in which case IDF->MongoDB hop would happen locally. So looks like forwarding at IDF level would lead to less latency, less failure conditions and better reuse of existing code.

[IDF Design Documents | IDF-IDF Sync on MongoDB]
## High-level design On the master cluster, each entity update / delete would get forwarded to the shard owner, the same way we do it now. But the shard owner wouldn't have any caches or etc. (at least not for the purpose of IDF sync), it would just own the timestamp sequencing (a.k.a. timestamp oracle). The shard owner would allocate a new db_modified_ts from the timestamp oracle (the same way we do now), and send update to MongoDB. In the find_and_modify condition we'd need to check that the new db_modified_ts is greater than db_modified_ts of the existing entity, this is needed to handle conditions when 2 updates of the same entity come at the same time and due to timing the update that got later db_modified_ts gets sent earlier to MongoDB. Once the update is successful (or we know for sure that update is rejected, e.g. cas failure or etc.), we'd send the update (or range without update) to the uploader (the same way we do it now) and update the completed timestamp (the same way we do it now). ## MongoDB Overview MongoDB is a "Document Database", the data unit in the data model is a document. Documents store data in BSON format (binary JSON), they are probably compressed on disk, but every document stores all field names. Each document must have an _id field (which can be provided by the user or auto-generated by MongoDB), the _id serves as the document key and the rest of the document serves as the document value. Documents are organized to collections, the collection semantics is somewhat similar to Cassandra's column family or SQL table or IDF entity type. The documents in the collection don't have to have the same schema, so document collection is basically a KV store, in that respect it's more similar to Casandra or IDF, than to SQL. Unlike Cassandra, Mongo supports secondary indexes on documents. Each index is a separate KV on-disk structure (B-tree in WiredTiger, but in RocksDB it's going to be LSM tree) that maps the value of the field to _id. MongoDB supports sharding. Sharding can be done based on any field. Sharding could be hash-based or range-based, this is similar to Cassandra. Sharding settings are per document collection, each collection could be sharded in a different way (or not sharded at all). Sharded document collections are stored in chunks, once a chunk reaches some max size (64MB by default), MongoDB splits the chunk in two and migrates as needed to maintain even distribution of data across the nodes. E.g. _md_ for the metadata nested document and then eid (for entity id), cas (cas values), cts (created timestamp), etc. The actual attributes are going to be fields in the document (as opposed to being a property bag of key-value pairs), so that we can efficiently run queries on them. E.g. if we have "ip_address" attribute in the entity, then the document is going to contain ip_address field. The value of the field is going a nested doc that would contain value and timestamp. For nested attributes, we need to save nested attributes in the actual doc, otherwise, they are not going to be visible to MongoDB queries. Adding / removing nested attributes would result in data update of the whole document collection. To avoid that, we'd either have to push nested attributes logic to MongoDB, or ask clients to translate protos into BSON. Both options are a fair amount of work (and BSON is likely going to take more space than compressed serialized proto), so in V1 we'd probably just

## Time Series Processing Integration As we plan to use MongoDB only for config data, time series data processing is going to be done by IDF (even if later we decide to use something else, IDF would still do the query integration). The current sharded functionality would work for time series data, and we can store data chunks in whatever persistent layer we end up using (RocksDB if we go with MongoRocks or MongoDB if we go with WiredTiger). The IDF store layer would have the cache for the chunks, the same way it does now, if we use RocksDB we'd probably take advantage of RocksDB merge functionality to minimize dirty metric data memory footprint and data loss. The persistence layer sharding is TBD. From the query execution standpoint, if a query involves metrics, generally we wouldn't be able to push it down to MongoDB completely. If the query has filtering / sorting / limiting on attributes and just returns raw data with some metrics, we can push down the query to MongoDB on the coordinator, and then fan out the entity ids to metric data shard processors to get the results. If we have group-by query that aggregates metrics, even if we're grouping on an attribute, we cannot push down the whole query to MongoDB, because we need entity ids to get and aggregate metric data. So in this case we'd need to issue a non-group-by query to MongoDB and then do grouping and aggregation at IDF level. We could push down the raw query on the coordinator, but that would limit horizontal

[IDF Design Documents | MongoDB _ IDF Integration]
case we'd need to issue a non-group-by query to MongoDB and then do grouping and aggregation at IDF level. We could push down the raw query on the coordinator, but that would limit horizontal scalability, because in the group-by case the coordinator would have to scale to the total number of entities, rather than with the number of groups (also, it would transfer a potentially large dataset between nodes). A more scalable way would be to fan-out group-by query at the IDF level, then each shard processor would issue a raw query to MongoDB for its local shards, then get metric data, do grouping and aggregation and return to IDF coordinator. This way, raw data processing is distributed between all nodes and the coordinator is handling aggregated data at the group level. Grouping on metrics would behave similarly. If we have filter / sort + limit on metrics, we would go through by-shard data to find entity ids that match the condition and then feed the entity ids to MongoDB to fetch the rest of the data. This needs to be done on shard processors. To support this functionality, we need to make sure that MongoDB can take queries with lots of ids, if it cannot, then we'd need to do a full scan of all entities (in the corresponding shards) and do an intersection with the entity id set we've got from the filter on metrics conditions. If we have filter / sort + limit both on metrics and attributes, we can first push down the attribute part of the filter to MongoDB, then apply

If we have filter / sort + limit both on metrics and attributes, we can first push down the attribute part of the filter to MongoDB, then apply additional filters based on the metric data values. As some of the queries are data-heavy on shard processor nodes, we need to make sure that the shard processing happens locally on the nodes (at least most of the time), which means that MongoDB shards need to be co-located with IDF metric data shards. ## Upgrade / Migration
When we upgrade the persistence layer from Cassandra to MongoDB / RocksDB, we'd need to migrate data from Cassandra to MongoDB / RocksDB.  The data migration shouldn't hold upgrade and will have to happen online, which means that we'd have to keep Cassandra running side-by-side with MongoDB / RocksDB during migration process.  We also should handle rolling upgrade logic, which means that the Cassandra-based query functionality needs to work side-by-side with MongoDB-based query functionality.
This is TBD, but we can use similar patterns and techniques that we've used when we implemented scaleout upgrade (except for stitching old and new metric format --metric data needs to migrate to the new format, because MongoDB / RocksDB cannot read Cassandra's data and we don't want to keep Cassandra running for a year waiting for all metric data to come out of retention period).
Alternatively, we can fork configurations and for new deployments use MongoDB, but for existing deployments keep Cassandra, but this would become quickly unmaintainable.

[IDF Design Documents | Business logic on ingest - 12_05_2014]
## Introduction
This is to capture discussions that we had on 12/05/2014 w.r.t. business logic that we may need to implement on data ingest.

## vdisk ⇒ virtual disk translation
The current implementation of the business logic in Arithmos can be represented by the following diagram:
On each CVM, Arithmos agent gets vdisk stats from local Stargate, and virtual disk information from the local Hyperint.  The virtual disk information contains the file path; the Arithmos talks to the NFS master and gets filepath ⇒ vdisk name translation.  Thus it gets to know how to relate vdisk stats from Stargate with virtual disk from Hyperint.  To keep things speedy, each Arithmos agent maintains vdisk ⇒ virtual disk map.  If Arithmos doesn’t get stats for a vdisk for some period of time, the vdisk is considered inactive and the mapping entry is removed.  Arithmos doesn’t store / report vdisk stats, it only stores the translated virtual disk stats.
The important point here to note is that the translation happens locally on each node, there is no agent-master communication required to do the translation.  The other important point is that it doesn’t actually need to store or access any database information, so the vdisk ⇒ virtual disk translation logic is effectively stateless.

[IDF Design Documents | Business logic on ingest - 12_05_2014]
## Container usage stats aggregation
Stargate only pushes stats for active vdisks.  For agreggating container usage stats, Arithmos needs all disks.  To get all vdisks, Arithmos needs to get vdisk configuration from Pithos and potentially scans data from Cassandra where Stargate stores usage stats.  The logic is the following:
On master, get vdisk configuration from Pithos and Cassandra partition information from Medusa.
On master, send aggregation requests to agents, such that each agent would preferably work with local Cassandra partition.
On each agent, scan the stats_realtime column family for the corresponding Cassandra partition, return results to master.
At this point it’s not clear to me if we’ll need to replicate this logic on ingest or this is going to be handled via the generic aggregation operation mechanism in the Insights DB.  As far as I understand, the reason this logic would need to exist on ingest is to avoid exposing raw vdisk stats -- in this case the Insights DB simply won’t have the raw vdisk information to aggregate.

## Miscellaneous notes
Note on Pithos watch: we probably want to have Pithos watch on the leader, not on each node.
Note on VM migration: we don’t get a special “VM migrated” event, but we get enough data to figure this out, if needed.  Hyperint always reports a list of running VMs.  The report contains host_id information.  If VM is moved to from one host to another, next time we’ll get a list of running VMs, the VM won’t be present on the old host and will be present on the new host.  Note that it’s possible to have a state such that a VM appears running on two hosts, but we don’t believe there is a possibility to have a state such that a VM is not running anywhere.

## Functional Requirement
For the bootstrapping / catch up flow, there are multiple entities in the range and the current implementation would wait for all entities to be replicated and then mark the whole range as complete if all replications are successful. If any of the replications fail, we  don't mark the whole rangeas completed. For sync barrier, we need to be able to properly calculate ranges when individual replications fails.
Example Scenario: - Let the starting missing range be [0 , kInfinity). Suppose we got 100-200 range, and entities with the following timestamps: 108, 123, 140, 165, 192. Let ReplicateEntity returns a failure for the entities with timestamp 123 and 165. The ordering of the entities can vary.

## Update on success.
Implementation: Update Missing Ranges for every entity success with range (t-1, t], where t is the timestamp of that entity. Update missing range with the specified range of the UpdateData set only if all the entities in that set has succeeded.

## Tags for entities One of the requirements for 4.2 is to support tags for entities. Tags should have the following properties: A tag may tag multiple entities An entity may be tagged with multiple tags There will be no tags on PE (at least for 4.2) Tags will exist on PC and may be applied to entities replicated from PE Each PC will have their own set of tags, even if data is replicated from the same PE Currently we don’t support repeated fields. Users can emulate repeated fields with a string, i.e. they’ll pick a delimiter and put all tags into a string, separated with the delimiter. This implementation has the following issues: Each user may pick their own delimiter, there is no unified way Database cannot do indexing / group by / etc. on tags, it’s opaque to the DB, so the client will need to use ‘where’ clause and handle grouping themselves To overcome these issues we may want to support repeated fields and then each tag will be an entity and other entities (e.g. VMs) may be linked to it via a repeated field. This is where we want to go, but if the work required for supporting repeated fields doesn’t fit into 4.2, then we can fallback to having delimited string solution. The other question was raised about data ownership. The way we have it now, the tagged entities are mastered in PE and the tags live in PC. So the entity data except for the tags attribute is going to come from PE and the tags attribute is going to modified on PC. There are multiple ways to solve this.

[IDF Design Documents | CPDB architecture for 4.2 - 02_17_2015]

The problem is that on the DB level we support a single CAS value for the whole object, so if we try to assume that the CAS value on the replicated entity is going to be always equal to the CAS value of the master entity, then updating the tags attribute will break this assumption. There are two classes of solutions here: don’t make this assumption don’t update the entity If we remove the assumption that the replicated CAS value must match the master CAS value, then we can force-override replicated data (i.e. when an update from the master comes, read the latest CAS from the replicated entity, merge in the latest tags value apply the update). For updating the tags attribute, we can use the CAS to enforce read-modify-write atomicity; we might get CAS errors because the master part got updated, in this case the client would read the updated entity and if the original tags attribute unchanged then save the data. The other way to do it, is to have PC-mastered part in a separate column. ## Insights Proxy and CAS vs. no-CAS entities
We had a discussion, that we may want to use no-CAS entities for data that is coming from Insights Proxy, because it’s mastered on PE and should override data on PC.  But it might create complications later because we don’t have a way to change no-CAS to CAS entity.  So what we could do, is to create CAS entities, but make Insights Proxy to force-override data by reading the CAS from the DB and then use it to save the data that came from PE.  This would effectively achieve no-CAS behavior on CAS entities.

[IDF Design Documents | CPDB architecture for 4.2 - 02_17_2015]
## Storing protocol buffers in DB We had a discussion on how we could simplify storing data in the DB. The scenario is that the consumers of Insights DB may have data in protobuf format and they would have to translate the data into Insights DB format (entities, attributes, metrics) in order to take advantage of indexing and querying. It’s easy to store protobuf in a string attribute, but the DB cannot do indexing and querying on the data inside the protobuf. One idea that we could implement would be to take the protobuf and auto-map all fields to attributes. For example, if we have the following protobuf: message Custom { optional string id = 1; optional string foo = 2; message Sub { optional int64 x = 1; optional int64 y = 2; } optional Sub sub = 3; } The the Custom would map to an entity type. The consumer would somehow communicate that the id field is the entity giud, so we could create an entity with the following attributes: “_2”, “_3._1” and “_3._2”. When we store the proto we copy the fields into the appropriate attributes and when we parse a query, we can take where condition as a proto and generate a where clause from the attributes that are set in the proto. This would work for simple data types, but becomes complex once the data types become more complex. One of the issues is how to represent nested repeated fields. We could represent them as entities, the consumer would communicate to us what field in the nested message is the entity giud and then we would store

[IDF Design Documents | CPDB architecture for 4.2 - 02_17_2015]
is how to represent nested repeated fields. We could represent them as entities, the consumer would communicate to us what field in the nested message is the entity giud and then we would store nested repeated fields as separate entities that would use the id field of the parent entity as the parent guid. This would work on a basic level, but raises issues with atomicity (we don’t support atomic updates / creates / deletes across multiple entities) and scalability (we’d need to support full updates vs. delta updates). The other issue is that some of the attributes could be metrics. So we need a way for consumers to specify whether a field is a metric or an attribute. Data / metadata bloat is also a consideration. Doing the mapping of the data into Insights DB format is a forcing function for consumers to think about their scenarios, what data they need to store and query for (and they can store the rest of the data as a serialized protobuf in the attribute). Automatic mapping removes this forcing function, so consumers would just store the whole proto in the DB which may lead to data / metadata bloat and high runtime costs. The decision is to wait for the first consumer to implement the Insights DB data translation and see how much work it actually is and if it worth it to go and solve it in a generic way.

The main difference between functionality available on PE and on PC/SRE/SaaS is determined by the resource constraints on PE (on PE the Control Plane shares resources with the Data Plane), so on PE the amount of data and the complexity of data processing is going to be limited (basic monitoring on PE vs. monitoring, analytics, RCA, prediction, etc. on PC/SRE/SaaS). Control Plane DB handles data upload from PE to PC/SRE/SaaS. The data always flows from PE to PC/SRE/SaaS. Control Plane DB doesn’t support data flow from PC/SRE/SaaS to PE. A PC/SRE/SaaS Control Plane DB may be configured to collect data from multiple PEs, in which case the PC/SRE/SaaS would support multi-cluster data processing and analytics. A PE may upload data to multiple remote destinations, e.g. a PE may upload its data to a PC that manages cluster in a branch office as well as to a PC that manages all clusters in the company. ## Insights DB architecture The Insights DB is at the core of data processing. The codebase is based on the Insights Server codebase. The Insights DB architecture can be represented by the following diagram: Insights DB functionality is accessible via protobuf-based RPCs. The API is described here. Queries are processed by the query processing layer. A query is given as an abstract syntax tree represented by a protobuf, so no parsing is needed. The query processing layer has the following responsibilities: Create a query plan of how data needs to be accessed from the cache / store layer Determine which nodes need to be contacted to get the data Send data access requests to other nodes Get data from cache and / or store layer Merge results from all nodes Filter, aggregate, sort, etc. Updates go through update processing logic. The update processing logic takes care of the following: Route request to the node that owns the data Downsample, if needed Trigger watches, if needed Pass update to the store layer Update the cache To avoid introducing latency into the update path, some logic is executed asynchronously in background. Examples of background services are: Background aggregation Alerts Downsampling of data older than full-fidelity storage period Removal of data older than retention period The cache layer provide single unified cache for entity types, metric types, entities (and attributes) and metric data. The cache features single-touch and multi-touch LRU pools for scan

[IDF Design Documents | Control Plane DB architecture]
of data older than retention period The cache layer provide single unified cache for entity types, metric types, entities (and attributes) and metric data. The cache features single-touch and multi-touch LRU pools for scan resistance. The cache is strictly partitioned, i.e. each node only caches data that it owns. This strategy allows implementing atomic strictly consistent updates and avoids cache coherency problems. The cache layer design is described here. The store layer provides low-level data access methods; manages data format, update buffering, secondary index, partitioning, and node assignment. The store layer master computes data ownership map, which is then used by other layers to determine which data is owned by each node. The map is broadcasted to all nodes (via Zookeeper/Zeus). The map is used by the query and update processing layers to route data access requests. The detailed data format is described here. We use Cassandra to persist the data. Let’s look into some layers in more detail.

[IDF Design Documents | Control Plane DB architecture]
## Query & update processing layers
Query and update processing can be initiated at any node.  The node that receives a request becomes the coordinator for the request and sends data access requests to other nodes as necessary.  The data access request routing is based on the data ownership map provided by the store layer.
The query processing interaction can be represented by the following diagram:
In this example, node 2 happened to receive the query request, so it became the coordinator for the query.  The query processing layer calculates the query plan and gets data from other nodes, in this example the query needs data from nodes 1 & 3.  Each node serves the requested subset of data from cache or gets the data from the store.  Once the coordinator gets the results from all nodes, it merges them into the single result and returns the result to the client.
Update processing happens in a similar manner, only the data flows from coordinator to the participating nodes.  The data is partitioned in such a way that atomicity guarantees can always be satisfied within one node, so distributed transaction processing is not required.

[IDF Design Documents | Control Plane DB architecture]
## Store layer The store layer master assigns data partitions to nodes and publishes data ownership map to store layers on other nodes (via Zeus / Zookeeper). On PE, the data ownership map is calculated such that the data for the node (e.g. VMs, CPU, etc.) is owned by the node. This way, ingestion of data that is scoped to the node is processed on the node. On PC/SRE/SaaS, the data ownership map is calculated to achieve uniform load distribution. The store layer master detects when nodes are added to / removed from cluster and re-calculates the data ownership map accordingly. To guarantee that only one node owns a data partition, the node claims locks (via Zeus / Zookeeper) on all data partitions that it owns. Each node watches changes in the data ownership map and if it detects that it doesn’t own a partition anymore, it invalidates the cache for that partition and releases the lock. If a node receives a data access request for a partition that it doesn’t own (e.g. because data ownership changed), it fails the request and the coordinator node would have to refresh the data ownership map and send data access to the correct owners. The store layer buffers some updates (e.g. stats) to reduce load on Cassandra. The store layer provides primitives for atomic operations on entities. Entities support a CAS id, that the clients get on read and send back on update. The store layer atomically checks and increments the CAS id to enforce that the update is based on the latest data. Paxos writes are needed only if multiple writers update the same column name. Otherwise, quorum reads and writes are enough to ensure read-after-write consistency. We don't need Paxos if columns are never overwritten (which is the case for time-series data), or if all access to a particular column go through one node which serializes the writes and reads. For non-Paxos column families, the extra overhead for each column is a single column timestamp, which is 8 bytes. TTLs are also per column, so enabling TTL adds an additional 8 bytes overhead per column. For time-series data in the current Insights server, we set the column name to be the time-stamp of the data. In this case, we could modify Cassandra to remove the extra bytes required for timestamp. We can also make TTL a per table value and remove that per-column overhead as well (a single TTL policy per table is sufficient for us). For Paxos column families, the extra overhead per column is much higher (about 100 bytes more). Each Cassandra row maintains column indexes etc., which can be about 100 bytes of overhead. This can result in a high percentage of overhead if we store one attribute per row (will not be an issue if each row stores hundreds of timeseries values for a metric). ## ENG-252632: Cherry-picking the changes for PC scalability feat from master to 5.14 branch Chitti Ankith Sep 2019 Jira: https://jira.nutanix.com/browse/ENG-252632 Summary: Currently, all the optimizations done in IDF and sync pipeline as part of PC scalability feat (FEAT-9680) are only checked-in master branch, we want those changes in 5.14 (euphrates-5.14-stable) branch. This task has been done for cherry-picking all of those optimizations to 5.14 branch. All these changes are properly tested and vetted on master and IDF's QI numbers are always above 95 with tests covering these workflows and optimizations. QI numbers for IDF master can be found in this link here Only the commits checked into master before September 3rd 2019 have been considered. The commit id’s included for this task along with their brief descriptions are listed below: 1) ENG-200185: Improve the logging for debug-ability in IDF-IDF sync Summary: 1. Print a warning if we avoid the sending of an RPC (update workflow or bootstrap) due to too many outstanding RPCs with respect to bootstrap calls (as here). 2. Fix the printing of the argument NodeRemoteTransferData/RemoteTransferData when there is no data but only shard ids. are non-CAS entities (we are converting the entities from arithmos format to IDF format). While performing entity updates/deletes, insights proxy (a component running on the PC that converts data from arithmos format to IDF format) sets the timestamp to the current time and if this time is older than a previous modified timestamp insights server will reject the updates/deletes with akInvalidTimestamp error. This scenario happens when the clocks are out of sync and then we bring it back to sync. The reason for this is because insights server provides a notion of rejecting updates and deletes if there is an indeterminate failure, in the absence of CAS values. If the service doesn't provide the timestamp, insights server auto-corrects the timestamp to last updated timestamp + 1 (more like a logical clock). [IDF Design Documents | ENG-281095 _ Oneof type support in interface class for flatbuffers and protobuffs]
Oneof type support in interface class for flatbuffers and protobuffs. Chitti Ankith Feb 2020 Introduction: As part of the PC scalability project to investigate the use of flatbuffers for entities in IDF, the use of interface class for flatbuffers and protobufs was decided. The interface class generates two files names, <proto_file_name>_generated_ntnx.h which contains convenient getters and setters for the fields similar to the protobuf methods and <proto_file_name>_generated_interface.h which acts as a multiplexer between protobuf and flatbuffer and calls the corresponding method based on the message type. Currently the insights_interface proto file has certain messages with ‘oneof’ fields whose support is not yet implemented in the interface class. In order to support the ‘oneof’ type in the interface class, the flatc compiler had to be changed because the oneof type can’t directly be translated to flatbuffer union due to its lack of support for primitive types which would cause the setters and getters to be different between a flatbuffer and a protobuf. (Eg: a primitive field such as ‘optional int64 int_val’ in a protobuf message would be set using the ‘set_int_value()’ method. However since flatbuffer unions expect tables, the same field would have to be set using mutable_<table_name>->set_int_value()’ in a flatbuffer). Therefore some sort of workaround had to be implemented which would cause both protos and flatbuffers to have the same methods while still supporting the

[IDF Design Documents | ENG-281095 _ Oneof type support in interface class for flatbuffers and protobuffs]
have to be set using mutable_<table_name>->set_int_value()’ in a flatbuffer). Therefore some sort of workaround had to be implemented which would cause both protos and flatbuffers to have the same methods while still supporting the expected functionality from a oneof field. Prior preparations: Before considering generating the interface class for the insights interface proto file, the bug in the idl_gen_ntnx.cpp which causes the templates for structs to be defined in the wrong order thereby leading to an implicit instantiation of undefined template error had to be fixed. Gerrit link for the same: https://gerrit.eng.nutanix.com/#/c/376325/ Even after fixing the bug, if there is a circular dependency between two or more messages in the proto file, the error would still persist as there is no way to forward declare the template classes without leading to an undefined template error. Since our main focus is on using flatbuffers for only entities, all the messages related to entity were moved to a separate file. Gerrit link for the same along with the tests to be used: https://gerrit.eng.nutanix.com/369099 Solutions: Right now two workarounds have been created which translate the oneof type appropriately into the interface class methods. Consider the following proto file structure which will be used to explain the two approaches: package oneof_support; message A { message B { repeated string value_list = 1; } message C { oneof decimal { optional float float_value = 2; optional

will be used to explain the two approaches: package oneof_support; message A { message B { repeated string value_list = 1; } message C { oneof decimal { optional float float_value = 2; optional double double_value = 3; } } oneof ValueType { optional string str_value = 4; optional B str_list = 5; optional C decimal_value = 6; } optional int64 int_val = 7; } Currently the oneof type in the proto structure above would be generated as an anonymous table in the .fbs file which would in turn cause it to be generated as an anonymous struct in the interface class as well: table Anonymous0 (proto_name: "oneof_support::A::C") { float_value : float; double_value : double; } table Anonymous1 (proto_name: “oneof_support::A”) { str_value : string; str_list : _oneof_support.A.B; decimal_value : _oneof_support.A.C; } table C (proto_name: “oneof_support::A”) { decimal : _oneof_support.Anonymous0; } table A (proto_name: “oneof_support”) { ValueType : _oneof_support.Anonymous1; int_val : int64; } Approach 1: All the fields in a oneof type would be added as fields of the parent table. The tables would now look like as shown below: table C(proto_name: "oneof_support::A”) { float_value : float; double_value : double; } table A(proto_name: "oneof_support”) { str_value : string; str_list : _nutanix._insights._interface.A.B; decimal_value : _nutanix._insights._interface.A.C; int_value : int64; } Additional information is added to the StructDef and FieldDef structs defined in the ‘idl.h’ file. ## Publish to Kafka After Ingestion into IDF [implemented outside of IDF]
From what I understood about XiS sync pipeline, the change is not acked to the “source” (whatever relay hop happens to be the "source") until it gets persisted to the store and Kafka, so the code to do this is already present in some form.  Also, from what I understood, it would be more work to call Kafka from C++ than from Python / GoLang, so the functionality should probably be implemented outside IDF anyway.  The algorithm would be the following:
Persist change to IDF (using the new ReplicateEntity RPC).  The result would tell the caller if the data is reordered.
Persist the change (as well as "is reordered" flag) in Kafka.
Ack to “source”.
If either of 1 or 2 fail, then Ack doesn't happen, so the push will be retried.
Given that this work doesn't require IDF expertise and requires Kafka expertise (and may involve some business logic to "enrich" Kafka data with XiS-specific info), I think it would be best to be done by XiS folks.
Work Estimate: 1 week (assuming that's done by someone with expertise in Kafka and XiS pipeline)

## Extend GetEWM to Return Latest as-of Start-time Values In some scenarios (e.g. XiS metering), the consumer app would need to know the latest value of a metric as of start time of a query range in addition to all the changes within the query range. For example, to measure the uptime of the VM within the last hour, the consumer app would need to know the powered_on state at the beginning of the hour as well as the changes that happen within the hour. To support that case, we can introduce a new Boolean flag include_latest_at_start_time, that would instruct IDF to fetch the latest value at the start time. When this flag is specified, the query would require an entity list to be provided by the caller and take no where clause. This is because our query logic operates on active entities, and here we need to get historical data for entities that may be currently deleted. We also need to store attribute deletions into the metric data, so that we can correctly handle deletions. The fetch logic is going to work as the following: Use the provided range the same way we do now, that would give us the samples within the range (aligned to hourly boundaries). If we can find the latest value as of start time in the fetched data, then we're done and can return the value. If the latest value as of start is not in the fetched data, then we issue a Cassandra scan in the by_entity CF and get the data from there, if any. This logic won't work for attributes, because there is no regularity in attribute updates. To support efficient retrieval of latest as-of time attribute values, we can re-purpose the snapshot logic for the entity trail, only instead of the entity trail, we'd use the metric data. ## 1 Goal The goal is to demo scaleout in terms no of entities and no of queries that can be supported. Today IDF with recent scaleup improvements has shown scale upto 12.5k entities, the goal is to show near linear scale with the number of nodes in the cluster. ## High level concepts At a high level, the basic idea of the scaled out distributed database is that an instance of Insights DF is going to run on every node and each instance is going to manage (or "own") a portion of data. To simplify cache coherence and implement concurrency control, a portion of data is managed by at most one node. Each instance of Insights DF is going to be capable of giving access to all data, by coordinating user requests to other instances. The extent of request coordination is going to vary depending on operation, and it could range from simple "forward to one node" or "fan out to all nodes" to complex subquery processing. In our consistency model, an entity is a unit of consistency guarantees, so it's convenient to partition data by entity id. Entities of the same type would generally have the same amount of data associated with them (attributes, metrics), so it's easy to achieve reasonably uniform distribution, if partitioning is going to be based on the entity id. To be able to coordinate the requests, each instance is going to have a way to know which instances owns which portion of data, so that it can route data access requests correspondingly. To implement such functionality we bucket entities' data into shards and then assign shards to the nodes. The reason for splitting data into shards is that we want to be able to: keep the map reasonably small, because it exists in all instances keep the number of shards reasonably large, so that it's

Basic assumptions: The number of shards is relatively small, in the order of 100s. E.g. 128 sounds like a good number. The number of nodes is less than or equal to number of shards, e.g. 128 at most. ## Shard shutdown on a node When a node discovers from a node assignment map, that it still owns shards that the leader assigned to other nodes, it initiates shard shutdown. On shard shutdown at a high level we need to do the following: Quiesce all operations on the shard. Invalidate cache. Release shard lock. (shard shutdown is complete at this point) Forward unflushed metrics. Quiescing all operations on the shard is done similarly to how the cluster unregistration is handled: each operation is going to grab a shard completion token that it would release at the end of operation. The shard shutdown logic is going to remove the shard from the set of shards immediately, so new requests are going to be rejected, then wait for all in-progress operations to stop. Once all operations are stopped, we invalidate the cache. For entities, the logic is going to be similar to how the cluster unregistration is handled -- we'll iterate over the entities and unload them from the cache. For metrics, we move dirty metric sets out of cache and put it to the "unflushed queue". Then we can invalidate the rest of metric data cache. The invalidation logic is the following. We're going to keep a transient "term" counter per-shard that the node increments every time it loads a shard. To release the shard lock, the node is going to delete its <blah>/insights/shard-<shard_id>/lock- Zookeeper node. To optimize inter-node traffic, we would like to assign shards to the same node where Cassandra persists the data that belongs to the shard.  The goal is that bulk of the data processing most of the time happens on the node where Cassandra stores data.
In our case, bulk of the data is metric data, and it seems to be relatively easy to achieve Cassandra locality if we do the following:
The hash for metric data rows is going to be a function of shard id (currently it's a function of entity type and metric name as well).
The leader would get token ranges from Cassandra from time to time and calculate shard assignment locality.
If current shard assignment don't match Cassandra locality, maybe reassign.

## Latest entities
The latest entities row key format is going to stay the same, but the shard id is going to be different.  In the leader-only solution, the shard id is always 0.  To migrate the data to the new format the following logic can be used:
Each shard would have an indicator of the upgrade status: migrating or sharded.
If upgrade status is migrating, then all updates are going to use the correct shard id, but on load the old data is going to be merged in from shard 0.
The migration process in background is going to flush all entities to correct shard.  To distinguish old data from new data, real shards are going to get non-0 ids (1..128).
Once all entities are flushed, the data is deleted from shard 0 and the status is moved to sharded.

In the leader-only solution, the range maps are stored for the shard 0.  We don't plan to migrate them, the sharded logic wouldn't find the range maps and case full resync, which should work fine given that we currently only replicate latest entities (no trail).

## Rolling upgrade from leader-only to sharded implementation
During rolling upgrade, some nodes may be upgraded to sharded implementation, while other nodes would be running leader-only implementation.  This means that until the rolling upgrade is done, we need to make sure that the data format stays the same and the leader-only and node-to-node protocols are both functional.
When the sharded server first starts up, the <blah>/insights/shard-map Zookeeper node is going to be missing.  The server will init it with empty map (otherwise cannot start a watch), and watch for changes.  The empty map is going to be a special state for the coordinator to forward requests to the leader instead of coordinating request among nodes.
When a sharded server acquires leadership and sees an empty map, it would check if the upgrade is going on and would work in backward compatible mode until the upgrade is done.  In backward compatible mode the leader does the following:
Generates a map that maps all shards to the leader, but does not save it in Zookeeper.
Entity updates happen with shard id 0.
Metric snapshot happens with shard id 0.
The leader from time to time would check if the upgrade is done.  When the upgrade is done, the leader would do real shard assignment and save the map in Zookeeper.  This would activate the real sharded functionality.

The Uploader uses shard information provided by the server, except for the heartbeat functionality.  The heartbeat would need to use a new server API to get a list of shards from the server.

## PE <-> PC compatibility in replication scenarios
Sharded PE would just work with leader-only PC (but this is probably a non-scenario as Prism would most likely disallow connecting newer PE to older PC).
To support leader-only PE, a sharded PC needs to implement request re-sharding and coordination.  When a request with shard 0 comes from PE, the request is forwarded to the leader, so that the leader updates range maps for the shard 0.  The leader then would re-shard the payload based on the entity->shard map so that the entity information gets applied to the correct shard, group by shards and forward it to nodes for processing.  Then when it gets the reply from the shards, it would update the range information for the shard 0.

all entity ids map (to do deletion)
We need to implement leader-only solution, so that we keep the mappings consistent.  The implementation is going to be similar to what we have in Insights now (leader does processing, non-leaders forward to the leader).
If a leader-only solution is not scalable enough, we can shard proxy state using arithmos id to determine the shard.

Swagat B, Ritu S, Sumit B, Devendra S, Pradhyumna K
January 2025

## Use-case:
Services on the PC now have requirements where they want to store data more than a few MBs in size. Writing this to IDF directly would be inefficient as IDF and corresponding backend stores weren’t primarily designed for high volume writes.
For instance, we have Reports & Images who have their large images or report files and perform their own lifecycle management. We also have CALM blueprints, LCM and Ergon (with task WAL) having similar requirements.
The other alternative is to use Objects-Lite on PC to now store the binaries/large objects on PC. However, the disadvantage is that Objects lack certain feature compatibility when compared to IDF like querying and notification.

## Solution and Scope:
The idea is to introduce the LOs in IDF. This is a standard feature which a lot of Databases like Postgres, Oracle etc where clients can store Large Objects like Binaries or Images in the database itself. IDF will rely on Objects-Lite on PC to take care of the operations with respect to the large binaries.
For now we want to limit the solution to entity types with a maximum expected scale of 10k entities. The column size is expected to be greater than a few MBs up to GBS.
Clients will directly interact with Objects for all the LO operations through IDF client. The operations not flowing through the server would avoid the extra latency of routing heavy objects through IDF.

[IDF Design Documents | LOs support in IDF]
## On PC:
The guarantees of durability of LO columns will depend on the guarantees offered by Objects-Lite on PC. At this point, it seems that it should be acceptable to lose the data on events such as PE-PC unpairing and PC disaster events as that is the support offered by Objects Lite.

## On SMSP:
The guarantees will be the same as guarantees of Objects on SMSP. However this would mean that along with NCM, now Objects deployment should happen. The details about having it as a new service in NCM env or using existing customer deployments needs to be looked into.

## Existing conditions from Objects-Lite (On PC):
Objects Lite, Phase-1 is being offered as a “temporary storage solution”. Interactions with PE and corresponding constraints:
Objects-lite picks up any registered PE to PC for data hosting. It is not possible to make it pick a specific PE. Node to check for:

/appliance/logical/component_configuration/objects_lite/data_hosting_pe_uuid
PE-PC un-registration, CMSP cleanup can cause data loss. However, there are pre-checks to prevent cluster unregistration unless the data cleanup is done.
Lack of support for PCDR.
Services like NCC, Images might not actually need PCDR because this data is not being backed up as of today.
Max outstanding of 8 is supported. Exceeding this might lead to unexpected behaviours
Restriction to Maximum object count of 20k.
Although internal docs support a count of 100k.
Won’t be supported on NC2 deployments

## How will LOs be introduced?
An IDF table can now have more than one column marked as Large Object.
Each LO column in IDF will be now stored as an individual object and the entity in IDF will just contain the reference and metadata to the object. The design would guarantee the atomicity of writes that, entire update including LOs would succeed or fail.
Each time a LO column is updated in IDF, a new Object will be created in Objects and the reference would be updated in IDF. When compared to overwriting the same Object, this offers the capability that the old version of the Object can still be read if the user has read the older reference from IDF.
Clients will be registering LO attributes by specifying the enum during registration at the attribute level. The details about the bucket name, configuration params wrt older version cleanup will be registered at the entity type level.

## Scope of LOs:
LOs can be created by the end clients for the following scenarios:

## 1. Object upload using IDF client
In this case, the service has the LO present within the memory or a file in the PC already. IDF will take care of life-cycle management of the column values in Objects. This would be used by clients like Reporting where the reports are created directly from client services. Column values will be stored in a specific format in Objects:

We need to explore this mapping as to when the need arises.

## AZ Attach For the AZ attach, in v1 can assume that the attached AZ has no consumer or global entities, so we don’t need to handle merge. To support this, during attach we need to have logic, that would check that the new AZ doesn’t have any consumer or global entities. The AZ attach would start with the process that’s similar to PE-PC pairing. To simplify connection routing, the AZ attach is always going to happen to the current cloud master. When the first 2 AZ are federated into a cloud, one of them becomes the cloud master (and it stays the cloud master until the admin explicitly designates a different AZ to become the master). The other AZ must be clean. We will need to implement logic to show which AZ is the cloud master and check that attach happens to the cloud master. We assume, that by the time we ship PC Federation, the reverse tunnel functionality is implemented, and links between AZs are asymmetrical (one AZ is initiator and the other is acceptor). So the AZ attach can either be initiated from the clean AZ to the cloud master or from the cloud master to the clean AZ. At the end of the pairing process (we’ll get into detailed pairing logic later), the entity that describes the new AZ is created in the master and gets replicated to all AZs (including the new AZ). The cloud-global data is replicated to the new AZ, so the new AZ becomes part of the Federation. At the IDF level, there would be a special RPC, TBD, to attach a new AZ, so that the entities that

At the IDF level, there would be a special RPC, TBD, to attach a new AZ, so that the entities that describe the federation could be only modified by IDF. When IDF first becomes the master (i.e. federation happens between 2 AZs that were not part of federation), then IDF creates entities in the following order: entity that describes cloud master AZ, entity that stores who the cloud master is, entity that describes the non-master AZ. The pairing process is going to be similar to PE-PC pairing, with the difference, that the AZ is going to be “paired” to the Federation, rather than to a single AZ. The pairing consists of 3 pieces of data: (1) the initiator needs to know the endpoint information on how to connect to acceptor; (2) the acceptor needs to have a certificate that trusted by initiator; (3) the acceptor needs to have a way authenticate initiator. The (1) is fairly straightforward (have DNS name or IP address + port number). There are multiple ways to solve (2) & (3), but assuming we picked a way to solve (2) & (3) for PE-PC pairing, the high-level modification is the following: (1) is going to be the same (stored locally in initiator’s AZ); (2) the acceptor certificate is either signed by the Federation-global CA trusted by all AZs (need to add the CA on the new AZ) or added into the list of trusted root certificates stored in the global data (need to set a watch on all AZs to update trusted root certificates);

## Inter-AZ Direct Links In v1, we require every AZ to have a direct link to other AZs (to avoid implementing request routing). The workflow for establishing a direct link would be similar to pairing, except there would be no need to establish trust. Each AZ would run a link heartbeat service, that would go through a list of AZs and try to ping them. If a direct link to an AZ doesn’t exist, the link heartbeat service would raise an alert that there is no link. If ping fails for a certain period of time, the link heartbeat service would raise an alert that the link is down. The link heartbeat service would know the list of AZs from the global entities that describe AZs in the cloud. Each AZ would provide a UX to show link status, and indicate the status (no link, link down). There would also be a UX flow (on each AZ), to initiate a link to any other AZ (i.e. become an initiator side of the new link). We just need to enter connection information (DNS name or IP address + port number), the AZ is going to initiate a connection to the other AZ, the mutual authentication will happen using the cloud-global trust information, and if it's successful, then the link entities are updated in both AZs. To reduce the amount of manual configuration, we can implement a gossip protocol to share known acceptor AZ connections. For links that AZ is initiator for, it would keep a list of remote AZs and connection info (DNS name or IP address + port number) it uses to reach them and update globally

If the connection heartbeat service detects that there is no link to an AZ (which can happen when a new AZ joins federation) or the link it down, it will try to re-establish the link using the gossip information. ## Global Data Remastering If the cloud master cannot be used for some reason (e.g. AZ is destroyed), the admin can manually designate another AZ to be a new cloud master. IDF will provide a new RPC, that will take the uuid of the new cloud master. The local IDF will forward the call to the corresponding AZ, then the new master IDF will remaster and update the entity that describes the current master to point to itself. The remastering of global entities happens lazily, whenever they are updated. When the entity that describes the cloud master is remastered to the new master, the incarnation id and the CAS value of the entity is set to the current timestamp (or previous value + 1). The assumption here is that the wall clock of the new master is reasonably accurate and remastering operation is extremely rare, so the new master’s incarnation id is going to be higher than the old master’s, so it actually becomes a new master (higher incarnation id will override lower). When the global entities are updated on the new master, they inherit the incarnation id and CAS values from the master record. When receiving updates for global entities, the IDF would check if it's the cloud master, and if it's not, then it will reject the updates. ## Estimating the IOPs needed by the PC In the current PC version, data ingestion is primarily driven by the Insights Proxy, which syncs PE data to the PC. Every 30 seconds, the Insights Proxy does one UpdateEntity call sper entity and one PutMetricData call per entity type. For this estimation we disregard all IOs except the ones issued by the DB (e.g., IOs due to alert manager). Let ET be number of entity types, E be the number of entities of all entity types, MT be the number of metric types across all entity types, and M be the total metrics across all entities. For each UpdateEntity, if the entity changed since the last update, the DB issues a Cassandra Paxos BatchMutate call to write the entity to the latest entities column family and a non-Paxos call to write to the entity trail. Currently, the entity trail is disabled, so the second call doesn't happen. So, for E entities, the DB may issue up to E BatchMutate calls to Cassandra. For each BatchMutate call, Cassandra does one commit log write, and since the commit log writes are O_DIRECT this results in a sync call to the underlying Stargate (assuming the PC is running on Nutanix DSF). Since commit log writes are sequential, Stargate does a sync write to the underlying device. So, the Proxy entity updates can result in up to (E / 30) IOPs. In 4.6, PutMetricData does not result in an immediate IO, as metric data is cached for an hour and written back in the background over the course of an hour. The DB writes back

[IDF Design Documents | PC IOPs estimation]
In 4.6, PutMetricData does not result in an immediate IO, as metric data is cached for an hour and written back in the background over the course of an hour. The DB writes back metrics every 15 seconds and it writes back one metric type at a time. We organize metrics into sets based on downsampling interval (raw and hourly for each metric type), so we can have up to 2 * MT number of Cassandra writes in 30 seconds. This gives MT / 15 IOPs for metric data writes. In the latest DB version, we also log PutMetricData arg to prevent metric data loss on a crash. Since the Proxy does one PutMetricData call per entity type every 30 seconds, this results in (ET / 30) IOPs for logging PutMetricData arg. From our current config file, ET=30 (excluding NVM and AVM entity types). Assume MT=750 (average of 25 metric types per entity type). Assuming a scaled up PC has E=30K and M=750K (average of 25 metrics per entity), entity updates can result in 30K/30 = 1K IOPs and metric data put can result in (750/15 + 30/30)=51 IOPs, for a total of ~1050 IOPs on a scaled up PC. Note that this only considers the IOs due to DB updates, and doesn't consider the IOs issued by Cassandra during compaction; since Cassandra issues large sequential writes during compaction the number of IOs should be much smaller in comparison. It also doesn’t consider IOs due to other services running on the PC.

[IDF Design Documents | PC IOPs estimation]
## Reducing the number of IOs used by DB
The majority of the IOPs are due to entity updates in the DB, which can be reduced by batching entity updates. One option is to do batching of Cassandra commit log writes. Earlier, Cassandra had an option to batch commit log writes but currently it is turned off (after Cassandra moved to O_DIRECT for commit log writes). But if a BatchMutate has multiple mutations, Cassandra batches the commit log writes for all the mutations. So, the DB can reduce the number of IOs by issuing multiple Cassandra writes in one BatchMutate call.
To do this, the DB can expose a new 'BatchUpdateEntity' RPC call that allows the Proxy to update multiple entities in one call. The DB can then issue the Cassandra writes for all the entity updates in a BatchUpdateEntity in one Cassandra BatchMutate call.
If the Proxy batches B entity updates in one BatchUpdateEntity call, we can reduce the number of IOPs due to entity updates from E/30 to E / (30 * B). So, if B=100, we can have the max number of DB IOPs due to entity updates be 10 IOPs and total number of IOPs for DB be less than 61 IOPs.

Data Ingest Support for Control Plane DB

## Background
Here is the data ingest architecture as I understood from the discussion on 11/20/2014:
Insights DB on CVM is going to ingest data from two types of sources:
Stargate and some other data plane services push data to Arithmos, which pushes it to Insights DB
PE data collectors (e.g. Hyperint) pull data from various sources and push data to Insights DB
Insights DB stores the data for its own purposes, and then pushes changes to the data uploader service (part of collector framework).  Continuing the tradition of using Greek mythology names, I named it Charon.
Charon receives data from the Insights DB and pushes it to remote destinations (e.g PC or multiple PCs, SaaS, SRE Insights, etc.).  Charon handles connections, authentication, synchronization, provides store-and-forward capabilities.
In addition to the data that is collected into the Insights DB, there is data that is collected only for the remote locations.  To distinguish collectors that collect data that is used on the PE (PE data collectors), I called the other collectors PC data collectors.  The exact semantic differences between PE data collectors and PC data collectors are out of scope for this document; the different names given here are just to reflect the fact that some data is collected for PE (and then forwarded to remote locations) and some other data is only sent to remote locations.

## Arithmos Options Currently, Arithmos ingests stats and responds to queries from Prism and other consumers. The functionality of Arithmos is going to be (at least partially) replaced by the Insights DB functionality, and it’s quite possible that Prism and other consumers of Arithmos will be eventually updated to query Insights DB. The data ingestion and business logic (e.g. mapping vdisk stats to virtual disk stats) is likely going to stay. While keeping the options open, I think it’s reasonable to make the following assumptions: we want to eliminate extra resource consumption due to duplicated functionality in Arithmos and Insights DB: simple data translation is ok; significant data or computation duplication should be avoided we want to minimize changes in the data plane services: simple replaces (renames, trivial changes of data format, etc.) are ok; significant changes of logic should be avoided even if Insights DB completely replaces Arithmos, it’s not going to happen overnight, so we’re going to have both Arithmos and Insights functionality side-by-side for some time DECISION: while discussing data ingest architecture on 11/20/2014 we decided that we want to keep Arithmos-related functionality (whatever is going to be left of it) separate from Insights DB core functionality, e.g. the business logic for mapping vdisk stats to virtual disk stats should not be a part of the Insights DB. We agreed, though, that this architectural separation of concerns, should not limit

[IDF Design Documents | Pulling data into insights]
functionality, e.g. the business logic for mapping vdisk stats to virtual disk stats should not be a part of the Insights DB. We agreed, though, that this architectural separation of concerns, should not limit our deployment options, i.e. Arithmos-related functionality could run in the same process as the core Insights DB without violating the requirement for architectural separation of concerns. DECISION: we discussed an option to keep Arithmos as it is now and have the collector framework pull data from Arithmos and push it to Insights DB, but we rejected it because it has too much runtime overhead (albeit this option requires the least change). The architectural diagram already reflects this decision. As I see it, we have two orthogonal sets of choices to make: deployment choice: two separate processes or in the same process data storage choice: two sets of data or adapters over one set of data The choices are orthogonal and we can pick any combination (which makes four options available). Here are the choices in detail.

[IDF Design Documents | Pulling data into insights]
## Two Processes vs One Process
Running Arithmos and Insight DB in separate processes has the following advantages:
Separation of deployment enforces separation of concerns
Arithmos functionality doesn’t have to be deployed on PC
… and the following disadvantages:
Interprocess communication overhead
More complicated failures modes (handle cases when one process is unavailable)
Overhead of of running two processes
Running Arithmos and Insights DB in the same process has the following advantages:
All communications are simple function calls
Synchronized failure modes (the same process is either available or not)
All library code (Zeus, etc.) is shared, smaller memory footprint
… and the following disadvantages:
Separation of concerns is not enforced (though we agreed that this is not an issue)
Arithmos functionality is going to be deployed on PC, even though it’s not needed there

[IDF Design Documents | Pulling data into insights]
## Two Data Sets vs One Data Set
Having Arithmos and Insights DB to keep separate data sets has the following advantages:
Less change to make -- we just can save stats in two locations on ingest
… and the following disadvantages:
More storage needed to keep redundant data
Data can get out-of-sync, need to handle that
Having Arithmos and Insights DB to work over the same data set has the following advantages:
No data redundancy, less storage required
No out-of-sync problems
… and the following disadvantages:
May need to implement adapters for translating data between Arithmos and Insights DB formats
Note that even if we pick the option to work on the same data, there might be some data that is unique to Arithmos logic (e.g. some data may be needed to translate vdisk to virtual disk stats), we’ll continue storing it.

[IDF Design Documents | Pulling data into insights]
## The Proposal
Given the listed choices and the goal of keeping resource consumption on CVM to a minimum, I think that we should merge Arithmos and Insights DB into one process and try to eliminate all redundant data.  In order to keep the codebase stable and operational during transition, I propose the following strategy:
link Arithmos code into Insights server binary and remove Arithmos binary
make Arithmos ingestion APIs forward stats to Insights DB ingestion APIs (just call the functions in the same process)
migrate Arithmos APIs to work directly with Insights DB data (rather than keeping its own data)
remove redundant / obsolete Arithmos APIs
The stability properties of this strategy is the following.  After step #2 we pretty much fulfill functional requirements -- the stats will get to the Insights DB.  Which means that if push comes to shove, we can ship even after step #2.  Step #3 can be done gradually and if needed we can ship releases in between.  After step #3 we pretty much fulfill performance requirements (i.e. eliminate redundant data), so step #4 doesn’t block a release.
I’ve updated the task list to reflect the proposal.

## 1. Introduction
Pithos stores the vdisk configuration information. Two messages VDiskConfig and StretchParams are defined in file pithos.proto, which defines the communication interface between Pithos server and client. The above two messages become two classes in the generated C++ header and source files. Vdisk information is actually stored in class VDiskConfig. When you search for the configuration information of a vdisk, the returned configuration data is stored in class VDiskConfig; also when you update the configuration of  a vdisk, the new configuration data should be stored in VDiskConfig and passed to update function as an input parameter.

## 2. Data VDiskConfig, the message in proto file and the corresponding class in the generated C++ header and source files, stores the vdisk configuration data and has the following fields, listed in the following tables. The table contains information of each field, including the name, type and desirability of the field. The desirability of a field can be required, optional or repeated. If a field is repeated, it means that it is an array of elements of a particular type and is required. The type of a field can be a primitive type such as int64, bool, string, etc., or a composite type, or an enum type. A composite type consists of primitive types, enum types and possibly other composite types. A composite type is represented by a data structure consisting of multiple fields and each of its field can have a primitive type, enum type or composite type recursively. If a field has a composite type, we store the name of the composite type in the column Type of its corresponding row in the table and store the definition of the composite type, i.e., the information of each field in it, in a separate table. For an enum type, we store the name of the enum type in the column Type of its corresponding row in the table and give the definition of this type, i.e., its possible values, later. All the fields, combined together, form the configuration of a vdisk, and this is the data stored in Pithos and returned to Pithos client. Please note that I do not provide the explanation of the

## 3. API Function Interface
Pithos provides 4 types of services, which are:
register
lookup
update
watch
In this documents, we provide brief explanation of lookup, update and watch.

## 3.1. Lookup
lookup service returns data, which is vdisk configuration, to the client. The client can search vdisk configuration and vdisk stretch parameters. There are two sets of lookup functions: Lookup* and TryLookup*. Lookup functions do not return the data, it prepares the client cache. That is, it checks if the searched item is in the cache; if not, try to load it into cache. If variable use_cache is false, it always pins the searched item and checks if the item in cache is older than that in database (master) and loads it if it is older in cache, i.e., lookup is forced to return the latest entry in database.

## 3.2. Update Update service allows client to update vdisk configuration and its stretch parameters. To update vdisk configuration, the client needs to specify which vdisk or vdisks to update and provide the new configuration data. To specify the vdisk or vdisks to update, the client should provide the information in data structure VDiskConfigEntry, which is defined in section 3.1.1. The new configuration data is provided in data structure VDiskConfig. The following are the API function interface: void UpdateVDiskConfig( VDiskConfigEntry::PtrConst old_entry, shared_ptr<VDiskConfig> new_data, const function<void(bool)> & done_cb ); void UpdateVDiskConfig( const std::vector<VDiskConfigEntry::PtrConst> & old_entries, const std::vector<shared_ptr<VDiskConfig>> & new_data, const function<void(bool)> & done_cb ); To update vdisk stretch parameters, the client needs to specify which stretch parameters to update and provide the new stretch parameters data. To specify the vdisk or vdisks to update, the client should provide the information in data structure StretchParamsEntry, which is defined in section 3.1.2. ## 3.3 Watch Watch service allows clients to set a watch on a vdisk configuration or vdisk stretch parameters so that the clients could be notified when an update is made to the watched vdisk configuration or stretch parameters. In this way, a client can monitor the vdisk configuration or stretch parameters it is interested in and update its cache when the watched configuration and stretch parameters are changed so as to make its cache always have the latest data. To set a watch on vdisk configuration, the client needs to provide vdisk_id to indicate which vdisk configuration it is interested in. The client could also provide a vdisk configuration category to monitor all the vdisks within the category. A callback function should also be provided so that appropriate action could be taken when an update to the watched configuration occurs.
