[IDF Design Documents | Service Data Insulation in IDF]
Service Data Insulation in IDF

## Why
In service-oriented model, multiple services may want to use IDF to store their data.  One way to do it is to have IDF instance for every service, but this would be expensive if the number of services is large, so this is suboptimal.  We want to provide a way for multiple services to share the same instance, such that the data for each service is insulated and only accessible to the service.

## What
This feature would make it possible to use one IDF instance from multiple services with strict insulation of service data (i.e. each service can only access its data).

## How
Assuming that the AuthN is going to be provided by common service communication framework, IDF should be able to get an authenticated service id and then provide data insulation based on that.  So the assumption that the following proposal explicitly makes is that IDF can get service id from the RPC layer.  If the service id is empty, the requests operate on data that belongs to no service (i.e. empty service id is treated as just yet another isolation boundary and doesn’t have special privileges).
In IDF, all entities and metrics are already scoped to an entity type, so we just need to provide scoping for entity types.  Whenever we refer to an entity type, we need to qualify the reference with service id.

[IDF Design Documents | Service Data Insulation in IDF]
## Implementation Notes
Internally, we can prepend service id to the entity type name (using our standard \xFF character as the separator).  The call that returns all entity types, would scope the results to only the service id it got from the RPC layer.  The CRUD data calls would amend the entity types that are passed by the caller with the service id, so that data access is properly scoped.  When doing entity graph traversal, the parent entity types in links are amended with service id.
Work estimates: 4 weeks
(Note the 4 weeks is not calendar time, it's effort size, calendar time depends on when the work is staffed and scheduled)

[IDF Design Documents | Tenant ID Phase 2_ Design]
## Overview
I am working implementing the following tenant ID features in IDF:
Use tenant ID to scope entities.
Observe tenant IDs in the query layer.
I am using this document to discuss design decisions as they become relevant.  Please feel free to comment on the data here or to point if I am missing a discussion on an issue.

## Query Layer
Either a query is a wildcard query (specifies only an entity type) or the tenant ID must be included along with the entity ID. (No queries that are wildcards on just the tenant ID.)
If no tenant ID is included but there is an entity ID, the default tenant ID for the entity type can be automatically used.  This is for increased backwards compatibility (similar to tenant ID stamping).
Internally, all data structures and function calls must support tenant ID and entity ID where the entity ID used to be used.

## Store Layer
Purge the tenant ID cache (this was a shortcut taken in phase 1 of the tenant ID implementation).
All data structures and function calls must support tenant ID and entity ID where the entity ID used to be used.

[IDF Design Documents | Tenant ID Phase 2_ Design]
## Design strategy: structs instead of tuples/pairs.
Many of the data structures that will need to hold the tenant ID make use of pairs and tuples.  As I modify these structures to hold the tenant ID, I propose to replace these tuples and pairs with simple structs.  This provides several benefits:
Code is more self documenting.  It is immediately obvious what data each field in the struct holds.  A std::pair<string, string, string, int> is not.
Simple methods (e.g. constructors) can be attached to the struct.  This will make useage cleaner.
Future extendability. These data structures can be modified in the future more easily.  When using tuples/pairs the data structure is defined in many places.
In terms of work required on my end, this is no extra.  I need to modify the data structures anyways.
From a memory perspective a struct is equally efficient.
The example below shows a struct for tracking an entity ID and a tenant ID together.

## Scaleout vs Non-Scaleout mode
Unfortunately, the behavior of entities with tenant IDs will differ between scaleout mode and non-scaleout mode.  The root cause is the function GetEntityCurrentStateRowKey. This function is used to create the row key for entities within Cassandra.  It returns two types of row keys: the old version (for non-scaleout mode) and the new version (for scaleout mode).  Unfortunately, the tenant ID is only a member of the new type of key.
This will lead to the following behavior when operating in non-scaleout mode:
Entities with conflicting (entity_type_name, entity_id) will not be able to coexist even if they have different tenant IDs.
Queries that specify a tenant ID in the GUID will not work.  Queries that use the pseudo-attribute for the tenant ID will still work. (Possibly not the case, need to investigate)

[IDF Design Documents | Tenant ID design & implementation]
This document explores the design and work-breakdown of Tenant IDs, a feature being added to IDF in 5.5.1. This feature is needed for Xi-CT.
The design of this feature has not yet been finalized, content in this document is still up for discussion and/or debate.

[IDF Design Documents | Tenant ID design & implementation]
## Background
The purpose of Tenant IDs is to allow entities to be scoped to tenants. This is needed for security (so entities with the same name on different tenants don’t conflict) and for developers (who can use the entity metadata to find which tenant owns a particular entity). One example use case for this is the Xi Metering service. Metering needs to compute the VM resource usage for each tenant, which becomes simple if each entity comes with the tenant id embedded as part of its guid (as proposed in this doc). That way Metering itself does not need to keep track of the tenant for each VM entity.
Previously, an entity could be uniquely identified by the tuple (entity type, entity uuid).  Under this new system, each entity is uniquely identified by the tuple (entity type, entity uuid, tenant ID).
Entities can be categorized into those that are tied to a particular tenant (e.g., VMs) and those that are multi-tenant and span tenants (e.g., nodes, clusters). We call the first category of entities as tenant-specific and the second category as tenant-general. For a tenant-specific entity, we use the id of the entity's tenant as part of its guid, whereas for a tenant-general entity, we use a special "general tenant ID" in its guid.

[IDF Design Documents | Tenant ID design & implementation]
as tenant-general. For a tenant-specific entity, we use the id of the entity's tenant as part of its guid, whereas for a tenant-general entity, we use a special "general tenant ID" in its guid.

Once an entity has been assigned to a particular tenant, its tenant cannot be changed. In particular, this also means that a tenant-specific entity cannot be made tenant-general and vice-versa.
An entity with a tenant ID belonging to a particular tenant is considered to be tenant specific.  In Xi-CT, a tenant specific entity does not live outside of its tenant cluster.
This goal of this document is to propose a solution to the problem of populating tenant ids in each IDF entity. One approach is to have each service populate the tenant id for each entity it creates, when it creates the IDF entity. However, this approach requires every service to change; this is risky given the short runway for Xi-CT.

[IDF Design Documents | Tenant ID design & implementation]
each service populate the tenant id for each entity it creates, when it creates the IDF entity. However, this approach requires every service to change; this is risky given the short runway for Xi-CT.

We propose a simpler approach for Xi-CT, given that in Xi-CT each PE and PC cluster is single tenant. The approach is as follows:
Each Xi-CT PE & PC cluster is seeded with its tenant id, which is stored in a ZK node.
When a tenant-specific entity is created, IDF adds tenant id to the entity guid by reading the ZK node. IDF determines which are tenant-specific entities based on the entity type -- each entity type is configured as tenant-specific or tenant-general in the IDF entity type configuration. Though some entity types (e.g., tasks, users) cannot be neatly categorized into tenant-specific vs tenant-general, the entities needed by Xi-CT services requiring tenant id (in particular, Metering) can be categorized; more on this later.
When a tenant-generic entity is created, IDF adds general tenant id to the entity guid.
IDF also adds tenant id for queries on the entities as needed.
https://jira.nutanix.com/browse/CPD-1702

## Data format of tenant IDs
We need to choose a data format for tenant IDs.  We propose 16 byte UUIDs (UUID4 format) stored as strings.  The general tenant ID should be “0” in the chosen data format, e.g. “0000-0000-0000-0000”.

[IDF Design Documents | Tenant ID design & implementation]
## Generation of tenant IDs
When a Xi-CT PE / PC is created, it is initialized with a unique tenant ID.  We propose that this is stored in the ZK node /appliance/physical/clustertenantid.
Team responsible: DCM?

## Retrieve tenant ID
Each IDF instance needs to be able to retrieve its tenant ID.
Team responsible: IDF (Cody)

## Entity type registration
When entities are registered they are marked as tenant specific or tenant general.
By default, entities are tenant-general.
Once an entity type has been configured as tenant-specific or tenant-generic, it cannot be changed later for Xi-CT. However, when migrating to Xi-MT, we can change as needed.
Team responsible: IDF (Cody), working with service teams responsible for entity types.

## Entity creation
When a tenant specific entity is created, the tenant ID is read from ZK and attached to the entity.
When a tenant general entity is created, the tenant ID is set to the general tenant ID. (“0000-0000-0000-0000”).
Team responsible: IDF (Cody)

[IDF Design Documents | Tenant ID design & implementation]
## Entities with mixed type
For entity types that can have both tenant-specific and tenant-generic entities (e.g., users, tasks), we propose that we make them tenant-generic for now. In other words, an entity type is configured as tenant-specific only if all entities of that type are tenant-specific (e.g., VMs). This should work for the use cases that we know of, in particular Metering. Since the tenant id for an entity cannot be changed after it is assigned, this config cannot be changed within the Xi-CT timeframe. When we migrate from Xi-CT to Xi-MT, we can change the tenant ids as needed in the migration script.
This proposal needs a design discussion (Vamsi, Jan, Vinod, etc.).
One way to do this would be to have an optional field for each entity type: access_groups. This field contains a list of “groups” (stored as strings) that are allowed to view this entity.  An empty access_groups list means that all tenants are allowed to access it.  Through zookeeper, each tenant keeps a list of the groups of which it is a member (e.g. “infra”). The access_groups list is ignored if the entity type is tenant-specific.
Team responsible: IDF

[IDF Design Documents | [ENG-683435] Request affinity for RPCs in IDF]
[ENG-683435] Request affinity for RPCs in IDF
Pradhyumna Komatineni
July 2024

## Problem statement:
As of today, we have 2 workflows which require node affinity:
Watches:
Requires all the requests post RegisterWatchClient to land on the same node.
Otherwise the functionality wouldn’t work.
Cursor queries:
Since the cursor query order is cached only on one node where the primary cursor is server from.

## 1.  node_handle in initial request:
Both the initial requests, RegisterWatchClient and PrimaryCursorQuery will now return a node_handle in the response. 

Or, we need to discuss if something needs to be passed in the headers or such. Like how we have handled client_service_name as of today.
This will be sent by clients in all the subsequent requests.
node_handle will be the same as what is written in ZK, so routing should be straightforward.

## Advantages:
No need of any state maintenance or node deduction overhead on the server
The cursor_id generated already has this mechanism for adding the node_handle: Code link
Both watches and cursors can use the existing mechanisms for CursorQueryInfo and WatchClientProto to consume the changes.

## Disadvantages:
Will require changes to be done on all languages of watch_client and all the clients should upgrade to the latest code version

[IDF Design Documents | [ENG-683435] Request affinity for RPCs in IDF]
## 2.  Hashing based on identifier of the requests:
Watch workflows have the client_name or session_id, either of them could be used as the identifier.

However for cursor queries, the identifier is generated after it lands on the node. This has to be changed to generate it on where it lands.
The hash generated will now rely on the existing shard distribution instead of adding new constructs.

## Advantages:
No changes would be required on the client side

## Dis-advantages:
Could lead to more dependency on node migration workflows going forward

As of today, all the above workflows will anyway get interrupted when there is a node addition/removal
Overhead of computing hash on every request.

Can be avoided by doing a mod on the last bytes if we can rely on uuid4

## Possible solutions:
Going ahead with Approach 1 of using node_handle.

[IDF Design Documents | Auto Purge entities during full restore from Snapshot]
Auto Purge entities during full restore from Snapshot
Devendra, Sumit
April 2022
In-progress
In this document, we discuss the high level design for Automatically Purging certain entities (some black listed entity types and replicated entities from PE IDF) from IDF during full restore from PCVM’s previous snapshots.
Since the PCVM disk snapshots will be older (at least few hours old) so PC recovered directly from them will have older state (compared to current state on PEs), we will purge entities synced from PEs and certain entity types like Task which can’t tolerate going back in time from PC during recovery itself so that client teams are not exposed to older state and PC do not enter into any inconsistent or unknown state.
In this document, we mention the design purely from the IDF side and coordination efforts needed from the PC/Adonis team for completing the PC recovery from the PCVM snapshots.
Already performed a POC for the amount of time taken to Purge entities during ShardLoad with varying scale.

## High-level order of events during recovery
Adonis/Prism create a ZK node mentioning that the PC is in full recovery mode.
IDF during its init sees the ZK node created in step 1 and starts entity data purging as needed (details mentioned in below sections).
After finishing entity purging (across all the shards in IDF), IDF can create another ZK node (or update the same node in step 1) to let Adonis/Prism know about completion of the purging phase.

[IDF Design Documents | Auto Purge entities during full restore from Snapshot]
## Entity Purge Decision
In phase1, we plan to purge entities falling in one of the below mentioned categories :-
IDF-IDF replicated entity from PE (decided by presence of _master_cluster_uuid_ in the entity).
If “purge_local_entities_on_full_restore” option is set to true in entity type config.
Introducing a new option in IDF entity type configuration for deciding whether to purge local entities for that entity type during full restore or not.
Sample configuration:-
entity_type_info_list {
entity_type_name : "sample_entity_type"
type_info {
track_attribute_changes : false
suppress_replication : true
enable_pulsehd_collection : false
purge_local_entities_on_full_restore: true
}
}
Implementation wise we can create a method (with above mentioned logic) either in InsightsUtil or EntityStore to decide whether an entity should be purged or not (whenever purging is needed during ShardLoad).

[IDF Design Documents | Auto Purge entities during full restore from Snapshot]
## IDF Entity Auto Purge Design Entities in IDF are uniformly distributed across 128 shards and those shards are uniformly distributed across nodes of the cluster (shard redistribution happens whenever any IDF instance is added/removed from the cluster). During bootstrap/initialization each IDF instance scans all the entities owned by shards assigned to it, called as ShardLoad operation. We can piggyback on the same ShardLoad operation and figure out the list of entities to be purged and purge them (here we have a decision of whether to mark the ShardLoad as completed before purging finishes or should we hold it until purging finishes). Since this operation of purging entities should be performed only during full restore, we will need some persistent marker, mostly a ZK node (path to be decided by Adonis/Prism team) from the Adonis/Prism team to signify if the PC is in full recovery mode. Moreover, for each shard this operation should happen only once (subsequent IDF restarts/ShardLoads should not trigger purging) so we can create a per shard zk node like “/appliance/logical/insights/full_restore_purging_status/<shard_id>” (signifying the completion of purging process for that shard). For updating the overall purging completion (across all shards) status in ZK, IDF leader can update/create a ZK node once all the shards finish their purging (IDF leader can keep a watch on “/appliance/logical/insights/full_restore_purging_status/” parent zk node and once it has 128 children

[IDF Design Documents | Auto Purge entities during full restore from Snapshot]
status in ZK, IDF leader can update/create a ZK node once all the shards finish their purging (IDF leader can keep a watch on “/appliance/logical/insights/full_restore_purging_status/” parent zk node and once it has 128 children (equal to number of shards in IDF), meaning all shards have finished their purging). Exact order of steps:- During init/bootstrap, IDF reads the zk node to decide if the PC is running in full restore mode or not and if we have not performed the purging already. During ShardLoad, we decide (based on zk nodes read in step 1) if auto purging needs to be performed or not for that shard. If needed, we start the purging as part of ShardLoad operation and ShardLoad waits until purging is complete. Once the purging is complete for this shard then IDF will write the zk node “/appliance/logical/insights/full_restore_purging_status/<shard_id>”. IDF leader node registers a watch on parent zk node “/appliance/logical/insights/full_restore_purging_status/” and once all the shards complete their purging process it can write the Zk node expected by Prism/Adonis to mark the completion of overall purging process. ## Overview
PCBR to PEs overview doc
PCBR to S3 overview doc
IDF’s native backup and recovery of entities is the core engine behind Nutanix’s PCBR (PC backup and restore) offering.
Currently, IDF supports backup and restore of Entities (configurable at entity type level) to/from below mentioned targets:-
To selected list of registered PEs
This is a continuous streaming backup
Can only retain latest data
S3 as well as any S3 compatible object store
Periodic snapshot of PC data backed up to object store
Can retain backups based on retention at bucket level (user configurable)

[IDF Design Documents | Backup of Namespaces]
## Namespaces Overview
Complete details about the Namespace feature and its guarantees can be found here.
The Namespace feature in IDF enables users to extend replicated entities to write extra attributes on replicas. In general,  replicated entities (IDF-IDF synced) are read-only on replicas but the Namespace feature provides a middle-ground to extend the replicated entity without need for multi-master writes and both-way replication.
High level guarantees of the Namespace feature:-
The lifecycle of all the Namespaces is attached to the Primary entity itself. On deletion of Primary entity all the namespaces will also get deleted.
Attributes belonging to a single Namespace can be updated in UpdateEntity RPC at a time.
Each Namespace will have its own metadata like cas_value, created timestamp, modified_timestamp etc. Namespace protobuf link
Namespaces created on local entities are neither Replicated nor Backed-up.
Almost all the Query functionalities like grouping, sorting, filtering, etc are supported on Namespace attributes.
Secondary indexing is also supported on Namespace attributes.

[IDF Design Documents | Backup of Namespaces]
## Upgrade and Version compatibility
For supporting full functionality of backup and restore of namespaces, we need both PE and PC to be upgraded to software version supporting backup and restore of namespaces (targeted for Iris).
PEs running older software versions will be able to persist the namespaces data coming from newer PCs (running newer software versions) but for PEs to support restore of namespace data we need PEs to be on newer software versions.
If PEs are running older software versions and PC is on the latest software version, existing features of backup and restore will keep working as is without any issues.

## Limitations/Restrictions of Namespace backup
Only the namespaces whose backup is enabled via schema (either config or RPC) will be backed up.
Namespaces created on replicated entities can be backed up using the similar schema changes.
Namespaces created on local entities :-
can only be backed up if backup is enabled at entity type level (if entity itself is configured for backup).
For Namespaces created on replicated entities :-
After recovery, they will only be visible when the original replicated entity syncs back to the recovered PC.
Will not be recovered if somehow a local entity with the same entity_id is present on the recovered PC before restore.
In events of namespace collision, we will always retain local namespace.

[IDF Design Documents | Backup of Namespaces]
## New metadata fields addition in Namespaces For supporting backup and recovery of Namespace data we had to add a few extra metadata fields to every Namespace. Below mentioned is the list of newly added metadata fields in Namespace proto  // Optional. Master cluster uuid representing the cluster where this // namespace was created. optional string master_cluster_uuid = 7; // Optional. The timestamp of server modification time (set by database). optional uint64 db_modified_timestamp_usecs = 8; // Optional. Internal field, to be used by database only during backup and // restore of namespaces data. optional uint64 incarnation_id = 9;  MasterClusterUUID Populated only on backup sites by replica InsightsServer. Similar to entities, this field can be used to identify if a namespace is local or replicated/backed-up. This field is added with future scope in mind, when we plan to support replication of namespaces, the same field can be used to identify local vs replicated namespaces. DBModifiedTimestampUsecs Populated on source InsightsServer. Whenever a namespace gets updated, InsightsServer will stamp this field with per shard Oracle timestamp (monotonically increasing timestamp stream kept at per shard level). IncarnationID Used during backup and recovery workflows only. During recovery, InsightsUploader will increment the incarnation_id for all the namespaces being restored. Moreover, currently it does not make sense to support attach-detach workflows for Namespace data

[IDF Design Documents | Backup of Namespaces]
Used during backup and recovery workflows only. During recovery, InsightsUploader will increment the incarnation_id for all the namespaces being restored. Moreover, currently it does not make sense to support attach-detach workflows for Namespace data because namespaces can not outlive primary entities.

## Entity transformations for Backup in source InsightsServer
Entities to be backed-up (with or without namespaces) will be transformed by source InsightsServer before forwarding to InsightsUploader. All these backup specific transformations are applied by function InsightsCommonStore::ProcessEntityForBackup
Clear namespaces which are not supposed to be backed-up
Namespaces that doesn’t have backup enabled in schema
Replicated namespaces, namespaces having non-empty master_cluster_uuid
Set entity’s incarnation_id as maximum of all local incarnation_ids, max(incarnation_ids of all local namespaces, entity’s incarnation_id if entity was locally created)
Set entity’s db_modified_timestamp_usecs as maximum of all local db modified timestamps, max(db_modified_timestamp_usecs of all local namespaces, entity’s db_modified_timestamp_usecs if entity was locally created)
For replicated entities
Set field ‘contains_only_namespace_data’ to indicate that we are backing up namespaces created on a replicated entity
Clear ‘attribute_data_map’ and ‘master_cluster_uuid’

[IDF Design Documents | Backup of Namespaces]
## Entity transformations for Restore
Increment incarnation_id for the entity during recovery
Increment incarnation_id for the Namespaces to be restored during recovery

## Recovery semantics on new PC
Local backed-up entities (with or without Namespaces) will be restored in normal state on PC and entities will be queryable after recovery.
For Namspace only backup
If the original replicated entity is present on the recovered PC then we will just merge the Namespaces into the existing entity on the PC.
If the original replicated entity is not present during recovery then we will just persist the empty entity having only namespaces data in Cassandra and not load the entity in cache. When the original entity replicates from PEs then we will merge these restored namespaces in that entity.

Aug 2021

## Problem Statement:
In multiple scenarios we've had requirements of cleaning up the replicated data on the replication site. For PC DR we have a similar requirement where on unregistration of a replica site we want to delete all the backed-up entities. These deletes should preferably be delete+purge if required.
One similar other use case in normal sync can be some clients trying to use PE uuid for PC-PE synced entities and not being able to do it because when PE is moved to another PC then entities don't sync due to the same incarnation_id and different master_cluster_uuid.

[IDF Design Documents | Cleanup backup data on replica on unregistration]
## Solution: Have a new zk node for IDF and add a new RPC in IDF to clear replicated data. In IDF we'll add an explicit RPC to clear up the DeleteReplicatedData similar to DeleteReplicationState where the clients will provide the cluster_uuid of the cluster being removed from backup. IDF leader will add a child entry in the zk node with cluster_uuid. All IDF instances will do the following after detecting the zk node: Check if the shards in the zk node are owned by that IDF instance. Exit if no shard is owned. Block RemoteTransferData RPCs from that cluster_uuid. Remove entry from registered_clusters map. What to do if a cluster is already unregistered? Then we'll have to directly scan from cassandra and do cleanup. Also, deleted entities won't be present in cache, a scan will be required for them as well. Clear up all the pending state queues such as sync_barrier queue. Also, we can clear up the queued ops, if serialization is enabled. Start iterating over each entity in the EntityIDSet and check if master_cluster_uuid == cluster being unregistered. Trigger delete if the condition is satisfied. Since this is backup data all entities won't have insights objects present. Also, the entity_id set will contain only live entities, deleted entities won't be present, but we'll have to somehow delete those entities as well. (One slow but correct option would be to trigger unregister workflow which will remove all entities from cache and then trigger a full scan and delete based on

[IDF Design Documents | Cleanup backup data on replica on unregistration]
somehow delete those entities as well. (One slow but correct option would be to trigger unregister workflow which will remove all entities from cache and then trigger a full scan and delete based on master_cluster_uuid) Remove the entry for the shard which is completed from zk and if all shards are removed, remove the cluster_uuid entry as well. All RemoteTransferData RPCs will be enabled for that cluster if it's still registered, put the entry back into registered_clusters map.

[IDF Design Documents | Enhancing Prism Central Backup & Restore Scale]
Enhancing Prism Central Backup & Restore Scale
[Devendra, Gaurav]
June 2024
[In-progress]

## Introduction:
The PCDRv2 solution for Prism Central (PC) configuration data backup & restore has been generally available since version PC.2021.7. This solution enables the backup of PC’s data to a few selected Prism Element (PE) IDF databases. However, a current scale limitation restricts the number of entities backed up to a Prism Element. This limit is set at 150,000 entities per PE node based on several benchmarks.
With the onboarding of new services onto PCBR, there is a critical need to increase the number of entities that can be backed up to Prism Element. This expansion is necessary to ensure that the backup solution can accommodate the growing volume of data generated by these new services.
This document outlines the enhancements required to increase the scale of entities that can be backed up to Prism Element.

[IDF Design Documents | Enhancing Prism Central Backup & Restore Scale]
## Memory Usage of Backup Entities on PE:
We store the entity ID set for backup entities in the IDF cache to support count queries.
We index the “_master_cluster_uuid_ attribute”.
Whenever we modify the backup data, we always load the entity into the cache from Cassandra.
We have addressed the first two points and removed them from the IDF cache, but as we do a Read Modify Write for entities to Cassandra, we can’t do much about the third point.
We considered two approaches to address the issue:
Continue storing the backed-up data in the same Column Family in Cassandra as we do for other entities.
Create a new Column Family specifically for the backed-up data in Cassandra.[ENG-700215]
The problem with the first approach is that as the volume of backed-up data increases, the IDF initialization time will also increase since we read the entire Column Family during initialization. Therefore, we decided to proceed with the second approach.

[IDF Design Documents | Enhancing Prism Central Backup & Restore Scale]
## Remove backed-up entity info from IDF Cache[ENG-658331]:
Currently, we store the “entity_id” set and also index “_master_cluster_uuid_” attribute for backed-up entities, which was required for supporting count queries on PE during Backup and Restore.
Now we have removed all the info, i.e., “entity_id” set and indexing for “_master_cluster_uuid_” attribute from IDF cache for backed-up entity types.
With this change, the following changes will be observed on PE for backed-up entity types.
GetEntitesWithMetric queries won’t be allowed for backed-up entity types. The “kInvalidRequest” error will be returned in response to any such queries.
Only point queries (i.e., with entity_id) will be supported for backed-up entities via GetEntities RPC.
Only Create Watches will be supported for backed-up entities.

[IDF Design Documents | Enhancing Prism Central Backup & Restore Scale]
## Writing the Backup entities to the new CF
Currently, IDF writes locally mastered, synced, and backed entities to the same column family (FLAGS_insights_entities_column_family_name) in Cassandra. Our goal is to move the backup entities to a different column family(FLAGS_insights_backup_entities_column_family_name). This change will offer the following benefits:
Backup entities will no longer be included in the IDF bootstrap, reducing IDF initialization time.
We will implement a change to allow only point reads on backup entities and disallow wildcard queries since these entities will no longer be maintained in the IDF cache.
This will reduce the memory load on PE IDF. As more services are onboarded for PCDR and with the limited RSS on PE IDF, this change will help alleviate memory pressure on PE IDF.
To implement this change, we need to consider the following scenarios:

## Handling the Brown Field Migration case
For PEs serving as backup endpoints for previous versions of IDF, the backup entities will remain in the latest_entities column family (CF). During the migration to the newer IDF version on a node, we will need to move the backup entities from the latest_entities CF to the new CF. Here are the tentative implementation details:

## Rolling Upgrades:
Since the IDF supports rolling upgrades, the leader node is aware of when all IDF instances have been upgraded.

[IDF Design Documents | Enhancing Prism Central Backup & Restore Scale]
## Upgrade Completion Check:
After the last IDF node is upgraded, use the watch on Zeus config (ZeusConfigUpdateCallback) to check if the cluster_upgrade_in_progress() field has turned to false.

## Migration Initialization:
Once the upgrade is complete, the IDF leader creates a ZK node(/appliance/logical/insights/migrate_backup/init) to indicate that the column family migration for backup entities should be initiated.
Both leader and non-leader IDF instances will watch this ZK node to start migrating backup entities to the new column family.
Once the nodes receive a watch callback, they temporarily block all incoming RemoteTransferData RPC requests for backup entities to maintain data consistency during migration. Before initiating the actual entity migration, each node waits for a predefined delay interval (FLAGS_insights_init_backup_migration_delay_msecs) to allow any ongoing requests to complete gracefully, ensuring a smooth transition.

## Shard Scanning and Migration:
After initialization and shard loading, each IDF node performs per-shard scans to locate backup entities in the latest_entities CF and migrate them to the new CF.
Once a shard migration is completed, the node that owns the shard updates the status of the shard in the ZK node at /appliance/logical/insights/migrate_backup/shard_status/<shard_id>, indicating the successful completion of the migration of the particular shard.

[IDF Design Documents | Enhancing Prism Central Backup & Restore Scale]
## Tracking Migration Status And Marking the Migration As Completed:
The IDF leader continuously watches the shard status ZK node at /appliance/logical/insights/migrate_backup/shard_status, and once it detects entries for all 128 shards, it marks the backup entity migration as complete by creating a ZK node at /appliance/logical/insights/migrate_backup/done.
Every node keeps a watch on the ZK node /appliance/logical/insights/migrate_backup/done, and upon receiving the watch callback, it unblocks the RemoteTransferData RPC calls for backup entities. From that point onward, all backup entities are written to and read from the new Cassandra column family.

## Note:
During the migration of backup entities to the new column family, all reads for the backup entities continue to be served from the old column family (FLAGS_insights_entities_column_family_name) until the migration is fully completed.

[IDF Design Documents | Enhancing Prism Central Backup & Restore Scale]
## Historical Timestamping Approach
Initially, while writing backup entities to the PE IDF, each entity was stamped with a backup_db_modified_timestamp. This timestamp was derived from an Oracle shard timestamp on the PE side. The purpose of this timestamp was to assist with bootstrap syncing during the initial phase of the restore workflow to the PC.
As a result, each backup entity on PE contained two timestamps:
backup_db_modified_timestamp: Stamped at the time of writing the entity to the PE IDF.
db_modified_timestamp: The original timestamp the entity had on the PC before being backed up.
During the restore workflow, the backup_db_modified_timestamp was used to identify and fill in the missing data ranges on the PC. When an entity was restored to the PC, its timestamps were set as:
db_modified_timestamp: Set to the value of backup_db_modified_timestamp from the backup entity.
source_db_modified_timestamp: Set to the original db_modified_timestamp of the backup entity (from the time it was stamped on the PC).

## Current Behavior with New Column Family
With the migration to a new Cassandra Column Family, backup entities no longer require a backup_db_modified_timestamp when written to PE, as these entities will not be loaded at all during bootstrap.

[IDF Design Documents | Enhancing Prism Central Backup & Restore Scale]
## Uploader Initialization and ZK Watch Setup
When the InsightsUploader starts on each node, it checks if a pc_backup_restore_config entity is present in the IDF. If this entity exists, it signifies that a restore process should be initiated. The uploader attempts to delete the ZK node (FLAGS_insights_uploader_resume_restore_zk_node) to reset the restore state. After this cleanup, it sets a watch on the same ZK node to monitor its creation, which will signal when restoration can proceed.

## Sync Barrier Creation by Uploader Leader
In the AlramHandler of the leader node of the InsightsUploader, if the pc_backup_restore_config entity is found and the backup migration is marked as completed (i.e., the ZK node /appliance/logical/insights/migrate_backup/done exists), it proceeds with a Cassandra scan.
This scan is done using the LoadEntityTrail RPC and is executed across all shards in the new column family. The purpose is to determine the maximum db_modified_timestamp for each shard. Once the scan is complete, the leader replicates a special sync barrier entity named pc_restore_idf_sync_marker, which includes these maximum timestamps for all shards.

[IDF Design Documents | Enhancing Prism Central Backup & Restore Scale]
## ZK Node Creation to Signal Restore Start
After successfully replicating the pc_restore_idf_sync_marker entity to PE IDF, the uploader leader creates a ZK node at /appliance/logical/insights/init_pc_restore. This node acts as a signal for all other nodes, indicating that they may now proceed with the actual restore process.
All uploader nodes, having set a watch on this ZK node, receive a watch callback upon its creation. Once the callback is received, the nodes move forward with restoring the data.

## Completion of Restore Process
The restore process is considered complete once the pc_restore_idf_sync_marker entity is successfully restored to the PC. This entity serves as a marker confirming that the IDF restore has been finalized and that all backup entities are now restored to a consistent state on the PC.

## Problem Statement
Prism Central is used by most Nutanix customers to manage their physical and virtual infrastructure. By 2021, we aim to have 100%-attach for Prism Central across the entire Nutanix customer base.
We at Nutanix have not provided customers with a single reference architecture for the management and operation of Prism Central. This coupled with various infrastructure constraints on the customer end has resulted in ad-hoc deployments of Prism Central, without a comprehensive view to high availability or DR.
Prism Central is also the management platform for running various services, so in addition to providing a HA/DR solution for Prism Central, we have to ensure that the solution enables HA/DR for all the services running within PC.
For HA/DR overview - https://www.wintellect.com/high-availability-vs-disaster-recovery/
This document describes a comprehensive view to Highly Available Prism Central Deployments.
Note : This document deals with Prism Central deployments on an AOS substrate only.
Note : For brevity, we use PC to refer to Prism Central and PE to refer to Prism Element.
Note: When referring to PC, this document assumes both single-node and Scale-out deployments unless where specified.

[IDF Design Documents | Highly Available Prism Central  Deployments]
## Types of Failures
Let us enumerate the types of failures that PC can be subjected to.
Node Failure : Single node on an AOS cluster goes down
Cluster Failure : A single AOS cluster goes down
Availability Zone (AZ) Failure : The entire AZ goes down.
Region Failure : The entire region goes down.
Short Term Network Failure (between PE and PC)
Long Term Network Failure (between PE and PC)
OS (or DB) corruption on the PCVM.
vdisk
Dependent System Failures : As PC gets deployed on hyper-scalars, systems which PC depends on might go down.
CVM

## HA vs DR vs Backup/Restore
It is important we are clear about HA vs DR vs Backup/Restore terminology to our customer. In general, our perspective is that
The difference between the 3 mechanisms will be based on the following:
The kind of failure it can handle (as listed above)
Infrastructure constraints (as listed below)
Recovery Point Objective (RPO), Recovery Time Objective (RTO)
Cost of implementing the solution

## Infrastructure Constraints
The following lists the infrastructure constraints that customers have for hosting their physical infrastructure. This in turn places constraints on the RPO and RTO that they can plan for.
Availability of a secondary data center : Many customers do not have access to a secondary data center. This limits their ability to plan around a disaster scenario.
Distances between datacenters : affects the latency of network traffic between datacenters.

[IDF Design Documents | Highly Available Prism Central  Deployments]
## Recovery Considerations
Restore behavior:
Point-in-time as Authoritative source
Point-in-time as a starting point + incorporate current changes
Backup/Snapshot behavior:
Number of copies to maintain
Differentiate between Metrics, Config data
For Config - Do we need to differentiate between entity vs policy data

## Desired Phasing
PC Metro for Cluster failure within a Region
PC Scale-out for Cluster failure within a Region
Backup/Restore for PC?
Async DR solution for PC for Region failures

[IDF Design Documents | Highly Available Prism Central  Deployments]
## Nutanix Architecture and Delivery Constraints
MSP : PC will move from the monolithic VM based architecture to a microservice based architecture with MSP. This means that high availability can no longer be thought of at the PC cluster level, but at the level of each of the microservices on MSP. Moreover, different microservices can have different availability guarantees.
PCaaS : PC will be delivered as a service, hosted on Xi to begin with, followed by the hyperscalers as we expand to a larger set of customers. The availability of this PC while running on the public cloud has a different set of constraints as compared to PC running on the customer premise.
PC-PE registration requirements : Today there seems to be a requirement that the hosting PE for a PC is registered to this PC. We need to find a way to remove this dependency
Note : There is an ongoing design discussion around how PCs will work in a hierarchical multi-tenant cloud model. Details are yet to be finalized. See here for details.

[IDF Design Documents | Highly Available Prism Central  Deployments]
## PC Time Machine
PC Time machine is the name given to a collection of micro-services that run on the PC cluster that enable the administrator to manage protection and recovery for the PC. Some of these components might make use of underlying AOS functionality, but this is an implementation detail. The administrator can do the following with the PC Time Machine. Ideally all of this functionality is available on the PC UI. In some cases, some of the workflows are made available on the PE UI (eg. for initial deployment with a given protected mode, or in the event the PC is down).

[IDF Design Documents | Highly Available Prism Central  Deployments]
## Setup During deployment of a PC, the administrator can choose a “striped” deployment of PCVMs. The administrator gives the choice of clusters that the individual PCVMs should reside on. The pairwise latency between each of the clusters must be <= 5ms. For brownfield deployments of PCs where all PC VMs are running on the same cluster, the administrator can choose to migrate some of the PCVMs to other clusters. The pairwise latency between each of the clusters must be <= 5ms. For a given PC deployment, the administrator can set up protection of the PC with the following possible RPO options. 0-RPO protection for the PC : This option allows the administrator to recover the PC without any data loss on PC. The administrator chooses a mirror cluster for each of the clusters that house each of the PCVMs. There is no requirement for the target clusters to be unique, i.e. it is possible for a 3 node PCVM cluster on the primary site to replicate to a single cluster on the secondary side. The latency between the primary site and secondary site clusters must be <= 5ms. The number of recovery points for 0-RPO protection of a PC is 1 by default. It is possible to configure more than 1 recovery point. Near-Sync RPO protection for the PC : This option allows the administrator to recover the PC with some data loss on PC. The extent of data loss depends on the change rate of data on the PC, as well as the latency between the primary and secondary sites. In most cases, the expected data loss

In most cases, the expected data loss could be of the order of a few seconds.The administrator chooses a mirror cluster for each of the clusters that house each of the PCVMs. There is no requirement for the target clusters to be unique, i.e. it is possible for a 3 node PCVM cluster on the primary site to replicate to a single cluster on the secondary side. Note that 0-RPO protection can only be achieved within a region, whereas Near-Sync RPO protection is possible for a PC managing clusters across regions.

## Recovery The recovery workflow corresponding to each of the failure scenarios listed below. The exact user experience for each of these cases is yet to be determined, and the details below should be taken for illustrative purposes only. Node Failure : AOS is already resilient to a single node failure by default. Some customers configure AOS clusters to be tolerant to 2 failures by setting FT2. Failures beyond the cluster level failure setting are handled by the remaining cases below. Cluster Failure : In this case, a single cluster hosting one or more of the PCVMs has failed. As long as there is an AOS cluster available hosting at least one of the PCVMs, an alert/icon appears on the PC UI showing the PC in “degraded” mode, along with an option to “fix”. The needed PCVMs are created, restoring the PCVM cluster to a healthy state. If all the PCVMs were hosted on the same AOS cluster, and this cluster has failed, this is equivalent to an AZ Failure from the perspective of the PC. The administrator has to go to the secondary AZ to perform the recovery workflow. This is described below. Availability Zone Failure : In this case, the entire AZ has failed. The administrator sees a “Recover” option on the appropriate clusters of the secondary AZ. This spins up a PC cluster on the appropriate clusters on the secondary AZ. Region Failure : In this case, the entire region goes down. At this point, the administrator sees a “Recover” option on the appropriate clusters in the alternate

[IDF Design Documents | Highly Available Prism Central  Deployments]
the appropriate clusters on the secondary AZ. Region Failure : In this case, the entire region goes down. At this point, the administrator sees a “Recover” option on the appropriate clusters in the alternate region. This spins up a PC cluster to manage the remaining clusters. Short Term Network Failure (between PE and PC): In this case 1 or more PCVMs lose connectivity with a given PE. There are no recovery steps here other than wait for connectivity to be restored, or assess if there is a long term network / cluster / AZ outage. Cluster / AZ outages are dealt with above, after the administrator makes said determination. Long term network outages are dealt with below. Long Term Network Failure (between PE and PC): In this case, the administrator has made the determination that there is a long term network outage between the PC and the PE. To continue operating on the cluster in question, the administrator spins up a PC on the cluster using the 1-click PC deployment workflow. Once the network connectivity is restored, this PC can either be registered with the aggregator PC as a master, or be destroyed, at which the PE can register directly with the aggregator. OS corruption on the PCVM: In this case, one / more of the PC VMs have data corruption. The administrator sees a “Recover” option on the cluster in the primary AZ, which walks the administrator through a workflow that ejects the corrupted PCVM from the cluster and creates a new PCVM to form the PCVM cluster.

## The Ideal PC Deployment
Here, we describe the ideal highly available PC deployment for a make-believe customer “ChromeDepot” that has AOS clusters across 4 locations across the US. The design to build a highly available PC deployment for smaller size customers is called out in the appropriate sections. Chad Phillips is the global IT administrator.

## Setup
10 AOS clusters in a single AZ in Seattle, WA - “aos-1” thru “aos-10”.
10 AOS clusters in a single AZ in Oakland CA - “aos-11” thru “aos-20”
20 AOS clusters in a single AZ in San Jose CA - “aos-21” thru “aos-40”
20 AOS clusters spread across different ROBO locations on the East Coast - “aos-41” thru “aos-60”. Each of these form their own AZ.
Latency :
1ms between Oakland CA and San Jose CA
50 ms between Seattle WA, and Oakland CA and San Jose CA.
100 ms between the US east coast and the US west coast.
50 ms between each of the east coast locations.

[IDF Design Documents | Highly Available Prism Central  Deployments]
## Deployment
Chad logs into pc.chromedepot.com - where he gets an aggregated view of all his AOS infrastructure. This PC runs in aggregator mode, with the following master PC instances registered.
PC-Seattle is a 3 node PC that runs in AZ-Seattle. The 3 PCVMs for PC-Seattle are PC-Seattle-1, PC-Seattle-2, PC-Seattle-3. Each of the PCVMs here run on a different cluster, say aos-1, aos-2 and aos-3 as part of the initial deployment. All Seattle based clusters (aos-1 thru aos-10) are registered with PC-Seattle.
PC-BayArea is a 3 node PC that runs in the Bay Area. The 3 PCVMs for PC-BayArea are PC-BayArea-1, PC-BayArea-2 and PC-BayArea-3, say aos-11, aos-12, aos-13 to begin with, which run in the Oakland AZ.
PC-Time-Machine is enabled for PC-BayArea, with RPO-0. The secondary AZ selected for PC-BayArea is AZ-San Jose.
PC-EastCoast is a 3 node PC that runs on the east coast. The 3 PCVMs for PC-EastCoast are PC-EastCoast-1, PC-EastCoast-2 and PC-EastCoast-3. All 3 PCVMs run on aos-41.
PC-Time-Machine is enabled for PC-EastCoast with Near-Sync RPO, with multiple sites selected as secondary, say AZ-50 and AZ-53.

[IDF Design Documents | Highly Available Prism Central  Deployments]
## Failure Tolerance
By default, Chad can recover all his PCs from OS corruptions, short and long term network failures. This is available by default on all PCs.
PC-Seattle can withstand node failures and cluster failures. There is no solution to a failure of the Seattle AZ/Region.
PC-BayArea can withstand a node, cluster and an AZ failure. There is no solution to a failure of the Bay Area region.
PC-EastCoast can withstand a node, cluster, AZ and Region Failure. Node, Cluster and AZ failure characteristics are similar to PC-Seattle and PC-BayArea. The distinction of a region failure here is that PC-EastCoast manages the various clusters across regions, as long as they are within acceptable latency bounds.

## Design Considerations for Nutanix Services
With MSP, we will have various services hosted as containers. For stateful services, MSP will provide an abstraction of a docker volume which can then be replicated via native Nutanix replication. Once this is available, PC Protection settings for 0-RPO or Near-Sync RPO do the appropriate work to set up Sync or Near-Sync replication for the VGs that back the docker volumes. Recovery flows around the PC also incorporate recovery of these docker volumes. MSP code takes into account the recovered docker volumes when the platform comes up.

Highly consistent backups for specific IDF entities (for PC Backup-Restore) (ENG-287337) IDF sync, as it is implemented today, works in an asynchronous manner. There is no guarantee that the a write performed on the source results in an immediate write on the replica and there is no guarantee that if two writes (A and B) happen then they are synced in order; unless sync-barrier is enabled. For the backup-restore workflow, this asynchronous nature can be a problem for some entities. These entities do not tolerate going back in time during the restore process. This is primarily because they use the PC entity as some sort of a WAL to perform actions across both the PE and PC. A more detailed description of an example of this is here: PC Backup and Restore ( Under the title ‘Reasons why we can’t afford the backup to lag behind actual PC’ ). Let’s call such entities as ‘special’ entities going forward. Other entities are called ‘regular’ entities. Definitions: Source PC: The PC which we’re backing up to the replicas.PC Backup and Restore Replicas: The replica clusters which would hold a backup copy of the entities from the source PC. For now, we’ll assume that these are all PEs (and the PC is able to securely communicate with these PEs). New PC: The new PC that would be deployed in the event of a failure and have all the backed up data restored into it. There are a few approaches to solve this issue. Approach 1: IDF provides an option in the UpdateEntity and DeleteEntity workflows

(Also, once an entity is marked as a highly consistent entity, it is forever a highly consistent entity even if this flag is not set for subsequent updates). 2) Then it does all the timestamp/CAS-version checking as it normally does by comparing against the entity(if it already exists) in the PC’s backend Cassandra store. 3) Then, in a IDF-Federation like workflow, it would start sending the write request (along with the modification to set the master-cluster-uuid and other metadata information saying that this is a backup entity to all the backups. (The entities sent to the replica would be transformed with a changed entity type name indicating that this is a backup entity). 4) IDF in the replicas would accept the entity as long as the ‘db_modified_timestamp’ is higher and the CAS is higher(not strictly monotonically increasing). And just responds yes/no depending on whether the write succeeded or not. 5) If IDF on the the source (PC) gets

Workflow for first completion and bootstrapping existing entities The existing entities already in the PC will make use of the ‘traditional’ IDF-IDF sync to sync the data. In order to facilitate the marking of this completion, we will create a sync barrier entity which will sync along the IDF-IDF sync pipeline. Once this entity reaches all the PEs, we consider the bootstrapping complete. Once that happens, we will mark the respective replicas as valid replicas. We would not honor any sync-barrier guarantees when this is done ( we don’t have to as this is not replication as intended between PE and PC. The sync-barrier flag on the entities will be maintained but the checks won’t be honored during the restore workflow). 2) We’ll add a marker sync-barrier entity which would be written to

[IDF Design Documents | Highly consistent backups for specific IDF entities]
PE and PC. The sync-barrier flag on the entities will be maintained but the checks won’t be honored during the restore workflow). 2) We’ll add a marker sync-barrier entity which would be written to the replica. Once that entity replicates to the new PC, the restore is complete. (For this particular entity, we will honor the sync barrier guarantees). 3) We would need to perform some transformations to the entity similar to what we do for regular entities during backup-restore. A brief explanation on versioning and how it works The key idea are the following: 1) The source of truth is the source (PC) when the source(PC) is functional. The replicas just act like a distributed backup store for the source. 2) The replicas are never ahead of the PC by more than one version. Since we commit the write to the source only after ALL the writes to the replicas succeed. 3) If different replicas are ahead of the PC by different versions of the entity or if they not ahead and on the same version of the entity; they’re all considered valid candidates for the restore workflow. Since each replica can at-most be ahead of the source by only one version, this is similar to the case(in our current IDF workflow) of an update getting committed to disk(Cassandra) but getting returned as a failure. We wouldn’t tell the client that the update succeeded in this case; but after a restart, we would load the updated state from Cassandra. In the restore workflow, the restoration can be likened to the

In the restore workflow, the restoration can be likened to the restart wherein we load an entity which is one version ahead that what we had. If subsequent updates fail, different replicas could end up with different versions of the entity (if the subsequent updates had different data for the entity). In this case as well, it is similar to the scenario mentioned above as each replica’s individual copy of the entity is ahead by at-most one version. Either of those two versions can be chosen during the restoration process. Drawbacks 1) The primary drawback is that this approach expects the functioning of all the replicas for every write. ## 1. Overview:
This document outlines the comprehensive backup process flow designed to ensure data integrity, minimize data loss, and provide efficient recovery options. The backup system is structured to meet specific Recovery Point Objectives (RPO) while ensuring scalability for large datasets. The process involves creating metadata, fetching data from IDF, chunking data, and securely storing it in S3.

## 2.1 AlarmHandler()
Purpose: 
The AlarmHandler() serves as the entry point for the backup process. It continuously monitors system conditions to decide if a backup process should be triggered.
Trigger Conditions: 
The backup is initiated when all the following conditions are met:
There is no active restore configuration.
No ongoing backup is in progress.
For any backup endpoint, the condition current_time - last_backup_time > RPO is true, indicating that the backup frequency requirement has been exceeded.
Outcome: 
When these conditions are satisfied, the process proceeds to StartBackupFromIDF() to initiate the backup process.

## 2.2 StartBackupFromIDF()
Purpose:
 This step initializes the environment for the backup process by creating the required directories and fetching metadata paths.
Tasks:
Create metadata and backup data directories to organize backup files and ensure proper storage hierarchy.
Fetch the Metadata Path Prefix, which acts as a reference point for locating metadata in subsequent steps.

[IDF Design Documents | IDF PCDR S3 Code Walkthrough]
## 2.3 StartTaskForSeedDataBackup()
Purpose: 
This step handles the seeding of initial data from IDF to ensure a reliable starting point for incremental backups.
Tasks:
Fetch PC seed data from IDF, which represents a stable snapshot of critical data.
Write the seed data to a local file for temporary storage before cloud transfer.
Transfer the seed data to all configured S3 endpoints to ensure redundancy and availability.
2.4 StartTaskForDataBackup()
Purpose: 
This phase initiates the backup of data that has been modified or added since the last successful backup.
Tasks:
Fetch the latest database modification timestamps for each shard from IDF to determine which shards require backup.
For each shard, the process triggers PerformLoadEntityTrailForShard() to manage the data extraction and chunking process.

## 2.5 PerformLoadEntityTrailForShard()
Purpose: 
This step reads data in manageable chunks to accommodate large shard sizes and maintain backup efficiency.
Tasks:
Call the LoadEntityTrail RPC for the given shard to retrieve data efficiently.
Create a backup file for each RPC response, ensuring data is stored incrementally to minimize performance impact.
If a shard requires multiple calls due to its size, create separate files using a chunk ID system.
File Naming Convention:
Files are saved using the format <shard_id>_<chunk_id>.
For example, if shard 1 has 20 MB of data (exceeding the 16 MB threshold), two files will be created:
File 1: 1_1 (16 MB)
File 2: 1_2 (4 MB)

[IDF Design Documents | IDF PCDR S3 Code Walkthrough]
## 2.6 CombineBackupChunksAndTransferToS3()
Purpose:
Ensures consolidated storage and smooth transmission of data to cloud storage endpoints.
Tasks:
Create a zip file named <backup_uuid>.zip that combines all the backup chunks generated earlier.
Generate a metadata file that logs essential details about the current backup, ensuring traceability.
Transfer the consolidated backup file and metadata to all configured S3 endpoints, ensuring redundancy and availability.

## 2.7 Backup Completion Check
Purpose: 
Verifies if the backup has been successfully uploaded to all endpoints to ensure data consistency.
Process:
If the backup is successfully transferred to all endpoints, trigger FinishCurrentBackup().
If any endpoint transfer fails, retry the transfer to ensure no data is left unprotected.

## 2.8 UpdateEndpointBackupTimestamp()
Purpose: 
Ensures backup records are properly synchronized for tracking and auditing purposes.
Tasks:
Update the pc_object_store_backup_sync_marker entity in IDF with relevant timestamps:
last_attempted_backup_usecs to reflect the time the last backup was attempted.
sync_completed_till_usecs to mark the point up to which data was successfully synchronized.

[IDF Design Documents | IDF PCDR S3 Code Walkthrough]
## 2.9 FetchAndUpdateBackupMetadataFileFromS3()
Purpose: 
Maintains a rolling metadata log to ensure only relevant backup records are retained.
Tasks:
Fetch the overall metadata file from S3 to get a consolidated view of recent backups.
Identify and remove backup records older than 30 days to optimize storage and adhere to retention policies.
Update the metadata with the details of the most recent backup.
Re-upload the updated metadata file to S3 for future reference.

## 2.10 UpdateObjectStorePCBackupMetadataInIDF()
Purpose: 
Ensures IDF holds the latest metadata details for efficient tracking and recovery.
Tasks:
Update the pc_object_store_backup_sync_marker entity in IDF.
Populate the object_store_backup_metadata attribute with the latest consolidated backup metadata for reference.

## 3. Summary
The backup process is designed to ensure reliable data protection while efficiently managing large datasets. By combining incremental data backup with efficient chunking, compression, and metadata handling, the system provides an effective solution for secure data storage and recovery. Additionally, the 30-day retention policy ensures old data is properly archived without occupying excessive storage space.

## 1. Overview
This document provides a comprehensive design of the restore process from S3 to IDF. The primary objective of this process is to ensure accurate data restoration from backups, maintaining data integrity and consistency.

The restore process involves:
- Identifying the required backup from S3.
- Downloading backup files in chunks.
- Parsing the files to extract data.
- Persisting the data back to IDF.
- Marking the restore process as complete.

## 2.1 AlarmHandler()
Purpose:
The AlarmHandler acts as the trigger point for the restore process. It checks for specific conditions to initiate the restore operation.
Conditions to Trigger:
1. Restore configuration exists.
2. No ongoing restore operation.
3. The system detects a need to restore data.
Action:
If all conditions are satisfied, the AlarmHandler triggers `BeginRestoreFromS3()`.

## 2.2 BeginRestoreFromS3()
Purpose:
This function initiates the restore process by setting up directories and fetching the necessary metadata.
Tasks:
1. Create meta and restore data directories.
2. Fetch Metadata Path Prefix.
3. Identify if a backup UUID is provided. If not, the latest backup must be identified.

## 2.3 ListObjectsFromEndpoint()
Purpose:
If no backup UUID is provided, this function lists all metadata objects available in S3 to identify the latest backup.
Tasks:
1. List all metadata objects.
2. Sort objects by timestamp.
3. Fetch the metadata file for the latest backup.

Limiting the number of entities backed-up
Devendra Singh, Sumit Bhatia
Jan 2021
In-Review
In PCDR, we take the backup of entities created on PC in IDF and store them on PE-IDF so that we can handle the scenarios of PC failure and can restore from one of the PEs which were selected as a backup location.
Recently, while discussing with multiple teams we realized that the number of entities on PC can be too many and many teams do not even have a max limit for their entities. So this can jeopardize PE-IDF’s functioning and lead to higher resource usage on the PE side if the number of entities being backed-up is not limited.
Below mentioned are a couple of approaches that we can use to detect when the number of entities backed-up on the PE crosses the threshold and we can pause the backup whenever this happens so that PE’s proper functioning is not at stake.
Irrespective of whichever approach we choose for this task we should also collect some data like total number entities backed-up (if possible per entity type also) via PulseHd so that we can use that data for further analysis while developing a new feature or simple scale numbers.

[IDF Design Documents | Limit number of entities backed-up]
## Approach 1
In this approach, we add the logic of counting the number of entities backed-up on the replica (PE) side, and once the threshold is reached, the replica will send a feedback/signal to the source for pausing the backup until some cleanup is performed.
The overall approach will look something like this:-
IDF on the replica (PE) side periodically checks the number of entities that have been backed-up from a PC.
If the number calculated in step 1 is more than our defined threshold then IDF will send this info to the uploader on the source side (PC) in response to the next sync request.
Uploader on the source (PC) side can act on the response and update the Backup Config entity to pause the sync or maybe set another flag also so that we know why it was stopped.
On the source (PC), we can have Prism watch on the Backup Config entity and whenever it gets stopped due to threshold exceeded, they can raise the Alert mentioning that backup has been stopped due to too many entities.
If we want to add a threshold per node (number of entities backed up per node) then we will have to get the number of nodes in this PE and enforce limits accordingly.

## Slightly complicated, need to implement a back-pressure / full feedback mechanism from PE to PC.
Once we hit the threshold then special handling is required to allow the deletes to be sent to replica so that cleanup can be done and backup can be re-enabled.

[IDF Design Documents | Limit number of entities backed-up]
## If we have too many entities to start with (while initiating the backup) then also the same issue might arise (this can be circumvented by adding a check for enabling the backup itself).
Difficult to implement per entity_type control in future since entity_types are auto-registered (we'll have to register restore entity_types via config file to enable this or do some translation from the config). Since the entity types are registered dynamically (auto-registered) during backup on the PE side we won't be able to provide per entity type max supported counts in the config file. Hence the concern that for providing per entity type threshold we should be able to provide the per entity type limits in the config file.

[IDF Design Documents | Limit number of entities backed-up]
## Approach 2
In this approach, we add the logic of counting the entities to be backed-up and pause the backup if the threshold is crossed on the source (PC) side itself by some orchestrator (maybe prism or uploader or some other service).
The overall approach will be like this:-
Workflow orchestrator on the source (PC) side makes periodic queries to local IDF and gets the number of entities that need to be backed-up.
If the number of entities calculated in step1 is above the threshold then Orchestrator can update the BackupConfig entity to pause the sync and also set a flag in it indicating why it was paused.
Prism on the source (PC) can watch on this BackupConfig entity and raise an alert when the backup is paused due to the number of entities crossing the threshold. If the Orchestrator is Prism itself then no separate watch is needed, they can do it inline with updating the BackupConfig entity.
If we want to have a per node threshold for backed up entities then the Orchestrator will have to get the number of nodes in each cluster (which are selected as backup location) and divide the total number of entities with node count and enforce the limits. In this case, we will only stop the backup for clusters that cross the threshold and not for all of them.

[IDF Design Documents | Limit number of entities backed-up]
## Pros:-
Common threshold controlled from a single place PC itself. No need for modifying/upgrading the replica.
PC side logic means faster and easier bug fixes and optimisations due to faster PC release cadence.
No special handling is required for enabling the Backup again. Once the threshold is hit and backup is paused, then cleaning up the entities from IDF will automatically enable the backup again (because the number of entities on source will go below the threshold).
No special logic required for handling the case when too many entities while initiating the backup itself. The Orchestrator will check the threshold whenever a new connection gets added and periodically also.
No count queries performed on the replica (PE) IDF so won’t increase the load on it and can be agnostic to the storage model on PE (whether we keep the entities in cache or not) and other such optimizations.
Simple implementation, no coordination needed from the replica (PE) side.
Easier to implement per entity_type control in the future.

[IDF Design Documents | Limit number of entities backed-up]
## CONS:-
It will be harder to implement features like suppress_backup at the entity level. We will have to iterate through all the entities and check if they have that suppress_backup set or not, this just makes the count queries expensive. Hence the term harder to implement features that involve extensive filtering during counting.
The same issue of checking the entity count periodically as mentioned above in Approach 1 as well.
All the above-mentioned approaches try to solve the problem of detecting (when we cross the threshold) and pausing the backup at the IDF level only. Minimal changes will be required from the Prism side to just watch on an entity and raise an alert if needed. Both the above-mentioned approaches are periodic and don't put a hard limit on the entities to be synced, it'll be based on the periodicity.

## Common task items for both the approaches
Introduce a new RPC in IDF to count the number of entities present for multiple entity types in a single RPC.
Changes in Orchestrator to update the Backup Config entity to pause the sync whenever the threshold is reached (by local calculation or when the replica gives this info).
Changes on Prism side to watch (if needed when orchestrator is not same as prism) on Backup Config entity and raise an alert whenever the Backup gets paused due to crossing the threshold.
Apart from the above-mentioned dev side tasks, we will need proper testing for this feature to be ready before V1.

[IDF Design Documents | Limit number of entities backed-up]
## First review with IDF-India team Below-mentioned are some decisions and tweaks in design which were discussed during review with the IDF-India team. We should go with the Approach-2 mentioned above (having the limiting logic on PC side) with some tweaks mentioned below. Instead of InsightsBackupUploader leader doing the query from IDF for entity counts and then updating the BackupConfig entity if the threshold is exceeded, we will move this logic to Prism backup and restore orchestrator service (Adonis). In this way, all the logic for orchestrating the backup and restore and enforcing such limits will reside in a single process so less moving parts and easy to maintain and handle. Decision to be taken from the IDF side whether we want to introduce a new RPC for counting entities of multiple types in a single query or modify the existing GetEntitiesWithMetrics RPC to serve this purpose also. So after the first review new design looks like something this: IDF will expose a new/existing RPC to get the number of entities for multiple entity types in a single query. Periodically, Adonis service will have to get the list of entity types from IDF which are marked to be backed-up. Then issue a count query to IDF for getting the entity count for these entity types and enforce the limits. If the overall backed-up entity count exceeds our defined threshold then Adonis will have to update the BackupConfig entity in IDF to pause the backup and also raise a corresponding Alert for it

[IDF Design Documents | Limit number of entities backed-up]
limits. If the overall backed-up entity count exceeds our defined threshold then Adonis will have to update the BackupConfig entity in IDF to pause the backup and also raise a corresponding Alert for it mentioning that backup has been paused due to this reason. If needed we can also add support in Adonis to remove the pause backup flag once the entity count comes below the threshold.

## Final Design for V1
Adonis / Prism on PC will act as the orchestrator for this workflow.
In V1 IDF’s existing API GetEntitiesWithMetrics can be used for getting the entity count for one type at a time.
In V2, IDF will either enhance the existing API to support counting of multiple entity types in a single RPC or add support for another RPC which handles this use-case. As this is a PC only feature and use-case so we should be able to release and upgrade very easily.

[IDF Design Documents | Limit number of entities backed-up]
## Changes needed from Prism/Adonis in V1
Please refer to Approach 2 mentioned above for the detailed plan. Moreover, list of tasks at higher level is mentioned below
Add a workflow which can get the entity types marked for backup from IDF and also fetch their corresponding entity count from IDF. And apply the defined thresholds in the collected count.
If the threshold exceeds then update the BackupConfig entity in IDF to pause the backup. And also raise an alert for the same mentioning the details.
The above mentioned workflow should be able to run periodically for continuous monitoring and on demand while adding the first backup end-point (to handle the case where the existing number of entities in IDF is above our threshold so we should pause the initial bootstrap sync also).
We also need to write a doc about how to resolve this, so that doc can come in handy when we encounter any oncall on this.
Also add some info to PulseHd regarding the total number of entities backed-up (can be done in V2 also).

## Changes needed from IDF side post V1
Enhance the existing GetEntitiesWithMetrics API to support count for multiple entity types in a single RPC or introduce another API for handling this use-case.

[IDF Design Documents | Limit number of entities backed-up]
## Changes needed from Prism/Adonis side post V1
If we plan to define and handle thresholds (number of entities that can be backed-up) per PE node then make changes in the count accordingly to handle this (we can get the number of nodes in the PE from IDF for the registered clusters).
When IDF provides support for querying count for multiple entity types in single RPC then Prism will have to make corresponding changes on their side as well.

## Summary
We ran multiple experiments in consultation with the CDP team on the basis of which they concluded that the numbers look acceptable from their end. We observed certain discrepancies from our end and performed some more experiments to find out the max number of entities that we could support. We have observed that when IDF is at 80-85 percent memory consumption on the PEs, IDF went into a crash loop when we tried to backup 100k entities per node. We found 50K per node limit to work fine with acceptable latencies for some of the other RPCs. However we recommend a max of 40K per node as the current limit. This is because in the current experiments we don't have any active/real-life workflows like VM Crud, DR, calm etc. on the cluster and we want to accommodate that, also this check would be running once an hour and the count could grow in that hour as well, exceeding the 50K limit, so a conservative limit would be the right way to go.

PC Backup Service Problem Statement Currently, if a PC goes down permanently, the data residing in the PC goes with it. The objective is to provide a scheme through which the data can be backed up to multiple locations. Restoration can happen manually when triggered from the user from one (or or more) of the backup copies to a freshly deployed PC. Data To Be Backed Up Broadly, the following are the data stores in PC: i) IDF config data replicated from PE (entities) ii) IDF config data mastered in PC (entities) iii) IDF stats replicated from PE iv) IDF stats mastered in PC v) Zookeeper config vi) Other components that need to be evaluated ( other DBs like Post-GRES used specifically by some teams, etc). Of these, we can ignore (i) and (iii) right away since re-replication automatically of the same happens when we attach the PEs to the freshly deployed PC. (iv) is something we’re ignoring for now considering the relative non-importance of it but we can think about adding support for this later. So, that leaves us with (ii), (v) and (vi). Two Possible Solutions Considered a) Backup the whole PC This simple approach involves using our VM replication services to backup the whole VM with very low latency (Near- sync or MetroDR). The advantage of this approach is that it provides a consistent snapshot of the entire PC VM capturing all the data. The obvious drawback is the size considering that this would include the stats in IDF which contribute to a significant majority of the data

[IDF Design Documents | PC Backup Service]
