The obvious drawback is the size considering that this would include the stats in IDF which contribute to a significant majority of the data in the PC VM. We had some ideas about selectively backing up certain files or disk paths but this doesn’t seem to be supported by the replication services mentioned above. The other drawback is that when a PC is restored, the state could go back in time. Certain config information in IDF (eg. tasks) do not tolerate going back in time as it stands today. The reason is that these entities are essentially used as a WAL to perform operations across the PC and the set of PEs attached to it. A more detailed description of an example of this is here: https://docs.google.com/document/d/1xTyntvqZ3aMtEOS5d-IllRK5dXOcowOyjO9P8cAN13w/edit#heading=h.lghetkdrc2wo ( Under the title ‘Reasons why we can’t afford the backup to lag behind actual PC’ ) Other considerations to check for include whether MetroDR supports multiple replicas and whether it can be restricted to a selection of virtual disks. b) Backup Individual Stores of Data Separately This involves providing a mechanism to backup individual sets of data independently from the different components ( data sets (ii) , (v) and (vi) mentioned above) The obvious drawback is the lack of consistency between the data stores in the backed up copies when the data needs to be restored. However, this is not a serious one as individual data stores should be

However, this is not a serious one as individual data stores should be silo-ed and not expect consistency across multiple such silo-es. The other question in mind again is the same problem mentioned in the previous approach: dealing with entities which cannot go back in time ever. For such cases, the idea is that these entities should stop assuming that such a guarantee is provided by default and instead make use of a special data store which can act like a replicated WAL. This special WAL will be distributed/replicated with strong consistency guarantees. The level of guarantee and further specifics of what this will be later in this doc. Since the second approach is more efficient in terms of space and also solves the issue with the entities which cannot tolerate going back in time; that’s the approach we’ll be going with. PC Backup and Restore
Devendra Singh, Swagat Borah
Jan 2020
In-progress

## Problem Statement:
In the event of PC unavailability, we lose all the data residing on PC (mainly the data which was generated on PC) so, we have to come up with a possible approach and design for having some kind of backup for PC.
We only have to take the backup of data generated on PC itself, data which was synced from registered PEs can be synced back again on registration.
PC has one main data store (i.e. IDF) and some configurations are stored in Zookeeper. For this reason, we have to take the backup of data residing in these two stores only. First of all, we have to identify the important data from IDF (i.e. the entity types) and zookeeper nodes which need to be backed up for restoring the PC back on a new VM.

## Solution:
After deciding on the entity types for which we have to take backup, we can forward all the creates/updates coming to IDF for these entity types to the backup endpoint also. We only apply the update locally on the primary PC after the backup endpoint was successfully applied. Otherwise, we fail the update. This is because we have to provide the strict guarantee that backup endpoint can not be behind the primary endpoint at any given instance.
If at the time of failure, the backup endpoint was lagging behind the PC then we might face issues related to tasks being incomplete and there will be a risk of the system going into an inconsistent state.

[IDF Design Documents | PC Backup and Restore]
## Reasons why we can’t afford the backup to lag behind actual PC: One of the major issues which could occur if the backup endpoint is lagging behind is related to when tasks are in incomplete phase and we might leave the system in an inconsistent state. One such example is explained below- VM restore workflow Say PC was running a task to migrate a VM from Cluster1 to Cluster2. VM migration task has multiple steps like delete the VM from Cluster1 then create the VM on Cluster2. If the PC failed between a VM migration task and right after the VM delete step from Cluster1 and say backup endpoint is running behind and this task (VM migration) is not yet there on the backup endpoint so when we recover from the failure by getting the data from backup endpoint, the new PC has no idea about the VM migration task which was in progress and even if the customer retries to migrate the VM, it will keep failing because we already deleted the VM from Cluster1 and system is now in an inconsistent state. VM create workflow A Metropolis workflow for a VM create operations creates a local Ergon task object on PC. Metropolis then triggers the VM create operation on the PE and when the VM creation completes on the PE, the associated ergon task entities are marked as complete and are then synced from PE to PC. These synced tasks then trigger a watch on PC which is used to mark the overall PC local ergon task as complete. If a PC crashes after the local PC task moves to completed state and is

[IDF Design Documents | PC Backup and Restore]
then trigger a watch on PC which is used to mark the overall PC local ergon task as complete. If a PC crashes after the local PC task moves to completed state and is restored to an older version where the PC local task is in pending state, then that task will be stuck forever in pending state. It is very difficult even on the client side to detect and recover from such a state. It is far easier if the state of the tasks move forward only; if it starts moving backwards as well, then the state transitions become very complex and would need a lot of custom client side logic to handle. Similarly, there might be other kinds of tasks/workflows that can leave the system in an inconsistent state if the PC is lagging behind connected PEs.

[IDF Design Documents | PC Backup and Restore]
## Approach 1: Using one of the registered PEs as the backup endpoint. We can use one of the registered PEs to the PC as the Backup endpoint, but we should not choose the PE where PC itself is hosted (if we do that then we won’t be able to handle a cluster failure which kind of defeats our purpose). We will use the IDF instance running on the selected PE for storing the backup data coming from PC. Pros:- As we already have PC-PE registration workflow in place so no need for new registration workflow for selecting the backup endpoint. No need for separate life cycle management for the backup endpoint. As the data will be stored in IDF instance so easy to restore. Cons:- We might overload Cassandra and IDF on PE because now they also have to handle the data coming for backup. As Stargate also uses Cassandra on PE so overloading it might have serious consequences. Will have to make non-trivial changes in IDF to not expose the backup data from normal read APIs and also evict it from cache for better memory footprint. For supporting point no. 2 we will have to distinguish between normal data and backup data in IDF on PE. Possible approaches can be: Add an extra flag in all backup entities to distinguish them from normal entities. Convert the entity types itself while storing the backup data (for example the “task” entity type becomes “backup_task”). This approach will enable us to easily evict entities from cache because in IDF evictability of entities is defined at entity type

[IDF Design Documents | PC Backup and Restore]
storing the backup data (for example the “task” entity type becomes “backup_task”). This approach will enable us to easily evict entities from cache because in IDF evictability of entities is defined at entity type level. While restoring the data we will have to remove the extra added flag or do the entity type name conversion (on the basis of which approach we take in above point) so that we can convert the data back to normal entities. Any bugs in backup logic on PE might need PE upgrades. This can be little tricky from the customer’s point of view.

[IDF Design Documents | PC Backup and Restore]
## Approach 2:
Using a separate thin PC instance just for backup.
We can have a separate thin PC instance which will be used as the backup endpoint. This thin PC instance will only run minimal required services only and not all of them. Like we need a transport service (mercury, gateway, etc.), zookeeper, Cassandra and IDF.
In this thin PC, we can still use the optimizations of making the entities evictable so that we don’t consume a high amount of resources on the backup PC.
During the recovery, a new PC will come up and will read the backed-up data from this backup endpoint.
Pros:-
We can separately manage (bug fixes, upgrades, etc.) the backup endpoint and not mess with prod PEs.
Restore will be easy as we don’t have to do any custom conversion of data.
No risks of overloading services in the Production environment.
Cons:-
Separate lifecycle management of this new backup PC.
We will have to design a new workflow for pairing PC with this new backup PC, something similar to PE-PC registration workflow we have today. This will need end to end (UI, UX, backend) changes.

[IDF Design Documents | PC Backup and Restore]
## Approach 3:
Using Active-Passive PC backup mechanism.
In this approach, we will use a separate PC instance for backup purposes. Initially, when everything is running as expected this new PC will act as a backup endpoint and whenever the primary PC goes down this PC can become the primary PC.
When the PC is in backup mode we can only keep the required services up and not all of them. During failover to this backup PC, we can change some configs and bring back all services. Similarly, in backup mode all IDF entities will be in evictable format and during failover we can switch the flag to make those entities normal again.
Pros:-
We can separately manage (bug fixes, upgrades, etc.) the backup endpoint and not mess with prod PEs.
Restore will be really fast and easy as we don’t have to do much, just a restart of IDF with some flag changes and bring back all services up.
No risks of overloading services in the Production environment.
Cons:-
Separate lifecycle management of this new backup PC.
We will have to design a new workflow for pairing PC with this new backup PC, something similar to PE-PC registration workflow we have today. This will need end to end (UI, UX, backend) changes.

## Context
PC resiliency story till date can be found here.
PCDR v2 overall solution design can be found here.

## Motivation
Below mentioned are some of the key missing features in existing IDF-sync based async PCDR solution (aka PCDR v2):-
No support for handling PC corruption and ransomware attacks.
No support for backing-up and restoring of PC metric data. After restore we do resync the metric data present on PEs but it has retention upto 90 days only so we lose all the metric data older than 90 days and PC local metric data. As mentioned by the PCDR team, this feature has been requested by a few big customers like Walmart and Carmax.
Missing support for LCM upgraded services. This is required to make the PC resilient with add-on services like Calm, Flow, etc.
Since in PCDRv2 we utilize PE IDF to backup the PC entities so there is scale limitation of up to 100k entities per PE node.
Integration with third party backup solutions like Hycu, Veeam, etc.
At Least 2 PEs are needed to provide cluster failure protection. This requirement especially in Cluster on AWS project adds the cost to run/maintain extra PE.

[IDF Design Documents | PC Backup]
## Potential Solutions
To overcome these limitations and provide a complete PCDR solution, we are discussing potential solutions for  PCDR v3 and have 2 broad solutions in discussion:-
IDF based async backup and restore to/from S3 compatible storage (can work with cloud as our inhouse object store). Complete design can be found here.
PCVM’s Snapshot based solution. Complete design can be found here.

## Evaluation
In this section we will evaluate both the proposed solution against the missing features discussed in the Motivation section.

PCVM size(RAM, vCPUs, Disk space), trust information, Zk nodes required will be saved in a new backup enabled IDF table on PC at the time of protection setup. Once the PC backup is setup, more replica PEs may be added later on as well. However the max replicas should be limited to 3.

## Zookeeper node and service reconciliation
When the new PC comes up during recovery in cases where services need a trigger to indicate that this is a PC recovery workflow we will create a Zookeeper node before the services are up. The presence of this node at service startup will indicate that its a recovery workflow. The zookeeper node could be /appliance/logical/prism/pcdr/recover.
Once services are up and finish reconciliation, they should then save the fact that reconciliation is complete so that upon subsequent restarts they do not trigger reconciliation.
This node will not be deleted and will remain in Zookeeper. Services, if they wish to, can create a child under this node and persist the fact that they are done with reconciliation.

[IDF Design Documents | PC DR Async Solution design]
## Pulse monitoring
Protection and Recovery workflows will insert the below data into pulse (nusights). This data can be used to monitor the usage of the feature, the steps in the workflow and gauge the time taken by the steps to execute. The entity_type_name for pulse for this feature will be pc_nearsync_idf_dr_stats.

## Single node/Scale out PC
The specs of the PCVM (VM Size, memory, disk, cpus, network) shall be saved in a new table in IDF as mentioned earlier in this document. On a single node PC, we will have a daily scheduled backup of this information at say 2am PTC (configurable) every day. However, on a 3 node PCVM we want this daily task to be run by only one of the 3 PCVMs. We will use Zookeeper write lock for this. The time at which the backup was taken will also be saved in another zookeeper node, say /appliance/logical/prism/pcdr/lastbackuptime. Whichever VM acquires the lock(implemented as distributed lock by zookeeper, the locknode is /appliance/physical/prism/pcdr/locknode) will inspect the lastbackuptime node and if the backuptime is less than one hour from current time, the lock will be released. If not, then take a backup, mark the completion time of the backup in lastbackuptime zookeeper node and then release the lock.

[IDF Design Documents | PC DR Async Solution design]
## Replicas being out of sync with each other
This is possible as the replicas may be on different networks having differing levels of connectivity with the PC. It's possible that one replica is disconnected for several days whereas the other ones are in sync. In case the PC goes down and the user now has to bring up the PC from any of the PE, the user on selecting the outdated PE and entering its credentials, will be able to see the last sync time of the PE with the PC. The user may then decide to either use a different replica PE or continue bringing up the PC with an older config.

## Failure to create PC during recovery
It is possible that the PC creation may not succeed during the recovery process. This could happen due to reasons such as resources(vCPU, memory) not being enough on the PE. The PC DR workflow triggers the PC creation in the same way as a fresh PC creation is triggered from the PE today. Therefore the same errors which happen there could be expected. If the user is unable to create the PC due to resource issues the possible solutions are to deploy the PC on another PE which has sufficient resources or to add resources to the PE.

[IDF Design Documents | PC DR Async Solution design]
## Failure to reach PC from the PE after creation
If the newly created PC endpoint cannot be reached from the PE then the PE will be unable to trigger the restore workflow on the PC. We could have a retry mechanism on the PE to try the PC restore n times over x minutes. Despite that if the PE cannot invoke the recovery API on the PC we should provide a command-line tool or UI for the same.
The tool will prompt the user to enter the replica PE IP and credentials and trigger the recover API on the PC with these inputs.

## Failure of the PC to reach the replica PE
The PC UI is going to show the status of restore.  The same UI should show any errors that occur during the restore. If the PC recovery task gets stuck, the user should be able to use a command-line tool to reset the state on the PC and restart the PC recovery.

## Failure in between when the IDF data restore is in progress
This could happen in many ways such as PC going down or the PE going down or the network going down while the IDF data restore was happening from PE to PC. Check with IDF team if the IDF will automatically continue restore when these conditions are fixed. The Prism orchestrator process should be able to clear old state and enable  restarting the recovery process at the PC from the beginning. This would be part of the recoverPCVM API.
If the recovery does not work for some reason, should we have a way to create a new  fresh PC from the UI?

[IDF Design Documents | PC DR Async Solution design]
## Failure during restoring data to file system or Zookeeper
Data from IDF tables on the PC will be copied to filesystem and Zookeeper during recovery. This step may fail due to factors such as Zk node write failure or disk write failure. This failure is unlikely but possible. We could develop an API that can restore data from IDF into zookeeper and the file system. A command line tool could be provided to invoke this API.

## Failure to clean the state from Zookeeper or IDF
At the end of the recovery process we will clear data from Zookeeper and IDF on the PC and IDF on the PE. If any of these steps fail, we will generate a warning alarm. To recover from the warning we can include option in the command-line tool to clean the IDF and Zk states and invoke the cleanup API on the PE.

[IDF Design Documents | PC DR Async Solution design]
## Old and new PC being up at the same time
Its possible that when the PC is down the user initiates the recovery of the PC and brings up PC’. Now the condition due to which the original PC went down is fixed and the original PC is also started. We have 2 PCs running with same clusterId and having the same PEs registered to them. This can lead to data corruption in the IDF on the PC as well as in the backup copies. It will also lead to PEs being confused as to which PC is the one they are registered to. This problem will exist in the initial version. We plan to fix this by using a solution such as a witness which will keep track of the current master. PCs will consult the witness upon startup to find if it can be the master. If not(meaning there is another master already), then it will terminate itself.

## Backup health
We should periodically query the last sync time of each backup from the pc_backup_config and if the time is greater than 24 hours, we should raise an alert saying that one or more of the replicas are not receiving the PC backup data. Its possible that not even one sync could be successfully completed to the selected PE. The same alert should be raised.

[IDF Design Documents | PC DR Async Solution design]
## Security - Recovery password
At the time of protection we expect the user to provide a recovery password which the user has to remember by committing to memory or saving it somewhere. This password will be used to encrypt the root and ica keys of the PC and then these will be saved into IDF and then transmitted to the backup PEs. At the time of recovery, the user is expected to enter the same password in order to restore the PC. Recovery will NOT be possible without this password as trust cannot be restored.

## Backup of LCM Managed Services Currently there are some services like Calm, Msp which depend on LCM for Life cycle Management. These services can be upgraded independent of AOS or PC releases. For instance, the PC's version is pc.2021.7. Now the calm and Msp binaries version can be 10.1 and it can be upgraded to 10.2 without upgrading PC. This introduces a new problem to solve in PC as we are backing up only PC versions and not the versions of all LCM managed services. So, when the PC is recovered, calm service will run on an older version which is packaged with PC binary. Inorder to solve this problem binaries of each of the LCM managed services needs to be backed up Approach 1 (IDF Based): Store all the LCM managed services binaries chunks in PC IDF which eventually gets backed up to PE IDF through IDF-IDF Backup sync. ## PC DR Mantle Integration Current Encryption Flow (v1): Generate a random string and store it in IDF Generate a new string by concatenating the string stored in IDF and Constant defined in PC DR code. Run it through PBKDF2 algorithm to generate a final Encryption key. This encryption key is used to encrypt all the secrets like the Root key. Current Decryption Flow (v1): Fetch the random string stored in IDF in Backup PE. Concatenate it with a constant defined in PCDR. Run it through PBKDF2 algorithm to generate a final Decryption key. The same key is used to decrypt all the files Proposed Encryption Flow (v2): Generate a random string in adonis by concatenating it with the constant defined in PC DR constants. Run it through PBKDF2 algorithm to generate an encryption key. Store the encryption key in all the backup PEs by making an RPC call from PC adonis. Store the encryption key in PC Mantle as well. This key will be used to encrypt the decrets during 30 min backup. This encryption key stored in PC Mantle is used for all kinds of PC DR secrets and files encryption. Proposed Decryption Flow (v2): When the recovery is initiated the PE on which recovery is initiated will make a call to Backup PE to fetch all the secrets. As a first step on receiving an api call from Recovery PE Backup PE will fetch the encryption key from Mantle. Fetched encryption key is used to decrypt the secrets. The Decrypted secrets are sent back to the Recovery PE which can be further used for PC

PC DR V1 final implementation at IDF/CPDB level Jan 2021 Devendra, Sumit PC DR Roadmap PC DR complete solution In this document, we will discuss the exact implementation level details for PCDR at IDF/CPDB level. As part of the PCDR project, IDF can take a backup of some entity types (specified in config) and store them in IDF running on one or more PEs (selected by the user from Prism UI on PC). When the original PC goes down, the user can login to any PE which was selected as backup for the original PC and trigger the PC recovery from there (recovery is triggered from PE and it will end up deploying a new PC with exact same config). As part of recovery, IDF will sync back all the entities to the new PC which were earlier backed-up from the original PC. After recovery, all the entities which were recovered from the PE will behave as local entities on PC and clients will be able to update/delete and query them similar to how they do for normal local entities. For debugging purposes, all the restored entities on PC will have some metadata info (called backup_info) in them for distinguishing them from locally created entities. For both backup and restore of entities we use the normal IDF-IDF sync pipeline. We have introduced 2 different types of uploader processes, BackupUploader running on PC and RestoreUploader running on PE. BackupUploader is responsible for performing the backup of entities from PC to PE, whereas RestoreUploader is responsible for doing the restore of

[IDF Design Documents | PC DR V1 final implementation]
of uploader processes, BackupUploader running on PC and RestoreUploader running on PE. BackupUploader is responsible for performing the backup of entities from PC to PE, whereas RestoreUploader is responsible for doing the restore of entities from PE to PC.

## Workflow overview
PC is hosted on PE2
PE3 and PE4 are configured as backup locations (backup PE has to be registered to PC in v1)
Backup here is done from IDF(CPDB) running on PC to IDF running on PEs.
For backup, we make use of IDF's native async replication solution.
Consider the scenario where PE2 (hosting the PC) goes down
The user will get an option to restore the PC from the remaining backup(PE3 and PE4) locations.
The one-click option from UI will end up creating and deploying a new PC and recovering it from the selected backup.
On the new PC the same backup locations will be configured automatically.
Restore here is done by the same IDF-IDF async replication.

Devendra, Sumit
Oct 2024
[In-progress]

## Overview
PCBR to PEs overview doc
PCBR to S3 overview doc
IDF’s native backup and recovery of entities is the core engine behind Nutanix’s PCBR (PC backup and restore) offering.
Currently, IDF supports backup and restore of Entities (configurable at entity type level) to/from below mentioned targets:-
To selected list of registered PEs
This is a continuous streaming backup
Can only retain latest data
S3 as well as any S3 compatible object store
Periodic snapshot of PC data backed up to object store
Can retain backups based on retention at bucket level (user configurable)

[IDF Design Documents | PCDR Infinite Scale]
## Namespaces Overview
Complete details about the Namespace feature and its guarantees can be found here.
The Namespace feature in IDF enables users to extend replicated entities to write extra attributes on replicas. In general,  replicated entities (IDF-IDF synced) are read-only on replicas but the Namespace feature provides a middle-ground to extend the replicated entity without need for multi-master writes and both-way replication.
High level guarantees of the Namespace feature:-
The lifecycle of all the Namespaces is attached to the Primary entity itself. On deletion of Primary entity all the namespaces will also get deleted.
Attributes belonging to a single Namespace can be updated in UpdateEntity RPC at a time.
Each Namespace will have its own metadata like cas_value, created timestamp, modified_timestamp etc. Namespace protobuf link
Namespaces created on local entities are neither Replicated nor Backed-up.
Almost all the Query functionalities like grouping, sorting, filtering, etc are supported on Namespace attributes.
Secondary indexing is also supported on Namespace attributes.

[IDF Design Documents | PCDR Infinite Scale]
## Upgrade and Version compatibility
For supporting full functionality of backup and restore of namespaces, we need both PE and PC to be upgraded to software version supporting backup and restore of namespaces (targeted for Iris).
PEs running older software versions will be able to persist the namespaces data coming from newer PCs (running newer software versions) but for PEs to support restore of namespace data we need PEs to be on newer software versions.
If PEs are running older software versions and PC is on the latest software version, existing features of backup and restore will keep working as is without any issues.

## Limitations/Restrictions of Namespace backup
Only the namespaces whose backup is enabled via schema (either config or RPC) will be backed up.
Namespaces created on replicated entities can be backed up using the similar schema changes.
Namespaces created on local entities :-
can only be backed up if backup is enabled at entity type level (if entity itself is configured for backup).
For Namespaces created on replicated entities :-
After recovery, they will only be visible when the original replicated entity syncs back to the recovered PC.
Will not be recovered if somehow a local entity with the same entity_id is present on the recovered PC before restore.
In events of namespace collision, we will always retain local namespace.

[IDF Design Documents | PCDR Infinite Scale]
## New metadata fields addition in Namespaces For supporting backup and recovery of Namespace data we had to add a few extra metadata fields to every Namespace. Below mentioned is the list of newly added metadata fields in Namespace proto  // Optional. Master cluster uuid representing the cluster where this // namespace was created. optional string master_cluster_uuid = 7; // Optional. The timestamp of server modification time (set by database). optional uint64 db_modified_timestamp_usecs = 8; // Optional. Internal field, to be used by database only during backup and // restore of namespaces data. optional uint64 incarnation_id = 9;  MasterClusterUUID Populated only on backup sites by replica InsightsServer. Similar to entities, this field can be used to identify if a namespace is local or replicated/backed-up. This field is added with future scope in mind, when we plan to support replication of namespaces, the same field can be used to identify local vs replicated namespaces. DBModifiedTimestampUsecs Populated on source InsightsServer. Whenever a namespace gets updated, InsightsServer will stamp this field with per shard Oracle timestamp (monotonically increasing timestamp stream kept at per shard level). IncarnationID Used during backup and recovery workflows only. During recovery, InsightsUploader will increment the incarnation_id for all the namespaces being restored. Moreover, currently it does not make sense to support attach-detach workflows for Namespace data

[IDF Design Documents | PCDR Infinite Scale]
Used during backup and recovery workflows only. During recovery, InsightsUploader will increment the incarnation_id for all the namespaces being restored. Moreover, currently it does not make sense to support attach-detach workflows for Namespace data because namespaces can not outlive primary entities.

## Entity transformations for Backup in source InsightsServer
Entities to be backed-up (with or without namespaces) will be transformed by source InsightsServer before forwarding to InsightsUploader. All these backup specific transformations are applied by function InsightsCommonStore::ProcessEntityForBackup
Clear namespaces which are not supposed to be backed-up
Namespaces that doesn’t have backup enabled in schema
Replicated namespaces, namespaces having non-empty master_cluster_uuid
Set entity’s incarnation_id as maximum of all local incarnation_ids, max(incarnation_ids of all local namespaces, entity’s incarnation_id if entity was locally created)
Set entity’s db_modified_timestamp_usecs as maximum of all local db modified timestamps, max(db_modified_timestamp_usecs of all local namespaces, entity’s db_modified_timestamp_usecs if entity was locally created)
For replicated entities
Set field ‘contains_only_namespace_data’ to indicate that we are backing up namespaces created on a replicated entity
Clear ‘attribute_data_map’ and ‘master_cluster_uuid’

[IDF Design Documents | PCDR Infinite Scale]
## Entity transformations for Restore
Increment incarnation_id for the entity during recovery
Increment incarnation_id for the Namespaces to be restored during recovery

## Recovery semantics on new PC
Local backed-up entities (with or without Namespaces) will be restored in normal state on PC and entities will be queryable after recovery.
For Namspace only backup
If the original replicated entity is present on the recovered PC then we will just merge the Namespaces into the existing entity on the PC.
If the original replicated entity is not present during recovery then we will just persist the empty entity having only namespaces data in Cassandra and not load the entity in cache. When the original entity replicates from PEs then we will merge these restored namespaces in that entity.

Based on PRD for FEAT-14057, below mentioned are the high level requirements from IDF side to add this support for PCDR from S3 for on-prem PCVMs.
[ENG-568073] Configurable RPO (specified options right now are 1, 2, 4, 6, 12, 24 hours)

[IDF Design Documents | PCDR On-prem to S3]
## Configurable RPO
In the previous version of PCDR using S3 (for NC2 deployments), we had a fixed RPO interval of 1 hour. Going forward we plan to provide the user with the option of configuring the RPO per endpoint (currently the RPO can be chosen from 1, 2, 4, 6, 12, 24 hours).
Based on the PRD, the RPO will be selected during the PCDR S3 endpoint creation itself and users will have an option to modify the RPO via UI as well.
In both the events (initial endpoint creation or RPO modification), Adonis will add the RPO interval in corresponding PC_Backup_Config entity in IDF.
Since S3 backup uploader process already has watches on PC_Backup_Config entity type so backup uploader will get the value for configured RPO for that endpoint via IDF watches.
Additional task needed in the backup uploader will be to design the scheduler and honor RPO for each configured endpoint.

[IDF Design Documents | PCDR On-prem to S3]
## Design The older design had a default RPO of 1 hr and every 1hr, we used to send the local backup to all the available s3 endpoints. However with the configurable RPO coming in with s3 On-Prem (where RPO can be 1, 2, 4, 6, 12, 24 hrs) this design would not work. Previously we maintained a last_backup_time_usecs variable that contained the backup start time for a successful backup. This time would also remain the same across all endpoints. However now we need to have a separate variable for each endpoint since the RPOs might be different. We plan to keep two timestamps per endpoint(last_backup_attempted_timestamp, last_successful_backup_timestamp). Both the timestamps shall be equal in case backup to the endpoint was successful else the last_backup_attempted_timestamp shall move ahead in case of failures. Both these timestamps should be persisted in IDF and only the last_attempted_backup_timestamp shall be cached in IDF. last_backup_attempted_timestamp as well as last_successful_backup_timestamp will be persisted in IDF in the pc_object_store_backup_sync_marker table. Next backup schedule shall depend on the last_attempted_backup_timestamp. We will need the last_successful_backup_timestamp for displaying it on the UI. Backup Scheduler: Currently we depend only on the last_backup_time_usecs for the next backup (If current_time - last_backup_time_usecs > 1hr then we take backup). However with endpoints with different RPOs we plan to do the following. We can modify this method

[IDF Design Documents | PCDR On-prem to S3]
on the last_backup_time_usecs for the next backup (If current_time - last_backup_time_usecs > 1hr then we take backup). However with endpoints with different RPOs we plan to do the following. We can modify this method GetAllActiveBackupEndpoints such that: Just like before, verify this condition before taking backup to IDF and again before sending to s3 (Because in between someone might delete the endpoint or change the RPO). This scheduler shall run as a part of AlarmHandler (we can keep this frequency as 1 min or 2 min), where we shall check if any endpoint needs backup based on the last_attempted_backup_timestamp or credential reset and schedule backup for them. Avoid frequent IDF backups: We want to avoid taking frequent backups from IDF since that might increase the load on PC IDF. So if any endpoint requests a backup within 30 mins interval (We can keep this gflag configurable) from where the last backup was taken from IDF, we can send the same local backup to that endpoint instead of taking a new one. We can plan to maintain a last_global_backup_timestamp which would be last_global_backup_timestamp = {Last successful backup timestamp for any endpoint} If any endpoint wants to upload data within 30 mins of the last_backup_global_timestamp, it can use the local backup available instead of taking a new one from IDF. However if no local backup is available we will have to take a new backup from IDF. We would not persist the last_global_backup_timestamp anywhere since on

instead of taking a new one from IDF. However if no local backup is available we will have to take a new backup from IDF. We would not persist the last_global_backup_timestamp anywhere since on any s3 uploader restarts the leader may change and it would be better to take a new backup from IDF. This would also help us save taking backup from IDF in case of RPO change for endpoint as well as credential reset.

## S3 Credential Management via Mantle
For PCDR via S3 in NC2 clusters we did not have the requirement to store and manage S3 creds because the access to S3 was provided via IAM rules.
For on-prem clusters, we will have to access S3 over the internet and S3 account will belong to Customer, they will provide us with the needed credentials to access S3 bucket specifically used for PCDR. Hence we need a secure way to handle/store these customer credentials.

[IDF Design Documents | PCDR On-prem to S3]
## Persist Backup Related Errors in IDF
As per the PRD, we have a requirement to log the recovery point failures in the IDF persistent store. To support this requirement we need to have the following things done from IDF side:
In case of backup failures in current snap-to-s3 design, we continuously keep retrying until we reach the time for next scheduled backup. To support the above feature, we shall mark a backup as failure after a fixed number of retries or after a fixed time interval and we shall persist the failure reason in IDF along with the endpoint address, RPO for the endpoint, backup attempted timestamp.
For this we would need to design a new schema (table) in IDF where we would persist all this information related to backup failures.
UI shall query from this table to display all the information related to backup failures.
We even plan to enable backup for this table, so that the user can see backup failure logs post recovery of the PC too.

[IDF Design Documents | PCDR On-prem to S3]
## Consolidated Backup JSON metadata file in s3
We want to maintain a consolidated list of all backups in a JSON file so that we have a list of available backups to restore from in the s3 console. By default we want to maintain a consolidated list of backups for the last 30 days. Changes from s3 uploader side will be as follows:
In case of successful backup, the s3 uploader needs to write the backup_uuid and the backup_timestamp to this consolidated JSON file.
For this we shall perform a GetObject call on this file. In case we get the file in response, we shall edit the JSON in memory by appending the latest backup information and removing any backup information which is 30 days older. We shall then write the JSON to the local disk from where it will be then sent to the s3 console.
In case of first backup, we shall not find any such consolidated JSON file in the GetObject call. In that case we create the JSON file on the local disk with information related to the first backup and then transfer that to the s3 console. We shall perform this step only if we receive a “NoSuchKey” error in the s3 error response. In all other cases we shall retry the GetObjects API call.
The consolidated backup JSON file shall be present at path /pcdr/<pc_cluster_uuid>/idf-data.

## Periodic IDF Backup to S3 July 2022 Devendra, Ritu, Sumit In-progress In this document we discuss the high level details about designing Periodic Backup of certain IDF entity types to S3 and restore procedure for the same. This is a requirement from the Clusters team for Amazon WAR certificate. More details can be found here. As we are not pausing writes to IDF during backup so Consistency guarantees (cross entity referential integrity might not be preserved) for this solution will also be same as PCDRv2 (async IDF based PC backup and restore). Moreover, as we are taking full backup of all IDF entities everytime so these will be full backups and not incremental. Currently, we have a genesis based InsightsDataTransfer(IDT) service responsible for IDF-IDF sync, Arithmos sync and PC backup and restore, we can extend the scope of the same service to include Backup and Restore from S3 as well. IDT has multiple processes under it, InsightsReceiver, InsightsProxy (runs only on PC), InsightsUploader, InsightsBackupUploader (runs only on PC) and InsightsRestoreUploader (runs only on PE). We can add another process in IDT with new uploader mode, running only on PC, named as InsightsS3PCDRUploader to have this responsibility of taking periodic backups from IDF and persist it in S3 (if configured) as well as Restore the IDF data from S3 whenever required. We will keep both Periodic Backup and Restore as the leader only solution in Uploader (if scale testing shows severe issues then we

[IDF Design Documents | Periodic IDF Backup to S3]
as well as Restore the IDF data from S3 whenever required. We will keep both Periodic Backup and Restore as the leader only solution in Uploader (if scale testing shows severe issues then we can reevaluate and scaleout the solution).

## Backing up to S3
As part of this solution we plan to take periodic snapshots from IDF (of all the required entities, having is_backup_required=true in the entity type config) and back it up in a S3 bucket (bucket will be auto provisioned as mentioned in this doc).
Default periodicity for backup will be 1 hour and also it will be configurable by a gflag.

[IDF Design Documents | Periodic IDF Backup to S3]
## Design for Dumping IDF data periodically IDF exposes an RPC “LoadEntityTrail” and it is currently used for Bootstrapping the IDF sync data, we will use the same RPC for taking a complete dump of all the entities per shard (configured to be backedup) from IDF. LoadEntityTrail RPC automatically does the pagination based on number of entities (3000 entities in single RPC) and overall size of the entities (8MB in single RPC) to be returned. We will build a solution using LoadEntityTrail to dump all the entities required to be backed up to s3 (note:- this RPC operates on a per shard basis so we will have to call it for all 128 shards to get all the data). If the uploader crashes in the middle of the Backup process then the new uploader leader will start the whole backup process again. Before taking a backup we will clear out older backup files, if any, present on the local disk. High level steps needed for Backup from IDF Insights uploader running in new mode for taking the S3 backup and restore registers a watch on IDF entity type “pc_backup_config” and watches for registered S3 endpoint to backup data to. When the end-point gets registered (by creating the corresponding IDF entity in pc_backup_config entity type), Uploader will start the periodic job of querying from IDF and persisting in S3. For backup from IDF, Uploader will issue LoadEntityTrail for each shard with missing timestamp range as [0, infinite) (timestamp mentioned here refers to a monotonically increasing,

[IDF Design Documents | Periodic IDF Backup to S3]
of querying from IDF and persisting in S3. For backup from IDF, Uploader will issue LoadEntityTrail for each shard with missing timestamp range as [0, infinite) (timestamp mentioned here refers to a monotonically increasing, called db_modified_timestamp_usecs, maintained per shard by IDF). We might have to do multiple RPC calls to fetch complete data of a given shard because internally LoadEntityTrail has pagination and returns upto 3000 entities or 8MB of data and also provides the time ranges covered by this set of entities, this can be used to make the argument timestamp range for next rpc. We can club responses of multiple batches from IDF to construct a single object in S3 (based on object size we want to store in S3). Instead of streaming Objects directly to S3, we can think of accumulating all the objects on the local file system and for finalizing the backup we can generate a meta-file corresponding to this backup. While persisting data to S3 we will upload the meta-file at the end, hence presence of meta-file for a backup in s3 will act as a marker that the backup is complete (more details about meta-file can be found in below section). Finalizing a backup locally will help us in reducing unneeded write/read/scans on S3 bucket in failure scenarios (like IDF, uploader crashed in middle of backup), if this is not a concern then we can even stream directly to S3. We will also explore compression for data files (if they exceed a certain threshold size limit).

[IDF Design Documents | Periodic IDF Backup to S3]
## Data format and object keys in S3 LoadEntityTrail RPC from IDF will return the data in proto format (with list of entities in it), we can use the same proto to serialize and persist in S3 objects. As mentioned in this doc, MCM will create and provision the buckets to be used for IDF backups in S3 and PCVM will have read/write permissions in those buckets. Adonis will add the S3 endpoint info in “pc_backup_config” entity and we will use the same to read/write from S3. For each backup we will have 2 types of objects in S3, actual data files and a meta file corresponding to each backup. Meta file will be uploaded to S3 at the end (after all the data files for that backup) so that the presence of a meta-file itself acts like a marker that backup is complete and can be used for Restore (we might have some incomplete backups in s3, specially in cases when uploader crashes in middle of uploading the data to s3). Object Key for meta file will look like:- Object Key for actual data files will look like:- Reason for keeping separate prefixes for meta and data files is, during restore we have to figure out the last complete backup and restore from that, there we can easily do a prefix list on meta files and download corresponding data files for the last backup and restore IDF. Meta files will have details like backup time, list of data files in this backup, if needed we can also keep checksum per data file for verification (but checksum calculations might consume high CPU on PCVM)

[IDF Design Documents | Periodic IDF Backup to S3]
will have details like backup time, list of data files in this backup, if needed we can also keep checksum per data file for verification (but checksum calculations might consume high CPU on PCVM) <Decision needed>. After every backup we will also update the corresponding timestamp in an IDF entity for Prism to consume and display on UI and the same timestamp can be used for alerting purposes to let the user know if there is no successful backup from the last few hours.

[IDF Design Documents | Periodic IDF Backup to S3]
## Restore IDF data from S3 Adonis will create an entity in the “pc_restore_config” table in IDF to trigger the restore from S3, this entity will have details for S3 endpoint and bucket to restore from. The Uploader process already has a watch on this entity type and will get to know whenever this entity gets created and will trigger the restore from S3. Initially to figure out the last complete backup to restore from, Uploader will perform a prefix list on S3 objects corresponding to meta files (presence of meta file itself is an indicator that backup is complete). Prefix used for the meta only list is “<base_path>/idf-data/meta/”. The meta file will have the complete list of objects part of this backup, we will download the corresponding objects from S3 and restore the entities data in IDF using the RemoteTransferData RPC (same RPC is used currently in IDF-IDF sync and PCDRv2) (Note:- we will need some changes in RemoteTransferData workflow to allow S3 data without registered cluster checks). As the RemoteTransferData RPC works in an idempotent way so even if Uploader crashes in between the restore process, performing the whole restore process again on new uploader leader will not cause any issues. Before downloading the backup files from S3 we will clear any backup files present on disk, if any, similarly we will remove the files after restore is complete. After restoring all the data in IDF we will update the restore finished info and corresponding timestamp in an IDF

[IDF Design Documents | Periodic IDF Backup to S3]
on disk, if any, similarly we will remove the files after restore is complete. After restoring all the data in IDF we will update the restore finished info and corresponding timestamp in an IDF entity, which can be used by Adonis and Uploader itself (in restart cases) to identify that IDF restore is complete.

## Open questions:-
Confirm with Adonis team that only one of Backup or Restore processes will be in progress at a time otherwise backups might not be full and consistent.
Discussion on Backup retention based on time or count? Should we design the cleanup from the uploader side itself or some other bucket level configs will take care of expiring older objects? If we don’t have any retention requirements and only need it for restore purpose then we can maintain 2-3 backups at most and implement the corresponding cleanup logic.:- Reply:- keep max 3 backups.
Details about S3 connection, is the SDK already present in our toolchain or we have to add it? Can we use existing s3 client created for objects?
Do we need to handle any AuthN for s3 connections?
Is it advisable to rely on timestamps for deciding the backup order? Or should we create a strictly increasing counter?
Do we need to encrypt the data at rest in S3 (does s3 provide bucket level encryption)?? At rest we need it.

[IDF Design Documents | Periodic IDF Backup to S3]
## Cleanup of older and incomplete Backups
Based on discussion currently we only need to maintain max 3 Backups in S3 so we will have to perform cleanup of older (if more than 3) backups and also the partial backups (without having the corresponding meta file). Partial backups might be present due to error scenarios like uploader crashing in the middle of uploading backup to S3.
Uploader will have a periodic job to cleanup partial(without corresponding meta file) backups, periodicity for this process will  be (Number of backups to retain * backup period) so default will be 3 hrs.
After successfully uploading the complete backup to S3, uploader will also remove all the older meta files (if number of backups more than 3) and then the periodic process will take care of deleting the actual data files (since these backups will now become partial as we are deleting their corresponding meta files).

Resolution on Highly Consistent Backups for Specific IDF entities This doc describes the resolution of the proposal discussed in https://docs.google.com/document/d/10HM1uY0VNzN9PqrWfUmK1dgO55eOfH9W67naCPLRPMs/edit?usp=drive_web&ouid=105375376357426482829 . This was taken after meetings with the IDF team, Ergon team, PC team and other stakeholders. The crux of the problem we are trying to solve as identified is entities(tasks) being used as a WAL to track progress of actions outside of the PC (in the PEs). If such entities go back in time to a previous state during backup-restore (this can happen due to the async nature of the backup process), there could potentially be some inconsistencies as described here https://docs.google.com/document/d/1xTyntvqZ3aMtEOS5d-IllRK5dXOcowOyjO9P8cAN13w/edit#heading=h.lghetkdrc2wo The decision reached was not to go ahead with providing this functionality and instead simply choose not to backup task entities. The following are the reasons: We already face this issue when we move PEs from one PC to another If we don’t backup any task entities at all, the situation would be analogous to the case of a PC getting corrupt and us registering all the PEs to a new PC. Whatever method we have for handling this case currently should prevent any inconsistencies happening . This might need some manual intervention on the PC side. And based on the information from the Ergon team, the PE state should be consistent regardless of what happens. PC scale-out

[IDF Design Documents | Resolution on Highly Consistent Entities]
inconsistencies happening . This might need some manual intervention on the PC side. And based on the information from the Ergon team, the PE state should be consistent regardless of what happens. PC scale-out across clusters subsumes this If the user wants to have a complete sync-replication solution - our upcoming efforts to make the PC scale-out across multiple clusters should enable that workflow. This essentially means sync replication across clusters. While it may be desirable to have the highly consistent entities solution as an in-between solution between sync and async replication (meaning we selectively choose a subset of entities to do sync based replication and leave the rest async); it would be difficult to enforce applications to use this only when absolutely necessary. Besides, the latencies involved in the sync-replication of the select few entities would creep up in the overall workflow anyway. Backup Restore without highly consistent entities solves the primary pain point The purpose of the backup-restore solution is identified as a way to provide an off-datacenter backup solution and it does not need to be sync-replication. A major chunk of the work the customer has to do when re-creating a new PC would be taken care of with the backup-restore solution - creating categories, policies, etc. If some of the recently created categories, policies go missing; it’s okay and the customer can just do the additional work of re-creating them. ## Restore without schema Currently in the PC restore workflow we skip entities which are not registered during the time of restore. Since many components are LCM based the version of backed up and initial restore PC for the services can be different. Even for the same versions many clients use dynamic registration. So many entity types will be registered on PC after restore has already been completed. One way to solve this problem is to restore the entities on PC even when schema for them is not available (populate in cassandra not in cache). Following workflow changes will be needed Restore without schema : If entity type on PC is not registered at time of restore, entity should be persisted to cassandra and not populated to cache. Entities in this hidden state won’t have any workflow support for query, watches, indexing, nested fields etc. http://codereview.nutanix.net/D19965 Scan on entity type registration : When entity types are registered range scans should be started asynchronously to populate all entities of the new type from cassandra to cache. See if error needs to be given to the client until data is loaded. Ways to handle client queries while entities are being loaded: Errors to all queries while entities are being loaded : Write Lock on all shards and populate cache for new entity type : This is the same as how we deal with metadata evictability change. Issue with this approach is that it can lead to overall IDF downtime during every dynamic entity type

Errors to clients which query only on the entity type which is loaded from cassandra : Keep a list of entity types pending for load on dynamic registration. Currently we have methods written in the InsightsUploader class for setting and exporting stats related to RPC calls made by the uploader. ENG-219834:Add Tenant Id support to Query layer
Uddhav Mishra, Aiswarya S
April  2019
In Review

## Customer use case:
Ref: https://jira.nutanix.com/browse/ENG-219834
For Xi-MT usecase, we need to make IDF client facing RPCs tenant aware.  Below we document the specifications and design considerations to make the GetEntitiesWithMetrics RPCs tenant aware. In GetEntitiesWithMetrics, we presently have tenant id support via the pseudo attribute ‘_tenant_id_’ . It is an explicit expression given by users and it is a costly operation.  Also it ignores the tenant id given in entity_guid. Since IDF exposes tenant awareness via tenant_id field in entity_guid, query layer should also be able to support tenant awareness using entity_guid list itself.

[IDF Design Documents | Adding tenant id support to query]
## Scope and Design Considerations: If a user specifies tenant_id and entity_type_name but not entity id in queries - it should be treated as a wild card query on entities with matching entity_type_name and tenant_id. There need not be any changes in the rest of the query flow. While populating the GetEntitiesWithMetricsRet, we should also populate tenant_id in entity_guids in raw_results. If no tenant id is specified in at least one of the entity_guids in the RPC, no other entity_guid should have tenant_id specified. Similarly if tenant_id is specified in atleast one of the entity_guids, other entity_guids should also have the same tenant id. This is common for wild card and non wild card queries. This is the expected use case. Supporting multiple tenant ids for limited use cases means changing query internal structures, which will affect query performance. We can revisit this if such a use case arises. If no tenant id or entity_id is specified in any of the entity_guids, the query layer fetches and processes all entity ids of that entity type irrespective of the tenant id. (Present workflow) If entity_id is specified in the entity_guids, and no tenant_id is specified, query layer processes all the entity_ids specified in the Query RPC. (Present workflow) If wrong (tenant_id, entity_id, entity_type) combination is provided in entity_guid, that entity_guid is treated as non-existent and ignored in the rest of the query flow. A similar support has to be added to cpdb_query as

[IDF Design Documents | Adding tenant id support to query]
wrong (tenant_id, entity_id, entity_type) combination is provided in entity_guid, that entity_guid is treated as non-existent and ignored in the rest of the query flow. A similar support has to be added to cpdb_query as well.

[IDF Design Documents | Adding tenant id support to query]
## Use GetEntitiesFromShardsByTenants instead of GetEntitiesFromShards in query layer
Presently query layer uses GetEntitiesFromShards to fetch entity data from store layer. We need to replace these calls with its tenant aware version :- `GetEntitiesFromShardsByTenants`. All references to GetEntitiesFromShards  has to be replaced with GetEntitiesFromShardsByTenants (or a wrapper on top of it) after processing entity_guid_list as required by the new method. We should also make sure the above specifications are followed. The method will create GetEntitiesStructByEtype structure and will further call GetEntitiesFromShards. It checks if provided entity_id_set has entries then tenant ids are inserted in the structure for each entity id. Otherwise it’s treated as wildcard query with tenant id.
Stats only queries
For non wild card queries which fetches only stats data, we may not call GetEntitiesFromShards.
As part of ParseEntityList in query processor for non wild card queries with tenant_id specified, we can use LookUpTenantId to check if the given <entity_type, entity_id, tenant_id> combination exist. If not, it should be treated as a non-existent entity.
Evictable Entity queries.
If the query is a wildcard query with tenant id specified, fill up `query_etype_to_entities_set_` , with the Index Map for pseudo attribute `_tenant_id_` in ParseEntityList and proceed as before.

[IDF Design Documents | Adding tenant id support to query]
## AddTenantIDsToQueryGroupResult
Here, if tenant_id is specified in the query arg entity guid, instead of looking up in store, we can directly  fill up the given tenant id.

Aggregating raw columns from multiple nodes The next steps for query processing is to perform sorting of raw columns, along with offset (to implement cursor) and limit (number of results to return). The query that the coordinator forwards to the individual nodes should be modified so that the offset is set to 0 and the limit is set to offset + limit. This is because final offset specifies the number of elements to skip in the final sorted result, and not individually sorted results. The coordinator pushes the results from individual nodes (shared pointer to NodeGetEntitiesWithMetricsRet) into a vector, that gets processed once all the nodes have responded. Each response is of the following format: group_by_column_value { str_value: "" } raw_results { entity_guid { .. } metric_data_list { name: "node_name" value_list { timestamp_usecs: 1477519721537470 value { str_value: "node-22" } } value_list { timestamp_usecs: 1477519721537470 value { str_value: "node-22" } } } metric_data_list { name: "disk_size_bytes" value_list { .... } } } The raw column values appear in raw_results (above). Since the value could be time series data, there could be multiple values for each raw column. Insights_node_query does some preprocessing to compute a representative value for each metric data (by using the appropriate sort key) and adds the corresponding value to the end of metric data list. Insights query should use the same logic for choosing the representative value. In order to avoid the

We don't expect the clients to send node queries directly to // insights server; node queries originate from the co-ordinator node. Status: Design Approved

## Background
The goal of this project is to come up with a system to process Insights metrics data in the background and keep all aggregated query results pre-computed and stored. This is needed to make the queries faster at runtime.

[IDF Design Documents | Background Aggregation]
## Overview The key design decisions to solve this problem are: 1. The system will be completely user query driven. The goal is NOT to build a generic SQL like query engine. Our system will only optimize on queries which have been registered by the user. 2. User must register new queries for different conditions even if some of them have common select conditions. Our system will NOT have the ability to make different querys’ execution plans re-use computed aggregations of each other. 3. Based on user registered queries, the system will have a periodic alarm handler which will check the query definitions and keep enqueuing them in priority order for execution. 4. Worker threads from a common threadpool will pick up tasks from the queue and execute them. 5. Query computation results will be persisted back into the data store. Since everything is query based, we will use the query name as unique hash to the computation results. 6. When users query for metrics, they should provide the unique query identifier and if rows are found in the db for that query. We will check for the presence of that identifier row key in the registered queries table and if found, we then scan the data table. If not found, we throw an appropriate error. 7. The data table is scanned using the existing get logic except that we filter the fetched rows in the end based on the query_name in the row keys. 8. All query computations are idempotent and we use this fact for retrials in case of process crashes.

## Query registration Any query which needs to be processed by the background aggregator should first be “registered” into the system. A new RPC method called RegisterQuery will be added into the Insights server interface. This RPC will take a query in almost the same form as the current GetEntitiesWithMetricsArg proto in insights_interface.proto. The proposed proto would roughly look like the following: We will use the query.query_name value as the unique identifier for the query. There will be validation in place to ensure it is unique. Query will be validated to be an aggregate query i.e. it should have a group by clause. These queries will be stored in Cassandra in a new column family called “query”. We will store only one version of any registered query. We can provide an “UnregisterQuery” RPC later to remove stale queries and also to add updated queries. Any update entity calls should lead to these tables being re-computed. These intermediate tables can be broken down further into two groups; common tables which can be re-used by all queries, registered or not, and query specific tables which would be used by a particular registered query only. Keeps Insights server process lightweight Will need caches to be duplicated in both the processes. Adds maintenance overhead - new process means more things to monitor. Run it as part of Insights server process but with its own threadpool Entity map caches can be shared by both the systems Also latest query results can be cached leading to faster subsequent searches. No need of inter process RPCs Does not let independent operation and maintenance of background aggregator Currently, the decision uses the second approach. Threadpool & AlarmHandler A periodic AlarmHandler thread will keep checking all query definitions every T interval. The T interval value will be selected to be more towards being fine grained. T will be set as a GFlag with default value of 5 seconds. The aggregation interval is used to by the alarm handler to determine when to schedule the query. No assumptions are made about the data that the query would process. The alarm handler simply schedules the queries based on their next scheduled run time and not based on the data size on which it would run. At each AlarmHandler run, it will calculate its next run time, AHNRT = current_timestamp + T (alarmhandler periodicity). Then for each query, it

If QNRT <= AHNRT, then the query is enqueued into a priority queue with the QNRT as key. The sampling interval is used by scheduler to figure out the range of the data which needs to be aggregated during each run of the query. The handling of query execution jobs is similar to a producer consumer scenario. The alarm handler is the producer which enqueues the queries based on their next run time while the scheduler is the consumer which takes these queries and executes them. The worker thread checks the last successfully sampled timestamp for that query and does the next aggregation from that time onwards till the next aggregation interval. The first time a query is registered, the worker thread initially computes the aggregated data from the query’s calculated start time to the current time at the aggregation interval rate. The first time a query executes, it is bound to take up a much longer time since it would have to aggregate a much larger set of data. To avoid these queries from hogging up all the resources of the thread pool and therefore, starving off the already existing queries, a proposed solution is as follows. Mark all the newly registered queries as ‘heavy queries’ and keep a threshold value (some percentage value) on the number of such queries which would be serviced by the threadpool at any given time. If the threshold value is already reached, then the execution of this query will be skipped for the current aggregation interval. The execution of this query will be retried during its next aggregation interval. For example, if the threshold value is 80% and the threadpool size is 10, then there will never be more than 8 ‘heavy’ queries running simultaneously as part of the background aggregation process. Any other heavy query that is scheduled during this time will be skipped and retried during its next aggregation interval. Cassandra data is the source of truth as far as progression of time is concerned and the latest timestamp written, if any, is taken as the start time for any new computation. This ensures that even after multiple lags or failures, any successful completion of the registered query will update the entire data set till the latest aggregation interval. Start time derivation - the thread will look at the latest value timestamp for the metrics belonging to that query. That timestamp should be the same for all the metrics in a query. The background aggregation is currently a single process system, just like how the Insights server is. It can be changed into a distributed system with background aggregation process running on each node in the cluster. A common task queue will hold the queries to be run and the process will keep picking up the queries from this queue. A master process which will be an alarm handler will figure out the next execution time for each query and populate the job queue accordingly. Master can be assigned through leader election, much like how Arithmos Master works.

## Get metrics flow Get calls for aggregated queries should have the query_name identifier provided in the payload using which, the results for that query will be fetched from Cassandra. The query_name identifier would be present in the FromClause of the Get query. There will be a validation check to ensure that the query_name refers to a valid registered query. The usual get metrics logic will be used here except that in the end, we filter the fetched rows based on the query name in the row key. Get calls reads the aggregated values for the specified entity type, entity id, metric and aggregation function from cassandra and returns the list of those values for the given time period. Get calls can specify an additional where clause over the results of the registered metrics provided it matches the following criteria the where clause refers only to columns present in the grouping clause and/or the select clause. Note that the aggregated value for a given time interval will be representative of the entire interval. Example, If the aggregation interval is one hour then results are stored for intervals, 10:00-11:00, 11:00-12:00 and so on. If query requests for data from 10:30 to 12:30, then internally, the value stored in 10:00-11:00 will be considered as the data point for 10:30, value at 11:00-12:00 will be the data point for 11:30 and for 12:00-12:30, aggregation will happen on the fly and the result will be the data point for 12:30. If the result is not already pre-computed by the background aggregation process and therefore, is not present in cassandra for the get call to read off directly, then the get call computes the result for either the entire time period or for the un-computed time period on the fly. However, such get calls do not write the result back. This ensures that data is mutated only by the background process and prevents any data corruption caused by race conditions. Worst case, two separate threads computes the same data but no complexity or corruption ensues. Get calls will be agnostic of any background aggregation processes; it will use the aggregated data whenever possible, otherwise it will compute the values on the fly like any existing un-optimised query. [IDF Design Documents | CPD - 1542 _ Skip ancestor tree walkup for certain entity types_]
As per IDF query semantics, if there is an attribute that is an entity type name, we consider that as an ancestor relation in the relationship graph. For instance: query { entity_list { entity_type_name: "alert" } .. group_by { group_by_column : “cluster” … } } Here, the client has requested alert entities from IDF, and wants the entities to be grouped on cluster. As per the current query implementation: we traverse the relationship graph. for each alert, we create buckets based on the values of “cluster” (result of relationship walk). Add the entities to the corresponding buckets. Entity & Metric type registration: While updating entities (using UpdateEntity RPC), IDF requires that entity attributes be pre-registered. For instance, while updating VM entities, if the VM “name” is updated, we expect “name” to be pre-registered. If not, we throw an error. However, we relax this constraint if the attribute name is an entity type name. For instance, if a VM has a cluster attribute, we don't throw an error if "cluster" is not registered. This allows the clients to create relationship between entities dynamically. Problem: The requirement from alerts team is that if the query refers to an immediate attribute of an entity in the group-by or filter clause, then IDF could use the value of immediate attribute and need not walk up the relationship graph. Also, walking up the relationship graph for evictable entities using reverse-indexes becomes complicated. One possible solution would

[IDF Design Documents | CPD - 1542 _ Skip ancestor tree walkup for certain entity types_]
then IDF could use the value of immediate attribute and need not walk up the relationship graph. Also, walking up the relationship graph for evictable entities using reverse-indexes becomes complicated. One possible solution would be to change the criteria for ancestor check in the query code to return true only if the attribute is an entity type (cluster, vm etc.) and is one of the metric types associated with the entity (type). But cluster need not be registered as a metric type for alerts (as explained above). Similarly, VM need not be registered as a metric type. Note that alert can be on any type. So as new types come in, we don't have to register the types. Let's say (hypothetically), we manage to register every attribute for entity type (by changing the UpdateEntity function to auto register metric types). And now, we skip ancestor walk if the immediate attribute is the requested group-by or filter column. This would fail other types of queries that have recursive structure as follows: Bar bar-1 { Bar: "bar-2" } Bar bar-2 { Bar: "bar-3" } Bar bar-3 { Bar: "bar-4" } where entity type "Bar" is a recursive structure, and we need to walk multiple levels to get the root. Proposal: 1. Explicitly specify that an entity type won't need ancestor walkup. For instance, alerts in this case. So, IDF query layer won't perform ancestor tree walkup for filtering and grouping for all queries of that entity type. This needs changes to the entity type proto in addition to query changes.

We won’t be able to support cases where some queries need to use ancestor relationships, while others don’t. 2. Specify in the query (QueryGroupBy and LeafExpression proto) that the requested 'column' is an ancestor or not, using a boolean flag: is_ancestor. By default, this is set to true. [IDF Design Documents | CPD-1168 Queries should return empty results for unregistered metric types]
## Problem
Currently, the query checks if the metric type is registered and fails the request if it's not. This may present a problem for a rolling upgrade when some nodes are running new consumer app code that asks for metrics that haven't been registered yet.

## Flag
Per CPD-1114 a new flag field has been added to the Query proto.  (Flags are bitwise or-ed together.)  A flag value, kReturnErrorForUndefinedColumn, can be used to revert the behavior introduced in this patch.

## Undefined column returned in raw results
The old behavior was as follows:
When a query requests a column (which has been registered) from an entity that doesn’t have value(s) for the requested column, the entity name was returned but not metric is returned.  When a query requests a column that has not been registered then an error was returned.
When an entity has an undefined column requested in the select clause (aka raw results), the entity is returned but no value for this entity is in the raw results.  If ALL rows had the same undefined column requested by the select clause then an error was returned.
The new behavior is as follows:
When a query requests a column that has not been registered then no error is returned.  Instead, the entity names are returned with empty metric values.
When no entity has a column requested by the select clause, entities are returned as normal.  The undefined column has no raw results returned.

[IDF Design Documents | CPD-1168 Queries should return empty results for unregistered metric types]
## Undefined column returned in aggregated results
The old behavior was as follows:
If some entities had an undefined column requested in aggregated results then those rows were simply omitted from the aggregated results.  If the column was defined nowhere (aka not registered) then an error was returned.
The new behavior is as follows:
No error is thrown, aggregated result for undefined column is not returned (aka an empty metric data list).

## Undefined column used as a group-by column
Even before this patch, it appears that undefined columns did not cause groupby to fail.  When asked to group by an undefined column, all entities are put into the default group.

## Undefined column used in where clause
Even before this patch, it appears that undefined columns in the where clause did not cause a failure.
If comparison operators such as == and < are used then entities with undefined columns do not match.
If the != operator is used then entities with undefined columns match.
If ==NULL is used then entities with undefined columns match.
If !=NULL is used then entities with undefined columns do not match.
