[IDF Design Documents | CPD-2127_ Raw sort and Limit using flatbuffers]
Implement Raw sort and Limit for Flatbuffer based Queries
Shrivatsan V,  Swagat Borah,  Aiswarya S
July 2018
In Review

## Scope
Flatbuffers based RPCs can offer performance improvement over Protobuf based RPCs, as documented here . For AFS use case, we need to support raw column fetch, sort and limit. The client should be able to issue a query using GetEntitiesWithMetricsFB client function and receive query response in flatbuffer format, which is consistent with the protobuf results, while offering performance improvement over the equivalent protobuf call.

[IDF Design Documents | CPD-2127_ Raw sort and Limit using flatbuffers]
## Design Considerations A FlatBuffer is a binary buffer containing nested objects (structs, tables, vectors,..) organized using offsets so that the data can be traversed in-place just like any pointer-based data structure[1]. It uses tables as opposed to messages in protobufs. A typical implementation can be found here . Every table references a vtable and stores field in a single block of memory. A table has no special rules about field ordering except fields must be properly aligned, and if they are ordered by size the will pack more densely but possibly more complicated to construct and the schema may provide guidelines on the preferred order[2]. For built in fields, the actual data is stored. Whereas, in case of variable length fields like strings, vectors and nested fields, an offset is stored instead of the actual values. This means such fields need to be serialised and stored in the given memory block, before their offsets are inserted into the parent flatbuffer object. This is in contrast with the elastic nature of protobufs, where we can mutate any fields of a message, when and where necessary. This makes it tricky for a case like GetEntitiesWithMetrics RPC, where the ret object is filled up at more than one locations. In the flatbuffer implementation, we have to fill up the individual pieces separately, store them separately and consolidate them at the final location to make the GetEntitesWithMetricsFB ret object, that can be send as response payload of RPC. In

[IDF Design Documents | CPD-2127_ Raw sort and Limit using flatbuffers]
have to fill up the individual pieces separately, store them separately and consolidate them at the final location to make the GetEntitesWithMetricsFB ret object, that can be send as response payload of RPC. In this implementation, we are reusing the existing protobuf based RPCs used in Nutanix. That means we would need corresponding Arg and Ret protobuf objects. For the flatbuffer case, Arg is still the same as existing RPC. Ret can also be the same, only that it won’t be filled up during query execution. Also the RPC functionality will remain the same, except that the response is filled up in response_payload and not the ret object. This means we can reuse the existing protobuf based GetEntitiesWithMetrics RPC, GetEntitiesWithMetricsArg and GetEntitiesWithMetricsRet. Only change will be that, now arg will have a special flag ‘ return_reponse_in_flatbuffer_format’. This flag will be used throughout the existing implementation to decide whether to fill up the protobuf ret or flatbuffer payload fields.

## Present Implementation based on Protobuf
Presently, raw_sort and limit are done at processor side and the co-ordinator side.
Sorting:- At the processor, We have a list of  references to the group results in the node_ret object. The raw results in each group are sorted with the std::sort function. The corresponding compare function compares the raw_sort_column in one entity to another. If a limit is specified, we use the std::partial_sort.  At the co-ordinator side, the results from all nodes are appended and sorted again. Then limit and offset are applied.
PreProcess/PostProcess:- If the sort_column has more than one time-value pairs, we use a representative value instead of the actual value for comparison. This is appended with the actual list values and removed only at co-ordinator
Multiphase Fetch:- In case the query exceeds the limit for single phase fetch(limits on raw_columns, number of entities, offset) , we use multi phase fetch. In multi-phase fetch - First, we fetch the sort column . For the 2nd fetch, we fetch only the entity ids within the given limit/offset constraints.

CPD-2216 - Better way to display query profiles on 2027 page.

## Jira Description
Since the query profiles are added very frequently, it's highly likely that we overrun the circular buffer. So, by the time we click on the profile, it gets deleted. A better way to do this would be to maintain a map of query name -> sliding stats of the query stages - this assumes that the stages for a specific query name is mostly the same. We'll handle cases where this invariant doesn't hold good.
query-1 -> stage1 -> sliding stat of latency
-> stage2 -> sliding stat of latency
One catch would be for cases where the clients are paginating the result – the exact query might be different with respect to (limit, offset) even though the query names are the same.

## 1.    ip:2027/query_stats_count
Displays per entity_type latency/count for GetEntitiesWithMetrics RPC for wildcard and non-wild card queries in a sliding time window of 1hr for 5 hr duration(Gflags)
Displays histogram  of latency across all queries  in a sliding time window of 1hr for 5 hr duration(Gflags)

## 2.  ip:2027/query_statistics (gflag enabled)
Displays per query_name count and latency for GetEntitiesWithMetrics RPC.  Since multiple queries can have same query name, there is a link in query name  to display per entity type count/latency for that particular query name
The stats are displayed in 30 s buckets for total duration of 1.5 minutes.

[IDF Design Documents | CPD-2216 - Better way to display query profiles on 2027 page]

## Improvements proposed upon existing profile data
Presently query_statistics(2) is available only for last 1.5 s  - We can change that to a sliding stat with 1 hr time window and 5 hr duration

entity_type ->sliding avg_latency/count stat (ip:2027/query_latency_stats?query_name=test_query)

CPD-2218 - Getting rid of entities_ map in query layer

## Description
‘entities_’ is a query layer structure  of format  {string -> {string -> Entity}}  stucture  used to store
{entity_type} -> {entity_id -> Entity}
This is a static object and  updated as part of  UpdateEntity calls.
Currently, entities_ map is used only:
To populate the set of child entities for entity tree walkup in case of wild card query and
To get the entity object (iterate over an entity's attribute) for performing wild card comparison expression in case of non indexed where clause evaluation.
We should get rid of entities_ map from the query layer and directly get the required information from the store layer assuming there is no performance impact.

IgnoreCase support in IDF Chitti Ankith Mana Agarwal May 2020 Requirement: There are a lot of cases where the following kind of filters are present in requests which are converted to regex queries in IDF "container_uuids==.*[c|C]2[e|E]95[e|E]9[a|A]\\-591[b|B]\\-47[e|E]1\\-[a|A][e|E][d|D]8\\-1[d|D][f|F]7[b|B]72[c|C]4648; name==.*[c|C][o|O][n|N][t|T][a|A][i|I][n|N][e|E][r|R]\\-[b|B][r|R][e|E][a|A][k|K][d|D][o|O][w|W][n|N]\\-[v|V][g|G]\\-0\\-[c|C][l|L][o|O][n|N][e|E].*" Adding a case insensitive option in comparison expression in the query layer would help simplify such queries and make them more efficient. Proposed solution: Introduce a ‘case pattern’ field in leaf expression of the where clause which would determine if the metric values are to be converted while filtering during query execution. The proto field looks as follows: enum CasePattern { kNotSet = 0; kLowerCase = 1; } optional CasePattern case_pattern = 5 [default = kNotSet]; If case_pattern is set to kLowerCase, then the attribute values of the entity would be converted to a lower case before comparing them with the RHS values present in the where clause. NOTE: Here the client has to take care that whenever the case pattern is set in the lhs, the rhs of the comparison expression should have the value in the desired lower case. Non Indexed attributes: Based on the value of the flag ‘use_indexed_columns_for_where_clause’ either the filter_metric_values_index_ or filter_metric_values_ map would be modified by

[IDF Design Documents | CPD-2583 _ IgnoreCase support in IDF]
of the comparison expression should have the value in the desired lower case. Non Indexed attributes: Based on the value of the flag ‘use_indexed_columns_for_where_clause’ either the filter_metric_values_index_ or filter_metric_values_ map would be modified by converting the string values if desired while fetching the where clause column values. Once the values are populated in the appropriate format, nothing else would be changed. Simply calling either CompareDataValues or EvaluateMetricExpressionFor(List/NonList)Values along with the map values will work. For Indexed Attributes: We fetch the index map from the cache and then evaluate the metric expression based on the values obtained from the map. Since the index map has the form (DataValue -> EntityIdSetPtr), converting the string values to lowercase and then checking the map would be pointless since we would be changing the keys of the map itself. Hence changes have to be made so that while creating and storing the index map itself, the corresponding changes to the values are made. For this a new field is added to the MetricType config proto which specifies whether the inverted index for the metric should be stored in lower case or not. optional bool store_index_in_lower_case = 31 [default = false]; The above flag would only be valid if the IndexType is kString and if the flag is set, while updating the index itself (in InsightsCommonStore::UpdateAttributeIndex), the string value would be converted to a lowercase and

above flag would only be valid if the IndexType is kString and if the flag is set, while updating the index itself (in InsightsCommonStore::UpdateAttributeIndex), the string value would be converted to a lowercase and stored in the MetricIndexInfo object. Due to the above change, if the indexed attribute is specified in the where clause then irrespective of whether the case pattern is specified or not the comparison would be done only with a lowercase string. Hence the same has to be passed in the query. For indexed attributes that don’t have ‘store_index_in_lower_case’ set in the MetricType config, if the case pattern is requested in the where clause for an indexed column, then we throw an kInvalidRequest error because otherwise we would have to scan through all the indexes of the index map, convert them to lower case wherever applicable and then do the comparison which would be very inefficient. Validations: As specified above, setting a case pattern on an indexed attribute which does not have store_index_in_lower_case specified in the metric config would result in an error. rhs of comparison expression cant have a case pattern. Wildcard comparison expression is not valid if case pattern is set. Comparison expression's case_pattern should correspond only to a string or string list in the rhs. Case pattern requires the operator to be kContains or kEQ or kNE or kIN or kAny. Case pattern on ancestor attributes for evictable entity types is not supported. (Should this be the

(Should this be the same for both the types of entities?) If a single leaf expression for a where column does not have the case pattern set, then the conversion wont be done for none of the other expressions containing that column as that would lead to inconsistent results. So either all of the leaf expressions having the same column should have the case pattern set or none of them should. (Should this scenario instead work in reverse or throw an error?) CPD-978 - Using internal MetricDataDB_ format instead of proto in Query layer
Aiswarya S
September 2018
Approved

## Problem Statement
When querying for metric data, we call the store->GetMetricDataFromShards method. Here the metric data is converted from internal memory structure representation MetricDataDB_ to protobuf format MetricDataDB.  This causes a deep copy of metric_data which is again copied to an internal map and then to ret.  Also the memory usage of MetricDataDB is higher than MetricDataDB_ as documented in CPD-708_design_doc.

## Proposed Solution -1
We can use the same in memory data structure MetricDataDB_ (used in store layer) to store the metric data in query layer as well. The processing done on metric_data(MetricDataDB) can be extrapolated to metric_data_obj(MetricDataDB_) with minimal changes to existing code. The detailed design approaches are  discussed below.

## Scope
Here after we refer to an object of MetricDataDB_ as ‘metric_data_obj’ and  an object of  ‘MetricDataDB’ as metric_data.
Presently we copy
metric_data_obj_store(MetricDataDB_) - > metric_data (MetricData) -> bucketized_raw_metrics/unbucketized_raw_metrics map -> ret.
With the usage of MetricDataDB_ ,  this becomes  :-

[IDF Design Documents | Comparison Expressions and lists]
The following issue is related to https://jira.nutanix.com/browse/CPD-1632.

## Problem
I have observed inconsistent behavior for the queries that have a where clause with list values.
Example:
Consider the following query:
Select A from B where A == {“val1”, “val2”}
If there is a single entity, E1(A:”not a list”), then this query does not fail, it returns empty results.
If there are two entities, E1(A:”not a list”) and E2(A:{“val1”, “val2”}), then the query errors out since the types don’t all match.
Other operators such as kIn will fail even with a single mismatched entity.
Flags
Further complicating behavior, when the flag use_indexed_columns_for_where_clause is toggled, this behavior changes.  This is because there are two implementations of the logic for evaluating where clauses, and these two implementations do not have exactly the same behavior.

## Solution?
Queries against entity types without matching types should not fail, rather, they should simply not match.  This is true for all types, including list types.
If types do not match, the kNE operator will/won’t match.
Query behavior with and without the use_indexed_columns_for_where_clause flag should be identical.  To enforce this behavior, tests in insights_node_query.cc should be run twice; once with and once without the flag.
Logic for evaluating comparison expressions should be merged if possible.  Part of the issue stems from two implementations of the same algorithm.
This issue will be resolved in 5.5

## What are derived metrics?
For example, a disk stats collector may only publish read IOPS and write IOPs for each disk, but a client may be interested in a disk's total IOPs (which is the sum of read and write IOPs). The client can define a "total_iops" metric as the sum of "read_iops" and "write_iops", and the DB would automatically compute "total_iops" using the "read_iops" and "write_iops" published by the stats collector.
There are two types of derived metrics that the DB supports:
Rollup metrics: These are metrics that are computed by roll-up aggregation along the entity relationship graph. An example of this is computing cluster "read_iops" by summing "read_iops" of individual disks belonging to the cluster (here we assume that disk “read_iops” are the metric data that collectors publish). These roll-up metrics are the same as results returned by an aggregation query with grouping by entity type.
Per-Entity derived metrics: These are metrics computed by combining metrics of the same entity. For example, computing the "total_iops" of a disk from "read_iops" and "write_iops", as described above.

[IDF Design Documents | Derived metrics design]
## High-level design Registering derived metrics A client can register a derived metric by specifying the metric name, the rule to compute the derived metric, and optionally the frequency at which the metric needs to be computed. If the frequency is not specified, it is taken to be twice the minimum bucketization interval of the metrics used to compute the derived metric. The rule for a rollup metric is the aggregation query that is used to compute the metric. The rule for a per-entity derived metric is an arithmetic expression on the raw metrics used to compute the metric (e.g., "read_iops + write_iops" for the "total_iops" example above). The derived metric type is registered against the group-by entity type for a rollup metric, and against the same entity type as the raw metrics for the per-entity derived metrics. The derived metric is always registered with kLast as the downsampling operator to handle the case when metric data that is ingested out-of-order needs to be recomputed. Derived metric computation There are two choices for computing derived metrics: (i) they can computed inline while the raw metric data is being ingested, or (ii) they can be computed periodically in the background. The advantage of computing derived metrics inline is that the derived metric data are up-to-date, unlike with background computation where the computation of derived metrics can lag the ingested metric data. However, inline computation can slow down the ingest path unlike background

[IDF Design Documents | Derived metrics design]
that the derived metric data are up-to-date, unlike with background computation where the computation of derived metrics can lag the ingested metric data. However, inline computation can slow down the ingest path unlike background computation. On a crash, both these methods can lose some data, and this can cause the derived metric data to be inconsistent with the source metric data. Another option (in addition to the above two options) is to compute derived metrics at query time, when the derived metrics are read. The advantages of this approach are that it does not result in any inconsistency (because there is no data loss) and it saves some storage space because the computed derived metrics are not stored in the DB; however, if the derived metric is repeatedly queried for, this can impose significant additional overhead. We don’t consider the additional storage for derived metric data to be a problem, because we expect that the number of derived metrics is relatively small compared to the raw metrics. Also, we want to avoid the repeated computation of the derived metrics; so, currently we do not consider this option of computing derived metrics at query time. Later, we may use it to fill in data that was lost due to crashes. Another advantage of computing derived metrics at query time (that we may make use of later) is that it allows for easy redefinition of derived metrics -- if derived metrics are computed in the background and stored, then a redefinition will require the

[IDF Design Documents | Derived metrics design]

The design we are currently going with is to compute derived metrics periodically in the background. To make this approach near real-time and efficient, we do the following: On metric data ingestion, we keep track of whether it is a metric that is an input to a derived metric computation. If so, we also keep track of the time ranges for the ingested data -- this helps us handle metric data that is ingested out of order. For per-entity derived metrics, we also keep track of the entity for which the data was ingested. A background alarm is set for an interval that is the GCD of all the derived metric frequencies. When the alarm fires, we compute only the derived metrics that need to be computed. Computing the derived metrics is relatively straightforward: for a roll-up metric, we just execute the aggregation query for the time ranges that it needs to be computed, and for per-entity derived metrics we read the raw metric values for the entities / time ranges that changed and compute the derived metric values. We do not do incremental computation of derived metrics because it is more complicated to implement, especially in the face of metric data that is ingested out of

Design Doc for Cursor Support The use case, overall specification and requirements for cursor support in IDF is mentioned in this document here. https://docs.google.com/document/d/1WbRZhdmFR3F-tJ8R_2ghR_KhGdMN46Voe-UDEsTGcig/edit This document describes the implementation details of this feature. The assumption here is that the cursor queries are for non-group-by queries. Terminology Cursor Query Set - The set of cursor queries sent to IDF to fetch the complete data set in chunks. Primary Cursor Query - The first query of the cursor query set which will mention the query and the associated cursor configuration. Secondary Cursor Queries - The subsequent queries of the Cursor Query Set after the primary query. Application Client - The application that is making use of IDF. Client Side Proto Changes The following fields will be added to the Query proto for the primary query: is_cursor_query -> If the previous field is not going to be created, we will make use of this field to let IDF know that this is a cursor query. v cursor_batch_size -> This tells the batch size for the cursor query response. There will be a global batch size limit set by a gflag on the server and if ‘cursor_batch_size’ is smaller than that, then this batch size will be made use of. Thi is to be set only during the primary cursor query. The response proto for each query in the Cursor query set (both primary and secondary queries) will carry with it the following information: ‘chunks_remaining’ -> The number

A ‘cursor_proto_object’ which carries has the following information: cursor_query_id -> This is the id which is used to correlate secondary cursor queries with the primary cursor query. This is set by the server and sent in the response to the primary query. cursor_query_chunk_number -> This tells the chunk number of the data in the current query response. Each subsequent response would have this incremented. cursor_batch_size -> The batch size being used (based on what the application client requested and the GFlag limits). This wouldn’t change between responses. query -> The query itself. For secondary queries, the client is expected to copy the ‘cursor_proto_object’ delivered in the response of the first primary query. Why we need chunk numbers An alternative approach to cursor objects containing chunk numbers could have been just a boolean field saying ‘is_continuation_of_query’ which implies that this is just a continuation of a primary query and to pick up wherever left off. IDF will first create a cursor_query_id for the new query. Then IDF will check whether the response can be cached. ## Problem
https://jira.nutanix.com/browse/ENG-147192
The following query is broken -- it returns entities that it should not be returning. Correct behavior is to return nothing.
The following conditions must be true for this query to break in the observed way:
“not_a_real_id” should not be a real entity ID.
The entity type should be evictable.
The where clause must be present.  The same query without the where clause has the correct behavior.
There must be at least one entity that is mapped to the same shard as “not_a_real_id”.  This entity must meet the conditions defined in the where clause.

## Root Cause Analysis
When a node receives a query it filters out all entity IDs that are not present on local shards and all entity IDs that do not exist (source).  We didn’t used to filter out non-existent entities for evictable entity types, but that was a bug that led to similar and more severe problems.
At the end of ParseEntityList, queries against non-evictable entity types abort if there are no valid entities and the query is not a wildcard query.  However, for evictable types the code would not abort.  This causes problems at later stages of the query where an empty set of entity IDs is interpreted as a wildcard query.

The max value that the bucket_boundary can support currently is around 4.2G which is very less when compared to TB. Hence, we need to increase this to uint64 so that we could have TBs in the bucket_boundary and UI can leverage the grouping correctly. The existing field will not be deprecated but its use would be discouraged. The existing clients which are using bucket_boundary field and their requirements fit well within the range of uint32 can continue to do so. This is done to avoid changing the client code. Force update timestamps even if all provided attribute values are same
ENG-426795
Lavish Gulati
October 2021

## Summary
This document explains the resolution for providing IDF clients to force update timestamps even if all provided attribute values are the same as what is already present in IDF, which was not supported earlier.

## Resolution Workflow
Before changes
After changes

## Example cases
Each example has an entity with two attributes: cluster and vm. Attribute values remain the same (to what is already present in IDF) for the new update.
Only the timestamp situations vary. Taking two timestamps for the cases: old_t and new_t where old_t < new_t (unless specified).
Specifying the attributes supplied in the update arg in brackets for the new entity.
Adhering to the ideology that a new entity should either go for update or throw an error (if it cannot be updated) if it is different (in form of value or timestamp). If new entity is exactly same as existing entity, there is nothing to update, so we should neither return error nor move forward for updation.

[IDF Design Documents | ENG-426795_ Force update timestamps]
## AttachEntity RPC vs CAS update discrepancy
There is a discrepancy in current behaviour with AttachEntity RPC when compared to CAS update.
CAS update
Let’s say we create an entity at timestamp T.
And we update this entity with the same attribute value but different timestamp_usecs (let’s say T+1)  while incrementing the cas_value.
The modified_timestamp_usecs of the entity as well as timestamp_usecs for the attribute are updated.
AttachEntity RPC
Comparing this to AttachEntity RPC, let’s say we create an entity at timestamp T:
And we update this entity with the same attribute value but different timestamp_usecs (let’s say T+1)  while incrementing the incarnation_id.
The modified_timestamp_usecs of the entity is updated but timestamp_usecs for the attribute is not updated.
RCA
The reason is that we do not have timestamp checks for incarnation_id in MergeEntityHelper and AreEntitiesEqualHelper but we have them for cas value. Putting similar checks for incarnation id as well will resolve this issue.

## Summary for AttachEntity RPC behaviour
force_update: false
force_update: true
Notes
Both entity and attribute timestamps should be updated.

ENG-532113 : Remove pre and post processing of data during query sort
Pradhyumna Komatineni
September 2023

## Motivation:
While making the optimisations for ENG-502546, it is seen that DoPostProcessSortLimit(processor)  and AddRawResultsToResponse(coordinator) were taking a significant amount of time. Adding a special check to sort entity_id and removing, pre and post process resulted in 78% reduction in latency of that phase.
For more details: proxfiling link.

## How does sort work:
To give a context about the sorting logic we have in brief, we support the following sort_keys:
Refer to the following code to see how each of the operations are performed: Code link
So when a sort_key is given:
computing the corresponding value according to the sort_key every time we perform a comparison is expensive
so we iterate over all the entities and all the sort columns and add a representative value to the value_list present in metric_data_list.
performed for both group_by and raw_column sort
also the representative values are sent from processor to coordinator, as we might have to sort the entities again on the coordinator
The representative values are removed on coordinator/processor depending on the type of query before the final response is sent to the client.

## Problem with existing implementation:
Although the above approach of pre-computing the value needed for sort is effective when there is a list of tv pairs and a sort key is given. It adds an overhead for cases where there is a single value present. Hence it’s always an overhead when sort is on attributes.

## Approach:
Skip computing the representative values when the sort is being performed on attributes or when the sort_key is kLast. This will reduce the memory overhead and CPU for DataValue creation.

ENG-555873 Perform raw limit and sort before populating data into response structures Mudit Wadhwa June 2024 In progress Motivation Based on query profiles seen on the scale setup, DoPostProcessUnsorted seems to take approximately 25-42% of time of the fanout request. Presently we are first creating the response structure for all the entities and copying the data to the ret first and then do sorting and limiting. Instead, we can skip creating intermediate response format structures and reduce some unnecessary copy of data. This will involve rearranging the existing logic and performing raw sort and limit using some custom data structures instead of performing it on ret directly. Implementation Details The current workflow looks like: Create group_result_list in ret and copy group by column value and aggregate results to ret if aggregation has to be done at the processor. Populate entity guid in ret by iterating over a set of entities based on groupby_key from entities_groups_ map. Iterate over the innermost group and populate raw results in ret. Perform group sort, raw sort and group/raw limit on the data. This can be changed to: Create group_result_list in ret and copy group by column value and aggregate results to ret if aggregation has to be done at the processor. Perform sorting and limiting across groups on ret. For the groups left after limiting, populate a custom structure for raw sort and limit purpose. The structure would look like: Since we are using heap in step 3,

limiting across groups on ret. For the groups left after limiting, populate a custom structure for raw sort and limit purpose. The structure would look like: Since we are using heap in step 3, raw sorting and limiting would automatically have been done by now. Populate raw_results into ret from the custom struct. Both single phase and multiphase queries are expected to benefit from this change. Will attach benchmark numbers shortly. Rolling Upgrade Since all the changes are in the processing side, there is no rolling upgrade impact. Future Work We can extend it to do multi-phase fetch from the store layer, sort and limit the results and then fetch remaining data from the store for the filtered entities. We already maintain entities_, parents_entities_ and children_entities_ in query layer statically. Every node will have this prebuilt for the shards hosted there. With Evictable entities this will change. 2. We can move that to insights_server object and change InsightsEntityTreeWalkup() to not take full leaf_entities just pass entity ids, this way you can eliminate the GetEntities() call in spotlight search, I have already done this in query layer. 3. You don't need to search for parent entities for each entity, its already available in parent_entities_

[IDF Design Documents | Entity tree walking for spotlight and query]
## Scenarios of entity tree walking
In both spotlight search and query, we often needs to access the relationship tree between entities. The following is a list of the typical scenarios where entity tree traversal is needed:
Scoping the entity in spotlight search by ancestor: We can limit spotlight search to only return entities that are children of certain entities. For example if we are only interested in VMs on node1, we can specify node1 in the  scope_entity_list in the spotlight search arg.
Relevance information by ancestor: This is used to assign different relevance number to matching entities based on their ancestors. The relevance number is used to sort the results of spotlight search. For example, if the client is more interested in VMs in cluster1. He can assign higher relevance number to all VMs in cluster1 using the relevant_ancestor_list field in the spotlight search arg.
Query by or filter by ancestor entity id in query: We may want to queries like “select entities where cluster_id is “foo”  and entity_type = “node”. In this query, the cluster_id is an attribute in the ancestor entities of node entities.
Roll-up groupby queries such as “select sum(disk usage) group by cluster” where the information about cluster has to be obtained from ancestor nodes.

[IDF Design Documents | Entity tree walking for spotlight and query]
## High level design of entity tree walking
I am assuming the we always start the entity tree walking from a set of entities found in the node processor. When a list of entities are given, the node processor iterates the attribute list of each entity to get a set of the guids of the parent entities.  After obtaining the set of the parent guids, it will partition them into sub sets so that all entity guid in the same sub set are owned by the same node in the cluster.  The node processor will then send out a  GetParentEntityGuids node RPC call for each sub set. The response of the GetParentEntityGuids call is a map<child guid, set of parent guids>. The node process will update a local map of the same structure with the response of GetParentEntityGuids call. After that it will put all the newly founded parent guids into a list and partition them according to shard ownership, and then send another round of GetParentEntityGuids calls. This process will repeat until no more unvisited parent guids are returned from the prior round of GetParentEntityGuids calls.
In this approach, we basically retrieve the subtrees that have the initial set of entities as their leaves. The number of iteration is equal to the height of the tree. The number of the RPCs is h*d where h is the tree height and the d is the number of nodes in the cluster.

[IDF Design Documents | Entity tree walking for spotlight and query]
## Code layout and data structure We will use a map <child entity guid, set of direct parent guids>. This map serves two purposes. The first purpose is to record the parent entities that have been visited, therefore we do not get into a loop and avoid querying for the same parent entities multiple times. The second purpose is to record all the edges from a child entity to its direct parents. This map will be returned as the result of tree walk-up procedure. Here is a detailed description of the steps in the tree walking, assuming all the action takes place on the node processor side. Input: A list of leaf entities S that match certain search criteria Initialize map<child entity guid, set of direct parent entity guids> M so that all entity guids in S is inserted as keys in the map and their values are the set of parent guids found in their attribute maps. Produce a set L that contains all the founded parent guids of the leaf entities. Remove in L the parent guids that exist in M as key. If L is not empty, partition L into sub sets according to shard ownership. Send out GetParentEntityGuids(set of entity guids) for each parent guid subset. Merge the response from the GetParentEntityGuids call into M and put all parent guids from the response into a list K. Set L to K and go to step 3. We will put the entity tree walking in a separate class, i.e. InsightsEntityTreeWalking. The class will take a list of leaf entites, and a pointer to InsightsServer object in its constructor. It

[IDF Design Documents | Entity tree walking for spotlight and query]
step 3. We will put the entity tree walking in a separate class, i.e. InsightsEntityTreeWalking. The class will take a list of leaf entites, and a pointer to InsightsServer object in its constructor. It will also have a public method Walk(done_cb) which will walk up the tree and when the walk is done, it will call the done_cb and the map<child entity guid, set of direct parent entity guids> will be a parameter in the call-back. The other parameter of the call-back is a status variable, indicating whether any error is encountered. If the status is not kNoError, then spotlight search or queyr will send kRetry error back to the client.

## Some use case
The InsightsEntityTreeWalking will take care of traversing the entity relationship tree and return the view of subtree that contains the leaf entities and their ancestors in the form of a map<child entity guid, set of direct parent entity guids>.
Let’s look at the four cases mentioned in the beginning of this doc and illustrate how we can make use of this class.

[IDF Design Documents | Entity tree walking for spotlight and query]
## Spotlight search
The initial set of leaf entities are obtained by call to GetEntitiesFromShards or GetEntities. It will filter out the entities according to the constraints like entity types, entity id set etc. The set of leaf entities are provided as input to the InsightsEntityTreeWalking in the constructor. After the walk up is done, a map<child entity guid, list of direct parent guids> is returned as a parameter to the done callback function provided to Walk method. This map is a subtree of the global entity tree graph. The subtree starts with the set of initial entities as leaves and go all the way up to the root.

[IDF Design Documents | Entity tree walking for spotlight and query]
## Spotlight search scope filter Initially all the leaf entities have a default value, kUnknown, about the scoping status. The default value is set before the tree walkup. When the tree walkup is done, we can do a reversed DFS, starting from the leaf entities. Normal DFS starts from the root, in the reversed DFS, it starts from a leaf. (If we reverse the parent child relationship, then it is normal DSF. Actually we can treat it as normal DSF pretending the leaves are the roots.) We will use a stack to track the DFS. The stack element will contain guid of the current entity, and an index in the parent guid set that we are currently exploring. Whenever an element is added to the stack, we will add the guid of it to a map<entity guid, scope_matched> M. When we visit any parent entity guid, we will check whether it matches any scope filter guid. If it does, we set the value of corresponding key in M to true. When we get to a parent guid that matches any scope guid, we will stop exploring from that parent guid and pop the top element from the stack. When we pop the top element from the stack, we check in M to see whether the popped element has scope_matched set to true, if so, update value corresponding to the key of top element in the stack to true. In this way, we are passing down the scope_matched flag from the parent to the child, and eventually to the leaf entities. This is the process of the backtrack. We will continue to pop until the stack is empty. To avoid loop, we will

[IDF Design Documents | Entity tree walking for spotlight and query]
from the parent to the child, and eventually to the leaf entities. This is the process of the backtrack. We will continue to pop until the stack is empty. To avoid loop, we will check whether a parent guid already exists as a key in M. If it already exists, then we will not explore from that parent by pop it from the top of the stack and still copy the scope_matched value of that parent guid in M down to its child following the above mention backtrack process. We will run one reversed DFS on each leaf entity. At the end of the multi-DFS, in M, we should know whether any initial leaf entities are scope matched or not.

## Spotlight search ancestor relevance
The process for ancestor relevance is similar to what we describe in the case of scope filter. We will use a map<entity guid, highest score so far> M. There are two differences however. The first is that when we meet a parent guid that matches some relevance ancestor, we will update M and continue the reversed DFS. The second difference is that when we pop an element from the stack, we will update in M the value corresponding to the key equal to the guid in the current top element in the stack. The new value will be the maximum of the relevance score of the popped element guid and the current relevant score in M for that guid.
Since in spotlight search, we often specify ancestor relevant and  scope ancestor in the same query, we can extend the ancestor relevant DFS to handle ancestor scope as well.

[IDF Design Documents | Entity tree walking for spotlight and query]
## Roll-up groupby
This query basically maintains a map<parent guid, a set of leaf entities>. Given the <child entity guid, set of direct parent entity guids> map, we can do a reversed DFS for each leaf entity, and if we find a parent entity guid that matches the type in the group by clause, we are going to insert that leaf entity to the set of the parent guid in the map. The reversed DFS will travel all the way to the root, as there may be multiple parent entities of a leaf entity that match the type in the group by clause.

## Filter by cluster name
For this case, the query can maintain a boolean flag for each leaf entities. Initially the flag is set to false. During the reversed DFS, if a parent guid that matches the where clause is encountered, we will set the flag of that leaf entity to be true and stop the DSF.  At the end of a DSF, we would know whether the leaf entity from which the DSF is started, is to be included in the result set or not.
We will repeat the reverse DSF for each leaf entity.

[IDF Design Documents | Fix IDF crash while sorting groups on aggregated values]
Sorting group results on aggregated column values could crash the server because of the following DCHECK failure: F0923 03:52:16.666767 162220 insights_query_util.h:152] Check failed: group_result.group_summaries_size() != 0 (0 vs. 0) The problem is as follows: Let's say we have the following 4 columns: Group-by-column value Aggregate value ---------------------------------------------------------- A 20 B 30 C 40 D 50 If the query requests sorting the groups ascendingly on aggregated value, with offset as 2 and limit as 1. The coordinator would rewrite the group limit as: offset = 0, limit = 3. The current logic on the shard processor would clear off the raw results, summary (aggregated) results and total entity count of the groups that fall outside the limit, thus making those groups invalid. The only reason they were sent to the coordinator was for computing the total entity group at the coordinator (group names are not unique). So, in this case, we would invalidate group 'D'. When the coordinator gets the invalid group, and tries to sort the group based on the aggregated value, it would fail because there are no summary results for group 'D'. A simple fix to this problem would be to clear off the invalid groups before sorting them. However this has another problem. Consider a query that was requesting average values of aggregates for a metric (i.e. aggregation operator is kAvg); and the query requests an offset of 2 and limit of 1. Column Sum (Aggregates) Entity count

[IDF Design Documents | Fix IDF crash while sorting groups on aggregated values]
a query that was requesting average values of aggregates for a metric (i.e. aggregation operator is kAvg); and the query requests an offset of 2 and limit of 1. Column Sum (Aggregates) Entity count Count Average (Aggregate) ----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- A 20 2 20 / 2 = 10 B 30 2 30 / 2 = 15 C 40 2 40 / 2 = 20 D 50 10 50 / 10 = 5 To sort the groups based on the average value of the aggregated metrics on the shard processor, we convert the aggregation operator to kSum. The intention was that the coordinator would divide the sum by the total number of entities in that group. We didn't want to compute the average on the node processor. So, we don't consider the entity count and perform sorting and limiting on the shard processor. For the above query, we clear off group 'D' and return 'A', 'B' and 'C' in that order. However, if we take the average values, then perform sorting and limit, the correct response should be 'D', 'A' and 'B'. For short term fix (Obelix), we won't convert the aggregation operator to kSum. That way the values computed will be the same both on the coordinator and shard processor. For long term fix (Obelix.1), we already have a ticket to fix how we perform grouping on aggregation values: https://jira.nutanix.com/browse/CPD-1589.

## Fix Impact of std::string Change With upgrade to gcc 7.3.0, the std::string implementation changed to use deep copy instead of copy-on-write. In IDF we explicitly (and implicitly) relied on the copy-on-write implementation to save memory and CPU (avoid allocations / copying). The change of string implementation caused regression (both in memory and CPU) that we need to understand and fix. The full extent of regression is unknown, but we already know of a few cases where it’s significant. In 5.9 and 5.10 we managed to revert std::string implementation to use copy-on-write, but in master we need to mitigate the regressions to acceptable levels before next release (most likely 5.11). First, we need to measure and understand the regressions, so that we can focus on fixing those that are important. Flatbuffers In IDF
Aiswarya Sreekantan, Nidhi Kadkol, Swagat Borah
Feb 18
In Progress
Table of Contents

## Objective
This documents lists our efforts to understand flatbuffers, its performance in comparison to protobuf and how we can use them in heavy payload RPCs like GetEntitiesWithMetrics, to improve their latency.
Goals for this project are:
Create a flatbuffer equivalent RPC of the GetEntitiesWithMetrics() RPC
This RPC should ideally work on the same IDF server handle, meaning the same IP and port
This RPC should lead to a lower latencies end to end for the client
This RPC should lead to a higher throughput for the client
This RPC should ideally not increase the server side memory usage
Should be easy for the existing clients to migrate to this RPC
Stretch goal : Existing GetEntitiesWithMetrics() RPC should also benefit from using Flatbuffers internally. This can be achieved by switching them completely to flatbuffer equivalents of the node to node RPCs.
Another optimisation is to move the coordinator logic to use flatbuffers for its in-memory structures as well.

## Milestones
To complete the above mentioned goals, the project has been broken down into the following milestones.

[IDF Design Documents | Flatbuffers in IDF]
## Understanding Flatbuffers Protocol Buffers: https://developers.google.com/protocol-buffers/docs/cpptutorial With protocol buffers, you write a .proto description of the data structure you wish to store. From that, the protocol buffer compiler creates a class that implements automatic encoding and parsing of the protocol buffer data with an efficient binary format. The generated class provides getters and setters for the fields that make up a protocol buffer and takes care of the details of reading and writing the protocol buffer as a unit. Importantly, the protocol buffer format supports the idea of extending the format over time in such a way that the code can still read data encoded with the old format. How to check if proto fields are set, and get their values: https://developers.google.com/protocol-buffers/docs/reference/cpp-generated#repeatednumeric Flatbuffers: http://google.github.io/flatbuffers/flatbuffers_guide_tutorial.html Definition - A FlatBuffer is a binary buffer containing nested objects (structs, tables, vectors,..) organized using offsets so that the data can be traversed in-place just like any pointer-based data structure. GetEntitiesWithMetrics RPC with flatbuffers Nidhi Kadkol, Aiswarya S, Swagat Borah April 2018 Work in Progress Introduction In a ‘flatbuffer based RPC’, we send the RPC response as a flatbuffer object ( set as RPC response payload) as opposed to protobuf format(Ret object). A detailed explanation can be found here .We have benchmarked the performance of existing ‘GetMetricTypes RPC against a flatbuffer based GetMetricTypes RPC. The results are very promising. The Client side latency is decreased by almost 3 times, for typical scenarios. (Results - 1) (Results - 2) This makes flatbuffers a promising candidate for performance critical RPCs like GetEntitiesWithMetrics. This doc investigates the design considerations for implementing a flatbuffer based GetEntitiesWithMetrics RPC. Design Considerations A FlatBuffer is a binary buffer containing nested objects (structs, tables, vectors,..) organized using offsets so that the data can be traversed in-place just like any pointer-based data structure[1]. It uses tables as opposed to messages in protobufs. A typical implementation can be found here . Every table references a vtable and stores field in a single block of memory. A table has no special rules about field ordering except fields must be properly aligned, and if they are ordered by size the will pack more densely but possibly more complicated to construct and the schema may provide guidelines on the preferred order[2]. For built in fields, the actual data is stored. Whereas,

[IDF Design Documents | GetEntitiesWithMetrics RPC with flatbuffers]
ordered by size the will pack more densely but possibly more complicated to construct and the schema may provide guidelines on the preferred order[2]. For built in fields, the actual data is stored. Whereas, in case of variable length fields like strings, vectors and nested fields, an offset is stored instead of the actual values. This means such fields need to be serialised and stored in the given memory block, before their offsets are inserted into the parent flatbuffer object. This is in contrast with the elastic nature of protobufs, where we can mutate any fields of a message, when and where necessary. This makes it tricky for a case like GetEntitiesWithMetrics RPC, where the ret object is filled up at more than one locations. In the flatbuffer implementation, we have to fill up the individual pieces separately, store them separately and consolidate them at the final location to make the GetEntitesWithMetricsFB ret object, that can be send as response payload of RPC. Note: Stargate team is actively working on flatbuffers, and they have implemented a wrapper to the flatbuffer object. There they use a single internal structure that stores these individual pieces. This can be used just like a protobuf. At the end we can call a ‘Finish’ function. This constructs the flatbuffer object bottom up and returns the final flatbuffer object. (Ref: https://gerrit.eng.nutanix.com/#/c/125765/ ) They are also working on a message format that can be used as a flatbuffer or protobuf (Ref:

For group-by on continuous values, we need the min and max values on the ‘group-by column’ values from all the nodes before bucketization of the results. For instance, let's say we want to group VM entities into 3 buckets according to their CPU usage. If we have VM entities with CPU usage ranging from 0 - 60% in one node. The bucket range is going to be 0 - 20, 20 - 40, 40 - 60. So, a VM with CPU usage 46% would fall into the last bucket. On the second node, if the CPU usage varies from 50 - 75%, the bucket range would be 50 - 59, 59 - 68, 68 - 77. [IDF Design Documents | Guardrail for preventing IDF from running into OOM when there is a query storm]
Guardrail for preventing IDF from running into OOM when there is a query storm Problem description: In IDF, we schedule a check every 1s to check if we’re close to the memory limit (> 75% of what’s allocated for IDF). This is our ‘memory limit alarm’. If we do, we try to clear up entries from the evictable cache and make it available. We keep trying this until we can’t evict any more entries or until we’ve gone below the memory threshold (75% of what’s allocated for IDF), whichever happens first. After this, we check if we’re exceeding the memory limit (100% of what’s allocated for IDF) and if we do, we crash. This logic helps in the scenario where there is a significant amount of memory used by the evictable cache and where clearing it would result in the memory usage going below the limit. However, if a large number of queries come in at the same time and get processed, the memory used by those queries for processing won’t be in the evictable cache. So, if the memory exceeds the limit due to a storm of heavy queries, we can result in a crash. This has been observed here: https://jira.nutanix.com/browse/ENG-165632?focusedCommentId=1375544&page=com.atlassian.jira.plugin.system.issuetabpanels%3Acomment-tabpanel#comment-1375544 We need a way to guard IDF from crashing when it receives storm of queries within a short period of time. Solution: The solution involves two parts: 1) Throttle incoming high-memory RPCs when there is memory pressure.

[IDF Design Documents | Guardrail for preventing IDF from running into OOM when there is a query storm]
way to guard IDF from crashing when it receives storm of queries within a short period of time. Solution: The solution involves two parts: 1) Throttle incoming high-memory RPCs when there is memory pressure. https://jira.nutanix.com/browse/CPD-2118 In this ticket, we queue up incoming ‘high-memory’ or ‘heavy’ RPCs (upto a certain queue size limit) when there is memory pressure (usage is above 90%). We drain from this queue using the following conditions: a) If there is memory pressure, we drain and process one heavy request if no request is being processed. If some request is already being processed, we don’t drain anything. b) If there is no memory pressure, we try to drain and process two requests from this queue when one request finishes. This exponential draining makes sure that we catch up on waiting requests. The above ticket is already checked-in to master and needs to be cherry-picked for AFS. 2) Prematurely finish ongoing queries if we are hitting memory pressure. Just using part 1 of the solution can result in a scenario where we can still crash even if throttle incoming high-memory requests. Consider the case, where there is a storm of heavy queries coming in: When they arrive at the server, we don’t throttle them as we aren’t hitting the memory limit and send them for processing. Then, all of them start to get processed and result in a spike in memory which exceeds the limit and eventually crash. This is exactly what’s happening here:

[IDF Design Documents | Guardrail for preventing IDF from running into OOM when there is a query storm]
limit and send them for processing. Then, all of them start to get processed and result in a spike in memory which exceeds the limit and eventually crash. This is exactly what’s happening here: https://jira.nutanix.com/browse/ENG-165632?focusedCommentId=1375544&page=com.atlassian.jira.plugin.system.issuetabpanels%3Acomment-tabpanel#comment-1375544 In order to prevent this, we shall do the following: 1) Provide an premature exit in every stage of the query pipeline so that the currently executing queries finish as soon as possible. We will just send the client a retry error when we have to exit in this manner. 2) Before we crash in the memory limit alarm, wait until we’ve actually completed execution of all the currently running queries. We will have a time limit for the amount of time we’re willing to wait for this cause in the alarm before timing out. The unaddressed part of this is other heavy RPCs which can spike memory. As we’ve seen this issue only for queries thus far, we shall focus the fix for just queries. If we hit the same issue due to other heavy RPCs, we can apply the solution for those RPCs as well.

[IDF Design Documents | Handling queries against entities with mismatched types]
## Problem
IDF is currently inconsistent in the way that it handles queries that have metric types different than the metric types of the entities in the database.
Most of the time, incorrect metric types (with respect to the where clause of queries) throws an error. But this is not always the case. For example, when investigating https://jira.nutanix.com/browse/CPD-1632 I found that the handling of mismatched list types varies depending on the state of FLAGS_use_indexed_columns_for_where_clause.  In another circumstance, I found that if all metrics had the wrong time was different than if only some metrics had the wrong type (an error was thrown in the mixed case).  Another example is in https://jira.nutanix.com/browse/ENG-113308 where there are errors for type mismatch for evictable entities.

## Proposed Solution
Queries will not return errors for mismatched types in the where clause.  Instead, the following rules will be used when there is a type mismatch:
==, <, >, <=, >=, kLike, kContains, kIN, and kAny will all fail (i.e. the entity will not match the where clause).
!= and kExists will always match
The behavior of these operators for mismatched types will not depend on evictable status, type (i.e. lists), or other factors.

[IDF Design Documents | Handling queries against entities with mismatched types]
## Alternate Solution
Queries always return an error for mismatched types.  This would require less of a change in current IDF behavior.  However, this seems to run contrary to some previous design decisions such as not enforcing metric types when entities are updated (except when there is an index for evictable entities) and ignoring unregistered metrics that are referenced in a query.

## Problem:
Please refer to the description in https://jira.nutanix.com/browse/ENG-293747 on the requirement of filtering on group_by results.
The problem basically reduces to two issues:
Extra/unwanted results being returned in the response even after filtering since, group_by_column is a list. Clients need to have a better control on the result provided by IDF.

Implement HAVING clause in query group_by which would do filtering based on either group_by column value or aggregate_columns.

Having clause on any column other than group_by_column or aggregate_columns (Invalid Request)

[IDF Design Documents | Having Clause in Query GroupBy]
## Evaluation of HAVING clause on the Processor nodes:
Pros:
Evaluating HAVING clause in the early stage of the query pipeline is more efficient and effective as we will have smaller ret to copy or send to the coordinator.
With increasing scale, this will reduce chances of hitting TCP payload limits since we are going to filter group results before sending them to the coordinator.
Cons:
Only limited queries will be supported. To be specific, only the queries with grouping done on the processor will be supported (discrete grouping queries and multi-phase continuous grouping queries).
HAVING clause on aggregate_columns won’t be possible since the final aggregation of the columns from all the nodes is done on the coordinator.
During rolling upgrades:
The clients will receive inconsistent results (as some nodes may be upgraded  while others are still on older versions). This could be solved by rejecting having clause queries while the upgrade is going on.
The query response could hit TCP payload limits (the group results may be unfiltered on some nodes). For this, the clients might want to wait for the upgrade to finish before executing HAVING clause queries.

[IDF Design Documents | Having Clause in Query GroupBy]
## Evaluation of HAVING clause on the Coordinator:
Pros:
Support for all types of queries no matter whether grouping is done on coordinator or processor nodes.
Can be further extended to aggregate_columns too in future without much hassle or code change.
Rolling upgrades won’t cause any issues since either the HAVING clause evaluation will be done completely or the query will be rejected depending on the version of the coordinator.
Cons:
HAVING clause will be evaluated at a very later stage of query pipeline i.e. after all the node results are collated. This will lead us to copying many results which might later be discarded after applying filter.
The node responses may hit TCP payload limit while sending the result to the coordinator.

## Phases of Implementation:
Dividing the work in the following phases:

## Phase - 1: HAVING clause in single dimensional grouping and only on group_by_column
If grouping is being done on the processor, we can implement HAVING on the processor itself. Else, on the coordinator.

## Phase - 2: HAVING clause in single dimensional grouping, on group_by_column as well as aggregate_columns
The evaluation has to be done on the coordinator after the responses are collated.

## Phase - 3: HAVING clause in multi-dimensional grouping queries, only on group_by_column
The evaluation can be done either on coordinator or processor.

[IDF Design Documents | Having Clause in Query GroupBy]
## Phase - 4: HAVING clause in multi-dimensional grouping, on group_by_column as well as aggregate_columns
The evaluation has to be done on the coordinator after the responses are collated.
For the first phase, we are planning to evaluate HAVING clause on the coordinator (after the node responses are collated) as it is more intuitive and would ease up our task for future phases when we add support for aggregate_columns as well. The HAVING clause will only be supported on group by column and single dimensional grouping queries for now.
Considering the clients’ use case (DR), filtering on coordinator makes more sense as the client is hitting TCP payload limits in their upgrade path (assuming that node results won’t hit TCP limits).

[IDF Design Documents | Having Clause in Query GroupBy]
## Update:
As per offline discussion with Artem and Brajesh’s suggestion, going with the approach of evaluating HAVING clause on the processor nodes itself.
Restrictions on HAVING clause queries:
HAVING clause is not supported for multi-dimensional grouping queries.
HAVING clause will only be supported on group_by_column
HAVING clause will only be supported for queries with grouping done on processor nodes. For queries which require grouping to be done on coordinator will be rejected if they have HAVING clause. This will cover most of the grouping queries that come to IDF.  In short, the following queries will be supported:
All discrete grouping queries
Continuous grouping queries with user defined buckets and FLAGS_insights_evaluate_user_defined_grouping_at_processor set to true.
Multi phase continuous grouping queries without user defined buckets.
HAVING clause evaluation can only be done if RHS is numeric type compatible or of the same data type as that of group_by_column_value.
HAVING clause queries will be rejected when rolling upgrade is going on from an unsupported to supported version. No issues in HAVING clause queries in case of rolling upgrade from supported to supported version.

Phase - 3: HAVING clause in multi-dimensional grouping queries, only on group_by_column

## Summary
This document explains the handling of empty attribute lists and captures the current behaviour from IDF for different query functionalities in presence of entities with empty attribute lists.

## How are we handling empty attribute lists?
For indexed attributes, entities with empty attribute lists are indexed by their respective empty data type attribute list. For example, the index key for entities with empty str list would be str_list { } and empty int list would be int_list { } and so on..
For group by query, entities with empty attribute lists are being assigned to the default group (“”).
For kContains operator, return false if lhs is empty list attribute.

entities with empty attribute lists are assigned to the default group (without kGroupByListValues flag set).
having_clause queries with kGroupByListValues set.

IDF Query Scaleout Design

## 1 Introduction
IDF Query offers a rich SQL-like interface capable of performing sophisticated queries on Entity Relationship Graph Database. Query follows a sequential processing pipeline which consists of broadly the following stages:
FROM
WHERE
SELECT

## 1.1 FROM
FROM clause suggests which entity type to operate on and specifically which entity ids to operate on or it can be wildcarded.

## 1.2 WHERE
WHERE clause is the filter clause evaluation stage which filters the entity ids to operate on.

## 1.3 SELECT
SELECT clause involves selecting the columns which can involve the following processing stages:
Groupby(Discrete, Continuous)
Group Sort, Offset and Limit
Aggregation
Raw Columns
Raw Columns Sort, Offset and Limit
Ancestor Rollup
Downsampling

## 1.4 Workflow
FROM and WHERE stages are basically `entity selection` phases which selects the exact entities to operate on, upon which SELECT processing stages are done to return the results.

[IDF Design Documents | IDF Query Scaleout Design]
## 2 Design
IDF Scaleout maps each entity to a shard and each shard is mapped to a node, in short each entity is mapped to a node. All associated data with the entity such as attributes and metrics are also stored along with entity in the same node.
Query processing pipeline is Associative by nature. Associative means an operation performed on a set of entities yields the same result irrespective of how they are grouped and the operation performed on them or in what order.
Example: Suppose we have query which operates on entity ids e1, e2, e3, e4, e5, e6 with WHERE clause and SELECT clauses. All the below are equivalent.
WHERE(e1, e2, e3, e4, e5, e6)
WHERE(e1, e2) + WHERE(e3, e4) + WHERE(e5, e6)
WHERE(e1, e6) + WHERE(e2, e5) + WHERE(e3, e4)
WHERE(e1, e2, e3) + WHERE(e4, e5, e6)

[IDF Design Documents | IDF Query Scaleout Design]
## 2.1 Common Case Workflow Query processing pipeline being Associative fits well with the IDF Scaleout sharding model. When a query is received at a local node(coordinator), first the entity guids are parsed and mapped to shards and the nodes which own them. Each processor node processes the entity ids it owns, process the select stages ie. Groupby, aggregation, raw columns and returns the results to coordinator node. The coordinator node collates the results, returns the results. The following will be the common case workflow when query comes to a coordinator node, the relationship graph scenarios are covered in the next section. Coordinator Node Processing Parse the query proto for errors Parse the entity guid list Map the entities to respective shards, if wildcard then map to all nodes Map the shards to respective nodes Prepend the shard -> node mapping to the query Send the query to shard owner nodes entity -> shard -> node Shard Owner Node Processing If entity ids are present, get the entities If wildcard then get all entities present for that entity type Parse the where clause Get the latest values for where clause fields Filter entities by where clause Get the time range(start time, end time) values for metrics Discrete Groupby Create groups by groupby field Continuous Groupby Create one group, return all raw results in it, as bucket boundary in each node could be different compared to when all results are present Aggregate if needed by aggregate op kMin: compute the

[IDF Design Documents | IDF Query Scaleout Design]
Create one group, return all raw results in it, as bucket boundary in each node could be different compared to when all results are present Aggregate if needed by aggregate op kMin: compute the minimum kMax: compute the maximum kSum: compute the sum kAvg: compute the sum, store the no of entries kCount: compute the no of entries Collect Raw Columns Sort Raw Columns if needed, merge sort can be done in coordinator Raw Column offset, limit is not done, its done in coordinator node after merging Sort Groups, groups merge sort can be done in coordinator Group offset, limit is not done, its done in coordinator node after merging Wait until all results are returned If Discrete Groupby, sort the groups If Discrete Groupby have offset and limit, extract the necessary groups Aggregate while merging using aggregate op If kAvg, merge using kSum and calculate using total no of entries Merge Raw Columns, if sorted then merge sort If Raw Columns have offset and limit, extract the result If Continuous Groupby, bucketize by bucket boundary if present Aggregate if needed by aggregate op kMin: compute the minimum kMax: compute the maximum kSum: compute the sum kAvg: compute the kAvg kCount: compute the no of entries Collect Raw Columns Sort Raw Columns if needed Compute Raw Column offset and limit If Continuous Groupby, sort the groups If Continuous Groupby, calculate offset and limit Return the query results

[IDF Design Documents | IDF Query Scaleout Design]
## 2.2 RelationShip Graph
IDF supports relationship graph queries. Entities could be connected together by relationship graph which could be queried by ancestor field. Ancestor field can be present in:
Where Clause
Groupby
Raw Column
Example: A common use case is below which could be queried to filter all VMs in a cluster or datacenter or groupby all VMs by cluster or datacenter.
VM -> Node -> Cluster -> Datacenter
The following are some design approaches to implement relationship graph.

## 2.2.1 No Caching
Here from leaf when you are traversing the tree up or rolling up we encounter a parent node, we send a special RPC to the node which owns that entity, if the entity has a parent node the node traverses up the tree and continues the RPC until we reach the ancestor we are interested in and returns to the originating node. The complexity of this approach is O(n) where n is the depth from leaf to the ancestor field.
Pros
Simple if first cut doesn’t have much depth
Cons
Can blow up into N x D calls where N is the no of entities and D is the Depth from leaf to the ancestor field

[IDF Design Documents | IDF Query Scaleout Design]
## 2.2.2 Cache Entire Tree
Build and maintain a entire relationship tree in every node. All parent updates are broadcasted to all nodes, updates on parent nodes are infrequent.
Pros
Simple
Cons
Maintaining consistency of the relationship tree, could have race conditions where stale data might be used.
The size of the tree scales with the total no of the entities in the PC cluster. For instance, if we have 5m entities in a 32 node PC cluster then the relationship tree of 5m entities which go upto 2x-4x no of entities has to be stored in each node. The entire entity is not stored just the entity id which could be 36 bytes worst case(uuids). Some optimizations to reduce the 2x-4x no of entities can be done by maintaining shared pointers, interning such that we don’t duplicate the parent and child nodes.
Challenges, if a node just got added or restarted, how does it build its tree upto date ? It has to query all the nodes and rebuild its tree.
Broadcast updates has to ACK from every node to maintain consistency guarantees. This could be tricky if there is network partitioning temporarily, how does it become consistent when network partitioning resolves. One way we could return kRetry to the client’s Update request since we couldn’t update all the nodes. Another way is if the partitioned node detects its Zookeeper was disconnected it rebuilds all over aga

[IDF Design Documents | IDF Query Scaleout Design]
## 2.2.3 Cache Partial Tree
Build and maintain a leaf to root path alone, not the entire tree.All parent updates are broadcasted to all nodes, updates on parent nodes are infrequent.
Pros
Simple
Less space, size doesn’t scale with total no of entities in the PC cluster.
Cons
Complexity in maintaining this could be same as caching the entire tree.
Challenges, if a node just got added or restarted, how does it build its tree upto date ? It has to query all the nodes and rebuild its tree.
Broadcast updates has to ACK from every node to maintain consistency guarantees. This could be tricky if there is network partitioning temporarily, how does it become consistent when network partitioning resolves. One way we could return kRetry to the client’s Update request since we couldn’t update all the nodes. Another way is if the partitioned node detects its Zookeeper was disconnected it rebuilds all over again.

## 2.2.4 Cache Subtree
In this approach we shard a root and its children together. For example a cluster and its children nodes, leaf VMs together. This is an approach we won’t go with for the following reasons:
The size of the subtree could be large causing overloading and imbalance between nodes
The approach may not work seamless across PE and PC, would require different design in PE and PC. For instance in PC there could be multiple clusters but in PE its all one cluster hence require a different way to shard.

[IDF Design Documents | IDF Query Scaleout Design]
## 2.2.5 Design
In first cut we should either go with No Caching or Caching Entire Tree because of its simplicity. We could evaluate the difficulty of both the approaches in case of complexity, we could go with the easier approach. One other midway approach to simplify Caching Entire Tree could be to keep the tree only in leader but the issues of network partitioning still remains at large.

## 2.2.5.1 No Caching
We will need to implement an internal node RPC which given an entity id,  if it has parent nodes, will recursively call the RPC for each parent node until there are no parent nodes(namely the root node is reached) or the parent node asked for is reached, collect the results and return to the calling node. The complexity of this N x P x D where N is no of entities, P is average no of parent nodes and D is the depth of the tree.

## 2.2.5.2 Cache Entire Tree
We will need a bootstrap logic when a node is added or IDF restarts to rebuild the relationship tree. In addition we will need a logic at a node level to know its fallen behind namely it has stale data and needs to catchup, this could be bootstrap logic to simplify.

[IDF Design Documents | IDF Query Scaleout Design]
## 2.2.5.2.1 Bootstrap
We will need to do GetEntities() and rebuild the relationship tree. In the scaled case this could be large amount of data, we could iterate for every entity type and do GetEntities() which would be manageable amount of data. There is risk of not having consistent data while this is happening that needs to be worked out, namely the parent entities are getting updated.

## 2.2.5.2.2 Broadcast Updates
Each UpdateEntity() will be broadcast to all nodes from HealthMonitor, unless they are ACKed we will return kRetry to the clients.The receiving nodes will process and maintain in memory relationship tree similar to current solution.

[IDF Design Documents | IDF Query Scaleout Design]

One downside of this when we cherry pick fixes from master to say branches 4.7.x, it won’t go through. For this reason we can keep it as is, make changes in Execute() and ExecuteInternal(). [IDF Design Documents | IDF Query Support for Multidimensional Grouping]
IDF Query Support for Multidimensional Grouping

## 1 Introduction
IDF Query currently supports groupby on a single column ie. single dimensional groupby. When grouping is enabled, based in the type of groupby discrete or continuous, the entities are bucketed into groups, the requested raw columns are populated, aggregation columns are calculated and added as group summaries. Additional operations such as raw sort and limit can be performed on the dataset inside each group. Overall group sort can be performed on specific column and limiting additionally done.
Example:
Grouping on memory and asking for raw column memory_usage would yield following results:
For more detailed examples and behavior of single dimensional groupby please refer to the Appendix.

## 2 Problem
Sometimes we have a need to do groupby on multiple fields. For instance we might want to know per cluster per severity per impact type how many alerts are there ? Another example, a user would want to find out for VMs per memory config, per vcpu count per memory usage what are the vm names ? It could be extrapolated per cluster, per VM per memory config, per vcpu per memory usage what are the vm names. This request translates to groupby on:
memory
num_vcpus
memory_usage

[IDF Design Documents | IDF Query Support for Multidimensional Grouping]
## 3.1 Scope The request is presented in a nested format and results are also returned in a nested format. Each table is nested inside one another. The number of nesting levels is equal to the number of levels of multidimensional groupby specified. Request format is defined as follows(Please refer to examples below and Appendix) Innermost Groupby group_by_column group_by_column_type num_buckets bucket_boundary aggregate_columns group_sort_order group_limit raw columns raw Sort raw Limit down_sampling_interval_secs Store_ds_interval Remaining Groupby group_by_column group_by_column_type num_buckets bucket_boundary aggregate_columns group_sort_order group_limit Response format is defined as follows(Please refer to examples below and Appendix) Innermost Group Result group_by_column group summaries raw results total entity count Remaining Groupby group_by_column group summaries total entity count A single grouping type is enforced at all levels namely all levels are discrete or continuous or ancestor. If there is a need to support mixed grouping type we can revisit this.). This design also aligns with requirements for Ancestor joins mentioned in references. Multidimensional Groupby: The semantics of the results are as follows. All the entities and raw results enclosed under a certain groupby column ie. Groupby Column1 is equivalent to groupby by Groupby column1. All the entities and raw results enclosed under nested Groupby column12 is equivalent to groupby by Groupby column1, Groupby column2 and so on and so forth. Group summary at each level nesting is aggregation performed on all enclosed entities. The results at each level can be group sorted by groupby column or optionally group summary value. The raw results are enclosed in the innermost group. This design also aligns with requirements for Ancestor joins mentioned in references. An example follows for the example mentioned above the results returned are shown below in color coded format. Yellow represents the memory, green represents the num_vcpus and violet represents the memory_usage. The uncolored columns represent the raw results returned which in this case is cpu_usage.The results are presented in a nested order such that we can do aggregation at each level i.e memory usage, num_vcpus, memory. In addition we can do group sort/limit and aggregation at any level of nesting. Aggregation can be done at any level starting with innermost grouping(level3), at level2 and level1 with group sort/limit applicable at any level, raw sort/limit applicable only at the innermost grouping. This makes is easy to answer the following questions: What are all the entities which match
