## 4.1 Option 1: Modify existing API
We can make group_by clause repeated. Each instance of the group_by clause sets the properties of the group_by_column whether is discrete or continuous, if continuous num_buckets, bucket_boundary etc. We will validate while all groupby are allowed to set groupby columns and properties, aggregate columns, group sort/limit but raw columns, raw sort/limit will be allowed only in the innermost groupby.
repeated QueryGroupBy group_by = 5;
group_sort_order will take any one of the group_by_columns specified and aggregate columns specified.
For the result proto we will make group_by_column_value a list, everything else remains.
repeated DataValue group_by_column_value = 1;
Pros:
One placeholder for group_by, no duplication of group_by functionality
Cons:
Client side has to change as we made group_by into list and result proto also the group_by_column_value becomes a list.

## 4.2 Option 2: Add new API
We can add a new clause mg_group_by. This is mutually exclusive to existing group_by clause. Each instance of mg_group_by sets the properties of the group_by_column. repeated QueryGroupBy mg_group_by = 6;
group_sort_order will take any one of the group_by_columns specified and aggregate columns specified.
The result proto will add new clause mg_group_results_list in which group_by_column_value will become a list,

New API doesn’t overlap with existing API

Phase 1 will implement support of aggregate columns, group sort/limit only in the innermost groupby along with raw columns, raw sort/limit and rest of the properties.
Phase 2 will implement support of aggregate columns, group sort/limit at all levels.

For discrete grouping the raw results from various nodes are collated indexing by the vector of group_by_attributes. For continuous grouping we need to strip out from the raw results, the latest group_by_attribute values per entity and calculate the min, max and bucket size per group_by_attribute, store this in a map. [IDF Design Documents | Indexes for query evaluation]
Indexes for IDF query evaluation
Shrivatsan Vasudhevan
July 2019

[IDF Design Documents | Indexes for query evaluation]
## Motivation: Data center entities such as VMs, Virtual Disks, Clusters, Alerts etc. are modelled as first class objects in insights server (a.k.a. insights data fabric). Each entity has an entity guid (entity_type, entity_id, tenant_id) and one or more attributes (such as “vm_name”: “vm1”). The attributes are config information that doesn’t change very frequently. One of the fundamental requirements from IDF was to perform fast reads of config data. To cater to this requirement, we started off caching the entities to its entirety in memory so that fetching the entity was really quick. With the introduction of Alerts, Snapshots and Events, the number of entities to grew to a few million and caching all of them in the memory became cost prohibitive. This lead us to divide entities into 2 broad categories: Non-evictable entities - Traditional entities such as VMs, Virtual Disks are cached entirely in IDF memory (hence they are referred to as non-evictable or un-evictable entities) with entity_guid as the key into an unordered map. As a result, there is no specific ordering of the entities in the cache. Queries that specify filters (i.e. the where clause) on non-evictable entities end up performing a linear scan of the entities to extract the values of attributes requested in the query. Even if there are multiple attributes in the filter clause, we do only a single linear scan. This worked reasonably well for a few thousands of entities. Evictable entities - Entities such as

[IDF Design Documents | Indexes for query evaluation]
query. Even if there are multiple attributes in the filter clause, we do only a single linear scan. This worked reasonably well for a few thousands of entities. Evictable entities - Entities such as Alerts, Audits and snapshots are made as evictable. This means that when the server runs low on memory, these entities get evicted from the (LRU) cache to make room for newer entities (or metrics which is not discussed in this document). We introduced secondary/reverse indexes in insights server to provide the clients the ability to index attributes that they’ll use in the queries.

## Reverse Indexes:
These indexes are created (modified, deleted) whenever the entities change. These indexes are used by the queries for filtering out entities that don’t match the specified criteria. The filtered set of entities are passed on to the next stages of the query processing pipeline.
For the in-memory index, we maintain an ordered map of attributes with the attribute value as the key for the map and the set of entities with that value as the mapped value. The attribute value is represented as a ‘DataValue’ which is a union of int64, string, boolean, int64 list, string list etc. This gives us the flexibility of specifying any type for the value. These indexes are maintained on a per entity type basis.

[IDF Design Documents | Indexes for query evaluation]
## Example:
For instance, let's say we have 4 entities:
{E1, "Alert", "T1"}: { "resolved": true, "created_timestamp": 1565133000, "detailed_msg": .. }
{E2, "Alert", "T1"}: { "resolved": true, "created_timestamp": 1565134000, "detailed_msg": .. }
{E3, "Alert", "T1"}: { "resolved": false, "created_timestamp": 1565135000, "detailed_msg": .. }
{E4, "Alert", "T1"}: { "resolved": false, "created_timestamp": 1565133000, "detailed_msg": .. }
We create two indexes on the attributes, “resolved” and “created_timestamp”. The in-memory index map will be as follows:
1) resolved:
2) created_timestamp:
If the query is:
Select ‘detailed_msg’, ‘signature’ from ‘alerts’
where ‘resolved’ kEQ false
kAnd ‘created_timestamp’ kGE 1565134000
The filter clause will be evaluated first.
We’ll fetch entity ids {E3, E4} that match the first criteria and {E2, E3} match the second criteria.
Perform a set intersection between the 2 (since the comparison operator is kAnd). This gives us entity E3.
For entity E3, we’ll fetch the values of ‘detailed_msg’, ‘signature’.

[IDF Design Documents | Indexes for query evaluation]
## Indexes for non-evictable entities:
We recently made a change in insights server to enable indexes for any entity type (whether the entities are evictable or not doesn't really matter any more). The indexes are a property of an attribute and they can be specified through the insights server config file.
For instance, to set an attribute “severity” of “alert” entity type as an indexed column, we’ll have to set “is_index_column” to true and specify the type of the data value that this attribute is expected. The metric type definition for this attribute will be as follows:
is_attribute: true
metric_name: "severity"
bucketize_timestamps_in_tsdb: false
entity_type_name: "alert"
user_metadata: "{\"data_type\":\"string\"}"
persist_attribute_as_time_series: false
is_index_column: true
index_type: kString

[IDF Design Documents | Indexes for query evaluation]
## A few things to note:
Indexing support is available only on attributes, time-series or metric data can't be indexed.
All the reverse indexes are maintained in memory. So, let's please index only the attributes that are being used in the filter clause. For this purpose, we request the teams to get approval from someone from the IDF team for any changes to the IDF schema file.
We’ll disable dynamic registration of indexed attributes.
The memory used by the map is proportional to the cardinality of the attribute value. If the values are sparse, the memory used will be more.
If some attributes used in the filter clause are indexed and some are non-indexed, we go through the non-index code path (primarily for ease of implementation and O(n) scan triumphs the logarithmic lookup in terms of run time complexity anyways).
We don't allow indexing attributes that represent parent relationships. This is because insights server ends up creating a relationship graph between the entities for such queries. Please refer to this document to understand parent relationship and relationship graph.

## Performance benchmark:
Our team (thanks to Aryan) did some benchmarking to compare the query performance as well are memory impact from using indexes. The results with indexing look significantly better. Please go through the following docs for Flow and Category API use cases.

[IDF Design Documents | Insights Query_ Alternate way to paginate results (raw columns)]
This document describes the current approach (as of Obelix) for paginating results, it’s drawbacks and alternate way for pagination, in order to scale. Pagination in IDF is achieved by specifying a limit and offset in the query: Limit controls the number of results returned. Offset specifies the number of elements to skip before accumulating the results to return. Pagination can be done for group results as well as the raw results within each group. For instance, if we have 5 groups: A, B, C, D & E, and we there are 10 elements in each group: A : [1, 10) B : [10, 20) C : [20, 30) D : [30, 40) E : [40, 50) If the offset for group results is 2 and limit is 1, and offset for raw result is 0 and limit is 1, we will return: C: [20]. This document primarily focuses on paginating raw results. Paginating raw results is mostly used in conjunction with sorting. In the scaled out version of IDF, the raw results for a particular group could be present in any IDF node of the cluster. When sorting and limiting is requested on raw columns, the offset and limit used in pagination specifies the offset and limit in the final sorted response and not in the individually response from each node. For instance, let’s say we have 12 vm entities with entity ids vm1..vm12, distributed among 3 nodes of a cluster as follows: Select “__entity_id__”, “vm_type”, “vm_name” from VM, order-by “__entity_id__”, offset = 1, limit = 2. The coordinator rewrites the query sent to the shard processor with an offset

[IDF Design Documents | Insights Query_ Alternate way to paginate results (raw columns)]
3 nodes of a cluster as follows: Select “__entity_id__”, “vm_type”, “vm_name” from VM, order-by “__entity_id__”, offset = 1, limit = 2. The coordinator rewrites the query sent to the shard processor with an offset of 0 and limit of 3. Rest of the query is unchanged. So, each node responds with “__entity_id__”, “vm_type”, “vm_name” for each entity and sorts the node based on the value of “__entity_id__”. The coordinator collates all the responses, sorts them again, and filters out the entities that fall outside the range. This becomes especially expensive when the response spans across multiple pages (each page requested translates to offset = 0 and limit = (page_number - 1) * page_size; page_number >= 1). The raw results returned by the shard processors for any previous page(s) are thrown away. For instance, if we have 1000 VM entities in the cluster, and each page displays 100 entities, for displaying the 10th page, the coordinator will rewrite the query to fetch all raw columns for all entities. So, in the worst case, the coordinator will have to sort all the 1k entities, and filter out entities 1 - 900. To solve this problem, we’ll use the following approach: If raw sort, offset & limit are specified in the query, we will rewrite the query so that it contains only the (raw) sort column in raw columns, irrespective of whether it is group-by query or not. We will retain the filter clause, if it exists in the original query. We will sort the response based on the value of the

[IDF Design Documents | Insights Query_ Alternate way to paginate results (raw columns)]
columns, irrespective of whether it is group-by query or not. We will retain the filter clause, if it exists in the original query. We will sort the response based on the value of the sort column, apply offset and limit. For the entities that are in the requested range [offset, offset+limit) , we send another query with the enriched raw columns. The entity ids are specified in the guid of the query. Consider the query: Select “__entity_id__”, “vm_type”, “vm_name” from VM, order-by “__entity_id__”, offset = 1, limit = 2. Top-level query: Select “__entity_id__” from VM, order-by “__entity_id__”, offset = 0, limit = 3. Node response(s): After performing raw sort, limit and offset we get: vm2, vm3. The second query becomes: Select “__entity_id__”, “vm_type”, “vm_name” from vm2, vm3. The response for this query is added to the final response. Implementation: With this approach, all the changes will be restricted to the coordinator.

[IDF Design Documents | Insights spotlight search for Delos - 04_02_2015]
## Introduction
This document reflects the requirements gathered at the meeting on 04/02/2015 as well as high level design for Insights spotlight search for Delos.

## Current state
The current implementation of spotlight search provides feature parity with Arithmos, which may not be powerful enough for Delos scenarios.  With the current implementation the caller may provide the following search criteria:
Search term.  Attribute values are checked for having the search term as a substring (case insensitive).  If not specified, all attribute values match.
Searched attributes.  If specified, only those attributes are searched, otherwise all string attributes are searched.
Entity types.  If specified, only entity of the given types are searched.
Ancestor entities.  If specified, the search is limited to descendants of the specified entities.
The results are returned as a list of entities with the corresponding matched attributes.  The caller may specify additional return attributes that don’t affect searching criteria, but their values are returned for each matched entity (this can be used for fetching friendly names of entities, e.g. “vm_name”, “cluster_name”, etc.).
The return results are not ordered in any particular way.  The order is not deterministic and depends on completion of asynchronous routines.

[IDF Design Documents | Insights spotlight search for Delos - 04_02_2015]
## New requirements
For Delos, the search needs to support ability to limit search results, which pretty much dictates the rest of the requirements:
Results need to be ranked and sorted (wouldn’t be useful to return 10 most random results)
Need to specify ranking hints
The requirements for ranking criteria are the following:
3 rank scores on match closeness: full string match, prefix match, any other match
Ability to specify “interesting” attributes: match in those attributes would make entity rank higher
Ability to specify “interesting” ancestors: if the entity is a descendant of an interesting ancestor, it would rank higher
Ability to specify “interesting” anchor entities: the rank of an entity is a function of the number of hops to that entity from the anchor entity (the path length between 2 entities on the entity graph)
During search, the matched entities are ranked according to the ranking criteria.  Then top N are sorted and returned.

## Design outline
The gist of the design is going to be defining the ranking criteria and the logic to combine rank scores into a single rank value.
Here are the ranking criteria in detail.  To keep things simple and fast, the various constants are limited to small number, we can reconsider in the future.

## Match closeness
For full string match assign rank score 2, for prefix match assign rank score 1, for other match assign rank score 0.  This logic is going to be hardcoded.

[IDF Design Documents | Insights spotlight search for Delos - 04_02_2015]
## “Interesting” attributes
The caller should be able to specify a list of attributes along with the “relevance factor”.  The relevance factor is a number 1-3 that denotes the relevance of the attribute (1 is lowest relevance, 3 is highest).  When an attribute matches, the search calculates the rank score based on the relevance factor.  For all other attributes the rank score is 0.

## “Interesting” ancestors
The caller should be able to specify a list of ancestors along with “relevance factor”.  The relevance factor is a number 1-3 that denotes the relevance of the ancestor (1 is lowest relevance, 3 is highest).  All descendants of an “interesting” ancestor get the rank score equal to the relevance factor of the ancestor. If an entity is a descendant of multiple “interesting” ancestors, then the rank score is the max of all relevance factors.  If an entity is not a descendant of an “interesting” ancestor, then its rank score is 0.

## “Interesting” anchor entities [NOT IMPLEMENTED]
The caller should be able to specify a list of “anchor” entities.    For each entity, the search would execute BFS over the parent-child links (treating it as undirected graph) with a max depth = 2, and then assign rank score of 3 to the anchor entity itself, rank score 2 to the neighbors, and rank 1 to the nodes that are reachable in 2 hops.

[IDF Design Documents | Insights spotlight search for Delos - 04_02_2015]
## Combining rank scores into a single rank value
When an entity is evaluated against multiple ranking criteria it gets a rank score of each criterion.  For example, entity VM#42 may get 3 because it’s a descendant of an “interesting” ancestor, and 2 because it’s a neighbor of an “interesting” anchor entity.  Moreover, there are 2 rank scores for each matched attribute (“interesting” attribute rank score and match closeness), so each entity gets a vector of rank scores and we need to order those vectors.  We’re going to define a simple way of calculating a value out of rank score vector, and we may tune the algorithm when we do some testing.
First let’s get a single score for an attribute match.  Each attribute match can have a pair of scores – the match closeness and attribute relevance.  Let’s define the combined score of the attribute to be a sum of the scores (a value from 0 to 5).  For the entity we pick the max of all attribute scores.
Now, we have 1 attribute score (a combined value) - X, 1 ancestor score - Y, and 1 anchor score - Z.  The rank value is going to be X*3 + Y*5 + Z*5.  The multipliers are needed to normalize ranges (0..5 for attribute score, 0..3 for the rest of the scores).
Once we have the rank value, it can be used for sorting.  Entity ids can be used to resolve ties, so that the order is deterministic even if multiple entities have the same rank.

## Work estimates:
1 dev week should be enough to accomplish the work.

[IDF Design Documents | Limit and sort data before copying to ret]
Limit and sort data before copying to ret
Mudit Wadhwa 2024

## Motivation
Presently we copy all the metric data to ret first and then do sorting and limiting. If  we reverse the order, we can reduce some unnecessary copy of data. This will involve just rearranging the existing logic and no major changes.

## Implementation Details:
Presently, after metric data fetch, we do ops in the order:-
DoPostProcessGroupBy - We iterate over entity_groups_ and perform aggregation for each group.
DoPostProcessUnsorted - Create group_results_list in ret and copy group by column value, Copy all metric data across all groups to ret.
DoPostProcessSortLimit - Do group sort/limit and raw sort/limit on the data.
This can be changed to
DoPostProcessGroupBy - Create group_results_list in ret and copy group by column value
DoPostProcessGroupSortAndLimit- do the sorting and limiting across groups(At processor, we always do sorting based on group by value)
DoPostProcessUnsorted - Fetch the aggregate values, entity_ids, sort column (if required) values.
DoPostProcessRawSortAndLimit - do the raw sort and limit of ret as before.
DoPostProcessMetricFetch - for all the entities, fetch the remaining metric data.

## Rolling upgrade:
Since all the changes are in the processing side, there is no rolling upgrade impact.

[IDF Design Documents | Limit and sort data before copying to ret]
## Future Work:
This can be converted to a multi phase fetch from store layer to fetch sort column first - sort and limit the results and then fetch remaining data from store for the filtered entities.

[IDF Design Documents | Lookup Support in IDF]
Lookup Support in IDF

## Introduction
After looking at what lookup support MongoDB has ($lookup operator) it looks like it should be fairly straightforward to implement some level of lookup support in IDF.  Effectively, lookup in MongoDB are nested queries that for each document in parent queries can return a subarray of documents according to some conditions that are passed from the current document.
Lookup in MongoDB has 2 flavors:
A simple field match that just fetches documents from another collection that matches the specified field value.
A more advanced form, where a nested pipeline can be specified to get any arbitrary results.
In either case, the results are returned as an array of nested documents.
In this project we implement semantics that fall in between and are expressive enough to support many scenarios used in our applications.  To implement #2 in general case it would require issuing a nested lookup query for each parent result, which is super expensive, and #1 is too restrictive (doesn't support nested, which is required for categories).  The API supports #2 syntax so when we get MongoDB to handle the queries, we don't need to change the APIs, just remove the restrictions.

[IDF Design Documents | Lookup Support in IDF]
## API Changes The QueryGroupBy is going to have a new member repeated Query lookup_query, which would have a list of nested queries to execute. Each nested query could have a nested query of its own, so queries can form a lookup tree. The top level query could be any query, a nested query has the following restrictions: cannot be a group-by query Boolean expression needs to contain lookup condition as the first member, and the rest of the expression (if any) needs to be combined with AND, e.g. (x kEQ y) AND (... blah ...) the lookup condition operator can be kEQ, kIN, kContains, kAny other operators are not supported the lookup condition supports kContains only for singular values on the parent side (i.e. value on the lookup side can be list value, but the value in the parent query needs to be singular) the lookup condition needs to be on one of the raw columns The QueryGroupResults would include repeated EntityWithMetricAndLookup lookup_query_results (see below for EntityWithMetricAndLookup definition), which would be used instead of raw_results. The reason for using it instead of raw_results is because raw_results use EntityWithMetric, that's used in many other places, so we don't want to add more fields to that. // Encapsulates entity with metrics and lookup results (used in queries // that have lookup subqueries). message EntityWithMetricAndLookup { // Required. optional EntityWithMetric entity_with_metrics = 1; // Lookup query results. The number and order of these

The number and order of these would match // the number and order of lookup queries at the corresponding nesting // level. repeated LookupQueryResult lookup_query_results = 2; } // Defines result for queries that have lookup subqueries. message LookupQueryResult { // Results. repeated EntityWithMetricAndLookup results = 1; }

## Query Execution The top level query is going to be executed as usual and then lookup queries are executed in the post processing phase, in batches. The query tree is traversed using DFS and then the results are correspondingly traversed to get lookup values from the results of the parent queries and issues nested subqueries and then fill out results at the corresponding levels. The subqueries are going to be formed as the following: iterate over parent results, collect values for the rhs of the lookup condition of the nested query once a certain threshold (say 512 entries) is reached, we're ready to issue a nested query we substitute the RHS lookup column name in the RHS with the list we've collected and add group-by-column to be LHS lookup column we substitute kEQ operator with kIN or kContains with kAny Assuming that values of one attribute would have the same type, which is true for our data, we just use the type of the first entry for the list value. Once we get the results of the query, we add the groups into a map and iterate over parent results, matching groups to the lookup column values. For the kIN operator, we'd need to do processing for sort / offset / limit (more details later). Let's consider an example. query { entity_list { entity_type_name: "vm" } group_by { raw_sort_order { sort_column: "cpu_usage" sort_order: kDescending } raw_limit { limit: 100 } raw_columns { column: "_entity_id_" } # implementation needs it raw_columns { column: "cluster" } #

Optimization of queries with continuous grouping
Shrivatsan Vasudevan, Aiswarya S
July 2019

## Problem Statement:
Ref:- https://jira.nutanix.com/browse/CPD-1837
Currently, the processor nodes just return the values for group-by columns as a raw column in case of continuous grouping and the coordinator performs the necessary grouping, followed by group-limit and raw sort/limit. This creates a bottleneck on the coordinator – both memory and compute wise.
Here we evaluate the usage of multi phase design to process continuous grouping queries.

[IDF Design Documents | Optimizing queries with continuous grouping]
## Implementation Details Presently the continuous grouping query workflow is as follows:- The coordinator sends the query to processor nodes The processor nodes send the continuous group by column and aggregate column as a raw column value Coordinator performs continuous grouping and aggregation based on the raw values returned by the processor The proposed workflow is:- If aggregate columns, raw_limt and/or group_limit is specified the coordinator uses multiphase fetch to get the max and min values of group_by_column first , creates buckets and use this buckets to fetch data from processors. In multi-phase fetch, The coordinator first sends a query (as part of DispatchQuery) - query_name_fetch_group_by_column. to fetch the maximum and minimum values from processor. Every field in the original query except the group_by column will be copied to the query_name_fetch_group_by_column . The group by clause will look like:- group_by { aggregate_columns { column: original_group_by_column downsampling_operator: kMax } aggregate_columns { column: original_group_by_column downsampling_operator: kMin } raw_limit { limit: 0 offset: 0 } } The processor processes this query using the existing workflow. The coordinator aggregates the response (as part of overall_done_cb of DispatchQuery) - calculate the overall max and min values, calculates the buckets using the calculated max and min values along with num_buckets provided in the query. The query is modified to replace the num_buckets

[IDF Design Documents | Optimizing queries with continuous grouping]
DispatchQuery) - calculate the overall max and min values, calculates the buckets using the calculated max and min values along with num_buckets provided in the query. The query is modified to replace the num_buckets with the new user defined buckets . The query processing will be done using the new modified query (by invoking DispatchQuery again) with newly defined buckets using the existing workflow.

## Extra notes:-
As an add on optimisation, we can avoid the copy of entities to the default group in the beginning in case of continuous grouping. This is done by creating the buckets first and then copying data from node_ret to corresponding buckets. This will be useful in case of regular continuous group by queries without multiphase. (Not part of this diff)
Presently, we use raw_limit as 0 to avoid any entity_ids to be returned from node rets. This still involves a copy of entity ids at the processor side - which can be a sizeable delay in case of > 20k entities. This can be avoided by doing SkipEntityGuids in processor side itself when the query does not have continuous grouping .

As of today if a metric is used in GroupBy, Where and Raw/Aggregate column, we fetch the same metric thrice from store. This might turn out to be expensive especially in case of derived metrics.

## Description: Ref: https://jira.nutanix.com/browse/ENG-199624 This document addresses thes following points:- Inconsistency in arithmos and IDF derived metric data. Presently derived metrics calculation is done as follows:- A) Create buckets according to the downsampling_interval_secs of the derived metric B) Sample the source data into these buckets (according to derived metric downsampling interval) and , if more than one value present in the bucket, take the last value in each bucket. (Ref: https://opengrok.eng.nutanix.com/source/xref/euphrates-5.10-stable/insights/insights_server/query/derived_metric.cc#450) C). Process each bucket according to derived metric expression D). Arithmos first down samples each metric (Derived and source metric) using the downsampling interval specified in the query and downsampling operator of the source metric. Then apply the derived metric calculation for each bucket eg: Consider query = ``` query { entity_list { entity_type_name: "vm" } group_by { raw_columns { column: "dm" } down_sampling_interval_secs: 300 } } ``` Let the derived metric (dm = a +b) has

But we still have to downsample the source data into buckets based on derived metric downsampling interval after derived metric calculation. Performance impact:- Here we downsample each source metric once before initiating all derived metric calculations. The purpose of this is to establish the semantics for the filter clause evaluation in an IDF query. It can be subsequently expanded to include other portions of the query as well. Query Filter Clause: The filter clause evaluation provides a way to limit the response returned to the client. Consider the following filter clause on VM entities: _master_cluster_uuid_ kNE empty kAnd is_cvm kEQ true This filter clause contains 2 comparison expressions: _master_cluster_uuid_ kNE empty - this fetches replicated VM entities (replicated VM entities will have non-empty values for _master_cluster_uuid_ pseudo attribute). is_cvm kEQ true - entities that have the ‘is_cvm’ attribute set to true. They are combined together using a boolean operator ‘kAnd’. So, the result would contain the entities for which both (A) and (B) evaluate to true. ## 3-value logic
We have a couple of options to implement 3-value logic, using a true-set + false-set or using true-set + unknown-set.  The former is somewhat simpler to implement and would be faster for Boolean expressions (at the cost of some comparison expressions), the latter would be faster for some common comparison expressions, but slower for Boolean expressions.

## True-set + false-set
With this option, each comparison expression calculates 2 sets: the true-set contains entity ids that would match the expression, false-set contains entity ids that don't match the expression, entities with missing values are not included in either set (except for the special case of comparing with NULL -- for kEQ NULL, entities with missing values are included in true-set, the rest of the entities are included into false-set, for kNE NULL, entities with missing value are included in false-set, the rest are included into true-set).
The Boolean operations are defined as the following:
AND: result-true-set = INTERSECT(true-set1, true-set2);  result-false-set = UNION(false-set1, false-set2);
OR : result-true-set = UNION(true-set1, true-set2);  result-false-set = INTERSECT(false-set1, false-set2);
NOT: SWAP(true-set, false-set)

[IDF Design Documents | Query semantics for filter clause]
## True-set + unknown-set
Here, each comparison expression calculates 2 sets: the true-set contains entity ids that would match the expression, unknown-set contains entity ids with missing values (again with the exception of the NULL expressions, for which unknown-set is empty).  This is faster for expressions like x = "foo", especially if there are not many missing values.
The Boolean operations are defined as the following:
AND: result-true-set = INTERSECT(true-set1, true-set2);  result-unknown-set=UNION(INTERSECT(unknown-set1, true-set2), INTERSECT(unknown-set2, true-set1), INTERSECT(unknown-set1, unknown-set2));
OR : result-true-set = UNION(true-set1, true-set2); result-unknown-set=DIFFERENCE(UNION(unknown-set1, unknown-set2), result-true-set);
NOT: result-true-set = DIFFERENCE(ALL, UNION(true-set, unknown-set)); result-unknown-set = unknown-set;

## kNOT pushdown
While thinking about 3VL logic and looking at alternative ways to achieve the same result, I realized that the kNOT pushdown approach that we talked about earlier would actually achieve the same semantics as the double-set logic and it's probably going to be more efficient (definitely more efficient than true-set + false-set option, because calculating false-set for every comparison expression is expensive).
Proof: assuming true-set + unknown-set approach is correct and there are no NOTs, the ANDs and ORs would transform true-sets independently, so the final true-set would be correct and unknown-set would be discarded.  If kNOT is pushed down to comparison expressions, it would work correctly.
Even pushing down kNOT to leaf level would mostly work (assuming we apply missing values appropriately), with the exception of kNOT(foo kNE NULL).

Querying for Latest Metrics with DownSampling Suresh Sivaprakasam Introduction When we query for latest metric values, we don't know when the last update for the metric happened, what we do is we go back in time for a specified period and check if there are metric values and return the last updated value. The specified period is calculated as metric's sampling period * query's num_intervals_for_latest_data. For eg. most metrics are of sampling period 30s and default value of num_intervals_for_latest_data is 10, hence its 30 * 10 = 300s or 5mins. If there are no values in the specified period, then client is expected to increase num_intervals_for_latest_data and query again etc. Problem Current implementation of downsampling works on timed ranges only and latest metric values by default looks at raw data like explained above. Design When a client asks for latest metric data with downsampling period/operator, what they expects is, from the last update, align it down to downsampling period, down sample for the last period using the configured down sampling operator or the default downsampling operator. We will use the same method for latest metric data, look back num_intervals_for_latest_data periods of max(sampling_period, downsampling_interval) so that if we find metric update we capture at least 1 down sample period. Example If sampling period is say 60s and last update is middle of an hour, say 5.30pm and goes back for 4 hours every 60s i.e 1.30pm to 5.30pm. Assume all

[IDF Design Documents | Raw sort and limit should be performed before fetching other raw columns._]
The query processing pipeline on the processor nodes is as follows (as of 09/17): Apply filter clause Performing grouping on the filtered entities For each group, fetch the raw columns for all entities. Paginate the entities in each group by applying offset and limit. One of the problems we have been facing with some memory intensive queries is that fetching all the raw columns for all entities (before applying the actual limit) could result in significant memory overheads. If a bunch of such queries run concurrently, it’s possible for IDF to run out of memory. There are 2 potential ways to fix this issue: The co-ordinator leverages multi-phase raw column fetch for all queries that requests pagination based on sorted raw column values. Pros: Minimal code change - modify LimitEntitiesBeforeRawColumnsFetch() to return true if a gflag is set (by default, let’s set the gflag to true) and if the number of requested raw columns == 1. We will piggyback on existing code that has been tested for a couple of releases. Tried this on a local PC, and with 20k VMs requesting for 4 raw columns, I see about 2.5x speed up. Cons: multi-phase (this involves 2 RPCs instead of 1) fetch could potentially slow certain queries. We need to measure the impact of this. Change processor pipeline to perform sorting of entities (based on raw sort column), followed by applying offset and limit; and then finally fetch the other raw columns for the ‘limited’ set of entities. Scale out design for Spotlight Search Spotlight search supports search for substring on attribute values on a given set of entities or entity types and support the scoping and relevance calculation based on ancestor entities. Of all the arguments for a spotlight search query, the following four fields requires changes to existing execution path. Entity_type_name_list Scope_entity_list Relevant_ancestor_list Query limit We will address them individually in the following sections. 1.1 Handling spotlight on a set of entity types entity_type_name_list specifies a set of entity types on which the spotlight search will be conducted on. When this set is empty, it will search on all entity types. Since sharding in IDF is based on entity ID, no matter whether the set is empty or not, we have to send the search request to all nodes in the cluster. 1.2 Handling scope entity list and relevant_ancestor_list The scope entity list limits the search on entities belonging to some ancestor entities. To determine whether an entity is a child of another entity, we need to walk up the entity relationship tree. The relevant_ancestor_list adds additional input on how the relevance information of the matching entities are computed. Entities of different ancestor nodes will get a relevance_factor associated with the ancestor node. Therefore we need to walk up the entity relationship tree too. This doc discusses the three options to handle the entity relationship graph.

[IDF Design Documents | Scale out design for Spotlight Search]
ancestor nodes will get a relevance_factor associated with the ancestor node. Therefore we need to walk up the entity relationship tree too. This doc discusses the three options to handle the entity relationship graph. https://docs.google.com/document/d/15bL2vUlhOa3yxnUJmdssHsTz6IpA48LPdCVil4WJVPw/edit?ts=575887af The walking up the tree will be handled by the processor node. If the tree is cached, the processor node will just start from any entities of the specific type, and walk up the tree by comparing the entity id to find out whether the entity is a child of the specified set of ancestor nodes. To calculate the relevance of all the matching entities, we will do another round of tree walk up. It is possible to combine the two phases of tree walk up into a simple phase. For example, for an entity whose attributes match the search term, we will walk up the tree to the top. During the traversal, if we found a matching relevance ancestor node, we can then update the relevant infor for the entity. If during the walk up, we did not find any matching scoping ancestor node then we can discard the match entity. If the tree is not cached, then the processor node will walk up the tree in multiple phases of fan-out RPCs. Each phase of the RPC calls will walk up the tree by one level. For example, let S1 be the set of matching entities, it will send out a set of RPCs to nodes that host the entities in S1. After getting the responses from all nodes, it will get a new set S2, which is

[IDF Design Documents | Scale out design for Spotlight Search]
matching entities, it will send out a set of RPCs to nodes that host the entities in S1. After getting the responses from all nodes, it will get a new set S2, which is the set of parental nodes for S1. Then it will send out another phase of RPC calls to get the parental nodes for entities in S2. The process repeats until the top of the tree is reached. 1.4 Handling of query limit The limit field controls how many entities will be returned to the client. It is handled on both the processor nodes and the coordinator node. Each processor node will return up to limit number of matching entities based on their local sorting of relevance. Once entities from all processors are received by the coordinator, the coordinator will merge-sort all the entities based on their relevance in decreasing order and return limit number of entities in the beginning of the sorted list.

[IDF Design Documents | Support DB query filters with loosely specified numeric types (CPD-621)]
Introduction
Currently, the DB query API requires clients to specify the correct RHS types for comparison expressions in where clauses. For example, in a where clause (num_iops > 50), where num_iops is int64, the RHS data value should have its int64_type set to 50; otherwise, the DB returns a kQueryGroupByInvalidComparisionExpr error.
CPD-621 tracks a request from the Prism Gateway team to support numeric comparison expressions with loosely specified RHS types. With this support, the client may specify the comparison expression with an RHS that is an double and the comparison would work even if the LHS was of a different numeric type—the DB would cast the LHS values to the numeric type of the RHS and perform the comparison. Using the example above, in a where clause (num_iops > 50), where num_iops is int64, the client can specify the RHS data value with its double_type set to 50, and the DB would perform the comparison correctly after promoting the LHS to a double.
In essence, the casting behavior of the DB is equivalent to the C++ reinterpret_cast of the LHS value to the RHS type. For numeric list types, the DB casts each individual element of the LHS list into the RHS numeric type.
Implementation
In InsightsQuery::EvaluateMetricExpression(), when CheckTypesCompatible() is false for numeric types, we cast the numeric types as specified above before calling CompareDataValues().

[IDF Design Documents | Two stage processing for continuous grouping]
ENG-226279:Do continuous grouping with user defined buckets at the query processor side
May 2019

## Introduction:
When user defined buckets are specified, we can do grouping at the processor side itself, without passing all the values to co-ordinator. This improves the latency of such queries by avoiding sending unnecessary data from processor as well as reducing the load  at the co-ordinator side

## Scope and Design Considerations:
The semantics for user defined buckets should be the same as existing.
Handle rolling upgrade scenario - both the existing and new code should be present in the  query layer. Switch to new behaviour via a Gflag only when the entire upgrade is done.
Group limit is applied at the processor and co-ordinator level.
Presently user defined buckets are specified only for non multi dimensional grouping case - so we dont need to consider the multidimensional scenario.
If grouping is discrete or if the continuous groupby is based on user defined buckets and the cluster is fully upgraded to present version, we do the group by step at the processor, else we do it at the co-ordinator

[IDF Design Documents | Two stage processing for continuous grouping]
## Proposed Approach -
Co-ordinator side - In the existing code we use the is_grouping_continuous_ flag to decide whether to keep the group_by_column_values populated by the processor  or create new groups. Instead of that we use a new flag to decide the same:-
use_group_results_from_processor =
!is_grouping_continuous ||                                 (group_by_->bucket_interval_separators_size() &&         FLAGS_insights_perform_user_defined_grouping_at_processor)
The rest of the processing is same as before.
Processor side:
Earlier, we used to add all entities to default group if the grouping was continuous. Instead, if use_group_results_from_processor is true, we add all the entities to the correct groups based on bucket intervals. We also fill aggregate results using similar logic, and the rest of the processing remains same.
use_group_results_from_processor
=(is_grouping_continuous &&  group_by_->bucket_interval_separators_size() &&         FLAGS_insights_perform_user_defined_grouping_at_processor)

## Handling rolling upgrade scenario
We need to check, when the cluster upgrades finishes by watching zeus config and set the flag FLAGS_insights_perform_user_defined_grouping_at_processor to true after that in all the nodes in the cluster.

It is possible that the intersection results in an empty set, in which case we ignore the index value from the result altogether. So essentially, we perform M * k lookups for getting the group buckets, as opposed to a linear O(M) scan. Because of the overhead of

[IDF Design Documents | parent_type_name Design Document]
## Problem
https://jira.nutanix.com/browse/CPD-1410
Currently, parent links are created via a name convention: if an attribute name matches an entity type name, then the attribute value is the parent entity it. This forces name convention to the clients which may break their name convention rules.

## Proposed Solution
First and foremost, this change will not affect behavior of existing workflows. Entity ancestor relationships defined using name conventions will continue to work as before.
Add an optional field to the MetricType protobuf: parent_type_name (a string)
If parent_type_name is not set then use the old behavior of determining entity ancestor relationships.
If parent_type_name == “__disabled__” then do not allow this metric type to connect to any ancestor, even if the metric type name matches an entity type.
If parent_type_name is set to any other value then use this value when determining entity ancestors.
In the original JIRA ticket it was suggested that once parent_type_name is set that it shouldn’t be able to be changed.  This seems like an unnecessary restriction.  I have currently not implemented this restriction.
After discussing with Artem, I have removed the feature that allows for parent types to be referred to in queries by their aliases. This has significantly reduced code complexity.  The challenges & implementation below is no longer relevant.

[IDF Design Documents | parent_type_name Design Document]
## Challenges:
Using this new schema a presents a challenge: given an entity type and a metric type name, determine if that metric type name is an ancestor of the entity type.
Previously this problem could be resolved by simply matching the metric type name against a set of all registered entity types.  In order to do this with the parent_type_name field, it is necessary to traverse the entity ancestor tree.
Consider the following examples:

## Example 1
Example 1 uses the old method of determining entity ancestors (aka string matching).
Entity type: test-cluster
Metric type name: attributeA
Metric type name: attributeB
Entity type: test-node
Metric type name: test-cluster
Metric type name: attributeC
Metric type name: attributeD
Entity type: test-vm
Metric type name: test-node
Metric type name: attributeE
MetricType name: attributeF
Question: does the string test-cluster refer to an ancestor of test-vm? Yes, since the metric type name test-cluster matches a registered entity type.

[IDF Design Documents | parent_type_name Design Document]
## Example 2
Example 2 uses the new method.
Entity type: test-cluster
Metric type name: attributeA
Metric type name: attributeB
Entity type: test-node
Metric type name: test-cluster-reference, parent_type_name: test-cluster
Metric type name: attributeC
Metric type name: attributeD
Entity type: test-vm
Metric type name: test-node-reference, parent_type_name: test-node
Metric type name: attributeE
MetricType name: attributeF
Question: does test-cluster-reference refer to an ancestor of test-vm? Yes, but you can’t just do string matching.  There is no entity type named test-cluster-reference.  In order to answer this question it is necessary to walk up the relationship tree starting at test-vm.

[IDF Design Documents | parent_type_name Design Document]

CPD-817 Implement metadata (entity types, metric types) caching on non-leaders

## Basic idea:
Metadata updates are going to be handled by the leader. All other nodes would watch for metadata changes and sync their caches from the leader. In Asterix, based on the cfstats in cassandra, the metric types metadata is round 1.2MB and the entity type metadata is about 57k (some overhead of keys are included). The amount of metadata is small but not small enough to be put in zookeeper. According to the config file in the main repo, we have 81 entity types and 2723 metric types.
The leader will be the only node that handles metadata related RPCs including read-only calls and during startup, it is the only node that loads the metadata from Cassandra and do the auto-registration. The non-leader node will always get the metadata by calling the GetMetadata internal RPC to the leader.
There would be a zookeeper node <blah>/insights/metadata/sha1, which is the SHA1 hash of the serialized metadata of the leader. Each non-leader node registers a watch on that zookeeper node and will call leader for latest metadata.
The GetMetadata internal RPC would return all metadata along with the corresponding SHA1 hash value of the serialized string representation of the metadata. So that the non-leader node knows whether the metadata is up-to-date or not. Implementation details
We will discuss the implementation details by going through a set of cases.

[IDF Design Documents | CPD-817 Implement metadata (entity types, metric types) caching on non-leaders]
## Non Leader initialization
Initially, every node is a non-leader, or to be more exact the leadership role is undetermined yet. During the initialization process, each node will volunteer for the leadership role and the eventually one node will be notified to be the leader and the other nodes will be non-leader. The leader election is done by zookeeper.
There are two components of the cache that an insight server initializes: the data cache and the metadata cache. Right now, the metadata cache is initialized before the data cache. We would like to keep the order in this design.
Before initializing the cache in init2, each Insight server will try to create a zookeeper node <blah>/insights/metadata/SHA1 and a zookeeper watch for any changes to that zookeeper node. If the zookeeper node does not exist, insight server will set the initial SHA1 to a string “0”.
Each insight server will have a local SHA1 value whose initial value is also string “0”.
When leader election is done, the non-leader will get the metadata from the leader by calling the GetMetaData RPC. If the response of the call is not kNoError, it will simply retry. After getting the metadata from the leader, the non-leader node will update its local metadata cache and then continue to load the entity data cache. After all data is loaded into memory, it will start the RPC services.

[IDF Design Documents | CPD-817 Implement metadata (entity types, metric types) caching on non-leaders]
## Leader initialization
When a non-leader is waiting for leader to get ready, it may be selected to become the leader. When a node becomes the leader, it will load the metadata from Cassandra and auto register the entity types and metric types from the config files. It will start the RPC service right after the metadata is loaded. After the metadata is loaded, it will compute a SHA1 hash of the serialized metadata string (it is the same as the serialized response from the GetMetaData internal RPC). The SHA1 will be put in the zookeeper node, so that the other non-leader node will be notified.
After loading the metadata, the leader node will continue to load the entity data based on the shard ownership. Before the entity data is loaded, any RPC request related to entities will be rejected.

## Non-leader to Leader switch
When a non-leader becomes leader, it will load metadata from Cassandra and auto-register the metadata. During the that process, it will disable the metadata related RPCs which includes both the external and internal metadata RPCs.  We can continue to allow other RPCs to flow in.
When the metadata loading and auto registration are done, the leader will turn on the metadata related RPC and then write the SHA1 hash of the metadata  to zookeeper so that other non-leader node will get the metadata update.

[IDF Design Documents | CPD-817 Implement metadata (entity types, metric types) caching on non-leaders]
## Handling metadata mutate RPCs
When serving a RegisterMetricTypes or RegisterEntityTypes RPC call, it will use a lock to block any concurrent metadata mutate RPCs. While holding the lock, it will apply the changes according to the arg, and compute the SHA1 hash of all metadata and put it to zookeeper. It will also store the SHA1 hash locally. After that, it will release the lock. The RPC call will return after updating zookeeper.
It is expected that there will be some delay in propagating the metadata changes to non-leader node. Therefore, non-leader node may update entities or metrics based on stale local metadata cache.
If there is error in updating zookeeper, for example, if the zookeeper is not available, the leader can just crash.

[IDF Design Documents | CPD-817 Implement metadata (entity types, metric types) caching on non-leaders]
## Zookeeper watch call-back
When receiving a zookeeper watch call-back, the non-leader node will check the current value in the zookeeper node with its local copy of the SHA1 value, if they match, then there is nothing to do (This may happen during the cluster start up due to race condition between zookeeper call-back and non-leader call to leader for metadata as part of non-leader initialization process). We will log it as a warning.
If the SHA1 value does not match, then the non-leader node will call the GetMetaData internal RPC to get the latest metadata. Upon getting response from the leader, the non-leader node will update the local SHA1 value and then apply the metadata update by replacing the current metadata value in cache with the value from the leader. If there is any error in applying the change, the non-leader shall just crash. After applying the change, the non-leader will compute the SHA1 hash of its local metadata, and it should match the one from the leader. If it does not match, it will log an error.

[IDF Design Documents | CPD-817 Implement metadata (entity types, metric types) caching on non-leaders]
## Handling of incoming RegisterMetricTypes and RegisterEntityTypes RPC calls.
In all modes including scale out demo mode, any node that receives the these calls will forward it to the leader. If the leader is not yet initialized (in kInitInProgress state), it will send a retry error back to the client. In this case, the client including the non-leader nodes is expected to retry after some time.
During the initial cluster startup, the leader will start RPC service right after metadata is loaded. After that moment, it can handle the metadata-related RPCs.
Action item: Try to see if we can use incremental SHA1 hash.

## Handling of nested fields
When a metadata get changed, it may involves changed to nested field definition. If so, on both leader and non-leader, we will need to re-compute the nested fields whenever nested field definition is changed. This is done locally on each node during the process of updating the local metadata cache.

Design on Shard Startup and Shutdown Introduction Rebalancing shards around the IDF cluster nodes is one of the most basic behaviors in scaleout mode. On each node, rebalancing involves loading and shutting down shards. This document describes the mechanism of starting and shutting down shards on a node. Major Design When the node receives a watch callback from the node map change in ZK, a new node map will be read from ZK. The new node map is compared with the current map to get all shards to be loaded and shutdown. All moving shards (that are going to be loaded or shutdown) will be queued in shard_status_map_ together with its operation (kLoad or kShutdown). ReadNodeMapEntryProto() then issues a thread calling MoveOneShard() for each moving shard. The thread will keep running until the queue for a shard is empty. During the time, new threads issued from ReadNodeMapEntryProto() (because of new node map changes) for this shard cannot take any operations from the queue if there has already been a thread working. Data Structure of shard_status_map_ shard_status_map_ currently is a hash protected by a mutex. It has shard IDs as the key and tuples as the value. The tuple consists of a queue of shard operation (kLoad and kShutdown), a flag indicating if a thread is working on the shard, and the volunteer ID when the node requests the ZK lock of the shard. Starting A Shard Move Moving a shard starts with a call of MoveOneShard(). The function is implemented as a forever loop. The

[IDF Design Documents | Design on Shard Startup and Shutdown]
volunteer ID when the node requests the ZK lock of the shard. Starting A Shard Move Moving a shard starts with a call of MoveOneShard(). The function is implemented as a forever loop. The thread exits immediately, if either of the following conditions is true: 1) the shard is not in the map, which means the shard has been removed from the node; 2) the queue of the shard is empty; 3) the flag indicating that a thread is already working on the shard move is set. If none of the conditions above is true, the thread first checks the number of operations in the queue: 1). If there are 2+ operations, pop out the first two because kLoad -> kShutdown or vice versa does not change anything. Then it continues another loop from the beginning of MoveOneShard(). 2). If there are only one operations, set the flag to indicate that a thread has started to work on the queue. It then calls LoadOneShard() to load the shard, or ShutdownOneShard() to shutdown the shard. Shard Load Loading a shard starts with sending a request for the shard ZK lock by calling VolunteerForLeadership(). It records the volunteer ID in shard_status_map_. After grabbing the lock, it checks shard_status_map_ again to see if there has been kShutdown scheduled in the queue. If there has been, it relinquish the ZK lock immediately and pops out kShutdown. It then clears up related status in shard_status_map_ and schedules another call of MoveOneShard(). If there hasn’t been, it sends the load to the store layer. It then

[IDF Design Documents | Design on Shard Startup and Shutdown]
lock immediately and pops out kShutdown. It then clears up related status in shard_status_map_ and schedules another call of MoveOneShard(). If there hasn’t been, it sends the load to the store layer. It then clears the status in shard_status_map_ and schedules another call of MoveOneShard(). The store layer loads all entities belong to the shard into the cache asynchronously. Once the load is sent to the store layer, the load must succeed and cannot be terminated. Shard Shutdown When a shutdown starts by calling ShutdownOneShard(), it first sets a flag in shard_set_ of the store layer to indicate that the shard is going to be shutdown so that all following RPCs should be returned with a kRetry error. It then checks the volunteer ID in shard_status_map_, which must be valid. This is because a shutdown is not scheduled until a load has sent the load to the store layer, which happens in the callback of grabbing the ZK lock. The shutdown waits until the shard is in shard_set_ of the store layer, which means the shard has been successfully loaded. After that, it relinquish the shard ZK lock and send the shutdown to the store layer. In the store layer, it first grabs the shard write lock (after waiting all pending RPCs complete). It then finds all dirty metrics which belong to the shard, packages them as a PutMetricData RPC, and sends it to the new owner of the shard. The RPC retries until success. Sending RPC is asynchronous. Then it remove all entities belonging to the shard

[IDF Design Documents | Design on Shard Startup and Shutdown]
packages them as a PutMetricData RPC, and sends it to the new owner of the shard. The RPC retries until success. Sending RPC is asynchronous. Then it remove all entities belonging to the shard from cache, clears the oracle time of those entities, and removes the shard from shard_set_, which officially means the shard has been removed from the node. Releasing the shard write lock concludes the shutdown process. RPC Service During Moving A Shard For each RPC, after arriving at the owner node according to the node map, it has to lock all shards to which this RPC is related by calling LockShards() in the store layer. If any shard fails in either of the following conditions, the whole RPC returns with an error of kRetry: 1). The shard must be included in shard_set_, which is the last step of loading a shard; 2). There must be no shutdown scheduled, which indicated by a flag in shard_set_; 3) It must grab the shard read lock.

[IDF Design Documents | ENG-140429_ node in crashloop]
JIRA: https://jira.nutanix.com/browse/ENG-140429

## Problem
Due to a configuration issue there is a node in a crash loop.  The reason why the node is crashing is an external issue and is not relevant to this ticket.
The other nodes are healthy.  However, IDF as a whole is unable to serve requests from the remaining healthy nodes.

## Root Cause
IDF delays the reallocation of a node’s shards for 2.5 seconds after it receives a “node is dead” alert.  If the node comes back online before the shards are reallocated then no reallocation happens.
In the above scenario the node is crashing and coming alive in less than 2.5 seconds.  This causes the node to hold onto shards -- even though the node is inoperable.
A similar problem could occur on a larger node.  A node in a crash loop that takes a long time to bootstrap could hold shards for long periods of time without being able to serve any requests.  Even though these shards would be released momentarily when the node crashes, it can grab more shards when it comes back online.
This issue is only present in clusters running in scaleout mode -- which is probably why we haven’t observed it until now.  In non-scaleout mode the leader holds all shards.  If a non-leader is in a crash loop the leader can still serve requests without problem.  If the leader enters a crash loop then another node is promoted to be the leader and it can start serving requests.

[IDF Design Documents | ENG-140429_ node in crashloop]
## Proposed Solution This particular ticket is caused by a crash happening when IDF attempts to load the metadata directory. Ensure that the metadata directory is set up prior to registering as healthy. If there is a problem with this process then the IDF instance will still die, but at least it will not make other nodes think that it is healthy. We can avoid the problem reported in the ticket by performing a series of checks prior to the health registration. These checks will determine if there are any configuration issues that will cause the IDF instance to crash during setup. If a problem is detected then IDF makes appropriate logs and dies. The node would still be in a crash loop, but it would never be reported as healthy. A tempting solution would be to simply wait until after setup before registering as healthy. However, some of the setup logic (including the metadata dir creation) has a dependency on the health registration. This is because health registration is required in order to initiate leader election. The pre-registration checks can be extended as needed if different setup problems arise. Although this would solve the immediate issue, I think that it leaves a deeper flaw un-fixed. Regardless of when we register the node as healthy, it is still possible that the node could die shortly afterwards. This could be during the initialization of the server or even shortly afterwards. This leaves open the possibility that the entire cluster can be disabled by a single

[IDF Design Documents | ENG-140429_ node in crashloop]
the node could die shortly afterwards. This could be during the initialization of the server or even shortly afterwards. This leaves open the possibility that the entire cluster can be disabled by a single misbehaving node.

ENG-471479: Double scan during bootstrap
Lavish, Sumit, Swagat, Devendra, Anand, Chitti
Feb 2023

## Summary
This document explains the design and implementation details of double scan for unevictable and evictable entities during bootstrap (ENG-471479). The last section also shares the benchmark results.
Currently, we scan both unevictable and evictable entities in one go. The main idea is to improve this by scanning unevictable entities first, and then evictable entities later since the majority of RPCs request for unevictable entity type and total number of unevictable entities are far lesser than evictable entities. This will enable us to return RPC results for unevictable entities faster after bootstrap.

[IDF Design Documents | ENG-471479_ Double scan during bootstrap]
## Shard Load Info Indicators ShardInfo ShardInfo is a struct which comprises of shard_start_time, boolean flag is_not_loaded and an unordered set of loaded_entity_types. is_not_loaded is initialized to true when the store layer is formed. As soon as an entity type is loaded from the backend, we mark is_not_loaded as false indicating the shard is at least partially loaded. Similarly, we initialize loaded_entity_types with an empty unordered set and keep on populating it with entity type names as they are loaded. Once a shard is fully loaded, we deallocate loaded_entity_types and assign it as nullptr since full shard load check will return true and we no longer need to check loaded_entity_types. shard_fully_loaded_ List of size equal to total number of shards containing 1s and 0s to indicate whether the shard is fully loaded or not. Each value in the list should always be atomically changed to avoid any race conditions. pending_first_phase_shard_loads_ Indicates the number of pending first phase shard loads. We do not start any second phase scan until all first phase scans are complete because we observed that insights threads may keep on picking second phase scan ops and block first phase scan ops rendering the whole double scan to be useless. Hence, this is used to prevent second phase scans blocking first phase scans of other shards. running_second_phase_shard_loads_ Indicates the number of currently running second phase shard loads. The number of running second phase scans

Hence, this is used to prevent second phase scans blocking first phase scans of other shards. running_second_phase_shard_loads_ Indicates the number of currently running second phase shard loads. The number of running second phase scans are controlled by a gflag insights_pct_threads_for_second_phase_during_bootstrap which indicates percentage of total threads assigned to IDF to use for second phase scans (currently 75%). This is done to throttle the number of threads used by second phase scans so that IDF is able to serve client RPCs using remaining threads.

If double scan is enabled, we increment pending_first_phase_shard_loads_ and call the first instance of StorePopulateEntityInfoInCache with first_phase_scan_done_cb as the callback. After first phase scan is complete, in first_phase_scan_done_cb, we decrement pending_first_phase_shard_loads_ and schedule the second instance of StorePopulateEntityInfoInCache with shard_load_done_cb as the callback. After second phase scan is complete, in shard_load_done_cb, we decrement running_second_phase_shard_loads_. We also increment running_second_phase_shard_loads_ if the current instance is second phase scan and take care not to schedule rescan workflow if the current instance is first phase scan. in double_scan_filtered_etypes, and finally populate rowkey_ranges with type range start and end tokens for these entity types and range_done_cb marks the entity type as loaded after each individual range scan is complete. ## Shard / Entity Type Load Status Check
Instead of just checking for full shard load, we now also need to check the status of entity types load (if needed) to accept an RPC.
For this, we first take read locks on the shards so that shard unloading doesn’t start while we are checking the status. We also introduced a flag check_shard_load in the existing ReadLockShards method which skips checking for shard load inside the method. If any of the given shards doesn’t exist in shard_set_ or we are unable to take read locks, we return false which means we cannot accept the RPC.
Then, we check whether all shards are loaded and accept the RPC if they are. Else, we check whether all entity types are loaded and accept the RPC if they are. If entity_type_set is nullptr, it means we only need to check full shard load and we shouldn’t accept the RPC. Similarly, if any entity type is not loaded, we shouldn’t accept the RPC. But before returning from the method, we ensure that we release the read locks we took on the shards earlier.

As a part of insights DF scale out, the insights leader has to assign shards to nodes. The leader will keep track of available nodes and use it to compute shard assignment. The leader will be responsible for rebalancing the shard when a node starts up or when an existing node dies. This document explains how the leader node does shard assignment and rebalancing. We'll be making use of the zeus library for achieving this. Node & Leader start up: 1. Enable component enables health monitoring by registering its handle (node_ip:port) with zookeeper (zeus::HealthMonitor). 2. Each component registers a callback with zeus to be invoked when contents of zknode: FLAGS_insights_node_map_zk_node_path changes. This zknode gives information about all the nodes (i.e. node handles) in the cluster and the shards that each node is responsible for. 3. The leader node will register a health watch callback to be invoked when an existing insights server component dies or when a new server component gets added. This callback is invoked with the peer handle whose health has changed (zeus::StartHealthWatch). 4. The leader starts off by getting the list of all the server components that have been registered using HealthMonitor (zeus::GetAllHealthy). The shards will be balanced equally across the available nodes: if there are 128 shards (1 through 127) and 3 nodes, a. shards [1, 44) will be handled by node 1, b. shards [44, 87) will be handled by node 2 and c. shards [87, 127] will be handled by node

[IDF Design Documents | Insights Scale-out_ Shard assignment and re-balancing]
127) and 3 nodes, a. shards [1, 44) will be handled by node 1, b. shards [44, 87) will be handled by node 2 and c. shards [87, 127] will be handled by node 3. Once the shard to node mapping has been established, the leader writes the protobuf consisting of nodes and the corresponding shards to the zknode at FLAGS_insights_node_map_zk_node_path. Since the contents of the zknode at FLAGS_insights_node_map_zk_node_path has been modified, each server components gets a notification. 5. Each server component maintains the following metadata: a. A node to interface map: given a node handle, whats the interface we can use to talk to the node? b. A shard to node map: Given a shard ID, whats the node handle of the corresponding node? Shard Assignment Change: So, when the shard assignment changes, we have to update the above mentioned maps accordingly. We'll consider the following scenarios: 1. Since the shard reassignment can take place when there are RPCs are on flight, we have to wait for the current operations on the shard to complete. To achieve this, each component should hold a shard lock in zookeeper and perform operations on that shards that it owns. We'll use zeus::VolunteerForLeadership() to obtain shard locks. Note that the zeus library creates a monotonically increasing sequence number for every volunteer that has been accepted by zeus. The library ensures that pending volunteers for the lock node are handled in order - the one with the lowest sequence number is elected the

[IDF Design Documents | Insights Scale-out_ Shard assignment and re-balancing]
for every volunteer that has been accepted by zeus. The library ensures that pending volunteers for the lock node are handled in order - the one with the lowest sequence number is elected the leader. Also, a volunteer can relinquish its intent for becoming a leader. 2. When a server component volunteers for leadership for a specific shard, it gets a volunteer id. Later, if it finds out that it’s no longer the owner for a particular shard, it should relinquish ownership for the shard by specifying its volunteer id. Hence the shard id -> volunteer id mapping is stored. Upon releasing the lock, the next volunteer will get the shard lock. 3. When a server component gets the leadership for a shard, it checks if it’s still the shard owner. If not, it has to relinquish the shard lock. #CPD-1719 Async recomputation of nested field attributes for existing entities on Schema change Devendra Shekhawat, Sumit Bhatia Dec 2017 In progress Requirements Currently on schema update for an entity type, the nested field recomputation is done synchronously for existing entities of that type. Issues with existing Implementation As the recomputation is done synchronously if the number of entities is huge like in case of evictable entities then this operation might take significant time and this can lead to RPC timeout. In the current implementation the recomputation is done by single thread but recomputation for an entity is independent of all other entities so we can employ multiple threads to process this task in parallel. Implementation As the recomputation of nested fields for an entity is independent of all other entities, so we can perform this operation in async manner. We will schedule multiple async tasks for recomputation of nested fields and when all of them completes then we can return success for the RPC. While scheduling the async tasks for recomputation of nested fields we also have to control the number of async tasks that we schedule otherwise we might overload IDF (mostly all threads will be working for recomputation this might introduce delay in other tasks). This problem can be solved by batching entities (say 1000 entities in a batch, BATCH_SIZE) for which we have to recompute nested fields. We also have to decide the number of concurrent batch

[IDF Design Documents | #CPD-1719 Async recomputation of nested field attributes for existing entities on Schema change]
tasks). This problem can be solved by batching entities (say 1000 entities in a batch, BATCH_SIZE) for which we have to recompute nested fields. We also have to decide the number of concurrent batch processing (num of async tasks) that we want to support, if we schedule so many async tasks together then most of IDF server threads might get busy doing only this task. The callback for each async request will check if there are any more entities left to process, if there are, then schedule one more async request with atmost BATCH_SIZE number of entities, if none are left, then the callback calls RpcDone and returns successfully. Support for Evictable Entities While recomputing the nested fields for an entity, check if it is non-evictable entity or evictable. If non-evictable then recompute the nested fields and update the entity in memory. If it is an evictable entity then first check is it available in memory (hydrated or dehydrated). If it’s available in memory then recompute nested fields similar to non-evictable entities. If this entity is not there in memory means its a dehydrated one then we don’t have to recompute the nested fields for this entity right now. Because as part of this update we will anyway update the schema and when this entity gets hydrated (or used next time) from cassandra then computation of nested fields will take place and that will take into account the updated schema. If updated metric is also registered as an indexed attribute then we also have to

[IDF Design Documents | Add support for non-cas evictable entities]
## Introduction
Currently, any evictable entity must be cas entity. That is to guarantee the read after read consistency. Consider the following example:
Read 1 comes in at T1, gets value=A, cas=10
Write comes in at T2, changing the value from A to B, cas from 10 to 11
Read 2 comes in at T3, gets value=B, cas=11
Read 2 returns first. It updates the cache with value=B, cas=11, and mark the InsightsObject as kMerged.
Read 1 returns later. It found the cas it has (10) is less than cache version (11). It will give up updating the cache InsightsObject.
The scenario doesn’t happen for unevictable entities because we assume that all entities will always exist in cache and thus the cached version will directly be returned even if it is kNotMerged. However, this assumption doesn’t hold when it comes to evictable entities, which may be evicted from cache. Thus, there can be multiple concurrent read, resulting in multiple versions of entities to be loaded into cache. So resolve this problem, we need to know if another reader has read something potentially newer.
Currently, we depend on the cas value to resolve this problem. Newer version of entity will have larger cas value. However, the replication logic saved all replicated entities as non-cas (kPaxos, vs. kPaxosWithCas). To support the replication of evictable entities, we need to support non-cas evictable entities.

[IDF Design Documents | Add support for non-cas evictable entities]
## New design
A new field named “ops_counter_” will be added to the InsightsObject. Whenever we update the cache, the counter will be incremented by 1. The logic will be as following:
When reading, take a note of the current counter value.
When updating the cache (whether resulting from read or write), increment the counter.
When updating the cache as a result of read
if the cached obj is empty, check if the counter is the same, don't update the cache if not.
if the cached obj exists, compare db_modified_timestamp and override and we've got newer version.
The reason we need to increment the counter even for read which updates the cache is that the read result can be evicted from cache before another read comes back. If we do not update the counter for read, take the first example above for instance:
The entity gets evicted between 4 and 5, Read 1 will find the cached object is empty, and the counter it has is the same as of cache. Then it will go ahead and update the cache with cas=10 which is wrong. Read 1 in this case does not know cas=11 has been read.

Mercury’s requirement for aggressive GC of their entity type
Jun  2022
Jineet Desai
In-progress

## Problem Statement
Mercury wants to increase the scale of their entity count to around 10k. While creating the entities they set the expiration_timestamp_usecs for the entity as {creation_timestamp of entity + 15 mins}. After 15 mins, they wouldn’t hold any account for those entities. However these entities can still remain in IDF upto 1hr (since the auto_delete frequency is currently 1hr for IDF). So it may happen that in 1 hr we can end up having 40k inactive + 10k active entities in IDF. Hence the requirement from their side is to configure the periodicity of auto_delete according to an entity type and do aggressive garbage collection for their entity type.

[IDF Design Documents | Aggressive GC of Mercury_s etype_]

(We now perform per shard per etype scan instead of per shard scan). Reference: http://codereview.nutanix.net/D20129 Here we can plan to have a field called auto_delete_periodicity_for_etype_secs in the EntityType proto.
