However the maximum frequency of auto-delete that we can have for an entity type is governed by insights_entity_auto_delete_process_schedule_interval_seconds.(we change the value of this gflag from 1hr to 15 mins). So even if you set a value for field auto_delete_periodicity_for_etype_secs that is lower than 15 mins, the auto-delete frequency for that entity type shall remain 15 mins. [IDF Design Documents | Atomic Batch Commit Support in IDF]
Atomic Batch Commit Support in IDF
Devendra, Sumit
July 2025
[In-Progress]

## Introduction
Current BatchUpdate and BatchDelete support in IDF is not atomic and the batch might fail/pass partially. This causes overhead on the client side to keep retrying until the whole batch is applied or rolled back successfully. Even adding retries on client side does not guarantee consistent state, as some other client might overwrite the entities in the middle of retries.
Multiple clients of IDF have expressed the need for Atomic Batch Commit support. In this document, we will discuss the design options available for adding the atomic batch commit support in IDF.

[IDF Design Documents | Avoid missing data caused by disabling the auto-registration (ENG-175605)]
## Problem
When replicating entities, we disabled the auto-registration of the entity type (ENG-144653). For PE->PC sync, we rely on the fact that PC should always be ahead of PE, so that PE should never see an entity type which is not on PC.
However, this does not hold anymore when it comes to PC->PE sync. Thus, when it replicates the entity, it finds that the entity type is not registered so it just logs error, calls the done_cb and returns: https://opengrok.eng.nutanix.com/source/xref/xi-5.10-EA/insights/insights_server/store/insights_replication_ops.cc#1618
As a result, this entity will be missing.
This could happen in the following scenarios:
When PE is being upgraded. The clients of IDF might have upgraded while IDF is still running in the old version. Such client might request for the new type while IDF is dropping all data of that type since it does not understand it.
If clients dynamically registers any new type on the master and expects to see the data of it on the replica, we will see this same problem since the type may/maynot exists in the replica. (Clients are discouraged from doing so)

[IDF Design Documents | Avoid missing data caused by disabling the auto-registration (ENG-175605)]
## Solution
We can do a stream per entity type (just for the missing types case).
We track all missing types of the <cluster, shard>. When the type is later registered on the replica, we'll associate the missing ranges with the type that is inverse of the current missing ranges (e.g. if the current missing ranges is [100, 200), [1000..INF), then the missing ranges with the type would be [0..100), [200, 1000)), then send back the current missing ranges and the missing ranges for the type, so that the master would only re-sync entities that belong to this type.

[IDF Design Documents | Avoid missing data caused by disabling the auto-registration (ENG-175605)]
## ReplicaRemoteData The replication of entities is range based. So the updating of the missing ranges map is done when the whole range finishes processing. Thus we collect all missing entity types of the whole range in a temporary set, which will be saved to the ReplicationStateObject (via PersistMissingTypes) before actually updating the missing ranges map (via UpdateMissingRanges). This will happen when the whole range has been processed. Here we need to persist the missing types before updating the missing ranges map so as to keep it update-to-date (any update in the missing ranges map must have been gone to the missing_types_and_ranges) Void PersistMissingTypes() { Auto obj = GetReplicationStateObject(); Auto current_inverse_ranges = GetInverseRanges(obj->missing_ranges_map); For entity_type in missing_types: Auto& existing_inverse_ranges_map = obj->missing_types_info[entity_type]; Merge(existing_inverse_ranges_map, current_inverse_ranges); ScheduleFlushReplicationStateToCassandra(); } After the whole replication payload has been processed, before collecting the remaining missing ranges (GetRangesToResend), we check if any entity_type is now registered. And if so, we will add the inverse_missing_ranges of the type to the reply payload. Void MaybeResyncEntityTypes(cluster_uuid, shard_guid, ret) { For entity_type_info in replication_state_obj.missing_types: Const string& entity_type = entity_type_info.first If entity_type is registered: AddMissingRanges(ret,

[IDF Design Documents | Avoid missing data caused by disabling the auto-registration (ENG-175605)]
## Pros & Cons
Pros:
Sync_barrier won’t be blocked since the missing range is filled up even if the data point is dropped.
If the type is dynamically registered, we could also catch up the data of this type when the type is registered to the replica side later.
Cons:
If the sync barrier is expecting any data of the missing type, this solution will mistakenly respond to the clients that the data has been replicated which in fact is not. This means the semantic of the sync barrier could potentially be broken during when there is any data of unknown types during replication.
Since we are cleaning up the whole missing range map of a shard, this could result in a re-sync of all data of that shard, which could be potentially huge (think of the evictable entities).
Currently, we do not have evictable types synced from PC to PE.

Batch Update / Delete Entities Cassandra only supports atomic operations on a single row. As a result, IDF only provides an atomic updating / deletion of a single entity and advises clients use a loop to send UpdateEntity / DeleteEntity request one by one. However, there is a requirement from NuCalm team on providing updating / deleting entities in batch, for potentially better end-end performant operations on large number of entities. This document describes the requirements from the client and design of the batch updating / deletion logic in IDF. Requirements from the Client The new API takes a list of UpdateEntityArg and returns a list of UpdateEntityRet for each entity; The API should support up to 1000 entities; The batch API is asynchronous, unordered, and non-atomic. Though operation on each entity will be still atomic, the operation on multiple entities cannot be atomic. Upon failures, the client is responsible for resending entities which have failed. “Unordered” means that the API does not support any specified sequence of the mutation of entities in IDF; Corresponding APIs should be provided in CPDB impl tools as well; A preliminary benchmark should be provided for the cost comparison with the existing UpdateEntity / DeleteEntity APIs; Design in IDF The implementation of the batch version of UpdateEntity / DeleteEntity will be basically a wrapper around the existing APIs. We will not do the batch in Cassandra APIs. This is because batching in the existing Cassandra

[IDF Design Documents | Batch Update _ Delete Entities]

This is because batching in the existing Cassandra API PaxosBatchMutate will not give us any benefits but add more complexity in the store layer of IDF. Coordinator RPC Layer Two new APIs BatchUpdateEntities and BatchDeleteEntities will be created, together with their arguments: BatchUpdateEntitiesArg and BatchDeleteEntitiesArg: message BatchUpdateEntitiesArg { // Required. Each item includes an entity which is going to be updated. repeated UpdateEntityArg update_entity_arg_list; } message BatchDeleteEntitiesArg { // Required. Each item includes an entity which is going to be deleted. repeated DeleteEntityRet delete_entity_ret_list; } In addition, a gflag insights_max_entities_for_batch_update_delete will be created to set a limit on the number of entities in BatchUpdateEntitiesArg / BatchDeleteEntitiesArg. If the limit is exceeded, kInvalidRequest will be returned. Node RPC Layer NodeBatchUpdateEntitiesArg and NodeBatchDeleteEntitiesArg will be created accordingly. Each NodeBatchUpdateEntities / NodeBatchDeleteEntities will wrap NodeUpdateEntity / NodeDeleteEntity for each entity into InsightsRpcFnExecutor. In NodeBatchUpdateEntitiesDone and NodeBatchDeleteEntitiesDone, the status of each entity will be collected and returned to the client. [IDF Design Documents | CPD-1026 Support Entity Purging High level requirements]
CPD-1026 Support Entity
Purging High level requirements

## Problem statement:
Similar to Metric Data Purging we need to add support for Entity Purging, as the deleted entities can grow to large amount and consume space. This is needed for Scale in Alerts, Snapshots. We have noticed in Scale setup with 9 million+ deleted entities which increase IDF startup time and also consume space.
Certain client (e.g. alert) would need IDF to perform entity deletion automatically based on certain predefined policy.

## Approach we agreed on:
Separate IDF TTL from Cassandra TTL
IDF TTL goes through the normal IDF DeleteEntity flow
Cassandra TTL only applicable on deleted entities tombstones.

[IDF Design Documents | CPD-1026 Support Entity Purging High level requirements]
## IDF-IDF sync, replication of delete operation from PE to PC relies on tombstone being present.
Sample scenario:
Assume initially PE and PC synced up and both have entity E1
PE detached from PC, then E1 got deleted from PE while the change couldn’t be sync with PC
Time has elapsed pass the retention period of E1 after the deletion and the tombstone got purged from Cassandra.
PE reconnected with PC and start the sync. PE send over the latest entities sync, however, since the deleted entities has been removed, the deletion won’t be able to sync to the PC.
The deleted entity might stay in PC forever.
Solution:
This is a realistic scenario that we need to address, solution might be to implement a “missing deletion” sync: PC to request a full snapshot of the current entity ids from the master (PE) and PC would remove any entity if the last updated time is less than the snapshot timestamp that doesn’t exist in PC. For more details about this functionality, please refer to following doc last paragraph (might need update).

[IDF Design Documents | CPD-1026 Support Entity Purging High level requirements]
## PC to PE fanout relies on GetEntites returning deleted entities to check for create+delete race conditions.
Sample Scenario:
PC Fan out number of entity creations to PE
PC checks on creation status by using GetEntity with deleted entities to capture the possible concurrent deletions.
If deleted entity got purged out, this request might never get any entities back causing the check to wait forever.
>> @Ramesh Are u aware of any client using this pattern to check on status of an entity creation?
Solution:
This is a highly unlikely scenario and unless the TTL is set to very small interval, the deleted entity tombstone should stay there by the the GetEntities request is sent.

[IDF Design Documents | CPD-1026 Support Entity Purging High level requirements]
## Today, we check for created ts > deleted ts and ensure increasing cas values when entity id is reused after delete. This relies on metadata stored with tombstone.
Sample Scenario:
PC has replicated entity E1
E1 got deleted
E1 then got recreated using the same ID after the tombstone TTL has elapsed and got deleted from Cassandra.
Any future update of the same entity won’t be able to pick up the last CAS value associated with last deletion operation.
If there’s a delayed update got replicated to the PC after this with an old CAS value lower than deleted cas value, that would have been applied and entity update would have been successful rather than being rejected.
Solution:
This is possible but unlikely scenario in practical as the TTL for tombstone should be practically long enough to make this scenario unlikely to happen. We might need to document this so that user be aware of this.

[IDF Design Documents | CPD-1026 Support Entity Purging High level requirements]
## Entity trail doesn't have latest update, it contains only updates prior to latest. Cassandra TTL purging has to ensure delete entity is placed in trail, otherwise after purging the trail will be incomplete.
Sample Scenario:
If the entity got deleted and the time elapsed long enough such that the tombstone got delete from Cassandra. The deleted entity won’t be written into the trail such that the full fidelity guarantee might be violated in this case.
Solution:
Today trail lives forever, one possible way address this while keeping the trail guarantee is to implement TTL on trail as well such as when a deleted entity got TTL purged from Cassandra. That means the life of the entity ends there , therefore corresponding trail could be purged as well.  But since currently we don’t have trail turned on either on PC or PE, therefore we could take it up for a separate task as a TODO.

PC to PE fanout relies on GetEntites returning deleted entities to check for create+delete race conditions.
Today, we check for created ts > deleted ts and ensure increasing cas values when entity id is reused after delete. This relies on metadata stored with tombstone.

Entity trail doesn't have latest update, it contains only updates prior to latest. Cassandra TTL purging has to ensure delete entity is placed in trail, otherwise after purging the trail will be incomplete.

[IDF Design Documents | CPD-1026 Support Entity Purging]
## Introduction
This document describes the implementation details for Entity Purging. For more information about the problem concerned, please refer to the CPD-1026 Support Entity Purging High level requirements doc.
The tombstone refers to entities which have been marked as deleted in the current logic. After the implementation of Entity Purging, the tombstones will still remain in DB, but instead of staying forever, they will be purged after a specific period of time.
The master and the replica are terms used during sync-up from PE to PC. When PE registers itself to PC, its data will be replicated/synced to PC. In the sync-up process, the data source (PE in this case) will be called master and the data target (PC in this case) will be called replica.
You may see the term auto-deletable entities, which refers to entities that needs to be automatically deleted (from cache). Please differentiate this from evictable entities. Besides, please also differentiate purge and delete. Delete means delete from cache (no longer accessible by user) and purge means the tombstone gets purged from DB.

[IDF Design Documents | CPD-1026 Support Entity Purging]
## Requirements
Automatically delete expired entities (defined as auto-deletable)
Clean up tombstones for deleted entities from Cassandra. Currently all deleted entities will be turned into tombstones. But however, they will stay in the Cassandra forever since we don’t have a mechanism to finally remove them from Cassandra which may cause some issues such as waste of storage and heavily slowing down the starting up of the cluster.
All tombstones should purged after some time.

[IDF Design Documents | CPD-1026 Support Entity Purging]
## Decide which entities need to be auto-deleted and when to auto-delete them.
Allow user to configure entity level expiration timestamp:
Add expiration_timestamp_usecs (optional) attribute to Entity proto. This is different from the TTL as it is an exact date instead of being related to the creation timestamp. (e.g 12/28/2016 14:22:56 GMT)
It is -1 by default, meaning not applicable.
User MUST set this field to non-negative if they want to auto-delete the entity (0 will be treated as not keep, and will get deleted once it is discovered).
Allow user to update the expiration timestamp via UpdateEntity rpc.
Implement a background process to scan periodically (interval is configurable by gflag “insights_entity_auto_delete_process_schedule_interval_seconds”, default to be 1 hour) on entities in cache and check for the expiration timestamp of auto-deletable entities.
The deletion is carried out entity by entity, by calling DeleleEntityFromShard() API (not batched).
NOTE: We do not auto-delete replicated entities on the replica. The deletion of replicated entities should always be synced from the master.

[IDF Design Documents | CPD-1026 Support Entity Purging]
## Have a mechanism to actually purge tombstones.
Add the deleted_entity_retention_in_days to TypeInfo proto. If this field is not set or invalid, it will be set to gflag “insights_deleted_entity_default_retention_in_days” (7 days by default). We use ttl rather than expiration date here since the time to purge is always based on the deleted timestamp. It is more an internal garbage collection mechanism than a user related functionality.
The cassandra doesn’t support ttl on the paxos column, so we need some mechanism to detect and actively purge the tombstones. Here, we have another background process which regularly scans the latest entities CF and check on the deleted timestamp. If the (now time) - (deleted timestamp) > (tombstone TTL), we will purge it by calling into the existing SchedulePurgeOldDeletedEntities logic.

[IDF Design Documents | CPD-1026 Support Entity Purging]
## Possible missing deletes The issue may occur because the incremental sync (PE sync every create/update/delete right to PC after the completion of the operation) may be interrupted because of disconnection which is longer than the TTL of the tombstones. If that happens, then the master will have no way of knowing that the entity has been deleted so neither does the replica. (Please refer to “IDF-IDF sync, replication of delete operation from PE to PC relies on tombstone being present” in the High Level Design doc for detailed info). So the basic question is “How does the replica know what entities have been deleted”. The solution is as following: Whenever a missing range is received by the master, besides processing the missing range (existing logic), it will also process the request for ids of active entities per shard (namely active_entities_info). Add new field “bool load_active_entities_info” to RemoteTransferDataRet proto. It is set by the replica, indicating that whether a new active_entities_info is requested from the master. The active entities info is used to be compared with the active entities on the replica. Those not exist in the snapshot but in the replica are considered as missing deletions and will be deleted. The replica keeps track of the timestamp of when the last active entities info was received. It is the time of receiving the snapshot instead of coming from the active entities info. This timestamp is used to calculate the ttl of the active entities

[IDF Design Documents | CPD-1026 Support Entity Purging]
last active entities info was received. It is the time of receiving the snapshot instead of coming from the active entities info. This timestamp is used to calculate the ttl of the active entities info (effectiveness). We use a gflag insights_active_entities_info_ttl_secs to control the ttl of this snapshot so that we do not send the request whenever the missing range is requested. When it passed the ttl, a request for a new active entities info will be sent along with the missing range. Create a new proto ActiveEntitiesInfo to represent the information needed in an active entities info: active_entities_info_timestamp_usecs: the time when the snapshot is taken. (This is the timestamp from the TimeOracle) entity_guid_list: ids of active entities by shard throughout the whole cluster. Add the new field “ActiveEntitiesInfo active_entities_info” to UpdateData proto so that we can incorporate this new logic into the current sync-up stream (all the active entities info, the missing ranges and the heartbeat are sent via the RemoteTransferData rpc). Add a gflag insights_active_entities_info_request_suppress_time_secs to suppress the duplicate requests for the same active entities snapshot (identified by shard id and entity type) so as to prevent the master from being bumped with the requests for active entities snapshot. The master will create a response which is stamped with the latest timestamp coming from the timestamp oracle (at the start time of the snapshot operation), and load

[IDF Design Documents | CPD-1026 Support Entity Purging]
the requests for active entities snapshot. The master will create a response which is stamped with the latest timestamp coming from the timestamp oracle (at the start time of the snapshot operation), and load the latest entities column family to get the ids of active entities and put them to the response. Then it sends the response back to the replica. Add a new rpc LoadActiveEntitiesInfo to allow the uploader to acquire the active entities info from the PE(master). Why we need a timestamp from the TimeOracle: For example, if a delete on entity E1 happens, then there is a snapshot taken, and then there is a recreation of this entity. It is possible that the recreation is received prior to the snapshot. Since the snapshot doesn’t include E1, the replica will update E1 (because of the recreation) and then delete it (because of the snapshot). When requesting the timestamp from the TimeOracle, an exclusive lock needs to be grabbed so that the “get timestamp from TimeOracle” and “modifying entities” cannot happen concurrently. All updates takes a shared lock so that they can happen concurrently. This lock is used to guarantee the atomicity between “acquiring time from oracle” and “successfully write to Cassandra”. We grab the write lock before taking the active entities snapshot so as to make sure all updates/insertions/deletions have completed (i.e. written to Cassandra). The lock is released as soon as it is grabbed rather than after the completion of taking the snapshot since

[IDF Design Documents | CPD-1026 Support Entity Purging]
snapshot so as to make sure all updates/insertions/deletions have completed (i.e. written to Cassandra). The lock is released as soon as it is grabbed rather than after the completion of taking the snapshot since we only need to get the timestamp so that later we can do the filtering on it. For example: Thread1 is going to insert entity A, got timestamp = 40. Snapshot thread took the latest value of the timestamp oracle: 50. (At this time, the 40 has NOT yet been written to Cassandra). Then if we first replicate the inserted entity with timestamp 40 and then apply snapshot with timestamp 50, we'll delete a newly inserted entity without the lock. If we have the lock, the 50 cannot be taken by the snapshot before 40 finished. We should scan the latest entities CF rather than the cache in this case. For example: New entity is inserted Successfully written to Cassanda, but failed to be written to cache Snapshot is taken and gets later timestamp Then the newly created entity will be deleted because the snapshot has a later timestamp. On receiving the active entities info, the replica will compare it with its own entities and delete those not exist in the snapshot via the ReplicateEntity() API. Notice that we are not using the DeleteEntity API since it doesn’t set the db_modified_timestamp correctly for replicated entities. The modified_timestamp_usecs and the deleted_timestamp_usecs of these entities are set to “modified_timestamp_usecs + 1” instead of “WallTime::NowUsecs()”

[IDF Design Documents | CPD-1026 Support Entity Purging]
we are not using the DeleteEntity API since it doesn’t set the db_modified_timestamp correctly for replicated entities. The modified_timestamp_usecs and the deleted_timestamp_usecs of these entities are set to “modified_timestamp_usecs + 1” instead of “WallTime::NowUsecs()” because we don’t know the actual time of the deletion. The clocks can be unsynced between PE and PC thus we should not use the clock on PC (WallTime::NowUsesc()) to set the deletion time. For unevictable entities, we will get the needed information from cache, while for evictable entities, we will load them from Cassandra. (Alternatively, we could index the db_modified_timestamp_usecs to avoid scanning the Cassandra. But considering this is low priority processing, do we want to keep that information in memory?)

## Auto-delete TTL
The alternative solution is to place the auto-delete ttl in the EntityType proto. The reason for this is because previously we assume that entities of the same time are expected to have the same behavior concerning the auto-deletion. However, this no longer holds due to the new  requirement from Alerts, e.g for resolved and unresolved tasks (different states) we may want to keep them for different time. So we need the ttl to be in smaller granularity (entity-based).

[IDF Design Documents | CPD-1026 Support Entity Purging]
## Expiration date vs. TTL
Originally, we call it TTL since we calculate the retention period based on the created timestamp. However, after later discussion, we find that it makes more sense if we allow more explicit control on the deletion rather than such a TTL. This TTL is based on the creation timestamp which may or may not be relevant to the time to delete. So we leave it to the user app to decide exactly when to delete the entity, e.g after the task is completed, IDF does not and should not know what “completed” means to the task.
Also, the new design (expiration date) can still support the old TTL semantic except that the user now needs to do the calculation.

## Future Work
How to clean up the historical data (old existing data might also need to be cleaned)?
We can schedule a upgrade time during which we read entities which need to be purged and write them back with the new attribute added.
Should we purge the entity trail as well?
Apply the same lock to LoadEntityTrail.

Have a mechanism to actually purge tombstones.

[IDF Design Documents | CPD-2069_ reducing contention for LookupTenantId]
## Problem
Looking up tenant IDs for entities via LookupTenantId(entity_type, entity_id) is causing performance issues due to lock contention.
This function walks the structure tenant_id_map_ in order to find the tenant ID for a particular entity.  If the entity is not in the tenant_id_map_ then the default tenant ID for the entity type is returned.
https://jira.nutanix.com/browse/CPD-2069

## Use a read locker
This will alleviate much of the issue.  Ning observed a 3x improvement for certain workloads with this modification.

## Keep a set of entity types that don’t all use the default ID
Assumptions:
Most entity types always use the default tenant ID
The set of entity types that do not use the default tenant ID does not change with high frequency.
Create a set etypes_with_mixed_tids_. This set is filled with the entity types that contain entities that do not have the default tenant ID.
Everytime LookupTenantId(entity_type, entity_id) is called, first do a lookup in etypes_with_mixed_tids_.  If the entity type is not present then immediately return the default tenant ID for that entity type.
Checking etypes_with_mixed_tids_ will only require a read lock, and since it will not be modified frequently there should be very little contention.  It will also me much faster to walk through this structure due to its small size.

[IDF Design Documents | CPD-2069_ reducing contention for LookupTenantId]
## Add optional arguments to LookupTenantId()
The purpose of this optimization is to reduce work when the caller is calling LookupTenantId multiple times in a row.

## Optional argument: default tenant ID
Allow the caller to provide the default tenant ID for the entity type.  This saves a cache lookup for the entity type.

## Optional argument: is the entity type in etypes_with_mixed_tids_?
Allow the caller to check if the entity type is in the set etypes_with_mixed_tids_.  This avoids grabbing a read lock in the common case.
headings: Keep a set of entity types that don’t all use the default ID
Optional argument: is the entity type in etypes_with_mixed_tids_?

CPD-2105 Metric data snapshot dynamic throttling to handle bursty client metric data

[IDF Design Documents | CPD-2105 Metric data snapshot dynamic throttling._]
## Problem statement We've seen multiple oncalls recently with customer that’s upgraded to 5.5 or 5.6 releases predominantly related with small PC 16GB going out of memory, one common scenario seems to be VMBL plugin running and inserting large amount of data, within one hour, it could insert upto 2500 VM metric data X 6 metrics x 21 X 24 hours which exceed the limit that IDF could hold up in memory within an hour boundary, so before IDF had a chance to flushing the data into the Cassandra, it will crash, as VMBL will continue inserting other metrics while this process goes on. As IDF crashes, VMBL may fail to record and checkpoint of the progress which will cause the same compute to repeat again which will lead to IDF crash again repeatedly. Some referenced on calls which pointed to the same issue are listed as following: https://jira.nutanix.com/browse/ONCALL-3916 https://jira.nutanix.com/browse/ONCALL-3983 https://jira.nutanix.com/browse/ONCALL-3722 https://jira.nutanix.com/browse/TH-424 https://jira.nutanix.com/browse/ENG-150803 https://jira.nutanix.com/browse/TH-455 Currently metric data snapshot logic use a simple throttling algorithm which statically divides the total number of metric data set that was buffered from the previous that needs to be saved to cassandra by the number of snapshot intervals (by default 240 * 15 seconds interval) within the snapshot window (default 1 hour), the algorithm will also continuously buffer up the metric data that is received within

[IDF Design Documents | CPD-2105 Metric data snapshot dynamic throttling._]
by the number of snapshot intervals (by default 240 * 15 seconds interval) within the snapshot window (default 1 hour), the algorithm will also continuously buffer up the metric data that is received within the current hour till the time window moves to the next hour and start flushing. This algorithm works well when IDF is under constant workload as the real time stats flow in. There are at least two scenario where this algorithm may face challenges where IDF may run into memory stress which could eventually lead to OOM. PE-PC bootstrap, where PE is trying to push selective historical stats for certain VM/VDisk/Vnic metrics for the last 3 month. VMBL background process perform compute on various metrics for all VMs which writes 3 weeks of future prediction metric data into IDF. Either of the above process would insert so much data into IDF in short period of time which IDF can not buffer for upto an hour which leads to the RSS to blow up.

[IDF Design Documents | CPD-2105 Metric data snapshot dynamic throttling._]
## High level design Assumption IDF should be able to handle normal real time stats workload without having to do any of the following changes. The proposed changes are meant to handle bursty short lived workload that is usually related metric data catch up, bootstrap scenarios, bulk writes mode as associated with certain client logic (such as VMBL prediction logic). Detailed design After a metric data set completes flushing to cassandra, the clean metric data objects (those has been merged, saved in cassandra) that are contained in the set still remain pinned in the set, only the set cache object is unpinned, the metric data will only be unpinned and removed from the set if the set itself got evicted. If by any chance the set is updated again (this is often the case with VMBL workflow where client keeps updating the same metric for different groups of entities) with some new data which belong to some other entities, the set will got pinned again and will not be flushed again for another hour. This could lead to those clean data which otherwise could have been removed from the cache after the snapshot force to remain in cache for much longer than needed. We could actually immediately unpin and remove the clean data from the set and mark the MetricDataSet to be kNotMerged status thus enable the clean metric data subject to eviction. The snapshot process issues ReadMetricData call to the dirty metric data set in order to merge the data, we will perform the clean up on the call

[IDF Design Documents | CPD-2105 Metric data snapshot dynamic throttling._]
the clean metric data subject to eviction. The snapshot process issues ReadMetricData call to the dirty metric data set in order to merge the data, we will perform the clean up on the call back of this specific Read. ReadMetricDataByShard call will also be used by the read path from user query, where the clean up will not happen so that the on-access cache functionality will not be affected. The above modification to the snapshot algorithm shall work well in relieving the memory pressure for the data that’s already been flushed in the current hour. However, it will not help should the burst metric data ingestion happens in the current hour where the snapshot won’t happen in the next hour. To address this, we could have a dynamically throttling mechanism that works as following: We shall check the current IDF RSS usage at the beginning of the snapshot cycle, If the RSS usage is under the low water mark FLAGS_insights_rss_low_watermark_pct, the snapshot process will continue the current pace without any changes, the number of metric data set that will be process shall be equal to the the total number of remaining dirty set divided by the remaining snapshot cycles remains in the current hour. If the RSS usage is above low water mark threshold as defined by FLAGS_insights_rss_low_watermark_pct or at the beginning of the snapshot process cycle, that’s indication that the snapshot might be lagging, or we could reasonably speed up the snapshotting by processing more metric data set

[IDF Design Documents | CPD-2105 Metric data snapshot dynamic throttling._]
defined by FLAGS_insights_rss_low_watermark_pct or at the beginning of the snapshot process cycle, that’s indication that the snapshot might be lagging, or we could reasonably speed up the snapshotting by processing more metric data set (by applying a predefined multiplication factor). The number of increased number of metric data set in the past cycle shall be kept till next snapshot cycle start. Should the memory usage continue exceeding the watermark thresholding in the current cycle, we shall continue applying the multiplication factors to the number of sets that was saved in the previous cycle and will save more metric data set in the current snapshot window. Should the memory usage not exceeding the watermark thresholding in the current cycle, we shall reset the number of metric data to be save to be normal as calculated in step a) We will also gauge the end to end latency for the current snapshot process, should the latency exceeds the snapshot interval, that’s indication that the pace of saving has exceed the speed that cassandra perform the persistences, therefore the in the next cycle we will not increase number of set to be saved even if the memory continue to exceed the watermark threshold, this is to properly ensure that IDF will not overwhelm the cassandra by writing too much data at any given cycle even if it is under the memory stress. If by any chance the complete set of the metric data has been exhausted by applying above “accelerated” snapshotting

[IDF Design Documents | CPD-2105 Metric data snapshot dynamic throttling._]
too much data at any given cycle even if it is under the memory stress. If by any chance the complete set of the metric data has been exhausted by applying above “accelerated” snapshotting throttling (step b, c and d) and memory is still exceeding the watermark, we shall start persisting the metric data set in the current snapshot bucket by applying the same rule as defined in step a, b, c., The initial set of metrics to be persisted will be fixed at a small seed number (such as 100) to allow as small as possible amount of metric data to be saved ahead of its expected snapshot window. If any time IDF is exceeding FLAGS_insights_rss_high_watermark_pct, it will start failing PutMetricDataCall which contains data that is beyond the boundary what it considered to be real time data (< current time - some hours or > current time + some hours) by kRetry error as a sufficient protective mechanism from failing on out of memory should the client continue inserting out of order data.

[IDF Design Documents | CPD-2105 Metric data snapshot dynamic throttling._]
## Limitations
If IDF ever runs into “accelerated” snapshot mode as described in b) and e) and eventually spill over to the current hour, we will be start snapshotting the data that’s stored in the current hour window, that means we could be saving data set that might be still keeping on accumulating. Which will cause multiple partial snapshot to a metric set. However, with the way is designed, I don’t expect this to happen so often unless IDF is really under significant data load is lasting long time which is not sufficient.  As the max number of data set to be save at each cycle is gated by the number as described in step d)  If the client continue to push data that far exceeding IDF could absorb. It will eventually fall into step f which will fall back to client retry error which should be extremely rare.

[IDF Design Documents | CPD-2205 design_ total entity quota]
## Problem
https://jira.nutanix.com/browse/CPD-2205
We need to enforce a limit on the number of entities that can be created.
The purpose of this feature is to make recovering from a type of client failure easier.  Sometimes a client will start creating tons of entities (while in an “error state”) which eventually overloads the system.

## Solution
The number of entities will be determined by two gflags:
FLAGS_insights_unevictable_entity_per_node_limit = ??
FLAGS_insights_evictable_entity_per_node_limit = ??
If the total number of entities exceeds one of the thresholds above then the error kTotalEntityCountExceeded is returned.
The entity count is tallied on a per-node basis.  This is simpler and has lower overhead than attempting to keep a global count.  Although this could lead to a situation where some entities are accepted and some are rejected, this doesn’t matter for the following reasons.
The number of entities sharded to one node does not put memory pressure of other nodes.
A significantly unbalanced shard map is unlikely as long as the client is using non-adversarially chosen entity IDs.
This limit is for the sake of preserving IDF’s sanity, not the client’s.  The client is already in an error state.

[IDF Design Documents | CPD-2205 design_ total entity quota]
## Allow creation of “low population” entities
Even if the total entity count gets very, very large we should allow the creation of entities that are not contributing to this problem.  This will allow services that are not in an error state to potentially continue to work.
If the total number of entities for a type is less than 80% of the count of the entities for the largest type then allow for the entity to be created.

[IDF Design Documents | CPD-2279 _ Fix Index map string intern regression]
CPD-2279 : Fix Index map string intern regression in MetricIndexMap
Uddhav Mishra, Aiswarya S
December 2018
In Review

## Customer use case
Ref: https://jira.nutanix.com/browse/CPD-2279
With the upgrade to gcc 7.3.0, the std::string implementation changed to use deep copy instead of copy-on-write. This resulted in multiple copies of entity_id while inserting into MetricIndexMap. This document describes an approach to resolve this issue.

## Suggested Approach:
We presently have a cache object that store Indexed values in the format
ObjectSet { [kMetricIndexMap, entityType] ->  {metric_name ->MetricIndexMap}}
where kMetricIndexMap is the cache key type,
MetricIndexMap is a map of metric value to list of entity ids. eg:
alerts -> { severity, resolved, etc }                    
severity -> true -> { id1 }        
severity -> false -> { id2, id4 }
here , true -> { id1 }, false -> { id2, id4 } are MetricIndexMaps for attribute severity.
With string interning not present, this can cause a lot of overhead. So instead of storing entity ids as strings, we store shared pointers with its values as string
The final MetricIndexMap structure would be:
<indexed_attribute_value> -> unordered_set<shared_ptr<entity_id>>

[IDF Design Documents | CPD-2279 _ Fix Index map string intern regression]
## Considerations
One entity id is stored only once. Whenever an evictable entity is created, we create a shared pointer of that entity and stores it in EntityUuidSet Cache (detailed below). For filling up MetricIndexMap, we use this shared_ptr.
Create, Update and Delete and access workflows remains the same except that we work with shared ptr of entity ids instead of actual values
Performance of the CRUD operations should not be affected.
Query layer also uses MetricIndexMap for faster where clause evaluation. The changes to cache layer should be extensible to query layer with minimal performance regressions.

[IDF Design Documents | CPD-2279 _ Fix Index map string intern regression]
## Changes to Cache Object Structures
We presently have two cache object types that stores evictable entity data. EntityUuidSet and                   MetricIndexMap.
These are the proposed changes in their structure:
EntityUuidSet : Currently stored as unordered set of entity ids. This can be changed to unordered set of shared_ptr of entity ids.
Present: Cache Object is of the format :-
typedef unordered_set<string> EntityIdSet;
<kEntityUuidSet, entity_type_name> -> InsightsObject<EntityIdSet>
Changed to:
Index map is presently stored in cache object in the following format.
Present:
(CacheKeyType::kIndexMap, entity_type) - > Set[
{(CacheKeyType::kIndexMap, metric_name)->MetricIndexMap}]
The MetricIndexMap  currently is a  <indexed_attribute_value> -> EntityIdSet map
Changed to:
<indexed_attribute_value> -> EntityIdPtrSet map
(EntityIdPtrSet is as defined above in EntityUuidSet)

[IDF Design Documents | CPD-2279 _ Fix Index map string intern regression]
## Create/Update/Delete Workflow changes
The IndexMap Cache and the EntityUuidSet Cache are updated by InsightsCassandraStore::IndexIfEvictableEntity method.
Create :-  Create a shared_ptr to the entity_id and add it to EntityUuidSet.  Add the same shared_ptr to MetricIndexMaps
Update:- Create a shared_ptr to entity_id. Use it to retrieve the shared_ptr of the entity_id stored in EntityUuidSet using EntityIdPtrHash . Add/Remove that shared_ptr<entity_id>  from relevant MetricIndexMaps
Delete :-Create a shared_ptr to entity_id. Use it to retrieve the shared_ptr of the entity_id stored in EntityUuidSet. Remove that shared_ptr<entity_id>  from MetricIndexMaps and from EntityUuidSet

## Access Workflow changes
Presently, the MetricIndexMaps are solely accessed by query layer to process queries for evictable entities in case of indexed columns. We access it via the metric value key and access the list shared_ptrs of entity_ids as a whole always. This returns a set of matched entity ids. after applying limits and/or after where clause evaluation, we copy the entity ids stored in them to query_working_entity_id_set in query layer for further processing. This can be optimised once the query layer and store layer can work with  list of shared_ptr<entity_id>s (eg.  in GetEntitiesFromShards,  GetMetricDataFromShards etc)

[IDF Design Documents | CPD-2279 _ Fix Index map string intern regression]
## Query workflow changes Presently, to evaluate where clause, for where columns for non-evictable entities , query layer creates a MetricIndexMap for each ‘where column’ in the query. This is to avoid multiple iterations over the entities. We have to change this MetricIndexMap also to <indexed_attribute_value> -> EntityIdPtrSet map. Along with that, we also have to maintain an QueryEntityUuidPtrSet to ensure a single point copy of the entity_id (The structure of QueryEntityUuidPtrSet is same as EntityUuidPtrset). After fetching a metric for an entity, we create a shared_ptr for that entity and check if that entity is present in the QueryEntityUuidPtrSet using EntityIdPtrHash. If not present, we insert that shared_ptr<entity_id> to QueryEntityUuidPtrSet and adds that entry to MetricIndexMap. If present, we use the shared_ptr<entity_id> from QueryEntityUuidPtrSet to add the entry to MetricIndexMap. This is local and created per query. ## CPD-708 Using customized data structure for in memory metric data cache
Ning Zhou
Mar. 31 2016

## Introduction
This document describe the high level design for the changes that replaces proto buffer messages with compact custom data structure for the in memory metric data cache.
CPD -708:   https://jira.nutanix.com/browse/CPD-708

[IDF Design Documents | CPD-708 Using customized data structure for in memory metric data cache]
## Current state Insights DB cache layer for metric data was implemented as write-back caching mechanism, through which the new metric data that are first copied into the cache layer which will only be persisted to the underlying cassandra store when snapshot process is periodically executed. Currently, when the samples of the metrics are pushed from proxy to the insights DB. They are transported in the form of protobuf messages and data points are copied directly in the original form to the cache layer. In which, each individual sample value were represented in a DataValue proto buffer message format. To understand the memory footprint of the metric data set that are stored in memory, we need to understand how google proto buffer messages in general are laid out in memory. Out of these integer type metrics/attribute, all of the metrics are defined as bucketized metric type. The distant second most common data type is “string” with only about 300 entries with most of them being attribute which belongs to the non-bucketized data set. The timestamp of the each data point can be inferred by (start time stamp + index of the data point * bucketize interval) within the array. When a data point is ingested into the system, it will be inserted into the right bucket within the array based on the timestamp value. Merging of two bucketized data set ordered by time as part of the snapshotting process. Copying of the data into Proto buffer data structure by the data query APIs. Support for Indexing Nested Messages (CPD-710) Swagat Borah March 16 Introduction Requirement document link. Certain REST APIs receive nested objects in the form of JSON which need to be stored in InsightsDB as part of certain entities. There is a need to index and query these entities by attributes within these nested objects. Insights Data fabric should provide a framework which would allow clients to define such indexes on nested objects and then be able to query them like any normal entity attribute, without worrying about the translation mechanism. Problem Currently, the logic to create these indexes rests on the client side where the nested objects need to be flatten out and registered as entity attributes. Each client needs to create their custom implementation and there is little scope of re-use, especially with clients written in multiple languages such as Java, C++ and Python. Nested objects are treated as opaque attribute values in Insights Data Fabric and there is no mechanism to define any metadata around its contents which could be used to query for these nested objects. Design All nested objects are defined in the form of protobuf to comply with the standard messaging format across Nutanix code base. Protobufs have built in support for nested structures which can be taken advantage of. The client should convert any nested objects in the form of JSON, etc to the appropriate protobuf message format The structure of the nested messages need not be provided to

[IDF Design Documents | CPD-710 _ Support for indexing nested messages]
be taken advantage of. The client should convert any nested objects in the form of JSON, etc to the appropriate protobuf message format The structure of the nested messages need not be provided to insights data fabric at compile time and the nested fields can be expressed in terms of indices. ## Introduction
This document addresses the requirements for purging the out of date insightsDB metric data as described in CPD-73 :   https://jira.nutanix.com/browse/CPD-73

## Current state
Currently there’s no age-out mechanism in insightsDB and metric data that gets stored indefinitely which lead to disk space outage.

[IDF Design Documents | CPD-73 Metric data aging]
## New requirements Allows user to specify global Retention period for the historical data for each of the following: Raw metrics data Hourly aggregated data Attribute/Metric specific retention period settings, this would override the global retention settings specified above. Add barrier to the PutMetricData API to drop any data that are older than the raw retention period. Design Outline . Add two gflag setting for specifying the retention period (in weeks) for raw metric data and 1 hour aggregated data. . Create a background data aging process that gets executed at a specific time interval (every 7 days) The aging process will perform the following tasks: . Perform a Full RangeScan on one of the insights_metric_data column family (insights_metric_data_by_entity) to gather the Row Keys for the metric data that are eligible for deletion. The row key format of insights_metric_data_by_entity CF is as following: [hash]\ff[shard]\ff[entity_type]\ff[entity_id]\ff[metric_name]\ff[ds]\ff[ReversedTime] The above format doesn’t allow us to figure out all the metric name and entity id that was collected for a certain timestamp period efficiently. As the row keys are clustered based on entity information (entity type and entity id) and metric names, not by time stamps. Collection of keys eligible for deletion without doing a full scan as for a given entity guid and metric_name, the rows for the metric data for various time frame is hashed across the cassandra token range. Cassandra API

[IDF Design Documents | CPD-73 Metric data aging]
for deletion without doing a full scan as for a given entity guid and metric_name, the rows for the metric data for various time frame is hashed across the cassandra token range. Cassandra API currently support sliceRange request which returns row keys only without sending any column information. However, the underlying implementation in cassandra still scans through the content of a the rows which is not efficient. A ticket has been filed for cassandra team to address this issue. https://jira.nutanix.com/browse/ENG-50033 . The scanning of the keys will be performed in batches in a simple iteration. Key scanning batch size could be much bigger than the current default value of 500. That’s because if the column information is not returned, the returned protoBuffer object could contain large number of keys without violating the proto-buffer size limit of 64MB. . Deletion for the rows in by_entity CF can happen in the same iteration by checking the the timestamp partition of the key. . Consider current time stamp is T1 (in usec), and a given row key to be examined has a timestamp T2. Considering F(T) being a function of a given timestamp in usec, it rounds down to timestamp of the the weekly granularity: F(T) = (T - T % (number of usec in a week)). If the Specified retention period for this data is R (in weeks). Then the row key with T2 will be deleted only if F(T1)-F(T2) > (D * (number of usec in a week)). . Assuming same metric data cell that is stored

## get_all_entities_of_entity_type (etype ET, shard S, time T)
Description:
Get all entity UUIDs from cassandra that belong to type E present in shard S at Time T
Workflow:
compute the week from Time T
Cassandra get slice query
column_family = entities
row_key = S.W.ET
column.slice.start = W, column.slice.finish = T
apply deltas on the starting values to get the state at T
Worst case cost analysis:
Cassandra RPCs = 1
Type of access = sequential access
Data Transfer from Cassandra =  less than 4 MB

Description:
Return the latest shard for the entity
Workflow:
compute the week W
Cassandra get slice query
column_family = entity_shard_map
row_key = E.W
column.slice.finish = T, column.slice.count = 1
Worst case cost analysis:
Cassandra RPCs = 1
Type of access = sequential access
Data Transfer from Cassandra =  Miniscule

Description:

Workflow:
compute the start week W1 and end week W2
Cassandra get range slice query
column_family = entity_shard_map
row_key.start_key = E.W1, row_key.end_key=W2
compute shard pairs [ S, [T1, T2] ]
Worst case cost analysis:
Cassandra RPCs = 1
Type of access = sequential access
Data Transfer from Cassandra =  miniscule

[IDF Design Documents | Cassandra DB Layout]
## get_entity_trail (etype ET, entity_uuid E, start_time T1, end_time T2)
Description:
Get the entity along with its attributes during the time T1 to T2
Workflow:
get_entity_shards (ET, E, T1, T2)
For each pair [ S, [T1, T2] ]
Cassandra get range slice query
column_family = entities
row_key = S.W.ET
column.slice.start = T1, column.slice.finish = T2
The above query will return all other entities that have been updated during T1 and T2, discard them and persist only the latest value for E
Worst case cost analysis:
Cassandra RPCs = # of shard changes for the entity during that time window (typically not many)

Data Transfer from Cassandra =  max. of 4 MB * number of weeks

compute the day D, from Time T
Cassandra get slice query

row_key = D
column.slice.finish = T, column.slice.count = 1
Worst case cost analysis:
Cassandra RPCs = 1

Data Transfer from Cassandra =  Miniscule

compute the hour H from Time T
Cassandra get row query
column_family = metric_data_by_shard
row_key = S.ET.M.T

Cluster Upgrading to Scaleout Mode Introduction Cluster upgrading from leader-only mode to scaleout mode includes two stages: the rolling upgrade and the data upgrade. Rolling upgrade is a process in which each node in the cluster reboots from the binary in leader-only mode to the binary in scaleout mode. It is completed when all nodes in the cluster are running the binary in scaleout mode. During rolling upgrade, some nodes are running in the scale-out mode, while other nodes are still running in the leader-only mode. However, client requests cannot be suspended, which means that until the rolling upgrade is done, we need to make sure that both the leader-only and scale-out mode can be supported in the same cluster. The rolling upgrade is marked as complete when Genesis sets the software version of each node the same as the release version of the whole cluster in zeus_config_. The update on zeus_config_ is notified to each node by a watch called ConfigUpdateCallback() in insights_server.cc. In leader-only mode, all data are stored in Cassandra in Shard 0 while in scaleout both entity and metric data are sharded in Cassandra. Data upgrade is a process in which all data are migrated from the old format (single shard) to the sharded format. Data upgrade follows the rolling upgrade. Please note this document does not include the details on data format upgrade. Instead, this document describes: how a node monitors and handles the rolling upgrade and, how the data upgrade in the

When a scaleout-mode node is up, it first reads the shard map from ZK (in ReadNodeMapEntryProto ()). If the shard map is not empty in ZK, it means the cluster has already been in scaleout mode and the status is set to kScaleout. The bootstrap process will follow the normal scaleout-mode routine without trigger any data upgrade. If the shard map in ZK is empty, it reads the configure file from ZK in ConfigUpdateCallback(). If the configure file shows the cluster is not in a rolling upgrade, the status is set to kStoreUpgrade, and starts a thread for the data upgrade. It won’t enter the scaleout mode until ReadNodeMapEntryProto() notifies it of the shard map is ready by the leader. If the node is the leader, it starts the data upgrade in the store layer. In the done callback of the data upgrade , it calls StartPeerMonitor(), in which a shard map is generated and uploaded to ZK and all nodes are notified, and hence the scaleout mode is started. ## Proposal:
The onerous of daily downsampling is the fact if the requested daily sample is not already in the cache, we need fetch up to 24 hours of raw data or houly (if available) in order to resolve the daily downsampled value for the requests, this could translate into lots of cassandra read if the data is not already in the cache (most likely not for that long period of time).
One way to address this is to find a way keep merged daily sample in cache for longer (for as long as upto 1 day while it keeps receiving raw data while merging into the existing data structure) to avoid the thrashing (eviction + reload + re-computation, or invalidation + reload + re-computation) cycles. As once the daily downsample data got evicted, to reconcile again, at the worst case it would require a recomputation of the entire 24 hour raw data or hourly data which is costly, especially if we want to snapshot the data periodically to cassandra.

[IDF Design Documents | Daily Downsample Design Proposal(1)]
## General
Introduce a new value in MetricDataDownSamplingInterval:  kDaily.
For downsample in memory as well as on-disk proto data structure, we could add two timestamp: “first_timestamp_usec” and “last_timestamp_usec” for keeping track of the range of the raw data that’s merged into daily downsample data structure so far. They represents the very first and the very last data points in terms of timestamp. If an ingested raw data timestamp is falling outside the range above, as it is the case of always monotonically increasing timestamp of new samples.  Only if the new ingested data timestamp falls into the range that’s represented by these two timestamp, the daily data cache object will be invalidated.  These timestamps will help DS metric cache data remain merged state for longer rather than being invalidated indiscriminately every time we received a new piece of data.
Introduce a new state : InsightsObjectMergedFromDatabase::kPartialMerge, this is specifically used to represent the state of a daily downsample (potentially for hourly DS data as well) such that the inmemory cache data could be potentially incrementally merged with the persisted (on-disk) version.

## Option To Directly Purge Tombstone via DeleteEntity
September 2025
[In progress]
Jineet DesaiPradhyumna KomatineniDevendra Shekhawat

## Introduction
Flow Team is planning to migrate some entity types from PC to Flow-SMSP in Janus. These entity types are currently owned/mastered/created on PC and also syncs to PE (from PC). After migration to Flow-SMSP they want these entities to sync from Flow-SMSP to PC as well as PE.
Migration process planned from their side is:-
Copy all the entities using CFS sync pipeline to Flow-SMSP
Delete these entities from PC after all the entities have been copied to SMSP
Register Flow SMSP with PC to enable entity sync from Flow-SMSP to PC and PE
Currently, deleted entity tombstone is also retained for up to 1 week and synced entities can not overwrite local (tombstone or alive) entities irrespective of incarnation ID also. This will hamper the entities for these entity types to sync from Flow SMSP to PC. Hence the Flow team requires a solution for sync to be enabled after migration from Flow-SMSP to PC & PE.
Ticket to track this change: https://jira.nutanix.com/browse/ENG-829333

[IDF Design Documents | Delete RPC_ Allow Tombstone Removal]
## Proposed Solutions
Option 1
Provide an option in the DeleteEntity RPC call to fully delete the entity from backend (i.e. leave no tombstone on the backend Cassandra or Chakr DB on a delete)
Option 2
Provide an option at entity type level to always allow overriding local tombstones with replicated entities.
One key concern with Option 2 is that it involves introducing a feature at the entity type level, solely to support a single team's use case and a one-time migration effort.

## Enhance the DeleteEntity RPC
As part of the solution, we propose introducing a new option directly_purge_on_delete within the DeleteEntity RPC. When enabled, this flag will ensure that entity deletion also removes the associated tombstone from the backend store (Cassandra/ChakrDb), rather than retaining it for the default tombstone retention period which is 1 week as of now.

[IDF Design Documents | Delete RPC_ Allow Tombstone Removal]
## Concerns with IDF sync due to removal of entity tombstones:
The removal of entity tombstones might introduce non-trivial risks for IDF-IDF sync, especially associated with the bootstrap scenarios.
When a DeleteEntity RPC with directly_purge_on_delete=true is issued:
The associated entity and its tombstone are completely purged from the backend store.
As a result, the Oracle timestamp (or db_modified_ts) associated with the deletion is also lost.
During an IDF restart, IDF reconstructs the latest_db_modified_ts for each shard based on entities present in the backend.
If the deleted entity was the most recently modified one in a given shard, purging it causes IDF to revert to an older latest_db_modified_ts, potentially leading to missed sync ranges during IDF-IDF bootstrap.

[IDF Design Documents | Delete RPC_ Allow Tombstone Removal]
## Example Scenario that could cause potential issues
Entity e1 belongs to shard s1.
Before deletion, the latest db_modified_ts for shard s1 is t1.
A DeleteEntity call with directly_purge_on_delete=true is issued for e1, with a resulting timestamp update t2(t2 > t1).
e1 is fully purged, including its tombstone.
If IDF restarts at this point:
e1 is no longer available in the backend to contribute to the latest_db_modified_ts reconstruction.
IDF infers t1 as the latest db_modified_ts instead of t2.
If the time range [t1, t2) has already been filled on the replica:
Bootstrap requests for that time range are ignored on the replica side.
Currently as a part of the bootstrap/catchup workflow in IDF-IDF sync, the replica requests the missing ranges from the source. Now if the missing range [t1, t2) has already been filled on the replica, the replica won’t request this missing range again
This leads to missed updates on shard s1 for [t1,t2) in cases where time jump happens on the system back into past.

[IDF Design Documents | Delete RPC_ Allow Tombstone Removal]
## Mitigation Strategy
While processing a DeleteEntity request with directly_purge_on_delete=true, let IDF not generate a new Oracle timestamp (db_modified_ts) for the deletion event. Instead, the deletion will proceed based on the last known db_modified_timestamp of the entity.
Let:
t = the last known db_modified_ts for the target entity
T_latest = the current latest_db_modified_ts for the corresponding shard
Before purging the entity and its tombstone, IDF will perform the following check:
This ensures that:
An entity's deletion is only allowed if its last db_modified_ts is strictly less than the shard’s current latest_db_modified_ts.
The latest_db_modified_ts for the shard will never regress, even after an IDF restart, thereby preserving sync consistency.
Upon receiving a kRetry response, the client is expected to wait for a short period and retry the DeleteEntity request. By the time of retry, it is expected that some other entity update on the same shard will have advanced T_latest, allowing the purge operation to proceed safely.
Since we can only hit this scenario in very rare cases when there was a time-jump and there are no CUD operation between a given entity's update and deletion so it should be ok to not allow deletes in this case and keep the system consistent instead of allowing the delete and hitting sync errors later on.

[IDF Design Documents | Delete RPC_ Allow Tombstone Removal]
## Delayed Replica Deletion via Active Entities Workflow
In scenarios where an entity is deleted and purged using directly_purge_on_delete=true, and that entity was originally eligible for sync, the replica will not be explicitly notified of the deletion. As a result, the stale entity may remain on the replica for up to 6 hours, until it is eventually removed by the Active Entities Workflow.

## Cassandra Ops Batching
We currently use the Paxos Column Family in Cassandra, where IDF-driven updates and deletes are batched using PaxosBatchWrite. However, our auto-purge workflow, which performs Cassandra row deletions, does not utilize batching.
We need to confirm from the Cassandra team whether we can send Cassandra row updates as well as deletes in the same batch for PaxosBatchWrite. If yes, this will require refactoring in insights_cassandra_ops.cc for PaxosBatchWrite.
A separate ticket has been filed from our side to track the changes pertaining to allowing batching with direct purge on delete as well: https://jira.nutanix.com/browse/ENG-847325

## Table
If t >= T_latest:
    Reject the delete request with a kRetry error

Detached Entity Reincarnation
Cody Littley, 8/30/17
Jira: https://jira.nutanix.com/browse/CPD-1488
Phabricator: http://codereview.nutanix.net/D15247

## Problem description
Entities can be detached.  Currently, you can recreate the same entity again on the same node without providing a higher incarnation ID.

## Proposed Solution
When creating a new entity, check if there are any “deleted” (aka detached) matching entities (with the same guid) that have the moved_to_cluster_uuid field set.  If so, ensure that the new incarnation_id is higher than the old incarnation_id.  If not, reject the new entity and return an error (kIncorrectIncarnationId).

## idf_cli test
The following script can be used to verify the new old/new behavior.  Similar test added to unit tests.
# register types
idf_cli register-entity-type etype1
idf_cli register-metric-type etype1 mtype1 --is-attribute true
# insert e1 into database
idf_cli update-entity etype1 e1 --string mtype1 'hello world 1'
# verify that e1 is in database
idf_cli get-entities-with-metrics --guid etype1 --raw-column mtype1 _ _
# detach e1
idf_cli detatch-entity etype1 e1 target_uuid
# verify that e1 is no longer in the database
idf_cli get-entities-with-metrics --guid etype1 --raw-column mtype1 _ _
# this SHOULD fail
idf_cli update-entity etype1 e1 --string mtype1 'hello world 2'
# verify e1 is still not in the database
idf_cli get-entities-with-metrics --guid etype1 --raw-column mtype1 _ _

[IDF Design Documents | Design doc for DIAL-29_ entity TTL variations break unit test]
## Problem
https://jira.nutanix.com/browse/DIAL-29
Unit test creates an entity with a short TTL.  We wait some time and check to see if the entity is still around.  Sometimes the entity is still present and the unit test fails.

## Root Cause
So far I have been unable to reproduce the issue and there were no errors in the IDF logs around the time of the failure.  After discussing with Peng I believe that the cause of the failure may be that an entity’s TTL is just an approximation and not exact measurement.  This means that a system missing the deadline to delete an entity is not necessarily in an error state.
What I can’t yet explain is what would cause IDF to not delete an entity right away (usually it is deleted very close to the requested time).  IDF allows the entity to live for at least 5 seconds past the TTL, I am not sure if this is long enough to cause concern.

## Proposed Solution
Preview: http://codereview.nutanix.net/differential/diff/63709/
Use the SleepUntil function to check to see if the entity has been deleted.  When it has been deleted then continue with the test.  If the entity is never deleted then the test will eventually time out.
Optionally we could also specify a maximum amount of time we are willing to wait that is shorter than the test timeout period.

Doubling the scale on PC from 5000 VMs to 12500 VMs - Insights Data Fabric Optimizations Problem Statement In release 4.7 and earlier, the memory requirement for a PC VM that manages 5000 VMs (which roughly translates to 30-40K entities, 500 total metric types, and 1.5 million metric data points per 30 seconds period) was 32GB total memory. Out of this 32GB, 24GB is assigned to Insights Data Fabric (IDF) for caching to achieve high performance of client requests. We needed to optimize the memory consumption of IDF for data caching to allow more optimal usage of memory amongst various PC VM components and also be able to manage more entities without having to increase the current memory requirement. Resolution In the Asterix release, Insights Data Fabric (IDF) has made a huge leap towards increasing the PC scale, specifically in terms of memory usage efficiency. A single PC VM with 32GB will now be able to handle 2.5X more number of entities than previous releases. (i.e., 12.5K VMs as opposed to 5K VMs). Internally, we are also actively testing a 3X scale (15K VMs/100K entities) setup with same PC VM configuration (which in 4.7 would have taken 3 PC VMs of 32GB each.) More details IDF has a caching layer, and a majority of that cache is used up for metric data. IDF has a write-back cache of the last one to two hours of each metric's data to avoid flooding Cassandra with metric data writes. IDF also has a LRU cache of metric data that was read from Cassandra during query

[IDF Design Documents | Doubling the scale on PC_]
the last one to two hours of each metric's data to avoid flooding Cassandra with metric data writes. IDF also has a LRU cache of metric data that was read from Cassandra during query processing, and this is used to optimize queries. Among these, the write-back cache consumes majority of the IDF memory; the size of this cache is proportional to the total number of metrics, as IDF stores the last one to hours dirty data for each metric in memory. Among the many IDF features in the Asterix release, these are a few major enhancements in the caching layer that deliver the much improved scale numbers: We purpose-built a compact in-memory metric data structure optimized for caching. That cut down the memory consumption by 50%. For metric data with integer types (which account for over 75% of all metric data), we specifically designed a data structure using variable-length encoding that reduces the memory footprint of the same data to as little as 1/10 of the original size. We normalized the structure of the cache keys from a plain string to a well-defined structure, which eliminates redundancy in the cache key components. We optimized the logic to fetch and merge data in the metric data cache, by tailoring it specifically for the new data structure. This helps in moving data in and out of the cache efficiently. Caveats - Supporting 2.5X entities on a single PC VM would require the disk space to be correspondingly increased 2.5X, since we are persisting 2.5X more data. This is a

of the cache efficiently. Caveats - Supporting 2.5X entities on a single PC VM would require the disk space to be correspondingly increased 2.5X, since we are persisting 2.5X more data.
