[IDF Design Documents | ENG-180667_ Issues when IDF cache entity is out of sync]
## IDF resync workflow: A create/ update of an entity can fail while writing to Cassandra in two scenarios. Either it succeeds on Cassandra write but the acknowledge fails or times out on IDF side or the write to Cassandra itself fails. In both these scenarios, the cached entity is now considered out of sync with the version in Cassandra and is moved into a kNotMerged state. When a subsequent mutate operation on the same out of sync entity is attempted, IDF does the following: Triggers a re-sync of the entity from Cassandra while moving the entity to a kReadInProgress state to avoid any race conditions. Once the re-sync is completed and the cached entity comes in sync with the Cassandra value, the incoming mutate operation is re-applied on IDF. Points to note: The behavior of this re-application should be exactly the same as if it were applied on a cached entity which was in sync with the Cassandra value. The re-sync logic should also be logically independent of the incoming mutate operation. This also means that the out-of-sync entity and the entity in Cassandra must at least have the same identifier which is the entity guid {entity_type_name, entity_id, tenant_id}. This re-sync is currently triggered by the incoming mutate operation but should not depend on the value of the incoming mutate operation since IDF does not know if the latter is a valid operation or not at this stage. The validation can only be done against the synced cache value and no assumption about its

[IDF Design Documents | ENG-180667_ Issues when IDF cache entity is out of sync]
operation since IDF does not know if the latter is a valid operation or not at this stage. The validation can only be done against the synced cache value and no assumption about its validity should be made beforehand.

## Problem statement:
In ENG-180667, it was observed the update/ delete of entity_snapshot entity did not succeed which made the cached version go out of sync with cassandra (kNotMerged state). Now a deletion operation of this same entity resulted in triggering a re-sync operation with cassandra. This re-sync didn’t find any entity in Cassandra and therefore, removed the cached entity as well, bringing the IDF cache in sync with Cassandra. The incoming delete operation is now re-applied which becomes a no-op (since the entity is no longer present in cache or cassandra) and succeeds. A subsequent GetEntities call, however, still returns this deleted entity.

## Root causes:
There are two problems here.

[IDF Design Documents | ENG-180667_ Issues when IDF cache entity is out of sync]
## Problem 1:
Note that
there are two places where the entity is kept in cache; 1) the per entity cache and 2) the per shard set.
GetEntities always refers to the per shard set for reading the entity and returns it whenever found in this set (irrespective of kNotMerged state).
DeleteEntity first checks the entity in the per entity cache first and then if found, deletes it from both these places.
The first problem is that when the re-sync workflow did not find the value in Cassandra, it deleted the per entity cache but didn’t remove the entity from the per shard set. When the incoming DeleteEntity was re-applied, it didn’t find the entity in the per entity cache and immediately returned as a success without touching the per shard set. The subsequent GetEntities was able to read this entity from the per shard set and therefore returned the entity even though the previous delete operation was marked as a success.

[IDF Design Documents | ENG-180667_ Issues when IDF cache entity is out of sync]
## Problem 2: Whenever a kNotMerged state was encountered for the cached entity, the re-sync of the entity was triggered. However, the second problem is that the entity guid of the incoming entity is used for querying Cassandra instead of using the guid of the cached entity. This breaks the above-mentioned semantics of keeping the re-sync operation independent of the incoming mutation. For workflows where tenant ids are not involved, the {entity_type_name, entity_id} tuple of both the incoming entity as well as the cached entity was the same and hence interchangeable. In workflows where tenant ids are involved, this presents a problem since IDF is yet to verify if the incoming entity has the correct tenant id or not. This is irrespective of whether the existing entity was auto-stamped with its tenant id or not. This is because even if we auto-stamp the entity with the default tenant id, the incoming entity may explicitly contain a wrong tenant id and IDF has no way of knowing this before the re-sync operation. Using the incoming entity’s tenant id results in IDF not being able to read the existing entity with the correct tenant id from Cassandra and the cached value gets removed. Now the incoming value is validated against a non-existent value leading to an incorrect state as seen in this bug. In this specific example, the DeleteEntity call did not have a tenant_id specified and was not auto-stamped either. The re-sync from Cassandra was attempted without a tenant_id whereas

[IDF Design Documents | ENG-180667_ Issues when IDF cache entity is out of sync]
state as seen in this bug. In this specific example, the DeleteEntity call did not have a tenant_id specified and was not auto-stamped either. The re-sync from Cassandra was attempted without a tenant_id whereas the entity in Cassandra was keyed with the tenant id. Therefore, the re-sync lookup failed to fetch the correct entity. This issue is not just confined to just the delete workflow but is prevalent in create/ update / delete and replication workflows where the incoming entity is used instead of the cached value for the re-sync operation.

## Fix for Problem 1:
The fix for the first problem is to remove the entity from both the per-entity cache and the per shard set whenever the re-sync workflow doesn’t find the entity in Cassandra.

[IDF Design Documents | ENG-180667_ Issues when IDF cache entity is out of sync]
## Fix for Problem 2:
The fix for the second problem is to use the cached entity’s guid whenever present while reading the entity from Cassandra.
Using the entity guid of the cached entity (whenever present) to query Cassandra always results in reading the correct entity, if present due to Point (3) mentioned in the previous section.
The only corner case is in the case of evictable entities wherein the entity got deleted from Cassandra but the acknowledgment to IDF failed. The entity also got evicted from IDF. In this case, the InsightsObject on the unevictable cache will always remain dehydrated and in kNotMerged state. In this case, IDF cannot ascertain the entity guid of the cached InsightsObject. The cache key currently contains only {entity_type, entity_id} and not the {tenant_id} but the key cannot be updated with the latter either since other components such as query and watches are not made tenant aware (as of 5.10 timeframe).
The solution here is to maintain the existing workflow of using the incoming entity’s guid so that this change does not cause a regression. Given that none of the current evictable entity types are tenant aware currently (as of 5.10 / Xi-1.0-GA timeframe), this corner case will not occur. This needs to be fixed when an evictable entity needs to be made tenant aware.
Note that both these fixes needs to apply to all re-sync operations present in create / update / delete / replication workflows.

[IDF Design Documents | ENG-180667_ Issues when IDF cache entity is out of sync]
## Action plan for Xi-1.0-GA:
Problem 2 is of higher priority and is being fixed as part of ENG-180667 for Xi-1.0-GA time frame since fixing problem 2 prevents the occurrence of problem 1 to a great extent by limiting it only to  the corner case where the entity got deleted and purged before the re-sync was triggered. 

This corner case is highly unlikely for Xi-1.0-GA time frame since the current default purging cycle for deleted entities is once per week and it is extremely rare for the cassandra write failure to coincide with purging schedule which deletes this entity before the re-sync happens. Problem 1 has existed since 5.5 (ever since entity purging feature was added) and we haven’t encountered it till date. Problem 1 and its fix will be tracked in a separate jira ENG-189363.
The proposed fix for problem 2 is being tested with and without the recent tenant id semantics change (tracked by the jira ENG-187654 and described in the doc here).The fix should work in both scenarios.
Once the proposed fix and associated diff is reviewed and approved, we will push it into master and 5.10/ Xi-1.0-GA branch if there is still time available, else this fix will have to go into the next available release branch although that should be the last resort since this issue can happen whenever any cassandra write fails and is not easily identified at a user level.

ENG-189227
Deleted entities are not being retrieved by GetEntities if they have a tenant_id
Currently, we keep track of all tenant_ids if it is specified by clients in a map. When the entity is deleted, the entry in the map gets removed accordingly.
When doing GetEntities with “included_deleted_entities” after the entity is deleted, the tenant_id provided by the GetEntitiesArg is not respected. Instead, we tried to find the tenant_id from cache and if not found, we will use the default tenant_id of the cluster (InsightsCassandraStore::LookupTenantId).
Solution:
Instead of looking up from IDF side, we should use the one in the GetEntitiesArg if provided, and only call the InsightsCassandraStore::LookupTenantId() if not provided.
Remained Problem:
If the client is not tenant-aware, and it wants to get the deleted entity which has specific tenant_id, it won’t be able to do so because we do not have any information about which tenant_id we should use for reading it from Cassandra.
Thus, either 1) we do a scan for this <shard_id, entity_type_name, entity_id> to get all entities related; or 2) tenant-unaware clients using “include_deleted_entities=true” against entities with specific tenant_ids will not get anything (existing behavior).

[IDF Design Documents | ENG-238000_ Evictable entities_ Indexing pseudo-attributes should be schema_config driven]
## Background
Currently, IDF forcefully indexes on 4 pseudo attributes (_created_timestamp_usecs_, _modified_timestamp_usecs_,  _master_cluster_uuid_,  _tenant_id_) for all evictable types. With the new client (Flow) coming, we will be hosting 1M entities in cache. The size of each such entity will be around 96 bytes - much less than the overhead of saving it as evictable (which is around 952 bytes as mentioned here). So we decide to save them as un-evictable entities.
Flow requires to filter based on created timestamp which is a pseudo attribute. With current implementation, for querying on pseudo attributes of un-evictable entities, we need to do cache lookup and get the body of each and every one entity of the type. And the whole execution is taking ~40s to complete.
This document will mainly discuss about an optimization on indexing pseudo attributes.

## Option 1
Adding a new field in entity type as following:
enum PseudoAttribute {
kCreatedTime = 0,
kModifiedTime,
kMasterClusterUuid,
kTenantId,
}
// Optional. Determining which pseudo attributes to be indexed.
repeated PseudoAttribute pseudo_attr_to_index = 15;
This field will be persisted in the metadata. When indexing the entity, we can get the pseudo attributes set from this field instead of hard-coding it.
Pros: This gives us the benefit of enabling clients to control which pseudo attributes to be indexed with minimal code changes.

[IDF Design Documents | ENG-238000_ Evictable entities_ Indexing pseudo-attributes should be schema_config driven]
## Option 2
Alternatively, clients can register pseudo attributes as normal attributes. When indexing the entity, IDF will recognize the attribute being indexed is a pseudo attribute and index on the corresponding field.
Pros: This gives the client a uniform syntax to control the indexing (just like how other indexed attributes are specified) instead of exposing a new structure.
metric_type_list {
is_attribute: true
metric_name: "_modified_timestamp_usecs_"
entity_type_name: "alert"
user_metadata: "{\"data_type\":\"int64\"}"
persist_attribute_as_time_series: false
is_index_column: true
index_type: kInt64
}
When processing the registration of pseudo attributes, we will do validations on the name and type. And we need to enable the registration of pseudo attributes for indexing purpose (which is currently disabled as here). If the “is_index_column” is false, we will return an error.
With the flexibility mentioned in either option, clients are enabled to have control over which pseudo attribute to be indexed, instead of letting IDF indexing all pesudo attributes for any eligible entity type.
The current decision is to go with the second option.

Although, the sync happens in batch but Cassandra Write happens for each individual entity. The RPC does not return success until the whole batch gets written to cassandra. We are not fully utilizing cassandra’s BatchMutate which supports multiple updates. This doc discusses batching cassandra writes for synced entities. This would increase the overall throughput under heavy load. Batching cassandra writes for UpdateEntity/DeleteEntity/BatchUpdateEntities/BatchDeleteEntities has already been done as part of this jira. In this doc, we will discuss about the changes required to integrate RemoteTransferData to the same pipeline. For more information on how writes are batched to cassandra, please refer to this doc. Changes Required: Recap: pending_write_entity_ops_: The map to hold all pending write entity ops to cassandra. These are all the ops that will be written to cassandra in one batch. total_expected_write_entity_ops_: Atomic counter which stores the count of all individual write requests that are about to be processed. This counter is decremented by 1 right before a write op is written to pending request map. Whenever the value of this counter becomes 0 or the size of pending request map becomes equal to the max ops that

1 right before a write op is written to pending request map. Whenever the value of this counter becomes 0 or the size of pending request map becomes equal to the max ops that we want to send in one batch, the pending request map is processed to be written to cassandra and we start with a new batch. We’ll be using the same map as well as the counter to batch write ops to cassandra in case of replication. ## ENG-264464: Squash entity updates when multiple facts are updated for the same dimensions
Nov 2019
<Approved>

## Background
The dimension-fact functionality is simulated by using the entity-metric model in IDF. Dimension will be the entity, and fact will be the metric. So facts (metrics) will only be queryable when the associate dimension (entity) is found. From clients’ perspectives, they might not even care about the entity itself. Thus, it requires IDF to internally maintain the life cycle of those dimension entities, including 1) creation, 2) keeping them alive as long as the facts are needed, and 3) deleting them when facts are no longer needed.
This document is solving a problem in 2). Following I will use dimension/entity and fact/metric interchangeably as they have the same meaning in this context.
Currently when processing dimension fact data, to make sure metric data is queryable, we need to extend the life time of associated entity. However, if there are multiple data points for the same dimension (entity), IDF may potentially issue multiple concurrent UpdateEntity on the same entity. Then some of them might succeed while others are bounced by UpdateInProgress error.
To solve the problem, we can squash duplicate updates on the same entity into one as following:

Every time when checking whether we need to update the entity, we check the map first. = [] () { ... rows = dimension_fact_map.find(entity_id); for row in rows: if update_success: rows_to_process->add(row.row_idx, row.start_index, row.status_vec_index) ... }; ... } This will make sure that for one ‘metric_data_sample_list’, we will issue at most one update for each entity, even if there are multiple metric data rows for it. ENG-305948: Delete Replicated Entities on Replica site
Mana Agarwal
Reviewed
April 2020

[IDF Design Documents | ENG-305948_ Delete replicated entities on replica]
## Requirement: In the current IDF behaviour, synced entities are read-only on replica side. However, there are certain use cases where clients need a way to clean up (delete) the replicated entities due to space constraints. Currently, Ergon keeps 4k tasks per PE (irrespective of the number of vms) which are synced to PC. This means (4k * number of register clusters) tasks on the PC. This will cause a problem when we scale PCs to a very high number of registered clusters even if we keep the overall number of VMs the same. With our current goal of 1000 registered clusters connected to a single PC cluster, this comes out to be 4M tasks on PC which is a very large number. Ergon's task scanner thread on PC today only deletes tasks on PC. The requirement is for this task scanner to be able to fetch all tasks (PEs included), ordered according to timestamp, limit the latest 100k tasks and delete the others. The alternative way for Ergon was to initiate a delete directly on the source PE. However, this has several disadvantages: PE level upgrade is required by customers to enable this feature. Similarly bug fixes would need both PE and PC side upgrade PE quota is now intertwined with the overall PC quota whereas the client, Ergon, would like to keep the two quotas, PE and PC, independent of each other. With this functionality: This becomes a PC only feature, so decouples the PE from any upgrades for enabling this feature or for further maintenance related bug fixes. PE quota remains

[IDF Design Documents | ENG-305948_ Delete replicated entities on replica]
independent of each other. With this functionality: This becomes a PC only feature, so decouples the PE from any upgrades for enabling this feature or for further maintenance related bug fixes. PE quota remains intact and independent of PC quota, allowing for more flexibility. This functionality can be considered analogous to client driven backup cleanup logic. No other modifications would be allowed on the replica side for such synced entities. This feature has other potential use cases in alerts, events, audits etc where a similar workflow around quota management can be applied.

[IDF Design Documents | ENG-305948_ Delete replicated entities on replica]
## Proposed Solution:
Solution is to introduce a new field in the entity type definition to indicate whether the entity should be allowed to be deleted on replica or not.  If yes, we mark the entity as deleted on replica and continue with the entity deletion (following the delete semantics of local entity delete to maintain consistency). Else, we throw an error.
NOTE:
Any subsequent operations (update/delete) on the source side would still sync as before  and override the locally (replica) deleted entity state.
The flag indicating whether the entity was deleted on replica or not is useful for watch processing at client side, for any reads on deleted entities as well as for debugging purposes.
Entities deleted on replica will not be purged until they are deleted from source. This will be useful for the scenario mentioned in the previous point. For the purge to happen for these entities, the delete on source should either sync to replica or happen due to active entities workflow.

## Delete Semantics:
For deletion of replicated entity on replica, we will follow the same delete semantics as that of any local entity delete:
Cas delete of any replicated non-cas entity is not allowed.
Non-cas delete of any replicated cas entity is not allowed.
Cas delete of any replicated cas entity is allowed only if it’s a valid cas value (current_cas_value == previous_cas_value + 1)
This is different from sync delete semantics where each delete is treated as a fresh one whether:
It is a cas delete of a replicated non-cas entity.
It is a non-cas delete of a replicated cas entity.
It is a cas delete of a replicated cas entity with any cas_value (higher, lower or same)
The above sync delete semantics remain unchanged.

## Rolling Upgrade:
During upgrade, the nodes which are on older versions will get an error on deletion of replicated entities until they get upgraded. On upgraded nodes, the deletion of replicated entities will go fine.
On the client side, this can be handled by enabling this functionality only after the cluster upgrade is complete. Ergon does this by using capabilities feature which writes a zk entry mentioning that this feature is active after the cluster upgrade is done. Once this capability is marked on zk, subsequent upgrades will continue using this functionality even during rolling upgrade.

ENG-331954: Store the IDs of entities deleted on replica in memory in IDF Approved Mana Agarwal July 2020 Jira: https://jira.nutanix.com/browse/ENG-331954 Problem: With the recent change for allowing deletion of replicated entities on replica, we read entities from cassandra during active entities workflow per entity_type per shard for which allow_entity_deletion_on_replica is set to true. This was done because some entities might be deleted on replica. If we read the entities only from cache, we will miss out on the entities which were deleted on replica. In that case, the entity would never get a source delete through active entities workflow and would never get purged. The entity tombstones of these entities will stay in cassandra forever. However, there is one potential problem with this approach. As and when the scale of the PC will increase, the number of cassandra scans on PC will increase thus leading to spikes every 6 hours (active entities are sent every 6 hours) in cassandra CPU usage. These scans are done per cluster per entity_type per shard basis. We need a way to reduce these frequent cassandra calls every 6 hours. Solution: Maintain an in-memory map in idf to store the entity ids of the entities which are deleted on replica on per cluster per entity type per shard basis. During active entities workflow, we will read all the existing entities from cache for every entity_type. For the entity type for which allow_entity_deletion_on_replica is set to true, we will

If yes, we will read only those entities from cassandra (since, those will not be present in cache as they are already deleted on replica) and process accordingly. ENG-99569 IDF should talk to available cassandra on the cluster when local cassandra becomes unavailable for extended period of time By: Ning Zhou 7/22/2017 Problem statement https://jira.nutanix.com/browse/ENG-99569 IDF uses Cassandra as the underlying data storage. Current assumption is that local Cassandra should always be available to handle request, in case of error conditions, cassandra should be able to forward the request to other nodes. However, this assumption might not hold true in a couple of scenarios: Cassandra in a prolonged crash loop where the request will always result in kTimeout or kUnavailable mode. Local cassandra in a bad state (e.g. detached from the ring) that it is incapable of processing data anymore which also result in kUnavailable errors. The timeout or unavailable error will get propagated all the way to the client applications of IDF, will eventually become user impacting. In the worst case, it could emerged into P0 availability issues eventually. In those instances, Cassandra processes on other nodes of the cluster might still be able to continue serving the client requests, but there’s no current mechanism for IDF to talk to any of the remote Cassandra node(s). [IDF Design Documents | Entity Data Upgrade]
Entity Data Upgrade In Asterix, entity data in both cache and Cassandra are flat on shards by using the default shard ID 0 in both cache keys and row keys. The document describes the process of changing the shard ID in cache keys and row keys from the default 0 to its real ID that the entity belongs to. This document will include all CRUD operations on entity data after the rolling upgrade finishes and how we migrate the old entity data into new format. The entity data migration process does not include entity trails, as they haven’t been enabled so we don’t have history entity trails to upgrade. And we will still disable this functionality during the data upgrade. We will use an enum status 'entity_data_upgrade_status_' to indicate whether the rolling upgrade has not started, or is running, or has finished. The candidate values are {kPreUpgrade, kUpgrading, kUpgraded} and the default value is kUpgraded (which stands for Obelix - scaleout). Once we start the rolling upgrade, this state needs to be set to kPreUpgrade, so as to force the Obelix code to operate in leader-only mode, so that all CRUDs are exactly the same as Asterix. Whenever we start (after the rolling upgrade finishes) the (or recover from the previous) entity data upgrade, we set the status 'entity_data_upgrade_status_' to kUpgrading. And set it back to kUpgraded when all entity data upgrade finishes. We will talk about it in the later paragraph. After all the entity data has been migrated to new shard, we will

[IDF Design Documents | Entity Data Upgrade]
And set it back to kUpgraded when all entity data upgrade finishes. We will talk about it in the later paragraph. After all the entity data has been migrated to new shard, we will purge them from shard 0. And when all entity data has been purged, we will turn the state to kUpgraded, saying we have finished the entity data upgrade, so the server will operate in Obelix scaleout mode.

## Cache Initialization
Generally, we add a new field ‘is_upgraded’ to each insights_object to indicate whether the entity has been upgraded or not. However, this is not enough. During initialization, the leader populates the cache by doing a full scan on the latest entities column family. Both shard 0 and shard N (new format shard) will be loaded. We additionally use a map ‘upgraded_map<type, set<id>>’ to keep track of entities which have been upgraded. The reason for this map is that delete entities will not be populated in cache and thus no insights_object will be found. Once an entity is loaded from shard N, it will be added to the ‘upgraded_map’.
The ‘upgraded_map’ is only used during cache population and will be deleted after that.
When an entity is retrieved from the latest entities column family in Cassandra, we check on the rowkey:
0:
If the entity is found in ‘upgraded_map’, which means it has been already upgraded, we skip this entity.
If non 0:
Add the entity to the ‘upgraded_map’
We need to delete the entity from cache if it has previously been loaded from shard 0.

[IDF Design Documents | Entity Data Upgrade]
## Before Upgrade: kPreUpgrade
All writes will still go to shard 0 in this state. However, when we turn the state into kUpgrading, there can be some unfinished writes on-the-fly. We have to make sure they are actually written to shard 0 rather than shard N to avoid uncertainty.
To solve this problem, we introduce a lock (‘sync_barrier_’ with ‘ENTITY_DATA_UPGRADE_BARRIER_LOCK_ID’). All writes during kPreUpgrade need to grab the read lock while entity data upgrade needs to grab the write lock. Thus the entity data upgrade cannot start until all writes during kPreUpgrade have finished and vice versa, but all writes can happen concurrently.

[IDF Design Documents | Entity Data Upgrade]
## During Upgrade: kUpgrading
Whenever we start the (or recover from the previous) entity data upgrade by calling into the function StartEntityDataUpgrade, we set the status 'entity_data_upgrade_status_' to kUpgrading.
Basically, in this state, all reads, which require to scan the Cassandra, need to load from both shard N and shard 0, and always take the new data (data from shard N) if there is any.
NOTE: When handling the new update to shard N, we won’t find anything from shard N, but we still need to load from shard 0 (even if we don’t care about the old paxos value) since we need to check on the master_cluster_uuid and etc. For example:
Entity E is in deleted states in shard 0.
Client starts an update on E which does not belong to it
The leader found E is not in cache, load it from shard N which returns kEntityNotPresent. Then the leader will write this update to Cassandra.
Now an update from a non-owner is applied to an entity.
Note that all the following CRUDs are in kUpgrading state.

## Read (Query)
When a new query (GetEntitiesFromShards) comes in, if it set the ‘include_deleted_entities’ to true, i.e. we need to load from latest entities column family, we need to read from both shard N and shard 0.

[IDF Design Documents | Entity Data Upgrade]
## Write (Update / Insertion / Deletion) Normally, all writes should be written to shard N after we start the entity data upgrade. However, to avoid the stale cache problem (see below), all write to Cassandra will first write to shard 0. And only when it succeeds, we can write to shard N. Stale cache issue: Current data in Cassandra: [shard 0, entity e1, paxos 2, cas 3, data A] IDF started write operation to Cassandra UpdateEntity: [s=0, e=e1, p=2, c=4, d=B] IDF crashed. New IDF instance loaded data from Cassandra Cache version: [e=e1, p=2, c=3, d=A] Write operation that the previous instance started finally completed in Cassandra (after the new leader populate the cache) DB version: [s=0, e=e1, p=3, c=4, d=B] Now new IDF instance has cache entry in kMerged state, but it does not correspond to the data in Cassandra (see 3.) If new IDF issues another update: UpdateEntity: [s=N, e=e1, p=0, c=4, d=C] On success, DB version: [s=N, e=e1, p=1, c=4, d=C] If client C1 load from DB (include_deleted_entities) between 4 and 6, another client C2 load from DB after 6, they will get same CAS=4, but different data: B vs. C. Briefly, for every write to Cassandra: If the entity hasn’t been upgraded -> write to shard 0 first: Success: Reset the paxos and write to shard N. And update the cache paxos accordingly on success. Error: kNotMerged Otherwise -> write to shard N directly. Creation(Insertion)/Update/Deletion: Almost the same as current flow, except: For loads, load from both shard 0 and

[IDF Design Documents | Entity Data Upgrade]
N. And update the cache paxos accordingly on success. Error: kNotMerged Otherwise -> write to shard N directly. Creation(Insertion)/Update/Deletion: Almost the same as current flow, except: For loads, load from both shard 0 and shard N. For writes, if non-upgraded, write to shard 0 first, then to N; if upgraded, write to shard N directly. For Insertion during kPreUpgrade, we need to mark it as non-migrated so that later we will be able to find out which entity hasn’t been migrated. For Insertion during kUpgrading, if the entity is not found in Cassandra, then it is a brand new entity and can be directly written to shard N. Replication entities should have similar behavior.

## After Upgrade: kUpgraded
We are in real scaleout now. Just follow the normal flow.

[IDF Design Documents | Entity Data Upgrade]
## Old Entity Data Migration (from shard 0 to shard N)
For the part of data migration (upgrade), when the upgrade process is triggered (by calling the method ‘StartEntityDataUpgrade’), the whole shard 0 in latest entities CF will be scanned:
For every entity read from shard 0, we reset the paxos to 0 and write it back to Cassandra. The write will go directly to shard N (rather than to 0 then to N)  since it is just loaded from shard 0 so that we should have got the latest paxos already.
On success, we add it to the purge batch and later purge it via the ‘SchedulePurgeOldDeletedEntities’. Update the cache object accordingly only if we managed to get it and to mark it as update in progress.
On error, we increment the failure counter: fail_cnt.
After the all shard 0 rows have been scanned, if the fail_cnt is not 0, we retry repeatedly until all succeed.
If the leader crashes during the upgrade, the new leader will repeat the initialization. Since previously upgraded entities will be found in shard N, we will be able to tell which entities have been upgraded or not.
When the migration process finishes, it will inform the server that all entity data upgrade has finished and change the upgrade state to kUpgraded. Then the leader can distribute the shard assignment information. Since we are running in leader-only mode during this upgrade, we don’t need to worry about the shard movement so as to simplify the issue.

[IDF Design Documents | Entity Snapshot Patch in Insights DB]
1. Introduction Entities in Insights DB are snapshotted periodically. However, back-in-time entity updates and race condition between updates and a snapshot process may cause incorrect snapshots. The mechanism of snapshot patch is to fix the existing snapshots. More specifically, we write a new column as a patch into the row to which the target snapshot belongs. Therefore, a complete snapshot includes the snapshot column itself and all those patch columns in the same row. The name of the patch column is the range start time of the row concatenated by the entity ID, while the value of the column is in the format of EntityList (but only include one entity), which is compatible with the snapshot column (which includes all entities in the latest cache when it is generated). 2. When a Patch is needed? There are three kinds of patches, depending on the sequence of four timestamps . Before explaining them in detail, let's define the following notations: finish_time: the time when an entity update/delete is completed after successfully writing to the latest CF; update_time: modified_timestamp_usec in the new entity value; initial_time: modified_timestamp_usec in the old entity value; time_before_completion: any time before finish_time. 2.1 New-entity Patches The first kind of snapshot patch is called “new-entity patches”. The name indicates that the value of the patch uses the new entity value. When update_time and finish_time cross snapshot boundaries (they do not fall into the same

[IDF Design Documents | Entity Snapshot Patch in Insights DB]
snapshot patch is called “new-entity patches”. The name indicates that the value of the patch uses the new entity value. When update_time and finish_time cross snapshot boundaries (they do not fall into the same snapshot window), a patch including the new entity value should be written to all rows whose range start time fall between them. This is because the new value is a back-in-time update and it overlaps the old value which has already been snapshotted. After writing the new value into the latest CF (the last step of updating an entity), the patch must be correctly applied to keep the DB consistency. Therefore, applying the patch cannot fail. If it fails, the previous step of writing to the latest CF must be rolled back. To avoid losing consistency due to crashing between the two steps (writing to the latest CF and applying a patch), WAL (Write Ahead Log) is introduced. We log the patch into WAL and remove the log after applying the patch successfully. If the system crashes before a successful patch, a recovery can be done by replaying the WAL. However, logging into WAL itself may fail. If the WAL logging fails after writing to the latest CF, the consistency is still spoiled. Therefore, WAL is logged before writing to the latest CF. Here it comes to time_before_completion. If it fails, the entity update request fails before it modifies the system. Before writing to the latest CF, finish_time is in the future and still unknown. But it must be later than the current time

[IDF Design Documents | Entity Snapshot Patch in Insights DB]
fails, the entity update request fails before it modifies the system. Before writing to the latest CF, finish_time is in the future and still unknown. But it must be later than the current time (time_before_completion). Therefore, it is reasonable to use time_before_completion to determine the new-entity patch. 2.2 Potential New-entity Patches Using time_before_completion (earlier than the real finish_time) before writing to the latest CF is sufficient to determine all the patches before time_before_completion. However, it may miss at most one more patch between time_before_completion and finish_time, if they cross a boundary as well. To address the problem, a buffer called insights_entity_snapshot_boundary_buffer_seconds is defined. If the distance from time_before_completion (the current time upon the decision is made) to the next snapshot range start time is smaller than the buffer. We assume there will be another patch needed for the next snapshot window, because it is possible that the finish_time is after the next range start time and that snapshot will have already started by finish_time. But whether this patch is really needed or not has to be determined after writing to the latest CF (at finish_time). If it is needed, it has to be logged into the WAL before writing to the latest CF; if it is not, it is better to be reverted from the WAL, and the final writing of patches to the trail should not include it. However, reverting it is not a must and not-reverting does not

[IDF Design Documents | Entity Snapshot Patch in Insights DB]
not, it is better to be reverted from the WAL, and the final writing of patches to the trail should not include it. However, reverting it is not a must and not-reverting does not hurt the consistency, because the snapshot should include it no matter whether it is patched or not. If the distance from time_before_completion to the next snapshot range start time is bigger than the buffer, it is impossible that finish_time will cross the boundary. Therefore, the potential new-entity patch is not needed. 2.3 Old-entity Patches The third kind of snapshot patch is called “old-entity patches”. The name indicates that the value of the patch uses the original entity value (the value which is going to be updated). When initial_time and update_time fall into different snapshot windows (cross boundaries) AND update_time and finish_time fall into the same snapshot window (do not cross snapshot boundaries), a patch is needed for the current snapshot window if the snapshot has not been completed upon finish_time, because the new value overlaps the old value.; no patches will be needed otherwise. For all other snapshots between them, no patches are considered, because no patches are needed if those snapshots has completed. This kind of patch can be determined before writing to the latest CF. The difference between time_before_completion and finish_time is covered by the case of potential new-entity patch. In addition, writing old entity values into the trail does not hurt the consistency.

[IDF Design Documents | Entity Snapshot Patch in Insights DB]
writing to the latest CF. The difference between time_before_completion and finish_time is covered by the case of potential new-entity patch. In addition, writing old entity values into the trail does not hurt the consistency. Applying old-entity patches can be combined with writing the old entity into the trail (the step before writing to the latest CF). Therefore, no WAL is needed for this kind of patches. 3. How a Patch is Applied? The patches are applied in the path of PutEntity and DeleteEntity. A WAL is used for all new-entity patches. A in-memory set is used to book-keep the logging/reverting patch records. In PutEntity/DeleteEntity, GetEntitySnapshotPatchNewEntity() is called to prepare all new-entity patches (including the potential ones) before calling EntityUpdateStateTransition(). All prepared patches are logging into WAL and recorded in the in-memory set. In WriteToEntityTrail(), GetEntitySnapshotPatchOldEntity() is called to prepare the old-entity patch and the old-entity patch is written to the trail together with the old entity value as part of entity updating/deleting. In the state of EntityUpdateState::kWriteToLatestEntitiesDone, FinalizeEntitySnapshotPatches() is called to determine the potential new-entity patch. If there are any new-entity patches left, the path is switched to EntityUpdateState::kWriteSnapshotPatchToTrail. The potential new-entity patch may be reverted in WAL and erased from the in-memory set. Finally, WriteEntitySnapshotPatchToTrail() is

[IDF Design Documents | Entity Snapshot Patch in Insights DB]
potential new-entity patch. If there are any new-entity patches left, the path is switched to EntityUpdateState::kWriteSnapshotPatchToTrail. The potential new-entity patch may be reverted in WAL and erased from the in-memory set. Finally, WriteEntitySnapshotPatchToTrail() is called to apply all new-entity patches. All committed patches are reverted in WAL and erased from the in-memory set. 4. How the Recovery is Done? During the recovery, we pair up all the records in WAL. If there is a record which does not have a corresponding "done", then this record should be recovered to achieve consistency. The checkpoint of WAL is generated periodically. When it is time to create a new checkpoint, all patch records in the in-memory set are logged into the new checkpoint, which “moves” all unpaired patch record in the previous checkpoint to the new one, while the paired ones are discar ded.

CouchDB’s automatic compaction daemon, internally known as “smoosh”, will trigger compaction jobs for both databases and views based on configurable thresholds for the sparseness of a file and the total amount of space that can be recovered. ref Smoosh works using the concept of channels. A channel is essentially a queue of pending compactions. Smoosh takes each channel and works through the compactions queued in each in priority order. Channels are defined as either “ratio” channels or “slack” channels, depending on the type of algorithm used for prioritization: Ratio: uses the ratio of sizes.file / sizes.active as its driving calculation. Introduction With the addition of VM snapshot entities (up to 128 snapshots per VM) and alerts, the number of entities in IDF can increase by two orders of magnitude. In the current design IDF requires all entities to be in memory, even if they aren’t frequently accessed; today, with 15K VMs and ~125K entities, IDF uses ~512MB to store entities, of which VMs + virtual disks + virtual NICs take ~400MB. Each VM snapshot entity on an average can be 10KB or more in size, since it contains the VM, virtual disk, and virtual NIC configuration. So, with 128 snapshots per VM, supporting snapshots for 15K VMs in the current design can take ~20GB of memory or more. This document outlines the design of evictable entities in IDF, where entities of some types need not always be in memory—they are fetched into memory on demand and evicted when not in use. This design fits well with entities like VM snapshots, events, and alerts, which are accessed frequently only for a short time after creation and after which they are infrequently accessed. Eventually, we may make all IDF entities evictable. Assumptions For evictable entity types, support for fetching all (or many) entities with GetEntities or GetEntitiesWithMetrics is not needed: supporting this in the current Get APIs (without real cursors) would need enough memory to store all evictable entities, which goes counter to our goal here. SpotLightSearch does not need to be supported for evictable entities (in v1) because SpotLightSearch

[IDF Design Documents | Evictable Entities in IDF]
APIs (without real cursors) would need enough memory to store all evictable entities, which goes counter to our goal here. SpotLightSearch does not need to be supported for evictable entities (in v1) because SpotLightSearch clients currently require arbitrary substring search. See future work section for discussion on how we can support this in the future. All entities of an evictable entity type are not actively updated all the time. For instance, we assume that we won’t have stats ingested for all VM snapshot entities every 5 minutes; otherwise, this can result in significant memory usage, and also cause the sizes of rows in the metric_data_by_shard CF to exceed Cassandra’s row size limits. The assumption is that at any time, only a few VM snapshot entities are being actively updated, with the older snapshot entities only being queried and not updated. High-level Design Add a flag to the EntityType proto that specifies whether entities of a type are evictable. The metadata for evictable entities (i.e., the insights object) is stored in unevictable cache and is always present in memory. The actual entity itself (i.e., the object_ in InsightsObject) is not always present in unevictable cache. The design of having metadata always in memory means that each evictable entity takes ~256 bytes of memory. This design was chosen as it simplifies implementation of evictable entities since the entity CRUD logic (which depends on entity insights object) can be mostly reused. During CRUD

After the operations finish, the insights object for the entity is dehydrated and object_ is set to null. IDF maintains in-memory indexes for evictable entity attributes. The indexes are stored in the unevictable cache in the store layer, and are used to execute queries and watches on evictable entities. On startup, IDF reads all the evictable entities from Cassandra to build the in-memory indexes but doesn’t store the entities in the cache. ## High level requirements In some scenarios (e.g. XiS metering), the consumer app would need to know the latest value of a metric as of start time of a query range in addition to all the changes within the query range. For example, to measure the uptime of the VM within the last hour, the consumer app would need to know the powered_on state at the beginning of the hour as well as the changes that happen within the hour. Sample scenario: User queries the power state of a VM over a period of time in order to generate the correct billing for the customer, to do that, they need to query all the past VM power on state including all the VM deletion transitions as VM may register and deregistered from the PC VM1 ========================================= T0 On T0 + 100 Off T0 + 200 On T0 + 250 On -- VM deleted. ⇒ Start_time_usecs (T0+300) T0 + 400 On T0 + 450 Off ⇒ End_time_usecs (T0+500) User queries VM power state between [T0 + 300, T0 + 500) with the latest value as of start time (T0+300). The expectation is to return the highlighted samples. The deletion event happened before the start time of the query needs to be returned along with the known state value of the power state as it represents a significant event, in the metering use case, if the “deleted attribute” value on T0+250 is not returned then previous known sample value was at T0+200 (on) which basically makes the metering service think the VM was powered-on between T0+200 and T0+450 which is inaccurate.

Garbage Collection of Dimension Fact Entities Dimension-Fact Table payload is composed of dimensions and facts. The attributes correspond to dimensions and metric data (stats) correspond to facts for a specified entity type. Key name for each row is generated by joining attribute values in defined order and Entity ID is derived by generating UUID from the Key name. Auto-deletion is support as part of infrastructure. Insights Periodic process performs scan on entities and deletes all the entities whose expiration timestamp is elapsed. As the dimension-fact entity is created implicitly using the generated UUID, the expiration timestamp is not set, resulting in entity not to be auto-deleted. The scope of this document is to define the expiration timestamp for the dimension-fact entities and the algorithm for calculation of expiration timestamp. The entity expiration timestamp is set such that the expiration timestamp should be in some future time with respect to the expiration time for any of the Metric Data associated with this Dimension-Fact entity. Besides the entity should not be updated on each Metric Data update to avoid too many writes to Cassandra. To avoid multiple updates the entity expiration timestamp is set after certain purge interval boundary from the Metric Data expiration time. Once the Metric Data expiration time crosses this interval boundary, the entity expiration timestamp is updated to next purge interval boundary. This will avoid excessive updates for

[IDF Design Documents | Garbage Collection of Dimension Fact Entities]
boundary from the Metric Data expiration time. Once the Metric Data expiration time crosses this interval boundary, the entity expiration timestamp is updated to next purge interval boundary. This will avoid excessive updates for entity. The bigger the purge interval, less is the entity update frequency. The purge interval is defined by introducing new GFLAG with default value as 7 days: insights_dimension_fact_entity_purge_interval_seconds Here are the steps to calculate expiration timestamp on entity create/update: TTL is calculated based on each Metric Type retention period. The algorithm goes over the list of metric types in the message header and fetch the Max TTL. Max expiration time is calculated as max_exp = max_ttl + now_time. If max_exp is within the set entity expiration time: No action required If max_exp is past entity expiration timestamp or expiration timestamp is not set: Expiration timestamp is calculated by rounding off max_exp to next purge interval boundary. Entity is updated/created with calculated expiration timestamp. Unit Test Cases: Create Dimension-Fact entity. Check expiration timestamp is generated and is set at purge interval boundary calculated from the metric data TTL. Update Metric Data with multiple times within the purge interval boundary. Check expiration timestamp is not updated and modified timestamp for entity is not updated since creation of the dimension-fact entity. Update Metric Data outside the last purge interval boundary. Check

[IDF Design Documents | Garbage Collection of Dimension Fact Entities]
the purge interval boundary. Check expiration timestamp is not updated and modified timestamp for entity is not updated since creation of the dimension-fact entity. Update Metric Data outside the last purge interval boundary. Check expiration timestamp is updated with new purge interval boundary and the modified timestamp of entity is updated.

Devendra S, Sumit B, Pradhyumna K, Vinay J
December 2024

## Setup 1:
PC with 1.5 Million entities:
With 750k of each type (evictable and unevictable).
Details of indexes:
5.2 Million unique values
16 Million IDs overall in indexes
IDF boot-up:
Time taken is 65 secs.
Around 1 minute for 1.5 million entities
Although system had 10 empty cores, IDF’s CPU consumption stayed at 3-4 cores

## Setup 2:
PC with 9 Million CALM entities:
90% of the entity types are of evictable type.
Most of the entities have nested fields enabled
IDF Bootup:
18k unique values (cause all entities in etype are copy of same entity)
78 Million IDs overall in indexes
IDF bootup:
Time taken without any CPU limits is 8 min 55 secs
Although system had 10 empty cores, IDF’s CPU consumption stayed at 2-3 cores for most of the time
As the index size increases, the CPU consumption seemed to further saturate
Disabling indexes alone increased CPU consumption to 500-600 cores

## Setup 3:
Scale CALM PC with 13 Million entities:
90% of the entity types are of evictable type.
Most of the entities have nested fields enabled
IDF bootup:
Time taken without any CPU limits is 20 min 30 secs
Although system had 14 empty cores, IDF’s CPU consumption stayed at 2-3 cores for most of the time

[IDF Design Documents | IDF Bootup Optimisations]
## 1. Increase observability on resource contention:
As of today, there was no insight into the exact cause of contention. Contention could be possible at various layers like Indexes, Common Unevictable Cache access, Other common structures. Exposed various observability stats via “/h/vars”.
Changes:
ENG-704509, ENG-707570
Exposed contention & op stats of cache and various entities with detailed split
Exposed a way to display contention of locks per object type
Exposed contention stats of other common structures
Observations:
EntityUuidSet seems to have around 70% contention
Unevictable cache had 10% contention
Too many Cache Gets have been observed

## a.  Avoid system calls for re-entrant locking  (ENG-707572)
Looking at the flame graphs and the system call logs, it was observed that there are a lot of SYS_gettid calls from all the Cache methods.
We track the thread holding the Cache lock at the Cache level to facilitate various operations during processes like Prune. However we are using gettide calls just to track the threads holding the locks. We moved to in-memory based thread::id class in cpp to reduce this overhead.
Post this, we have seen a decrease in CPU consumption and the amount of system calls during bootup.

[IDF Design Documents | IDF Bootup Optimisations]
## b.  Bifurcate Unevictable Cache (ENG-705506)
Due to a lot of Get and Inserts happening at the same time on Cache, we have seen a 10% contention. As of today, all the Cache entries of Unevictable type are stored in the same shard. We have identified that some CacheKey types like Metadata are way more frequently accessed than the other types.
This high amount of reads were causing contention to CacheInserts. Sharding of Unevictable cache based on Key types, like EntityType data, MetricType data, Entity, IndexMap etc. had to be introduced. This reduced the contention on Cache and helped scale the inserts.

## 3. Nested Attribute computation:
Nested Attribute computation is one of the most expensive things we perform during bootup. As of today IDF doesn’t pre-compute and store the nested attribute details because of flexible schema.

## a.  Optimise nested attribute parsing (ENG-704508, ENG-676526)
As of today, parsing nested attributes especially from nested proto structures including parsing each nested message once per each nested attribute using it and also the base attribute parsing was being done for each nested attribute. We can avoid doing this and instead use a short lived cache for the lifetime of parsing the entity to solve the former. It has been seen that the attributes share a common path of 32% overall.
We have only made the changes concerning the base attribute at this point.

[IDF Design Documents | IDF Bootup Optimisations]
## b.  Skip computing non-indexed nested attributes for evictable entities (ENG-707757)
Nested attribute computation is expensive especially given the high number of evictable entities. Since we discard the entities anyways, we only have to compute nested attributes which are indexed during bootup. Only 30% of the nested attributes seem to be indexed. So skipping the others should save a significant amount of cycles.

## a.  Reduce contention (ENG-692936)
To update the index maps for a given entity type, we lock all the index maps and update them one by one for each entity. This is done to have a consistent view of indexes for query execution with simultaneous updates. However, this is not required during bootup because queries across shards that are being loaded won’t be served.
This along with bifurcating cache solved the issues wrt to contention letting IDF scale upto 6-8 cores. With this on deployments like PC where there are CPU limits set and most of the other services would be waiting for IDF shard load, this will give us good benefits.

## b.  Optimise Index Structure Value (ENG-705514)
Although changes were not planned as part of bootup, the current Index value structure was designed to support various types of entity-id sets like string set, ptr set, value-index set. However, this was causing a lot of relative overhead on indices with a lot of unique values.
The improvements observed were more on the memory side but not significant wrt bootup time/CPU.

[IDF Design Documents | IDF Bootup Optimisations]
## a.  Reduce metadata lookups during bootup (ENG-692936)
There seem to be a lot of redundant metadata lookups for entity and metric types. This would cause additional burden on the Cache. Refactored the code to reduce the lookups by multiple folds.

## b.  Remove stale query layer cache (ENG-506143)
One of the query layer cache which stores the shared pointers of the entities was once used for the majority of the query workflows. However, most of the heavy workflows have been moved out of this to avoid heavy contention. Migrated rest of the less used workflows to get rid of the cache.

IDF Metadata Management RPCs
IDF Metadata Management RPC behaviour
November 2025

## Metadata RPCs:
In most forms of deployments, config management for IDF is done predominantly using config files.
But IDF has the following RPCs for Metadata management and here is the current behaviour:

## RegisterEntityTypesArg
To only register/update multiple EntityTypes and define the corresponding behaviour of the EntityType. Check the following arg to understand various configurations possible at an EntityType level: TypeInfo.
However, the following restriction is present for the dynamic registration compared to the config approach:
Changing the status of evictability of an entity type is not supported. (updating entity type from evictable to un-evictable and vice-versa is not supported)

[IDF Design Documents | IDF Metadata RPCs]
## RegisterMetricTypesArg
To only register/update MetricTypes and define corresponding behaviour of MetricType like Indexability, Nested field Information, Time-series properties. Check the following arg to understand the configurations: MetricTypeArg
However, the following restrictions are present for the dynamic registration compared to the config approach:
Changing the status of indexing (enabling/disabling indexes) is disabled.
Changing index column data type is disabled.
Registering indexed attributes which have nested fields is not allowed.
Adding indexed attributes for evictable entities is  not allowed.
Most of the above restrictions can be removed with a gflag. But however, 3&4 in RegisterMetricTypesArg would require a minor code change to make it gflag enabled.
Note that unregistration of EntityTypes and MetricTypes is currently not supported.

[IDF Design Documents | IDF Metadata RPCs]
## Note to clients:
Currently the metadata management in IDF is done in a leader only fashion. Currently the Metadata RPCs are just responsible for saving the metadata on the leader, and initiate the propagation to all the nodes in the cluster, waits for configurable wait time (default 15s) for the other nodes to get the changes. The actual application of metadata happens asynchronously. Refer to the section below for more details on the actual flow of the RPCs.
While metadata propagation is instantaneous under ideal network conditions, its application can be delayed by factors like system scale and disk latency. This creates potential issues for services.
Metadata updates are serialized in IDF. So it would be ideal to club the metadata updates in a single call. Also, it is suggested to have a higher timeout for all the config RPCs. Atleast, over a minute.
Although new metadata is queryable, dependent operations may fail with errors related to missing entity or metric type definitions until the metadata is fully applied. Note that there is currently no mechanism to automatically handle these "missing metadata" errors.

[IDF Design Documents | IDF Server to remote cassandra communication]
## IDF Server to remote cassandra communication
Mana Agarwal
In progress
October 2021
Jira: https://jira.nutanix.com/browse/ENG-263270
(IDF shards not available when Cassandra in crash loop on one node)

## 1. Motivation:
IDF uses cassandra as the underlying data storage. It relies on local cassandra to handle all the requests. In case of error conditions, the node goes into a forwarding mode where it forwards the RPC to another node and the request is still served. However, this does not work in all the cases:
When local cassandra is in a crash loop. This will result in continuous kTimeout or kUnavailable errors from cassandra. The node will eventually go into kForwarding mode due to frequent restarts but until that happens the client will receive errors.
When local cassandra is down. In this case it will be detached from the ring and will be unavailable to serve requests. However, the node will take some time to be detached from the ring and until that happens the client will receive kUnavailable errors.
In both of the above cases IDF server doesn’t FATAL/crash instead it keeps on retrying. These errors get propagated all the way to the IDF clients (which require IDF interaction with cassandra) leading to their operations being stuck.
The other cassandra nodes might still be healthy and serving client requests but currently, IDF (or infact cassandra client) doesn’t have any mechanism to switch to healthy (and remote) cassandra nodes in such scenarios.

[IDF Design Documents | IDF Server to remote cassandra communication]
## 2. Solution
Client needs to switch to remote (healthy) cassandra in case local cassandra is down/unavailable or in a crash loop and switch back to local cassandra once it is up and healthy.
The solution can be broken down into three broad categories:
Detecting that the local cassandra is down
Selecting the remote cassandra to switch to
Monitoring the status of local cassandra and switching back to it once it’s healthy

## Approach 1:
Overall approach:
Maintain a collection of available and healthy (Normal mode) cassandra endpoints that is running across all the nodes of PC/PE  cluster.
Monitor the liveness change of the cassandra node and update the status accordingly.
Use one of the healthy Cassandra Client endpoints to issue the request with the local node being the highest priority.
A mechanism that automatically puts the alive nodes into cooldown mode in order for them to become stable before they can be used again to serve requests.

## 3.1 Detect Unreachable Cassandra Node
The health of local cassandra node can be guessed using the following options:
Zeus health watch to monitor the liveness change of cassandra client. The worst case delay for this is 20s.
RPC failure rate - Keep a lower threshold of rpc error count (kUnavailable or kTimeout error) within a specific amount of time. If the error count crosses this threshold, we switch to another healthy cassandra node.
Update: We are going to use point 1 in our final implementation.

[IDF Design Documents | IDF Server to remote cassandra communication]
## 3.2 Select Remote Cassandra Create a list of backup healthy cassandra nodes on startup and use any one of the available nodes as the new endpoint. This list will be updated based on zeus health watch callback (node addition or deletion) and the node status from zeus_config (to filter out nodes which are in forwarding mode). The logic of selecting a “healthy” cassandra endpoint is following steps in the order of priority: Check whether the local Cassandra Endpoint is healthy. If yes, use it. If 1) is not available, randomly pick a Cassandra Endpoint from the healthy end point pool. Healthy endpoint pool will guarantee that all the endpoints present in it are in normal mode. If no healthy_client is available, take one of the endpoints from cooldown mode with local being the highest priority. If both healthy_client_ and cooldown_mode_client_ are empty, use the local endpoint. (If this scenario happens, that means cassandra is not available on any of the nodes and nothing is going to work). Collection of “healthy” Cassandra client endpoints status ( e.g ClientStatus): typedef tuple<Cassandra::Ptr, /* Cassandra client */ uint64, /* error count */ uint64, /* error time */ bool, /* is_alive */ int64 /* incarnation id */> ClientStatus; typedef shared_ptr<ClientStatus> ClientStatusPtr; // Healthy cassandra nodes map. unordered_map<string, ClientStatusPtr> healthy_client_; // Nodes in cooldown mode. unordered_map<string, incarnation_id> cooldown_mode_node_map_;

[IDF Design Documents | IDF Server to remote cassandra communication]
uint64, /* error time */ bool, /* is_alive */ int64 /* incarnation id */> ClientStatus; typedef shared_ptr<ClientStatus> ClientStatusPtr; // Healthy cassandra nodes map. unordered_map<string, ClientStatusPtr> healthy_client_; // Nodes in cooldown mode. unordered_map<string, incarnation_id> cooldown_mode_node_map_; vector<Cassandra::Ptr> remote_endpoints_(ft+1)

## Initialization logic:
Collect a list of healthy cassandra node endpoint information by doing :
zeus_->GetAllHealthy(Zeus::kCassandraHealthNamespace,
all_healthy_cb);
and populate the CassandraStatus for each observed healthy node (which is not
in forwarding mode) in healthy_client_ map accordingly.
Start the zeus health watch on Zeus::kCassandraHealthNamespace namespace and update the healthy_client_ map on every liveness change.

[IDF Design Documents | IDF Server to remote cassandra communication]
## 3.3 Monitor Local Cassandra Status
If the cassandra endpoint was switched to some node other than local cassandra node, we need to monitor the status of the local cassandra node for sometime and switch back to it once it’s stable. The node can be put in cool down mode and be moved to healthy_client_ only after it has passed its cool down period.
The logic for monitoring the status of endpoint could be as follows:
Put the node in cool down mode on liveness change (node addition). This not only applies to the local node but to all the nodes of the cluster as we want to monitor the stability of the endpoint before moving it to healthy_client_.
Send empty MultiGetSlice RPC to the node in cool down mode and keep track of the RPC response. If there are no errors (kUnavailable or kTimeout) during the cool down period, move the node to healthy_client_.
Update: We are going to use point 1 in our final implementation.

[IDF Design Documents | IDF Server to remote cassandra communication]
## Status Update Logic:
On observation of any liveness changes, the ClientStatus instance of the corresponding endpoint will be updated with the latest liveness flag as well as the incarnation_id.
If a healthy endpoint has a state changed to unhealthy, the ClientStatus instance will be removed from healthy_client_.
If an unhealthy endpoint has a state changed to healthy, the endpoint would be put in cool down mode before being put in healty_client_.
RPC failure rate: Keep a lower threshold of rpc error count (kUnavailable or kTimeout error) returned by cassandra client within a specific amount of time. If the error count crosses this threshold, switch to another healthy cassandra node.
Update: We are going to use point 1 in our final implementation.
Note (TODO): We should not remove the local node from healthy_client_ on first crash as it might be a one off scenario and we wouldn’t want the client to communicate to remote cassandra for one off failures. For local node, we could wait for 30s before another failure happens (or could keep a failure threshold) before removing it from healthy_client_.

[IDF Design Documents | IDF Server to remote cassandra communication]
## Decisions to be taken:
We need to decide where to implement the solution.
The above solution could be implemented both in IDF as well as cassandra client. However, it’s better to implement the solution in cassandra as other clients of cassandra face the same problem as IDF (Eg. Pithos) and could leverage the same solution instead of each client having their separate solution.
Please refer to ENG-99569 IDF should talk to available cassandra on the cluster when local cassandra becomes unavailable for extended period of time
for the implementation details of the solution in cassandra client.
The benefit of the above solution is that it is completely abstract from the clients. Clients are not required to handle anything from their side. They will be unaware of which endpoint is actually serving their requests. All they need to do is create a CassandraMultiNodeOps object (instead of CassandraOps) and use the same in their code for sending RPCs. CassandraMultiNodeOps will handle all the work of detection of unavailable endpoint, connecting to a healthy endpoint and switching back to the local endpoint.
The following are the tunables whose default values need to decided:
Cool down period after which the endpoint will be moved to healthy_client_.
RPC error count threshold
Time window period for deciding if the endpoint is reachable or not.
The clients will be allowed to set custom values based on their use case, load, frequency of RPCs etc.

[IDF Design Documents | IDF Server to remote cassandra communication]
## Cassandra:
If the node is in normal mode and there are absolutely no crashes in the system, then the RPCs should always be served given that there are no CPU/disk issues.

## Zookeeper Watch:
On every crash, there will be a new zookeeper session created and the old session will expire. When the session expires, the ephemeral node tied to the health of the session is deleted and the watch is fired. There are three ways the session can be expired:
By the zookeeper server: This will happen when the service doesn't come up within session_timeout secs. In that case, the zookeeper server expires the session.
By the service whose health is being monitored: If the service comes up quickly (before it's session timeout), it will expire the old session and create a new session.
There was no progress being made by the service after the last transaction (due to network issues, CPU issues etc.). In this case, the session will be expired and the service will FATAL.
The max time taken for the watch to be delivered is session_timeout secs. session_timeout is set per service. Low session_timeout means expiring the session more quickly even on very short unavailability and FATALing the service which might be harmful.
Zk watches are fired on every event (node going down and node coming up) and are received in the same order in which they are fired. The incarnation id will be monotonically increasing but need not necessarily be incremented by 1.

[IDF Design Documents | IDF Server to remote cassandra communication]
## Approach 2:
Another approach is for IDF to unload its shards on that node (on detection of local cassandra unavailability) and go into forwarding mode. Then switch the operations back to the node and migrate the shards once the local cassandra becomes stable.
Detection of local cassandra unavailability and monitoring of local cassandra will still be required to be done using either zeus_config or zookeeper health node.
Pros:
IDF will always talk to local cassandra.
The changes are specific to IDF code base, no changes required in cassandra client.
Cons:
Loading and unloading shards is a heavy operation and will lead to idf unavailability while the shards are migrating.
Once local cassandra is stable, shards need to be migrated back.
Can’t be leveraged by other clients, the changes will be specific to IDF.
One more hop as the RPC request will be forwarded to the node which holds the required shards.
A healthy idf instance won’t be utilised for doing any form of processing other than just forwarding the requests.
Wastage of CPU and memory.
Puts more load on the other IDF instances.

Lazy Loading Entities

## Problem
For 400k VMs, it takes 290+ seconds to bootstrap IDF. For 8800k Alerts, the time is ~1080s, which turned out to be similar to VMs. The time for bootstrap is proportional to the total number of entities. When the number of entities increase to millions, it takes ~20 minutes, which is unacceptable.

[IDF Design Documents | Lazy Loading Entities]
## Solution
There are basically 2 types of entities: operational (i.e. VMs, VNICs, VDISKs) & historical (alerts, events, tasks). We do not expect huge number of operational entities (currently we only support 12.5k VMs, but definitely not millions), but we could potentially have huge number of historical entities (500k Alerts in the large PC setup. The number could go to millions with the coming of Audit Events).
Historical entities are not always needed in cache, while operational entities are required for functioning properly. From this point of view, we could separate the loading of historical and operational entities as to reduce the total number of entities loaded at bootstrap time.
The idea is quite straightforward:
We could load based on priorities. The priority can be at the level of entity type. Currently, loading entities is on the basis of per shard and shards can be loaded in parallel. Then we could further narrow down the loading granularity to per type (i.e. shard + entity_type). The loading of different will be sequential, i.e p0 -> p1 -> p2 -> ...
We would need a status (is_loaded) indicating whether the data of an entity type is loaded or not. If !is_loaded, we will return kRetry for the request. After all data has been loaded, we can change the bootstrap_completed to true.

## Metadata Registration for LCM based services
July 2021
Work In Progress

[IDF Design Documents | Metadata Registration for LCM based services]
## Problem Statement: As of today, metadata registration happens via client config files where clients put their IDF schema in protobuf text format for entity_types and metric_types. IDF also provides RPCs to register the schema for clients. But the RPC based metadata registration lacks full fledged feature support. For example, clients can't register indexed attributes via RPCs. This files based schema registration has worked perfectly for a unified release cycle model for PC and PE. With the increasing acceptance of LCM based upgrades in nutanix for services, almost all new services on PC are being added to this independent release model. With this new model coming in, the schema being present as part of the PC makes the services dependent on PC releases if they depend on the file based schema registration, as operations to IDF on entity_types can't happen unless the schema gets registered. Clients can use RPC based schema registration(e.g. Calm), but they can't register secondary indexes as well as evictable entities even if the scale is high, because of limitations such as indexed attribute registration. There are other limitations of dynamic registration on sync/backup/restore but those are not covered as part of this doc. With big-bang, even the clients depending on schema registration and common release cycle, want to maintain the config files in their own respective branches instead of ntnxdb-client branch to speed up their development, without waiting for LKG of

[IDF Design Documents | Metadata Registration for LCM based services]
clients depending on schema registration and common release cycle, want to maintain the config files in their own respective branches instead of ntnxdb-client branch to speed up their development, without waiting for LKG of schema file commits. This also enables separation of ownership and tighter control of their schema (disallowing clients modifying each other's schema).

[IDF Design Documents | Metadata Registration for LCM based services]
## Suggestion:
Suggestion would be to implement approach 2 totally with adding asynchronous registration of indexed attributes for clients like calm already using approach 1, if it's not easy to move to approach 2.
Tasks:
Approach1:
Support evictability change on leader after RegisterEntityTypes RPC.
Support indexing change on leader after RegisterMetricTypes RPC.
Asynchronous execution of nested field recomputation.
Handle conditions like successive schema modifications should fail until 1-3 above are completed.
Approach2:
Check if components can have a PC version as dependency while using new fields/moving from RPC to schema file.
Check if LCM can put files to IDF config directory, for LCM based components/it should be file level overwrite, not directory level.
Check if we can watch config files for their modifications and trigger registration. Or periodically check the file contents/file modification times.
Trigger registration whenever a file changes at runtime without restart on leader.
Check if unknown fields can be ignored from file parsing text to proto, in case LCM client puts a new file and IDF is old. (not needed if clients are ok with point 1)

[IDF Design Documents | Metadata Registration for LCM based services]
