Currently, this document mentions the high level solutions possible to fix the above problems with their pros and cons.
In all the below mentioned solutions there is a common issue, client upgrading after PC and trying to register backup/sync for registered entity_types, in this case the client will have to do dummy updates on all entities if backup/sync site is already registered, and that is not handled as part of this doc.

[IDF Design Documents | Metadata Registration for LCM based services]
## Approach1:
Add support in IDF to support schema registration dynamically.
PROS:
This solves both the above mentioned issues.
CONS:
Clients might get upgraded before server and when clients register their schema IDF protobuf would be old and won't recognize some fields in the schema, later when IDF gets upgraded, the client wouldn't know it has to re-register schema again with the fields that were unknown in previous versions.
Solution here could be to take the protobuf from the client as text and try to parse known fields, but persist all text. During bootstrap verify whether all unknown fields are now recognizable.
Assume that whenever clients use a new field they'll depend on the min version of the PC in which IDF will have that field.
Currently, the schema registration is synchronous on the leader and asynchronous on non-leaders. Adding indexed attributes/nested fields has to iterate over all entities and might have to read data from cassandra in case of evictable entities. The synchronous part would be time taking and often lead to timeouts so even on leaders we might want to make it asynchronous.
Also, there will be behaviour of call succeeding but schema still not taken effect. This expectation exists even today also, but the time taken will be higher since cassandra reads will be involved for indexing.
No visibility to the IDF team about rogue clients as all registration will be hardcoded in clients code.

[IDF Design Documents | Metadata Registration for LCM based services]
## Approach2: Allow clients to add schema files to /home/nutanix/config/insights/ done on LCM based upgrade of the component, which is the same as IDF config files directory with a specific prefix/suffix to denote entity_type and attribute config files. IDF leader can watch on these files and apply schema in case of any change in these files, and decide whether to apply it directly/restart IDF, followers will apply schema in the same way as now. Bootstrap will be the same as current, but read all entity_type files followed by metric_type files. The restrictions of parent entity_type/base attributes being present before child entity_type/nested fields still stays, so preferable if they are registered in the same file, else behaviour could be random as we're not mentioning any sequence of reading config files. Instead of directory we can also have clients specify an exact list of files in IDF, downside of this being the first time release of the component will be dependent on a PC release, successive releases will be independent. We can check with LCM if the first release of a component is already dependent on the PC. PROS: This solves both the above mentioned issues and most issues mentioned in the previous approach. This also solves the issue that client has to detect IDF upgrade and re-send the config registration APIs. There will be no API timeouts involved since everything is being done internally in IDF. IDF team can verify these files in oncalls and see which client is

[IDF Design Documents | Metadata Registration for LCM based services]
and re-send the config registration APIs. There will be no API timeouts involved since everything is being done internally in IDF. IDF team can verify these files in oncalls and see which client is rogue in case of issues. IDF team can be added as reviewers for these files as well. CONS: The clients might get upgraded first and put fields in the schema file which aren't known to IDF protobuf, currently converting text to proto gives errors in case of unknown fields, we'll have to find a way to ignore unknown fields and apply the schema. Allow the clients to publish and retrieve entities and attributes without registering them with defaults and later when IDF schema gets upgraded with the PC.
CONS:
Many of the clients planning to use this are depending on nested fields, so they'll only be publishing __zprotobuf__ and reading/filtering on other attributes. While most features in IDF can work with defaults and later tuned (e.g. indexing/retention/evictability).
features like nested fields have no default and won't work in this approach.

LCM based release for IDF configs.

[IDF Design Documents | Metric Data Loss Prevention on Crash]
## Introduction
This document addresses the mechanism of preventing metric data loss on node crashes, which was described in ENG-44207.
Metric data updates are returned to clients after they are properly stored in cache. They are written to disks periodically by a separate snapshotting process at a configurable interval. If a node crashes before they are persistent to disks, data loss will occur.  Obviously, the longer the period of snapshotting, the higher probability of data loss, and the more data loss.

[IDF Design Documents | Metric Data Loss Prevention on Crash]
## New Design To prevent metric data loss from memory when a node crashes, all updates need to be logged to a persistent storage before returning clients with success When a node crashes before snapshotting (and after returning clients with success), a replaying process can recover all non-snapshotted data upon restarting. In addition, the persistent storage of data should be purged after they are successfully written to disks (snapshotted). Therefore, the design should include the following three parts: Metric Data Logging There are two sources of places where metric data should be logged. One is from the RPC of PutMetricData in the RPC layer, and the other is from PutEntity() in the store layer when an attribute change should be logged as a metric. Considering this, metric logging will be done in the beginning of PutEntityWithMetric(). PutMetricDataArg is converted into IOBuffer and then the IOBuffer is logged into on-disk files in PutEntityWithMetric(). The logging can be done in two ways: sync and async. A new parameter will be added into PutMetricDataArg to let clients specify sync and async. In sync, the IOBuffer is logged into files before PutEntityWithMetricInternal() is called; in async, the IOBuffer is put into a queue and a separate process writes IOBuffers from the queue to files. To avoid contention during logging, each thread appends IOBuffers to its own logging file. The file name is the thread ID. A new file with the same name is created in every snapshotting

[IDF Design Documents | Metric Data Loss Prevention on Crash]
files. To avoid contention during logging, each thread appends IOBuffers to its own logging file. The file name is the thread ID. A new file with the same name is created in every snapshotting window (FLAGS_insights_metric_data_write_to_cassandra_delay_seconds) and is put in a sub-directory named after the beginning timestamp of the corresponding snapshot window. Since one file may have metric data from multiple calls, each metric data logging begins with a payload. The payload has 9 bytes. 8 of them represents the length of the metric data and the other one indicates whether the metrics are attribute or not. Log Replaying During a restart, after the cache population, a new thread is generated to go through all log files in all directories, reconstruct the parameters in PutEntityWithMetric(), and replay them one by one. Since the log replaying may co-exist with new coming requests, all pre-exising directories (divided by snapshotting windows) are recorded before starting the thread of log replaying. Log Purging At the end of each metric data snapshotting process, all directories with the timestamp name which is smaller than the starting timestamp of the previous snapshot window are deleted. Since the thread of log purging might co-exist with the thread of log replaying as log replaying may take a long time to finish, the target files in the purging thread should not be recorded by the thread of log replaying.

[IDF Design Documents | Metric_data_layout]
Metric_data_by_entity row:  1 week worth of raw data for a given Entity Type/ Metric Name chunked into 168 Hourly data.
Metric_data_by_shard row: 1 hour data for a given Metric Name through ALL entities of the same entity type.   These N 1 hour data chunks are are serialized as one proto buffer object is then compressed to be stored as a binary blob.  The compression ratio is usually 3:1 – 4:1 as observed from the testing environments.
Metric_data_by_entity_ds: Each row stores 1 week worth of hourly aggregated data for a given Entity Type/ Metric Name chunked into 168 pieces.  Each chunk contains 6 aggregated (min, max, avg, sum, last, count) values.
Metric_data_by_shard_ds:  Each rows stores 1 hour worth of data chunks of a given Metric Name for ALL entities of the same entity type.  These N 1 hour data chunks are combined together serialized as one proto buffer object is then compressed to be stored as a binary blob.  The compression ratio is usually 3:1 – 4:1 as observed from the testing environments.

[IDF Design Documents | Multi-node metric data log replay]
Multi-node metric data log replay Our current metric data replay implementation works well in a single node deployment, but it wouldn't work well in multi-node deployment (whether it's a leader-only or sharded solution) because after the node crashes the data ownership may change (in leader-only it's almost guaranteed to change as the leader most likely is going to be re-elected on a different node). In this case, metric data replay would be delayed indefinitely (until the node becomes the leader again, which may not happen for a while). To mitigate this issue, we need to somehow get the metric data from the node that doesn't own the data any more to the node that now owns the data. One way to do it is to make each node read the metric data log from the local file system and forward it to the current data owner (leader in the leader-only solution). The solution should handle the following scenarios: the new leader may restart while the previous leader (now follower) is still forwarding the data the follower may restart a few times before finishing metric data forwarding the new leader needs to delete old log files after the data is flushed to Cassandra The first solution that comes to mind is to initiate metric replay on node start (regardless whether it's the leader or not) and then just forward the metric data to the leader, so that the leader would ingest the data and eventually flush it. It turns out this solution has some problems handling the abovementioned scenarios:

[IDF Design Documents | Multi-node metric data log replay]
and then just forward the metric data to the leader, so that the leader would ingest the data and eventually flush it. It turns out this solution has some problems handling the abovementioned scenarios: if the leader restarts, it would lose the data that the follower has already sent if the follower restarts a few times, it's going to resend data a few times, which can lead to incorrect data for metric data downsampled with kSum and kAvg coordination needs to be done between new leader and the followers so that the logs are deleted To avoid these problems, the "chain of custody" approach can be used -- the followers would forward a chunk of metric data to the leader, the leader would write it to its own log (and apply to the metric data cache), ack to the follower, after which the follower would mark the data as "sent". To avoid double replays, we can calculate SHA-1 of each chunk and keep a set of all chunks that the leader has applied (either from its own log or forwarded from other nodes). The easiest way to implement chunking is to chunk data when saving into the metric data log into ~10MB files. I.e. watch for the current file size and if grows bigger than ~10MB then start a new one. This way it's easy to implement "chain of custody" -- read chunk, forward it, get ack, delete on the source. It's also easy to keep track of what chunks are replayed -- just calculate SHA-1 of the chunk and put it into the set. Note that because the set of chunks' SHA-1s is not persisted,

[IDF Design Documents | Multi-node metric data log replay]
also easy to keep track of what chunks are replayed -- just calculate SHA-1 of the chunk and put it into the set. Note that because the set of chunks' SHA-1s is not persisted, it's still possible to get double-replays if a follower sent a chunk, crashed before receiving the ack, then was down for a while, and sent the chunk again. This should be fairly rare, so I think this is an acceptable imprecision. We could mitigate it further by storing log chunk SHA-1s in the MetricDataDB (then we would be able to read metric data from Cassandra and know what log chunks it has incorporated), but I'm not sure if it's worth the trouble. The only case that this model wouldn't handle is kLast -- as the data may come in any order, logically older values may override logically newer. We could take couple approaches here: Do nothing. We have this problem regardless of metric data log replay and generally we get one sample per downsampling interval anyway, so reordering doesn't cause issues in practice. Actually fix kLast -- we already have an extra field to store count for averages, we can use this field to store latest timestamp for kLast (which would be real timestamp of timeseries data, not ingest time), then reordering won't present a problem. In any case, if we decide to fix kLast, this should be done in a separate change.

[IDF Design Documents | Orphan Entity Auto-Deletion]
Orphan Entity Auto-Deletion
April 2025
Devendra ShekhawatSumit BhatiaJineet Desai
[In-progress]

## Problem Statement
IDF currently supports auto-deletion of entities based on expiration timestamp only. Some clients have use cases to automatically cleanup/delete entities after their parent / linked entity has been deleted. This feature is pretty similar to Cascading Deletes in relational databases, with major difference being, IDF will cleanup / delete the orphaned entities in the background periodically instead of inline deletion along with parent.

## Solution
For supporting this feature of Orphan entity auto-deletion first we need to define how to link entities.

## Linking of Entities
In general, there are two ways to link entities (or form parent child relationship) to be used for auto-deletion of orphaned entities:-
Child entities provide a link to the parent entity.
The parent entity provides the information for all the children entities.
In IDF, we will use Option-1 to define the relationship between parent and child entities (where all the child entities will provide a link to their corresponding parent entity).
The reason for choosing Option-1 is figuring out children to clean up from deleted parent entities will be expensive as we might have to retain attributes in a deleted entity and also read those from disk.

[IDF Design Documents | Orphan Entity Auto-Deletion]
## Actions/Configuration needed from client services.
The client service is required to register the attribute attr_name for the child entity type. This attribute will be used to establish a link between the child entity and its corresponding parent entity by storing the UUID or entity_id of the parent.
Additionally, the client service must update the schema of the child entity type to include a background_cleanup_config section. This configuration should specify the following:
The name of the parent entity type
The name of the parent mapping attribute (i.e., attr_name)
The namespace of the parent mapping attribute
All schema modifications are to be applied solely to the child entity type. No changes are required on the parent entity type.

[IDF Design Documents | Orphan Entity Auto-Deletion]
## Cleanup Behaviour based on schema
If the entity type name mentioned in the field “parent_entity_type_name” is not a valid/registered entity type in IDF then cleanup will not be performed.
Attribute name mentioned in the field “parent_mapping_attribute_name” should either have a valid/registered attribute name or a pseudo attribute name.
Attribute mentioned in the field “parent_mapping_attribute_name” should have string value (str_value) only. If any other type of value is populated then cleanup will not be performed.
If either of the fields “parent_entity_type_name” or “parent_mapping_attribute_name” are left empty then cleanup won’t be performed.
If the child entity type is evictable then the attribute name mentioned in the field “parent_mapping_attribute_name” should be marked as an indexed attribute.

## Rolling Upgrades
This feature can only be reliably honoured by IDF after all the nodes in the cluster have been upgraded.

[IDF Design Documents | Orphan Entity Auto-Deletion]
## Overall Feature Limitation/Guarantees
Entity ID reuse in the parent table (recreating entities with the same uuid again) might cause issues with auto-cleanup of child entities.
When configured at entity type level, IDF will perform the cleanup in the background periodically. By default we are planning to keep the periodicity at 1 hour (might change based on design review and discussions with client teams).
Since the cleanup will be in the background and will be performed in batches so it is hard to provide a strict upper time limit for cleanup to happen.
Cleanup can only be performed for local entities. Cleanup will not touch replicated entities.
Modifying parent links and related schema at runtime might have unknown effect because cleanup running in background might use older or newer schema.
Once cleaned up, entity data can not be restored by IDF.
In case the parent entity is a replicated entity, then on cluster unregistration parent entity will be removed from IDF, this will lead to deletion of child entities as well.
Currently we won’t support n level traversal for parent-child relationships. Hence if we have a chain of entity types registered for cascading deletes (for e.g. e1->e2->e3->e4), then the deletes would happen eventually. Deleting e4 should eventually delete e1,e2,e3.
Client needs to ensure that the parent-child relationship links form a tree structure and has no cycles.

[IDF Design Documents | Orphan Entity Auto-Deletion]
## Having tenant-id as a part of the background_cleanup_config
During recent discussions, we evaluated whether the tenant_id corresponding to the parent entity should be explicitly included in the background_cleanup_config of the child entity type. If adopted, this change would require the client to configure the following additional metadata in the child entity type’s background_cleanup_config:
Name of the parent entity type
Name of the parent mapping attribute
Namespace of the parent mapping attribute
tenant_id (i.e., the tenant space associated with the parent entities)
Pros and Cons of Adding tenant_id
Cons:
Users would have to register an extra attribute/metric in addition to the parent_mapping_attribute_name. However this new attribute need not require any sort of indexing.
The internal GetEntities call, which would be used to fetch active parent entities, would set the tenant_id in the GetEntitiesArg. However, the current implementation of the GetEntities RPC is not tenant-aware, which means including the tenant_id provides no immediate functional benefit.
It remains to be confirmed whether components such as Task or Ergon WAL are aware of and propagate the tenant_id context when registering child entity types.
Pros:
Tenant-aware readiness: Including the tenant_id enables a smoother transition when IDF workflows become tenant-aware in the future, reducing the need for further configuration changes at that time.
headings: Having tenant-id as a part of the background_cleanup_config

## Orphan Entity AutoDeletion Implementation Doc
May 2025 [In progress]
Jineet DesaiSumit BhatiaDevendra Shekhawat
To support automated deletion of orphan entities, we propose introducing a new periodic process, independent of the existing auto-deletion mechanism. This process will be responsible for identifying and deleting orphaned child entities whose corresponding parent entities no longer exist.
Characteristics of the periodic process:
It shall run at a frequency of 1hr for now, to clean up orphan entities.
We shall introduce appropriate jitter in order to avoid parallel scans/processing with other periodic processes(like AutoDelete and AutoPurging).

[IDF Design Documents | Orphan Entity Deletion Implementation Details]
## Orphan Entity Process Description Overall the periodic process would perform the following set of steps for orphan entity deletion: Identify the relevant child entity types: Load into memory the child entity types that have background_cleanup_config populated in their schema. From here fetch the parent_entity_type and the parent_mapping_attribute_name(this attribute belongs to the child entity type). Fetch Referenced Parent Entity IDs: Once we have this list of child entity types, the next task is to fetch the uuids or entity_ids of the parent entities(may be in a batch of 500 or 1000) from the “parent_mapping_attribute_name” attribute in the child entity. This list can be fetched in memory from IDF or by performing a scan on Cassandra. The pros/cons for both the approaches are discussed in detail in the next section. Note: This attribute is populated by the client(as in the child-parent link is established by the client). Not populating this attribute will not perform orphan entity cleanup. Verify Existence of Parent Entities: With the gathered list of parent entity IDs (processed in batches of 500–1000), issue a fan-out query across all IDF nodes to retrieve existing entities of type parent_entity_type that match the entity_id’s. Maintain an in-memory map of parent_entity_id -> child_entity_id to facilitate the lookup for child-parent relationship. Determine and Delete Orphaned Child Entities: Identify parent entity IDs that are missing from the query response, which

[IDF Design Documents | Orphan Entity Deletion Implementation Details]
entity_id’s. Maintain an in-memory map of parent_entity_id -> child_entity_id to facilitate the lookup for child-parent relationship. Determine and Delete Orphaned Child Entities: Identify parent entity IDs that are missing from the query response, which indicates that the parent entities have been deleted. For each missing parent entity, delete the corresponding child entities. We shall directly use the store function DeleteEntityFromShard to remove this entity from IDF.

## In Memory Fetch v/s Cassandra Scan
Let us discuss the approach for reading the child entities in memory versus performing a Cassandra scan just like the normal auto deletion process.

## In-Memory Approach
Cons:
Need to enforce indexing on the “parent_mapping_attribute_name”, if the child entity type is an evictable entity type.
Would increase the memory overhead with indexing coming into picture.
Pros:
The code framework becomes easy with the in memory approach as fetching the parent entity ids(from parent_mapping_attribute_name) just requires a query to the local IDF node(for child entity types). This can be a NodeGetEntitiesWithMetrics query if appropriate shard locks are grabbed. Else we can just issue a normal GetEntitiesWithMetrics query with shard_list provided to grab child entities on that node.
As mentioned above, the flow for this goes through the query layer of IDF.

[IDF Design Documents | Orphan Entity Deletion Implementation Details]
## Cassandra Scan Approach:
Cons:
We might want to scan the child entities and obtain parent entity ids in batches. We do not want to block the thread performing the scan while we process one set of parent entity ids. For this we might need to add a construct to pause Cassandra scans and resume once one batch has been completed.
Another periodic process that requires additional Cassandra scan.
Pros:
No indexing required for this approach.
headings: In Memory Fetch v/s Cassandra Scan

## Problem statement: Aryan and Aman have run extensive benchmarks around various combinations of minio instances and buckets and we have come to the conclusion that the OSS stats resource requirements (memory, cpu, disk) for 1 million buckets and 32 minio instances are not feasible for OSS 1.0 GA unless we revisit the stats framework workflows. To provide more details, we currently have two main tables: poseidon_cluster_dimension_fact_table: For storing UI stats. Cardinality of {bucket_id} poseidon_instance_dimension_fact_table: For storing internal performance stats for debugging purposes. Cardinality {bucket_id * minio_id} For a single tenant, 1M buckets, 32 minio instance setup, the first table creates 1 million entities whereas the second creates 32 Million entities, which means that the second table contributes to ~97% of the total resource consumption irrespective of the percentage of active buckets that we write to. Even in the smallest possible setup, we would have 3 minio instances which means that this second table still contributes 75% of all resource consumption. In terms of actual numbers: 500k Buckets and 32 Minio instances (16.5 million entities) requires 26 GB of memory in IDF and a few GBs of memory in Cassandra totaling to roughly 30 GB of memory for single instance IDF container. (This is with evictable entities enabled) This is just for the entities and without any regular stat injection. (We evicted the stats that is required to trigger the creation of

[IDF Design Documents | Proposal for changes of OSS stats model]
single instance IDF container. (This is with evictable entities enabled) This is just for the entities and without any regular stat injection. (We evicted the stats that is required to trigger the creation of these entities). To reach 1M buckets, 32 minio instances would mean roughly double this number. Currently, only the first table stats are queried for by UI and there aren’t any queries for the second table. AFAIK, the second table is to shortlist the problematic Minios from the total list of Minio instances and then figure out the problematic process by referring to counters (which is not targeted for GA 1.0). We can try to optimise on the total resource consumption from IDF by introducing several new changes such as evictable entities for dimension fact tables combined with lesser overhead of indexes, spilling indexes onto disks, faster expiration and deletion of un-used dimension entities etc but sooner or later, we would hit scale issues because of the high cardinality of this second table (75% - 97% of overall). IMHO, even a different data store will have similar resource issues at a certain scale since the number of stats and entities can grow exponentially. [IDF Design Documents | Reasons for IDF requirement of CAS from the underlying persistence]
## Reasons for IDF requirement of CAS from the underlying persistence
Devendra, Sumit
Feb 2022
This doc discusses the scenarios due to which IDF requires CAS support from the underlying persistence store.
In case of happy path(success scenario), IDF marks an entity as 'kUpdateInProgress' and sends a write request to cassandra and then after the write is successful applies the same in-memory, clears the 'kUpdateInProgress' and returns success to the client.
Any parallel updates during this duration are rejected by the server. So there shouldn't be a need for CAS support for these scenarios in general since the server is doing the concurrency control here which would be enough.
But, CAS support is required in case of failure scenarios to avoid invalid state from previous failed write in case and, in case of restarts to avoid write issued before restart, to overwrite later writes.
High level points to consider while working on top of non-CAS based store:
Make sure no parallel writes from normal workflows are ongoing for the same keys.
Writes after crash should not be overwritten by earlier issued writes for the same key.

[IDF Design Documents | Reasons for IDF requirement of CAS from the underlying persistence]
## Scenario 1 Local writes:
IDF server receives an update for entity1 for state s1 and issues a write to persistence store and crashes.
Before the update reaches the persistence or before the persistence IDF server restarts and reads state s0 and receives another state s2 and issues write to the store and it succeeds before s1 and later s1 succeeds in absence of CAS. And IDF returns success to the client who expects the state in db now to be s2.
In the absence of CAS s1 should have failed and been lost but here s1 is the final state in the persistence which is unexpected.
There could be similar variations of this with other error scenarios like timeout.

[IDF Design Documents | Reasons for IDF requirement of CAS from the underlying persistence]
## Scenario 2 Backup/Sync: entity1 gets updated with state1 with db_modified_timestamp as 5. The update is sent to the replica and gets persisted with CAS say 5 and corresponding missing ranges are also filled. Now, entity1 has two quick successive updates with db_modified_timestamp 6 and 7. The update with timestamp 6 reached the replica and replica server compared it against the previous db_modified_timestamp 5 of the entity and found that 6 was greater and issued a write to cassandra(before the write could succeed the server crashed and restarted) (In case of CAS the write would have been issued with CAS value 6) On the restarted server, the entity1 with db_modified_timestamp 7 came, read the value as 5 and issued a write again which immediately succeeded. (The previously issued write came later to s3 and overwrites this). The final state on replica persistence should be 7 but without CAS support it is 6 which is invalid. Server would ack the db_modified_timestamp 7 as success and it'll never be retried. In case of CAS writes only one of the updates would have succeeded and would have helped avoid invalid final state in the persistence store by failing one of the two writes. A variation of the same scenario would be timeout error, in case the entity state s1 reaches the persistence layer after the client side timeout and if an update comes in with state s2 and reaches persistence between the client side timeout and s1 reaching persistence. The final state in the db will be

[IDF Design Documents | Reasons for IDF requirement of CAS from the underlying persistence]
after the client side timeout and if an update comes in with state s2 and reaches persistence between the client side timeout and s1 reaching persistence. The final state in the db will be s1 instead of the expected s2 state.

[IDF Design Documents | Reducing cassandra ops lock contention]
JIRA: https://jira.nutanix.com/browse/CPD-1878

## Problem
There is a lot of lock contention in the function DispatchCassandraOp.  This is happening in two places.
ops_mutex_, which is locked when reading the size of outstanding_ops_ and when inserting an operation into the op queue.
PutOpQueueStats, which grabs the mutex store_stats_.cassandra_OP_que_mutex internally.

## Make outstanding_ops_ atomic
If the variable outstanding_ops_ is made atomic then we don’t have to grab the ops_mutex_ lock unless we actually need to insert into the ops queue.
This is an easy fix and will definitely reduce contention, but I suspect that it will mostly reduce contention when the system is not under high load.  Under high load many (if not most) of the operations will be placed into the ops queue, requiring us to grab the ops_mutex_ anyways.

## “fuzzy” outstanding_ops_
If we are willing to accept slightly out of date value for outstanding_ops_ we can store the value locally in the thread.  Every several iterations we can read the real value.
I suspect that will result in a minor reduction of contention, so we need to decide if it is worth the loss of accuracy in the outstanding_ops_ variable.

[IDF Design Documents | Reducing cassandra ops lock contention]
## Use multiple queues for cassandra_ops_queue_ I suspect that optimizing cassandra_ops_queue_ will lead to the greatest performance improvement. Here is a sketch of an algorithm to do that. Algorithm properties: Operations put into the data structure may be re-ordered when they are taken out. This already happens with a monolithic queue due since worker threads may have different speeds. The Get operation may return an op that was added to the structure after the get operation is started. This is not a problem -- all we really want is for the worker thread to have an op to execute. The Get operation may return “no ops found” when there are actually ops in the queue. However, any ops in the queue will be ops that were added after the get operation was started. This is not a problem, since it is reasonable to return “no ops found” if the data structure has no ops when get is started. Instead of using a single queue, use N queues (configurable). Each queue contains the following variables (in addition to a queue data structure): lock: a mutex used to protect the queue and the queue’s variables. is_empty: an atomic boolean, indicates that queue is empty. This enables a thread to determine that the queue is empty without locking it. delta: an integer, used to track the change in size of the queue. Is lazily flushed to total_count when it’s absolute value exceeds some constant. There is also a variable of type atomic integer: total_count. This variable holds the approximate total

[IDF Design Documents | Reducing cassandra ops lock contention]
change in size of the queue. Is lazily flushed to total_count when it’s absolute value exceeds some constant. There is also a variable of type atomic integer: total_count. This variable holds the approximate total number of ops in the data structure.

## Algorithm for Insert
A thread has an op that it would like to insert into the queue.

## Algorithm for Get
A thread would like to pull an op off of the queue (if any ops are actually present).

## Use ThreadSafeSlidingStat
This may be more efficient since it uses spinlocks.

## Use “fuzzy” values.
Instead of updating the log after every update, cache data locally and update the log periodically.  This will reduce the accuracy of the logs but reduces the number of times that a lock needs to be acquired.

[IDF Design Documents | Resolve kNotMerged State for InsightsObject]
## Resolve kNotMerged State for InsightsObject
https://jira.nutanix.com/browse/ENG-363442
Uddhav Mishra
March 2021
Currently, when IDF gets a timeout from Cassandra we're not sure whether the write might have happened or not, so we put the entity in a kNotMerged state and then try to resolve the state in case of successive write retries from the client, in this case, if the client loses that entry or doesn't retry, and the write to Cassandra had succeeded, the state  in Cassandra and IDF memory will be out of sync for a long time until the shard reloading happens.

[IDF Design Documents | Resolve kNotMerged State for InsightsObject]
## Approaches We can resolve this state by 2 approaches: To resolve this issue during normal updates whenever we mark any object as kNotMerged we should schedule an event that will be executed after a couple of minutes to resolve this kNotMerged state. The scheduled event should read the latest entity from cassandra and update the InsightsObject accordingly. Pros: The object state will be resolved in matter of few minutes after the incomplete update (gflag driven) Cons: To avoid cases where the client retries for same entity and the Resolve process is also trying for the same entity we might have to keep track of the event added(inmem entity type and id) and cancel in cases where an update for the same entity is received in IDF. The cached entity type and id can lead to OOM issues if not controlled with a max limit if cassandra is down for a long time.(If cassandra is continuously giving errors we mostly will have a bigger problem than this to deal with) Have a periodic process that iterates through all entities and resolve the object state for the entities in kNotMergedState Pros : In cases where cassandra times out continuously for a small period of time due to some issue for a large no. of updates, this won't affect IDF since all the unresolved objects will be picked in the next iteration of the periodic process. Cons : Since this involves iterating through the complete object set for entities it won't be efficient. Even if we store the entity_type and entity_id object

[IDF Design Documents | Resolve kNotMerged State for InsightsObject]
in the next iteration of the periodic process. Cons : Since this involves iterating through the complete object set for entities it won't be efficient. Even if we store the entity_type and entity_id object info, the process will be periodic and during the intermediate time the object will be in the same state.

[IDF Design Documents | Resolve kNotMerged State for InsightsObject]
## Proposed Approach and Implementation
Since we do not expect too many cassandra timeouts in ideal cases  , Approach 1 would be suitable for this task.
Whenever any update fails and the cache object is marked as kNotMerged, an event(ResolveObjectNotMergedState) will be scheduled in ed to execute after some time( maybe few minutes , flag driven) which will read the latest state from cassandra and would resolve the object state to kMerged.
We will also store store the event_id of the added function in a map structure to keep track of scheduled events resolving state of objects
unordered_map<pair<string /* entity_type */, string /* entity_id */>,
int64 /*event_id */>> pending_entities_to_merge_events_map_
In cases where update for same object is received before the the event gets executed the pending event for same entity to resolve should be cancelled, since the object state will be resolved as part of the new Update op( read from cassandra and new update), In cases of failures in new update leading to kNotMerged state a new event will be added to resolve the state.
For ResolveObjectNotMergedState we can call MergeNewEntityToCache with done_cb that reschedule the same in case of failures or clears the event entry from   pending_entities_to_merge_events_map_ in case of successful update of kNotMerged state.

At some point we might need to tweak the logic to optimize for Cassandra shard locality (so IDF shard would be assigned to the same node which hosts the Cassandra data for that shard). In order to achieve Cassandra shard locality in the future, we need to design row keys such that all (or at least most of) the data that belong to the same IDF shard would be hosted by one Cassandra node. We need to structure the metric data row keys in such a way that it would keep the shard data together. For entities, we already plan to group data by shard. The current key structure is the

Key key; // The value for the cache entry. Therefore the same shared pointer was also stored in the LRU list. However, this is not required as we could

[IDF Design Documents | Store in-place ContentBuffer instead of shared_ptr for Cache Entries]
might need move to the front of either LRU list to avoid value copying. Therefore the same shared pointer was also stored in the LRU list. However, this is not required as we could safely use a raw pointer to the ContentBuffer value in LRU list, this is because the a ContentBuffer being present in one of the LRU list also means they are present in the cache hashmap. Having a shared pointer wrapper around ContentBuffer introduced extra 16 bytes of minimum overhead per cache entry. That also means extra memory allocation during the cache insertion and more fragmentions will occur when cache entry is removed. Additional overhead occurs when we move the ContentBuffer shared pointer into the LRU list where a copy of the shared pointer was made and locks were taken where it updates the ref count. [IDF Design Documents | Support for Entity Type Evictability Change in Scaleout Mode]
Support for Entity Type Evictability Change in Scaleout Mode (CPD-2131) In scaleout mode, changing entity type evictability and column indexability are not allowed. The purpose of this doc is to design the appropriate approach to support evictability changes (both directions) at any time (both bootstrap and dynamically). Evictability change includes two directions: 1) unevictable -> evictable; 2) evictable -> unevictable. For unevictable -> evictable, index maps are firstly established, and then entities of the entity type are dehydrated; for evictable -> unevictable, entities are firstly rehydrated and then all index maps are removed from cache. If the change only includes metric types which become indexable from non-indexable, or vice versa, then index maps are added or removed and no entity rehydration / dehydration. For simplicity, we refer to “evictability change” as the actions mentioned above. Race Conditions with Other Workloads Evictability changes have the following race conditions with other workloads: Race with UpdateEntity: in the path of UpdateEntity, IsEvictableEntityType() is checked for a couple of times for dehydration or establish index maps. Race with Shard Load / Unload: For shard loading and unloading also rely on IsEvictableEntityType() to add / remove index maps. Race with Cluster Register / Unregister: For cluster registration, the race is similar to shard loading. For unregistration, it should be exclusive to evictability change as well. Race with

[IDF Design Documents | Support for Entity Type Evictability Change in Scaleout Mode]
add / remove index maps. Race with Cluster Register / Unregister: For cluster registration, the race is similar to shard loading. For unregistration, it should be exclusive to evictability change as well. Race with Concurrent Query: The query layer has different policies for evictable and unevictable entities. For evictable entities, queries usually rely on indexes for filtering. However, indexing might not be completed yet after the entity type evictability flag in the proto is changed to be evictable, which might result in inaccurate filtering results. Race with other metadata updates in the middle of evict change. To avoid the aforementioned race conditions, metadata updates including evict changes should not be applied in cache (after that, other workload can see the changes) until the logic of evict change has taken the following locks: 1) SERIALIZE_SHARD_LOAD_AND_CLUSTER_REG_LOCK_ID to exclude shard load / unload, cluster registration / unregistration; 2) write lock of all shard hosted in the node to exclude RPCs such as queries, entity updates, etc. Besides these two locks, we also need to set a flag metadata_evictablity_change_starting_ at the very beginning of evict change. The flag blocks RPCs RegisterEntityTypes / MetricTypes which do not require shard locks, and also it blocks incoming RPCs so that the evict change logic is easier to take the write lock of all shards. Therefore, the logic of evict change should follow the following steps: When the evictability is

[IDF Design Documents | Support for Entity Type Evictability Change in Scaleout Mode]
blocks incoming RPCs so that the evict change logic is easier to take the write lock of all shards. Therefore, the logic of evict change should follow the following steps: When the evictability is about to start, it firstly sets a global flag metadata_evictablity_change_starting_ to true. Take the write lock of all shards. Apply the metadata updates including evict changes in cache. Release SERIALIZE_SHARD_LOAD_AND_CLUSTER_REG_LOCK_ID so that shard loading and cluster registration are unblocked. However, shard unload and cluster unregistration are still blocked due to the shard write locks. It starts the evictability change shard by shard: adding / removing indexes and dehydration / rehydration. Once it completes a shard, it releases the write lock of that shard. When all shards are done, the whole evictability change is completed. Set metadata_evictablity_change_starting_ false to unblock incoming RPCs. But the RPCs might be still blocked by the shard write locks. We are going to have the following cases: To add indexes for evictable entities, we scan the the entities from cassandra and build the indexes; If adding indexes comes with unevictable -> evictable changes, as we dehydrate the entities, we establish the index maps. To remove indexes, we simply remove the corresponding index maps. If it comes with evictable -> unevictable changes, we load all the entities to cache. Since blocking all shards may block shard loading/unloading, most queries, entity sync, etc, it might

[IDF Design Documents | Support for Entity Type Evictability Change in Scaleout Mode]
the corresponding index maps. If it comes with evictable -> unevictable changes, we load all the entities to cache. Since blocking all shards may block shard loading/unloading, most queries, entity sync, etc, it might “freeze” the whole IDF cluster for a while (the time need to be tested). To alleviate the freezing time, we can considering blocking one shard one time. However, since evict change happens rarely, we can block all shards for simplicity for now. The logic of blocking one shard one time is introduced in the section of alternatives, which can be taken when the aforementioned assumption is not correct any longer. The evictability change can take place from two paths: by configuration file and by dynamic change. Evictability Change By Configuration File Evictability change by configuration file can only happen when the leadership changes. In bootstrap on the leader node, auto-registration updates all entity types and metric types separately in InsightsServer::BatchedRegistration. During auto-registration, all metadata updates including evict changes are skipped and recorded in a new data structure. At the end of auto-registration, if there are recorded updates, the evict change is triggered. After the write lock of all shards have been taken, the recorded updates are sent to be registered by calling InsightsServer::BatchedRegistration. On non-leader nodes, metadata are pulled from the leader and then call InsightsStore::UpdateMetadataCache to update both entity types

[IDF Design Documents | Support for Entity Type Evictability Change in Scaleout Mode]
all shards have been taken, the recorded updates are sent to be registered by calling InsightsServer::BatchedRegistration. On non-leader nodes, metadata are pulled from the leader and then call InsightsStore::UpdateMetadataCache to update both entity types and metric types. Similar to the leader node, entity types and their metric types which are going to have evictability change are recorded and skipped. After the evict change has taken the write locks of all shards, the recorded updates are applied in cache by calling InsightsStore::UpdateMetadataCache again. Dynamic Evictability Change Sometimes clients may not apply the evictability change by the configuration file, but by sending metadata update RPCs dynamically, e.g., evictability change for a dynamically registered entity type. Dynamic evictability change are done by two RPCs: RegisterEntityTypes and RegisterMetricTypes, to update is_evictable of the entity type and the indexable attributes, respectively. The two RPCs may be sent independently. Unlike the evictability change by configuration file, entity types and metric types are done separately. The updates are persisted in Cassandra first. If it succeeds without any error, the evict change is triggered. After it has taken the write lock of all shards, the updates are applied in cache; if it returns from Cassandra with errors, the metadata insights object will be in kNotMerged state. The evict change is not triggered until kNotMerged state is resolved by the next

[IDF Design Documents | Support for Entity Type Evictability Change in Scaleout Mode]
are applied in cache; if it returns from Cassandra with errors, the metadata insights object will be in kNotMerged state. The evict change is not triggered until kNotMerged state is resolved by the next update. Cluster Upgrading This feature is planned for shipment in 5.12. If the upgrading happens between builds after 5.12, the evict change can take place as the logic introduced above. However, if the upgrading happens between a pre-5.12 build and a post-5.12 build, the leader node might transition between the old build (which does not support the evict change) and the new build. In this case, the dynamic metadata updates including evict changes should be disallowed until the rolling upgrade is completed. For the change from config files, the leader node (with the new build) will hold the evict changes until the rolling upgrade is completed. When the leader node is notified by the zookeeper that the rolling upgrade is done, if there are evict changes which are being held, it starts the evict change logic by taking the serializing locks as introduced above. Alternatives During evictability changes, instead of blocking all the shards, we can also choose to block one shard a time. Shard loading inserts the shard into shard_set_ right before the loading starts, and takes the write lock immediately. When the evictability is about to start, grabs shard_set_lock_ and copies all shards in shard_set_ into a new global unordered_map evictablity_change_shards_status_, which records the

[IDF Design Documents | Support for Entity Type Evictability Change in Scaleout Mode]
before the loading starts, and takes the write lock immediately. When the evictability is about to start, grabs shard_set_lock_ and copies all shards in shard_set_ into a new global unordered_map evictablity_change_shards_status_, which records the evictability change status for each shard. The initial value is false, indicating the evictability change is not done yet. Holding shard_set_lock_, it flips is_evictable in the entity type proto. It then releases shard_set_lock_. This is to prevent evictablity_change_shards_status_ missing new shard loading which uses the old value of is_evictable. It takes the write lock of each shard in evictablity_change_shards_status_ and start the evictability change. If it complete one shard, it sets the status of the shard as true in evictablity_change_shards_status_. Once all shards are done, evictablity_change_shards_status_ is emptied for the entity type, which marks the end of evictability change. If a concurrent RPC request checks the evictability of the entity type (it should have taken the shard read lock), it checks if the corresponding shard is in the map: 1) if it is in the map and the status is true, it takes the value of is_evictable; 2) if it is in the map and the status is false, it takes the complement value of is_evictable; 3) if it is not in the map, which means the shard loading starts after the change of is_evictable, it takes the value of is_evictable. Compared with “Block All Shards”, this mechanism only blocks one shard

[IDF Design Documents | Support for Entity Type Evictability Change in Scaleout Mode]
it is not in the map, which means the shard loading starts after the change of is_evictable, it takes the value of is_evictable. Compared with “Block All Shards”, this mechanism only blocks one shard a time. Requests to other shards might have different evictability view of the same entity type depending on whether the evictability change has been completed for that shard. But for RPCs which visit all shards will still get rejected. Since evictability change is not expected to happen often, we can block all shards for simplicity. In the future, if blocking all shard incurs big performance penalty, we can switch it toe block shard one by one. Implementation Plan The full support will be completed in two diffs: Unevictable -> Evictable (4-5 days) Evictable -> Unevictable (~2 days)

[IDF Design Documents | Tracking memory utilized by insights cache]
Tracking memory utilized by insights cache. The premise behind this document is to propose a solution for tracking the memory consumed by insights cache. For the first cut, we will primarily focus on entity and metric type cache objects. We won’t keep track of the memory consumed by other cache entries such as watches, entity trail objects, snapshot history etc. To solve the problem, we will provide a base class for the cache objects: InsightsObjectBase, that provides a virtual function: Size() that returns the size of the object that it wraps. class InsightsObjectBase { public: typedef shared_ptr<InsightsObjectBase> Ptr; typedef shared_ptr<const InsightsObjectBase> PtrConst; virtual ~InsightsObjectBase() {} virtual size_t Size() const = 0; }; We will have InsightsObject and the WatchMapper classes extend the InsightsObjectBase class. Class InsightsObject : public InsightsObjectBase { …. virtual size_t SpaceUsed() const { return SpaceUsed(object_); } private: template<typename U> size_t SpaceUsed(shared_ptr<U> object) const { return 0; } size_t SpaceUsed(const shared_ptr<interface::Entity>& entity) const { return entity->SpaceUsed(); } size_t SpaceUsed(const shared_ptr<store::MetricDataDB_>& mdata) const { return mdata->SpaceUsed(); } … We could have the watch mapper class make use of InsightsObject for wrapping the watch objects. The downside to this is that an instance of InsightsObject class is about 256 bytes, which is probably wasteful. We will also maintain a top level

[IDF Design Documents | Tracking memory utilized by insights cache]
use of InsightsObject for wrapping the watch objects. The downside to this is that an instance of InsightsObject class is about 256 bytes, which is probably wasteful. We will also maintain a top level stats for unevictable cache (and potentially evictable cache) that will be displayed on the 2027 page. This would give the total size used by the unevictable and evictable caches. To get advanced stats that would give insights into how much memory individual metrics use, we will present a separate page. When the page gets loaded, we will go through the cache entities and cast the key to the appropriate type and sum up the memory used by metrics (CPD-904). Re: I think we should not scan the cache just to get the cache size, that will cause massive cache contention while user is trying to load the page which may disrupt the server operation. What we are building here is a diagnostic tool. If we want to get advanced details about the memory utilized by entity type + metric type, there will be cache contention. With this new proposal, there will be no change to the existing put path when the diagnostic page is not loaded. An alternate solution would be to use a separate map, for instance map[entity type + metric type] => size used. This results in extra memory for the map and contention during the put time [to insert the appropriate data into the new map].

[IDF Design Documents | Trail per master cluster]
## Introduction
As I’m going forward with fleshing out specific snapshot logic for replicated entities, I’m getting convinced that things are going to be much easier if the entity trail is going to be partitioned by master cluster.  This approach should also align well with our efforts to limit the amount of data that goes into the trail row: partitioning the trail by the master cluster would help to make sure that if data fits into the row limits on each PE then it’s going to fit into the row limits on PC that may get data from multiple PEs.
Here is the design outline.

[IDF Design Documents | Trail per master cluster]
## Current behavior Currently entities are stored as the following: Latest entities (‘entities’ CF) are stored as one entity per row, row key: {shard, type, id}, range scan prefix: {shard, type}, column key: “1” Trail (‘entity_tail’ CF) is stored in fixed time chunks, row key: {shard, type, start_range_time}, range scan prefix: {shard, type}, column key: {time, id} All entities have the master_cluster_uuid field that currently does not participate in partitioning. For entities that are created on the local Insights DB the master_cluster_uuid is empty. All entities regardless of the source go to the abovementioned CFs. A modification operation works as following: Copy the current latest entity value to the trail using the {shard, type, start_range_time} as the row key, and {time, id} as the column key Update latest with the new value using the {shard, type, id} as the row key An operation to get all entities as of time in the past works as following: Get entities from latest using {shard, type} as the scan prefix Entities that have timestamp <= specified, go to the results Entities that have timestamp > specified, retrieved from trail as following: The specified time becomes the start of the range scan The last snapshot time (taken from snapshot map) becomes the end of the range scan Get trail records between {shard, type, start_time} and {shard, type, end_time} The changes come in reverse order, to the first change we find for an entity becomes the value An operation to get

[IDF Design Documents | Trail per master cluster]
scan Get trail records between {shard, type, start_time} and {shard, type, end_time} The changes come in reverse order, to the first change we find for an entity becomes the value An operation to get specific entities as of the time in the past is similar to getting all entities with one notable difference: the entities are first retrieved from cache and if all entities are present in the cache, then reading data from latest entities CF is not needed. An operation to get entity trail for a time range works as the following: Get entities from latest entities CF using {shard, type} as the scan prefix Skip entities that have timestamp >= end of range, save others entity_id => entity_trail map Scan trail between {shard, type, start_time} and {shard, type, end_time} (the start time is taken as the latest snapshot before specified start range) The changes come in reverse order, so the entity_trail is built in reverse I’m ignoring entity snapshotting functionality as for the local entities it’s going to be unchanged (it’s just going to skip entities with master_cluster_uuid set) and for replicated entities it’s going to be driven from replication state by the snapshot logic.

[IDF Design Documents | Trail per master cluster]
## Proposed changes The latest entities storage format is unchanged. The trail row keys are going to use the master_cluster_uuid as the shard id. The trail modification operation is changed as the following: now the master_cluster_uuid field is used as the shard id to form the key. If master_cluster_uuid is empty, then the shard id is the “0” constant as before. The operation to get all entities as of time in the past is changed as the following: now when the entities are retrieved from the latest, we group them by master_cluster_uuid. Then we do trail retrieval operation for each group, the actual trail retrieval is largely unchanged, with the obvious change of using the master_cluster_uuid as the shard id in the scan range for each group. Then all group results are merged together (the returned sets are disjoint, so merge is just moving the results for each group into a single result set). The operation to get all entities for the time range is changed as the following: now when the entities are retrieved from the latest, we group them by master_cluster_uuid (even if skip an entity timestamp >= end of range we make sure that its master_cluster_uuid is represented in the groups). Then we do trail retrieval operation for each group, the actual trail retrieval is largely unchanged, with the obvious change of using the master_cluster_uuid as the shard id in the scan range for each group. Then all group results are merged together (the returned sets are disjoint, so merge is

[IDF Design Documents | Trail per master cluster]
with the obvious change of using the master_cluster_uuid as the shard id in the scan range for each group. Then all group results are merged together (the returned sets are disjoint, so merge is just moving the results for each group into a single result set). The snapshot timeline is going to be independent for each master cluster (the local snapshotting logic is going to stay unchanged). So when the trail retrieval is done for each group, the scan is going to consult the cluster-specific snapshot state and calculate the range for the scan accordingly. This would avoid the need to coordinate snapshot state between the master clusters and the local changes (some clusters could be newly joined and not completely bootstrapped, some could be active with lots of recent changes, some could be inactive with no recent changes, etc.). Note that this functionality relies on the fact that we keep deleted entities in the latest entities CF. When we stop doing that, we'd need to use a set of cluster uuids to lookup the trail records in case all entities for a master cluster are currently deleted. I plan to make this change before the snapshot syncing logic for replicated entities.

[IDF Design Documents | [ENG-654871] Drop auto-indexing for  evictable entities]
Drop auto-indexing for evictable entities
[ENG-654871]
April 2025
[Done]

## Proposed changes:
Currently we have auto-indexing on a few pseudo attributes enabled for evictable entity types and entity type name attributes. For pseudo attributes, we want to move away from auto-indexing to config controlled indexing as it might not make sense for all the entity types to have the fields indexed.
The existing list of attributes is also static and not configurable. The current list of fields that are automatically indexed are:
_created_timestamp_usecs_
_modified_timestamp_usecs_
_tenant_id_
_master_cluster_uuid_
As of today, only “_master_cluster_uuid_” is needed by IDF, to clear out entities from cache on a cluster unregistration and also used in active-entities workflow. Indexes on the other 3 fields can be chosen by the client based on entity type specific requirements.
So these are the proposed changes:
Reduce the list of auto-indexed attributes to _master_cluster_uuid_
Make the list of auto-indexable pseudo attribute configurable via a gflag
Make the necessary config changes with indexes enabled for the 4 attributes for all the evictable entity types
The objective of the change is only to make it optional for the clients and also to not cause any regression to the existing client queries on the system.

[IDF Design Documents | [ENG-654871] Drop auto-indexing for  evictable entities]
## Existing issues with configuring indexes:
However, another issue with the current code we have is that, any config change to enable index(even on an already indexed pseudo attribute) will trigger the entire evictability change workflow. Which includes scanning all the entities from Cassandra and attempting to re-index the attributes.
Given the fact that we are enabling indexes for all the entity types, the upgrade to the new version might now trigger a scan of a huge proportion of total entities from Cassandra and might cause huge unavailability during upgrade on high scale setups.

[IDF Design Documents | [ENG-654871] Drop auto-indexing for  evictable entities]
## Solution:
The solution would be to add a check in the evictability workflow that if all the indexes that are newly added belong to the auto-indexed list, then we can skip the scan and the re-index workflow.
We’ll do the following changes to handle the same:
We’ll hold back the config registration of these specific pseudo attributes till all the nodes are upgraded to the latest version so that we don't end up performing a re-scan.
After the new config is applied, we drop the old list and start using the new list after 60 mins to ensure that we give enough time for the config to get applied.

This should also consider the possibility of ongoing shard load, previous config update being in progress, cluster registration etc.
This will also ensure that there will be no failures of queries end-clients perspective with respect because of missing indexes.
TODO:
We need to revisit the 60 mins interval and see if it needs to be further increased. There is no harm in delaying it for a couple of hours.
Time for dropping indexes needs to be benchmarked.

[IDF Design Documents | [ENG-654871] Drop auto-indexing for  evictable entities]
## Alternative for dropping indexes asynchronous to config propagation:
The following change in logic can be made for config propagation between nodes:
The leader keeps a track of applying the new configuration post the upgrade.
Which would be the first configuration post the upgrade and creates a marker node
Non-leader requests Leader for the latest metadata:
Leader checks if any marker node has been created for the node for this schema
If not, leader creates a node before returning the latest schema: “disable_auto_pseudo_attr_indexing/<follower-ip>/config_requested”
Non-leader applies the config and check if marker node has been populated by the leader to ensure that the desired schema was returned in this rPC:
“disable_auto_pseudo_attr_indexing/<follower-ip>/config_requested”
If populated, non-leader applies the configuration changes internally. Then drops the indexed attributes and populates the following marker node:
“internal_upgrade/disable_auto_pseudo_attr_indexing/done”
This ensures both seamless support for queries and also quick drop of indexes post the metadata is applied.
Not going ahead with this approach, as it would be complicated to keep track of the exact hash of config that has been applied. And the guarantees with async approach should be good enough.

## Changes to overall code base:
1. New zk node: 
   `/appliance/logical/insights/disable_auto_pseudo_attr_indexing_status`

[IDF Design Documents | [ENG-654871] Drop auto-indexing for  evictable entities]
## Init workflow:
1. TryCreate zk node: `/disable_auto_pseudo_attr_indexing_status`
2. Checks the value of the zk node: 
     `/disable_auto_pseudo_attr_indexing_status`
a. If yes, Initiate store with new dynamic attribute list.
b. Else, init with the legacy attribute list.
Register a watch on:     
        `/disable_auto_pseudo_attr_indexing_status/`.
On a callback of node creation:
Invoke a delayed callback with the following changes:
          - `insights_drop_pseudo_attr_indexes_delay_secs` 
              → Will be the amount of delay.
- Hold the lock `SERIALIZE_SHARD_LOAD_AND_CLUSTER_REG_LOCK_ID`

[IDF Design Documents | [ENG-654871] Drop auto-indexing for  evictable entities]
## Leader config init changes:
AutoRegisterMetadataFromConfig:
- If current_upgrade_version_ < kDisablePseudoAttributeAutoIndexing:
We postpone the metric registration by scheduling UpgradeCallback.
In UpgradeCallBack:
- Complete the auto registration locally.  
        - Update the metadata hash node on Zeus,
        - write `kInitiated` in:
            `/disable_auto_pseudo_attr_indexing_status` node.
- Else:
- If: value of upgrade node is not `kInitiated`
        - Post the metric registration, we populate `kInitiated` into
          `/disable_auto_pseudo_attr_indexing_status` node before we log 
          `Auto-registration of metadata completed successfully`
          (This only happens when the previous leader died either during

## EvictabilityChange:
1. Skip indexing attributes which are auto-indexed for evictable entities.

[IDF Design Documents | [ENG-654871] Drop auto-indexing for  evictable entities]
## Expected error scenarios:
The shard_lock write lock is taken to drop indexes and will end up blocking operations of read and write during this time. The index drop operation should be very quick and shouldn’t take more than a few milliseconds. Request failure during this time is expected.
If the config propagation takes more than 60 mins from the moment the leader applies it. The node will fail queries on the indexed attributes and IDF also might have some downtime (twice) while trying to drop and re-index the attributes again. The latter would be noticeable.
The upgrade workflow is only capable of handling the cases where the new configurable list is just a subset of the existing list of 4 attributes.
The newly introduced gflag can’t be updated dynamically and requires a re-start of IDF.

[IDF Design Documents | [ENG-661651] IDF Tombstone retention]
IDF Attribute retention in Tombstones
Devendra S, Sumit B, Pradhyumna K, Ricky P
July 2024

## Problem statement:
IDF sync disconnect between PE and PC can be caused by a lot of common factors on the customer environments. This was causing certain challenges to Ergon who have their data spread across PE, PC and take actions on PC based on sync.
Consider the following scenario:
Task 1 is created on PC with Task 2 as the child task on PE.
PE gets disconnected from PC
Task 2 is now marked completed on the PE.
Ergon’s garbage collection on PE gets triggered and removes Task 2.
PE-PC sync gets fixed. 
The tombstone of Task 2 gets synced to PC.
But it's practically not existent to the client and the tombstone doesn’t have attribute data as of today.
Now the end state of Task 2 is always lost to the PC. So none of the actions either on the Parent or the dependent tasks can’t move forward.

## Solution:
The following approaches have been discussed:
Increase wait minimum wait time of task deletion on PE
PE IDF doesn’t sync deleted tasks to PC
PE Ergon doesn’t delete the task till sync happens to PC
Have attribute retention in tombstone and let the clients access the attributes
Archival table for deleted tasks
More details about each approach can be found here: Doc link
Conclusion after considering all the parameters was to go ahead with Approach 4.

[IDF Design Documents | [ENG-661651] IDF Tombstone retention]
## Implementation details:
One thing to consider was that the level of retention configuration should be exposed at a per etype, entity or attribute level. Configuration per entity type or below seemed fit, but to check if the retention had to be made at the attribute level, tried the following benchmark
Tried to populate 550k entities on a PC. Here is how the bootup time looked like:
With no attributes retained: 53 secs
With all attributes retained : 60 secs
Since there is no significant difference between bootup times, deciding to go ahead with entity level retention to keep things simple.
The following changes are required for the same:
Watch layer:
[ENG-680614] Support watching on synced deletes

As of today, the existing watching mechanism doesn’t support notifications when a tombstone syncs from other clusters. Changes are required on the server and in the watch clients to support notifying clients when a delete syncs.
[ENG-680617] Support fetching Current State of entities from Tombstones

If the entity is deleted and a watch is registered on it, the Current State will be empty. We have to now support new params in watches to facilitate the same.
[ENG-680624] RPC Layer:
Expose special params in DeleteEntityArg to retain the attributes of the entity post deletion. It has to be ensured that these attributes are also available on the destination post replication.

## Test plan:
Link to test plan

[IDF Design Documents | [ENG-676523] Proto parsing optimisations]
[ENG-676523] Proto parsing optimisations
Pradhyumna Komatineni
June 2024

## Problem statement:
This doc is majorly about the changes tried to optimise nested field parsing latencies. As of today, on regular PC setups(without portfolio enablement) it is observed that nested field parsing takes approximately 25% of the bootup latency.
The idea is to use CodedInputStreams instead of the existing method to parse into empty proto and iterate over the unknown fields.

## Existing code flow:
Code link:
https://sourcegraph.ntnxdpro.com/ntnxdb-master@eb2dc0ad4fdb4391eab7e49426e5c0bdbc852156/-/blob/ntnxdb_server/insights/insights_server/store/insights_store_nested_fields.cc?L1119
Get the base_attr_set which contains all the nested attributes associated with it.
Uncompress the base attribute
Iterate through all the nested field metrics, and for each metric:
Unmarshal the base attribute to empty proto
Do a BFS on all the unknown_fields:
If an unknown field is a node and is of type delimiter, we unmarshal the proto present at that field. And goto 3.b again.
If the unknown field is of type leaf, then we copy it to DataValue.

[IDF Design Documents | [ENG-676523] Proto parsing optimisations]
## Solution:
Move 3.a out of the loop. There is no reason why the parsing has to be performed multiple times since we never use Move or Swap semantics while extracting the fields from the proto. Reason being, it's not possible to Swap primitive types in proto (not even for strings).
Note that we are not optimising multiple parsings being done, if the same path is being used again in 3.b.i.
For example, say we have 2 nested attributes, [1, 2, 3] & [1, 2, 4], the unmarshalled message at level [1, 2] will get unmarshalled twice.

## Change 2: Use CodedInputStreams
We have certain heavy entity_type like recovery_point, check_schema, nucalm_substrate, nucalm_deployement, recovery_plan where there are a lot of complex nesting/ too many attributes in the client proto. But only a few of them are being used as nested attributes.
As of today, there are 3 copies of the data that happen:
Once from the serialised proto to the empty protobuf created.
Then the required nested fields from proto to temporary variable
Then from temporary variable to DataValue.
Say total data is t and nested field data is n.
This would mean t + n*2 amounts of data is copied.

[IDF Design Documents | [ENG-676523] Proto parsing optimisations]
## Solution:
After Change1, use CodedInputStream to directly iterate through the input proto and copy the nested fields. This will eliminate 1. Which would bring down the copies from “t + n*2” to “n*2”.
Also, we do multiple parsing on the nested field info data in the metric type.
To resolve this, the proposal is to have a data structure per node which would contain the tree structure of nested fields for every (etype, base_attribute) combination. There are around 1600/5000 nested attributes to total attributes. And there are almost 2500 instances of nested_field_index. But since the overhead of the structure is less, not expecting more than a few MBs of overhead because of this.
Apart from that we can try to refactor the existing base metric data set and this would give us memory saving anyways.

-- Batching Cassandra ops for BatchUpdateEntities/BatchDeleteEntities

## Problem:
Currently, there are many places in the code where we access Cassandra for every individual entity operation, both read and write.
For all UpdateEntity/DeleteEntity RPCs, either creation or update or deletion, we issue a Cassandra write for each individual entity. The BatchUpdateEntities/BatchDeleteEntities RPCs are based on UpdateEntity/DeleteEntity, thus the internal processing of the batch is actually per entity, which is not fully utilizing the Cassandra
In the creation path, we need to load from Cassandra to do some validations, meaning we issue a Cassandra read for every creation operation. In some use cases (e.g. Calm), it introduces a lot more unnecessary overhead and thus impacts the performance

[IDF Design Documents | [IDF-PG parity optimizations] -- Batching Cassandra ops for BatchUpdateEntities_BatchDeleteEntities]
## Solution: For the first issue, we can easily batch the columns to be written in WriteToLatestEntities() by adding the information of write operations to a pending batch. The processing of the list is as following: Iterate through the list and prepare the arguments for CassandraPaxosBatchMutate(). Prepare the done callback to handle each individual error status. Schedule the next processing. Issue the Cassandra batch write. As the size of the payload could be determined by the payload, we could set an expectation (N) of how many write operations there should be. Then at the backend, we would send the next batch when the size is met or when expected operations reduce to 0 (i.e. the last batch may not be filled). Increases the number of expected operations by N (total number of write operations within the batch. For single UpdateEntity/DeleteEntity, N = 1). Every time we reach the WriteToLatestEntities(), we decrement the number of expected operations (N -= 1). If it reduces to 0, send the batch. If we hit the batch size, send the batch. If the validations failed before getting to WriteToLatestEntities(), we need to decrement N by 1 (N -= 1). For the second issue, we can obviously use the same solution as the first one. However, one thing to be thought of is: do we really need to do the read for all creation? There are 2 cases that we do not find the entity in cache: 1) the entity has been deleted; 2) the entity does not exist at all. When we directly write into Cassandra

[IDF Design Documents | [IDF-PG parity optimizations] -- Batching Cassandra ops for BatchUpdateEntities_BatchDeleteEntities]
creation? There are 2 cases that we do not find the entity in cache: 1) the entity has been deleted; 2) the entity does not exist at all. When we directly write into Cassandra without doing the read, if we encounter 1), the write will receive Cassandra::kEpochMismatch since we do not have the correct epoch and paxos_instance. Then we can piggy back to what we are doing now, i.e. read from Cassandra and do all those validations. If we encounter 2), the creation will succeed and we are good to go. This way, we can avoid much overhead for clients who need to do a lot of creations (e.g. Calm). The cons for this approach is that if the majority of creation requests are resurrecting deleted entities, then we are actually introducing unnecessary overhead (the first write attempt). So the assumption is that most of the creation requests are indeed creating brand new entities rather than resurrecting deleted ones (e.g. Alerts).

When this number is met, start processing the current batch. We could find the explanation below as of why we are reusing this gflag. BatchUpdateEntities / BatchDeleteEntities / UpdateEntity / DeleteEntity: For each individual write request within the batch, count the total number of individual write ops, and add that to the total_expected_write_entity_ops_: total_expected_write_entity_ops_ += expected_write_entity_ops; For UpdateEntity / DeleteEntity, expected_write_entity_ops = 1 Before writing to Cassandra, i.e WriteToLatestEntities(), any validation failure should decrement total_expected_write_entity_ops_ by 1, as this write operation has failed and should not be scheduled for the following processing. WriteToLatestEntities(): New bool flag should_be_batched indicating whether we should batch the operation or not. This could avoid touching the existing logic of other places calling into WriteToLatestEntities(), e.g. AttachEntity, ReplicateEntity, etc.
