the following processing. WriteToLatestEntities(): New bool flag should_be_batched indicating whether we should batch the operation or not. This could avoid touching the existing logic of other places calling into WriteToLatestEntities(), e.g. AttachEntity, ReplicateEntity, etc. Otherwise, we would need to increment/decrement the total_expected_write_entity_ops_ here and there (e.g the replication logic needs to retry/write to trail/write to latest. ) instead of calling directly the CassandraPaxosBatchWrite(), add to the list and decrement total_expected_write_entity_ops_ by 1 (as we found one write operation). if 1) current_batch size reaches FLAGS_insights_max_concurrent_entity_batch_updates, meaning the list is full; or 2) total_expected_write_entity_ops_ reaches 0, meaning there are no more batch ops to be processed, start processing this batch of write operations (i.e schedule to write to Cassandra) by calling ProcessBatchWriteOps(). The gflag FLAGS_insights_max_concurrent_entity_batch_updates was originally used to control the max concurrent entity batch update requests by throttling the total number of threads used to do the processing. Within each thread, each individual request is called sequentially. Thus we could expect at most this number of requests coming in at any point of time. If we have a larger batch queue size than this number, we could end up in a deadlock since the queue could never be filled up if there is only one batch request. Thus we are using the

Thus we are using the same gflag to determine the size of the batch queue. With this mechanism, we would actually mix operations from different update requests (e.g multiple BatchUpdateEntities, or BatchUpdateEntities with BatchDeleteEntities, or single UpdateEntity with BatchUpdateEntities) into one batch. If one batch queue is incomplete, it must be the last batch of all requests; otherwise we'll get complete batches (ops from next requests would complete the batches that are not completed by previous ones). In the kWriteToLatestEntitiesDone: if the status is kCassandraMutateEpochError: If is_first_try_insertion == true: we will try to load from Cassandra by getting into kReadFromLatestEntities state(fall back to the existing workflow). The is_first_try_insertion will be set to false then so that the retry will not be handled specially. Else: reset the status to kCassandraMutateFailed(as what it is before) and fall back to the existing workflow. --------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------

## Alternative timeout based solution
One obvious solution for batch processing, is timeout-based, i.e. having a timeout after which we start processing the list of operations.
From a 3 nodes PC cluster with 230k entities (8k VMs), the UpdateEntity rate is [~15/s, ~200/s]. So if we have a queue with specific size (e.g. 25, which seems to be the optimal size during the POC against PostgreSQL) and a timeout (e.g. 1ms, as the same reason above), it would be hard to fill in such queue as we need 25k/s UpdateEntity/DeleteEntity requests, which is not usual. But when clients use the batch RPC, there would be a burst of write requests, which is probably larger than 25k/s.
So we are adding unnecessary delay for single UpdateEntity/DeleteEntity. This could be resolved by the proposal discussed above.

## Alternative batch-transition solution
Given that the BatchUpdateEntities already contains the information about “how many entities in the batch”, instead of having a queue waiting for those randomly coming UpdateEntity requests, we can directly process the whole batch altogether at every stage, i.e validation, state transition, write to Cassandra and etc.

It collects all status or each individual entity within the batch and return as a whole. If the validation failed for one entity, just set the error status, do not return: SET_ERROR_AND_RETURN -> SET_ERROR In EntityUpdateStateTransition(), since we are going to remove the Read for creation case, and the trail has been disabled (we could return an error for the entity with trail enabled for now), then the only thing we need to deal with is the write. It is similar with the other solution, i.e queuing up the batch, besides that we already know the queue size thus no timeout is needed. And each batch update has its own queue instead of sharing the same queue. We will call the EntityUpdateStateTransition() for every entity in the batch independently, and add them to the queue instead of writing to Cassandra directly in WriteToLatestEntities(). In the creation case, if it failed because of Cassandra::kEpochMismatch (meaning that it has the tombstone), we will load those entities from DB and do the validations as we’ve done in the EntityUpdateState::kReadFromLatestEntities. Then we will try to write these entities to Cassandra again. Other entities will wait for this write to finish. (We could have a separate ticket removing the read for creation first.) ## Problem statement In light of multiple on call issues that dealt with large amount of data, one of the major pain point was that we are lacking effective diag tool to inspect the large IDF raw data set (e.g. metric data) when it is needed to. Also, when we detect there are some anomalies from cassandra cfstats (e.g. very large rows, rows with many columns, too many rows for a certain column families, too much data added in certain time), we have no way to drill down to the cassandra column family to determine where the hotspot are. Cassandra’s Medusa printer helps in some degree but it lacks the IDF specific logic and data structure and row key structure to fully understand the data set to be helpful, for example majority IDF data payload are compressed, unless medusa printer understand these specific logic , it will be not much useful to use that. The only way to fetch that information is to manually construct IDF queries/get request which is quite cumbersome and limited in nature , as we can not fetch all the raw data due to the IDF processing of the query and get requests. Active Entities for Multi-Hop Sync
Devendra, Gaurav
March 2026
[In-progress]

[IDF Design Documents | Active Entities Workflow For Mutli-hop Sync]
Context: The Active Entities Workflow ensures that replicas don’t keep stale entities when sync is down. If the connection between the source and replica breaks, and an entity is deleted from the source (and purged from its backend database), the replica won’t be aware of the deletion and will continue to retain the entity once sync resumes. To handle this, the source periodically sends a list of all active entities to the replica. The replica compares this list against its own data and removes any entities that no longer exist on the source. This check also happens automatically whenever the replica hasn’t received an update for a set amount of time. Currently, the workflow only sends the list of local (source master) entities. But with the introduction of the Infrastructure Domain (ID) and multi-hop IDF sync, we also need to include the synced entities (not just the local ones) in the active entities list at every hop. For example, consider a sync path PE → ID → PC and ID->PC Entities e1 and e2 are created on PE and synced to ID, and then from ID to PC. Entity e3 is created on ID and synced to PC. Now, if the connection between ID and PC breaks: Suppose e1 is deleted from PE. The deletion syncs to ID, and e1 is purged from both PE and ID. When the connection between ID and PC resumes, ID must send its active entities list, which includes both local entities (like e3) and entities that flowed through ID as a hop (like e2). PC compares its own entities with this list, detects

ID must send its active entities list, which includes both local entities (like e3) and entities that flowed through ID as a hop (like e2). PC compares its own entities with this list, detects that e1 is missing, and deletes e1 as well. Edge case If PE unregisters from ID and active entities reach PC before the config update, PC might incorrectly delete PE's entities rather than hide them.

## Solution
Group active entities by master_cluster_uuid at each hop, so replicas can track and delete entities per source cluster.
Key Changes
Source
Group active entities by master_cluster_uuid (includes local + synced entities)
Destination
Process deletions per master_cluster_uuid independently

[IDF Design Documents | Active Entities Workflow For Mutli-hop Sync]
## Edge Case Analysis Consider a scenario where PE->ID->PC are paired, and bi-directional sync(PE<->ID<->PC) is functioning correctly. Assume there is an entity type (etype1) whose schema allows entities to sync from PE → ID → PC. Suppose 10 entities of this type are created and successfully synced from PE to ID, and then from ID to PC. Now, PE gets unregistered from ID. According to the design: ID should maintain registration-related zk nodes of all registered PEs. PC should maintain information about all registered IDs, as well as the PEs associated with those IDs via ZK nodes. Upon PE unregistration, the corresponding ZK nodes should be cleared from both ID and PC. However, consider a case where: The ZK nodes are successfully cleared from ID. But they are not yet cleared from the PC. At this point, if PC requests the list of active entities from ID: ID, having already removed the ZK nodes for the PE, will exclude all entities that were synced from that PE. As a result, those entities will not be included in the active entities response sent to PC. When PC processes this updated active entities list: It will interpret the missing entities as deletions, And consequently delete all existing synced entities associated with the PE’s master cluster UUID. Impact: Incorrect entity visibility on PC; i.e., PE-synced entities should have been in a hidden state on PC, but are now being deleted from PC. Proposed Solution Design Overview The solution involves grouping active entities by master_cluster_uuid at each hop: Source-side changes: Active entities must be grouped per master_cluster_uuid source (in addition to existing tenant_id grouping) Only entities eligible for replication should be selected at the source The selection logic will need enhancement to determine replication eligibility Destination-side changes: Use the same grouping logic on the destination Finding deleted entities should happen at a master_cluster_uuid level Compare entities per source cluster independently Implementation Details Destination when asking for active entities from source will now also specify the format in which the active entities data should be sent, i.e., whether it should be grouped per cluster or not.

The logical stream type. optional StreamType.Type stream_type = 1; // Required. If true, the source should send active entities in the // new format with per-cluster grouping. optional bool request_active_entities_per_cluster = 3 [ default = false ]; } // The missing ranges

by // master_cluster_uuid. The execution time taken by this rpc on the insights server // side in microseconds. optional uint64 rpc_execution_time_usecs = 2; } Note: The destination cluster should set the new field only when the entire cluster is upgraded.

Now, there can be two scenarios on Source. The source can be upgraded to understand this new field, or it hasn’t been upgraded yet and wouldn't understand it.

[IDF Design Documents | Active Entities Workflow For Mutli-hop Sync]
On Upgraderd Source: The upgraded source will honour this new field in RemoteTransferDataRet and will send the active entities to the destination grouped per cluster with an identifier as well to indicate that the data is in a new format, i.e., grouped per cluster. To achieve the same, we need to make the following changes in the ActiveEntitiesInfo proto message ActiveEntitiesInfo { // Required. The start time of the taking the snapshot. optional uint64 active_entities_info_timestamp_usecs = 1; // The entity info data for a given entity type. message EntityInfo { // The entity info data for a given entity type restricted to a tenant_id. message EntityInfoPerTenant { // Optional. The tenant id. optional string tenant_id = 1; // Optional. Ids of active entities. repeated string entity_id_list = 2; } // Required. The entity type name. optional string entity_type_name = 1; // Optional. The entity info for each of the tenants. repeated EntityInfoPerTenant entity_info_per_tenant_list = 2; } // Optional. The active entities info. repeated EntityInfo = 2; // Grouped active entities per master cluster UUID message ClusterActiveEntities { optional string master_cluster_uuid = 1; repeated EntityInfo entity_info_list = 2; } // New format: active entities grouped by source cluster repeated ActiveEntitiesPerCluster entity_info_per_cluster_list = 3; optional bool is_active_entities_grouped_by_cluster = 7 [default = false]; } On a non-upgraded source: The non-upgraded source will continue to

[IDF Design Documents | Active Entities Workflow For Mutli-hop Sync]
} // New format: active entities grouped by source cluster repeated ActiveEntitiesPerCluster entity_info_per_cluster_list = 3; optional bool is_active_entities_grouped_by_cluster = 7 [default = false]; } On a non-upgraded source: The non-upgraded source will continue to send the active entities in the older format, i.e., grouped by per-shard, per-entity_type, per-tenant, as it won’t recognize the new field in RemoteTransferDataArg.

Now, when active entities' info reaches the Destination, there are two scenarios.
Either the data can come from an upgraded source, i.e., grouped by master_cluster_uuid, or from a non-upgrade source.

The destination should be able to handle both scenarios.

When active entities come from an upgraded source:
Destination will check whether is_active_entities_grouped_by_cluster is set to true; if so, it will process active entities per cluster by reading entity_info_per_cluster_list.

When active entities come from a non-upgraded source:
Since the source is not upgraded, it will continue to send active entities in the old format. The destination will again read the value of is_active_entities_grouped_by_cluster, which will be set to the default value false; hence, the destination can continue to process older-format info by reading entity_info_list.

[Arithmos & Metric Collection | Arithmos Sync integration with ID]
Arithmos Sync integration with ID

## Context
Arithmos is the time-series database responsible for storing all time-series metrics on PE, along with a small subset of configuration entities such as cluster, disk, and container. These entities are currently synced from PE to PC IDF using the Arithmos-IDF sync mechanism. With the introduction of an intermediate ID layer between PE and PC, Arithmos sync must now support syncing entities to both ID and PC.

## Problem Statement
Since IDF does not yet support syncing metric (time-series) data, a fully cascading model (PE → ID → PC) cannot be established for all entity types. To accommodate the new architecture, two potential approaches are being considered.

## Approach 1: Dual Arithmos Sync (PE → ID and PE → PC)
Under this approach, PE continues syncing all Arithmos entities directly to both ID and PC.
* **Pros:** Simplifies implementation with minimal code changes.
* **Cons:** Once IDF adds support for metric sync, migration and cleanup will be required to consolidate data under a cascading model (PE → ID → PC).

[Arithmos & Metric Collection | Arithmos Sync integration with ID]
## Approach 2: Split Responsibility Sync
In this approach:
PE → ID Arithmos sync handles both configuration and time-series entities.
PE → PC Arithmos sync sends only time-series data.
Config entities flow from ID → PC via IDF sync.
This avoids the need for migration in the future because PE → PC metric sync can simply be disabled once IDF supports metric sync.
Pros: No migration or cleanup effort when IDF metric sync becomes available.
Cons: Currently, entities synced from PE → PC via Arithmos are created as local entities on PC. Local entities allow direct client updates (e.g., cluster updates via Zeus sync). If config entities start flowing from ID → PC, those entities become replicated (read-only) on PC, breaking existing client write workflows.

## Proposed Solution
To preserve client write capabilities on PC, certain attributes of Arithmos-synced entity types will be converted into namespace attributes. This will allow clients to continue updating these fields even if the entities become replicated and read-only on the PC.

## Note
We are evaluating workflows that directly read or modify attributes of Arithmos-synced entities on PC. Based on this analysis, the final decision between the two approaches will be made.

## Batching Arithmos Sync Calls At Insights Proxy
Devendra, Sumit
April 2021

## Problem Statement:
As seen by Aryan in testing ENG-382171, if the same data is sent broken into multiple RPCs vs in the same RPC the cpu resources of IDF is very low when it's sent in a single RPC. So this doc is to mention the approaches to reduce the number of calls by batching data at proxy layer.

[IDF Design Documents | Batching Sync Calls At Insights Proxy]
## Batching all entity_types from a single cluster: Modify AgentSendPersistEntities to take list of SendPersistEntitiesInfo instead of a single SendPersistEntitiesInfo. At the coordinator break the data coming inside TransferArithmosData into two args: one of the scaleout entity_types to be sent to local and the other of leader-only entity_types to be sent to the leader. On the processor the lock will be acquired for the received entity_types(currently there is locking per cluster,etype pair, now we'll try to acquire lock for all entity_types received for that cluster), arg will be converted to IDF arg and lesser RPCs sent to IDF as all entity_types will be batched. PROS: All entity_types will be batched per cluster. The batching might be higher even in low PE count PCs. Since we're sending all entity_types in one call we're sure even if there is just 1 PE connected to PC batching will happen. Since batching is fixed the number of RPCs to IDF would come down to a minimum 3 from current 30+ RPCs CONS: No cross-cluster batching, but very high per cluster batching. The coordinator should take care the processor is upgraded to use the new arg parameter. Changes will be needed in the Prism side to use the list attribute of AgentSendPersistEntities. This will only be needed to support this optimization in 5.15.x. Else we can ignore this. No adverse effect on prism side sync workflow. Need to make sure that the coordinator to processor payload doesn't cross 16mb RPC limits.

[IDF Design Documents | Batching Sync Calls At Insights Proxy]
to support this optimization in 5.15.x. Else we can ignore this. No adverse effect on prism side sync workflow. Need to make sure that the coordinator to processor payload doesn't cross 16mb RPC limits. Currently, we don't hit this since the PE-PC payload is compressed and PC internode RPCs are for a single etype. Possible solutions: Could be solved by compressing again while forwarding to the processor if required. (Extra compress/decompression overhead). Can also be solved by breaking arg based on the count/size of entities payload.

[IDF Design Documents | Batching Sync Calls At Insights Proxy]
## Batching calls across clusters:
Create a queuing class that will intercept all BatchUpdate/PutMetricData going from Proxy to IDF and batch them based on a timer as well as counter.
Batching quantification can't be said definitively.
PROS:
No changes required in Prism, automatic batching for all sync requests.
Historical requests will also be batched automatically.
Since it's an ops queue it can be used to do rate limiting to IDF.
Won't hit 16MB RPC limits since payloads are only per entity_type.
CONS:
If the PE count is low, the batching effect won't trigger and the timeout will end up slowing down all requests.
To get the real benefit we'll have to process the entity_types parallelly instead of the current sequential flow, the parallel processing was reverted due to oom issues earlier.
Potentially high memory usage.
Since there are 33+ entity_types being processed sequentially by the coordinator the queuing timeout has to be small to not cause overall sync RPC timeouts.
Batching effect could possibly be lower even in high PE setups since proxy has fewer threads and only be able to process 2 RPCs at a time.

## Not clearing backup db modified timestamp from pending updates set affects the Active Entities Workflow and the fix for time-skew. Jineet Desai Feb 2022 ENG-449494: Remove backup db_modified_timestamp from pending updates oracle timestamp set JIRA: https://jira.nutanix.com/browse/ENG-449494 We maintain an ordered set oracle_time_set_for_pending_updates_ per shard in order to record oracle time for all pending updates. Whenever an update comes to IDF server(normal update or backup entity from PC), we call the following method GetDbModifiedTimestamp to get the db_modified_timestamp for the shard. This method internally inserts the db_modified_timestamp returned to the oracle_time_set_for_pending_updates_ set. In case of a normal update/restored entity we set the db_modified_timestamp_usecs field of the entity with the db_modified_timestamp value returned from the GetDbModifiedTimestamp method. However for backup entity coming to PE, we store this db_modified_timestamp value returned into the backup_db_modified_timestamp_usecs field of the entity. Code reference: https://sourcegraph.canaveral-corp.us-west-2.aws/ntnxdb-master/-/blob/ntnxdb_server/insights/insights_server/store/insights_store_entity.cc?L1471:40 Once the update is complete in case of normal update/restored entity, we remove the db_modified_timestamp_usecs from the oracle_time_set_for_pending_updates_. However we do not remove backup_db_modified_timestamp_usecs from the set for a backup entity, due to which those

[IDF Design Documents | Bug_=ENG-449494]
the update is complete in case of normal update/restored entity, we remove the db_modified_timestamp_usecs from the oracle_time_set_for_pending_updates_. However we do not remove backup_db_modified_timestamp_usecs from the set for a backup entity, due to which those entries would always remain in the oracle_time_set_for_pending_updates_ set(unless the IDF server restarts). Issues Caused: In case of pending updates, LoadActiveEntitiesInfo always gets a smaller oracle timestamp than all the pending updates so that the pending updates aren’t snapshotted. So if the backup_db_modified_timestamp_usecs entries remain in the pending_updates set, then we may not be able to send the latest active entities info to the replica side. Thus the active entities workflow would not work as expected. [IDF Design Documents | CPD-2084_ RPC v2 updates for IDF adoption]
https://jira.nutanix.com/browse/CPD-2084

## What
Currently the RpcServerV2 class only supports a single RPC service.  We would like to enhance RpcServerV2 so that it supports multiple services, similar to the RpcServer class.  Additionally, we need to introduce multithreading to HttpServerV2 via the event driver.

## Why
IDF is migrating to RpcServerV2, but in order to support existing workflows we need the RpcServerV2 class to support multiple services (i.e. client interface, node-to-node interface, and replication interface).

## Interface
The original constructor for RpcClientV2 will continue to be supported.  Additionally, a constrictor that accepts a list of services will also be supported.
Unlike RpcClient, RpcClientV2 will not support ExportService().  This is to eliminate the need to protect the set of services with a mutex.

## RpcClientV2 Changes
The modifications to RpcClientV2 required to support this new functionality are minor.  RpcClientV2 just needs to add the service name (which it already knows about from the service descriptor) to the RPC header.  This is similar to HTTP mode, which puts the service name into the request URL.
The only change to the RpcClientV2 interface is the addition of an optional argument to the constructor: server_exports_single_service (default true).  If the target server is only exporting a single service then there is no need to pass the target service name in the RPC header.

[IDF Design Documents | CPD-2084_ RPC v2 updates for IDF adoption]
## Multiplexing RPC Services
When it has multiple RPC services, the RPC server needs to be able to decide which service to use to handle each individual RPC.
This will be done by adding a field to the RpcRequestHeader protobuf called service_name.  This field has a type of string and contains the name of the service to which the RPC belongs.  Together, service_name and method_name will uniquely identify the exact RPC being invoked.
All services will be stored in an std::map named rpc_svc_map_.
map is implemented using a binary tree (as opposed to unordered_map which uses a hash table).  Since the total number of interfaces will likely always be small (i.e. 2 or 3), map will have no significant performance disadvantages compared to unordered_map (it may even be faster).  It also has a smaller memory footprint.
A pointer will be kept to the “default” service.  This service is used whenever the client doesn’t specify the service_name (i.e. when there is an “old” client that isn’t populating service_name in the RPC header), for the sake of backwards compatibility.  The default service is always the service provided to the constructor or the first service exported if there is no service provided to the constructor.
If a client requests a service_name that does not exist then the RPC server will return a RpcResponseHeader::kTransportError with an appropriate error message.

[IDF Design Documents | CPD-2084_ RPC v2 updates for IDF adoption]
## Backwards Compatibility
RpcServerV2 will be fully backwards compatible with old versions of the V2 client due to the default service described in the section above.  Since there is no change in how it handles HTTP requests, V1 clients will also continue to be compatible.

[IDF Design Documents | CPD-2084_ RPC v2 updates for IDF adoption]
## HttpServerV2 Event Driver
HttpServer version one calls the RPC event handles on seperate threads (via the event driver).  In order for IDF to adopt RpcServerV2 and HttpServerV2 this is a necessary feature for IDF.  IDF RPC handlers operate under the assumption that they are not blocking incoming messages.
This issue was previously discussed for SimpleHttpServer here.
In HttpServerV2::HandleMessage and HttpServerV2::HandlePacket, if the event driver has qmore than one worker thread then work will be passed to the event driver instead of executing it on the local thread.  The event driver will be passed to the HttpServerV2 in its constructor.
This new functionality in HttpServerV2 will be toggled by the optional argument schedule_rpcs_on_event_driver in its constructor.  By default the HttpServerV2 will use the old behavior of executing the RPC callback on its own thread.
Question: should the handlers for flatbuffer communications also be handed to the event driver?  This feature is not required by IDF (since we are not using flatbuffers), but it would make the overall pattern of HttpServerV2 more self consistent.
IDF will wrap some of its longer running RPCs in an event driver context.  HttpServerV2 will not do this automatically.

[IDF Design Documents | CPD-2084_ RPC v2 updates for IDF adoption]
## Testing
Since this touches code outside of the IDF project I am unsure the requirements for testing, automated tests, etc.  One major test is to enable the use of this new functionality in IDF to ensure that it works as advertised… although I don’t think this alone is sufficient.  We will also want some sort of performance testing as well.

CPD-2350 - Introduce per entity sync filtering capabilities
Aiswarya S,  Swagat Borah
January 2019

## Customer use case:
Ref: https://jira.nutanix.com/browse/CPD-2350
Draas is introducing a new service called Polaris in Xi-MT time frame. This new service will create a bunch of task entities on Xi-PE that need not be synced to Xi-PC. Currently all task entities are synced from Xi PE to Xi PC since the replication is set at the entity type level. We need to filter out these task entities created by Polaris and prevent them from syncing without affecting the other task entities created by other services. Polaris can tag their task entities with any metadata / attribute which can help IDF identify which entities to not sync.
DRaas team has use cases around syncing policies from PE to PCs of certain Availability zones and not to others. This will be required by DRaas Team for them to move to PC Federation. The above feature covers this use case also.- (Ref: https://docs.google.com/document/d/1kqfAM5b1ej2pIWkcFC3DFd-vpmhtEKZoeg1bqlmgS-M/edit#)

## Other use cases:
This feature can also be extended to other local entities like tasks,  intent-specs etc. that can be selectively synced.
PC Federation :- Once we have the per entity sync framework  available in IDF, we can extend it for PC Federation use case which also require per entity sync filtering.

[IDF Design Documents | CPD-2350_ Per Entity Sync Filtering_]
## Scope and Design Considerations:
In addition to `is_suppress_replication flag` and `replication_control_list` that specifies entity_type level sync restrictions, we need parameters per entity level to filter or to specify whether that particular entity needs to be synced or not.
This feature needs to be generic and extensible enough to support upcoming sync use cases around PC Federation and other per entity sync filtering scenarios as well.
The filtering can depend on multiple attributes of that entity  as well as cluster wide parameters.
To future proof, We should be able to specify different filters for each {from-to} combinations of sync (eg: PE->PC, PE-Xi-PC) with minimum duplications.
It should provide the same  guarantees as the existing `is_suppress_replication’ flag for upgrade/ config change and sync barrier related workflows.
Proper semantics should be defined to determine which filter to apply when.
The implementation should be as optimised as much as possible w.r.t to memory and processing overheads.

[IDF Design Documents | CPD-2350_ Per Entity Sync Filtering_]
## New Metadata Field per Entity Approach: We can add a new metadata field to IDF entities - ’sync_list’. This can be of type:- enum ClusterConfiguration { kNone = 1; kPC = 2; kPE = 3;} message SyncInfo { ClusterConfiguration replicate_to = 1; (Can this be same as ReplicationControlList?) } message Entity { ... repeated SyncInfo sync_list = 17; // SyncInfo can be replaced with ReplicationControlList } The user will specify the cluster configurations to which the entity is to be synced. If it needs to be synced to all the connections, the sync_list will be empty. If it need not be synced to any configuration, cluster_configuration = kNone. If it needs to be synced only to PE , `replicate_to = kPE`. eg:- for our use case , All Polaris task entities will be contain the metadata :- sync_list = [(kNone)] Pros: Simple, No significant processing overhead at IDF level. No need to look up metric types/entity types. Extensible to future use cases where uses need to specify connection_uuids based on their application. IDF need not do application logic processing. Cons: Memory overhead to store the metadata list. The sync_list values should be consistent and decodable during upgrades (in case additional fields are added to `SyncInfo` . his approach is extensible and IDF need not do the application specific processing. This can be done at uploader side, after combining with other PC federation filters (based on tenant_uuid and federation_id etc). As a simplified version of this, we can go

[IDF Design Documents | CPD-2350_ Per Entity Sync Filtering_]
do the application specific processing. This can be done at uploader side, after combining with other PC federation filters (based on tenant_uuid and federation_id etc). As a simplified version of this, we can go with a boolean flag metadata field for now and later add the SyncInfo field (similar to `is_suppress_replication` and `replication_control_list`) . A possible concern is the extra overhead for this boolean flag . Discussed this approach with Ergon and Draas team and they are good with this.

## Plan of Action
As a first step, we can go with a boolean flag metadata field for now and later add the SyncInfo field (similar to `is_suppress_replication` and `replication_control_list` in entity_type) . A possible concern is the extra overhead for this boolean flag . This filtering will be done at the Server side. Expected by end of April.
The next set of change will include supporting the filtering based on SyncInfo field.      This will be  done at  uploader side - as detailed in the doc. Expected by October.

[IDF Design Documents | CPD-2350_ Per Entity Sync Filtering_]
## 1) Filters in Metric Type config :
Approach: Add a new field called  ‘suppress_replication_value’  to the metric type. If the metric  value equal to the suppress replication value - do not sync it.
eg: for metric type ‘component’ in ‘task’ entity, add  ‘suppress_replication_value = “polaris”’ as part of metric type config info. To decide if a  ‘task’ entity need to be synced,  check the metric type config for this entity type, check the ‘suppress_replication_value’ of metric type ‘component’ and check if the current entity has an attribute which matches this value. If matches don’t sync, else sync the entity.
Pros :- Simple and straightforward. 
Cons :- May not be suitable for future requirements - where sync filter criteria may depend on multiple attributes( eg. component = “polaris”  AND status = “completed”) and  multiple ‘from-to’ configurations

[IDF Design Documents | CPD-2350_ Per Entity Sync Filtering_]
## 2) New Metadata Field per Entity.
Approach : We can add a new metadata field to IDF entities -’to_be_synced’. Users can set it to true or false depending on whether to sync or not.
eg: When user creates a task entity with  component = polaris, the user will send it with ‘to_be_synced’ = false.
Pros:
Simple, No significant processing overhead at IDF level.
No need to look up metric types like approach [1].
Cons:
May not be convenient for future requirements - where sync depends on multiple attributes ( set by different users or in different updates) and multiple configurations.
There are memory overheads to store the flag (or list of flags in case we need to support   multiple from-to configurations).

[IDF Design Documents | CPD-2350_ Per Entity Sync Filtering_]
## 3) New Metadata Field per Entity and Filter per Entity Type.
Approach: As part of the entity type config, we add a new config field ‘sync_filter’. In addition, we can add a new metadata field ’to_be_synced’ to  entity proto. For any new updates, IDF evaluates the ‘sync_filter’ on the entity and sets ‘to_be_synced’ accordingly.
eg. Add a new filter in entity type config of ‘task’:
sync_filter = {component!=”polaris”}.
When the task entity is created with component=”polaris”, IDF evaluates this expression  ‘sync_filter’ and sets the metadata field ‘to_be_synced_’ to false. Thus the entity is not synced.
Pros:- We have to calculate the field only once - per update. Can depend on multiple attributes and values.
Cons:- Memory overheads to store the value. It can extend to a list if we want different filters per {cluster_from-cluster_to} sync conditions.

[IDF Design Documents | CPD-2350_ Per Entity Sync Filtering_]
## 4) Entity Type per filter Approach: We add a new field to the replication control list proto in Entity Type config - a Boolean expression object called ‘Sync filter’(In the replication control list, we presently have {from, to}). We evaluate the sync filter when we initiate a sync of that entity. If the sync filter evaluates to true for the present entity, we sync the entity for that sync case. Else we don’t sync. eg. We add a new entry in replication_control_list {from: NotSet, to: NotSet, Sync condition: “component” != “polaris”} of the entity type ‘task’ . During sync, IDF will evaluate this condition on each task entity before attempting to sync this entity . Pros : Suits the present and future use cases where we need to filter based on entity attributes , other cluster wide attributes required in future. Less memory overhead than approach (2) and approach (3) since we have only one config entry per entity type level Can be extended to multiple from-to sync configurations by specifying the sync filter as field in the replication control list entry (as shown in eg. above). We can avoid redundancies of having the same filter condition across multiple from-to sync configurations by introducing the semantics of a wildcard approach for them, i.e if the from/to configuration are kept empty, then the filter is applied on all possible values of that from/to entry respectively. (Explained in more detail below) Cons: We may need to calculate the boolean expression every time a

are kept empty, then the filter is applied on all possible values of that from/to entry respectively. (Explained in more detail below) Cons: We may need to calculate the boolean expression every time a sync operation is initiated. Since any user can modify a filter expression in entity type, other users can get unexpected results due to an unintended change by a different user. To be synced or not , will depend on the entity type config at the time at which the sync happens and not during the CRUD operations.

## Introduction
This is the capture of the discussions that we had on 12/04/2014, the decisions that we made w.r.t. high-level architecture and the open issues that we need to address.

## Requirements
We identified the following requirements for data transport functionality:
PE may not be co-located with PC
Need ability to ship data to PC w/o storing it on PE
PC + SRE Insights is one product to support
Sync data from PE to PC
Local collection of data on PC (e.g. metrics & health of PC itself)
NOS-independent collectors
Multiple transport options (SMTP, HTTP, …)
Secure transport channel (Auth, Auth, encryption)
Multiple channels (QoS) of transport
Multiple endpoints (data from PE may go to multiple PCs, SaaS, etc.)
Note: we don’t need to handle data flow from PC to PE, i.e. the data is always mastered (collected) on PE and gets replicated to PC.  The Acropolis team is planning to do Acropolis-to-Acropolis communication (i.e. Acropolis running on PC will send the data to Acropolis on PE), so we don’t need to provide this service for them.

[IDF Design Documents | Data transport architecture - 12_04_2014]
## High-level architecture The high-level architecture can be represented by the following diagram: The data that is collected from Stargate, Pithos, Hyperint, etc. goes to the Ingest proxy that supports Arithmos interfaces (the Arithmos service will be removed), and from the Ingest proxy it’s pushed to the Insights DB. The Insights DB pushes data to the Transport service which pushes the data to one or more remote destinations that run Prism Central services (that could be running on-premise or potentially in the cloud). Each PC would have Transport services to receive the data and deliver it to the Insights DB on PC. In addition to the data that gets through the Insights DB on PE, there is a set of collectors that push data directly to the Transport service. We have pretty good understanding and agreement on the Ingest proxy, collectors and Insights DB components, and now we’re trying to get clarity on who’s going to provide transport services and how. I’ll get into the details of transport options in a moment, but let me first to list the requirements for the Transport service that were discussed: Authentication Encryption Compression Store & forward QoS / channels Multiple destinations Bootstrapping Multiple transport protocols Access control Notes on authentication and access control: at the beginning we don’t need elaborate access control and probably going to just support the model “if you managed to authenticate, then you have access”. In the future we might need to

[IDF Design Documents | Data transport architecture - 12_04_2014]
control: at the beginning we don’t need elaborate access control and probably going to just support the model “if you managed to authenticate, then you have access”. In the future we might need to support RBAC, but not likely in this version. Notes on multiple transport protocols: for this version it’s probably ok to support HTTPS only. HTTPS would give us encryption and cert-based authentication (and maybe even compression, depending on what library we use). Notes on bootstrapping: bootstrapping is a protocol for pulling data from Insights DB running on CVM (PE) to Insights DB running on PC when a new PC gets added (or after a PC was offline long enough for the queued incremental updates to expire). Notes on store & forward: the Insights DB on CVM (PE) already has persistent copy of the data that it pushes to the Transport service, so technically it doesn’t need the Transport service to provide store & forward. But for simplicity we initially will implement store & forward functionality that would work uniformly both for Insights DB and collectors (the latter do require Transport service to store the data).

[IDF Design Documents | Data transport architecture - 12_04_2014]
## Current state
To provide context, here is how the data transfer happens now:
PE pulls data from Arithmos, sends it to PC and pushes it to Arithmos on PC.  Store & forward is not needed, because the data is stored in the Arithmos on PE and can be re-retrieved from there if the transfer fails.
The Arithmos service will be removed, so the current implementation has to change.  We considered two options:
Use Prism as a channel for the data transport
Fully implement transport service end-to-end
Let’s consider the options in more detail.

[IDF Design Documents | Data transport architecture - 12_04_2014]
## Use Prism as a channel for the data transport
In this case we would implement uploader service that would push data to PE and will tell it where the data needs to be sent, the PE will contact the corresponding PC and the PC will push the data to the receiver service, which would push the data to the Insights DB.
Here is the diagram that represents this option:
The uploader / receiver pair is going to implement the following functionality:
Store & forward
QoS (send now or lazily)
Multiple destinations
Bootstrapping
Prism is going to handle the following:
Authentication
Encryption
Compression
Access control
The following changes would be required for Prism:
Provide interface for uploader to push data into (instead of pulling from Arithmos)
On PC, push to receiver (instead of Arithmos)
The endpoint information is going to be provided by uploader
Support bootstrapping protocol
Pros of this option:
Reuse existing Prism functionality for data transfer
Cons of this option:
Multiple moving parts
Cross team dependencies in the middle (we own both ends, Prism owns channel)

[IDF Design Documents | Data transport architecture - 12_04_2014]
## Fully implement transport service end-to-end
In this case, we’ll implement the Transport service end-to-end.  We will port the functionality that Prism currently provides, so the Transport service would take care of transferring the data and supporting all the requirements.
Here is the diagram that represents this option:
Pros of this option:
Transport components are tightly integrated
End-to-end ownership
Build on top of infrastructure that is proven to scale for remote data transfer
Cons of this option:
Potentially need to re-implement functionality currently provided by Prism
Implementation note: should the Transport service run as a daemon or as a library?  We decided that the Transport service is going to run as a daemon to avoid implementing the functionality for multiple languages.  If this happens to be a problem, we can re-implement it as a library in the future.
Implementation note: we may be able to use websockets.

## Open issues
It seems like the Transport service would be generic enough to be used from other components to transfer the data.  So we need to figure out what other components would benefit from using the Transport service:
Prism transfers Zookeeper data, would they delegate this to Transport service?
Prism transfers Alerts data, would they delegate this to Transport service?
Acropolis may need to transfer data, would they use Transport service for that?

[IDF Design Documents | Data transport architecture - 12_04_2014]
## Product-wide data transport vision [12/05/2014] On 12/05/2014 we continued the discussion of transport options and arrived to the idea of architecturally separating Transport functionally from Tunnel functionality. A Tunnel service would be a first-class citizen in Prism, a user would be able to configure a Tunnel that could be used for transferring data between two locations. Once a Tunnel is configured, it can be potentially used by multiple services (Insights DB, VNC, etc.). A Tunnel service would provide the following capabilities: Authentication - make sure that the two endpoints are allowed to talk to each other Multi-protocol - may be implemented on top of different protocols: HTTPS, SSH, etc. Encryption May provide compression A Tunnel connection is always between two locations, it doesn’t provide multi-point, broadcast or etc. capabilities. A Tunnel connection doesn’t provide data persistence for guaranteed delivery (e.g. store & forward). The Tunnel service is currently in the vision stage, there are no resources allocated for its implementation. The Transport service would provide the following capabilities: Store & forward QoS (send now or lazily) Multiple destinations Bootstrapping These capabilities are required by Insights DB and it’s going to be implemented by the Insights DB team. Given the functionality that we have now, it’s reasonable to say that Transport service is going to have Uploader and Receiver parts, so the architecture can be represented by

[IDF Design Documents | Data transport architecture - 12_04_2014]
by the Insights DB team. Given the functionality that we have now, it’s reasonable to say that Transport service is going to have Uploader and Receiver parts, so the architecture can be represented by the following diagram: The user will have one or more Tunnels configured, each Tunnel configuration would contain the information that is necessary to connect and authenticate to the remote location (e.g. server address:port, proxy address:port, certificate, etc.). The Tunnel configuration would be provided independently of Insights DB data transport, in fact there could be Tunnels that are not used by the Insights DB data transport: in the diagram above there are 4 Tunnels, 3 of them are used to transport Insights DB data to their corresponding remote locations (they could also be used by other services) and 1 of them is not used by the Insights DB (could be used by other services). The Uploader service would be configured to use one or more Tunnels to transport data to the corresponding locations. The Tunnel ID (uuid or name or etc.) would be provided to the Uploader service and it would use the Tunnel ID + service ID to create connections to the remote destinations (service ID would identify the service, in our case it’s going to be “insights” or something like that). The uploader would maintain per-connection the state that is necessary for store & forward functionality (e.g. persistent queue) and etc. Is Tunnel service going to be implemented as a daemon or as a library? I

[IDF Design Documents | Data transport architecture - 12_04_2014]
uploader would maintain per-connection the state that is necessary for store & forward functionality (e.g. persistent queue) and etc. Is Tunnel service going to be implemented as a daemon or as a library? I think this is an implementation detail and it possible that some types of Tunnels would be implemented as a daemon and other would be implemented as a library. The Tunnel service API is just an abstract interface that would map to multiple implementations. Like I mentioned earlier, the Tunnel service is currently at the vision stage, so we don’t have concrete APIs to use or even a team tasked with defining the APIs. Does this block us? I don’t think so. Without loss of generality, we can assume that the Tunnel service API is going to provide four primary functions in some form: connect listen send receive connect would take the {Tunnel ID, service ID} pair and establish a connection to the remote location. listen would take {[Tunnel ID], service ID} pair and wait for a connection from the remote location (Tunnel ID is optional -- can listen on all Tunnels). send would send some data, receive would receive some data. With that assumption, until the Tunnel service API is defined, we should be able to use existing protocols. The transition to the Tunnel service APIs should be fairly easy -- e.g. the BaseTransport interface should be similar to Tunnel API and it would be just a matter of changing some calls to use Tunnel ID instead of the rest url.
headings: Use Prism as a channel for the data transport

## Ensure Replica never goes ahead of Source in IDF-IDF sync
Devendra Singh
Sep 2018
In-progress

## Problem Statement:
According to the current implementation, the IDF Replica side can go ahead of IDF Source side in case of below-mentioned events:-
Entity E1 (state s1) gets created in the IDF on the source side and also gets replicated to the Replica side.
An update on entity E1 (state s2) came to IDF on the source. IDF was able to write this update (state s2) to Cassandra but the acknowledge for the write to IDF failed so IDF will declare this update as failed and will mark the entity in kNotMerged state (which will be resolved on next update/write for the same entity) and marking state s2 as tentative value and while s1 remains the finalized state and all subsequent reads for entity E1 will get state s1.
If sync bootstrap/catchup logic happens before next update on the same entity then Replica will go ahead of source because in bootstrap/catchup logic we read from Cassandra and Cassandra already have an updated state (state s2). As IDF cache on source has state s1 while Cassandra has s2 state so Replica goes ahead of source on sync.
For sync catchup/bootstrap we can’t avoid reading from Cassandra otherwise, we will miss on deleted entities (deleted entities are not there in IDF cache and we won’t be able to sync them in this case) and anyway we have to go to Cassandra for Evictable entities.

[IDF Design Documents | ENG-172868_- Ensure Replica never goes ahead of Source in IDF-IDF sync]
## Possible solutions: Solution 1:- Resolve kNotMerged state on reads also When an entity is in kNotMerged state, it is possible that IDF cache is behind Cassandra for this entity (if we were able to write to Cassandra but the response from Cassandra to IDF failed). Currently, we only resolve the kNotMerged state of a cached entity only on subsequent update/write for the same entity. Therefore, all the reads, before the kNotMerged state is resolved, will read the previous version of the entity (finalized value from InsightsObject in cache for that entity). If we resolve the kNotMerged state on both subsequent reads and writes then we will bring IDF cache in sync with Cassandra on reads also. This will solve the problem of Replica going ahead of Source upto some extent because for someone to notice that Replica is ahead of source they will have to do a read, which will internally bring the cache in-sync with cassandra and return the latest up to date state of the entity. Cons:- If some client is solely relying on watches for keeping their cache in-sync or maintaining the state of entities then they will have the old state of the entity until some client issues an explicit read or write on the same entity. Reads might become expensive because now reads can also go to Cassandra for resolving the kNotMerged state. Solution 2:- Resolve kNotMerged state on LoadEntityTrail also (Cassandra scan done for sync catchup/bootstrap logic) Another possibility is that we resolve kNotMerged

[IDF Design Documents | ENG-172868_- Ensure Replica never goes ahead of Source in IDF-IDF sync]
now reads can also go to Cassandra for resolving the kNotMerged state. Solution 2:- Resolve kNotMerged state on LoadEntityTrail also (Cassandra scan done for sync catchup/bootstrap logic) Another possibility is that we resolve kNotMerged state when we do a read from Cassandra for sync catchup/bootstrap logic. In that way we ensure that replica never goes ahead of Source. This approach also solves the problem for clients who were maintaining their cache/entity states using watches because in this approach we bring the IDF cache on source side in-sync with Cassandra before syncing, which in turn makes sure that replica IDF never goes ahead of source IDF. Cons:- We might compromise on read after read consistency (if catchup/bootstrap logic happened between the two reads then we will get different state of the same entity on 2 consecutive reads and clients might see this as an abnormal behaviour). All reads will return the previous version of the entity until the bootstrap/catchup logic happens, this can be upto 5 minutes according to current frequency of bootstrap logic (this is similar to current behaviour of IDF reads (where we resolve the kNotMerged state on subsequent write/update) so not really a regression). Solution 3:- Combination of both Solution1 and Solution2 If we resolve the kNotMerged state of the InsightsObject for an entity either on next subsequent read/write or on next read from Cassandra done for catchup/bootstrap logic, whichever happens first. This approach

and Solution2 If we resolve the kNotMerged state of the InsightsObject for an entity either on next subsequent read/write or on next read from Cassandra done for catchup/bootstrap logic, whichever happens first. This approach solves the problem for clients who were maintaining their cache/entity states using watches because in this approach we bring the IDF cache on source side in-sync with Cassandra before syncing, which in turn makes sure that replica IDF never goes ahead of source IDF. This approach also solves the problem of read after read consistency because second read can only give different value if there was a failed write in between first and second read. Recommended Solution:- On the basis of Pros and Cons of all the above mentioned possible solutions. Solution3 seems a viable option because it solves the problem without any severe side effects and also do not break any of the current sync guarantees.

## ENG-560805 : Insights Uploader getting stuck in timeout loop
June 2023
Jineet Desai, Devendra Shekhawat
Recently we have seen multiple instances where the insights uploader continuously gets timeouts for all the RemoteTransferData calls that it makes and gets stuck in a timeout loop. Logs for the insights uploader would seem something like:
I
We have done a detailed analysis for this with the mercury team and the summary of the analysis can be found in this ticket: https://jira.nutanix.com/browse/ENG-560805
The issue can be shortly summarized as follows: There is some bug in Http Client or RPCClientOnAplos, the http responses are not delivered to the caller (in this case the caller is insights uploader) and the connection remains stuck forever until the http connection is recreated.

## Why doesn’t our ncc heartbeat check catch this issue on setups?
This is because the NCC check is designed to catch the complete halt and failure of IDF-IDF sync pipeline i.e. there are no requests passing from PE to PC. But in this case there is a unidirectional behavior where requests from PE to PC are reaching PC and hence the heartbeat timestamp gets updated on PC. Hence PC thinks that the sync pipeline is working fine (NCC check passes since it will get the latest heartbeat timestamp) but the response is not reaching the PE resulting in the calls getting timed out on PE.

[IDF Design Documents | ENG-560805 Insights Uploader getting stuck in timeout loop]
## Workarounds to solve the issue
We can simply restart the insights_uploader(it's under the insights_data_transfer service on our clusters) or mercury service on the nodes where we see this issue. Restarting mercury or insights uploader re-creates the http connection and solves the issue.

## Solution from our side
We have added a change in insights uploader as a workaround to re-create the http connections in case of request(RemoteTransferData calls) failures.
Code review link:  http://codereview.nutanix.net/D20604
Gerrit link: https://gerrit.eng.nutanix.com/#/c/main/+/763889/
However we still need to find out the actual RCA for this issue.

## Flush Uploader Data on Sync Barrier Updates
[In Progress]
Jineet DesaiDevendra ShekhawatSumit Bhatia

## Sync Barrier Updates
The current behavior of IDF-IDF sync is asynchronous. This implies that while updates are replicated across clusters, strict ordering of replication is not guaranteed. In particular, the order in which updates are applied on the target may differ from the order in which they were issued on the source.
Certain clients may require ordered sync of entity updates, for e.g. for tasks it may be necessary to ensure that all sub-task updates are replicated before the final completion state of the parent task is synced. To support such use cases, IDF provides a sync barrier construct. This construct allows clients to explicitly mark specific entity updates as sync barriers which ensures that all entity updates before this update are synced to replica.
When an entity update is marked as a sync barrier:
It ensures that all updates prior to this sync barrier are replicated before the sync barrier update itself is replicated to target.
The sync barrier update stamps the latest_db_modified_timestamp_usecs across all 128 shards
This update is only replicated to the target after the first start missing ranges across all shards have been caught up to the recorded timestamp.

[IDF Design Documents | Flush Uploader Data on Sync Barrier Updates]
## Insights Uploader
In a steady state workflow, IDF sync works via a push mechanism where any syncable updates on source IDF would be pushed to the local insights uploader. Post that insights uploader will batch these updates and send them to the insights receiver on the target via some transport service (e.g Mercury).
To manage the transmission of updates and missing range information, the uploader employs two types of configurable timeouts:
Urgent timeout: The urgent timeout is used when a syncable update is generated on the source IDF. In such cases, the uploader is immediately prompted to push the update—batched along with any other pending updates and missing range information. This transmission is expected to occur within 200 ms.
Normal timeout: For non-syncable updates coming on source IDF, we might need to fill the missing ranges corresponding to this update on target indicating there was nothing to sync. Or it can even be the case that there was no update for this local insights uploader to send. To address this, the source IDF requests the uploader to issue a heartbeat to the replica, conveying the current state and any inferred missing ranges. This heartbeat call would have a timeout of 30 secs.
Detailed description and overview of the sync barrier can be found in this documentation: IDF-IDF-sync-client.

[IDF Design Documents | Flush Uploader Data on Sync Barrier Updates]
## Problem Statement
Consider a scale-out IDF deployment consisting of three nodes managing shards:
Node 1: Shards 1–42
Node 2: Shards 43–85
Node 3: Shards 86–128
Insights Uploader on each node operates independently based on update activity in local IDF.
Now, consider the presence of a sync barrier update u1 on Shard 45, which is handled by Node 2. In order for this sync barrier to be replicated to the target IDF, the system requires that missing ranges for all shards (across all nodes) are fully caught up to the their corresponding latest_db_modified_timestamp_usecs / sync_barrier_timestamp associated with the sync barrier update.
Suppose Node 1 (Shards 1–42) has only received non-syncable updates, and therefore has not triggered any urgent timeouts on insights uploader. In this case, the uploader on Node 1 will only communicate its missing range state for shards 1-42 using the normal 30-second timeout. As a result, the sync barrier replication u1 is blocked until all the missing ranges for shards 1-42 are updated on replica. This might take 30 secs of time resulting in a delay of 30 secs for replicating sync barrier entities.

[IDF Design Documents | Flush Uploader Data on Sync Barrier Updates]
## Proposed Solution
To address this latency issue, we propose introducing a mechanism that proactively flushes the uploader’s batch when a sync barrier update is received on any IDF node. This ensures that all shards, including those with no recent syncable activity, promptly report their missing ranges to the replica in an event of sync barrier update.
The high level idea for this is as follows:

[IDF Design Documents | Flush Uploader Data on Sync Barrier Updates]
## Insights Server
When a sync barrier update occurs on any IDF node, that node issues a fanout call (NodeGetSyncBarrierInfo) to all peer nodes to fetch the latest DB modified timestamps across all 128 shards.
Receipt of this fanout request on a node serves as a signal of an impending sync barrier update. The receipt of a NodeGetSyncBarrierInfo request on an IDF node serves as an implicit signal of an impending sync barrier update. Upon receiving this request, the Insights Server on the node should issue a force flush command to the local Insights Uploader. This indicates the local Insights Uploader to flush all currently batched entity data and missing ranges information.
To support this mechanism, the UploadData RPC (from Insights Server to Insights Uploader) may be extended to include two additional parameters:
shard_timestamp_list :
This will carry the current sync barrier timestamps for all local shards. These timestamps will also be recorded in the sync_barrier_info to be stored as part of the sync barrier metadata.
force_flush_uploader:
A boolean flag that indicates the uploader batcher to flush all data in the current batch.
Sample proto changes would look as follows:

[IDF Design Documents | Flush Uploader Data on Sync Barrier Updates]
## Insights Uploader When the UploadData RPC is received by the local Insights Uploader, the uploader must track sync barrier timestamps per shard to coordinate the flushing behavior. This ensures that updates to entities and missing ranges are flushed to replicas before the corresponding sync barrier is replicated. To facilitate this, the uploader maintains an in-memory timestamp map for all shards, tracking the sync barrier timestamps and when they were recorded. shard_sync_barrier_timestamp: The sync barrier timestamp received from the Insights Server during sync barrier update. record_timestamp: The local wall clock time when the above timestamp was recorded or received on Insights Uploader. Each record_timestamp entry for a shard has an expiry duration. The expiry is controlled via a gflag: Records older than this gflag time shall be purged from the uploader_per_shard_timestamp_map. This can happen if there haven’t been any further sync barrier updates in IDF in which case the map would not be updated resulting in stale entries. A new sync barrier update shall always update the map entry. UploadData call from Insights Server to Insights Uploader can take at max 30 secs owing to RPC timeout. Hence we plan to set this expiry gflag to 30 secs. When an UploadData request is received with a force flush flag, the uploader must immediately initiate a RemoteTransferData request for: All current data in the uploader batch, and Any missing ranges within the batch. For all the

[IDF Design Documents | Flush Uploader Data on Sync Barrier Updates]
request is received with a force flush flag, the uploader must immediately initiate a RemoteTransferData request for: All current data in the uploader batch, and Any missing ranges within the batch. For all the subsequent UploadData calls post the force flush call: Following a force flush invocation, the Insights Uploader processes subsequent UploadData requests as follows: For each entity/missing range in the current uploader batch, the uploader evaluates the following conditions: The range_begin_timestamp is less than the corresponding shard_sync_barrier_timestamp. The record_timestamp associated with the sync barrier has not expired, i.e., it is still within the configured timeout window. If any entity satisfies both of the above conditions, the uploader must send the current batch using a RemoteTransferData request with kUrgent priority (200 ms). This behavior continues for each UploadData request until all relevant record_timestamps for the corresponding shards have expired.

## OVERVIEW IDF is our internal key-value store implementation that stores NOS management data on PC (Prism Central) and PE (Prism Element). The NOS management data includes spec, status and stats for VM, VNIC, VDisk and other entities. The ownership of these various entities in NOS is divided between PE and PC. For entities whose state is fully managed within a PE such as VM, VNIC, VDisks etc. are owned by PE while global config data such as SSP user, group info, authorization and access control policy info etc. is owned by PC. The IDF DBs on PE and PC sync the state of these entities with each other to keep the IDF DBs on both sides up to date and reflect the changes happening on one side to the other side. The IDF Sync mechanism syncing entities (and stats) between different IDF DBs follows master-slave relationship established between DBs for entities getting synced. The entities to be synced can only be updated (written) at the master IDF DB and these updates eventually get synced to the slave (replica) IDF DB. The entities that are owned by PE are mastered at PE and PC acts as the slave (replica) and vice versa for entities owned by PC. The IDF sync follows eventual consistency model where there is no guarantee on when and in which order the updates for various keys will get synced from master IDF DB to slave (replica) IDF DB. The only guarantee that IDF sync offers is that sync always progresses forward - once the slave IDF gets a newer update for a key, then the older

[IDF Design Documents | IDF Sync Barrier]
DB to slave (replica) IDF DB. The only guarantee that IDF sync offers is that sync always progresses forward - once the slave IDF gets a newer update for a key, then the older update for the key will not show up on slave IDF.

[IDF Design Documents | IDF Sync Barrier]
## IDF Sync and ordering (or lack thereof) of updates The sync between IDF PE and PC is not only eventually consistent but also has no ordering guarantee for updates to different keys(/tables/entities). This means that if key k1 was updated on master IDF before key k2, it’s possible that update to key k2 shows up on slave IDF before the update to key k1. This can cause headaches for applications trying to reason about the IDF state between PE-PC. Consider the following scenario where Metropolis service on PC asks Acropolis service on PE to do a certain operation on its behalf and relies on IDF sync mechanism to keep track of progress of the task - Metropolis on PC asks Acropolis service on PE to do some VM operation(s). Acropolis on PE reports back to Metropolis and provides the task ID for the request to track its progress. This task ID is an entity in IDF in PE. Metropolis on PC now relies on the syncing of the task ID in IDF to keep track of progress for the task. Acropolis on PE can now issue different actions and change the VM state (multiple entity updates in IDF). Finally when all the VM operations are done, Acropolis would mark the task as done by updating the task ID status in IDF. The task ID status gets synced from IDF PE to the IDF PC. Once Metropolis sees the task status as done in IDF in PC, it reports back to the client about the task as being finished. Note that even though the task is marked finished on PC IDF, the other IDF entity updates from step 4) may

[IDF Design Documents | IDF Sync Barrier]
PC, it reports back to the client about the task as being finished. Note that even though the task is marked finished on PC IDF, the other IDF entity updates from step 4) may not have been synced to the PC IDF. This lack of ordering for updates in the sync mechanism between PE-PC IDF would make it hard for clients reason about the PC IDF state. The client presumes that task having been reported as done in step 5) would mean that the VM status changes are also done but on reading the PC IDF state for the VM, it may find the VM state to be stale. This would be the case when the IDF updates for VM from PE have not been synced. To get around the above problem, the client (Metropolis) requires a way to guarantee that all master (PE) IDF updates are synced (visible) to slave (PC) IDF before the master IDF syncs a particular update (task getting marked done). In short we need a Barrier for IDF-IDF syncs.

[IDF Design Documents | IDF Sync Barrier]
## Problem Description
As documented above, currently IDF-IDF sync doesn't provide any ordering guarantees between entities.  For each individual entity, each replica would see timeline-consistent view (once a replica sees a new version of the entity it won't see older version), but if on the master entity e1 is updated before entity e2 is updated, a replica can see e2 update before e1 update.
There are cases when it's important that the replica (slave) sees certain updates in the same order they were made on master, because it represent causality between events.  A typical example is a task entity that represents an operation that updates other entities (e.g. vms, virtual disks, etc.).  When a task is marked as "completed", it's expected that all the entities that it worked on are updated (e.g. if the task created vm, then the vm entity would be created, virtual disks are attached, etc.).  On PE (IDF master), this is guaranteed by the service (the service would make sure that task is not marked "complete" until all entities are updated), however on PC (IDF replica) the task entity update could be replicated before other entities, so on PC the user can see that a task is completed but the other entities (e.g. vms) are stale or missing.

[IDF Design Documents | IDF Sync Barrier]
## Sync Barrier in IDF To express cross-entity ordering requirements, IDF would provide a "sync barrier" construct. The UpdateEntity / DeleteEntity (as well as the corresponding batched versions and attach / detach) operations would support a new sync_barrier flag, that the service can set. This would specify that the modification contains a sync barrier. Specifying a sync barrier for a modification would guarantee that the modification will be seen in a replica only after all previous modifications to all entities are replicated. For example, for the following sequence UpdateEntity(vm1) UpdateEntity(virtual_disk1) UpdateEntity(task1, sync_barrier=true) UpdateEntity(vm2) would guarantee that the IDF slave (replica) won't see task1 until vm1 and virtual_disk1 have been synced. The other relative ordering is not defined. E.g. the IDF slave may see virtual_disk1 being synced before vm1, it may even sync vm2 before vm1 (and before task1) but IDF would guarantee that vm1 and virtual_disk1 updates are synced before task1. As sync barrier would cause cluster-wide synchronization both on master and on replicas, as well as cluster-wide serialization on replica (most modifications with sync barriers are serialized between each other on the replica), it is expected that services would use it sparingly, so that updates that don't require ordering guarantees could be replicated independently. For now we the top level task entity setup at PE IDF would be updated with ‘sync_barrier’ as

[IDF Design Documents | IDF Sync Barrier]
would use it sparingly, so that updates that don't require ordering guarantees could be replicated independently. For now we the top level task entity setup at PE IDF would be updated with ‘sync_barrier’ as true.

[IDF Design Documents | IDF Sync Barrier]
## Design (IDF Implementation Details) The IDF DB consists of 128 shards that are independently mastered on the various IDF instances. Client generated keys in IDF get hashed (mapped) to these 128 shards. The updates/reads for a key are serviced by the IDF instance that owns the shard for the key. At a time a shard is owned by a single IDF instance, this ensures consistency of reads and writes for key in IDF. Updates to each of these shards get synced independently to the IDF slave. Each shard maintains a timestamp that is incremented with every update for key belonging to the shard. Each of these key updates in a shard gets tagged with this unique shard timestamp. The shard timestamp is used by IDF master and slave when syncing updates for a shard. The ordering of updates for different keys across (and within) shards is not guaranteed when syncing to IDF slaves. This means for updates to two keys that belong to same or different shards there is no guarantee for ordering of sync updates for these keys. For implementing the sync barrier, the IDF master DB would need to note down the shard timestamp of each shard with the value that contains the sync barrier update. So for an entity that contains a sync barrier write, IDF would put 128 int64 values (shard timestamps) as metadata for this update. These shard timestamps would be used by the IDF slave to ensure that the sync update for the barrier entity is accepted only once the syncs for all the shards are past the shard

[IDF Design Documents | IDF Sync Barrier]
These shard timestamps would be used by the IDF slave to ensure that the sync update for the barrier entity is accepted only once the syncs for all the shards are past the shard timestamps noted. To find out the shard timestamps for all shards, the IDF master would send a node-node RPC to all IDF instances to get current values of all shard timestamp. If a modification operation (UpdateEntity or DeleteEntity) has the sync_barrier=true the IDF master will get the shard timestamps from all IDF instances and store this list of shard timestamps in the new field of the entity metadata (sync_barrier_info). Once the sync_barrier_info field is set in the entity metadata, it needs to be inherited by further modifications of the entity (unless the new modification operation is issuing a new sync barrier request). To support sync barrier for updates that do deletions, we may possibly be required to store deletion tombstones for a longer time window. If the tombstone gets purged, the sync barrier info would get lost, so we need to make sure that the tombstone lives long enough to cover race condition window (currently default tombstone retention period is 7 days, which should be plenty -- if we have trouble replicating for 7 days, we'd probably have bigger problems than reordering of updates). As the sync barrier info is persisted with the entity (or entity tombstone in case of delete) and inherited by further modifications, all replicas will get it regardless of whether they receive the

[IDF Design Documents | IDF Sync Barrier]
updates). As the sync barrier info is persisted with the entity (or entity tombstone in case of delete) and inherited by further modifications, all replicas will get it regardless of whether they receive the update as a normal push flow as part of bootstrapping / catch up flow, and regardless of whether a replica got the modification that issued the sync barrier or a later modification. The modification operations with sync_barrier=true may come in bursts, we'll try to get the same sync barrier info for all operations that come within a time window (e.g. 50ms). This would help to avoid serialization on the replica (see the description of sync barrier wait logic later in the doc). To accomplish that, instead of calling the node-node RPC directly for each operation, the sync barrier requests would go through batching logic. The batching logic would work as the following: If a batch is not pending, create a batch handle, add callback to the list of callbacks, send node-node RPC to get all shard timestamps. Once node-node RPC completes, schedule batch completion in 50ms, once the batch completion happens, call the callbacks, remove batch handle. If a batch is pending, just add callback to the list of the callbacks. The batching logic is going to happen on every node. If this is not good enough, we can make the leader do batching for the whole cluster. When a replica receives an entity with sync barrier info set, it would verify that replication of all shards has advanced enough

[IDF Design Documents | IDF Sync Barrier]
enough, we can make the leader do batching for the whole cluster. When a replica receives an entity with sync barrier info set, it would verify that replication of all shards has advanced enough to satisfy the sync barrier. The check for the sync barrier is to just make sure that there is no missing ranges below the sync barrier's timestamp value (i.e. check that the bottom of the missing ranges map is >= timestamp). If sync barrier is not satisfied, then the node would not apply the entity modification, but wait for shards to catch up. If the node crashes (or shard is unloaded), the pending update would get lost, but it'll get re-sent as part of bootstrapping / catch up flow. Given that most of the time under normal circumstances (good connectivity) the changes are replicated near real time, the wait for sync barrier is not going to be long. The sync barrier wait for individual updates (push flow) is fairly straightforward because there is only one entity in the range. For the bootstrapping / catch up flow, there are multiple entities in the range and the current implementation would wait for all entities to be replicated and then mark the whole range as complete if all replications are successful. If we just do sync barrier wait within the ReplicateEntity function, we'll stall other updates and actually can deadlock because the sync barrier may be waiting on the ranges that would be applied as part of this replication operation. To avoid this problem, we need to implement

[IDF Design Documents | IDF Sync Barrier]
