To avoid this problem, we need to implement the following: Support updating ranges on partial success. If ReplicateEntity returns an error, we would knock out the hole in the range for the failed entity, so we can apply the range for the entities that are successfully replicated. This would work for any error, not just sync barrier. If sync barrier is not satisfied, ReplicateEntity would return an error (so the original range will get a hole), and then wait until the sync barrier is satisfied, and then it would apply the hole to the range. For example, suppose we got 100-200 range, and entities with the following timestamps: 108, 123, 140, 165, 192. The entities with timestamp 123 and 165 have sync barrier, ReplicateEntity would return a failure for both, then we knock out the holes to make the ranges look like this: 100-122, 123-164, 165-200 (we could've knocked out larger ranges, for the first entity we could've knocked out 109-123 but it's more work for no apparent benefit). When the sync barrier is satisfied for entity with timestamp 123, it would apply the 122-123 range to close the hole, and etc. In the case of new PE registration, we would get all completed tasks during replica bootstrapping process. Currently we keep about 2000 completed tasks on PE, we were also talking about bumping up this limit to 500 completed

Currently we keep about 2000 completed tasks on PE, we were also talking about bumping up this limit to 500 completed tasks / node (so on a 30 node PE we'd have 15K completed tasks). Assuming all completed tasks would have a sync barrier, most of the completed tasks would be serialized one after the other. The original thinking was that waiting could be implemented as simple check every second or so if the barrier is satisfied, which would work for normal (push) flow. For bootstrap, it would mean that we would be able to update about 1 task per second, so 15K tasks would be become visible in 4 hours (and while they are serially replicated, no new task completes will be visible). then it should be ordered before. Long poll is issued when the first request is added to the priority_queue. If a new update gets added to the queue such that it waits for earlier state than the rest of the updates, a new long poll is re-issued. The long poll rpc would take the master cluster uuid and the sync barrier (list of shards with timestamps). When a node receives long poll, it would check the ranges in all loaded shards, for any shard that the sync barrier is not satisfied for, it would add a waiter to the queue with the value to wait for an callback to the ReplicationStateObject of the shard. As the missing range map gets updated, if any of the waiters is satisfied, the callback will be called with the new bottom of the missing range map. Once all pending callbacks are called, the long poll RPC would return; once all long poll RPCs from all nodes are returned, the node that was waiting for the sync barrier would check if the returned values now satisfy the sync barrier. Shard load / unload is handled as the following. If the shard is unloaded from the node that is waiting for sync barrier (has priorty_queue of pending changes that would be applied on this node once the sync barrier is satisfied), the priority_queue is traversed and the changes that belong to the unloaded shards are removed from the queue (they will get re-replicated via bootstrapping logic, so we don't do any handoff to the new shard owner). If the shard is unloaded from the node that received long

[IDF Design Documents | IDF Sync Barrier]
are removed from the queue (they will get re-replicated via bootstrapping logic, so we don't do any handoff to the new shard owner). If the shard is unloaded from the node that received long poll rpc, then rpc completion can happen before the sync barrier is satisfied for that shard. To account for that case the node that issued long poll rpc must use the returned values to check if the sync barrier is satisfied. When a shard is loaded on the node that received long rpc, the callbacks are not added as part of the shard load, they will be added when a new long poll rpc comes. The long poll logic is per master cluster (so if PC has 100 PE registered, there would be 100 queues, 100 long polls, etc.). The missing ranges map is flushed with delay up to 30 seconds. If a few update to missing range map are lost there was no user-visible effect -- the replica would just re-request a little bit of extra changes from master. The sync barrier creates user visible effect -- visibility of an update could be impacted. To minimize this, we should reduce the delay to 1 second. The other thing that we need to do is to reverse the order of bootstrapping chunking. Currently, bootstrapping logic chunks the requests to go in reverse order (to support entity trail). Going in reverse order would delay sync barriers until bootstrapping reaches the beginning of the range. Reversing bootstrap logic would break entity trail bootstrapping (it's indexed in reverse order), but it's ok, as at this point

[IDF Design Documents | IDF Sync Barrier]
reverse order would delay sync barriers until bootstrapping reaches the beginning of the range. Reversing bootstrap logic would break entity trail bootstrapping (it's indexed in reverse order), but it's ok, as at this point it's unclear if we ever support it. If serialization of most sync barrier replication requests presents a tangible performance problem, we may consider relaxing barrier to exclude some entity types from sync barrier check (of course, we need to check if it works for the IDF clients). For example, if we never need a sync barrier between 2 tasks, then we can exclude tasks from sync barrier checks. There would be a flag on an entity type that would specify that the type is excluded from sync barrier checks. To achieve that, we'd keep 2 missing range maps: one would track completed replications and another would track pending replications. Entities that are excluded from sync barrier checks would add their range into pending replication range map as soon as we receive replication request, but normal entities would add their tange to pending replications only after the are finished replicating. The sync barrier wait would happen on the pending replication ranges. Another potential optimization that would avoid serialization of most sync barrier replication requests, would be to specify a sync range, rather than a barrier. In that case, the client would specify whether the update should start a sync range or end a sync range. E.g. when the client creates a task

[IDF Design Documents | IDF Sync Barrier]
a sync range, rather than a barrier. In that case, the client would specify whether the update should start a sync range or end a sync range. E.g. when the client creates a task entity it would specify that it should get the start of sync range (which is also just a list of shards and their timestamp oracles), and when the client marks the task entity complete, it would specify that it should take the end of sync range. Assuming the client does the bracketing right, then the replication of completed task would wait only for updates that happen while the task was pending. We can implement this as a future optimization, if needed.

## Backward Compatibility
If the IDF master is older version that doesn't support sync barriers, it's not a problem, because the replica just won't see the sync barrier info.  If the IDF replica is older version that doesn't support sync barriers, then replica would ignore sync barrier information.  In our specific deployment, we enforce that PC is always newer than any PE that is registered to it, so for that PE->PC replication, we should never have a case when PE issues a sync barrier that PC doesn't respect.
So at the IDF level, we don't need to do any additional logic to handle backward compatibility scenarios, but at the service level, the service on newer PC would have to still handle the data from old PEs that don't set sync barriers and do the ordering (if any) at the service level.

[IDF Design Documents | IDF Sync Barrier]
## Rolling Upgrade
On the master, the sync barrier operations won’t be available until all nodes in the cluster are upgraded to the IDF version that supports sync barrier.  If sync barrier is requested on a node that has newer IDF version, it will fail because it won’t be able to get sync barrier info from older versions (they don’t support node-node RPC); if sync barrier is requested on a node that has older IDF version (which should never happen in our deployment as all services use local IDF), then the sync barrier would be ignored (as the older version wouldn’t know anything about sync barrier).  The services on PE need to properly handle rolling upgrade and not rely on sync barrier until the cluster is fully upgraded.
On the replica, during rolling upgrade, if a modification comes to a node that knows how to handle sync barriers, then it will fail (and will be replicated again later via bootstrapping / catchup), if a modification comes to a node that doesn’t know how to handle sync barriers, the sync barrier won’t be respected.  In our specific deployment, we enforce that PC is always newer than any PE that is registered to it, so for that PE->PC replication, we should never have a case when PE issues a sync barrier to a PC that doesn’t know how to handle it.

[IDF Design Documents | IDF Sync Barrier]

Implement new sync_barrier flag in all IDF RPCs and cpdb_impl.py - 1 day
Implement new NodeGetSyncBarrierInfo RPC and call it on master for entities with sync_barrier=true - 2 days
Implement updating ranges on partial success - 5 days
Implement new NodeSyncBarrierWait long poll RPC - 10 days
Implement priority_queue and barrier checking logic - 5 days
Implement reverse order of bootstrapping chunking - 5 days
Implement batching of sync barrier requests on IDF master - 3 days
Miscellaneous - 5 days

Design Doc: Multihop IDF Sync – Detailed Design

## 1. Overview
The Infrastructure Domain (ID) introduces a new intermediate control layer between PEs and PC, designed to improve scalability. This design specifically focuses on IDF–IDF entity synchronization; metric synchronization will be designed separately. To ensure consistent entity replication across this multi-layer architecture, the existing single-hop IDF–IDF sync framework must evolve into a multi-hop (cascading) sync model.
Today, IDF–IDF sync supports only direct source–replica pairs (e.g., PE ↔ PC). However, the new architecture introduces PE ↔ ID ↔ PC chaining, where each hop acts both as a replica (to its upstream) and a source (to its downstream).
This enhancement guarantees near real-time, eventually consistent replication of entity data across multiple layers, even during transient failures, while maintaining sync-barrier semantics and ordering guarantees at every hop.

## High-level Data Flow
PE ↔ ID ↔ PC is the only valid sync path (no direct PE ↔ PC sync when ID is present).
PC → ID → PE reverse sync will follow the same route (always via ID).
Each hop (PE→ID, ID→PC) acts as an independent replication boundary, ensuring localized ordering and failure recovery.

[IDF Design Documents | Infrastructure domain- IDF]
## 4. Dependencies Mercury – Transport layer for bi-directional data sync between PE ↔ ID and ID ↔ PC. Cassandra / ChakrDB – Persistent storage for IDF. Prism (Zookeeper Registration Info in Zookeeper) In the existing PE<->PC registration, the clusters rely on the ClusterExternalState ZK node to determine which cluster trusts which other cluster. When a cluster is unregistered—e.g., during a PE → PC unregistration—the PC uses the PE’s clusterExternalState entry to hide the entities that were previously synced from that PE, and vice-versa. To achieve the same behavior in the ID-based architecture (PE → ID → PC), the trust info needs to be extended across all three layers: A PE must know the ID it is registered to and the PC that the ID is registered to. The PC must know all PEs registered under all IDs connected to that PC. This is required so that: PE can hide PC-synced entities when an ID gets unregistered from PC. PC can hide PE-synced entities when a PE unregisters from an ID that is connected to the PC. This extended visibility and trust propagation ensures that entity cleanup and hiding semantics remain consistent in the new PE–ID–PC infrastructure. Also, as a part of unregistration with the cleanup of trust ZK nodes, we should also be calling an IDF RPC to clear the replication states of the replicas. So let's assume an architecture PE->ID->PC where ID has the missing range of PE and PC has the missing ranges of ID. Now, let's say we unregister PE from ID as a part of

## 5. Arithmos Sync Integration Context: Arithmos is a time-series database responsible for storing all time-series metrics on PE, along with a small amount of configuration data (e.g., cluster, disk, container, etc.). These entities are synced to PC IDF via Arithmos sync. With the introduction of the intermediate ID layer between PE and PC, Arithmos sync must now support syncing data to both ID and PC. As IDF currently does not support metric (time-series) data sync, we cannot yet establish a fully cascading model where both config and metric data flow through IDF. Two approaches are being considered: Approach 1: Dual Arithmos Sync (PE → ID and PE → PC) Pros: Simpler implementation with minimal code changes. Cons: Once IDF metric sync is introduced, migration and cleanup will be required to consolidate data under the cascading model (PE → ID → PC). Approach 2: Split Responsibility Sync Design: PE → ID Arithmos sync will handle both config and time-series data. PE → PC Arithmos sync handles only time-series data, while config data flows from ID → PC via IDF sync. Pros: No migration or cleanup will be required once IDF metric sync is supported; we can simply stop sending metric data directly from PE to PC. Cons: In the current Arithmos architecture, entities synced from PE to PC are created as local entities on PC, allowing direct client updates (e.g., cluster entity updates via Zeus sync). If config data starts syncing via ID → PC through IDF, those entities become replicated

[IDF Design Documents | Infrastructure domain- IDF]
PC are created as local entities on PC, allowing direct client updates (e.g., cluster entity updates via Zeus sync). If config data starts syncing via ID → PC through IDF, those entities become replicated (read-only) on PC, causing client write operations to fail. Proposed Solution: We will go ahead with Approach 1 for Kronos. Arithmos data from PE will be synced directly to ID and PC separately. Note: There will be no support for Metric Sync in IDF in Kronos, i.e., Metric Data from ID can’t sync to PC and vice-versa)

## 6. PC Backup and Restore
PCBR is an admin-driven workflow in which the admin has direct visibility into the PEs. Because of this direct relationship, the PCBR workflow remains unchanged even after ID is introduced into the architecture.
PCBR data can continue to sync directly to the PEs, as this is required to support direct PC recovery. Introducing ID into the data path is not necessary for the current recovery model.
If, in the future, PC recovery via ID is required, we can extend the design to support cascade replication through ID.

## 7. Summary
Multi-hop IDF Sync introduces a cascading data replication model.
Sync always flows via ID.
Ensures consistent, scalable, and fault-tolerant propagation of entity data across the infrastructure hierarchy.
PC Backup and Restore will continue to happen to and from PE.

Support for cascading / multihop config sync in IDF. Bi-directional entity sync for PE <-> ID <-> PC.
Support sync from ID to Flow-SMSP
Continue supporting sync barrier semantics across hops.
Within ID, all IDF features, including metrics, will be supported.
However, metric sync from ID to PC is not part of v1 because there are currently no requirements.

PE will directly sync Arithmos data to both ID and PC.
Refer this for more information

## Table
Guarantee | Description
Eventual Consistency | All entities will converge to the same final state across hops.
Sync Barrier | Sync barrier guarantees will be extended to cover both replicated entities and local entities that are scheduled to sync to the next hop
Cascading Propagation | Each hop only syncs to its direct upstream/downstream, ensuring consistent and isolated replication boundaries.
Backward Compatibility | Legacy single-hop schema remains supported alongside the new cascading schema.

[IDF Design Documents | Insights Proxy Leader only solution]
Insights Proxy Leader only solution. Insights proxy maintains an in memory state of entity IDs (per PE cluster) for which it has received updates from the gateway. For instance, if at time T1 it received updates for VM entities with IDs e1, e2, e3 from PE cluster pe1; and at time T2, it received updates for entities e1 and e2. By computing the difference, proxy infers that VM entity e3 was deleted between T1 & T2 and triggers a DeleteEntity(e3) to IDF on PC. In the scenario discussed above, if at time T1' (T1 < T1' < T2) proxy gets restarted, it should still be able to deduce that e3 got deleted. To achieve this, proxy preloads the non-deleted entity-IDs from insights upon start up. Because proxy is state-aware, it is necessary to support a leader-only solution as a part of IDF scale-out. Otherwise, the updates from Prism Gateway might go to random nodes, each maintaining its own cached ID sets, thus making the updates to IDF incoherent. Eg: in the above scenario, we don't want the first update to do to node1 and the second update to go to node 2 (on which case, the delete of e3 will be missed). This document proposes a leader-only solution for insights proxy where all the RPCs from prism gateway will be forward to the leader instance. Implementation: Insights proxy maintains 2 main classes: InsightsProxyServer and ArithmosRpcSvcImpl. The InsightsProxyServer class provides the functionality to access the zeus config, the ability for a proxy instance to be elected as a leader

The InsightsProxyServer class provides the functionality to access the zeus config, the ability for a proxy instance to be elected as a leader (by calling zeus' VolunteerForLeadership function) and set watches on proxy leadership changes. When a leader has been elected, rest of the proxy instances get notified of the leadership changes. The ArithmosRpcSvcImpl exposes RPCs that PG calls to persist entities and stats. The in-memory states are stored as data members of this class. So, when a leader is elected or when the leadership changes, the proxy server should call into arithmos rpc class to start the bootstrap process to read the entity IDs from IDF. ## Current Architecture Overview
IDF is deployed using Helm Charts. IDF runs in a StatefulSet in scaleout mode with 3 replicas. Each pod runs 3 containers - 1 for insights server and 2 for insights uploaders.

## Running proxy and receiver in the same pod as server and uploader
Pros:
Affinity for uploader and server will be maintained
Lower operational complexity with fewer pods to manage
Reduced network latency between tightly coupled components
Simplified networking - all components can communicate via localhost
Cons:
A liveness probe in any of the containers would lead to restart of the whole pod
Issues can be caused in scheduling due to high resource requests from a single pod
Difficult to scale individual components independently

## Server and uploader run in a single pod. Proxy and receiver run in another pod with only 1 replica.
Pros:
Proxy and server can run with different numbers of replicas
Better fault isolation between server and data transfer services
Cons:
Insights proxy can run into scale issues
Network overhead for inter-pod communication
Single point of failure for proxy functionality

[IDF Design Documents | Insights Proxy in SMSP]
## 1 statefulset for insights server. 1 pod for Insights Data Transfer Service (runs uploader, insights proxy, insights receiver)
Pros:
Clear separation of concerns between data processing and transfer
Easier to apply different resource limits and requests
Cons:
Insights data transfer service can run into scale issues
Insights data transfer service could become a bottleneck for sync pipeline
More complex networking configuration required

## Proposed Architecture
Insights server runs in a StatefulSet. Insights data transfer service (uploader and insights proxy) run in a single pod with only 1 replica. Insights receiver logic will be integrated in the insights server.

## Current Configuration Management
Currently our helm charts have boolean fields isSMSPToPCSyncEnabled and isSMSPToPESyncEnabled for enabling PC uploader and PC uploader respectively.

## Adding similar booleans for enabling insights proxy and further instances of uploaders. Clients set all the booleans in their umbrella charts.
Pros:
Simple and straightforward configuration approach
Granular control over individual component enablement
Backward compatible with existing deployment patterns
Cons:
Umbrella charts need to set too many variables
Need to add different booleans when more uploaders need to be enabled

[IDF Design Documents | Insights Proxy in SMSP]
## Adding similar booleans for enabling insights proxy and further instances of uploaders. A mapping is maintained for the number of uploaders to be enabled and proxy status based on deployment type. Clients only pass the type of deployment in the umbrella chart.
Pros:
Umbrella charts do not need to set all variables. Only a single variable sets other boolean variables
Reduces configuration complexity for end users
Enforces consistent deployment patterns across environments
Easier to maintain standard configurations
Cons:
New mapping needs to be added for new environments
Less flexibility for custom deployment scenarios
Requires maintaining mapping logic and documentation

## Taking a list of uploaders from the client which provides the target  host and port. The number of uploaders and target is decided based on the list. Proxy is enabled based on a boolean.
Pros:
Scalable solution for onboarding new clients
Future-proof design that can accommodate new environments
Reduces need for code changes when adding new targets
Cons:
Implementation can be tricky
Potential for misconfiguration with complex list structures
Validation complexity increases with flexible configuration

## Current Containerization Strategy
We have 2 docker images - 1 for insights server, 1 for insights uploader.

[IDF Design Documents | Insights Proxy in SMSP]
## Keeping a single image with 2 binaries - insights proxy and insights uploader.
Pros:
Easy to maintain as there is only 1 image
Keeps the overall package size light
Reduced registry storage requirements
Cons:
Unused binaries will be packaged for scenarios where only 1 of them is required

## Different images for insights proxy and insights server
Pros:
Separate images for separate binaries
Only required binaries will be packaged
Cons:
2 images will be packaged
Overhead of maintaining 2 different images

## Proposed Containerization Strategy
Keeping a single image with 2 binaries - insights proxy and insights uploader. Managing a single image is easier. The unused binaries add only a few MB’s in an image whose size is around 1.5 - 2 GB. So this approach is a clear winner among the two.
Summary:
1. We will be running Proxy in a different pod (with or without receiver depending on if we can merge receiver into server in janus timeline)
2. Uploader will be running in same pod as that of server as a different container
3. We will be running 2 uploader containers, one for ID->PC and other for ID->PE

## Config Files required for insights proxy
Files from the data_sender directory will be copied to the container.
Arithmos_entity_operation.proto will be mounted from configmap. This keeps it modifiable.

## Metric sync: is_replicated flag is not effective
Peng Huang
November 2019

[IDF Design Documents | Metric sync_ is_replicated flag is not effective]
## Background When syncing metric data from PE to PC, proxy will send the payload with is_replicated set to true. When the store layer sees the is_replicated flag, when creating the metric data cache object, it will use the kLast as the downsample operator, overwriting the one from the schema (metric type). This is assuming that one metric type (of a specific entity type) should only have one source (either generated locally, or replicated remotely, not mixed). And replicating metric data is not always idempotent, thus we need to use the kLast ds operator. This is working fine if there is no data of the metric existing in cache (i.e. no cache object). However, if the cache object has already been created, with a default downsample operator (from schema), the is_replicated flag will be ignored. This can happen in 2 cases: If the metric data forwarding happens, the forwarding logic will send the data without setting the is_replicated flag. Hence the replicated metric data will be treated as locally generated data, and the cache object created will use the default downsample operator instead of the kLast. Later when new metric data gets replicated, we will run into the issue mentioned above. (https://jira.nutanix.com/browse/ENG-261856) Another case is if the metric data is loaded from Cassandra (e.g. to serve the query), it will use the default schema since there is no way to tell whether the metric data is replicated or not. Later if new metric data comes in for the same metric

For the forwarding, when extracting the dirty metric data from the set, we need to get the ds operator and set the is_replicated if it is kLast.
For the other case, when injecting new metric data, if it is replicated, we need to overwrite the downsample operator of the existing cache object with the kLast.

Have a metric type level field which tells that the metric will be replicated and set that field for all replicated metrics.

Moving Arithmos Sync logic to Uploader
Devendra Singh, Uddhav Mishra
March 2019
Reviewed

## Introduction
In this document, we will discuss the plan for moving Arithmos (PE) to IDF (PC) sync logic to InsightsUploader. We will cover the work required in Arithmos, InsightsProxy, InsightsUploader, and PrismGateway for completion of this task. We will try to cover the implementation details as much as possible.
Let’s start with the existing implementation and working of sync pipeline from Arithmos (PE) to IDF (PC).
Understanding the below diagram,
PrismGateway on PE pulls the entities and stats to be synced to PC, from Arithmos and then forwards them to PrismGateway on PC.
PrismGateway on PC, after performing some validation on timestamps, forwards the sync payload to InsightsProxy on PC.
InsightsProxy on PC does Arithmos to IDF data format conversion and publishes this data (stats and entities) to IDF on PC.
When the PrismGateway on PE gets the response that data has been successfully synced, it updates the timestamps in Zookeeper (for tracking how much we have synced and the same timestamp is used in case of PrismGateway restarts).

[Arithmos & Metric Collection | Moving Arithmos Sync logic to Uploader]
## Proposed design In the existing design, PrismGateway has the logic for pulling the data from Arithmos and then transferring that to PrismGateway on PC side, which then eventually gets stored in IDF on PC. PrismGateway on PC also has some logic related to sync timestamp validations. As part of our new design, we want to move this sync logic out of PrismGateway on both PE and PC. On PE we will move this sync logic from PrismGateway to InsightsUploader whereas, on PC the logic will be moved to InsightsProxy. The benefits of moving this sync logic out of PrismGateway include, we won’t have any direct dependency on PrismGateway and can easily use the upcoming new transport service, Mercury, or as a matter of fact, we can easily make use of any transport service by merely changing some GFlags. Apart from this, we will be able to scale, optimize and add new features in one place for all type of PE to PC sync (Arithmos to IDF, IDF to IDF, etc.), all these motivations are documented here in detail. In this new design, InsightsUploader on PE pulls the data from Arithmos and then transfers that to PC using a transport service (can be PrismGateway, Mercury, etc.). Transport service on PC will forward this sync payload to InsightsProxy, which will do the Arithmos to Insights data format conversion. Finally, the data gets stored into Insights on PC. When InsightsUploader on PE receives the success signal (when sync RPC finishes successfully), it updates the timestamps in zookeeper

[Arithmos & Metric Collection | Moving Arithmos Sync logic to Uploader]
Arithmos to Insights data format conversion. Finally, the data gets stored into Insights on PC. When InsightsUploader on PE receives the success signal (when sync RPC finishes successfully), it updates the timestamps in zookeeper (these timestamps are used when InsightsUploader restarts).

## Implementation
In the first version (V1), we will port the code for Arithmos sync from Prismgateway [Java] to InsightsUploader [C++] as it is and then in the next versions (V2 and later), we will add support for extra functionalities like black-listing of stats, pagination in current sync, moving PC side logic from PrismGateway to InsightsProxy, etc.

[Arithmos & Metric Collection | Moving Arithmos Sync logic to Uploader]
## Prism Gateway
In the current implementation, PrismGateway has two separate dedicated threads for Arithmos sync, one for HistoricalDataSync and one for current data sync. HistoricalData sync gets triggered when the PC-PE registration happens for the first time or when the sync delay between PC and PE increases more than 3 hrs (maybe because of network failures or any other errors) and HistoricalSync only syncs the historical stats ([current_time - 90 days, current_time - 3hrs]). On the other hand, current sync is responsible for syncing the current stats, it periodically queries from Arithmos (for all the entities of all the entity types, with some exceptions) and syncs the data to PC.

## 1) Support for Blacklisting stats
As of now we only allow for stats to be whitelisted, this puts an extra limitation that if we want to stop sync for a couple of stats then we will have to list all the remaining ones and keep adding all the newly coming stats to this list and it gets very tricky if we have dynamically registered stats. If we provide blacklisting support then we don’t have to keep a list of all remaining stats, we can simply ignore the stats which are blacklisted and in this way we can handle dynamically registered stats better.

[Arithmos & Metric Collection | Moving Arithmos Sync logic to Uploader]
## 2) Pagination support for Current Arithmos sync
Currently, the current sync tries to sync all the stats in one single RPC for current sync. If there are many entities then this RPC payload might get very high and can cause issues.
For supporting pagination in current sync we might have to make changes in Arithmos RPC (cursor support for GetInMemoryTimeRangeStatsForEntitiesRequest RPC) and also in the way we use sync timestamps today (single timestamp for all the entity types). Currently, PrismGateway has a hard limit of only syncing upto 5000 entities of an entity type, with pagination we can remove this limitation completely and sync as many entities as we have in the system.

[Arithmos & Metric Collection | Moving Arithmos Sync logic to Uploader]
## 3) Stop sending complete entity id list in every sync request
As per current implementation, we sync the current state of each entity from PE to PC, the only way of figuring out the deleted entities on PC is via tracking the previously existing entities and compare that with the current set of active entities. So, in each sync request, be it from current sync or historical sync flow, we send the list of all active entities. InsightsProxy uses this list of active entities from each request and decides which entities are stale and deletes them from Insights.
Instead of sending this list of active entities in each and every sync request, we can send this list periodically and set a flag in sync request while sending it and this flag can be used by InsightsProxy to figure out when to take the diff with existing entities and delete the stale entities. This will require changes in both sender’s (InsightsUploader on PE) as well as the receiver's side (InsightsProxy on PC). This will also help us in the efficient implementation of above-mentioned enhancement (pagination support for current sync).

Multihop IDF Sync
Devendra, Gaurav
Sept 2025
[In-progress]

## Overview
The IDF-IDF sync workflow is responsible for near-real-time entity data replication from a source to its replicas, following async replication and the eventual consistency model. (for example, sync VM entities to PC from all the registered PEs). Currently, IDF-IDF sync does not support syncing stats/metrics data; however, we have Arithmos - IDF sync for this purpose.
Some highlights of IDF-IDF sync:
Near real-time replication: If all the IDF services are running fine, we expect the entity updated on the source to sync in almost real-time to the destination.
Eventual consistency: Although the time of replication could vary (on the underlying infra), the latest state of the entity would be synced from source to destination.
Catch up on failures: If the replication to the replica fails due to some failure(connection/transport failure), IDF sync catches up on those failures and tries to make the replica side the same as the source.
IDF-IDF sync overview doc

[IDF Design Documents | Multihop IDF Sync]
## Problem Statement
The current IDF–IDF sync framework supports only direct, single-hop replication between source and replica clusters (e.g., PE ↔ PC). This model does not accommodate the evolving requirements of the Infrastructure Domain (ID), which introduces an intermediate layer between PEs and PCs.
To support this architecture, IDF–IDF sync must evolve into a multi-hop (cascading) sync model, where entity updates flow seamlessly across PE ↔ ID ↔ PC. Without this capability, data consistency cannot be guaranteed across all layers of the infrastructure hierarchy.

Current Architecture For ID(Zagreus):

[IDF Design Documents | Multihop IDF Sync]
## Solution To support multi-hop (cascading) IDF–IDF sync, the framework must evolve beyond single-hop replication and introduce sync-barrier semantics at every hop. This ensures both: Local entities created at a hop, and Synced entities received from the previous hop follow strict ordering guarantees when propagating to the next hop. Cascading Sync Model In a cascading replication setup, each IDF only communicates with its immediate upstream and downstream neighbors. No hop can directly sync entities to non-neighboring members (e.g., PE cannot directly sync to PC in a PE → ID → PC chain). Sync-Barrier Semantics Across Hops In the current single-hop model, if an entity update E3 is marked as a sync-barrier, the framework guarantees that all prior updates (E1, E2) are replicated before forwarding E3. However, in multi-hop sync workflows (e.g., PE → ID → PC), this guarantee breaks down. Example: On PE: E1, E2 are created, followed by E3 (a sync-barrier). The sync barrier framework ensures E1 and E2 are replicated to ID before E3. But if ID creates another sync-barrier entity E4, the current sync barrier framework does not guarantee that E3 reaches PC before E4. Required Enhancement To achieve correct sync barrier ordering at every hop: Restamp Sync-Barrier Timestamps When a synced entity arrives at an intermediate hop (e.g., ID), its sync-barrier timestamp must be restamped with the local hop’s barrier timestamp. This ensures downstream hops evaluate barrier ordering using the

[IDF Design Documents | Multihop IDF Sync]
## Introduction of new uploader modes
Currently, the uploader mode determines the default sync pairs if both enable_replication_from and enable_replication_to are not specified in the RCL (Replication Control List). To support the new Infrastructure Domain, we need to introduce a new uploader mode for ID, extending this behavior to handle PE↔ID and ID↔PC sync flows.

The newly added metadata fields represent the following: replication_chain_uuids Stores the list of cluster UUIDs through which the entity has been replicated. Example: At C1: [] At C2: [ "U1" ] At C4: [ "U1", "U2", "U3" ] replication_chain_cluster_types Stores the cluster types corresponding to the replication chain. [IDF Design Documents | Multihop IDF Sync]
## Entity transformations for multihop IDF-IDF sync Let’s consider a multi-hop sync path: PE → ID → PC Step-by-Step Explanation At PE (uuid1): Entity Creation When the entity is first created on PE, i.e, it's a local entity, master_cluster_uuid is kept empty. PE stamps its local db_modified_timestamp (t1) and sync barrier info (s1). No replication history exists yet, so replication chain lists are empty. Replica fields are also empty because PE is not a replica—it’s the source. At ID (uuid2): First Sync Hop (PE → ID) Once the entity reaches ID, we mark PE as the original owner. This means master_cluster_uuid = uuid1. ID carries forward PE’s values for db_modified_timestamp (t1) and sync_barrier_info (s1). ID then updates the replication history by adding PE’s UUID to replication_chain_uuids and PE’s type to replication_chain_cluster_types. ID stamps its own local values in the replica fields: replica_db_modified_timestamp_usecs = t2 and replica_sync_barrier_info = s2. At PC (uuid3): Second Sync Hop (ID → PC) When ID forwards the entity to PC, the following happens: Promotion of replica fields: The replica values from ID (t2 and s2) are promoted into the main entity fields. So, db_modified_timestamp becomes t2. sync_barrier_info becomes s2. The master_cluster_uuid still points to PE (uuid1) because the master cluster of the entity (by definition, means where the entity was created) PC now extends the replication chain: it adds IDs, UUID, and cluster type to the lists. Finally,

[IDF Design Documents | Multihop IDF Sync]
PE (uuid1) because the master cluster of the entity (by definition, means where the entity was created) PC now extends the replication chain: it adds IDs, UUID, and cluster type to the lists. Finally, PC stamps its own replica values: replica_db_modified_timestamp_usecs = t3 and replica_sync_barrier_info = s3. Extension to further hops This transformation persists even when more clusters are added. For example, if we add NC after PC, the replication path becomes: PE → ID → PC → NC At each hop, the chain metadata grows, and the new replica fields are updated with the local cluster’s values.

[IDF Design Documents | Multihop IDF Sync]

Current schema  for enabling IDF sync:
To support multi-hop sync, we need the schema to represent a full replication path (with ordered From → To hops) in a single block.

## Adding support for missing ranges for chakrdb as an IDF-backed store
Since ID will run in the SMSP environment, we need to add support for handling missing ranges in IDF, backed by ChakrDB. This will allow the ID’s IDF to function as a replica, by persisting the missing ranges from the source into ChakrDB.

[IDF Design Documents | Multihop IDF Sync]
## Active Entities Workflow The Active Entities Workflow ensures that replicas don’t keep stale entities when sync is down. If the connection between the source and replica breaks, and an entity is deleted from the source (and purged from its backend database), the replica won’t be aware of the deletion and will continue to retain the entity once sync resumes. To handle this, the source periodically sends a list of all active entities to the replica. The replica compares this list against its own data and removes any entities that no longer exist on the source. This check also happens automatically whenever the replica hasn’t received an update for a set amount of time. Currently, the workflow only sends the list of local (source master) entities. But with the introduction of the Infrastructure Domain (ID) and multi-hop IDF sync, we also need to include the synced entities (not just the local ones) in the active entities list at every hop. For example, consider a sync path PE → ID → PC and ID->PC Entities e1 and e2 are created on PE and synced to ID, and then from ID to PC. Entity e3 is created on ID and synced to PC. Now, if the connection between ID and PC breaks: Suppose e1 is deleted from PE. The deletion syncs to ID, and e1 is purged from both PE and ID. When the connection between ID and PC resumes, ID must send its active entities list, which includes both local entities (like e3) and entities that flowed through ID as a hop (like e2). PC compares its own entities with

[IDF Design Documents | Multihop IDF Sync]
and PC resumes, ID must send its active entities list, which includes both local entities (like e3) and entities that flowed through ID as a hop (like e2). PC compares its own entities with this list, detects that e1 is missing, and deletes e1 as well.

[IDF Design Documents | Multihop IDF Sync]
## LoadEntityTrail RPC Changes:
In the bootstrap/catch-up workflow, IDF uses this RPC to load entities from the backend DB to fulfill the missing ranges requested by a replica. At present, this RPC only loads local entities and sends them to the replica to address its missing ranges.
With the introduction of multi-hop/cascading IDF sync, each hop must now load not only its local entities but also the synced entities that are marked for propagation to the next hop. These entities should be included in the LoadEntityTrailRPC and forwarded to the next hop so that it can fill the missing ranges corresponding to its immediate upstream hop.
Important: For creating the missing ranges on a replica, we always use the UUID of the previous hop.
Example: Sync pipeline PE → ID → PC
On ID, the missing ranges are created for PE.
On PC, the missing ranges are created for ID (not PE), i.e., always the hop just before the current one.
Now, let’s assume entities are syncing from PE → ID → PC, and in addition, local entities on ID are also syncing to PC. If there is a connectivity issue between ID and PC, once the sync resumes, PC will request the missing ranges for ID.
To fulfill this request, ID must send:
Its local entities, and
The entities received from PE are marked to be synced to PC.
This ensures that the PC can update the missing ranges for ID correctly.

[IDF Design Documents | Multihop IDF Sync]

## Cluster unregistration/registration
When an ID is registered to PE and PC, IDF sync requires a trigger to detect the newly registered cluster. To support this, the following ZK node info is required per cluster:
On PE:
Zk nodes for directly connected PCs
Zk nodes for directly connected IDs, including some marker indicating which PC each ID is registered with
On ID:
Zk nodes for directly connected PEs
Zk nodes for directly connected PCs
On PC:
Zk nodes for directly connected PEs
Zk nodes for directly connected IDs, including some marker indicating which PE each ID is registered with
TBD: TO discuss with the Prism team on trust zookeeper node structure and lifecycle.

NOTE: PC should be aware of all the registered IDs as well as all the PEs registered to those IDs.

[IDF Design Documents | Multihop IDF Sync]
## Brownfield Scenarios
Consider the following scenario: initially, PE1 was directly registered with PC, and Arithmos config data was synced from PE1 to PC1 via the Arithmos-IDF sync. During this flow, Insights Proxy creates local entities (for example: e1) in PC1 IDF. With the introduction of ID1, the sync flow changes to PE1->ID1 via the Arithmos-IDF sync, followed by ID1->PC1 via the IDF-IDF sync. In this model, Insights Proxy creates e1 as a local entity in ID1, which is then synced to PC1 as a replicated entity.
An entity that already exists as a local entity in PC1 cannot be converted into a replicated entity; therefore, we need to have some cleanup mechanism to delete entities that were previously synced directly from PE1 to PC1 via Arithmos-IDF sync.
When an ID is unregistered and removed from the topology, PE and PC become directly connected again, and IDF–IDF config sync resumes directly from PE to PC. In this transition, the replication ranges associated with PE1 must be cleared from PC1.
Without this cleanup, entities that are local to PE1 and were previously replicated via ID (for example, e1) may not be modified after ID removal. As a result, the corresponding entities on PC1 would continue to retain replication-specific metadata (such as replication_chain_uuids, replication_chain_cluster_types, etc.), which is no longer valid in a direct PE → PC sync model.

[IDF Design Documents | Multihop IDF Sync]

We need to define whether a PE can migrate from one ID to another, and if so, what restrictions or validation rules will apply.
How will brownfield migration work?
In cases where an existing PE was already registered to a PC, and now the model changes such that the PE is registered to an ID, and the ID in turn is registered to the PC, does IDF need to perform any additional cleanup or migration steps to maintain consistency?
How will we handle entity schema modifications when ID is introduced?
For static configurations, we might modify the schema to convert the current RCL structure into CRLC. However, we need to determine an appropriate approach for dynamic schema changes.
What will be the exact cluster type for ID?
Clear replication states as part of unregistration?

## Adding the Sharding logic in InsightsProxy [Sumit]
Arithmos and IDF uses different attributes for entity IDs so InsightsProxy has to keep a mapping from Arithmos Entity ID to Insights Entity ID for handling the delta updates coming from Arithmos sync and that delta update might not have the attribute required for building the Insights Entity ID. Today only proxy leader maintains this Entity ID mapping and all the requests which makes use of this map has to go through InsightsProxy Leader node.
To remove this hard dependency of every request (which needs entity mapping) going through InsightsProxy leader we can shard the requests coming from PEs on the basis of Cluster Uuid and then every InsightsProxy Instance will generate the Entity ID map for Clusters it serves, By this approach we expect a uniform distribution of requests / metadata on InsightsProxy instances and avoiding the scenario of overloading Leader instance.
This sharding logic will be very similar to how we implement sharding in IDF today and if a Proxy instance receives a request for some Cluster Uuid which is not owned by it then it will forward that to corresponding shard owner.

## Uniformly Distribute the requests coming from registered PEs to the PC in the 30 secs interval. To avoid the problem of all PEs sending data to PC at the same time and causing CPU and Memory spikes on PC at that particular moment. We plan to distribute the requests (Arithmos current sync requests) coming from various PEs across a 30 secs interval so that PCs do not get data in spikes. Devendra, Sumit
Oct 2024

[IDF Design Documents | PC-PC IDF Synchronization]
## Overview IDF is our internal key-value store implementation that stores NOS/AOS management data on PC (Prism Central) and PE (Prism Element). IDF has the native capability of supporting replication across multiple IDF clusters. Below mentioned are the high-level guarantees provided by IDF-IDF synchronization:- IDF-IDF replication is Asynchronous in nature and provides eventual consistency. IDF-IDF replication depends on the Transport layer (Mercury) for secure and authenticated data transfer between source and destination. Entities replicated by IDF-IDF sync are Read-only on destination. IDF-IDF sync only supports replication of Entity Data and not time-series data. IDF-IDF sync design is highly scalable and can easily handle replication of millions of entities. An Entity Type in IDF can contain Replicated as well as Local entities. On a cluster unregistration, IDF removes all the entities replicated from that source cluster and these entities won’t be accessible anymore. In this unregistration workflow, entity delete watches won’t be provided, this behavior is for handling scale of entities and firing millions of watches in a minute might kill most of the services hence we have an option to just receive a Reset on the WatchClient in such cluster register/unregister workflows. IDF-IDF sync can be configured at EntityType level by providing the Source Cluster type. For example:- below schema means that Entities of type “entity_type” will replicate from kNDFS cluster to

[IDF Design Documents | PC-PC IDF Synchronization]
such cluster register/unregister workflows. IDF-IDF sync can be configured at EntityType level by providing the Source Cluster type. For example:- below schema means that Entities of type “entity_type” will replicate from kNDFS cluster to endpoints connected with it. entity_type_info_list { entity_type_name : "entity_type" type_info { suppress_replication : false replication_control_list { enable_replication_from : kNDFS } } } 

## Problem Statement
IDF can fundamentally support replication between any two IDF clusters but currently, the replication is enabled for below mentioned paths only:-
PE (from kNDFS) to PC
PC (from kMulticluster) to PE
FSVM (from kMinerva) to PC
Today, 2 PCs can be paired with each other using AZ pairing workflow and multiple components have a use case of replicating data across PCs that are paired by AZ pairing workflow. We need to configure and enable IDF synchronization across PCs also.
<TODO> :- Discuss with PC, DR team on how to detect paired PCs uuid. Either some ZK node or IDF entity.

[IDF Design Documents | PC-PC IDF Synchronization]
## Solution As per current schema definition, sync can be configured at EntityType level based on source cluster type only (using field `enable_replication_from`). This schema works for current use-cases because of the assumption that every cluster will have to replicate to a single type of cluster only, for example: PC will only replicate to PE, PE will only replicate to PC, FSVM will only replicate to PC, etc. With the use case of PC to PC sync (where PCs are paired using AZ pairing), now a PC has to replicate to two types of target clusters (registered PE and paired PC). To support this, IDF schema needs to evolve to support `enable_replication_to` as well at EntityType definition level so that every EntityType can be configured to be replicated to all the needed target cluster types. New Schema for Replicating an EntityType to paired PC only will look like:- entity_type_info_list { entity_type_name : "entity_type" type_info { suppress_replication : false // Rule for replicating from PC to PC replication_control_list { enable_replication_from : kMulticluster enable_replication_to : kMulticluster } } }  For Replicating an EntityType from PC to PE as well as paired PC:- entity_type_info_list { entity_type_name : "entity_type" type_info { suppress_replication : false // Rule for replicating from PC to PC replication_control_list { enable_replication_from : kMulticluster enable_replication_to : kMulticluster } // Rule for replicating from PC to PE replication_control_list {

[IDF Design Documents | PC-PC IDF Synchronization]
: "entity_type" type_info { suppress_replication : false // Rule for replicating from PC to PC replication_control_list { enable_replication_from : kMulticluster enable_replication_to : kMulticluster } // Rule for replicating from PC to PE replication_control_list { enable_replication_from : kMulticluster enable_replication_to : kNDFS } } } 

## Schema Backward Compatibility
We need to define and honor the schema in such a way that we can maintain backward compatibility. For the existing schema only the field `enable_replication_from` will be specified and `enable_replication_to` might or might not be present.
For backward compatibility wherever `enable_replication_to` is not present, we can treat default targets as below:-
PC as default target where only `enable_replication_from : kNDFS` is present
PE as default target where only `enable_replication_from : kMulticluster` is present
PC as default target where only `enable_replication_from : kMinerva` is present
TBD, the default target for enable_replication_from: kXiVM
TBD, the default target for enable_replication_from : kAGSCluster
TBD, the default target for enable_replication_from : kIAMCluster

## PC version compatibility
All the AZ paired PCs need to be at least on the version that supports PC-PC IDF sync.

[IDF Design Documents | PC-PC IDF Synchronization]
## Rolling Upgrades
During PC upgrade from non-supported version to supported version of this feature, the sync to other PCs should only be expected after all the PC nodes have been upgraded. Since we are adding a new schema we will need all the IDF instances (running on all PC nodes) to be upgraded for honoring all the sync guarantees.

## PCBR Impact
Currently, after recovery of the PC, Adonis clears replication ranges from registered PEs so that future sync from PC to PE does not encounter any issues (even when there are time jump scenarios). We will need to work with Adonis team to also clear replication ranges from PCs paired with this PC to handle all the scenarios.

## Guarantees when schema mismatch between paired PCs
For PC-PC synchronization, we will keep the guarantees similar to existing PE→PC and PC→PE IDF-IDF sync.
EntityType needs to be registered on both source and target for replication to happen.
Normal attributes (non-nested) will automatically get registered on the target PC, if not registered.
For nested attributes, the schema of the target PC will apply and unregistered attributes will not get auto-registered on the target PC.
When replication is enabled for an existing EntityType, IDF will replicate all the changes (CUD) in the table after replication is enabled. Entities which exist from the time when replication was not enabled, will only replicate if the entity gets modified after replication was enabled.

Extend IDF entity type registration schema to support `enable_replication_to` rule at per entity type level. Internally build and honor the default replication target based on cluster type in cases when `enable_replication_to` is not present.

LoadEntityTrail RPC is used for bootstrap and filling missing time ranges, in this workflow we will have to add logic to filter the entities scanned from DB based on replication rules configured at the corresponding EntityType level. (Done)
Similarly, we will have to filter the entities in LoadActiveEntitiesInfo as well. (Done)

[IDF Design Documents | PC-PC IDF Synchronization]
## Insights Uploader Changes
Introduce a new mode in InsightsUploader to forward the IDF-IDF sync data via Mercury to all the available PC endpoints. This new mode needs to be enabled only on PC. (Done)
Endpoint Detection. Similar to IDF, InsightsUploader will also need to detect the addition/removal of PC endpoints and start/stop various sync workflows for those endpoints. We can use the existing ZK nodes used for PC-PC AZ pairing or rely if they exist. (Done)
Pass/relay the upload mode info to InsightsServer in LoadEntityTrail and LoadActiveEntitiesInfo to only send data meant for PC-PC IDF sync. (Done)

## NCC Check Changes
Currently, we have a NCC check to track the status of IDF sync and raise Alerts when sync is stuck for a long duration. Check name is idf_db_to_db_sync_heartbeat_status_check. This check runs on replica and tracks last sync request received timestamp.
We will need to enhance this NCC check to also monitor sync from paired PCs and show similar Alerts on failures.

## Prevent Entities Deletes From PC IDF Incase Arithmos Is Down
ENG-412294
Devendra, Gaurav, Sumit
October 2021 [in-progress]

## Problem Statement:
Currently, if Arithmos is down on any of the nodes then entities owned by the Arithmos agent on that particular node are not synced from PE to PC. This behavior results in InsightsProxy (on PC) deleting the entities owned by Arithmos on that particular PE node from PC IDF.
Below mentioned are a couple of scenarios where this behavior is observed:
When a node goes down during upgrades then its relevant entities are deleted from the PC and as soon as the node comes up its relevant entities start reflecting on the PC.
Suppose a category is defined for a particular node entity on PC and due to the Arithmos instance going down on a node its relevant node entity will be deleted from PC and via categories cleanup logic any category defined on that particular node entity will be deleted. Though the node entity will come back on PC once the Arithmos instance comes up on that node since Category is a user-created workflow it won’t be restored.

[Arithmos & Metric Collection | Prevent Entities Deletes From PC IDF Incase Arithmos Is Down]
## Background:
Arithmos sync from PE to PC is a periodic workflow (where InsightsUploader on PE queries data to be synced from Arithmos master), as sync is periodic and we only get the current entities available in Arithmos, so we have to explicitly identify the deletes happening in Arithmos and sync them to PC.
For every sync call Arithmos master collects all sync related data from healthy Arithmos Agent(i.e ignores Agents which are down) as well as its own entities. InsightsProxy on PC receives the sync request and processes all the entity updates i.e attributes as well as the stats.
For identifying deletes happening in Arithmos, InsightsProxy on PC maintains an in-memory map(created at the Proxy startup time) of all the entity ids that were synced from Arithmos to  PC IDF. Entities to be deleted are figured out by taking the set difference of entities which were synced earlier (present in in-memory map) and incoming entity list in sync request. If some Arithmos agent on PE is not healthy then InsightsProxy won’t receive entities owned by that agent in sync request and will trigger a delete for those entities from IDF as well.

[Arithmos & Metric Collection | Prevent Entities Deletes From PC IDF Incase Arithmos Is Down]
## Approach 1:
Whenever one/more Arithmos instances goes down Arithmos master will notify InsightsProxy via a flag that the data synced from PE to PC is incomplete and hence Proxy will not initiate the delete workflow for that sync request. All the entities and stats will be synced as usual. Once all the Arithmos instances come up InsightsProxy can initiate the deletes of the entities from the PC on receiving subsequent sync calls.
PROS:
Easy to implement as this will only require a flag to be set from InsightsUploader side on PE in case of Arithmos instance down which will be used by Proxy on PC to avoid entity deletes.
CONS:
If one or more Arithmos instances are down in a PE any delete operation on Arithmos Agent owned entities will not be reflected on PC (however creates and updates will keep working as expected) till all the Arithmos instances come back to a healthy state. Hence stale data(in case of delete operations) can be present on PC till all the Arithmos instances are healthy. Since arithmos deletes itself are rare and chances of deletes in conjunction with node down is pretty rare so we should be good in most of the scenarios unless some service has a strict requirement for it.
Note: With this approach only agent entities deletes will will preventedin PC IDF.

[Arithmos & Metric Collection | Prevent Entities Deletes From PC IDF Incase Arithmos Is Down]
## Approach 2:
We can construct a mapping of entities owned by each Arithmos Agent by modifying the MASTER_GET_IN_MEMORY_TIME_RANGE_STATS_FOR_ENTITIES_NAME RPC which can add a Arithmos Agent identifier to all entities and forward that to uploader and eventually to InsightsProxy on PC. We will also be sending the identifier(node ip or uuid) for all the nodes in the cluster with the Arithmos Sync RPC which will help us to handle node removal scenarios. Proxy on init can create a grouping of entities in IDF on the basis of per Cluster per Node. On receiving sync requests Proxy can check for the entity  in all the node groups for that cluster (Note: This is done to handle entities movement from one node to other) and if entity is not found in any of the node mapping it can initiate deletes for those entities only.
PROS:
Handles all the scenarios related to entity deletion correctly with no stale data.
CONS:
Major changes in the Arithmos sync pipeline as we have to pass the entity to Arithmos instance mapping from Arithmos to InsightsUploader to InsightsProxy on PC.
Complex logic in InsightsProxy on PC to handle different versions of registered PEs.
Difficult to handle duplicate entities across Arithmos agents in the same cluster.

Purging off Hidden entities on replica after Cluster Unregistration. Jineet Desai Feb 2022 Problem Statement Currently, whenever unregistration takes place, we hide the entities synced from the source cluster(only the IDF-IDF synced entities, this does not apply to Arithmos synced entities) to the replica cluster (i.e. they are completely removed from the insights cache and no operation/queries can be performed on those entities). However these entities still remain in Cassandra of replica and occupy the disk space and impact IDF bootup time as well because we have to scan through all the entities before we skip entities belonging to an unregistered cluster. So we aim to clean up these hidden entities from cassandra on replica once cluster unregistration takes place. Proposed Solution Currently based on the watch on cluster external state zk node on a cluster, we detect the registration/unregistration of a cluster and corresponding to that we maintain the registered_cluster_maps_(PE will contain entry for registered PC and PC would contain entries for all registered PEs). For all entities on replica having a master cluster uuid not present in the registered_cluster_map_, we mark those entities as hidden and remove them from the cache. Along with this, in the callback pertaining to removal of these entities from cache, we can also issue a DeleteReplicationState rpc to erase all the replication info from the replica pertaining to the unregistered source. (So next time the

(So next time the source cluster gets re-registered on this replica, we would re-sync all the entities to the replica.) For purging the entities actually from Cassandra, we can have a periodic process(just like AutoDelete, Purge) running on replica, that will scan all the entities from Cassandra and for all the entities having a master_cluster_uuid that is not present in the registered_cluster_map_(entities from unregistered source cluster), we can remove those entities from Cassandra. Thus this would ensure a periodic cleanup on the replica side. With the approach mentioned above for deleting the cluster replication state on cluster unregistration we may face an issue: Let's say the cluster gets unregistered but due to some issue(node going down for eg.), the DeleteClusterReplicationState RPC for that particular cluster_uuid may fail and it may not end up being deleted from Cassandra. Thus before we delete hidden entities from Cassandra, we need to make sure that we delete the replication state for that particular cluster_uuid. We propose 2 solutions for this: While performing Cassandra scans for deleting hidden entities, we can check if the replication state for a master_cluster_uuid of an entity has been deleted or not. If not, we can issue a DeleteClusterReplicationState RPC

While performing Cassandra scans for deleting hidden entities, we can check if the replication state for a master_cluster_uuid of an entity has been deleted or not. If not, we can issue a DeleteClusterReplicationState RPC for that particular master_cluster_uuid. This would involve Cassandra scan of entities only once. But we would need to wait for the DeleteClusterReplicationState RPC to finish before we proceed ahead with scanning other entities. Second solution would be to scan all the entities, and for master_cluster_uuid of all hidden entities, we delete their replication states from Cassandra. Then we issue scans again on all the entities and delete the hidden entities from Cassandra. Problem with this approach would be that it would increase Cassandra scan ops being issued.

## Taking the approach of doing the scan on entities only once: We can maintain an atomic bool variable(false by default) to track any cluster unregistration or shard load since the previous run of our periodic process. If it remains false till the next run of our periodic process, no need to perform any scans since no unregistration of the cluster or shard load would have taken place. If it turns true then we need to perform scans to delete the replication state of that cluster and delete the hidden entities for the shard that was recently loaded. We should acquire the sync_barrier_ lock(SERIALIZE_SHARD_LOAD_AND_CLUSTER_REG_LOCK_ID) to avoid any cluster registration/shard load while we are deleting the replication state of the cluster. We would also acquire read locks on shards that would prevent any shard migration to happen during our process(since shard migrations need to acquire write lock on shards). While deleting the hidden entities from Cassandra, we would have acquired the read lock for loaded shards. We may need to exit early if Data upgrade is in progress. In this case, we can exit early and release all the locks acquired. We need to keep a flag to determine whether we want to purge backed up entities on PE or

cluster registration. In this case, we can exit early and release all the locks acquired. We need to keep a flag to determine whether we want to purge backed up entities on PE or not(by default lets not purge backed up entities). For each col_done_cb of scans, issue the DeleteReplicationState RPC(from leader_interface_??? [IDF Design Documents | Replication State per Shard]
## Semantic Considerations Currently, we have a logical stream (timestamp oracle, range tracking, bootstrapping) per shard per entity type. This explodes the number of logical streams to be in 10s of 1000s and is only going to grow in the future as the number of entity types grows. To avoid this growth and make the system scale well in the presence of large amount of entity types, the proposal is to keep a logical stream per shard (i.e. all entity types are going to be in one stream). The original decision to make logical stream per entity type had 3 considerations: Control replication settings per entity type. Partition bootstrapping by entity type. Entity trail. The current semantics of suppress replication is similar to breaking a connection for a stream: if entity type replication is suppressed, then replication doesn't happen, but if it's turned back on, then all changes that happened while the replication was suppressed will get replicated. This happens because the replication range tracking happens per-entity type so that replica knows which changes are not replicated. So enabling replication for an entity type will get this entity type in sync. With stream-per-shard, replication range tracking is going to be done for all types together, so if an entity type replication was suppressed at time T1 and re-enabled at time T2, the changes between T1 and T2 may not get picked up because they may be already accounted for by replication of entities of other types. So enabling

[IDF Design Documents | Replication State per Shard]
time T1 and re-enabled at time T2, the changes between T1 and T2 may not get picked up because they may be already accounted for by replication of entities of other types. So enabling replication for an entity type may not get this entity type in sync, only the new changes will get replicated. Given that the difference in semantics happen only if the replication suppression is changed and we don't really have scenarios when replication suppression is changed dynamically, the semantic differences are immaterial. If push comes to shove (e.g. made mistake in entity type definition), we can provide a tool to clear replicated ranges which would cause full resync and bring systems in sync. The other consideration is that bootstrapping is partitioned by entity type. Currently, bootstrapping has to scan all entities within a logical stream to get changes that happen within a time range. This happens because entities are not indexed by time. When bootstrapping happens, the chunking logic chunks data by range (because that's the only way to partition the data space), so for every chunk there is a full scan. This shouldn't cause a regression in the short term, because we're actually splitting the data into 128 shards, while previously data was concentrated in 3-4 entity types. In the future, we can also introduce chunking by entity guid, so that we can track entity guid ranges for bootstrapping and that would solve the bootstrapping problem. I honestly don't remember the details of

[IDF Design Documents | Replication State per Shard]
the future, we can also introduce chunking by entity guid, so that we can track entity guid ranges for bootstrapping and that would solve the bootstrapping problem. I honestly don't remember the details of complications for entity trail implementation, I think it's related to the fact that snapshots are done per-entity type, so in order to track snapshot replication progress we'd need per-entity type markers or something like that. In any case, we don't support entity trail now, so the point is moot. As far as backward compatibility is concerned, we're going to do a full re-sync when we upgrade from Asterix to Obelix (which is also the case with our current implementation). The full resync wouldn't have any visible functional consequences. The full re-sync happens due to the fact that replication ranges in Asterix are tracked at shard 0 x entity type, so when ranges are going to be tracked by shard 1..128, it would seem to the replica that all changes need to be replicated.

[IDF Design Documents | Replication State per Shard]
## High-level Design
At the high level we have 3 workflows:
Normal entity update push.
Bootstrapping / catch up.
Heartbeat.
For normal entity push, we need to change the cardinality of the timestamp oracle to be per shard.  The entities that are not suppressed from replication would work exactly the same way they worked.  The suppressed entities are not sent to the target system (if the entity is not replicated at all from this source, the server can just avoid sending it to uploader, but the uploader may need to do more control if the entity is replicated not to every target).  Note, that this approach would leave holes in the ranges during the push, but the bootstrapping would close them, so it shouldn't be a problem.
The LoadEntityTrail call would be per shard.  Initially, we can iterate through all entity types and if the entities of this entity type are replicated, then we add them to the payload (the range filtering and chunking logic is going to stay the same).  This would work functionally, but it would result into a scan per entity type.  Most likely it should be good enough for Obelix.  In the future, we can start one scan and skip entities of the types that we suppress replication for.
Heartbeat is going to happen per shard.  We'll remove the logic that checks if the replication of the type is suppressed because type is not going to be present is the stream info.

[IDF Design Documents | Replication State per Shard]

LoadEntityTrail 	- 5 days
Normal push 		- 1.5 days
Heartbeat 		- 0.5 day
Total - 7 days

[IDF Design Documents | SMSP-PC_PE IDF Synchronization]
SMSP-PC/PE IDF Synchronization
Devendra, Sumit
Jan 2025
[In-progress]

[IDF Design Documents | SMSP-PC_PE IDF Synchronization]
## Overview IDF is our internal key-value store implementation that stores NOS/AOS management data on PC (Prism Central), PE (Prism Element) and SMSP (Objects, NCM, Flow) clusters. IDF has the native capability of supporting replication across multiple IDF clusters. Below mentioned are the high-level guarantees provided by IDF-IDF synchronization:- IDF-IDF replication is Asynchronous in nature and provides eventual consistency. IDF-IDF replication depends on the Transport layer (Mercury) for secure and authenticated data transfer between source and destination. Entities replicated by IDF-IDF sync are Read-only on destination. IDF-IDF sync only supports replication of Entity Data and not time-series data. IDF-IDF sync design is highly scalable and can easily handle replication of millions of entities. An Entity Type in IDF can contain Replicated as well as Local entities. On a cluster unregistration, IDF removes all the entities replicated from that source cluster and these entities won’t be accessible anymore. In this unregistration workflow, entity delete watches won’t be provided, this behavior is for handling scale of entities and firing millions of watches in a minute might kill most of the services hence we have an option to just receive a Reset on the WatchClient in such cluster register/unregister workflows. Currently, IDF allows replication configuration based on source cluster type (NDFS, Multicluster, etc.) and replicates the data to all the endpoints available, IDF

[IDF Design Documents | SMSP-PC_PE IDF Synchronization]
receive a Reset on the WatchClient in such cluster register/unregister workflows. Currently, IDF allows replication configuration based on source cluster type (NDFS, Multicluster, etc.) and replicates the data to all the endpoints available, IDF sync does not allow selective replication as of now (meaning replicate to only these PEs and not all). IDF-IDF sync can be configured at EntityType level by providing the Source Cluster type. For example:- below schema means that Entities of type “entity_type” will replicate from kNDFS cluster to endpoints connected with it. entity_type_info_list { entity_type_name : "entity_type" type_info { suppress_replication : false replication_control_list { enable_replication_from : kNDFS } } } 

## Problem Statement
IDF can fundamentally support replication between any two IDF clusters but currently, the replication is enabled for below mentioned paths only:-
PE (from kNDFS) to PC
PC (from kMulticluster) to PE
FSVM (from kMinerva) to PC
Portfolio services are moving out of the PC to a separate SMSP cluster. For example, AIOPs and Calm are moving to the NCM SMSP cluster, Flow and Networking are moving out to a separate SMSP cluster.
Since most of these services are using IDF as their metadata store, we have use-cases of replicating IDF data from SMSP to PC and similarly from SMSP to PE as well.
In this document, we will discuss the infrastructure pieces needed to support SMSP to PC IDF replication and similarly SMSP to PE replication.

[IDF Design Documents | SMSP-PC_PE IDF Synchronization]
## Solution As per current schema definition, sync can be configured at EntityType level based on source cluster type only (using field `enable_replication_from`). This schema works for current use-cases because of the assumption that every cluster will have to replicate to a single type of cluster only, for example: PC only replicates to PE, PE only replicates to PC, FSVM only replicates to PC, etc. With the use case of SMSP to PC and SMSP to PE sync, now a single IDF source has to replicate the data to two types of target clusters (PC and PE). To support this, IDF schema needs to evolve to support `enable_replication_to` as well at EntityType definition level so that every EntityType can be configured to be replicated to all the needed target cluster types. New Schema for Replicating an EntityType from Flow-SMSP to PC will look like:- entity_type_info_list { entity_type_name : "entity_type" type_info { suppress_replication : false // Rule for replicating from Flow-SMSP to PC replication_control_list { enable_replication_from : kFLow_SMSP enable_replication_to : kMulticluster } } }  Similarly schema for replicating an entityType from Flow-SMSP to PC as well to PE will look like:- entity_type_info_list { entity_type_name : "entity_type" type_info { suppress_replication : false // Rule for replicating from Flow-SMSP to PC replication_control_list { enable_replication_from : kFlowSMSP enable_replication_to : kMulticluster } // Rule for replicating from Flow-SMSP to PE

[IDF Design Documents | SMSP-PC_PE IDF Synchronization]
{ entity_type_name : "entity_type" type_info { suppress_replication : false // Rule for replicating from Flow-SMSP to PC replication_control_list { enable_replication_from : kFlowSMSP enable_replication_to : kMulticluster } // Rule for replicating from Flow-SMSP to PE replication_control_list { enable_replication_from : kFLow_SMSP enable_replication_to : kNDFS } } } 

[IDF Design Documents | SMSP-PC_PE IDF Synchronization]
## Infrastructure Needed to support SMSP to PC and PE replication
Mercury service to support FanoutProxy calls from SMSP –→ PC, SMSP —-> PC —-> PE. For this trust setup is needed between PC and Flow-SMSP.
Information needed in Common ZK running in Flow-SMSP:-
Stamp with the correct cluster type (like kFlow_SMSP) in Zeus config. See the proto for more details.
Paired/Registered PC details for IDF and mercury to detect registered endpoints.
List of PE UUIDs registered to the paired PCs. This is needed by IDF to sync data to all the PEs (we will issue a nested fanout call from SMSP to PC to PE via mercury). This list of clusters should be updated whenever a new PE gets registered or unregistered to PC.
Currently, IDF does cluster UUID validation on the destination side as well from the list of registered cluster UUIDs. For supporting replication from Flow-SMSP to PE, we will need the PEs to be aware about Flow-SMSP cluster UUID. Similarly, remote cluster uuid is also used to load the entities of registered clusters only on IDF bootup and unload on cluster unregistration.
Similarly, PCs also need to be aware about registered Flow-SMSP cluster uuid.

[IDF Design Documents | SMSP-PC_PE IDF Synchronization]
## Restrictions for Sync from SMSP to PC/PE
Current design needs changes on PE side as well so PEs will also need to be on a supported version to handle sync from FLow-SMSP to PE.
Since we plan to use recursive/nested fanout calls for data transfer from Flow-SMSP to PE (via PC) so PC and PC-Mercury needs to be available for data sync to PEs.
Since IDF in SMSP will be independently replicating the entities to PC and PE, there won’t be any sequencing guarantees between data syncing to PE and PC.
The current proposed design is to have independent sync from Flow_SMSP to PC and PE directly, this is not a multi-hop sync. Hence, both the destinations (PC and PE) will eventually be in sync with Flow_SMSP IDF. Furthermore, any namespaces created on a replicated entity in PC won’t be synced to PEs.
