## Sync NCC check stats(error, check scores) from PE arithmos. Jun 2023 (Kumar Gaurav, Jineet Desai, Devendra Shekhawat, Sumit Bhatia) With the v4 APIs coming into picture there is a requirement from the NCC team to sync all the NCC check related stats like error & check scores stored in PE arithmos to PC IDF for their health page. These check related stats are dynamically registered by ClusterHealth service in Arithmos when the check is run. Currently we only sync the overall check score to PC IDF. To accomplish this feature requirement we are considering two approaches: Modify the arithmos.json file to have all the entries for the NCC related stats: There is a caveat in this approach. We may have to add around 400-500 stats in the arithmos.json file, which would rather be very unclean. To counter this we can add a regex support in arithmos.json file so that we can sync all the stats to PC IDF that match a particular regex. Pros: We would just have to add the regex support in arithmos.json file and all stats matching that regex can be synced. Testing this change would be easier since there is no change in Arithmos workflow as such Cons: Further filtering of stats or getting a subset of stats would lead to frequent changes in regex expression and misuse of the workflow. Arithmos fails the query if some requested stat is not registered. So adding the entries directly to the arithmos.json file might not work. Allow Arithmos to change schema dynamically: Apart from the

[Arithmos & Metric Collection | Sync NCC check stats from PE Arithmos]
the workflow. Arithmos fails the query if some requested stat is not registered. So adding the entries directly to the arithmos.json file might not work. Allow Arithmos to change schema dynamically: Apart from the arithmos.json file, we sync stats from Arithmos to PC IDF when they have the current_sync_to_pc field set to true in their schema. Currently Arithmos does not allow schema changes once the schema has been registered. We can consider making a change to allow modifying the current_sync_to_pc field(make it true from default false value) for the stats that we want to sync. In this approach we might require extensive testing of the arithmos workflows. Pros: This seems to be a cleaner and easier approach for the clients. They just need to modify the schema field. We won’t have to do extra computations for regex. Cons: This change would need extensive testing since initially we did not allow schema changes in Arithmos. So with this change there would be a lot of unknowns present.

[Arithmos & Metric Collection | Sync NCC check stats from PE Arithmos]
## Questions and Concerns:
Since the changes are in Arithmos and on the PE side, only the upgraded PEs will be able to sync these extra stats to PC and PEs on older versions won’t be syncing these stats. Cluster Health v4 API will have to handle these scenarios on the PC side during querying.
The NCC release version should be aligned with the AOS version(else their calls would fail if the stats are not present on PC).
Since the insights uploader on PE pulls the stats to be synced from Arithmos at a specific frequency (15 min depending on the flag value) we can expect a delay in the initial syncing of stats to PC. After initial detection of stats to sync to PC, uploader will sync the stats data every 30 secs.
RPC to change the schema should be fired only after upgrade is complete on all the PE nodes.
With so many stats now a part of the PE Arithmos to PC sync pipeline, we need to check the impact on PC load. (We may require this to test with our simulator).
We should check the retention of stats in PC IDF. Since dynamically registered stats in Arithmos will get auto-registered in IDF on PC via sync pipeline with default config and retention.
Question on historical sync requirement. With any of the above mentioned approaches we won’t be able to support historical stats sync so confirm from the Cluster-Health team if this is required or not.

Syncing PC only stats from PE to PC
Devendra Singh, Sumit Bhatia
April 2021
In-progress

[IDF Design Documents | Syncing PC only stats]
## Problem Statement
As of today, all the stats required on PC are stored in Arithmos on PE and synced to PC by InsightsUploader (via PrismGateway in version older than 5.17), most of these stats are used on both PE and PC (and some of them require historical sync also) so it makes sense to store them in Arithmos also on PE. Arithmos sync uses a static whitelist to decide the stats to be synced to PC and is not able to sync the dynamically registered stats in Arithmos to PC.
There is a requirement for new kind of PC only stats (these gets generated on PEs but used only on PC and no real consumer on PE), the first client team having this use-case is AHV team. As discussed with the AHV team, historical sync is not needed for these stats and no real need for storing them on PEs as they will only be used on the PC. As these will be dynamically registered stats in Arithmos so we also need to add support for dynamically registered stats to be synced and can’t rely on a static whitelist for sync.
There are various approaches that we can use to handle PC only and dynamically registered stats to be synced to PC. As these are dynamically registered stats on PE and we do not sync schema as part of Arithmos/IDF sync so on PC these new stats will be registered with default config (like Downsampling interval of 30 secs, default retention period, etc.). We will discuss each solution in detail in the below sections:-

[IDF Design Documents | Syncing PC only stats]
## Client teams (like AHV) directly sending stats to IDF on PC
Client teams (whoever owns PC only stats) can directly send the stats to IDF on PC via direct ApI calls using transport layers like Mercury or v3 calls.

## Pros
No resource impact on Arithmos
Skips the conversion from Arithmos data type to IDF data type in InsightsProxy.
No changes needed in Arithmos or sync pipeline.

## Cons
Each team has to build the logic for calling the API based on their sampling interval and retry mechanism. Duplication of code and effort.
Overall number of calls between PE and PC will increase, putting more load on Mercury, IAM, etc.
No control and limit on the parallel number of calls coming to IDF on PC. IDF might get overloaded on PC if each PE node starts sending some stats.
Can not make full use of batching, each client will send a separate API call based on their sampling interval.

## Buffer PC only stats in Arithmos for minimal required time
We can use Arithmos to store the PC only stats totally in-memory for a very small period of time (5-10 mins) and enhance the existing sync pipeline to support dynamically registered stats also. And then existing Arithmos sync workflow will take care of syncing these stats also to PC.

## Pros
Number of calls between PE and PC will remain the same. Noo extra load on mercury , IAM, etc.
Batching can be used effectively for sending the sync payload.
No specific logic to be handled on the client side.

[IDF Design Documents | Syncing PC only stats]
## Cons
Little extra load on Arithmos (shouldn’t be very high considering the small number of new stats ~50).
Historical sync can’t be supported because we plan to store the stats for minimal time in arithmos.
As the stats are kept in-memory only in Arithmos so Arithmos restart/crash can skip some data points from syncing.
As we're only keeping 5/10mins worth of data on PE side. So if sync lags more than that time then data on PC will not be present for that time.
As Arithmos will mostly reside in CVM only so won’t be able to leverage the niceties of the whole MVM plan (where mgmt services move to a separate VM outside the CVM).

## Make a dedicated service (can be uploader itself) to buffer the PC only stats
We can introduce a new service or enhance the existing insightsUploader to buffer the PC only stats. Client teams can send their PC only stats to the uploader, that will internally take care of syncing them to PC by leveraging the existing sync pipeline.

## Pros
Same as approach 2.
No need to add support for dynamically registered stats in Arithmos.

## Cons
Same as approach 2 if we plan to keep the stats in-memory only.
More design and implementation efforts needed as compared to other approaches.
Same thing can be achieved by giving some extra resources to Arithmos and we don’t have to build everything from scratch.

[IDF Design Documents | Syncing PC only stats]
## Conclusion
Based on the current requirements (from AHV team only, ~50 stats for node entities), it will be better and faster to go with Aapproach 2 mentioned above.
To be decided and finalized.

## Handling infinity and in-progress updates
The replica may request changes in the range of [timestamp..+INF), e.g. on initial bootstrapping.  To properly handle infinity, the master need to be able to figure out the ranges for completed operations, so that it can reliably identify ranges that cannot be updated in the future (failure to do so may result in missing updates, because the replica would think that it got all data for the range and won’t report that the update is missing).
After the entity updates are timestamped on the master, they can happen concurrently, so even though the timestamps define total ordering, the results are inconclusive until the data is persisted in the database.
To handle updates in progress, we use a missing ranges map to track completed operations on the master.  The map is not persisted as it’s only used for requests that are actually running on the server.

mark update in progress
get update range from timestamp oracle
when the operation completes, add the range to the completed operations map

## Handling inconclusively completed operations As far as I understand, the consistency model in Cassandra provides no locks, there is no way to protect a value that’s read from Cassandra from a write that is in progress. This means that on crash/restart we can have modification operations pending in Cassandra, that may complete after we read data on startup on Cassandra error (e.g. timeout, network hiccup) the operation may complete after the value has been read from Cassandra The problem that it presents to the replication is that if we base our range calculation on the data that we read from Cassandra on restart and we tell the replica that there are no updates since the max read timestamp, then we may miss in-progress writes. One (and probably the only) way to guarantee that a value cannot be updated by a pending write (assuming that we make sure that the server has exclusive access to Cassanrda), is to successfully update the value in a Paxos CF to move forward the Paxos instance counter (so that even if an operation is pending it would bounce off the new Paxos instance counter). So one way to cancel all pending operations on restart is to update all latest entities. But I presume that we don’t want that, so here how we’re going to deal with this problem in replication scenarios. We’re going to make an assumption that a pending operation in Cassandra must complete within a certain amount of time, say 5 minutes (configured with gflag). Let’s call it “uncertainty period”.

[IDF Design Documents | Transport design]
in replication scenarios. We’re going to make an assumption that a pending operation in Cassandra must complete within a certain amount of time, say 5 minutes (configured with gflag). Let’s call it “uncertainty period”. So if the server has owned a shard for longer than uncertainty period long, then it can be guaranteed to read the current values from Cassandra. This “uncertainty period” isn’t going to affect the master functionality, it’s only going to affect the accounting of replicated ranges. To support this, the completed operation map is initialized to timestamp oracle’s initial value minus uncertainty period, and the range for the uncertainty period, put to a queue of inconclusive ranges so that it can be marked as completed after the uncertainty period amount of time has passed. The other scenario is Cassandra update failure. Even though for some errors it’s possible to say that this update operation is not pending any more, in general this assumption cannot be made. So when there is a failure to update the latest entities happens, the operation is not accounted for in the completed operations map, instead its range is put to a queue of inconclusive ranges so that it can be marked as completed after the uncertainty period amount of time has passed.

## Handling time skews
The timestamp oracle is wall clock-based and it has some advantages (the values represent server time, they can be co-indexed with client timestamps, updates on different nodes can be loosely correlated based on the server timestamps, etc.).  The disadvantage is that it’s possible to get the wall clock time can be different on different nodes.  We generally can assume that the clocks are synchronized reasonably well, but there still could be small skews.
To mitigate this problem, we assume that the time skews are going to be bound by some value, say 5 seconds (gflag), let’s call it max time skew.  We’re going to have a Paxos value that stores the shard start time.  When the shard starts, it gets the last shard start time, takes max of last shard time and current time, adds max time skew value and that becomes the value that the timestamp oracle is initialized to.  Then it writes the new shard start time.  So for the first 5 seconds or so the timestamp oracle is going to be in the future.
The server would also check if any of the entities have DB modified timestamp that is greater than initial timestamp oracle value and fail to start the shard if such entities are found.

## Introduction
This document describes the discussion and decisions that we made on 04/03/2015 and 04/09/2015 about using Insights Transport service for PC in the cloud (a.k.a. SaaS a.k.a. SRE Insights a.k.a. PulseHD) solution.
Currently, our SaaS solution is a completely independent solution from Prism Central (PC).  The data collection, transfer, and mining is done by Insights software stack.  Giving that Insights is going to be the Control Plane DB for new Prism Central, it’s beneficial to converge PC and SaaS into a single platform that would use the same software stack.  To do so, we need a transport solution to transfer data from PE to PC in the cloud.

[IDF Design Documents | Transport for PC in the cloud - 04_09_2015]
## Cloud deployment architecture
To keep cloud deployment scalable in the presence of variable incoming data traffic, it’s beneficial to decouple data ingestion from data mining, in the manner similar to what’s currently done with the Insights receivers.  The architecture could be depicted by the following diagram:
The data from Nutanix cluster (PE) is sent to a network load balancer (NLB).  The load balancer sends data to a farm of receiver servers.  The data has no affinity to the receiver servers: any receiver server may store a slice of any cluster’s data.  The receiver servers save data to storage (could be local disks, could be cloud storage, etc.)  This way the cloud solution may ingest data in a scalable fashion even if PC is not ready for it.
The data slices that are stored by the receiver servers are identified by the originating cluster uuid and the timestamp of collection.  To load all data that corresponds to one cluster, the corresponding data slices from all receiver servers need to be merged together.
Let’s see what functionality may be needed to enable such deployment.

[IDF Design Documents | Transport for PC in the cloud - 04_09_2015]
## PE to PC data pipeline architecture in 4.2.1
The CPDB 4.2.1 roadmap document describes the PE / PC architecture pertaining to Insights DB.  The full data flow in 4.2.1, however, isn’t completely managed by Insights; Prism gateway continues to transfer Arithmos, Alerts and Zookeeper data.  The Arithmos data on PC is redirected to Insights DB, but Alerts and Zookeeper data continue to flow to their corresponding components.
Here is a diagram that depicts the Prism gateway data flow in 4.2.1:
The arrows show data flow direction, not control flow.  Prism gateway on PE polls Zookeeper, Alerts and Arithmos data and then transfers the data to the Prism gateway on PC, which forwards the data to the corresponding services on PC.  This functionality exists today.
In 4.2.1 we’re planning to add new data flow (colored in green).  Insights DB on PE and collectors are going to push data to Insights Uploader service, which would push it to Prism gateway on PE.  The Prism gateway on PC would forward Insights data to the Receiver service which would forward the data to Insights DB on PC.  In addition, we intercept Arithmos data via Insights Proxy, translate it into Insights format and forward it to Insights DB on PC.

[IDF Design Documents | Transport for PC in the cloud - 04_09_2015]
## Cloud deployment design considerations We would like to achieve feature parity and software reuse for the PC in the cloud, however, after careful consideration (see Alternative design), it looks like the amount of work that it requires would be too high. Given that the plan is to move all data to Insights DB in the future, we think that it’s OK if PC in the cloud runs slightly different software and will merge with on-prem PC in a future version. Thus, the architecture of PC in the cloud is going to look more like the final architecture, where all data is going to come from Insights DB on PE and collectors: On this diagram, each receiver server node runs Insights Receiver service in queue-to-storage mode, which writes the data to storage (e.g. local disk). On PC, the Receiver service runs in deque-from-storage mode, where it would be configured to know what clusters it is interested in and where the source data is stored (e.g. on the receiver server’s disks). The Receiver server on PC reads data from all source data locations, finds the data that came from the clusters of interest and forwards it to the Insights DB. On the PE side, we need to provide a way to collect data that is only sent to cloud. So when a collector sends data to the uploader service, it should indicate whether the data should be sent to on-prem PC. The reason for this distinction is that some data (Arithmos, Alerts, etc.) is going to be transferred by Prism, so an on-prem PC wouldn’t need the data that

[IDF Design Documents | Transport for PC in the cloud - 04_09_2015]
should be sent to on-prem PC. The reason for this distinction is that some data (Arithmos, Alerts, etc.) is going to be transferred by Prism, so an on-prem PC wouldn’t need the data that collectors pull from Arithmos. The various data flows are depicted on the following diagram: The data flow in red denotes the data that is sent to both on-prem PC and PC in the cloud. This is the data from Insights DB and collectors that don’t pull the data from sources that are replicated by Prism (Arithmos, etc.). The data flow in yellow denotes the data that is sent only to PC in the cloud. This is the data from collectors that pull data from Arithmos, Alerts, and Zookeeper. The data in blue denotes the data that is send only to on-prem PC. This is the data that is pulled by Prism from Arithmos, Alerts, and Zookeeper. The data in orange indicates that it’s a mix of red and yellow flows. This is the data that is sent to cloud. The data in purple indicates that it’s a mix of red and blue flows. This is the data that is send to on-prem PC.

## Work estimates
Here are the tasks that need to be accomplished to support the described design along with rough estimates in dev weeks (the time includes design and implementation):
Add support for Receiver service to run in queue-to-disk mode - 1 week
Add support for Receiver service to run in dequeue-from-disk mode - 2 weeks
Add support for replication state tracking on the uploader side - 2 weeks
Add support for “cloud-only” flag that collectors can use to indicate that this data should be only sent to PC in the cloud - 1 week
Cleanup collectors naming convention so that all names / types are consistent both in on-prem PC (that gets data directly from Arithmos) and PC in the cloud (that gets data from collectors) - 1 week
Add deployment / configuration scripts for setting up tunnel (assuming we’re going to use SSH or stunnel, so we can just use our RPC over the tunnel) - 1 week
Total: 8 weeks

[IDF Design Documents | Transport for PC in the cloud - 04_09_2015]
## Alternative design We considered an alternative design, that would achieve maximum feature parity and code reuse for both on-prem PC and PC in the cloud. To implement the desired cloud deployment architecture, we need to be able to do a couple things: capture data that’s received by Prism gateway and store it read the stored data from multiple receiver servers, merge it and forward to the corresponding services on PC Here is the logical picture that illustrates the requirements: The red line denotes the place where the data flow needs to be intercepted and redirected to storage. So the cloud data pipeline would look like this: Each receiver server would run Prism gateway and Receiver Proxy that would intercept data for all services and store it (e.g. to disk). The PC in the cloud would run Data Loader Proxy instead of Prism gateway. The data loader would be configured to know what clusters it is interested in and where the source data is stored (e.g. on the receiver server’s disk). It would read data from all source data locations, find the data that came from the clusters of interest, merge the data by the timestamps and forward the data to the corresponding services. Multipoint Currently, Prism gateway on PE can only send data to one PC. This is OK in the cases when the customers don’t have on-prem PC and just want to use PC in the cloud. For many deployments, however, lack of multipoint support would be a limiting factor, and it would be very desirable to be able to

[IDF Design Documents | Transport for PC in the cloud - 04_09_2015]
on-prem PC and just want to use PC in the cloud. For many deployments, however, lack of multipoint support would be a limiting factor, and it would be very desirable to be able to send PE data to at least 2 destinations. Sending to multiple destinations is supported in Insights Uploader, so the data that comes through the Uploader (Insights DB & Collectors) can be easily forwarded both to on-prem PC and PC in the cloud. For 4.2.1, however, Insights DB on PE stores only fraction of the data, so if we want PC in the cloud have feature parity with on-prem PC, we need to forward that data to the cloud as well. ## Problem to resolve
Currently, we do not support the ActiveEntitiesInfo sync for evictable entities. To make the ActiveEntitiesInfo sync logic function well with the existence of evictable entities, we need a mechanism to:
ignore evictable entities in the replica side when processing the ActiveEntitiesInfo payload
suppress in the master side as to avoid unnecessary scan on the Cassandra for evictable entities.

## Solution
When processing the ActiveEntitiesInfo payload, the replica will collect all evictable entity types(from the payload) and send them back to the master in the return payload(RemoteTransferDataRet). This list will be passed to the LoadActiveEntitiesArg so that the master can avoid loading entities of types in this list.

Requirements The following watches are to be supported as part of this: Watches when new entity types are created. Support for Conditional Watches Swagat Borah Dec 16 Approved 1. Customer requirement (CPD-1025) 1) Create-entity callback on entities with an attribute value from a given list. e.g. notify if an alert entity is synced from PE to PC having cluster value in ["abc", "pqr", "xyz"]. If the "in" operator is not supported we can work around by creating a watch for each of the required clusters. 2) Update-entity callback if an attribute x is updated for entities having attribute y value in the given list. e.g. notify if severity is changed for an alert entity having cluster value in ["abc", "pqr", "xyz"]. "in" operator workaround is applicable here too. 3) Large number of watches is not expected but the watches will be applicable on a large number of entities. 2. Translation of requirement to design Existing watch framework supports the following kind of watches on entity types. Watch framework also supports watches on specific entities as well as on entity / metric schema changes. Watch on create of entities of a given entity type Watch on update of given attribute of entities of given entity type Watch on delete of entities of a given entity type If we interpret the alerts use case into a generic feature, then the feature is the ability to provide additional conditions/ filters on the above mentioned watch types. The filter is currently specified as a single conditional expression of the type attribute OP value Or more specifically for this use case attribute IN {value_list} =>

[IDF Design Documents | Conditional Watches]
filters on the above mentioned watch types. The filter is currently specified as a single conditional expression of the type attribute OP value Or more specifically for this use case attribute IN {value_list} => cluster IN {cluster_list} This can be further extended to a series of conditional expressions which could be joined with an AND or an OR expression based on the use case. To keep this feature flexible enough to meet all existing and future use cases, we can use the existing BooleanExpression grammar definition for implementing conditional watches. The BooleanExpression structure is the traditional grammar based expression tree capable of expressing any complicated filter logic and is currently used in the filter expression for IDF query evaluation as well. The filter support will be applied on all the existing watches. This would mean that the filter would be applied on the fired watches after the existing rule engine evaluation but just before the dispatch operation, effectively limiting the fired watches to the set of entities which satisfy the BooleanExpression. 3. Definition of current state for conditional watches The filter condition will be applied even on the entities returned as part of current state for all applicable watches. Only entities which currently satisfies the filter condition would be considered part of current state. 4. Scope of Filter columns We would support only attributes of the given entity type as filter columns for the first version. The

[IDF Design Documents | Conditional Watches]
satisfies the filter condition would be considered part of current state. 4. Scope of Filter columns We would support only attributes of the given entity type as filter columns for the first version. The filter conditions cannot be Non-attributes or stats Attributes belonging to different entity types (ancestors, child etc will also fall in this case) Metadata of the given entity type, including entity id. Metadata of any other type, ancestor and child entity types included. We can easily extend it to include (3) metadata of the given entity type, but that would be done based on future requirements. Update(Obelix): (3) has been implemented currently in master and is present since 5.5. Most of the metadata can be used in conditional watches as pseudo attributes, i.e, adding underscore ‘_’ as a prefix and suffix to the metadata name. Eg: _entity_id_, _modified_timestamp_usecs_ etc. 5. Filter Set Modification The effective list of entities, on which the watches would be triggered, gets limited to a set of entities which currently satisfies the given filter condition. Lets call it the filter_set. For example, for alerts use case, only the entities of alert types which currently belong to the given set of clusters will be eligible for watch evaluation and therefore, belong to this filter_set. The user may also need to know if existing entities are added or deleted to this filter_set. This can happen if the user maintains a cache of entities on its side based on entities which are

Insights DB Watches
rpaul@, sborah@
Status - Work-in-progress

## Background
Main goal of Insights DB watches is to let various components monitor changes in the DB to track operation progress, changes in the cluster setup, cluster health and other alerting needs that each component might have.

[IDF Design Documents | Deprecated - Insights DB Watches - Design notes]
## Scope
For V1, we want to support the following types of watches:
1.  Watch on entity creation, updation or deletion. This can either based on an entity type or an entity UUID
E.g. Watch on any new entity created of type VM
Watch whenever VM UUID “abc123” changes i.e. any attribute of VM abc123 changes
Watch on whenever a new entity is created with UUID “xyz444”
2. Watch on any attribute value change at any point of time.
E.g. Watch on power_on attribute value change on VM UUID "abc123"
Watch on an attribute value change by a certain delta or %.
3. Watch on any metric stat value crossing a certain threshold at any point of time.
E.g. Watch if the disk_usage of disk UUID "pqr1334" goes beyond X.
Watches related to time series or historical data will NOT be supported in the first version and may be supported in future releases based on their needs from other components. E.g.
N alerts fired over the time interval T.
Crossing of a fixed threshold over a time interval T.
Change of value of a metric by a certain %.
Change of value of a metric by a certain % over a time interval T.
Watches will have the following limitations:
Watches cannot be defined over data from various entities.
Watches can not be set on a range of DB rows.

## Terminology
Watch - A monitor set up on the DB to look for a specific change in the data in the DB.
Alert - An instance of notification generated due to a watch condition being met by a particular DB data update.

[IDF Design Documents | Deprecated - Insights DB Watches - Design notes]
## Design
Note: this doc talks about a single leader based design. There will be a separate doc or section added to this same doc later for sharded architecture based design.

## Watch library Translates any Create/Update/Delete operation payload into watch language. E.g. if an entity is created, it translates that Create payload into a WatchObject message where the EntityGuid is populated with the properties of the entity being updated and the watch type is set as create. Maintains a cached copy of the registered watches and also contains a reverse-indexing strategy to quickly get the filtered list of watches which pertain to the context of a CUD operation. The context for a watch is basically the associated WatchObject. There will be typically three reverse indexed maps - 1) By entity type 2) By entity UUID 3) By attribute / metric Contains methods to do various types of watch rule evaluation. Contains a queue where fired alerts are enqueued. Maintains separate queues per client. These queues are later dequeued by the watch server to send the fired alerts RPCs to the respective clients. Evaluation of registered watches: For entities, entity types, metrics and attributes: Insights RPC server makes a call to the Watch library for every CUD RPC on successful completion of the RPC. Watch server, on being called by the Insights RPC server, delegates the task of evaluating that CUD operation to a thread from amongst a threadpool. Watch server will translate CUD operation into watch language (WatchObject proto) and then reverse index on the registered watches to get only those watches which pertain to the context in the WatchObject. It then evaluates

It then evaluates all those filtered watch rules. If any watch matches, an entry is made into the DB in alerts column family and the alert is also queued up to be sent as RPC notification to the respective client on being dequeued. If any watch matches, the following sequence of events take place: Client entry in DB is updated to update the sequence number with paxos write. If this write fails, this step is retried before proceeding to the next step for this fired watch. Entry is made into metrics CF for the fired watch. ## Watch server
A new service hosted on Insights server.
Runs on a specific port. This can be maintained in Zookeeper too but basically clients will know about this one port where the server is running.
Keeps the list of registered watch clients along with their ports cached.
Maintains a cache of sequence number per client.
Issues RPC calls to the respective clients when alerts are queued up.
Will not retry any failed RPC call to the client. It’s upto the clients to later poll and get missed alerts.
For stats:
Watch server periodically wakes up and goes over all the registered watches filtering out the non-stats related watches.
For the rest of the watches, it translates the watch definition into a GetEWM query and gets the raw stats for the current execution period.
It then will do the watch rule evaluation on those raw stats.
Notification
For non-critical watches, Watch server will NOT directly notify the client whenever a watch fires. The client is expected to poll and receive the fired alerts information.
For critical watches, Watch server can use zeus config sections for faster, “push” based notifications. (needs more discussion)

## Watch Client Client library for watch server. Registers with zookeeper to stay updated about watch server status. Is an RPC service by itself which listens on an unused port. It listens for any alert fired for its client. At startup, registers the containing component to the watch server using a unique client_id and port number (takes up any unclaimed port). Is used by the component to register watches. The client library keeps polling the watch server asking for new alerts fired for its client_id At a very sparse periodicity, keeps polling the server for missed alerts. Client will reset any time it perceives that the system has gone into an undefined state: Reset means it will issue an RPC to the watch server asking for Resetting of sequence number for itself and missed watches since the last successfully received timestamp sequence number. If it comes to know that the server has changed port, then it re-establishes the connection. Will also reset if the server has sent a force reset call. Maintains the last_alert_timestamp sequence number in a local file. This is the timestamp sequence number of the most recent alert received by the client. Component (e.g. acropolis) must provide a callback function which accepts a list FiredAlert protos. In this function, the component defines what they want to do further with the fired alert information. Watch client will also queue up the incoming fired watches sorted on the sequence number and then dispatch the watches to the

[IDF Design Documents | Deprecated - Insights DB Watches - Design notes]
defines what they want to do further with the fired alert information. Watch client will also queue up the incoming fired watches sorted on the sequence number and then dispatch the watches to the callback function in order.

## Client and server up but both unreachable to each other
Server sends some alerts to client and bumps up the sequence number.
Client does not receive those packets so its sequence number stays stale.
Client-server communication restored.
Server sends some new alerts with new sequence numbers.
Client realizes that it has not received all alerts or received them in wrong order - so it will issue a reset call asking for alerts since its last successfully received timestamp sequence number.
Server resets the sequence number for this client and sends the alerts again.

## Client up but server goes down
Client’s RegisterWatch calls will fail hence it will re-try those calls.
Same for Reset calls.
Meanwhile server comes back up. It will read the DB and establish RPC connections with all clients again.
Server also sends force reset calls to all the clients so that they reset their connections and sequence numbers.

## Server up but client goes down
Client re-registers and let’s its new location be known.
Gets a sequence number from the server as part of the registration call.

[IDF Design Documents | Deprecated - Insights DB Watches - Design notes]
## Open Issues
Should the client be intimated on what actually triggered the alert? Or we just intimate them that the watch triggered and leave it to the client to read the DB and figure out the diff. -- Since server maintains per client queuing of fired watches and client checks the sequence number (basically ordering of received alerts ensured), server will also send the actual data which triggered the alert.
How do we handle de-duplication of registered alerts? At what granularity?   --We don’t. Clients should not register such overlapping watches and if they do, they should deal with the alerts.
How do we handle very noisy alerts? Do we handle it at the registration phase itself or later on depending on how frequently that alert gets called. -- Later on on alerts frequency. Server will do some rate limiting but this is not targeted for first version.
Max number of watches to support at any point in time?  -- Acropolis team would set up watches in the order of a few thousands at any given point of time but most watches are expected to be based on tasks which are short lived watches, hence Acropolis will unregister them as soon as they fire.
How to handle missed DB updates i.e. watch server is down for some time and misses processing of some DB updates during that time. -- Server going down means Insights server itself will be down. So Watch server per se, won’t miss any update.

E.g.

Alternately, we can store the watch firing logs as metrics in the existing metrics CF. The EWM proto will hold the entity and metric context (along with new value) while the row key will be as follows:

<hash>.client_id.watch_name.metric_name.<reverse sequence number> | FiredAlert | This CF can have a retention of 1 day. The need for going back to more than a day old alerts seems minimal.

For many use cases, only a subset of attributes may be required for the end user. Instead of returning the entire payload, it will be useful to only return the attributes that the client is interested in. This smaller payload will help in 1. bringing down the memory footprint of IDF and help in scaling to higher capacities 2. would also lead to faster processing on client side 3. Lower latencies because of lower payloads for the RPCs to handle Use Case: The primary user of projection feature will be Prism Notification Service. Reducing redundancy in watches in case of restarts via persistent watches Terminology 1) Application - The application making use of the watch client 2) Watch Client - The Watch Client library provided by IDF 3) Server - The IDF server. Current design The current watches mechanism works the following way: the client registers a watch on an entity or entities of an entity type during which the current states of entity(s) is returned and subsequent updates are delivered via callbacks. This design is totally ephemeral and the expected behavior from clients during errors is to re-register and do the above process from scratch. This can lead to some strain on the application making use of the watch client if it has to reprocess all the entities (which are returned as current states) every time the client re-registers (due to errors or whatever). Secondly, if a delete happens and application wants to be notified of it in order to perform an action (in case of re-registration), it would have to maintain a local cache and do a diff of the current state received after re-registration to see which ones got deleted. Proposed design The primary objective is to prevent the sending of all the entities as part of the current state and only let the application know about the changes that took place when the watch client or the IDF server was down. This would require persisting some additional data in IDF w.r.t to the clients. Secondly, the application will get notifications of deletions that

Shard Based Filtering for Watches
Aiswarya Sreekantan, Sumit Bhatia, Swagat Borah
June 2018
In Review

[IDF Design Documents | Shard Based Filtering for Watches]
## Customer Requirement:
Currently IDF watches are shard agnostic. Requirement is to provide additional filtering on entities based on the shards that they belong to. One use case which drives this requirement is from Alerts team with the detail as follows:
Action Service (AS) is listening to alert entity creation in IDF. Since AS uses scale out model, it will distribute IDF shard numbers among AS instances. That means, each AS instance cares only about a subset of the alert entities which watch client reports (as of today, watch client report any alert entity changes to all clients care about alert entity changes):
For example:
AS1 : shard 1- 42
AS2 : shard 43 - 86
AS3 : shard 87 - 128
So, when AS1 register a watch client to IDF, it should be able to specify a filter like “SHARD_IDS” so that only the entities belonging to the given set of SHARD_IDS are returned for the given watch client for AS1. This will be similar to the shard id based filtering which the query layer currently provides here. (Refer to field shard_id_list in message Query in insights_interface.proto)
A watch client can watch many entity types.  One entity type may use this filter and the other entity type doesn’t. For example, the watch client watches for alert change, at the meantime, it also watches action service rule change. So the use case would look like
alert entity changes being sharded
action_rule entity changes being not sharded.

[IDF Design Documents | Shard Based Filtering for Watches]
## 1. Provide one set of shard ids per watch client All watches registered against this watch client will automatically get filtered based on the given shard id list. This shard filter will be applied in addition to the respective watch definition. Backward compatibility: Yes. Shard id list can be uninitialised which means that no shard based filtering will be applied. Pros: Simple design and easy to understand. Implementation is easy with minimum changes on IDF server side and IDF watch client side. On IDF server side, an additional set inclusion check needs to be performed as part of watch processing. On IDF watch client side, an additional shard id list needs to be provided as part of the watch client registration process as part of the constructor. No changes required to all the watch registration wrapper methods. Cons: Inflexible. If there are certain watches which do not need shard based filtering, then a separate watch client needs to be instantiated for the same. Multiple watch clients are more expensive than multiple watches for both client and server side. For example, IDF watch clients need dedicated threads, some fixed internal structures, etc on the client instance. On IDF server side, we have alarm handlers and heartbeat mechanisms per watch client, each requires more threads and memory. there is no scope of enhancing it to filtering on different shard id lists. Same inclusive filter on shard ids is applied to all watches. No scope for performing range checks on

[IDF Design Documents | Shard Based Filtering for Watches]
and memory. there is no scope of enhancing it to filtering on different shard id lists. Same inclusive filter on shard ids is applied to all watches. No scope for performing range checks on shard ids or any other advanced filtering options. The shard based filtering by default will be ANDed to the existing filters of attribute watches, conditional filters etc. There is no option to change this. Moderate space usage. One exhaustive set of shard ids to be stored per watch client on IDF server side.

[IDF Design Documents | Shard Based Filtering for Watches]
## 2. Provide one set of shard ids per watch client with an opt-in / opt-out switch per watch
A single shard id list per watch client. Each watch registration will now have a boolean switch to specify if they want to include shard based filtering or not on top of their watch definition. This shard filter will be applied in addition to the respective watch definition.
Backward compatibility:
Yes. Shard id list can be uninitialised which means that no shard based filtering will be applied on any of the registered watches. The default value of this switch can be opt-out which means that the watch will not use shard based filtering by default even if the watch client provides a shard list. Only watches that need shard based filtering would need to set this switch to opt-in.

[IDF Design Documents | Shard Based Filtering for Watches]
the watch will not use shard based filtering by default even if the watch client provides a shard list. Only watches that need shard based filtering would need to set this switch to opt-in.

Pros:
Simple design and easy to understand.
More flexible than option 1 and fully supports the above given alerts team’s use case. A single watch client will suffice instead of having two watch clients.
Cons:
Big code change. 
Implementation is similar to option 1 but with an added change of including an optional opt-in/ opt-out boolean flag. This will require changes to all the wrapper methods for watch registration across watch clients in four different languages, namely C++, Python, GoLang and Java. Server side implementation remains the same.
Inflexible.
there is no scope of enhancing it to filtering on different shard id lists. Same inclusive filter on shard ids is applied to all watches.
No scope for performing range checks on shard ids or any other advanced filtering options.
The shard based filtering by default will be ANDed to the existing filters of attribute watches, conditional filters etc. There is no option to change this.
Moderate space usage
One exhaustive set of shard ids to be stored per watch client on IDF server side.

[IDF Design Documents | Shard Based Filtering for Watches]
## 3. Provide a different set of shard ids per watch Each watch definition will now have an exclusive set of shard ids set. There will be no shard ids at the watch client level. This shard id list will be empty by default meaning no shard based filtering will be applied on that watch. This shard filter will be applied in addition to the respective watch definition. Backward compatibility: Yes. Shard id list will be uninitialised by default which means that no shard based filtering will be applied on any of the registered watches. Only watches that need shard based filtering would need to specify the shard id list. Pros: More flexible than option 1 and 2. Now each watch can have a totally different set of shard ids to filter on. It fully supports the given alerts’ use case while leaving ample scope of expansion for future use cases where different shard id lists may be required for the same watch client instance. Cons: Big code change. The amount of change required is at a similar level as option 2. This will require changes to all the wrapper methods for watch registration across watch clients in four different languages, namely C++, Python, GoLang and Java. Server side implementation remains the same as option 1 or 2. Inflexible. No scope for performing range checks on shard ids or any other advanced filtering options. The shard based filtering by default will be ANDed to the existing filters of attribute watches, conditional filters etc. There is no option to change this.

[IDF Design Documents | Shard Based Filtering for Watches]
shard ids or any other advanced filtering options. The shard based filtering by default will be ANDed to the existing filters of attribute watches, conditional filters etc. There is no option to change this. High space usage One exhaustive set of shard ids to be stored per watch on IDF server side which leads to a high space usage. Moreover, for most of the use cases including the current alerts use case, this introduces a high level of redundancy when multiple watches have the same shard id list to filter on.

[IDF Design Documents | Shard Based Filtering for Watches]
## 4. Provide support for shard_id as a pseudo attribute for Conditional watch filtering
Instead of specifying any shard id list as part of watch client registration or watch registration, simply provide support for shard_id as a pseudo attribute in conditional watches. Similar to all existing pseudo attributes, the shard id value is computed inline whenever any entity is processed for potential watches and since we only evaluate one entity at a time, there is minimal processing and memory usage involved in this. No watch client side changes are required for this approach. (Thanks to Sumit Bhatia for proposing this option.)

[IDF Design Documents | Shard Based Filtering for Watches]
Example filter condition: Note that these filter conditions can be combined with any existing filter conditions using the boolean expression operators AND, OR, NOT. Contiguous shard id ranges. This is the Alerts use case given above. As per the example mentioned in the requirements section, the corresponding filter conditions are Discrete, non-contiguous shard id case Suppose the use case requires a discrete shard ids for filtering (preferably for non-contiguous shard ids). In that case, the filter condition examples are as follows. Backward compatibility: Yes. This approach works with the existing conditional watch framework. Older watches where shard id is not specified as a pseudo attribute will continue to work as before. Watches which need shard based filtering will use this new pseudo attribute as part of its filter condition as per the specific use case. Pros: Easy implementation. Scope of change is similar to adding a new pseudo attribute which is pretty straightforward. This requires no IDF watch client change which is a huge plus. Most flexible approach among the list. Each watch can decide whether it wants shard id based filtering or not. No need to have multiple watch clients. Full flexibility of filtering on different shard id lists. Instead of specifying an exhaustive set of shard ids, a simple range check can be applied on a contiguous set of shard ids. Similarly advanced filtering options can be applied on shard ids too using the full set of conditional

[IDF Design Documents | Shard Based Filtering for Watches]
of shard ids, a simple range check can be applied on a contiguous set of shard ids. Similarly advanced filtering options can be applied on shard ids too using the full set of conditional operators that conditional watches provide. This approach is even more flexible than what the current query based approach described in the use case. The query API allows specifying an exhaustive set of shard ids and that shard id based filter is ANDed to the existing query filters. This watch implementation does not enforce any such restrictions and allows full control to the user to specify custom filters on shard ids. Low memory footprint Typical use cases work off contiguous shard ranges instead of discrete, non-contiguous shard id values. In this scenario, the shard based filtering can take advantage of range filters and significantly reduce the memory footprint of watch registrations. In the worst case scenario of discrete, non-contiguous shard id values, the memory footprint will regress to the footprint of option 3. Cons: Worst case memory footprint is high Given the flexibility, the same contiguous shard id set can be expressed as an explicit set of shard ids instead of utilizing the range filter operators. This can potentially lead to a high memory usage for watch registration especially if there are a lot of watches which requires shard id filtering. This can be avoided by proper documentation and proactively informing the clients of the best practises but there cannot be enforced

[IDF Design Documents | Shard Based Filtering for Watches]
especially if there are a lot of watches which requires shard id filtering. This can be avoided by proper documentation and proactively informing the clients of the best practises but there cannot be enforced via any code validation. May theoretically hit filter clauses limit There is a strict upper limit on the number of filter conditions (gflag controlled here) that IDF can currently support which is a factor of the protobuf RPC limitations itself. Since this approach requires two filter expressions per shard id range, theoretically, this may possibly reduce the amount of filtering that the client can provide on a given watch. In most practical use cases, the current limit of 30 clauses is more than sufficient for any existing or potential future use cases.

## Chosen Approach:
Given the pros and cons discussed above, we are going ahead with Option 4. This is the most flexible and has the highest pros versus all the other approaches. The cons are mostly theoretical issues and should not be much of a concern in the near future.

[IDF Design Documents | Shard Based Filtering for Watches]
## Implementation notes:
We already have added multiple pseudo attributes to conditional watches (Recent example here) so adding shard_id as another pseudo attribute is a simple, iterative change. Moreover, shard_id can be easily computed inline from the given entity id using a standard hash function. The watch evaluation based filtering is done one entity at a time and all processing happens on in-memory data as part of the CRUD operation. Therefore, this implementation adds a marginal increase in the computation time of the existing conditional watch filtering implementation (equivalent to evaluating two more conditional expressions.)

## Timelines:
Alerts team needs this feature by mid June 2018 (two weeks from the time of writing this doc) well in time for 5.9 release which is a good enough timeframe to complete the implementation using the pseudo attribute approach as per option 4.

## JIRA Link:
https://jira.nutanix.com/browse/CPD-2078
Due date: 15-Jun-18

[IDF Design Documents | High availability deployment with rack resilience for IAM_IDF services_]
## Problem statement
IAM for XI is a tier 0 service that’s deployed in the MSP framework that needs to meet high availability serviceability requirements.
IAM uses IDF which is the control plan data store for the data persistence. On the high level, there are three distinct HA requirements that IAM that needs to meet.
No single point of failure
Minimal downtime upgrade
Rack level resiliency, i.e. if a single rack fails, IAM still needs to be available to other racks within DC
Since IAM is a stateless service, these HA requirements naturally fall back to the underlying IDF which is used to maintain the persisted state.
The purpose of this document is to focus on the rack level resiliency solutions, the rest of the requirement is taken up by separate discussions and might already be covered by the IDF scale out architecture as well as the rolling upgrade capability.
In the case of unplanned rack failure within a DC, all the services that are hosted by the MSP running on that rack will become unavailable, that would include underlying stargate, cassandra, zookeeper, IDF and IAM.  Hence all the data that are stored physically on the same rack will become unavailable, we need a resilient way to keep the service running under such circumstances without data loss and with minimal service down time.

[IDF Design Documents | High availability deployment with rack resilience for IAM_IDF services_]
## Assumptions
All dependent services of IAM including IDF/Cassandra/Zookeeper are all deployed by proper placement and configurations by MSP framework in a rack aware manner.
The underlying AOS cluster shall be running on each rack that forms isolated protection domains.
Cassandra and zookeeper cluster can both be deployed over different subnet through proper configurations.
Cassandra and zookeeper can both be deployed in a rack-aware manner to protect against a single rack failure.
Cassandra provides its own data protection domain through RF replication without dependency on the underlying AOS data replication.
IDF container or cassandra container (when cassandra is segregated into its own containerized service), is backed by vdisk(s) from underlying AOS cluster which is mounted onto the IDF container using the volume group plugin. Vdisk is replicated by Stargate so the underlying data has HA in the case of node failures.
In the current form of deployment, whenever a single IDF container goes down, MSP detects it and brings the container back up and mounts the same vdisk onto it and all services resume after that with no config data loss. This downtime in case of such unplanned failurers is similar to the one we currently have even in our scale out PC / PE IDF setup wherein zookeeper detects a node going down (maximum of 20 secs heartbeat timeout).
The bootstrap time of IDF for IAM data should be negligible due to the small amount entities involved.

[IDF Design Documents | High availability deployment with rack resilience for IAM_IDF services_]
## Proposal for solutions
MSP is going to be running across racks, on top of multiple AOS clusters (potentially different subnets) such that to perform service deployment and orchestration across racks and across different AOS clusters.
IDF, cassandra and zookeeper services are going to be segregated into their own container and are going to be deployed by MSP.
MSP will place all above mentioned services in a rack-aware manner (e.g. Having IDF, zk, cassandra running across different racks with minimum 1 instances of IDF and cassandra and zk running on each rack.)
IDF/Cassandra/zookeeper shall form clusters from the instances running in each of these AOS clusters across racks through proper configuration and orchestration from MSP.
The HA event could happen in the following ways:
If MSP detects a service container failure, it will bring it up on another node joining the cluster.
The existing health monitoring HA mechanism through zookeeper heartbeat shall continue to work seamlessly. For example: In the case of IDF container’s failure to respond to the zookeeper heartbeat either because of service down or rack down event. That will trigger an IDF shard reassignment event which will happen within <= 20 seconds of heartbeat failure.

[IDF Design Documents | High availability deployment with rack resilience for IAM_IDF services_]
## Data redundancy and recovery in rack failure scenario
Each IDF instance running on each rack owns certain logic shards of user data marked by shard ID, which is derived from the hashing of the primary keys of the entities.
Actually data of each of those logic shards will map into a certain token ring range which is managed by one of the cassandra node, which may or may not be colocated on the same rack.
Each of those shards’ data will be replicated according to the RF specification.
Because cassandra is deployed in rack aware manner, therefore, each of the shard will be replicated to the cassandra node that are deployed on different racks.
In the case of rack failure, zookeeper heartbeat will detect both cassandra and IDF failure will trigger HA migration within 20 seconds (can be configured if so required).
IDF will invoke shard reassignment logic in the cases of such HA event and “move” the shards which were owned by the failed node into the existing healthy nodes.
The actual data will be bootstrapped from the local cassandra store which are already available due to the RF replication.

[IDF Design Documents | High availability deployment with rack resilience for IAM_IDF services_]

Zookeeper containerization (Zk team)
IDF container disaggregation from Cassandra and zookeeper (Cassandra tem, IDF team)
IDF container support for scale out mode. https://jira.nutanix.com/browse/CPD-2456
(IDF , MSP team)
MSP to be deployed over multiple AOS cluster across multiple racks  (MSP team)
MSP support for rack aware deployment and orchestration of services (MSP team)

[IDF Design Documents | High Level Design for Xi-MT]
High-level Design for Xi-MT
Sumit Bhatia
March 2020
In Review

## In order to achieve multi-tenancy in the cloud there are three options:
Xi-CT design where each tenant will have a dedicated cluster. This would be inefficient and expensive since there will be no sharing of resources. From the changes side, no changes would be required in the components.
Make all the components tenant aware and then use the Xi-PE and PC along with these tenant aware components where multiple users can access their tenant-specific data.
Another option is to have multi-tenant data in the PE and PC and create an upper-level abstraction which is tenant PCs where the data would be synced per tenant. In this case, the sync will have to be tenant-specific, but all the read components can read the data from local IDF without being tenant aware and it won't be an issue since the local IDF for them will have only that specific tenant's data.
In this case both the publisher(on both PE and PC side) and IDF will have to be tenant-aware but the read APIs/ reader components can be tenant agnostic.

## Current design:
In the current design, the components are not fully tenant-aware and we are using one PE-PC setup per tenant i.e. Xi-CT.

[IDF Design Documents | High Level Design for Xi-MT]
## Sync filtering based on particular attribute/metadata field which in this case is 'tenant_uuid':
The multi-tenant PCs will now start sending data to single-tenant PCs (tenant-specific PCs) and the destination will be decided based on the tenant_uuid field. So, IDF sync destination will have to be based on the 'tenant_uuid' attribute from entity_guid, as part of all workflows: active sync, bootstrap, active entities.

## Multi-hop sync for IDF-IDF:
doc
In current design the synced entities are only sent 1 hop i.e a VM from PE (source) is sent to PC (replica) or from PC (source) to multiple PEs (multiple replicas). However, it is not propagated further from these replicas to more PEs or PCs. 
Now, IDF sync will have to be multi-hop since the synced entities from multi-tenant PC will have to be again synced to single-tenant PC. Also, the multiple hops will have to be defined as a path (list of source-destination pairs). Chain replication in case level1 PC keep all the data.
Sync from PE(source) ---> PC(replica_level1) and PC(replica_level1) ----> TenantPC(replica_level2).

[IDF Design Documents | High Level Design for Xi-MT]
## Implement Stat Sync from IDF-IDF:
IDF sync doesn't support stat sync. This hasn’t been an issue since PE-PC stat sync happens from Arithmos-IDF via arithmos_data_sender and we didn't have a use case yet for IDF-IDF stat sync. For this approach, we'll have to implement stats sync in IDF. These stats could also be synced multi-hops. Currently, since there is not stat sync implemented yet, so there is no concept of source and replica for stats. We can write stats for replicated entities directly on the replica side. So we just need stats to be synced from PC to TenantPC.

## Sync Barrier guarantees:
The sync barrier guarantees should remain similar to what they are currently. The PE sync barrier entity should be applied on the tenant PC only after all the updates previous to it on the same PE were applied. Currently, there are no guarantees in particular across PEs which would remain the same.

## SLAs for IDF-IDF sync:
Since now the sync would turn from one hop to two hops considering the batching of 200ms it would take twice as long for the data to reach the tenant PC, so we might have to tune the batching times and other SLA related parameters in order to maintain current SLAs. Or explore using some network efficiency algorithms, one of the suggestions that came up in the meeting was Nagle.

[IDF Design Documents | High Level Design for Xi-MT]
## Retention on multi-tenant PC:
As PC is just an intermediate hop for the synced data, some of the data on PC would be needed by services like scheduler but most of the remaining data would not be needed and we should explore removing such data from the PC one it has been synced to tenant PCs this would help keeping the PC resource consumption light.

## Changes Needed in IDF server/ client libraries:
IDF already has support for the 'tenant_uuid' field in entity_guid in order to support multi-tenancy.
Fill in all gaps(if any), for all the RPCs and server workflows to be tenant aware across all use cases.
Add support for the same in commonly used client libraries.

## Currently, arithmos on PE has no notion of tenants. So there will have to be some logic to publish tenant_uuid in arithmos.
One possible approach can be to let publishers on PE publish the entities normally along with a 'tenant_uuid' field. This won't require changing arithmos to be tenant aware. While syncing data to PC via proxy we'll convert 'tenant_uuid' field from PE into 'tenant_uuid' field in IDF's entity_guid. This approach will since no one will directly interact with so queries will not need tenant support.
Other approach would be to enable multi-tenancy in arithmos both write and read flows.

[IDF Design Documents | High Level Design for Xi-MT]
## Security related:
The sync would take care of syncing only the entities using tenant_uuid. But it is upto individual component owners that they make sure they do not make fanout calls to the multi tenant PC from tenantPC and fetch any data that belongs to other tenants.

## Open questions:
Do entities in PE arithmos need to be tenant_aware or are they hardware-level entities and won't be shown to the end-user?
Ans: Arithmos itself won't be tenant aware, the entity will have tenant_id stamped and sync would be tenant aware.
The tenant level entities would be stamped with tenant_id and will be synced to that particular tenant PC.
The hardware entities would be stamped with nutanix tenant and synced to a nutanix tenant PC.
Do we need any form of QoS between config and stat data?

## Features The main piece of data is KeyValue, key is bytes and value is bytes. The data is ordered by keys. There is create_revision and mod_revision. There is also a version of the key, when deleted it's reset to 0. There is also lease id, when the lease expires the key is deleted. Another piece of data is Event. It can be a PUT or DELETE event and it contains kv and prev_kv. This is probably similar to the FiredWatch construct. The keys are expected to be sorted, there is a notion of range. The RangeRequest can be used to query the KV pairs (or just the keys). The requests can be sorted by key, value, revisions (mod / create) or version. The request can go over an older revision. The query can be marked as serializable (as opposed to linearizable, which is the default), which means the reads could be potentially stale (the underlying implementation is that reads can be served from followers, and if the follower is lagging, the read could return stale data) . The range could be filtered by min / max mod / create revisions (convenient for getting changes since or between revisions, e.g. for incremental replication). All responses have ResponseHeader that contains cluster id, member id, revision and raft term. Other than the revision, it's not clear what to do with other data. etcd supports transactions, they are somewhat similar to how Pithos allows conditional dependency checking, but the conditions are more elaborate. Each transaction request contains a list of predicates

[IDF Design Documents | Etcd Evaluation]
what to do with other data. etcd supports transactions, they are somewhat similar to how Pithos allows conditional dependency checking, but the conditions are more elaborate. Each transaction request contains a list of predicates and two actions: one action (the "true" action") would run if all predicates evaluate to true, and another action (the "false" action) would run otherwise. Each predicate would specify which property of a KeyValue to compare (value, version, create revision, mod revision, lease) with what value and the comparison operator. E.g. a predicate could be 'version of key "foo" is equal to 42', and the the action could be 'update value of key "bar" to 75'. The action could be another transaction, so there could be a tree of if-then-else structures. etcd supports watches. A watch can be set on a key, a range of keys or all keys with some prefix. A watch can watch for event starting with a certain revision (if revision is not specified, the watch starts from latest revision). I presume that all events will come in order (even events that involve different keys). The watch interface uses the "stream" feature of proto3, both the request and response are streams, the client can create and delete watches using the request stream and get the events from the response stream. etcd supports leases. The client can start a lease with a certain id (the client can pick an id or can let the server generate an id). When keys are created they can be attached to a lease. When

can start a lease with a certain id (the client can pick an id or can let the server generate an id). When keys are created they can be attached to a lease. When a lease is revoked, all keys that are attached to the lease are deleted. A lease has a TTL, if the server doesn't get a keep-alive request before the TTL expires, the server will revoke the lease. etcd supports security model. It has a built-in IDP (i.e. there is API to add users and roles), and it's possible to set read / write permissions on the key or a range of keys. There is an option to turn off auth.

## Implementation Notes Etcd uses raft (https://raft.github.io/raft.pdf) as the consensus algorithm. All etcd nodes operate on a single replicated data set, there is no sharding. Raft achieves consensus on all replicated logs, each node has a copy of the log and applies the log to the state. Writes are performed by the leader, reads can happen from any node. The persistent state is managed by a B-tree implementation written in Go (bbolt). The implementation is similar to Berkeley DbOpen (almost exactly same data formats and terminology). It mmaps the file for reads (there is no buffer manager) and it writes modified pages to disk on every update. Only one update at a time can happen, but multiple keys can be updated in the same update. Once update is ready, the pages are just written to disk and then the file is fsynced. I presume that if there is a crash and a page is partially written (torn page) or there is a B-tree split and only part of it is written, the B-tree would just corrupt itself -- I don’t see any logging or other recovery mechanism to achieve write atomicity. The keys in the B-tree are actually revisions and the data stores the actual user-provided key-value data. When a node starts, it reads all data from disk and builds an in-memory index key -> {revN, .., rev1}. I honestly don’t understand why they chose B-tree as on-disk data structure in this case -- the data is pretty much sequence ordered, so a log (or some other form of queue) would be more efficient

[IDF Design Documents | Etcd Evaluation]
don’t understand why they chose B-tree as on-disk data structure in this case -- the data is pretty much sequence ordered, so a log (or some other form of queue) would be more efficient and easier to provide write atomicity and do compaction. WAL just uses buffered IO and fsync to flush it to disk. The same sector can be updated and flushed multiple times, so unless the underlying storage guarantees sector write atomicity, the previously committed records can be lost if the sector overwritten to commit new records. The requests go to the raft state machine directly. Raft is implemented as a library (which is also used in other projects). The raft library takes proposals and then drives the state machine: it lets the server know what needs to be saved to the log, what messages to send, which entries to apply. The requests are written to the raft log as is, and once committed (i.e. log is replicated to the quorum) are applied to the current state. The conditions are checked and revision is generated when requests are applied, so application of requests to the current state is not idempotent. I spent a bit of time looking for logic that at least tries to provide idempotency, but from the code it looks like if etcd crashes after applying operation to the B-tree store (which would increment revision), on restart the raft log entry can be applied again and increment revision again (and now the state is different on different nodes, even if the logs are the same). Pros: the smallest startup cost -- start with what we have, fix the functional issues. Cons: long term we can run into scalability issues (no scale-out, load all keys in memory) and miss on features like Federation. So long term it may be an expensive investment to design and implement missing features. Implement etcd APIs on top of some other DB that Nutanix has already invested in (or plans to invest in the future irrespective of etcd). The communication protocol for the APIs is gRPC, so it should be fairly straightforward to implement them in any language, but the semantics could be challenging to implement efficiently. E.g. to implement it on top of IDF looks like the biggest gap in generally useful semantics would be the ability to support transactions. Pros: piggyback on existing investments into scale, perf and features. Cons: there could be features that are specific to etcd only, re-implementing those may be expensive (both in development and runtime cost) and not as generally useful (e.g. keeping an arbitrary history of revisions). Replace etcd backend with some other backing store. This would require a bit of research. ## Global Sequence Number Etcd updates need to be globally ordered, i.e. if a KV pair "a" got modified after a KV pair "b", it would have a later sequence number. This is needed so that a single number could represent a consistent point in time. Assuming we cannot rely on TrueTime, all modifications need to go through global coordinator that would sequence them. The sequence coordinator needs to do 2 things: Allocate sequence ids, in such a way that higher sequence id can represent later modification. Serialize completions in the order of sequence ids (so that all operations with lower sequence ids complete before operations with higher sequence id). The easiest way is to forward all requests to the leader, so that the leader can do sequencing. In normal processing, sequence id allocation is just an in-memory increment. After the sequence id is allocated, the leader can forward the request to the corresponding shard processor. The leader would keep track of completed sequence ids (just a counter) and if a request completes out-of-order, it would hold completion until previous requests complete. For example, suppose there are 3 requests and the current sequence id is 42, and completed id is 42. One of the requests would get id=43, another would get id=44, and the third one would get id=45. Then if the request with id=45 completes first, the leader would hold it. Then if request with id=44 complete. the leader would hold it as well. Then when the request with id=43 completes,

[IDF Design Documents | K8S DB Requirements]
id=45. Then if the request with id=45 completes first, the leader would hold it. Then if request with id=44 complete. the leader would hold it as well. Then when the request with id=43 completes, the leader will see that this follows the completed id, increments completed id and returns result to the client. After that the leader can process completions of the requests with ids 44 and 45. If the request to the node processor fails, the leader would send a read request to get the result of the operation. It will keep trying until the read succeeds. The operation completions with later sequence ids are going to be held until the previous operations results are fully known. When the leader crashes and another node becomes a leader, the new leader needs to learn the completed sequence id from shard processors. It would fanout the requests to the shard processors, shard processors would wait until pending operations are completed and then return the last sequence id known to them. The leader would then take the max as the global completed sequence id. To prevent any pending operations from completion later, the leader would have a term id that is incremented every time leadership changes. The shard processors will remember the term id of the new leader and reject any operation that comes with the old term id. The globally sequenced watches are registered on the leader. The leader pushes the results to the watch queue in the order of completion, so there is global ordering between
