## Consistent Point-in-time Queries To support point-in-time queries, we'd need to keep multiple revisions of records. One way to do it is to keep Cassandra WAL per shard. Each update of a sequenced entity would go to the WAL first (both new version and preimage), then upon success, the operation is completed and the entity can get to the entities CF in the background. The reason preimage goes to WAL is to simplify log truncation. The old revisions are stored in memory, and on restart are recovered from the WAL. WAL is truncated from time to time, by starting a checkpoint, and waiting for some time (e.g. 5 min) to complete it (all records before the start will get deleted, but the 5 min of history will get retained). When checkpoint is started, we wait for all delta records to be completed. This is so that records are not reordered around truncation point (in general, records can be reordered, i.e. a later delta record could store an update with the smaller sequence id). Then in the checkpoint, we store the max sequence id that we've wrote to the WAL. If a request comes later with the id that is less than or equal to the max sequence id we store in checkpoint, we reject the request. After some time (e.g. 5 minutes), we complete the checkpoint and truncate the in-memory representation using the max sequence id from the last checkpoint. We immediately start the next checkpoint. In memory, old revisions are stored in the map sequence id -> entity, each entity would also have

[IDF Design Documents | K8S DB Requirements]
representation using the max sequence id from the last checkpoint. We immediately start the next checkpoint. In memory, old revisions are stored in the map sequence id -> entity, each entity would also have weak_ptr to previous version. When entities get truncated, they are just removed from the map, and would get destroyed. The sequence id that we use as the key is the sequence id of the next revision - 1. Let's consider an example. Suppose we have the following history: seq -> key#version 42 -> a#1 43 -> b#3 44 -> c#1 45 -> b#4 46 -> a#3 Then the latest entities (our current data structure) would look like this: {a#3, b#4, c#1}. The old version map would look like {45->a#1, 44->b#3) (45 is because a#3 has sequence id 46 and etc.). If a new update comes, say 47->c#2, then the latest would look like {a#3, b#4, c#2}, and the old version map would look like {46->c#1, 45->a#1, 44->b#3}. If we want to truncate such that the last sequence id we could retrieve is 45, then we remove all data with sequence id less than 45, so the the map would look like {46->c#1, 45->a#1}. For deleted entities, we'd need to keep tombstones in the cache (so that we could go back to previous versions), until the tombstone falls off history. So when we truncate deletions, we need to check if a tombstone needs to removed from the cache. The lookup for a point-in-time revision would go against the latest values (that would include tombstone), but if the latest sequence id is greater than the provided

[IDF Design Documents | K8S DB Requirements]
tombstone needs to removed from the cache. The lookup for a point-in-time revision would go against the latest values (that would include tombstone), but if the latest sequence id is greater than the provided point-in-time revision, we would follow the links until we find the value with the version that is less than or equal to the requested revision (if we don't find such a version, then the query would fail). To get a consistent query for the latest data, we'd ask the leader for the latest completed sequence id, and then use it as the argument for point-in-time query.

## Point-in-time Watches
All watches for globally sequenced entities are coordinated on the leader.  When a watch has a point-in-time sequence id, the watch is started at the current sequence id, but the fired watches are held at the leader.  Then the leader would get all events from shard processors that happened between the requested sequence id and the current sequence id.  The results are merged and sorted by the sequence id and then pushed to the watch queue, then the new fired watches are pushed, so that the client gets all fired watches in order.
When the shard processor gets the request to get all event is in the range (between point-in-time sequence id and current sequence id), it would get all entries from the latest version and old revision maps that fall into the given range.

[IDF Design Documents | K8S DB Requirements]
## Lease Manager
In etcd, the user can create a lease and associate KV pairs with the lease.  The lease is identified by a numerical id (just a number), and if it expires, all KV pairs associated with the lease get deleted.  The client can send keep-alive RPCs to extend the lease.  K8S actually doesn't use keep-alive RPCs, because it uses leases to implement TTL (i.e. it associates keys with a lease and lets it expire).
To implement leases, we can add lease id into entity metadata.  The leader would manage leases.  Creating a lease would create a row in Cassandra (could be an entity of a _lease_ type).  The lease would have an expiration time, and when the lease expires, the leader would broadcast requests to all nodes to delete all entities associated with the lease.  We need to check validity of lease and handle lease expiration race conditions, TBD.

IDF Update Workflow (Client side) June 2022 Chitti Ankith Summary: This document explains the client side semantics for creating / modifying an entity within IDF. Clients are expected to issue the UpdateEntity RPC while trying to create / modify an entity within IDF. If the entity object does not exist in IDF cache, then the RPC would be considered a create operation, otherwise it would be an update operation. The semantics for UpdateEntity RPC are described below: entity_guid : Specifies the pair of entity type and entity id of the entity to be created or updated. entity id is a unique identifier for each entity in IDF. It can be similar across entity types but each entity type would only have a single entity with the same entity id. timestamp_usecs : Timestamp of the entity update. If not specified, it is set to 1) 'created_timestamp_usecs' (see below) for a create operation if it is provided 2) Current server time otherwise. This timestamp is propagated to the replica DB when the entity is replicated. created_timestamp_usecs : The created timestamp of the entity. This field if set cannot be later than the modified timestamp of the entity. For new entities, if the 'created_timestamp_usecs' is not provided then it is set to 'timestamp_usecs' in the arg. If 'timestamp_usecs' is not set, then it is set to the server time. NOTE: The modified_timestamp of the entity is set to ‘time_stamp_usecs’ if specified, otherwise its set to the ‘created_timestamp_usecs’ if specified for

[IDF Documentation & Guides | IDF Update Workflow (Client side)]
If 'timestamp_usecs' is not set, then it is set to the server time. NOTE: The modified_timestamp of the entity is set to ‘time_stamp_usecs’ if specified, otherwise its set to the ‘created_timestamp_usecs’ if specified for creations. For updates modified timestamp is always inherited from the current entity in cache. expiration_timestamp_usecs : If set, the entity will be automatically deleted after the specified expiration time. If it is not set, the corresponding field of the entity set previously will be cleared. cas_value : Set if the entity is supposed to be a cas entity. For all such entities, the entity has to be created with a CAS value of 0 and the client should increment it every update by 1 for every update. Once the entity is created with cas_value, non CAS updates are rejected by the DB. Similarly, if the entity is not created with an initial cas_value, CAS updates are rejected by the DB. The below snippet shows an example of an entity being created as a cas_entity and with an expiration timestamp of 1hour meaning that the entity will get deleted after an hour. entity_guid { entity_type_name: "vm" entity_id: "entity_id" } cas_value: 0 expiration_timestamp_usecs: 86400 Since in the above example, timestamp_usecs or crreated_timestamp_usecs are not specified, they would be set to the current server time by IDF. On successful completion of the update, the cas value would be increased by 1 for succesive updates. attribute_data_arg_list : Repeated list of attribute

[IDF Documentation & Guides | IDF Update Workflow (Client side)]
they would be set to the current server time by IDF. On successful completion of the update, the cas value would be increased by 1 for succesive updates. attribute_data_arg_list : Repeated list of attribute values to be populated for the entity. Each attribute data in the list specifies the operation to be performed on the attribute i.e either clear the attribute or set it (default would always be the set op), and the attribute name and value. If the attribute is not registered against the entity type of the entity, a validation error would be thrown. Let’s say we want to update the above created entity with some attribute values, the RPC arg would be as shown in the following snippet: entity_guid { entity_type_name: "vm" entity_id: "entity_id" } attribute_data_arg_list { attribute_data { name: "vm_name" value { str_value: "blah_blah" } } } cas_value: 1 Since it’s a cas entity, the cas_value needs to be incremented. The above RPC arg would set the ‘vm_name’ attribute value in the entity. NOTE: attribute values can be set at the same time the entity is created. full_update : By default all IDF updates overwrite the current state of the entity in cache. This means that if an update comes in on some entity with certain attribute values set, any previously set attributes of the entity which are not part of the current update payload would get cleared. In order to avoid this behaviour, clients can set this field to true in order to specify only the changes in the entity so that

[IDF Documentation & Guides | IDF Update Workflow (Client side)]
part of the current update payload would get cleared. In order to avoid this behaviour, clients can set this field to true in order to specify only the changes in the entity so that the existing state of the entity is merged instead of overwritten. Say for the above entity, we issue an update as such: entity_guid { entity_type_name: "vm" entity_id: "entity_id" } cas_value: 2 attribute_data_arg_list { attribute_data { name: "node" value { str_value: "node_1" } } } This would cause the previously set ‘vm_name’ attribute to get replaced and the entity would only have the single ‘node’ attribute set. Storing zprotobuf and nested fields
Ricky Patel, Pradhyumna
June 2024
With time, clients started storing data as blobs in IDF. Storing data as a blob had the following issues:
Blobs have large sizes, leading to slower read and write operations and hence impacting the database performance
Difficulty in fetching the inner attributes
Querying and indexing blob is more complex and less efficient. Blobs are not easily searchable and cannot be partially fetched in most of the cases
Other database operations like sorting, filtering, and grouping can also not be easily performed on blobs

[IDF Documentation & Guides | Storing protobuf and nested fields]
## What is __zprotobuf__ Basically in IDF, each entity (similar to a row) has attributes (similar to columns). Some clients have data in the format of protos defined in the client-side interfaces/code. If they want to store their data in IDF, they have two options: Approach 1: Clients can define a new entity_type in IDF and register all the attributes/metrics to that entity type which are defined in the original proto Now, for creating entities, clients would have to fetch values for all the attributes from the original object and pass them as values to the corresponding attributes defined in the IDF proto like attr1:value1, attr2:value, attr3:value3, etc. in the UpdateEntityArg of IDF. This approach is pretty standard similar to other DBs where you just send the value for columns explicitly as you want to update Approach 2 (__zprotobuf__): Storing data as __zprotobuf__ along with nested fields. Using the __zprotobuf__ way, clients just pass their complete proto to IDF, and then based on nested field definition (attribute schema mentioning the proto field indexes), IDF will derive all the nested fields by looking inside the proto given by the client Clients can store compressed serialized protobuf in an attribute (let’s call it the base attribute). Clients can define the attributes of the original protobuf as nested attributes of the base attribute in the proto defined in IDF This attribute which stores the compressed serialized string can be given any name just like any

[IDF Documentation & Guides | Storing protobuf and nested fields]
attributes of the original protobuf as nested attributes of the base attribute in the proto defined in IDF This attribute which stores the compressed serialized string can be given any name just like any other attribute. __zprotobuf__ was the name used in some client libraries and everyone started using the same. __zprotobuf__ is not any special datatype/naming convention defined in IDF

## Advantages of using __zprotobuf__:
Easily store data of different proto objects in IDF
If clients want to convert from their proto format to IDF proto format, then there is no need to store value for every attribute/arg you can just pass a compressed proto of their format and it will automatically be converted to IDF format based on the nested field definitions
Clients don’t have to form the whole argument attribute-wise while updating an entity. They can just send the proto and read it back from IDF. Parsing to/from IDF RPCs arg/ret is not needed
When the client’s proto is huge and they only want to use a few fields for sorting/grouping/filtering then just mark them as nested and the rest of the proto remains compressed in IDF so saves some memory in these cases.

[IDF Documentation & Guides | Storing protobuf and nested fields]
## Disadvantages of using __zprotobuf__:
There would be higher CPU consumption both on the client side and server side (serializing and compressing on the client side, uncompressing and deserializing on the server side)
Even if the client wants to update just one field, they will have to update the entire zprotobuf. For all the remaining fields, the client will need to pass the old value otherwise the values of those fields will be lost as we overwrite the old zprotobuf entirely with the new one. This is because nested fields can’t be directly updated for consistency reasons
The above point restricts the client to use only the read-modify write mechanism whenever they want to update any data stored inside ​​the __zprotobuf__ attribute.

## When to use __zprotobuf__?
If clients have a large blob and want to store the entire blob in IDF then it is ideal to use zprotobuf as it will help in saving the total size
It will also be helpful when clients want to fetch only 2-3 attributes very frequently out of a large blob
Some things to keep in mind:
IDF is unaware of the data stored inside __zprotobuf__ and the actual definition of the proto. IDF extracts fields from the proto based on schema provided by clients (nested field index and data types mainly).

[IDF Documentation & Guides | Storing protobuf and nested fields]

If the value is kNone, then it contains uncompressed data and no need for decompression) and derive nested fields based on schema provided by clients. ## Problem:
Currently, we have the following config files for storing the entity_type and attribute definitions:
ntnxdb_client/installer/config/insights/entity_type_config.proto.template
ntnxdb_client/installer/config/insights/entity_attribute_config.proto.template

For some entity_types, the client team requires indexing on specific cluster types only.
Let’s say some client has registered entity_type “etype1” and attribute “attr1”. Let’s say they want to index this attribute only on PC and not on PE. Currently, we don’t have any such functionality. As a result, indexes would get created on PE unnecessarily. These indexes consume memory in IDF which could be potentially saved.
Currently, we are targeting to provide support for overriding only the attribute definitions.

[IDF Documentation & Guides | [ENG-685822] Independent Indexing on PE and PC]
## Solution:
We plan to have separate config files:

pe_override_entity_attribute_config.proto.template
pc_override_entity_attribute_config.proto.template
afs_override_entity_attribute_config.proto.template

pc_override_entity_attribute_config

## Introduction to Namespaces:
Namespaces are contained within an entity (can be considered as sub-entities, entities within an entity). The semantics of each namespace is similar to what we have for an entity today: a namespace has its own set of metadata (like cas value, timestamps) and attribute data.  Attribute namespaces let different clients add different attributes in the same entity. It provides a Merge solution - to save data from different sources in the same entity without stepping over each other. For instance, entities that have synced from PE to PC, can’t be modified directly on the PC. In such cases, a namespace can be registered on the PC and all the new data can be written into the namespace. Each namespace can be created / deleted / updated atomically, but there are no atomicity guarantees across namespaces.
The "primary" entity's data is contained in the default namespace, which mostly has the same semantics as any other namespace within the same entity, with one notable exception: when the default namespace is deleted, all other namespaces attached to the entity are deleted as well.

[IDF Documentation & Guides | IDF Namespaces - V1]
mostly has the same semantics as any other namespace within the same entity, with one notable exception: when the default namespace is deleted, all other namespaces attached to the entity are deleted as well.

Namespaces are to be used to persist subordinate data (data that exists only when the primary data exists). If the data to be stored needs to have its own life cycle, i.e can be created/deleted independent of the primary entity, then it should not be represented as a namespace. One use case for namespace is: an entity is mastered in PE and replicated to PC. On PC, though the primary entity can’t be modified, users can add new attributes in a namespace to manage it.
‘Sub-entity’ & ‘namespace’ will be used interchangeably in this doc.

## Indexes:
Indexing for namespace attributes is supported for all attributes other than pseudo attributes. The metric schema is very similar to that of an attribute in the default namespace. The metric schema for the required namespace attribute should have the ‘is_index_column’ set to true.
Sample metric config:

[IDF Documentation & Guides | IDF Namespaces - V1]
## Creates and Updates:
Attribute namespaces can be created/updated via UpdateEntity RPC like how _default_ namespaces are created/updated. We need to set the namespace field in UpdateEntityArg. As of today we can only update namespaces one at a time via UpdateEntity RPC.
IDF stores both the primary and sub-entities/namespace in the same cache entity in IDF(Insights Object). Hence concurrent updates on primary / multiple namespaces for the same entity are not allowed. Updates to more than one namespace for the same entity can’t be sent in a single BatchUpdateArg rpc.
Each namespace has its own set of metadata (like cas value, timestamps) and attribute data. And the metadata of namespaces is independent of each other. A sub-entity can be created with a cas-value even though the primary entity may not be a cas entity. Another point to note here is that the modified timestamp of the parent doesn't get updated when the sub-entity is created / modified.
Example:

[IDF Documentation & Guides | IDF Namespaces - V1]
## Deletes:
Deleting the primary entity would cause all the existing namespaces to be deleted as well.
In order to delete a specific namespace, we just have to mention the namespace name in the DeleteEntityArg.
Sample query:
Note that on deleting a namespace, we will still maintain the metadata of the namespaces in a tombstone like we do for parent entities. We do this so that we can restore the cas_value on recreation of deleted namespaces.
Sub-entities will be auto-deleted and purged together with primary entities. Setting expiration_timestamp_usecs for a namespace is not valid.

## Reads:
Currently, GetEntities RPC returns the complete entity including the namespaces. Retrieving individual sub-entities is not supported. But GetEntitiesWithMetrics RPC supports scoping for namespace attributes.

[IDF Documentation & Guides | IDF Namespaces - V1]
## Watches:
Currently we only support watches on the operations on the default namespace. We don’t support watching individual namespaces or the entity as a whole.
When a watch gets triggered, FiredWatch will contain the whole entity along with all the namespaces.
Going forward we have plans to enhance watches and provide features to watch on individual namespaces and the entity as a whole.
Doc link for planned watch related changes: Doc Link

## Sync:
As of now namespaces are not synced and also not backed up.
The typical use case of sub-entities is when an entity is replicated from PE to PC, services on the PC can add some additional information to that entity, despite the fact that the entity is replicated. As of now, we clear sub-entities before replication such that sub-entities are only meaningful locally to a cluster. The same semantics also apply for backup and restore.
NOTE: While replicating an update for an entity, we don't overwrite any existing namespaces on the synced entity.

## Rolling Upgrade Scenarios:
We disable all the namespace related registrations, creates, updates and queries while IDF is upgrading from a version that does not support namespaces to one that does. Once the upgrade is done all namespace operations will be allowed as usual.

[IDF Documentation & Guides | IDF Namespaces - V1]
## Limitations from external services:
Apart from some of the missing feature support mentioned in above sections. This covers the missing support from external services for client planning to consume namespaces:
As stated above, sync is not supported for namespaces. Hence PCDR of namespaces is not supported as of today.
Note: The design discussions are in progress. Will be picked up soon.
Query layers like groups, v4 platform currently don’t offer query support from attributes inside namespaces. Clients will have to write their own custom logic to handle it as of today.
This might create problems to display or use this data for UI pages directly.
Pulse data collection is also currently not supported for namespace data.

IDF query evaluation Shrivatsan April 2018 Currently, the query processing pipeline is as follows: 1. Evaluate the filter/where clause. 1a. Fetch the where columns. 1b. Perform where clause evaluation. This gives us the set of query entities. 2. Create buckets for the entities, and add the entities to the corresponding groups. 2a. Fetch group by column. 2b. Depending upon the type of groupby, create groups for the entities (either continuous, discrete or ancestor). 2c. Depending on the value of the groupby column, segregate the entities into created groups. 3. For the entities in the groups, fetch all the requested 'column' values. This includes the aggregate columns as well. 4. Perform aggregation of 'aggregate' columns. 5. Sort and limit the response. The way we evaluate the filter clause is as follows: - Query layer caches a copy of all the entities. For each entity (of the query entity type) in the set of entities 'query_entities_', fetch the values for the where 'columns' in the query. - Store {entity type, entity id, metric name} -> DataValue of the metric in map ‘filter_metric_values_’. - For each entity in 'query_entities_', evaluate the expression. If the expression evaluation fails, remove the entity from 'query_entities_'. - At the end of expression evaluation, 'query_entities_' contains all the entities that match the boolean expression. In this document, we propose a more performant approach where instead of iterating over every entity and evaluating the boolean

Semantics of Derived Metrics Computation
Pradhyumna, Aryan Rai
May 2024
This doc is to explain the high level semantics of Derived Metrics based on a given comparison expression.
Derived Metrics relies on the following constructs:
They are always computed on the fly
Derived metric is only computed for timestamps where the data is present for all the source metrics
Derived metric data is first computed and then downsampled
In a divide by 0 case, the derived metric value is treated as 0

## Derived Metric computation:
Consider the following example where:
metric1 has ds interval of 20 secs
metric2 has ds interval of 30 secs
derived metric formula is (metric1 + metric2). Check “Config 1”
Since the derived metric is calculated only when both the values are available:
So value of derived metrics will only be present at time intervals of LCM of the base metrics

## Downsampling of kRaw derived metrics:
Consider the following example where:
metric1 has ds of 10 secs
metric2 has ds of 20 secs
derived metrics is (metric1/metric2)
So with derived metrics and downsampling on kRaw metrics,
raw values of the base metrics are taken first and then the raw version of derived metrics is computed
then the derived metric is downsampled as per downsampling operator and downsampling interval of the metric

[IDF Documentation & Guides | Semantics of Derived Metrics Computation]
## How is downsampling operator decided?
IDF as of today provides 6 downsampling operators: Link to definition
kSum, kAvg, kFirst, kLast, kMin, kMax
For downsampling operator, this is order of priority:
if there is a down_sampling_operator passed in the raw_column during query
query_down_sampling_operator present in the metric configuration
down_sampling_operator present in the metric configuration
kLast is the default downsampling operator
Check the code snippet below for examples.

## How is downsampling interval decided?
For downsampling interval, this is the order of priority:
if there is a down_sampling_interval_secs passed in the group_by of the query
down_sampling_interval_in_secs if set in the metric configuration
30 secs is the default downsampling interval
Check the code snippet below for examples.

## What are kHourly metrics?
For all the metrics stored in IDF, we store the hourly downsampled values if opted
There is one value stored every hour, with all the downsampling operators applied. Which is 6 values per hour for a given metric (check the above section of downsampling operator)

[IDF Documentation & Guides | Semantics of Derived Metrics Computation]
## So when are kHourly metrics used?
When a query is made with the following conditions, then we read the kHourly metrics:
ds_interval is explicitly set to kHourly instead of kRaw
down_sampling_interval_in_secs set in group_by is a nonzero multiple of hour
down_sampling_interval_in_secs set in group_by is greater than flag value of  “min_threshold_hrs_for_hourly_downsampling” (default 5)
So the computation will be similar to kRaw where now the values will be present at the start of applicable hours. But the question is which downsampled metric (out of 6) will be considered for the source metric for the computation?
For kHourly cases, the downsampling operator of the derived metric will be used to pick the value from the 6 ds value present in the source metrics.

## Derived metrics and latest queries:
In latest queries(meaning if no time-range is specified), the metric data is returned for the last
few down_sampling_intervals of the derived metric. How many numbers of intervals is decided in this order:
If num_intervals_for_latest_data is specified in the query.
Else, the default value of 10.
For derived metrics, the source metrics are fetched for the time-range of:
[curr - num_intervals_for_latest_data*down_sampling_interval of derived metric, curr)
Now the derived metric is computed for the range and then downsampled.

IDF cache eviction logic Chitti Ankith Cache overview : IDF cache (defined here) is a singleton class which can be used to store key-value data, where the key is a string and the data can be a shared_ptr to an arbitrary type. We maintain a single instance of unevictable cache, and 17 instances of the evictable cache (insights_cache_num_shards). Every object inserted into the evictable cache is sharded based on its key in order to determine which cache it needs to access. The cache maintains two queues namely single-touch and multi-touch LRU queues. When an item is first inserted in the cache, it is inserted into the single-touch LRU queue. When the item is accessed a second time, it is promoted to the multi-touch LRU queue. This provides scan resistance because a scan accesses many items exactly once and all these items pollute only the single-touch LRU queue and not the multi-touch queue (which over time accumulates the most accessed items). The ratio of the multi-touch LRU queue size to the single-touch queue size is configurable via a gflag. (multi_touch_pct) The cache supports pinning of certain items. Pinned items are not evicted from the cache until they are unpinned. After a formerly pinned item is unpinned, it is placed in the single-touch or multi-touch LRU queue, depending upon whether it was accessed once or multiple times in the past. Eviction of items in the cache can be done explicitly by using the Evict() call or it is done automatically when memory runs out.

CASCADING REPLICATION CONTROL (CRCL)
OVERVIEW
Cascading Replication Control List (CRCL) enables IDF clients to define a
complete replication path by specifying an ordered chain of replication
control entries within a single block.
Each replication control entry defines:
- enable_replication_from : Source cluster type
- enable_replication_to   : Destination cluster type
CRCL supports multi-hop synchronization by allowing multiple replication
control entries to be chained in order. CRCL provides more capabilities than Replication Control List (RCL), while fully supporting all functionality provided by RCL. Existing RCL functionality remains supported for backward compatibility.
EXAMPLE
If a client wants to enable synchronization for the following paths:
1) PE → ID → PC   (multi-hop)
2) ID → PC        (single-hop)
The entity schema would look like:
OPTION 1: MIXED USAGE
(Single-hop via RCL, Multi-hop via CRCL)
OPTION 2: UNIFIED USAGE
(All paths expressed using CRCL)
KEY POINTS
- Single-hop synchronization can be expressed using CRCL.
- CRCL supports both single-hop and multi-hop replication paths.
- The existing replication_control_list field remains supported for backward compatibility.
- CRCL is the recommended approach for new multi-hop configurations.

IDF-IDF Sync Workflow
Jineet Desai
Apr 2022

## Introduction
The IDF-IDF sync workflow is responsible for near real-time entity data replication from a source to its replicas. (for eg. sync vm entities to PC from all the registered PEs). Currently IDF-IDF sync does not support syncing stats data, for which we have Arithmos - IDF sync.
Some highlights of IDF-IDF sync:
Near real time replication : If all the IDF services are running fine we expect the entity updated on source to sync in almost real-time to the destination.
Eventual consistency: Sooner or later we end up syncing the entity data from source to destination.
Catch up on failures: If the replication to replica fails due to some failure(connection/transport failure), IDF sync catches upon those failures and tries to make the replica side same as that like source.

## Replication Paths Present
PE ⇒ PC : Sync entities like vm,alerts,tasks,etc
PC ⇒ PE : Sync the DR entities, lincense_info, etc
Xi Portal ⇒Xi PC
Minerva ⇒ PC

[IDF Documentation & Guides | IDF-IDF-Sync]
## Sync Pipeline
Services running as a part of sync pipeline on their respective ports of CVM: InsightsServer(2027), InsightsUploader(2029), InsightsReciever(2028)
General IDF sync pipeline is as follows:
InsightsServer on c1 pushes the updates on InsightsUploader of c1 (UploadData)
InsightsUploader of c1 pushes these updates to InsightsReciever of c2 (RemoteDataTransfer)
InsightsReceiver of c2 pushes these updates to InsightsServer of c2.
Various transport services available are Mercury, Aplos, Prism Gateway. Since 5.17 mercury is used as the transport service for all PE->PC, PC->PE related sync replication paths. Mercury gateway runs on port 9444 of CVM. Before that Prism Gateway was used as a transport service for PE->PC sync.
NOTE: Currently as a part of recent change we may merge the InsightsReciever service into InsightsServer itself. Refer to https://jira.nutanix.com/browse/ENG-200560 for more details.
PCDR uses the same sync pipeline for its backup and restore workflow. We have separate backup uploader and restore uploader running for this. Workflow for an insights uploader process is determined by the following gflag: insights_uploader_workflow_mode

[IDF Documentation & Guides | IDF-IDF-Sync]
## Cluster Registration Whenever a PE gets registered to a PC, Prism creates a zookeeper node: /appliance/physical/clusterexternalstate/<cluster_uuid> on both PE and PC. PC cluster_external_state zk node will have child nodes corresponding to all registered PE cluster uuids and PE cluster_external_state zk node will have child node corresponding to the PC cluster uuid. Given below is a 1 node PE - PC connection. These zk nodes are watched via Zookeeper watches by Insights Server. Even RC entities are created upon PE/PC and XiVM/PC connection. InsightsUploader watches upon these RC entities through IDF watches. Currently we monitor the PE->PC connection end-points via the cluster external state zk node whereas for PC->PE, XiVM->PC, Minerva->PC connections the source uploader watches on the RC entities. The replica side always uses the cluster external state zk node to read the connection endpoints. Code reference: Link Upon cluster registration the insights server on the replica side loads the existing entities(hidden entities) and the replicated ranges corresponding to the connected cluster from Cassandra. When cluster unregistration takes place, the zk nodes and RC entities would get deleted. Insights server on replica side would unload all the replicated entities from cache(would hide those entities, not delete them from Cassandra). Insights Uploader on source would stop pushing any data further. NOTE: As a part of recent change with the deprecation of RC for PC->PE

[IDF Documentation & Guides | IDF-IDF-Sync]
from cache(would hide those entities, not delete them from Cassandra). Insights Uploader on source would stop pushing any data further. NOTE: As a part of recent change with the deprecation of RC for PC->PE connections, we will now watch on the cluster external zk node for PC->PE connections. Refer to https://jira.nutanix.com/browse/ENG-461086 for more information.

[IDF Documentation & Guides | IDF-IDF-Sync]
## Regular Sync Workflow Insights Uploader consists of the following three inner classes: Channel : The channel manages multiple endpoints and sends data (calls the RemoteTransferData RPC) to one or more endpoints from the uploader. Transfer Batcher: Transfer batcher batches multiple requests to transfer data from Uploader of source to insights server of replica. Its batches request until the data size of request exceeds threshold or there is a heartbeat timeout in which case the batched data is sent to the Channel. Bootstrapper: It is responsible for handling the bootstrap/catchup workflow wherein we load the data for missing ranges from Cassandra and send it to replica. Normal sync flow diagram: When an entity gets updated on the source side, the source insights server checks whether the update needs to be replicated to the replica, and makes a UploadData RPC call to local Insights Uploader(in case of backup workflow, it's the backup Uploader). The update range covered by the UploadData call will be the (last_used_oracle_timestamp, current_db_modified_timestamp of shard]. Insights Server method that makes this call : MaybeForwardEntityToUploader(https://sourcegraph.canaveral-corp.us-west-2.aws/ntnxdb-master/-/blob/ntnxdb_server/insights/insights_server/store/insights_store_entity.cc?L2101). We create an uploader interface only for normal workflow and backup workflow. There is no uploader interface for restore workflow since it has only static backup data to send and hence

[IDF Documentation & Guides | IDF-IDF-Sync]
call : MaybeForwardEntityToUploader(https://sourcegraph.canaveral-corp.us-west-2.aws/ntnxdb-master/-/blob/ntnxdb_server/insights/insights_server/store/insights_store_entity.cc?L2101). We create an uploader interface only for normal workflow and backup workflow. There is no uploader interface for restore workflow since it has only static backup data to send and hence uses only the bootstrap part of IDF-IDF sync. We remove the namespace fields, if any present in the entity being sent(since currently we do not support sync for namespaces.). We even modify the backup entities to contain the backup prefix in their entity type name. We send data to the uploader with 2 types of priorities 1) kUrgent(if any entity update is being sent) 2) kNormal(if there is no entity update to send, we just fulfill the missing ranges of the uploader). The uploader Transfer Batcher batches these updates from insights server and fires the RemoteTransferData RPC under 2 scenarios The batch size exceeds 10 MB(insights_uploader_batch_size_kb) Urgent or normal update timeout triggers(insights_uploader_batch_urgent_timeout_msecs~200ms, insights_uploader_batch_normal_timeout_msecs~30s) NodeRemoteTransferData calls the ReplicateRemoteData store method. ## Bootstrap Workflow Bootstrapping happens when a new cluster is registered to replicate the existing entities on source to replica. Bootstrap logic is also used to catch up on missing updates from source if the regular sync workflow for updates fails due to some connection issue, transport issue, etc. Bootstrapping is triggered by the Insights Uploader on source by sending a heartbeat(RemoteTransferData call) to the replica Insights Server. Insights Server on replica responds with a list of unreplicated ranges(RemoteTransferDataRet) to the source uploader. Insights Uploader on source stores/queues these unreplicated ranges and requests the entities corresponding to these ranges to the local Insights Server by issuing a LoadEntityTrail RPC call. The LoadEntityTrail RPC call would scan these entities from Cassandra and return the ( fulfilled ranges, entities) to Insights Uploader. Insights Uploader on source would then make RemoteTransferData RPC calls to the replica with these entities and fulfilled ranges. There are restrictions on the amount of data syncing/the number of entities syncing at a given time in bootstrap Insights_uploader_bootstrap_send_size_kb ~ 16MB Insights_uploader_bootstrap_send_num_entities ~ 3000 The number of RemoteTransferData RPC calls during bootstrap is also limited by the following flags Insights_uploader_max_bootstrap_rpc_queue_length_per_endpoint : Calls limited to one replica per node ~ 36 Insights_uploader_max_bootstrap_rpc_queue_length_total :

## Active Entities Workflow Active entities are the current set of entities that are present in the source Insights DB. Consider a situation where an entity E gets replicated from source to replica through IDF sync. Let's assume that the connection between source and replica now gets disrupted(i.e. IDF sync stops). During this time entity E got deleted and purged from source. Now the connection resumes again. Presently E would be present on replica but would not be present on source. Since E would be missing from the source Cassandra, there is no way LoadEntityTrail can detect the deletion of E and E would continue to exist on the replica. As a solution to this problem we send a list of active entities on source periodically to replica, to do a comparative existence check and delete entities from replica that do not exist on source. The Insights Server on replica has a timeout from when it last received active entities information for a given shard(determined by FLAGS_insights_active_entities_ info_ttl_secs ~ 6hrs) and responds to the RemoteTransferData RPC call with an active entities info request. Uploader on source takes a note of this and queues a LoadActiveEntities request for that shard. It then issues LoadActiveEntitiesInfo RPC to the source Insights Server to get a list of active entities on shard by scanning Cassandra. Once the Uploader receives the current entities on the shard, it makes a RemoteTransferData RPC call to the replica InsightsServer with an

[IDF Documentation & Guides | IDF-IDF-Sync]
to get a list of active entities on shard by scanning Cassandra. Once the Uploader receives the current entities on the shard, it makes a RemoteTransferData RPC call to the replica InsightsServer with an active_entities_list. Replica Insights Server compares the replicated entities with the active_entities_list in the RemoteTransferDataArg, and deletes the entities which are not present in the active_entities_list. ## Oracle Timestamp V/S Latest DB Modified Timestamp Oracle Timestamp: The oracle timestamp provides a hardened timestamp where it guarantees that the timestamps are unique and monotonically increasing (can be considered a strictly increasing monotonic function). It has 2 aspects: Like a physical timestamp, it is wall time based(or server time based). Like a logical timestamp, it provides strict sequencing. The Oracle Timestamp object provides a method CurrentUsecs to get the current timestamp and the previously used timestamp. The return value of this method is the current timestamp that satisfies the strict increasing ordering defined by the timestamp oracle. It uses the following formula to get the db_modified_timestamp values during entity updates db_modified_ts = max(last_used_oracle_ts + 1, current_time=Walltime). Latest Db Modified Timestamp: The Latest Db modified timestamp contains the maximum of all the ‘db_modfiied_timestamp_usecs’ of all the entities owned by the shard(including all the deleted entities as well). When an update/delete to an entity is successful(PutEntitySuccess/DeleteEntitySuccess) we issue a call to InsightsCommonStore::UpdateLatestDBModifiedTimestamp(shard_id, db_modified_ts) to update the latest db modified timestamp for a given shard. This info is made to use when setting the sync_barrier_info for a sync barrier update. From the formula mentioned above we can safely say that the Latest Db modified timestamp value is derived from Oracle

[IDF Documentation & Guides | IDF-IDF-Sync]
info is made to use when setting the sync_barrier_info for a sync barrier update. From the formula mentioned above we can safely say that the Latest Db modified timestamp value is derived from Oracle Timestamp value(since all the db_modified_ts are derived from it), however at a given point in time for a shard, these values may not be the same. An entity’s db_modified_timestamp that is obtained from the Oracle timestamp increments the value of Oracle timestamp irrespective of whether the update of entities succeeds in Cassandra or not, whereas Latest DB modified timestamp reflects just the last successful update for a given shard. WHY USE LATEST_DB_MODIFIED_TS VALUE? For eg. Let say an entity e1(shard_id = s1) got updated at time=t1 sec, and due to some reason the update to Cassandra failed. The Oracle Timestamp would surely reflect this value. Let say at time=t2 (>t1) a client issues a sync barrier update on some entity e2(shard_id=s2). Now lets say the insights server fetches the latest Oracle timestamp for all the shards(instead of latest_db_modified_ts) and puts them in the sync barrier info of e2. Now the timestamp that would be set for shard s1 would be t1. If the client does not retry update for entity e1, then the sync-barrier update for entity e2 would be stuck indefinitely on the replica, since for shard s1 the updates would not have been synced up to time=t1 on replica. Hence we use the latest db modified ts that just reflects the time of the last successful update

since for shard s1 the updates would not have been synced up to time=t1 on replica. Hence we use the latest db modified ts that just reflects the time of the last successful update for a shard.

## Sync Barrier Workflow As discussed in the previous section, we maintain the latest_db_modified_timestamp for each shard after a successful update. Even during bootstrap or shard loads, we go through all the entities and update this value for a shard if needed. Now when a sync barrier entity is updated, we fetch the latest_db_modified_timestamp for all the shards(residing on different nodes) through the NodeGetSyncBarrierInfo RPC. Then the latest_db_modified_timestamp info for each shard is stored in the sync_barrier_info field of the sync barrier entity object. The sync barrier entity will have this field set for all 128 shards. After update on the master goes through, the sync barrier entity arrives on the replica side and it will go to the node that holds the shard that the sync barrier entity belongs to. Here it will check whether the IDF-IDF sync replication has caught up to at least the timestamp value for each of the shards in the sync_barrier_info of the entity(i.e. the latest_db_modified_timestamp). The replica maintains the sync barrier processing information which holds the first missing replication range for each shard of the node (it's called the first_range_starts_cache). If for any shard, the first missing range is earlier than the latest_db_modified_timestamp value in the sync_barrier_info of the entity, this means the replication hasn’t caught up. The sync barrier check will fail and the entity will be added to a sync_barrier_queue. However if the sync

[IDF Documentation & Guides | IDF-IDF-Sync]
latest_db_modified_timestamp value in the sync_barrier_info of the entity, this means the replication hasn’t caught up. The sync barrier check will fail and the entity will be added to a sync_barrier_queue. However if the sync barrier check passes, then the entity will be replicated. Snippet for sync barrier criteria check: In order to process this sync_barrier_queue, we send NodeSyncBarrierWait long poll RPCs to each node. It checks whether all the shards owned by that node have caught up to the timestamp value mentioned in the sync_barrier_info field of that shard. The RPC returns either after all shards are fulfilled or either after it times out. We then iterate over the queue and replicate all the entities for which the sync barrier condition is fulfilled. If some entities still remain in the sync barrier queue, then we fire another set of NodeSyncBarrierWait RPCs and wait for the sync barrier condition to get fulfilled.

## Deleting Replicated Entities IDF provides a feature for users to delete synced entities of certain entity types on the replica. In usual cases IDF would throw an error saying “Cannot update replicated entity”. We have certain fields in the EntityType proto which can help us enable this feature. allow_entity_deletion_on_replica: This flag indicates whether IDF should allow deletion of replicated entities of this entity type on the replica or not. This flag would allow only the existing replicated instance to be deleted on the replica i.e. if the entity is deleted on the replica and a subsequent CUD operation comes on the source for this entity, then the entity would still sync and become available on replica. direct_purge_on_replica_delete: This flag indicates whether to directly purge the entity on replica deletion. If set to true, IDF will directly auto purge the entities which are deleted on replica irrespective of whether the entity has been deleted on source. If false, we wait for the entity to be deleted on source in order to purge it from replica. We also maintain an in-memory replica_deleted_map for maintaining all entities whose entity types allow deletion on replica but do not allow direct purge on replica (i.e. allow_entity_deletion_on_replica=true and direct_purge_on_replica_delete=false). IDF Watches - Client Guide
Pradhyumna K
March 2024

## Introduction to IDF watches:
IDF Watches is a non-persistent notification mechanism for clients to get updates on IDF metadata(entity types and metric types) and config data(attributes). IDF watches provide diverse functionality such as watching over: an entire entity type, single entity, single attribute across the table, updates satisfying a filter criteria or a certain type of operations (C/U/D or composite). Watches offer near real-time delivery of watches under no-error scenarios.
As mentioned above, IDF Watches don’t offer any persistence on updates and there is no guarantee of updates during the time when the session gets reset.
Let’s look at some of the constructs and guarantees of a watch client.

## Watch Client:
The Watch Client objects present in Java, Python, CPP, Golang abstract session creation, polling for updates, ensuring updates are not being dropped etc. Letting the client focus on just handling the updates and Watch Reset scenarios.
Clients provide callback functions while registering watches and the updates are provided as arg to callback functions.
A Watch Client offers the following operations to be performed:
Register & Unregister Watch Client.
Multiple Register & Unregister Watches
Start & Stop streaming the updates

[IDF Documentation & Guides | IDF Watches - Client Guide]
## Register Watch Client:
The first step of the Watch Client initiation is the client registering the Session on the server. All the operations pertaining to the Watch Client are only performed as long as the Session is alive.
Each Watch Client establishes a new session with the server with a Watch Client Name and Session ID.
The Watch Client Name is expected to be unique across the IDF cluster.
It is strongly recommended to avoid using UUIDs/random strings as WatchClient name on every watch create because that might cause watch client leaks lie undetected and tough to catch.
The Watch Client object can only serve one Session and no operations can be performed on the Watch Client once the session expires. 
(Except for golang implementation, where it can be reset using Reregister method).
Once the registration is done, users can start performing actions on the Watch Client.
Implementation detail:
In C++ and Golang, users have to specifically call the Register() method to register a Watch Client.
In Python and Java, initialization of objects ensures that registration of Watch Client is done.

[IDF Documentation & Guides | IDF Watches - Client Guide]
## Watch Client Reset & Unregistering: “Watch Client Reset” means the current Watch Client Session getting terminated. Session can be terminated under the following conditions: A new session registration with the same Watch Client Name. Insights Server or Client is restarted (on any of the nodes) Client explicitly chooses to Unregister the watch client. Server/Client chooses to terminate the Session due to various error scenarios. Once “Watch Client” is “Un-regeristered”, server stops keeping a track of all the updates and no further actions can be taken on the client. All the ongoing operations like RegisterWatch/UnregisterWatch and Start will result in a failure. Error callback will be invoked in other languages and the client should reset the Watch Client. “Watch Client Reset” can happen due server/client session termination in the following scenarios: Any one of the nodes in cluster going down (especially during upgrades) Node addition or node removal workflows on the current cluster. Any IDF instance getting restarted. Updates between IDF <-> IDF nodes or IDF <-> Client getting dropped due to timeouts. Client not able to sustain the rate of updates and the pending updates growing beyond thresholds. Lack of communication from client to server over a period of time. Watch Client sends a long poll request for updates after Start(). In cases of CPU starvation, Client might not even get the CPU required to make calls. This will result in a Session termination. Note: Failure

[IDF Documentation & Guides | IDF Watches - Client Guide]
sends a long poll request for updates after Start(). In cases of CPU starvation, Client might not even get the CPU required to make calls. This will result in a Session termination. Note: Failure of the Unregister Watch Client method can be treated as a no-op. Because the client is automatically registered when the Watch Client objects are destroyed.

## Watch Client Reset handling:
Clients will have to create a new Watch Client and have to again perform the actions performed on the previous Watch Client. All the updates during this time will be lost and the user is expected to reconcile with the state present in IDF after the reset. These updates won’t be delivered to the client after registering the Watch Client again.
Once a watch client throws a reset error. Clients can skip Unregistration of the watch client.

## Register & Unregister Watches:
More than one watch can be registered under a Watch Client.  Once registered, the watch keeps working till the Unregister is performed or the watch client session ends. Re-registration of watch need not be done on every update.
Watches can be registered on the following:
Schema Watches (Schema changes in IDF).
Registration/modification of Entity Types and Attr/Metric Types in IDF.
Entity Watches (Config data in attribute.)
Any modifications to existing entities present in IDF.
The user can perform an UnregisterWatch for a given watch if the updates are no longer required.

[IDF Documentation & Guides | IDF Watches - Client Guide]
## Schema Watches:
User can choose to watch to have one or more of the following functionality:
Creation of any/a new entity type
Update on any/a entity type
Registration of any/a new metric type for any/a entity type.
Update of any/a new metric type for any/a entity type.
Ordering of Schema Watch: updates is guaranteed to be the same as occurred on the server side. And the server guarantees to provide all the operations, hence all the state transitions of the schema.

## Entity Watches:
Entity watches provide the following functionality and can be used in combination:
Watch on changes on entire entity type or a single entity
Watch for one or more operations of Create/Update/Delete. (Composite Watches in Entity Watches)
Watch for changes on entire entity or a single attribute
Pseudo attributes aren’t supported.
Watch on actions which satisfy a given filter criteria (Filtering in Entity Watches)
This can be done by providing a where_clause on attributes of the entity
Limit the attribute data in the entity to certain attributes (Projection in Entity Watches)

[IDF Documentation & Guides | IDF Watches - Client Guide]
## Ordering guarantees of Entity Watches:
Ordering of updates of a particular entity are delivered to client in the same order as happened on the server
However, there is no guarantee provided across multiple entity types. Reordering of updates can occur.
All the state transitions of an entity are returned, there is no batching or grouping of updates 
(However replicated entities have different constructs. Refer to Sync section for more info)

## Previous State/How will I know what changed in an update?
Both Entity and Schema watches allow the user to choose to get the “Previous State” along with the new state. Which means if the entity changes from s1 -> s2, by default the watch callbacks only provide new state s2. Upon requesting for a previous state, s1 will also be provided to the client. So that client can take actions based on what changed in the entity.

## Current State/What if updates happen while RegisterWatch is in progress?
There can be some modifications to the data while registering a watch. Register Watch lets the client prevent the scenario of missing updates by providing the option of “Current State”. While registering the watch the user can choose to get the “Current State”, which will give all the data. For example, all the entities are returned when a watch is registered on the entire entity table requesting “Current State”.  And from that state of data, all the updates are guaranteed to the user.

[IDF Documentation & Guides | IDF Watches - Client Guide]
## Start & Stop:
Start() and Stop() are WatchClient level constructs which instruct the Client to start and stop streaming the updates respectively. Start() and Stop() can be executed only once in the entire lifecycle of a Watch Client.
Note that callbacks are always invoked sequentially per watch client.

## Start vs Register Watch/ What’s the difference? Won’t I get updates after registering watch?:
A RegisterWatch call will only instruct the server to start collecting the updates on the server side. The client will start fetching the updates from the server and invoke callbacks only what Start() is invoked. If a RegisterWatch is performed after Start() is executed, then updates can be expected to be delivered once the RegisterWatch call is a success.
Once Stop() has been executed on the Watch Client, no other actions can be performed.

[IDF Documentation & Guides | IDF Watches - Client Guide]
## Synced data and Watches:
Because of the guarantees offered with the sync layer there are a few scenarios which needs to be specially handled for Entity Watches:
Missing exact state transition updates as on source:
On PE, suppose the entity went from 0 -> s1 -> s2 -> s3. If a user has registered a watch on PC and lets say the sync wasn’t functioning during this time due to network failure. After a while, when the sync resumes the PC will directly get the entity created with state s3. So there will only be one Create Watch fired as:(null /* previous_state */, s3 /*current status*/)
During non-failure scenarios, usually all the states are updated to PC and hence all the watches would be triggered.
Unregistration of cluster is not considered as deleting synced data:
For example, consider the ‘node’ etype on PC. These entities are populated in IDF via sync workflow, hence when a PE is unregistered the ‘node’ data will cease to exist on IDF for all client use-cases. However a user who has registered a delete watch on ‘node’ won’t be getting notifications that the ‘node’ entities corresponding to that cluster have been deleted.
Re-registration of cluster might not be considered as creates or updates:

[IDF Documentation & Guides | IDF Watches - Client Guide]
who has registered a delete watch on ‘node’ won’t be getting notifications that the ‘node’ entities corresponding to that cluster have been deleted. Re-registration of cluster might not be considered as creates or updates:

For example, in the above case consider 2 nodes n1 and n2 with state n1-1 and n2-1 when the cluster got unregistered. Consider the user has registered a Create Watch and an Update Watch on the ‘node’ table. When the cluster got reregistered, assume the states are n1-1 and n2-2 (meaning n2 has a different state now)
In this case, only an Update Watch will be fired for entity ‘n2’. Neither Create Watch for n1 or n2 will be fired.
Missing Delete updates for an entity due to network interruption:
On PE, suppose an entity got created and deleted like this: 0 -> s1 -> d1. If the user has registered a Delete Watch on the PC on this entity and there was network interruption during the entire time. When the network gets back to normal, the delete would be sync to PE and an entity tombstone is created. In this case delete watches are not fired unless clients opt-in using this field: link.

## Options provided wrt sync:
To help clients handle sync workflow, IDF Watch clients in all languages are given an option to get a Watch Reset on a cluster registration/unregistration so that the user can reconcile with the new state of the DB.

[IDF Documentation & Guides | IDF Watches - Client Guide]

Since PC will be receiving data from SMSP, the following zookeeper path needs to be populated, corresponding to SMSP:

## Index memory consumption:
Today, we use DataValue as the key to r-Index maps in memory. This is very inefficient because we always enforce IndexMaps to always have data of only a certain type. An empty DataValue itself is observed to take around 48 bytes. For indexes on fields like timestamps, this would be unnecessarily huge consumption of memory. However for indexes on large string fields, this might not give much benefits.

Explanation:

The upgraded IDF should know that data migration is in progress and do not start another data migration due to a newer data format. IDF should wait for the on-going data migration to be completed. An example is data migration from leader-only to scaleout is in progress and the software is upgraded to a version that stores the evictable entities in mongoDB. To accomplish this, IDF needs to persist the current data format and the target data format (if any) in Zookeeper node. If the target data format is present, it means data migration is in progress. Once the data migration is completed, the current data format will be set to target data format. The target data format will either be removed or set to a newer target data format. The second decision is which IDF instances should perform the data migration for scaleout IDF. There are two choices. are two choices. The first choice is the IDF leader reclaims back all the shards and the IDF leader performs the data migration. The second choice is the IDF instances who own the shards perform the data migration for the data in the shards. The second choice should be more performant due to higher parallelism. Thus we will go with the second choice. To accomplish this, IDF needs to persist the data migration status for each shard so that when the shards are assigned to new IDF instances, the new IDF instances know whether the data migration is completed for the shards. The third design decision is during data migration, the target store can have partial data set. To avoid resolving conflicts between the data from target and source store during bootstrap or query time, it is easier to keep the data in source store and always query from the source store. Data Migration Workflow During startup, the IDF instances load and watch the data format protobuf from the Zookeeper(data_format_zknode). If the Zookeeper doesn’t allow watches on a non-existent zk node, the first IDF instance will create data_format_zknode with uninitialized values so that watches can be set of the zk node.

[MongoDB Integration | Data Migration To MongoDB]
During the IDF leadership callback or during Zeus configuration callback, the IDF leader updates the data format protobuf if the value is uninitialized and adds the target data format if data upgrade is needed. This is only done when the cluster has at least kEvictableEntityInMongoDB upgrade version (a new upgrade version) and not in the middle of software rolling upgrade and there is no on-going data migration. If software rolling upgrade is in progress, the IDF leader registers the callback which will be invoked when the upgrade version reaches kEvictableEntityInMongoDB. The IDF leader also creates the list of shards with status Uninitialized for the data type that needs to be upgraded. Upon receiving Zookeeper notification on new target data format, the IDF instances will wait for 60 seconds for any writes from previous incarnation to be finalized in the persistent store. Then the IDF instances will first get the sync barrier lock to stop further updates and wait till all the updates to be done. Then the IDF instances will wait for 60 seconds for the in-progress updates in the persistent store to be completed. The IDF instances will update the status of the shard to StartedMigration in the Zookeeper node. The state StartedMigration allows IDF instances to start data migration immediately without waiting for another 60 seconds again if the IDF instances restart. After this, the IDF instances will copy the data from source store to target store in batches. After each batch

migration immediately without waiting for another 60 seconds again if the IDF instances restart. After this, the IDF instances will copy the data from source store to target store in batches. After each batch copy, the IDF instances will persist the progress info in mongoDB. This enables the IDF instances to continue copying the data from where they leave off if restarts happen. After all the data has been copied, the IDF instances will update the shard status to Migrated. Once all the shard status has been set to Migrated, the IDF instances will wait for at least 50 seconds (20 seconds for Zeus notification to all the nodes + 30 seconds for on-going query) before starting purging the data from the source store and from the memory, including indexes. The IDF instances will also start serving the query from the target store and allows data updates. Once the shard data has been purged from source store, the IDF instances will update the shard status to Done. After all the shard status is Done, the IDF leader will update current data format to target data format. [MongoDB Integration | ENG-275464_ IDF_Mongo integration_ Implement filtering of entities based on shard-id_]
## Background
The notion shard is originally designed for the purpose of data distribution in IDF. Only the owner of the shard will be able to process the request for that shard, while others (non-owner) will forward the request to the owner. However, as the first release for IDF-Mongo integration, we haven’t got to the phase of sharded Mongo data, so it is tempting to think we need not keep the shard anymore. Unfortunately, other than the reason mentioned above, we do have some other logics relying on this functionality.
For IDF-IDF sync, the sync pipeline is also on the basis of a shard, including heartbeat, missing ranges tracking, active entities tracking, etc. This works naturally with the existing sharding mechanism. If we remove the sharding, the sync feature will be heavily impacted. For example, to fetch data of one shard, we will need to do a full scan of a collection in Mongo, and then do the filtering in IDF.
Furthermore, IDF has exposed the shard information to clients (GetEntitiesWithMetricsArg::shard_id_list here), so that clients will be able to do filtering based on shards. For example, UDA (Alerts team) has built some features based on this functionality.
With these being said, shard is still necessary for IDF.

[MongoDB Integration | ENG-275464_ IDF_Mongo integration_ Implement filtering of entities based on shard-id_]
## Indexing
Solution 1
Since shard information is not needed by all data, it is unnecessary to index the shard_id for all entity types. To determine which type needs the shard_id to be indexed, we can expose an option in the config file, such that clients can opt to index as needed.
message TypeInfo {
optional bool is_shard_aware [default = false];
}
For types to be synced via IDF-IDF sync, we can internally add the index for them instead of specifying the field in the config file, since clients do not need to understand this.
The only concern is if later we determine to shard on all types (e.g. we need to integrate the IDF shard with Mongo shard), it will be moot to have such a field in the proto.
Solution 2
We can just hardcode this logic to force indexing on some specific types (e.g. VM, types with suppress_replication=false …, etc).
Solution 3
We can expose the shard_id as a pseudo attribute. Then enabling the indexing on shard_id is nothing different than indexing on a pseudo attribute. This also requires internal logic to force enabling the indexing on shard_id for replication types.

## Other Changes
Add the shard_id when persisting to Mongo, similar to the entity_id, tenant_id, etc.
Query layer needs to parse and process the shard_id_list.

[MongoDB Integration | ENG-280288_ IDF_Mongo integration_ Grouping on list values]
As currently implemented, the group-by on list values is not supported: MongoDB would treat the whole list as a single value, instead of work on each element of the list.
This can be solved by utilizing the $unwind operator in MongoDB aggregation pipeline. If the field has a singular value, it will be treated as one element array by $unwind.
I did a simple experiment on a setup with 257K entities with an average size of 5.5KB. All attributes have a singular value.
From the table below, there is no obvious relationship between the latency and the number of attributes being unwinded. This reveals the fact that it does not introduce significant latency unwinding singular value.
(The index does not really help the $unwind operator as it is doing the COLLSCAN here)
Due to the fact that IDF does not enforce the type of the value of an attribute - we can have attribute Foo with both singular value and list value in the same table, we may unwind all group-by columns to cater for both singular and list values in this case.

[MongoDB Integration | ENG-280288_ IDF_Mongo integration_ Grouping on list values]
## Future work
According to the documentation of Mongo:
Each document is identical to the input document except for the value of the sizes field which now holds a value from the original sizes array.
It means $unwind will pass <X * N> (X as the number of input documents, N as the number of values of the unwinded field) documents to the next stage.
If we group-by 3 attributes, each has a list value with 10 different elements, $unwind all 3 attributes will process 10 * 10 * 10 = 1000 times the number of original documents.
The actual impact of this needs to be further investigated.

[MongoDB Integration | EntityGuid]
EntityGuid
Entity Guid consists of entity type, entity id and tenant id. Since we have a collection per entity type, we only need entity id and tenant id for the entities in the collections. MongoDB supports string and binary data types. String should be utf-8. However MongoDB allows writes and reads of binary data on string data type. The equal operator also works. The operators that do not work are regular expressions and document conversion to Json because Json does not support binary data.
IDF clients usually use UUID in string format for entity id because the clients would convert the protobuf to Json and pass it to external clients through REST API. Since IDF doesn’t use regular expressions on entity id and tenant id and doesn’t convert documents to Json (only for vlog), it is better to store entity id and tenant id in string data type for debuggability through Mongo shell. However, IDF should handle the case of binary data as entity id because there is no enforcement. Below are four approaches for storing entity id and tenant id in MongoDB. We consider two main operations when designing the indices.
Find entities through entity ids.
Find entities through tenant ids.
We choose approach 1 because it should be the best.

[MongoDB Integration | EntityGuid]
## Approach 1
_id: auto generated id (20 bytes)
entity_id: usually uuid in string format (36 bytes)
tenant_id: uuid in string format (36 bytes)
Unique compound index on <entity_id, tenant_id>
Finding entities through entity id can utilize the compound index. Since the cardinality of tenant id is small, the index range scan should be fast. We do not create an index for tenant id because currently we only support single tenancy where tenant id should be the same for the entities of the same type. Collection scan should be equal to index scan in this case. This can change in future when multi-tenancy is supported.

## Approach 2
_id: auto generated id (20 bytes)
entity_id: usually uuid in string format (36 bytes)
tenant_id: uuid in string format (36 bytes)
Unique compound index on <tenant_id, entity_id>
Index on entity_id
This is worse than approach 1 because of an extra index. When multi-tenancy is supported, approach 1 is still better because the index size of tenant id is smaller than the index size of entity id. The reason is the cardinality of tenant id is lower than the cardinality of entity id.

## Approach 3
_id: <entity_id, tenant_id> (36 + 36+ 1 separator = 73 bytes)
tenant_id: uuid in string format (36 bytes)
The idea is to use the default index on _id and prefix match the entity id when finding the entities. This won’t work because MongoDB prefix matching only works on utf-8.

[MongoDB Integration | EntityGuid]
## Approach 4
_id: { entity_id: uuid1, tenant_id: uuid2 } (around 32 + 32 = 72 bytes)
tenand_id: uuid in string format (36 bytes)
The idea is to use the nested document as _id to avoid an extra index. The assumption is wrong because by default MongoDB will create an index on _id which can’t be used to find the entities using only entity id. An extra compound index is needed on the entity id and tenant id in the nested document.
