Evaluation of InfluxDB

## Why
As we are investing into MongoDB as the backend, significant effort went into proto-typing, validating, benchmarking the time series model by storing the stats using mongo documents.
InfluxDB is one of the most widely used and claimingly highly scalable open source time series DB, it will be good to use it as a reference point to compare if there are any significant red flags and show stoppers in our proposal of using MongoDB as the backend.

## How
We tried to evaluate the basic functionalities and quantify the perf/scale in the following perspectives, we also tried to use the same baseline data set so that we can draw some meaningful comparison to our current mongoDB time series model.
Underlying Storage Engine
DataModel
Data Ingestions.
Data storage.
System resources usage.
Usability and debug-ability
Query performances.  (TBD)

[MongoDB Integration | Evaluation of InfluxDB]
## Storage Engine The InfluxDB storage engine is based on LSM Tree implementation (which uses Level Compaction algorithm. It has a write ahead log and a collection of read-only data files which are similar in concept to SSTables in an LSM Tree. TSM files contain sorted, compressed series data. Cache - The Cache is an in-memory representation of the data stored in the WAL. It is queried at runtime and merged with the data stored in TSM files. TSM files are a collection of read-only files that are memory mapped. The structure of these files looks very similar to an SSTable in LevelDB or other LSM Tree variants.TSM files store compressed series data in a columnar format. Compactor - The Compactor is responsible for converting less optimized Cache and TSM data into more read-optimized formats. It does this by compressing series, removing deleted data, optimizing indices and combining smaller files into larger ones. So, in general, influx DB shares some similar characteristics as our own Cassandra data store and will likely show incremental penalty in terms of disk IOs when datasizes grows bigger due to compaction, TSM uses Level compaction algorithm (Level 1-4), a new data point will have to re-written multiple times in order to traversing to the final Level 4 TSM table. And should the updates happen, multiple copies of the data point will likely be stored in TSM table, It’s unclear at what degree that a full compaction will be triggered to merge all the duplicated data or query

[MongoDB Integration | Evaluation of InfluxDB]
happen, multiple copies of the data point will likely be stored in TSM table, It’s unclear at what degree that a full compaction will be triggered to merge all the duplicated data or query performance will likely suffer because it will have to read all the data and discard the old version. Key take aways is influx might be good for real time stats use cases, but might not be suitable for the analytics data use cases as the same perf /scale issue might arise should the data size becomes significant.

[MongoDB Integration | Evaluation of InfluxDB]
## DataModel Influx’s data model is fairly simple and each every data point that is pushed into influxdb is model after a JSON like structure as the following: { "measurement": entity_type, "tags": { "entity_id": entity_id, "week": week, }, "time": timestamp, "fields": { Metric_1 : value1 Metric_2 : value2 ... } } measurement - is equivalent to the table or collection in MongoDB that we know. tags - metadata that are associated with each data point that user might be using for querying, grouping etc., All tags are indexed, and all the fields that a user intend to use for GROUPBY operation needs to be placed in tags. But it’s unclear how exactly the index work, (e.g. like a composite index or works individually). The measurement + tags tuples uniquely identified a unique time series that is queryable. time: Time stamp of the data point(s). fields: Actual value of one or many metrics, fields are not indexed. This structure has a lot of similarities to IDF’s dimension fact table, which allows a client to push multiple data points for multiple entities at the same time. InfluxDB seems to advised against put a high cadinatilities values in tags due to exhaustive memory usage of the indexes of high values count: https://docs.influxdata.com/influxdb/v1.7/concepts/schema_and_data_layout/#discouraged-schema-design Also, InfluxDB seems to have a hard limit on the cardinality we have in a single database. For example, during my evaluation, influxDB seems to start rejecting new data

[MongoDB Integration | Evaluation of InfluxDB]
of high values count: https://docs.influxdata.com/influxdb/v1.7/concepts/schema_and_data_layout/#discouraged-schema-design Also, InfluxDB seems to have a hard limit on the cardinality we have in a single database. For example, during my evaluation, influxDB seems to start rejecting new data whenever the cardinality reaches 1Million and work around is creating multiple databases but it is quite cumbersome in terms of deployment or orchestrations. The impact of memory usage is characterized in the following benchmark result: https://www.influxdata.com/blog/the-effect-of-cardinality-on-data-ingest-part-1/ https://www.influxdata.com/blog/path-1-billion-time-series-influxdb-high-cardinality-indexing-ready-testing/ From this article, it appears that influxdb has addressed this issue by some degree in making the index evictable, however, it’s unclear what’s the performance impact of the DB should the index gets cold and flushed to disk, whether the entire indexed needs to be bootstrap from the disk in order to effectively serve the requests. This cardinality issue in our use case may be worked around by putting shard ID in the tag and flatten the entity ids into the fields (without index), this is conceptually equivalent to our by_shard row column family. In the case of Mongo, large indexes for btree index can be partially loaded into memory for the value ranges of queries. One noticeable limitation on InfluxDB data model is once a measure field is written with some value of type X,

[MongoDB Integration | Evaluation of InfluxDB]
btree index can be partially loaded into memory for the value ranges of queries. One noticeable limitation on InfluxDB data model is once a measure field is written with some value of type X, it can’t be changed and will be strictly enforced, it will start rejecting accepting data should it comes in with different type.

## Data Ingestions
Influx supports 2 basic mechanism to ingest data  1) HTTP (rest) API 2) Bulk import API through CSV, for all the practical purposes of integrating with other services through programmatic interfaces, HTTP API is probably the only way to push data into influxDB.  All the available “drivers’ are built on this HTTP protocol which internally transmit the influx Line Messages to the server to ingest data.  (Java; https://github.com/influxdata/influxdb-java  C: https://github.com/influxdata/influxdb-c  ) and some of them seems quite outdated.
The HTTP protocol supports ingestion for multiple data points it’s unclear what’s the max limit on the number of data points per message (subject to the http message transmit limit).

[MongoDB Integration | Evaluation of InfluxDB]
## Disk space usage
I couldn’t manage to successfully ingest the entire 2 hour worth of prism metric data set (100Mil data points) into the influx due to various reasons (i.e. high cardinality tags etc), but from the values that manage to get into the system, we can extrapolate the disk space usage for the data set is around 500-600MB which is quite comparable with MongoDB  -490MB.  Data compression was enabled in both cases.  The measured disk IO is actually more than MongoDB case probably due to the data compaction.

## Memory usage.
Influx supports configuration that limit the cache memory usage through this setting:  cache-max-memory-size, however it appears that it failed to honor this setting, at least it appears that during the heavy load of data ingestion, the memory usage of influx might go much higher than being specified and there seems to be no clear way to explicitly control it. For example, the RSS of influxdb shot up to as high as 10GB when I continuously ingest data for the 2 hour worth of data set which is much bigger than IDF evictable cache, In the case of mongo DB, I managed to perform the ingestion with just 2GB of wire tigher cache without observing any noticeable churn on the disk/CPU usage.

[MongoDB Integration | Evaluation of InfluxDB]
## Usability and debug-ability
Influx supports SQL like query language allows client to easily drill into the data set for debugging purposes. The same query language is also supported through HTTP API, it’s not conclusive whether any other native query driver is supported.

## Horizontal scaling
Open source version of influxDB does not (in contrast to tools like Cassandra and Elasticsearch) come with support for distributed deployments (clustering), despite the fact that the underlying database was designed for it. You need to upgrade to the paid InfluxEnterprise or InfluxCloud versions to distribute your database across node.

[MongoDB Integration | Handle the group sort and limit for multi-dim groupby queries [In Progress]]
The group sort and limit in multi-dim group-by query is different in IDF and MongoDB. In IDF, the group sort and limit are supported in the innermost layer, while in MongoDB, they are for total groups. For example:
group by <foo, bar>, sort on <bar, desc>, limit = 1
e1: foo: "a", bar: 1
e2: foo: "a", bar: 2
e3: foo: "b", bar: 3
IDF return:
group<a>
<2> e2
<1> e1 (this will not be returned because of the limit)
group<b>
<3> e3
MongoDB return:
group<b, 3>: e3
group<a, 2>: e2
group<a, 1>: e1 (e1 and e3 will not be returned)
The group<a, 1> and group<a, 2> will be in separate groups, and the sort will be across all groups (irrespective of the other group-by fields, i.e. "foo" in this example). So after the group limit 1, only one group will be returned.

IDF Attribute Type Scraper Script

## Motivation
As part of IDF’s migration to MongoDB as a backend, we are planning to deprecate a number of attribute types from IDF (see design doc). In order to do this successfully, we must ensure that clients of IDF will not be impacted by this change. As a part of this process, we want to identify which entities in IDF have attributes of these forbidden types.

## Goal
Use a script to scrape a system test cluster and obtain representative data-set from IDF. Identify the entity types of all entities containing attributes of forbidden types.

[MongoDB Integration | IDF Attribute Type Scraper Script]
## Flow

## Current data models and challenges On-disk data model For a given resolution (e.g. raw, hourly) IDF persistence data model stores metrics data hourly chunks in one of the two column families: metric_data_by_shard - (data of multiple entities of the same hour on the same row) metric_data_by_entity. - (data of multiple hours of the same entity on the same row) metric_data_by_shard column family was designed to efficiently retrieve stats for a large group of entities, metric_data_by_entity column family was designed for efficiently answering point queries of one or small number of entities over a long time period of time. We store duplicate data set in two CFs assuming there are sufficient use case for either one which can provide significant benefit over another. However, the benefits seem to be diminished for the following points: Most of the use cases for real time stats are limited less than just a few recent hours of data, so either by_entity or by_shard read doesn’t appear to have a significant edge over one or another. We are taking significant penalty of extra disk space usage by maintaining duplicate data set. by_entity CF row number grows with the scale of entities, which leads to increased burden on cassandra maintaining the meta/indexed in memory. To fully assemble a by_entity row of data for a week for real time stats, the row will be updated written upto 168 times (number of hours in a week). That leads to significant compaction cost and write amplifications.

In-memory data model IDF maintains metric data hourly chunks uniquely identified by <entity_type, metric_type, entity_id, hourly_time> tuple. Dirty metric chunks stays pinned in memory for up to an hour, anticipating continually filled with new data points till the hourly chunk is fully assembled. However, this caching model doesn’t work well for analytics data, in which case, data chunks are usually ingested fully assembled for the entire range. As a result, IDF consumes a significant amount of memory resources holding the dirty metric data.

## Sharding strategy We need to decide on the mechanism to partition the metric data collections properly, and ideally we would like to have data affinity from the IDF logical shard(s) to the physical mongo shard running on that node for the following reasons. In the case of wildcard group by queries, which could land on any of the IDF nodes, the node will fan out the query to all IDF node to distribute the query. Assuming data that is stored in IDF node has an affinity to the logical shard that it owns, then the fan out request will just fetch data from local MongoD process without having to traversing to one or many network hops to other remote mongod shards. As we see in the later sections, if we were to go with the document model of storing metric data from multiple entities in the same doc. Multiple document updates might be involved from multiple IDF nodes. If the logical shards of IDF is bound to the physical data partition of a mongod shard). Then the data ingestion request will be forwarded to the owning IDF node which subsequently translate into a consolidated update request. One way to accomplish this data affinity is the following: IDF can remain the orchestrator of the logical shards assignment/placement logic, which means IDF owns the decision of the shard set to node mapping as in the case today The mongo collection can then be sharded using a shard key that have embedded the IDF shard ID information. Using mongo zone-sharding configuration (https://docs.mongodb.com/manual/tutorial/manage-shard-zone/) IDF can assign a unique zone tag(s) for each individual mongo shard. (i.e. one zone for each mongo shard) as part of the shard assignment workflow. IDF can then push down that shard-map → zone knowledge through sh.addTagRange API that maps the document that contains the specific IDFs shards to the mongo shard. When the cluster topology permanently changes (i.e. add node, remove node), IDF will perform shard map reassignment which will subsequently push the updated shard key ranges to zone tag through sh.removeTagRange and sh.addTagRange calls. MongoDB shall perform the automatic chunk migration to the new zones that the chunks are mapped into. Once this is all configured, the data that belongs to a certain shard key will always confined to the node that maps to the zone that shard key belongs to, hence the data affinity from IDF logical shard to the mongo shard. For the RPC that needs data affinity (such as PutMetricData), the request will be forwarded to the node that owns the shard to process, so that the write/read request will not again traverse to other remote node. Dec 10, 2020
(IDF-Mongo) Retain Attributes for Deleted Entities

## Overview
Recently, we have seen an on-call where the client had accidentally deleted some entities from IDF. We want to make sure that we don't clean up the attribute_data_map for such entities so that they can be resurrected at a later point in time if needed.
Today, when entities are deleted in IDF, the corresponding document in the Mongo store is modified so that:
The deleted timestamp field (“_dts” in Mongo) is set to indicate when this entity was deleted
The entity is replaced with a new entity which contains only the following fields from the old entity:
Entity ID
Tenant ID
Shard IF
Created timestamp
Modified timestamp
DB Modified time
Some of the above fields are updated to reflect the deletion as well. There are other fields which are optionally kept as well (source).

## Design
Introduce the GFLAG “insights_retain_all_attributes_on_deletion”, which controls whether this feature is enabled.
If this flag is set to true, then when IDF is processing a DeleteEntity, it will copy all fields from the old document to the new document, instead of just keeping the fields listed above.

[MongoDB Integration | IDF-Mongo Retain Attributes for Deleted Entities]
## Implementation
In the Mongo driver, find_one_and_update takes an optional argument `projection`. If this is not provided, then the operation will not do any projection on the found document. Instead, it will return it with all fields present. See the documentation for more details.
For entity deletion: modify InsightsMongoStore::StoreDeleteEntityFromShard so that if this flag is set, do not construct a pipeline for the `project` argument, but instead pass an empty BSON document. CHANGES BELOW IN RED.
On entity recreation: modify InsightsMongoStore:PutEntityToShard to not do a partial update when creating entities

Deprecating IDF Entity Types incompatible with MongoDB
1st September 2020

## WHAT
As part of IDF’s migration to MongoDB as a backend, we will only be supporting entity/attribute types that are native to MongoDB. Namely:
int64
double
bool
string
byte strings
Lists of any of the above
In particular, moving forward, we will be deprecating these types:
uint64
float
We have not yet decided which release we are going to target for this change. We are currently benchmarking performance and running regression tests to close the functionality gap between Cassandra-backed IDF and Mongo-backed IDF.

## WHY
MongoDB is a NoSQL database which stores data in a BSON format. When clients put an entity to IDF, the corresponding protobuf must first be converted into BSON before being handed off to MongoDB’s storage engine. Since MongoDB supports only a limited set of types, any incompatible types must be converted to a compatible type. Specifically:
Float type is converted to Double
Uint64 type is converted to Int64
This is problematic for two reasons:

## Problem 1
Since int64 has a smaller range than uint64, an exception may be thrown by Mongo if it is given a value too large.

[MongoDB Integration | IDF-Mongo Type Deprecation]
## Problem 2
IDF does not guarantee strict typing–there is currently no way for IDF to “remember” the types of data given to it. As a result, when clients then do a subsequent get, IDF will return protobufs with fields of types that do not match what the client expects. For example, see JIRA ENG-319209:
This behavior is legal (but not intended) as a side effect of how our RPC Protobufs are formatted. See insights_interface.proto:420
Here, DataValue fields are generic in the sense that they can accept any value type. Therefore, it is permissible for IDF to populate responses to GetEntities with whatever type it receives from Mongo, regardless of the client’s type requirements.

## Build functionality to maintain type consistency from Put to Get
This is the worst solution, as it will require IDF to somehow “remember” the data type of each field. Since Mongo does not operate on a schema, we would have to add an extra “Type” field for every single data field stored. This quickly spirals out of hand.

## Notify clients when a type conversion happens
This is also impractical. When doing a put operation, Mongo does not return the entity persisted. Therefore, IDF would have to do a “fetch after put” to confirm whether a conversion has occurred, which seriously affects performance. Avoiding this path by hard-coding these errors does not fix Problem 1 above.

[MongoDB Integration | IDF-Mongo Type Deprecation]
## Deprecate all incompatible types
Double type has more precision than float type, so changing these should not cause issues for clients. On the other hand, changing uint64 to int64 may be problematic. If clients require the extra range of uint64, they may store data as blobs (byte strings) or some combination of fields. However, clients would then lose the ability to do any filtering (i.e. where clause, group by, aggregation).

[MongoDB Integration | IDF-Mongo Type Deprecation]

## Write Path Before Optimization (Vanilla non-Paxos column family) Single PC: 1 replica Scale out PC: 3 replicas The write is persisted in commit log for durability (1 disk write). The write also goes to the memtable. Once the memtable is full, the memtable is flushed to disk as sstable (1 disk write). In the background, compaction combines multiple SStables (can be more than two SStables, usually 4 to 8) to one SStable. After compaction, the input SStables are deleted. Compaction removes garbage and combines the columns for rows. If all the columns for a particular row are in a single SStable, read will be faster. The compaction selection policy is size based. Cassandra will try to compact a few of similar size SStables. Usually the small SStables will be compacted to medium SStables and medium SStables will be compacted to large SStables. This avoids compacting large SStables with small SStables which does not provide any benefits. A single row contains metric data for 1 week and each column has 1 hour of metric data, therefore there are 168 columns in a row. The columns are written in different hours and should be in different SStables initially. Assuming 4 input SStables compaction, we need 5 compactions to compact the 168 SStables into 1 SStable. Worst case write amplification: 1 (commit log) + 1 (sstable) + 5 (assuming 4-way compaction) = 7 Scale out PC write amplification = 7 * 3 = 21 Time Series Column Family Single PC: 1 replica Scale out PC: 2 replicas

[MongoDB Integration | Metric Data Optimization]
+ 1 (sstable) + 5 (assuming 4-way compaction) = 7 Scale out PC write amplification = 7 * 3 = 21 Time Series Column Family Single PC: 1 replica Scale out PC: 2 replicas (investigating to keep only 1 replica for older metric data) The write skips the commit log and sacrifices durability. First Approach: Bucketize the SStables The row key-value pairs in the SStables also have expiration time information. The min and max expiration time is calculated for each SStables. The SStables are assigned to buckets based on max expiration time. When all the SStables in a bucket has expired, all the SStables in the bucket are deleted. Size based compaction only works on the SStables within the buckets. Cassandra doesn’t compact SStables from different buckets. When flushing memtables to the disks, the memables are split into different SStables based on buckets. Problem: The memtables can contain key-value pairs of different expiration time. Thus multiple small SStables can be created. This increases the number of compaction required to compact the small SStables and causes Cassandra to hit the max SStable limit (400 SStables per sub-shard for a column family). Second Approach: Reduce the number of SStables To resolve the issue in the first approach, Cassandra decides not to split memtable entries into multiple SStables based on buckets when flushing. Also, the memtable sizes are increased from 32 MB to 128 MB. Problem: This creates another problem where the SStables won’t get deleted until

Problem: This creates another problem where the SStables won’t get deleted until all the all the entries have expired. Since the entries can have very different expiration times, Cassandra holds on to a lot of stale data. Third Approach: Self Compaction (What we are using today) To resolve the issue in the second approach, a background scrubber is introduced. If the SStables contain many stale entries, the scrubber will perform compaction on the SStables themselves to remove the stale entries. ## Read Path
Row cache is disabled for time-series column family. Every SStable has 2 index files and a bloom filter. The 2 index files are used for level index where first level index points to a section in the second level index and second level index contains all the row keys. The first level of index and bloom filter is cached in memory. When reading a column for a row, Cassandra will read from the newest SStables to oldest SStables. It first checks the bloom filter whether the row is in the SStable. Bloom filters can be false positive but not false negative. If the row might be in the SStable, Casandra reads the first level index in the cache and figures out the section of second level index that should be read (1 disk read). If the row is not in the second level index file, then the SStable doesn’t have the data and Cassandra will continue with older SStables. Else, Cassandra reads the SStables for the data (1 disk read). If the column data is in the SStable, Cassandra returns the data to the client. Else, Cassandra will continue with older SStables. If the clients specify the column names, Cassandra will stop reading from older SStables once it gets all the columns.
Worst Case (assuming no compaction and 95% bloom filter accuracy): 5% of (number of SStables * 2 for index file read).

## MongoDB
MongDB uses WiredTiger btree (b+tree) as the storage engine. MongoDB internally creates record id for each document when writing to WiredTiger. An index from document _id to record id is created. Record id is monotonic increase. WiredTiger uses variable length internal pages and leaf pages for its btree. The pages are immutable. Modification involves read-modify-writes into new pages. When a leaf page changes, all the parent pages up to root have to be changed as well.
Writes will first go to the journal first and memory blocks (index and data blocks) are allocated and changed. Periodically (every 1 minute), checkpoint is taken by flushing the memory blocks to disks.
One key concept for btree performance is localized changes. The more localized the changes are, the more performance we get. Example is when two keys are far apart in the btree, modify the values for the keys requires reading and writing more internal and leaf pages. The worst case being 2x the pages being modified compared to the best case.
Another key concept is caching. If the pages are cached, then btree doesn’t need to read the pages from disks.
More info:
http://source.wiredtiger.com/mongodb-3.4/tune_page_size_and_comp.html
https://engineering.mongodb.com/post/breaking-the-wiredtiger-logjam-the-write-ahead-log-1-2

## Write Path
For new writes, MongoDB record id->doc btree writes will be localized since record id is monotonic increase. Index btree _id -> record won’t be localized if _id is random. In this case, if N new documents are added, the worst case is reading and writing N leaf pages for the index btree. If the _id is ordered, then only 1 leaf page needs to be read and written if all the new keys can fit into the a page.
For overwrites, the difference is the record id->doc btree needs to be read and written to new pages.

[MongoDB Integration | Mongo Container Infra Change]
The goal is to reuse the same Mongo container image for multiple components. Another goal is to support the PC with multiple data disks. To reuse the same Mongo container, the Mongo configuration is abstracted out of the Mongo container image. The clients specify the configuration through the Mongo configuration file. For example, idf mongo configuration file is located at /home/nutanix/config/mongo/ idf_mongod.conf. Genesis copies the Mongo configuration file to a data disk directory before starting the Mongo container. Genesis needs to copy the configuration whenever starting up the Mongo container because the configuration can change across software versions. The Mongo container mounts the data disk directory and picks up the configuration file in the directory. Different clients should use different component names for isolation. The component names decide the directory names in the data disk. This enables multiple clients to have different directories for different Mongo container instances. To support multiple data disks (vdisks), the first time Genesis starts up the Mongo container, Genesis will pick one of the data disks to be used for the Mongo container. Then Genesis persists the chosen disk id to disk so that same disk will be used subsequently. Todo: Delete old Mongod log files. Adjust Mongod wired tiger cache based on PC memory. [MongoDB Integration | Mongo for IDF  - FAQ]
Mongo for IDF - FAQ
June 2020

## Life cycle management (start/stop) of Mongo
Mongo will be deployed in a container on the PC and Genesis will manage the Mongo service on the PC.
See this doc on how to start and stop mongodb using Genesis:
<checking the commit id, commit date for Mongo>

## Entity types that going to reside in Mongo
All the evictable entity types are going to reside in Mongo.
Controlled by a flag: `insights_mongo_evictable_entity_types`. Ref: insights_common_store.cc#39
This flag should not be changed during the lifetime of IDF. The reason is the data migration to MongoDB can be completed and changing the gflag won’t trigger another data migration.

## Will evictable entity types have any entry in the IDF cache ?
No, not even the dehydrated evictable entity will be present in IDF cache. Cache is used during the duration of an update - to handle concurrent updates for watches purpose.

## Indexing of evictable entity type attributes
This will now be done by Mongo. Mongo will honour the IDF schema and index the same set of attributes. IDF cache will not have any index for evictable entity type entities.

[MongoDB Integration | Mongo for IDF  - FAQ]
## Nested fields
Before IDF persists the document(entity) to MongoDB, IDF expands the protobuf and populates the nested field values.
Mongo is not aware of nested field logic, so IDF expands nested fields before saving them to Mongo. Right now, the logic to recompute nested fields is not implemented (not sure if we get to do it in V1), but IDF will have to physically rewrite all entities if metadata for nested field changes.

## Schema Changes
<Adding/Switching new evictable entity type>
IDF only moves entity types in gflag insights_mongo_evictable_entity_types to MongoDB. New evictable entity types added after that won’t be moved to MongoDB.
<Adding new attributes >
This will update the metric type collection in MongoDB. It doesn’t impact existing entity documents in the MongoDB.
Behaviour relating to enabling and disabling indexes for attributes will remain the same. It will be done through schema file change. The IDF leader creates or deletes indexes in MongoDB based on the metric type definition. The behaviour does not change regarding dynamic addition of indexes. It will still be blocked by IDF. Mongo supports dynamic indexes, we are not using that feature right now.
Clients don’t directly interact with Mongo. All the schema related information is held by IDF. No changes in behaviour there.

[MongoDB Integration | Mongo for IDF  - FAQ]
## Resource constraints
We can define the memory limit for MongoDB. From experience, MongoDB can exceed the limit up to 512MB. Therefore, we need to have a higher memory limit for the container.

## Attribute level timestamps
Mongo does not persist attribute level timestamps. We just use the modified timestamp to maintain semantics.

## Thread count
<How many threads does Mongo have ?>
I do not know how many threads MongoDB has. IDF instances use connection pool to connect to MongoDB. Each instance can have up to gflag insights_mongo_max_connection_pool connections to MongoDB.

[MongoDB Integration | Mongo-Cassandra Feature Gap]
Mongodb vs. Cassandra IDF Feature Gap
This is a list of features or functionality which are intended to be different between Mongo-backed IDF and Cassandra-backed IDF

## Removing support for certain metric types
Along with the release of Mongo-IDF, we intend to remove support for attributes/metrics of the following types:
Uint32
Uint64
Float
Uint32_list
Uint64_list
Float_list
The initial problem was reported here (JIRA). A writeup of the motivation and action plan for this change can be found here.

## Raw sort with limit on non-indexed attribute for evictable entity
In Mongo-IDF, we are adding support for GetEntitiesWithMetrics with group-by clauses where:
The entity type is evictable, and
A raw limit is specified
A raw sort order is specified over a non-indexed attribute
This is not supported in legacy IDF. See the ticket here (JIRA). This type of query is not supported in Cassandra-IDF, and will be explicitly blocked (JIRA).

## Group sort over one of the aggregate columns for evictable entities
In legacy IDF, we only support GetEntitiesWithMetrics with group sort over an aggregate column for non-evictable entities. In Mongo-IDF, we will relax this restriction and allow such queries for evictable entities too.

[MongoDB Integration | MongoDB Retrospective Document]
MongoDB Retrospective Document The primary goal of MongoDB project is to utilize an open source database without further developing features like on-disk index and transaction in IDF. Initially Nutanix had the aspiration of rolling out MongoDB as a service to end customers. Thus the project also has the long term goal of building a team of people who are familiar with MongoDB and supporting the effort of MongoDB as a service. However the aspiration is no longer there. For Xi, we no longer want to introduce more services including MongoDB. For on-prem (ERA), MongoDB is not requested by customers and ERA team is focusing on PostgreSQL instead. We hit multiple query performance issues. Since the long term goal of MongoDB as a service no longer exists, it doesn’t make sense to invest in learning and fixing MongoDB, which is a huge effort. Therefore we decided to end the project. Lessons learnt: Evaluate technology based on target workload Although MongoDB is widely used in the industry and highly recommended by people who have used it, MongoDB is mostly used for non-critical workloads. In the paper “Tunable Consistency in MongoDB” published in 2019, 99.86% of the reads use read concern levels less than “majority”, which can return stale or uncommitted data. 84.14% of the writes use write concern less than “majority”, which can result in data loss. Meanwhile our use case requires high availability, strict consistency and fast query response time with least amount of resources. We

[MongoDB Integration | MongoDB Retrospective Document]
the writes use write concern less than “majority”, which can result in data loss. Meanwhile our use case requires high availability, strict consistency and fast query response time with least amount of resources. We should not assume that if MongoDB works for others, it should work for us. Verify documented behavior MongoDB documentation says it supports index intersection. However MongoDB rarely performs index intersection and only supports intersection up to 2 indexes. These behaviors are not clear and not documented. Also detailed information that is essential for evaluation is hard to get. For example, it lacks details about consistency behavior. When asking the questions to MongoDB, MongoDB folks would only answer our questions after we pay them and tried to convince us that we don’t need strict consistency. It took us a lot of time to figure out the consistency behavior by reading papers and emailing the authors of the papers. Hard to quickly conduct representative tests (hire people with deep understanding of MongoDB query optimizer) Even though the POC goal is clear - get all the queries, understand their performance requirements and test them using Mongo queries, this task is very difficult. IDF doesn’t know the complete set of queries and their performance requirements. Many teams issue IDF queries and the developers who wrote the codes have moved on. Database query optimization is complicated. Queries that are similar in nature like queries that have two filter

[MongoDB Integration | MongoDB Retrospective Document]
performance requirements. Many teams issue IDF queries and the developers who wrote the codes have moved on. Database query optimization is complicated. Queries that are similar in nature like queries that have two filter conditions can have different physical execution plans. Without deep understanding of database query optimization, it is hard to quantify the query performance. The only way to expedite the POC is get people that have a deep understanding of MongoDB query optimization. If not, we should invest time in learning and understanding MongoDB ourselves. Breadth first performance tests We focused on testing queries that are specific to IDF (raw results, total entity count, multidimensional grouping) because we expected performance degradation. We saw degradation and we focused on solving that. Strategy-wise it's a reasonable distribution of efforts to the areas of most risk. We assumed that queries that mapped 1:1 to Mongo queries would have performance in the ballpark and that was a wrong assumption. In retrospect, we should've gone breadth first and benchmarked as many queries as possible. Replacing a purpose-built database with a generic database is never going to be easy. It is almost guaranteed to have performance drop because a purpose-built database only needs to handle one workload really well. Database is a complex system. We should spend more time evaluating, testing and understanding a database system at a deeper level before using it. Better still is to

[MongoDB Integration | MongoDB Retrospective Document]
to handle one workload really well. Database is a complex system. We should spend more time evaluating, testing and understanding a database system at a deeper level before using it. Better still is to hire contractors/developers with expertise in the specific database. I hope we can apply the lessons learned when evaluating other database systems like Postgres, etcd and Prometheus.

## Poor Index Intersection Support
SERVER-13740. Index intersection is critical for database performance when there are many documents. Index intersection should produce the document ids that fulfill the filter conditions and the database only loads those documents from memory/disk. Index intersection has a huge performance impact when the index is selective. Since MongoDB has poor index intersection support, the workaround is compound indexes. The number of compound indexes can be much higher than the number of singular indexes with index intersection. For example, we need 24 compound indexes to cover all the queries that can be supported by 4 singular indexes. Therefore it is not a good workaround.

[MongoDB Integration | MongoDB Retrospective Document]
## Inefficient Index Scan
SERVER-23406. MongoDB uses different on-disk and in-memory formats for indexes. WiredTiger, the storage engine for MongoDB, caches on-disk format for indexes. When the indexes are consumed by the query layer, the on-disk format needs to be converted to in-memory format. This requires many memory allocations and deallocations, which makes using indexes ineffective. Therefore MongoDB prefers collection scan over index scan, which can result in loading unnecessary data to the cache when the queries can be covered by indexes.

## List Values Do Not Use Index
SERVER-37470, SERVER-32549, SERVER-45823. Without using index, list value operations like filtering and sorting are inefficient.

## Non Existence Check Do Not Use Index
SERVER-18861. This is critical if clients perform existence check on many documents without other filter conditions or filter conditions that are not selective.

## Covered Queries Not Supported on Certain Operators
Covered queries are important performance features of databases. With this support, databases can reply to the queries using only the indexes. Operators like $unwind, $type and etc. disable the use of covered queries.

## Read After Write Consistency
To achieve read after write consistency, we need to use lineralizable reads which translate to majority writes before returning the data to the clients.

[MongoDB Integration | MongoDB Retrospective Document]
## Replica Status
In replica set setup, we cannot differentiate between newly added replicas or replicas that are out of sync with the leader. In both scenarios, the replicas have “recovering” states. The only way is to scan MongoDB logs to differentiate the two. For replicas that are out of sync with the leader, we need to manually (can be automated by script) re-sync the replica with the leader again.

## Supportability
MongoDB community version is not supported.

For example, when updating “foo.a” and “foo.b” fields, IDF creates two subdocuments for foo, one contains a and another contains b. Instead IDF should create one subdocument that contains both a and b for foo. More details are in experiment 1. ## Categories of problems:
List value in filter - setIsSubset() is used. This is not going to use an index. We need to separate list vs singular value processing.
Group-by doesn’t use index
Convert group-by queries into 2 phases:
Fetch the values of group-by columns using distinct command
Sort / limit the values. (what if the group is empty / only contains deleted documents)
Send the group-by-column values as a filter in the second query - lookup query.
All indexed columns will be the first ‘index’ of compound index of:
<column_name, mcid, deleted_timestamp>
For total entity count, we can use _dts index.

[MongoDB Integration | Query_ groupby with raw sort & limit memory issue ($push)]
In our current implementation, if raw sort and limit are specified with groupby, we use $push to get all raw results and then do sorting and limiting inside IDF.
This will result in all raw columns of a group being gathered inside one gigantic document, exceeding the 16MB size limit (or even 100MB limit for the $push processing).
https://docs.mongodb.com/manual/core/aggregation-pipeline-limits/
This document discusses some potential solutions.

## Solution1 - Multi-phase query
This is similar to what we are doing right now in our query pipeline. In phase 1, we will try to get the entity_id and sort_column first. After doing the sorting and limiting, we fetch the rest raw_columns in phase 2.
The problem with this solution is that even only entity_ids may not fit in the 16MB limit.
16MB / 36 (uuid bytes) ~= 400K uuids.

## Solution2 - $slice
We can use $slice to split the raw_columns into batches and query them separately.
We need to make sure that the order of $group -> $push is fixed, so that $slice will be able to split the raw_columns into batches and hence fetch them separately.
This will solve the problem of that the returned document exceeds the 16MB limit.
However, in v4.0.14, there is a memory limit of 100MB for $push processing (not even with allowDiskUse=true). So we might still exceed the size limit.
(https://docs.mongodb.com/manual/reference/operator/aggregation/push/#memory-restrictions)
Each uuid is 36B, so 100MB can hold 100 / 36 ~= 2.5M uuids.

[MongoDB Integration | Query_ groupby with raw sort & limit memory issue ($push)]
## Solution3 - one query for each group
In the first query, we can just get all the groups. Then for each group, we use the where clause and sort + limit to get the results.
This will solve the problem of size limit, since we can push the sort and limit to Mongo.
However, it brings about the problem of latency and scalability since the number of RPCs to be  sent to Mongo will be proportional to the combination of values of the groupby columns.
One way to reduce the impact is to parallelize the sub-queries by issuing multiple such queries (each for one group) concurrently.

## Solution4 - $out
$out allows us to redirect the output to collection, which can be further used for second phase query. But it does not solve the $push size limit issue. Also, it might introduce significant performance issues because it needs to copy the data to another collection.
Another thing to be noticed is that it does not work with “majority” read concern in v4.0 (v4.2 works fine though).
https://docs.mongodb.com/manual/reference/operator/aggregation/out/#majority-read-concern

## Solution5 - $mapReduce
If we really want to return document > 16MB, we need to use $mapReduce
https://docs.mongodb.com/manual/core/map-reduce/
Haven’t drilled into this.

[MongoDB Integration | Query_ groupby with raw sort & limit memory issue ($push)]
## Solution6 - $lookup This is the most promising workaround as of now. $lookup has a field “pipeline”, which allows self-join. With this, we will be able to specify sort and limit within each group. For example: db.alert.aggregate([ { $match: { "resolved": false } }, { $group: { "_id": { _1: "$cluster", _2: "$impact_type", _3: "$severity" }, "count": {$sum: 1} } }, { <---------- The groupby results will be used as an input for the $lookup $lookup: { from: "alert", let: { "cluster": "$_id._1", "impact_type": "$_id._2", "severity": "$_id._3" }, pipeline: [ {$match: {"$expr": {$and: [ {"$eq": [ "$cluster", "$$cluster" ]}, {"$eq": [ "$impact_type", "$$impact_type" ]}, {"$eq": [ "$severity", "$$severity" ]} ]} }}, {$sort: {"_cts": 1}}, {$skip: 0}, {$limit: 1}, {$project: {"_eid": 1, "_id": 0, "_cts": 1}} ], as: "_new_rr_" } } ]) The result will be returned as one document for each group (same as what we need). The advantage is that we can sort and limit within each group inside Mongo, without the need for getting all the raw_columns and then process inside IDF. It is faster than Cassandra backed IDF (which takes 10+ seconds). [MongoDB Integration | Query_ improve the performance in $lookup (2-phase query)]
Today in Mongo-IDF, when the group-by query asks for raw results, we make use of the $lookup to fetch the raw results (See here for more details). However, if the group-by field(s) contains list values, the index of those list fields won't be utilized by the $expr properly (the indexes on list fields are called multikey indexes. And the $expr does not support multikey indexes - see here and here.). And hence the performance degrades drastically. This problem does not exist if all group-by fields are in scalar values. A straightforward workaround is getting all the groups in one query, and sending a separate query for each group such that we can get rid of the $expr. However, the number of queries will then be proportional to the number of groups. To avoid sending so many queries to MongoDB, we try to batch those queries by gathering multiple lookup stages in one query. And each lookup will cover one group. To avoid using the $expr, we hardcode the value instead of matching it with the input document (e.g. {$match: {$expr: {$eq: ["cluster", "$$v1"]}}}). [MongoDB Integration | Replicating existing entities when replication is newly enabled on an entity type]
Replicating existing entities when replication is newly enabled on an entity type Currently, when an existing entity type is modified such that replication is freshly enabled, the existing entities in the source cluster would not automatically replicate to the replica cluster. The entities would get synced only if they were later updated/deleted in the source cluster and the updates get carried through to the replica. Since this is a common enough use case, the solution would be to implement this functionality fully in IDF with no additional intervention required from the clients. By nature, just like our regular IDF sync workflows, this will also be asynchronous. Proposed Solution The proposed solution tries to leverage the existing IDF sync bootstrapping and active entities pipeline. Modifications to ActiveEntities Workflow 1. In the LoadActiveEntities workflow, instead of just sending the entity_ids from the source cluster to the replica cluster; we would also send the db_modified_timestamps of the corresponding entities. 2. In the replica, when processing the active entities info; we would also check for any entities which are present in the source but not in the replica. If we encounter such entities, we create holes in the corresponding replication ranges map. Following our regular bootstrap workflow, these holes would get filled and the existing entities for which we created the holes would sync. So with just the above changes, we can expect the entities to sync within 6 hours. [MongoDB Integration | Reporting Mongo Query Performance]
Oct 20, 20203
Reporting Mongo query performance on 2027 page

## Overview
In order to provide more debugging information for Mongo-backed IDF. We would like to display the profiling information generated by MongoDB for Mongo queries on the 2027 page. This profiling information will contain more granular query latencies that what can be measured in IDF, in addition to useful qualitative info about queries (More details in MongoDB manual.)

[MongoDB Integration | Reporting Mongo Query Performance]
## Two Approaches
1. Set profiling level to max and collect info on all queries on a rolling basis as they are executed.
See Ghazanfar’s notes on this
Likely fewer changes needed to code (just need to set profiling level in config, then fetch and save profile doc during query execution)
Significant performance degradation.
2. Use `db.collection.explain()` to re-execute (and profile) the query on-demand.
Will give all of the information available from `system.profile`. In addition, can be tuned to show all of the unsuccessful plans generated for the query.
Results may not be consistent from original query to `explain` query, either because the winning plan changed, or the data changed
Assuming queries are not that heavy, the overhead on loading 2027 will be minimal. We could possibly have different behaviors for normal queries and heavy queries. ( for example, `explain` on page load for normal queries, and have a clickable link for heavy queries.
Likely requires significant code changes, i.e. accessing `insights_mongo_ops.cc` from `insights_stats.cc`, as well as setting up clickable link/page for  `explain`.

[MongoDB Integration | Reporting Mongo Query Performance]
## Design: display the explain results in 2027/query_recent page
By default, we select “queryPlanner” verbosity level for the Explain output. At this level, we would only see the winning plan chosen by the query optimizer for each query.
The page will accept a new URL argument “verbosity”. If this argument is provided (for example, set to “true”), we will select “executionStats” verbosity level instead. At this level, MongoDB will re-execute the winning plan, and we would see the plan along with its execution statistics for all the Mongo queries in the IDF query at once.
For convenience, a link will be added to the page to provide this additional argument. Clicking said link will re-render the whole page. Running explain in verbose mode will take some time, so a warning will be added to use this sparingly.

[MongoDB Integration | Reporting Mongo Query Performance]
## Implementation Details
Introduce InsightsMongoOps::Explain(string database, bson::document::value&&), which, given a Mongo query/command in BSON format, executes explain() with said query asynchronously, and returns the resulting document
InsightsMongoOps::Explain() will use InsightsMongoOps::RunCommand, a more general implementation of InsightsMongoOps::RunAdminCommand (implemented here), which asynchronously executes a command against the Mongo backend. InsightsMongoOpsRunCommand will be implemented in Ghazanfar’s replica set change.
Refactor code in InsightsStats to support Explain(). Two concerns arise:
Explain calls are asynchronous, but the page needs to be populated by “GenerateQuerProfileTable” before an HTML response is emitted
There may be multiple queries to explain, and they must all be added to the same HTML table, and in the correct order.
Refactor code in InsightsStats to support the “verbose” argument.

[MongoDB Integration | Reporting Mongo Query Performance]
## Implementing a way to Explain() a query
This feature can take one of two forms:
A standalone function in InsightsMongoOps which takes a BSON document representing the Mongo operation to be explained. The burden of creating this document falls on the user (in this case, InsightsStats)
An overload for InsightsMongoOps::Aggregate, which takes an additional argument “verbosity”. The idea is to eventually have an overload for every explainable InsightsMongoOps operation. Having this will save the user having to worry about BSON specifics. However, since we don’t have any additional use cases for this right now, we’ll go with the first approach.

[MongoDB Integration | Reporting Mongo Query Performance]

We can do this by passing the query to the Mongo shell on the The Mongo shell treats all sufficiently large numbers as float/double. When using bsoncxx::to_json to convert a Mongo aggregation pipeline object to a string, numerical literals are printed as is, and are not decorated with any type specifier. This is problematic because if a query contains a sufficiently large integer (i.e. in64, long), the Mongo shell would not be able to recognize it as an int64 or long, treating it instead as a float, which will give unintended query results. To mitigate this, we must explicitly declare the type numeric literals in the query string. To do this, we must iterate through the query’s bson document to examine the types of fields when doing the conversion to string. Jan 7, 2021
Reporting Latencies of Concurrent Mongo queries
ali.dowair@nutanix.com

## Background
Today in IDF, performance and latency measurements are collected on a per RPC basis. For each RPC, a `QueryProfileRecord` object exists. Timestamps are taken at different stages of execution of an RPC and are stored in its associated `QueryProfileRecord` object, in a vector like so:
After execution, stage and substage latencies are calculated from these timestamps as follows (this is simplified for demonstration purposes): for each stage, indicated by an element in the above vector, the latency is calculated as the difference between its timestamp and the timestamp of the following element.
The latencies are then displayed on our 2027 page as follows:
Clearly then, the current design only supports timing stages/substages which occur serially and successively. We have no way of cleanly timing an operation in IDF which is concurrent with, or independent from, any other operation.

[MongoDB Integration | Reporting latencies of concurrent Mongo queries]
## A bad solution (proposed changes in red)
Instead of storing points in time in the `QueryProfile`, and subsequently calculating latency as the difference between timestamps, we could instead store the latency value for each stage directly:
This allows us to be able to “start” and “stop” the timing of operations individually and independently. The downside of this, however, is that timing any one operation will need two commands instead of one. Note that the profiling architecture is used by both Cassandra and Mongo backed IDF. While implementing this timing design (start+stop) should be simple for Mongo backed IDF, it will be difficult and time consuming to do for Cassandra backed IDF.

## An alternative
For each Mongo backed RPC, both a `QueryProfile` and `MongoQueryProfile` are created and persisted. Instead of modifying the existing profiling design, we could instead store the latencies specifically for Mongo queries in the existing `MongoQueryProfile` member of `QueryProfile`:
This saves us going through the effort of changing the existing profiling design and associated code in Cassandra backed IDF. However, this means we will now have two separate sets of timestamps and latencies to record, manage, and display on the 2027 page.

And for the count query:

[MongoDB Integration | Sharding with Mongo Backend]
11/5/2020 Meeting Minutes (Karan, Artem, Vatsan, Chern) Goals Scalability with larger configurations. Support join across entity types by utilizing Mongo join. Items Without sharding, Mongo should be sufficient for current scale ~ 25k to 35k VMs. Scale is measured by the number of entities. We need to know the scale that can be supported without sharding. For scalability in future, sharding on cluster id is the way to go. The assumption is most of the queries are bounded by clusters. Mongo supports sharding. However Mongo sharding sacrifices join ($lookup). Join only works from sharded collection to unsharded collection. Doesn’t work from sharded to sharded collection or unsharded to sharded collection. Therefore we couldn’t use join (goal #2) with Mongo sharding. Another idea is application level sharding. The sharding is done by IDF on individual Mongo instances. These Mongo instances do not talk to each other except for Mongo replication. IDF can perform static sharding or dynamic sharding on cluster id. Static sharding requires data upgrade to move entities from the source Mongo instance to the target Mongo instance. Dynamic sharding is preferred because we can group certain clusters together and can skip data upgrade. In this design, cluster-level entities like VMs and virtual disks are sharded while global-level entities like policies are replicated across all Mongo instances. Then IDF can utilize Mongo join on cluster-level entities and also cluster-level and

[MongoDB Integration | Sharding with Mongo Backend]
design, cluster-level entities like VMs and virtual disks are sharded while global-level entities like policies are replicated across all Mongo instances. Then IDF can utilize Mongo join on cluster-level entities and also cluster-level and global-level entities. IDF couldn’t utilize Mongo join on entities in cluster A with entities in cluster B. In this design, IDF is responsible for aggregating data across clusters. Note: Beware of cluster id of entities can change. For a 3-node PC, for read performance, there is not much difference between sharding with replica set and non-sharding with replica set. This assumes that we can enable local replica reads for the non-sharding Mongo and reads are the majority of the workload. Sharding only helps with PC larger than 3 nodes. Nothing is required now to prepare IDF for sharding model in future. PC federation is orthogonal to IDF sharding.

[MongoDB Integration | Tenant Id]
Tenant Id
Tenant id is created for multi-tenancy. Currently IDF supports entities from multi-tenants with the restriction that entity id should be unique across tenants. In Cassandra, the entity row key includes entity id and tenant id. This is to avoid expensive development cost in data upgrade when entity id should to be scoped by tenants. On the other hand, in MongoDB, the entity can be uniquely identified by entity id. The uniqueness of entity id is enforced through a unique index. To support entity id scoped by tenants in future, we can replace the unique index with a unique compound index on <entity_id, tenant_id>.

[MongoDB Integration | Tenant Id]
Details about tenant id in Cassandra store can be found here https://sites.google.com/a/nutanix.com/corp/engineering/idf_internal#TOC-Tenant-ID The goal of this document is to describe how Mongo store can achieve the same behavior as Cassandra store in handling the tenant id. Cassandra store behavior: Entity creation with tenant id and entity creation without tenant id. Default tenant id is used when tenant id is not provided. Entity update and delete should not change the tenant id. If input tenant id is different, an error should be thrown. We should also enforce this when the entity has a tombstone. Entity read supports reading entities by entity ids, by tenants and by <entity_id, tenant id>. The entities in query result have their tenant ids populated with the cached tenant ids before returning to the clients. Similar behavior is needed in Mongo store. Since entity id alone is enough to identify the entity, Mongo store can skip caching tenant ids for entity CRUD. It needs to ensure that the entity’s and tombstone’s tenant ids do not change after entity creation. For populating entities in query result, IDF can populate them with default tenant ids if the entities do not have tenant ids set in MongoDB. The only place IDF needs the tenant id is when inserting and updating the metric data to Cassandra or MongoDB. The reason is for Cassandra, Cassandra row key includes tenant ids. For MongoDB, metric data is a separate doc not in entity doc. Therefore we need to cache the

[MongoDB Integration | Tenant Id]
data to Cassandra or MongoDB. The reason is for Cassandra, Cassandra row key includes tenant ids. For MongoDB, metric data is a separate doc not in entity doc. Therefore we need to cache the tenant ids if the entities in MongoDB have metrics. In the first release, we only move entities that do not have metrics to MongoDB. Therefore we can skip caching the tenant ids in tenant_id_map_ for the entities in MongoDB. In subsequent releases, unevictable entities will be moved to MongoDB. Unevictable entities have metrics. Therefore we need to cache the mapping from entity ids to tenant ids for such entities. The mapping will only be used for metrics operation. Entity operations should only update the mapping and not look up the mapping. We allow metric data to be created for entities that have not been created yet. This is problematic because the creation can use wrong tenant ids for the metric keys. Since no issue has been reported so far, this should be rare and we can ignore it.

## Changes in First Release
Modify Mongo store’s entity update and delete to ensure tenant ids do not change if clients provide the tenant ids. If clients do not provide tenant ids, entity ids alone should be enough for the operations.
Modify Mongo store’s entity read to support getting entities through only entity ids alone and also getting entities for specific tenants.
Populate default tenant ids on the query entities that do not have tenant ids set. This can happen on entities that are created on old software versions without the tenant ids. If we can populate the tenant ids during data migration, we can get rid of this, which seems to be a cleaner solution.
Modify data migration path to handle the case where Cassandra has multiple entities with similar entity id with different tenants. This can happen because Cassandra does not enforce unique entity ids.

## Summary 1
To summarize, the most important problem to solve here, is that $expr does not support multikey indexes.
This issue seems to be tracked by https://jira.mongodb.org/browse/SERVER-37470 and https://jira.mongodb.org/browse/SERVER-32549.
From the IDF side, the best thing we can do is to send separate queries for each group so that we can avoid using the $expr, which may hence benefit from the multikey index.

[MongoDB Integration | Slow query_ groupby + raw_columns [IN PROGRESS]]
## Solution 1 - Multiple $lookup in one query Since the problem is with the $expr on array fields, we can try to avoid using the $expr in the $lookup. So in this solution, we will do 2-phase query: In the first phase, we get all the groups by issuing a group-by only query. In the second phase, we issue one query with multiple $lookup's, and each $lookup takes care of one group by matching the group_id which is a constant string. Multiple $lookup within one query will be concatenated during processing - meaning the output from the previous $lookup will be passed as input the next $lookup. And if we do not do $group before $lookup, we will end up doing the $lookup for every single document from the collection. Federation Re-Mastering
This document is in extension to Artem’s high level document on remastering: https://docs.google.com/document/d/1KobcmPYxHUCBuit556URvYamWtoQ5u3yE2v6BHMzayM

## Use Case
Client can have 2 independent Federation Sets and want to converge them as Single Federation Set. Remastering makes the master cluster of one federation as replica of other federation.

## IAM Use Case 2 (On-Prem PC Federation <-> Xi Federation)
Note: Use Case 2 requires Hierarchical model support. Though remastering logic will apply to both, but few aspects like Staging on all the Replicas will be covered separately once Hierarchical support will be added.
Terms Used to define Master and Federation Sets:
Federation-1: Federation which will be remastered.
Federation-2: Federation to which 1st Federation is remastered and will become the one complete Federation
Local Master: Master of Federation-1 as all client interaction is happening on this cluster.
Global Master: Master of Federation-2 as this will be the Master of converged Single Federation.

## Remastering Expectations
IDF Clusters can have both Global and Local Data. Re-mastering will only apply to Global Data Set.
Global Data on Federation-1 is merged with Global Data on Federation-2.
Local Master will become Replica within the Federation-2.

[PC Federation & Multi-Cluster | Federation Re-Mastering Design Document (Under Construction)]
## New IDF Functionalities for Remastering
At high level the global entities on both the Federation Set need to be merged before the federation can be remastered. To support merging the entities, remastering step needs support of new functionalities:
Write Lock Support (On Local Master and on Global Master).
Setup Staging Area for Merged/Resolved Data between Global Master and Local Master. Client will fetch Data from both Federation Set and write to the staged area on Local Master.
Flushing Data from Global Master to Federation-1.
Remastering process is done exclusively on the Local Master with the exception of configuring remote endpoints on Global Master for syncing data.

[PC Federation & Multi-Cluster | Federation Re-Mastering Design Document (Under Construction)]
## Remastering Steps:
Each of the remastering steps is triggered by Client.
Initialize Staging for Merge Data: The staging area (cache and cassandra column) will be set on Local Master. All the global data writes will go in staging area while Query requests will be processed as in normal case. For IAM use-case 2, staging is set on Master as well as all the Replicas of Federation-1.
Remaster Federation-1: This is done by setting up cloud master entity on Local Master with cluster UUID of Global Master.
Write Lock on Global Master: To disable writes outside the scope of merge process. This step simplifies the merging process without worrying for CAS errors.
Allow updates on Local Master: As part of Init staging, updates were disabled on Local Master.  As Global Write Lock is taken, we can enable the updates.
Query Data: Client will Query Global Entities from:
Global Master using Strict Consistency
Local Master using Eventual Consistency
Merge Data: Client will Delete/Update/Add Entities according to their Merge rule. The merged entities are saved in Staging Area.
Flush Data: All the Global entities are flushed from Global Master to Local Master.
Flush Data to Replicas (Hierarchical Model): Local Master need to flush data to its Replicas. (Required on if there are Replicas configured).
Release Write Lock on Global Master.
Commit Staging Area: Staged area is now the regular data store.

## Design Details The write lock is ttl based. Client will issue WriteLock rpc to request for the lock and WriteUnlock rpc to release the lock. And client will be responsible to refresh the lock before it expires, which can be done by calling the same WriteLock rpc. In response of the WriteLock request, there will be a lock_id which will be used by the client for future CUD operations after the write lock is taken. When the WriteLock is received by the replica, the lock_id will be populated if it is not provided by the client yet (and it should not). The lock_id will be set to cluster_uuid of the replica cluster. Then the request will be forwarded to the master. Only the leader node on the master will handle this request; non-leader nodes will forward it to the leader. And all operations on the lock will be serialized - guarded by a local exclusive lock. All clients on the same replica cluster will share the same lock_id since the lock_id is automatically stamped by the replica cluster by using the cluster_uuid. Thus any client will be able to get the lock_id even if the write lock has been grabbed by other client on the same replica cluster. (The current implementation of lock_id is designed to let one AZ block data modifications from other AZs belonging to the same federation. If this does not hold in the future, we can re-think about it.) The lock related information will be saved in zookeeper (FLAGS_insights_federation_write_lock_state_path). During bootstrap, all nodes

During bootstrap, all nodes on the master will sync-read from zookeeper for the latest lock information and cache it in memory. The lock information persisted is as following: <lock_id, sequence_id, lock_state>. Same information will be saved in local cache. Additionally on the leader node, there will be a <expiration_time> saved. lock_id: provided in the WriteLockArg sequence_id: monotonously incremental integer, generated locally on the master leader node. It will be needed when unlocking the lock on non-leader nodes. It will NOT be returned to the client. lock_state: enum LockState (kUnlocked / kLockInProgress / kLocked). The kLockInProgress state will be treated the same as kLocked in most cases unless specially mentioned (e.g. for the leadership transfer [see “Bootstrap / Recovery” section]). expiration_time: current_time + FLAGS_insights_write_lock_ttl_msecs, which is kept in cache only on the leader node in federation master cluster. The server will regularly validate the write lock and release it if expires.

## Lock state transition:
The version with higher sequence_id wins (sequence_id is starting the 0).
If sequence_id is the same, kUnlocked state wins.
Changing the state of the lock needs to exclude all write operations.
For simplicity, we can just grab the shard write lock. The only concern is it will also block read operations. If later it becomes an issue, we can rethink about it.
There are some special handling in different scenarios. Please refer to the corresponding sections for more details.

## Bootstrap / Recovery: All nodes will sync-read the lock state from zookeeper on bootstrap (including the leadership transfer) and update the cache. The leader will do a sync-read after it gets the leadership. All nodes will do a sync-read after it grabs the first shard lock in ZK. This is to solve the following issue: WriteLock comes in, leader is writing to ZK New node joins, reads the stale lock state The new lock state is written to ZK. Leader then sends NodeWriteLock to all nodes except the new node since it does not yet know about it Leader returns success to client Shard reassigned. The new node starts processing request. But it thinks the lock has not been grabbed because it hasn’t received either the NodeWriteLock request, or the watch callback All nodes will watch on the lock information in zookeeper. Every node will registe r one watch - no new watch will be registered on leadership transfer. The main reason for the watch is to notify non-leader nodes about releasing the lock. The data pulled from zookeeper may not be up-to-date (e.g. old leader crashed during writing the lock to zookeeper, the new leader may pull stale lock information before the previous write actually completed), in which case we need to rely on the watch to get the leader in sync with zookeeper. Thus other than following the general lock state transition, there is some extra work to be done when handling the watch callback on leader: (Since lower sequence_id will be discarded, following we

Reseting the expiration_time is to avoid the potential discrepancy of system time between different IDF nodes. ## Grab the lock: The lock_id in the WriteLockArg should not be provided by the client. It is filled up by the replica cluster. If it is provided, it will be treated as a renew operation, and will be rejected if the lock is not taken yet. The processing of the request will be handled by the leader. The WriteLock request will be allowed if lock_state = kUnlocked (grabbing the lock). lock_state = kLocked, and the lock_id matches with the arg (renewing the lock). For lock_state = kLockInProgress, the request will be rejected by returning kLockInProgress. We do NOT depend on the expiration_time to determine whether we can grab the lock or not. The previous lock has to be released first before the new lock can be grabbed. If allowed, leader will generate a valid sequence_id (prev_sequence_id + 1), persist the new lock information <new_lock_id, new_sequence_id, kLockInProgress> to zookeeper, update its local cached lock info, and set the expiration_time. This kLockInProgress state is only meaningful for leader. For non-leader, it will be treated as kLocked. Persisting to zookeeper and updating the local cache need to be atomic. Otherwise, we may grant a second lock while the previous one was already granted (since we are checking the cache to determine whether the lock should be granted or not). Then, leader sends NodeWriteLock RPCs (which contains all shards belonging to that node according to the leader’s perspective) to all nodes as to update the cached lock information.

This guarantees that the lock is grabbed on the node only if the node has the same view (shard ownership) as the leader does. ## TTL expiration: Leader will maintain an alarm to regularly check the effectiveness of the expiration_time. If current system time has passed the expiration_time, it will release the lock as mentioned above. When leader changes, the new leader will reset the expiration_time if the current lock is valid. Non-leader does not keep the expiration_time information as the lock state is completely depending on either the commit request from leader, or the zookeeper. Process the NodeWriteLock: Arg: lock_id Non-leader will just follow the state machine of updating the lock. Renew the lock: Client is responsible for refreshing the lock before it expired. The renew will be done via the WriteLock rpc with lock_id specified. When the leader receives the request, it will check if the renew request is valid (lock_id matches and the current lock status is kLocked). If not valid, the request will be rejected; otherwise leader will reset the expiration_time and return success. Note that we only matches the lock_id, not the sequence_id. Write operations: Any UpdateEntity / DeleteEntity operation and its batch-version needs to have the lock_id attached after the lock is grabbed. Otherwise it will be rejected with error kGlobalDataWriteLocked. When checking the validation of the lock_id, the processing node only checks the lock_id, NOT the sequence_id. The pros of this solution is if the master took the lock but the response to client failed, the client can still continue with the previous lock

The pros of this solution is if the master took the lock but the response to client failed, the client can still continue with the previous lock since the lock_id is the same. Also, if client wants its own exclusive lock (per client lock), it can provide its own lock_id in the WriteLockArg by paying the price mentioned earlier.

## Alternative Solution - Per shard lock
Instead of one global lock, the shard owner will write the lock_id for every shard it owns, e.g. shard/lock_id: 1/10000. So when receiving all watch callbacks for all shards, the lock is considered grabbed.

## Introduction
The current plan is to implement phase 1 first: https://docs.google.com/presentation/d/1sAbSp47Nzj3nIHOPwXrIvzyp816gc3L0Fjy_25WUBYo/edit#slide=id.g1fa4530043_0_10.  The phase 1 scenarios are pivoted to support Xi MT, if we want PC federation for on-prem need to do some of the phase 2 work as well.

## AZ Attach For the AZ attach, in v1 can assume that the attached AZ has no consumer or global entities, so we don’t need to handle merge. To support this, during attach we need to have logic, that would check that the new AZ doesn’t have any consumer or global entities. The AZ attach would start with the process that’s similar to PE-PC pairing. To simplify connection routing, the AZ attach is always going to happen to the current cloud master. When the first 2 AZ are federated into a cloud, one of them becomes the cloud master (and it stays the cloud master until the admin explicitly designates a different AZ to become the master). The other AZ must be clean. We will need to implement logic to show which AZ is the cloud master and check that attach happens to the cloud master. We assume, that by the time we ship PC Federation, the reverse tunnel functionality is implemented, and links between AZs are asymmetrical (one AZ is initiator and the other is acceptor). So the AZ attach can either be initiated from the clean AZ to the cloud master or from the cloud master to the clean AZ. At the end of the pairing process (we’ll get into detailed pairing logic later), the entity that describes the new AZ is created in the master and gets replicated to all AZs (including the new AZ). The cloud-global data is replicated to the new AZ, so the new AZ becomes part of the Federation. At the IDF level, there would be a special RPC, TBD, to attach a new AZ, so that the entities that

[PC Federation & Multi-Cluster | PC Federation Infra V1 Plan]
to the new AZ, so the new AZ becomes part of the Federation. At the IDF level, there would be a special RPC, TBD, to attach a new AZ, so that the entities that describe the federation could be only modified by IDF. When IDF first becomes the master (i.e. federation happens between 2 AZs that were not part of federation), then IDF creates entities in the following order: entity that describes cloud master AZ, entity that stores who the cloud master is, entity that describes the non-master AZ. The pairing process is going to be similar to PE-PC pairing, with the difference, that the AZ is going to be “paired” to the Federation, rather than to a single AZ. The pairing consists of 3 pieces of data: (1) the initiator needs to know the endpoint information on how to connect to acceptor; (2) the acceptor needs to have a certificate that trusted by initiator; (3) the acceptor needs to have a way authenticate initiator. The (1) is fairly straightforward (have DNS name or IP address + port number). There are multiple ways to solve (2) & (3), but assuming we picked a way to solve (2) & (3) for PE-PC pairing, the high-level modification is the following: (1) is going to be the same (stored locally in initiator’s AZ); (2) the acceptor certificate is either signed by the Federation-global CA trusted by all AZs (need to add the CA on the new AZ) or added into the list of trusted root certificates stored in the global data (need to set a watch on all AZs to update trusted root certificates);

This way, the acceptor certificate would be trusted by any AZ of the cloud and the initiator credentials could be validated at any AZ of the cloud.
