## Inter-AZ Direct Links In v1, we require every AZ to have a direct link to other AZs (to avoid implementing request routing). The workflow for establishing a direct link would be similar to pairing, except there would be no need to establish trust. Each AZ would run a link heartbeat service, that would go through a list of AZs and try to ping them. If a direct link to an AZ doesn’t exist, the link heartbeat service would raise an alert that there is no link. If ping fails for a certain period of time, the link heartbeat service would raise an alert that the link is down. The link heartbeat service would know the list of AZs from the global entities that describe AZs in the cloud. Each AZ would provide a UX to show link status, and indicate the status (no link, link down). There would also be a UX flow (on each AZ), to initiate a link to any other AZ (i.e. become an initiator side of the new link). We just need to enter connection information (DNS name or IP address + port number), the AZ is going to initiate a connection to the other AZ, the mutual authentication will happen using the cloud-global trust information, and if it's successful, then the link entities are updated in both AZs. To reduce the amount of manual configuration, we can implement a gossip protocol to share known acceptor AZ connections. For links that AZ is initiator for, it would keep a list of remote AZs and connection info (DNS name or IP address + port number) it uses to reach them and update globally

[PC Federation & Multi-Cluster | PC Federation Infra V1 Plan]
For links that AZ is initiator for, it would keep a list of remote AZs and connection info (DNS name or IP address + port number) it uses to reach them and update globally visible "gossip" data (e.g. an entity of the gossip_links entity type with id = initiator_AZ_uuid and attributes containing acceptor AZ link info). If the connection heartbeat service detects that there is no link to an AZ (which can happen when a new AZ joins federation) or the link it down, it will try to re-establish the link using the gossip information. Note, that gossip may not always work, because the DNS name or IP address may not be public. Work: Implement link heartbeat service - 10 days Implement UX to show link status - 10 days? ## AZ Decommission In v1, we won't support attaching AZs that global or consumer data, so once AZ is detached from the federation, it can only be attached back if all data that it has is removed (i.e. purely as provider resource pool). To avoid implied expectation that AZ detach operation would leave an option for re-attach, we use the AZ decommission terminology. The primary scenario for AZ decommission is the physical loss of an AZ. If an AZ is temporarily disconnected from the Federation, the AZ is still logically considered a part of Federation and will function as a part of Federation (the global data may become inconsistent until connectivity is restored). If the current cloud master is partitioned from Federation and the connection cannot be quickly restored, the global data can be remastered by an admin, the logic for remastering will be described later. The AZ decommission flow will be an explicit user action. The action would probably be initiated from cloud status page. A current cloud master cannot be decommissioned, a new AZ needs to be chosen as the cloud master (manual remastering workflow). The UX needs to show a warning that this action is irreversible and etc. Once the user agreed to proceed, the decommission flow will delete the entity that describes the AZ from the master. The deletion will propagate to all AZs in the cloud via the normal global data replication flows. The decommissioned AZ (if it wasn’t destroyed prior to decommission), will retain its

The decommissioned AZ (if it wasn’t destroyed prior to decommission), will retain its data. It won’t be able to initiate connections to Federation AZs, as acceptors won’t accept connections from decommissioned AZ, as it’s trust information is removed from the global data. The Federation AZ won’t initiate connections to the decommissioned AZ. ## Global Data CRUD In v1, the way to specify whether an entity is a global or a local would be a property of the entity type. I.e. an entity type could be marked as "global" (e.g. users, categories, etc.) and then for all entities of that entity type IDF would go through global data CRUD logic. UpdateEntity / DeleteEntity / PutMetricData and the corresponding batched versions would check if the entity type is global, and for global entity types they would check who the current cloud master is, and if the current cloud master is not the current AZ, then issue a corresponding remote RPC call to the cloud master. When the UpdateEntity / DeleteEntity return from the master with success, they will return the new entity and try to apply it to local replica. If replication doesn't succeed, then the request fails. This way, if local IDF returns success, it means that the change is applied to master and local replica, so within one AZ we guarantee read-after-write consistency on the global entities. For PutMetricData we don’t do this logic to avoid double-counting and just rely on normal replication flows. For read operations (GetEntitiesWithMetrics, GetEntities, SpotlightSearch), we'll provide an option to specify whether the caller wants strictly consistent data or can use eventually consistent data. The default is going to be eventually consistent (which will help with latency and availability). If the operation is eventually consistent, then the data is fetched from the local

can use eventually consistent data. The default is going to be eventually consistent (which will help with latency and availability). If the operation is eventually consistent, then the data is fetched from the local replica (i.e. this is a normal local request as we have today). If the operation is strictly consistent and the current AZ is not the cloud master, then the request is sent to the cloud master. Watches on global entity types are going to be set on the replicated data, so no logic change is required. Note that in v1, we assume that all AZs have the same entity types marked global, so that we don't need to worry about metadata synchronization and reconciliation. ## Global Data Replication To support global data replication, we need to support replication control based on the destination type (enable_replication_to). Currently, we only support replication control based on the source type (enable_replication_from). The entity types marked “global” would have enable_replication_to set to some type, TBD. The links between AZs are going to be of the type that the global data is set to be replicated to. The server would check the enable_replication_to type and pass it to uploader. The uploader would have the pipeline (channel / batcher / bootstrapper) for each destination type, so when it receives request from the server, it would pass it to the batcher that corresponds to the passed destination type. The uploader would also send ranges with empty update and normal priority to other destination types (the same logic that we have in the server for entities which have replication suppressed). The LoadEntityTrail / LoadActiveEntities RPCs would take the replication_to as an argument, the uploader pipeline would pass it in. The server would use the argument to only fetch entities that have the corresponding enable_replication_to set. We need to update all entities types that are currently replicated from PC to PE, to explicitly set the destination type to PE, so that global data doesn’t get pushed to PE. ## Global Data Remastering If the cloud master cannot be used for some reason (e.g. AZ is destroyed), the admin can manually designate another AZ to be a new cloud master. IDF will provide a new RPC, that will take the uuid of the new cloud master. The local IDF will forward the call to the corresponding AZ, then the new master IDF will remaster and update the entity that describes the current master to point to itself. The remastering of global entities happens lazily, whenever they are updated. When the entity that describes the cloud master is remastered to the new master, the incarnation id and the CAS value of the entity is set to the current timestamp (or previous value + 1). The assumption here is that the wall clock of the new master is reasonably accurate and remastering operation is extremely rare, so the new master’s incarnation id is going to be higher than the old master’s, so it actually becomes a new master (higher incarnation id will override lower). When the global entities are updated on the new master, they inherit the incarnation id and CAS values from the master record. When receiving updates for global entities, the IDF would check if it's the cloud master, and if it's not, then it will reject the updates. The admin can initiate remastering from the cloud status page. We'll print a warning about consequences of remastering, then if the admin agrees, we'll call local IDF to do remastering. ## Federation of AZ-local Data Each AZ would be capable of operating the whole cloud. To support that, in addition to the global data support, we also need to stitch together AZ-local data from all AZs. The read operations (GetEntitiesWithMetrics, GetEntities, SpotlightSearch) would have an option to indicate if the request just goes to the local IDF or it would need to get data from all AZs. If the information is needed from all AZs, then the local IDF acts as a “super-coordinator” that would fan-out requests to other AZs and collate results. The “super-coordinator” functionality is going to be very similar to a single-cluster coordinator, the same principles would apply, only instead of direct Node* RPCs, it would call remote RPCs in other AZ’s IDFs. As AZs failures shouldn’t affect other AZs, we need to return partial results if some AZs are not reachable. The operations will return a list of AZs we’ve got the results from and AZ that we got the error from. The UI / UX of services would need to present the partial results to the user. The GetEntitiesWithMetrics would support the _az_ pseudo-attribute. When a list of entity ids and tenant ids is specified in the GetEntitiesWithMetrics argument and the flag is set to fetch data from all AZs, the query would cache {entity_type, entity_id, tenant_id} -> AZ mapping and would use it to optimize the fanout. The functionality can also be used by the services to issue a query for _az_ pseudo-attribute with a list of entity ids and

[PC Federation & Multi-Cluster | PC Federation Infra V1 Plan]
-> AZ mapping and would use it to optimize the fanout. The functionality can also be used by the services to issue a query for _az_ pseudo-attribute with a list of entity ids and tenant ids to find the AZ of the entity for service-level fan-out operations. The query would try to serve this information for the local cache, if available. ## IDF Work
To decouple IDF work from Transport / Security work (and to support easier unit testing) we’ll allow specifying one of the AZ’s IDF handles (IP:port) in the AZ record.  This will take care of server, for global data CRUD and federation of AZ-local data.  For uploader, we can set direct connection info in ZK.

## High Level Traffic Flow
Each Xi-AZ has a L7 proxy that is responsible for incoming traffic authentication, routing and outgoing traffic routing. The outgoing traffic to other customer site deployed clusters is delivered through reverse tunnels established by the on-prem cluster L7 proxy. In the on-prem PE cluster envoys on all nodes OR a single leader envoy on the leader node or can act as the proxy layer for traffic to other clusters or Xi-AZs [ustomers who want outgoing traffic to be through a single IP will override the default to single leader envoy].

## Transport Service Interface
The transport service acts like a forward proxy and transparently forwards messages as required to deliver to the destination. However, to make it easy for developers transport service is made available through a library that exports RPC Client interfaces in C++, python and golang similar to existing RPC Client interfaces. In each hop the two envoys open mTLS connection between them and guarantees `confidentiality` but not service to service authentication. SvctoSvc encryption within DC is punted to when svc-to-svc auth is implemented. Later, that will be done by the transport lib.
Transport lib reaches out to envoy using ‘proxy’ as DNS name which resolves to localhost on-prem and to mercury/transport service in the Xi AZ.

[PC Federation & Multi-Cluster | Transport Service]
## Reverse Tunnel Setup The cluster that is behind a NAT or firewall is responsible for establishing reverse tunnels with all other clusters that it is paired with. The Tunnel Controller learns from the IAM pairing database that its local cluster is behind NAT/firewall. Tunnel Controller instructs all ingress envoys to establish a reverse tunnel with all AZs (and clusters) that cannot reach this cluster. The envoys use external facing APIs to establish connections (APIs discussed later) passing its endpoint-instance-name to the AZ. The Envoys need credentials (certificates) to establish the connections. The TC gets the information about all the paired clusters and AZs including the credentials from IAM. All incoming reverse tunnel connections are registered in the service registry as service-endpoints. The endpoints are later used in defining egress routing rules for services on remote cluster. Note that in a Xi-AZ the L7 proxy layer (transport and mercury) consist of many L7 proxies. A remote cluster opens numerous reverse tunnels to a Xi-AZ for performance reason and to avoid head of the line blocking. However, each remote cluster surely does not have reverse tunnels open with each and every envoy in the L7 proxy layer. The transport lib randomly picks a envoy to send the outgoing request to a cluster. If that envoy does not have a reverse tunnel to the cluster then it forwards the request to the envoy that has the connection (also performing load balancing across all open

[PC Federation & Multi-Cluster | Transport Service]
to a cluster. If that envoy does not have a reverse tunnel to the cluster then it forwards the request to the envoy that has the connection (also performing load balancing across all open reverse tunnels). In case of streaming services like storage services the extrahop above may be cause of loss of streaming performance. The performance of transport can be optimized by having the receiving envoy send an HTTP Redirect to the transport lib: (i) if the next hop is a different envoy that has a reverse tunnel open or (ii) if the destination or next hop is within the DC. The transport lib handles HTTP redirections transparently.

## On-prem svc to on-prem svc (same cluster, different cluster)
Any service that wants to talk to its well-connected peer (on the same cluster or different), can do so using the legacy IP based approach (which is supported for backward compatibility). If the service using the new SPIFFE handle, then the request is routed to the local envoy proxy as usual, and the traffic is directed to the next logical envoy on the path to the destination service.

## Xi-MT cluster in one AZ talking to another Xi-MT cluster in another AZ
All pairing between AZs is to be done at the logical tenant level. All service discovery is also done at a logical tenant level. So, when the discovery service running in one AZ asks the destination DS for the list of services, the destination AZ only sends it the list of services that are visible to the tenant UUIDs that have paired with the destination AZ. The same SPIFFE can redirect to different service instances based on tenant.
Two services in different Xi-MT AZs should be able to talk to each other without any change in behavior when compared to a single-tenant on-prem to Xi-MT usecase. Single-tenant on-prem is simply a “currently one-tenant MT AZ”. That is how the transport and the discovery service shall be designed.

That is because the DC Ingress Rotor will have programmed the allowed routes across all the envoys in the DC. ## Envoy Design Patterns
Following is a list of design patterns used in L7 proxy deployments in modern services based architecture. These patterns are used in this design.

[PC Federation & Multi-Cluster | Transport Service]
## Standard North-South Ingress Proxy
A single Envoy can be deployed as a N-S load balancer and service proxy. The configuration required is :
Route: Rules that match URLs and headers to one of the services
Clusters: this is the list of `services`
Endpoints: set of endpoints that export a service
Load Balancing policy: policy for load balancing across endpoints in a service cluster.
A set of envoys with same config can be deployed as a scalable L7 proxy layer with a L2 or L4 proxy in front of it.
A example of this is following configuration of the N-S Envoys:
route : match URL /v3/vm to service `vm` and map URL /v3/storage to service `storage`
clusters : vm, storage, …
endpoints : vm = {ip1, ip2, ip4},  storage = {ip5, ip6, ip7}

[PC Federation & Multi-Cluster | Transport Service]
## Floating Leader Based Service Routing Envoy supports a feature where : EDS can tag endpoints Envoy can tag incoming requests based on rules or a custom filter The load balancer can be configured to choose only the subset of endpoints that have the same tags as the request. See https://www.envoyproxy.io/docs/envoy/v1.6.0/intro/arch_overview/load_balancing#load-balancer-subsets Consider we have service where There are number of endpoints that export the same instance of the service however only one endpoint called leader endpoint can receive certain type of requests (say requests that modify/update/create) but all endpoints can receive other requests (like requests that only read) The leader endpoints could change to any one among the set of endpoints. If a client sends a leader request to a wrong endpoint then the non-leader endpoint forwards the request to the leader. Load balancer subsets can be used to implement request routing for such services. This will work as follows : The service client sending the request can add a header specifying that the request need to be send only to the leader. The endpoint on the host that receives the request will first tag the request with tag like tag : “<service-name>-leader” and value : “true” The service load balancing is configured to use subset load balancing with tag specified as tag: “<service-name>-leader” and value: “true”. The envoy control plane has a service that discovers which endpoint is the current leader and updates the

[PC Federation & Multi-Cluster | Transport Service]
is configured to use subset load balancing with tag specified as tag: “<service-name>-leader” and value: “true”. The envoy control plane has a service that discovers which endpoint is the current leader and updates the EDS endpoint definitions with appropriate leader tags. Please note that Envoy supports dynamic configuration updates, thus once the control plane discovers the leader it will soon be known to the data plane. Immediately after the leader changes its possible that some requests will still be sent to the old leader till the data plane has learnt about the new leader.

## Multiplexing Ports on Single HTTPS
Consider the scenario similar to services running on CVM. Each host runs multiple independent service endpoints (processes) that listen on their own ports. All incoming request to all services on a host can be received on single https port by a proxy and by using URL matching rules forward the request to corresponding ports. This requires that the URL has enough information to match to a service.

## Transport Service Design The transport service design: Interface : Provides a http proxy service which is responsible for routing and transporting the http request to the destination through a encrypted channel. Components: Envoy proxy data plane, control plane, discovery service and reverse tunnel service. Envoy Proxy: Each host runs a Envoy proxy. All service to service traffic leaving the cluster is proxied through the envoy. This is relatively easy since all services use different library calls to send messages on same cluster and remote cluster. Envoy Proxy Layer: Each AZ runs a set of Envoys which operate as egress routing layer. This Envoy layer is like the `router` layer described in the design patterns above. Service Discovery Service: Runs on each cluster and in a AZ. This service is responsible for building registry of all the services and endpoints on all paired clusters / AZs. For its own services this service talks to ZK to gather information on (i) list services (NOTE: in PE the services information is all hard coded compiled in), (ii) list of nodes/endpoints (basically each CVM is a endpoint) and (iii) current leader endpoint of all floating leader based services. This information is exported to other discovery services on paired clusters and AZ. ## Current Solution for Xi-CT
The current solution for this problem is called Xi Secure DR and it works as follows:
As evident in the above diagram, it is possible to have overlapping IP ranges for the CVMs between OnPrem and Xi. So, it is required to have a NAT layer in both directions to translate IPs between the two sites. This is achieved through two logical components that provide IP routability between OnPrem and Xi clusters:
OnPrem Load Balancer IP (used for configuring routability from Xi CVM to OnPrem CVM) - referred to as OLB henceforth
Xi Load Balancer IP (used for configuring routability from OnPrem CVM to Xi CVM) - referred to as XLB henceforth
The way it works is:
The PC nodes and PE nodes in Xi are deployed with cluster external IPs. Ports 9440 port for PC, and 2009 (stargate), 2020 (cerebro) and 2074 (NGT) on the PE are open.
If a node is added/removed to/from the cluster, an update of the IP mapping is done. This is done by VIP agent running on each PC.
VIP master running in the PC in Xi cloud provides the APIs to VIP agents for updating the XLB and OLB mappings.
Site to site VPN is used for encrypting traffic between the clusters.

## Problems with the solution:
Requires two physical load balancers in XI cloud.
Requires non standard ports to be opened on Xi cloud.
The requirement (2) to (4) above essentially reflect the limitations in the current implementation of communication between stargates and cerebro services on different clusters. The limitations are as follows:
Transparent Load Balancing at destination / Client side load balancing: When one stargate wants to talk to another stargate on different cluster to replicate data for a given vdisk the stargate first talks to a service (cerebro) on the other cluster and finds out the right stargate (depending on load and which stargate currently has the vdisk mounted) to talk to.
Binding to non-standard ports: On each CVM there are more than one process/service running; there is no single proxy/webserver on the node that binds to standard http ports and routes the incoming traffic to different services. In absence of that the service binds to separate known ports and any other service requiring to talk to this service has to send traffic to this port.
Service Naming: As we see above services are addressed as slave_ip:port instead of servicename.

Dictionary iteration
for attr_name, data_value in attributes.items():
Will be changed to
for attr_name, data_value in list(attributes.items()):
This change is not required and can be ignored.
raise db_interface.DbError, dbe, sys.exc_info()[2] will be replaced by raise_(db_interface.DbError, dbe, sys.exc_info()[2]). We used raise_with_traceback(db_interface.DbError(dbe)) instead. from future.utils import raise_with_traceback

## Common changes
uuid needs a byte string. So convert your string “abc” to b”abc” to make it a byte string.
imap, ifilter, izip will be replaced by map, filter, zip respectively. from builtins import map, zip, filter will be added. This import is good to have as it will use the iterator based implementations imap, izip, ifilter internally instead of lists.
Python 3 has nothing called as long. It replaced long with int. To specifically use long, use from past.builtins import long
5L needs to be replace by long(5)
Using mox
import sys
if sys.version_info[0] == 2:
import mox
else:
from mox3 import mox
Integer Division
a / b gives float in Python 3 and int in Python 3. a // b gives int.
Futurize will change this with old_div. We used // instead of importing an extra dependency.
If you are using /= anywhere, it will not be fixed by futurize.
xrange can be safely replaced with range when using from builtins import range.
range might need to be replaced with list(range()) since range returns an iterator now instead of a list.

Now when the cluster is unregistered, these replicated entities remain in a dormant state in the replication sites. In one such specific case, xi_tenant entity type had some stale replicated entities left on a null PE cluster node. This can happen if these entities were mastered on a PC, got replicated to the PE and later on the PE was unregistered from the PC and the PC was also destroyed. Hi all,
This is a heads-up to all components on PC consuming any stats synced from PE to PC.
Please note and respond to the following changes we are planning in 5.11 for metric sync from PE to PC !
What is changing
As part of FEAT - 6439 and to help address related customer issues caused by Sync payload bloat, we need to optimize the PE to PC metric sync pipeline. Two of the most impactful changes planned in this regard are:
- To downsample all stats from 30 secs to 5 mins before syncing them to PC. The stats on PE will remain unaffected.
- Identifying stats which are not used on PC so that we can skip syncing the same.
We are targeting this feature for 5.11. We have done some initial vetting with some of the  heaviest stats consumers, such as UI, Search, Capacity Planning. We will be enabling this change on master by EOD 17-Dec-18 IST so that we have sufficient time to identify and fix any unanticipated regressions on UI / PC workflows.

[IDF Processes & Operations | IDF - ES Architecture Review]
IDF - Iris ES Architecture Review
June 2025

## Scaleout Architecture
IDF truly supports both Horizontal as well as Vertical Scaling. All the components within IDF are designed to support this scaleout architecture.
IDF can dynamically add or remove nodes from the cluster as needed. Similarly, resources (Memory, CPU) can be added to IDF at runtime to support vertical scaling.

## Data Sharding / Shard Migration
IDF internally distributes all the data in 128 shards. IDF also supports dynamic migration of shards across nodes for uniform data distribution.
For example, 16 Shards and 3 nodes in the cluster.

## Scaleout query processing
IDF has a distributed query engine which can coordinate across nodes for query processing.

## Scaleout Watch Processing
IDF watch processing layer also supports scaleout architecture by design.

## IDF QA Qualified Scale Iris
Scaleout architecture of IDF and various improvements done has allowed us to qualify 50k VM scale on PC in IDF.

## Conclusion
IDF as a component was tested with 50k VMs scale. IDF was able to sustain the load of 50k VMs within allocated resources (CPU and Memory).
Based on this architecture of IDF, giving needed resources to IDF should help us in achieving the desired scale without updating / modifying the architecture.

## ONCALL-4682 : Gemeente Eindhoven - High latency and mostly unavailability of ncli/Prism due to Arithmos 100% CPU usage on one CVM.
Symptoms: Arithmos on one node kept crashing due to OOM.
Root cause: There was too much data VM and virtual_disk data on one agent node of arithmos, which was stale but arithmos could not come up to allow Acropolis to delete those VMs.
Resolution: (Option1 was used)
Option 1:
Check using top whether the system has enough free memory, increase RSS memory of Arithmos:
To increase the Arithmos rss limit.
 1. shutdown the arithmos instances
 allssh genesis stop arithmos

2. create genesis.gflags file with the following content in /home/nutanix/config/ directory.
 --arithmos_rss_mem_limit=<new limit>

3. copy the config file to all other CVMs.
 for ip in `svmips`; do scp /home/nutanix/config/genesis.gflags $ip:~/config; done

4. restart genesis on all the CVMs for the new gflag to be picked up.
 allssh genesis restart

5. Start Arithmos on all the CVMs.
 cluster start
Check whether all the stale entities are deleted from Arithmos.
Change RSS memory limit back to normal.
Option 2:
To start from clean state, we can stop Arithmos on that node, delete the persist directories and start arithmos again. To delete the persist directories, you can do
rm -rf /home/nutanix/data/arithmos/arithmos_persist_*
Will lose the stats for last few hours.

## Insights Data Fabric ON-CALL Process
To properly support Nutanix software that runs in production, the engineering team may need to help with investigation and root cause analysis of support cases.  Here is the process that we use in the Insights Data Fabric team to handle ON-CALL issues.

## Triage
New ON-CALL requests are sent to the InsightsDataFabric-Leads email alias.  The leads do triage and assign the issue to an engineer to help with investigation / RCA.

## Investigation / RCA
The ON-CALL engineer works with SRE and customer to investigate the issues.  The InsightsDataFabric-Leads should be kept in the loop whenever is practical (CC on email).
The ON-CALL engineer should keep the document trail of the investigation whenever is practical and at the end of investigation create a document in Insights Data Fabric > RCAs folder, that would capture the issue summary as well as the communication trail.

## Mitigation / Fix
After the root cause is determined, the ON-CALL engineer should work with SRE to propose a mitigation / workaround, if possible.
In any case, for every ON-CALL issue we should come up with a way to fix the product (and file a ticket) so that the issues of this class don’t happen again.  Once the a ticket is filed, the ON-CALL duty is complete (the actual fix may be implemented by someone else in a priority order).
During the ON-CALL duty, the activity related to ON-CALL should be treated at top priority.

Prism Central Serviceability

## 1 Introduction
Prism Central(PC) is an appliance (VM) providing a single, centralized management interface for managing multiple Prism Element(PE) Clusters. It also provides additional operational insights across multiple PE Clusters by way of ‘Capacity Analytics’, ‘Intelligent Workload Alerts’ and ‘Contextual Search’ to name a few.

## 1.1 Prism Architecture
Prism Architecture
(Courtesy: Steven Poitras)

## 1.2 Prism Central Form Factors
PC currently supports single VM deployment form factor with 2 sizes (Small and Large). Small form factor VM is 4 vCPU, 12 G of Memory and 500 G of Disk space whereas Large form factor VM is 8 vCPU, 32 G of Memory and 2.5 TB of Disk space.

[IDF Processes & Operations | Prism Central Serviceability]
## 1.3 Prism Request Handling
A Prism service runs on both PC as well as PE with an elected leader responsible for handling HTTP requests. Similar to other components which have a Master, if the Prism Leader fails, a new one will be elected.  When a PE which is not the Prism Leader gets a HTTP request it will permanently redirect the request to the current Prism Leader using HTTP response status code 301.
Prism Services - Request Handling
(Courtesy: Steven Poitras)
When using the cluster external IP (recommended), it will always be hosted by the current Prism Leader.  In the event of a Prism Leader failure the cluster IP will be assumed by the newly elected Prism Leader and a gratuitous ARP (gARP) will be used to clean any stale ARP cache entries.  In this scenario any time the cluster IP is used to access Prism, no redirection is necessary as that will already be the Prism Leader.

## 1.4 Prism Central Navigation
Prism Central contains the following screens:
Home Page
Multi pane dashboard which shows detailed information on cluster wide view of Storage, CPU Usage, Memory Usage, Latency, Controller IOPs, tasks and Capacity Planning.
Explore
Entity browser which provides a single pane view across clusters, nodes, VMs, Disks.
Analysis
Detailed performance analysis tab where charts can be pinned to get hourly, weekly, monthly view of statistics.
Planning
Capacity planning page which shows current runway for all clusters.
Alerts
Consolidated view of alerts across all clusters.
Tasks Icon
Get a detailed view of current tasks.
Search
Spotlight search across clusters, vms, actions etc.

## 2.7 Unable to unregister PE from Prism Central
Check that PE is still registered to PC.
Use ncli multicluster get-cluster-state command on PE/PC to check current status of the registration.
Verify that the credentials provided are valid.
Is the username / password correct?
Do the credentials have admin privileges?
Is the PC reachable and running?
Has manual PE unregistration been attempted from PC?
Check the command ncli multicluster get-cluster-state to verify on both PE and PC side.
If only half the connection is present, then use ‘ncli multicluster delete-cluster-state’ to remove the registration info.
If nothing else is working, use the backdoor commands to delete the registration info.
zkls /appliance/physical/clusterexternalstate
zkrm /appliance/physical/clusterexternalstate/<uuid>
Repeat steps above for the zookeeper node paths /appliance/physical/clusterdatastate and /appliance/physical/zeusconfig.

## 2.8 Clusters got automatically removed/unregistered from PC
Clusters get automatically unregistered in the following situations:
The other end ran the backdoor command to delete the cluster state.
Cluster is destroyed and re-created. The temporary user used for PE-PC communication is deleted and so the PC automatically unregisters the cluster.
The SSL certificate on Prism was changed when an existing PE-PC registration exists. This causes the heartbeat to fail with unauthorized error. If this certificate change is on PC, all PEs registered will remove the connection to PC. In turn, PC will find that it is not authorized to talk to PE and will unregister the PEs.

## 2.9 Unable to launch NCLI on PC
Check that the Prism gateway service on PC is up and running.
NCLI may fail to launch if it is running into Out of memory (OOM) errors. In this case, check the top output and look at the free memory to see if it is sufficient.  At startup NCLI requires about 400 MB+ of memory. So if total free memory on CVM is less than this, NCLI may fail to launch.

## 2.11 User account gets locked out after password reset attempts
This issue is only applicable for Asterix.1 or later.
Run the following commands to reset your admin password:
sudo faillock --user admin --reset
#if that doesn't help..

sudo passwd admin

## 2.12 Communication between PE and PC failing with network connectivity issues
Connectivity issues between PE and PC can happen for a variety of reasons:
PE and PC cannot ping or reach each other.
PE is configured with a Virtual IP (External IP). This IP may not be reachable from PC.
PE and/or PC are behind a NAT / firewall.
Check the firewall to confirm that port 9440 is reachable.
The CVM IP is not reachable directly, since it is NATd. There is no support for communication with servers behind a NAT today.
External IP address has been misconfigured.
The external IP should only be set by editing the cluster properties via Prism UI or NCLI. If the same is attempted by trying to adding a NIC on the VM from outside (e.g. by logging into vSphere client), that would not configure the VIP correctly and the PE would become unreachable.

## 2.13 Specific clients are unable to connect to Prism.
Certain browser clients or SDK clients may be unable to reach Prism service. When this happens check if:
Client auth has been enabled by the cluster.
ncli> authconfig get-client-authentication-config
Auth Config Status        : true

In this doc, we will discuss the high level manual steps needed to perform PCDR using older IDF backups present in S3 bucket.

## Background
For Snap2S3 and PCs running in AWS we have designed PCDR to backup and restore from S3 natively. IDF has the capability to backup and restore from S3 bucket (bucket LCM is taken care of by the end user and configured while protecting PC).
As of today, IDF takes periodic full backups (by default hourly) from PC and keeps 3 (configurable by gflag insights_uploader_max_num_backups_retain_in_s3) backups in S3 and automatically uses the latest one to recover from during PC recovery. In situations where a user wants to recover from previous backups (not the latest one), for example:- maybe LTSS was not able to restore VMs after recovering the PC from the latest backup or some other error scenarios (like latest backup objects are corrupted in S3).

[IDF Processes & Operations | V4 Guidelines from IDF side]
Guidelines from IDF side for v4 GA API’s
June 2023
Complete
In this document we have defined a set of guidelines from the IDF side for teams onboarding to V4 for APIs that depend on IDF for their v4 workflows. These guidelines are to ensure proper functioning of the PC as a whole and provide a seamless and scalable Manageability Platform to our end customers.
Based on the experience with older v2/v3 API’s and some of the recent requests seen regarding v4 API’s. We have come up with the following set of guidelines:
Measure resource consumption of IDF for new v4 API’s
Indexes for “Latency Critical Queries” only
Well defined default projection list for read APIs (no select *)
Mandate non-empty $select for metric queries
Select * from IDF shouldn’t be done
Enable Backup only for types that are not reconstructable after PCDR
Unique Request/RPC ID for each workflow to track originating workflow
Move from uuid to _entity_id_
Adding pre-computed data to PE origin(replicated) entities.
Query guidelines to optimize workflows.

[IDF Processes & Operations | V4 Guidelines from IDF side]
## IDF resource consumption for v4 APIs:
We want to ensure that we account for the additional resource consumption on IDF(if any) for the new v4 API’s being added.
Also ensure that the queries are optimized and are not causing any spikes in memory/CPU during execution. Because we have observed many API’s in the past which had very inefficient queries, fetching a lot of data (sometimes unnecessary) and causing OOM’s and timeouts for other clients as well. For example, we still have the v2/host, which requests around “164 attributes” and metrics for all the nodes in the system. Also the downsampling interval isn’t specified in the query. Such queries had led to ONCALL and never got fixed and still leads to on-calls. We have also recently seen Flow query asking metric data for 10k entities for 24 hours with 30 sec ds causing huge CPU and Mem spikes in IDF causing timeouts for other clients. And this was in a direct user UI workflow.
This should either be tested per API or during system tests runs so that APIs with inefficient queries will never happen to get released. And also to ensure that IDF is given required extra resources for supporting the new workloads on the PC.
Teams can either:
Get this monitored via the Performance Benchmark done for v4 APIs on the perf test tool.
Teams can use the “Resource Tax Calculator” tool where you can compute the combined resource usage of IDF for all the new workflows introduced per release. Link to resource tax

[IDF Processes & Operations | V4 Guidelines from IDF side]
## Indexes
Almost every database supports creation and utilization of Secondary indexes to improve latencies of critical/foreground queries. But these secondary indexes come with an associated cost; usually higher memory and disk usage, added latencies in creates/updates, higher init times. Similarly, in IDF we have support for Secondary Indexes and utilizing them is advised for latency sensitive queries and for required use cases (like queries for Evictable entity types).

[IDF Processes & Operations | V4 Guidelines from IDF side]
## Impact of Indexes in IDF As per IDF’s implementation of indexes, each new index has a direct impact on Memory consumption and Bootup time of IDF. Currently, IDF keeps all the secondary indexes in-memory and because of this it needs to rebuild the entire index on service restart hence having too many (specially unneeded) secondary indexes can have negative impact on the overall performance of the system and resource usage. We have recently seen teams indexing attributes to fall in the 200 ms bracket. Upon further discussions, in some of the cases it was seen that it was to support few niche use-cases. This cannot be supported because there will be severe implications for IDF and other applications on the PC which depend on IDF. The memory consumption will increase, the bootup times will grow, having a direct implication on upgrade time of the PC. For a team which had 8 indexed attributes on an entity type which has a per node scale of 100k entities. We have seen the RSS increase by 130 MB and the bootup time by 15 secs. There are over 34 teams and easily up to 35 entity types. Each individual team adding indexing will have a severe impact on the overall health of IDF and PC. To ensure practicality, we recommend to divide the API’s into 3 broader categories: Latency critical APIs Frequently used APIs Analytical/Debugging APIs And create indexes only for critical use cases and should prevent over usage. Don’t add indexes to fasten the queries for analytics or debugging.

[IDF Processes & Operations | V4 Guidelines from IDF side]

Don’t add indexes to fasten the queries for analytics or debugging. Indexes can’t be added for all attributes exposed for filtering/sorting. Also, going forward request for any new index addition should be documented in the following sheet: Link

## Have a well defined default projection list for a read APIs (no select *):
A lot of fields in the API might just be present for completeness sake, niche use cases, debugging or UI specific use-cases etc. Like:
fields like “description” or other long string fields will take higher deserialisation times
non-indexed fields for evictable entities will increase the overall API latency because data has to be fetched from the store.
fields that need a lot of backend processing like data fetch from multiple services/requiring joins etc. And these fields can get expensive to compute.
All of this data is tough to convey to clients and there is a high chance that they might use that API’s without explicitly setting $select parameters. This will cause unnecessary load on the system. So it’s better to identify and not compute expensive attributes by default.

[IDF Processes & Operations | V4 Guidelines from IDF side]
## Mandate non-empty $select for metric queries:
All the metric based endpoints exposed via v4 should make $select a mandatory non-empty and should disable use of select *. The metric reads are heavy and expensive, hence allowing select * will have a severe impact on the system.

## Select * from IDF shouldn’t be done
As mentioned in “IDF resource consumption for v4 APIs” we have seen clients often fetching all the raw_columns or way more raw_columns than which are actually needed. Clients need to be mindful of the columns requested and attributes should be requested on a need-only basis. One of the major reasons behind this has been the use of common utils.
So we request the clients to be very mindful of the attributes being requested and also the common utils being used. Please request only the attributes and metrics that are absolutely needed.

[IDF Processes & Operations | V4 Guidelines from IDF side]
## Enable Backup only for types that are not reconstructable after PCDR
For enabling PCDR for new entity_types, we are severely restricted based on resources available on the PE. Since the backups are stored on the PE and given that a PE node has limited resources can only store 120k entities, backing up all the entities on PC is not an option.
So backup can only be enabled for entity types which cannot be reconstructed after bootup and are critical. The guideline in general is to backup only user input data but not data generated by internal services on account of the user input data. The expectation is that, during restore the services should re-create the data based on the restored input data.

[IDF Processes & Operations | V4 Guidelines from IDF side]
## Uniquely Identifiable Queries
In previous v2/v3 API’s and in multiple other services, we have seen that a lot of workflows don’t have a uniquely identifiable query name. This causes multiple issues, especially during debugging because we won’t be able to track the workflows making a given query. We have faced this problem during on-calls extensively and client teams also took a lot of time to identify the workflow.  In the past we have seen cases where all workflows in a service use a common hardcoded query_name. We have seen cases where service owners were also not able to find the source of queries.
The client facing RPC requests will soon expose a “source_id/query_name” field which should contain the service and exact workflow which generates the query. Also should include the context about the service. Ensure that the fields are getting set in your code and also the common utils that are being used by your service.

[IDF Processes & Operations | V4 Guidelines from IDF side]
## Move from uuid to _entity_id_ possible
We have seen this practice across multiple entity types in Nutanix that clients have chosen to use the “uuid” field (often having the same value as Entity ID) as if it’s a primary_key for the entity type. IDF doesn’t support making explicit attributes as a primary key and IDF considers the Entity ID itself as the primary_key and having queries based on Entity ID are more efficient (especially for point reads, sorting, filtering, joins etc). Refer to the “Queries” section for more information around point reads.
Hence it is recommended to move away from “uuid” workflows. If your legacy API stack is based on this field, now is a good time to get out of this practice. With “uuid”, scaling to higher scales might not be possible.

[IDF Processes & Operations | V4 Guidelines from IDF side]
## Pre-computed/additional data for PE origin entities
We have seen it as a pattern that a lot of teams want to do some precomputation or have some additional data for entities that have replicated from PE. However IDF doesn’t support modifying synced entities on the replica. In some cases, teams have created a different entity type and write the data there and try to maintain a 1-1 mapping between tables. This is highly inefficient and also would limit a lot of querying capabilities.
As a solution to the above use-case, we have come up with writable partitions on replicas called Namespaces. A brief description of Namespaces:
Maximum of 255 namespaces can be registered under an entity_type.
indexed, non-nested attributes can be registered under a namespace.
The query capabilities are similar to what the attributes of the entity_type have.
A namespace can have its own lifecycle, cas_value within the lifecycle of the parent entity.
Some limitations with namespaces:
We don’t support any sync of namespaces, hence PCDR cannot be performed on these entities.
Also groups and other layers have to enhance to support namespaces queries
Currently there is no support from v4 platform side for the same.
Pulse data collection is also currently not supported for namespace data.
Please refer to the following doc for more details: Doc link

[IDF Processes & Operations | V4 Guidelines from IDF side]
## Query guidelines for specific workflows:
We have found a few common patterns and use-cases in queries and we have some optimized query workflows for the same.

## GetEntities vs GetEntitiesWithMetrics:
To fetch a few attributes, given a set of _entity_ids, we have often seen clients confused between using GetEntities vs GetEntitiesWithMetrics.

Don’t use GetEntities if the entity contains any heavy attributes with long strings or bytes such as _zprotobuf_ or _protobuf_. Also if the number of entities is higher, it’s suggested to use GetEntitiesWithMetrics. In other cases, either should be fine.

## Point queries vs passing _entity_id_ in the filter criteria:
A very common use-case we have seen is, fetch the entities with a list of entity ids. We have often seen clients specify this in the where_clause of the query. If the Entity IDs are mentioned in the where_clause, the latency is linearly dependent on the total number of entities in the table and at scale query latency will be very high to even fetch one entity.
Avoid this and mention the Entity IDs in the entity_list param of the query. This is very efficient and will reduce the amount of processing on IDF. (Link to param)

## Cursor queries:
We have seen use-cases where clients want to read the entire table. In such cases, instead of using queries with increasing offsets, it’s suggested to use cursor queries with _entity_id_ as the sort column. For more info on cursor queries: (Link to param)

[IDF Processes & Operations | V4 Guidelines from IDF side]
## Fetching latest metrics:
In cases where metrics are fetched along with attributes, we have seen instances where there was no downsampling interval mentioned in the query. IDF by default considers 10 ds intervals worth of data in such scenarios. For queries where ds interval is say one hour or one day, IDF has to process 10 hours/10 days. This slows down the query.
So please ensure that the queries don’t have any metrics unknowingly. And if the latest query has metrics being fetched, provide the appropriate sampling interval or the max intervals read for the latest query if the metric has a higher downsampling operator (Link to param).

## Fetching counts/groups/unique values:
We have often seen clients having workflows where they want to only get the total count of entities satisfying a given filter criteria, or number of entities present per group or to only get the unique values of a given column. In this case, there is no need to get all the Entity GUIDs. 

	For such use cases, we have a flag “kSkipGuidsForRawColumns”. Please refer to this link for more details: Proto link

## Fetch total unfiltered entity/groups counts in the same query:
It is a common use-case for our clients to fetch the total number of entities/groups present along with the filtered entities. Clients end up firing an additional RPC for the same. To avoid that, we have exposed 2 new flag in the query: kFetchTotalUnfilteredEntityCount & kFetchTotalUnfilteredGroupCount. Proto link

[IDF Processes & Operations | V4 Guidelines from IDF side]
## Left outer joins/Lookup queries:
We have seen clients fetching data across multiple entity types as a part of separate queries. IDF now supports lookup and can instead rely on lookup instead of firing multiple queries.
Link for more details: Proto link

## Optimal filtering:
We have often seen clients overuse regex and nested boolean expressions in the past. Regex evaluation is very expensive and should be used only when utmost necessary.
For use-cases like filter entities for which string field “a” has value “a1”, “a2” or “a3”. We have seen regex queries like: a=kLike=”a1|a2|a3” or (a==a1 || a==a2 || a==a3).
Instead please use the appropriate operators like kIn. 

Link to detailed description of all the supported operators: Proto link

Select * from IDF shouldn’t be done
Enable Backup only for types that are not reconstructable after PCDR

## If you CAN NOT login to cot01/cot02:
Are you part of the group that is allowed to connect to COT servers?
If you were just added to one of the COT groups give it few minutes time to sync that information - logging constantly to cot servers will not speed up this process it might delay it,
Verify what is your correct username (your main username), it is in LDAP/AD the field sAMAccountName, cot servers are running Linux and they are case sensitive, make sure the username that you are using is typed exactly the same way as the sAMAccountName field.

## We have got a new/different remote tunnel, what it can do:
connect you to a cluster via the remote tunnel ,
download files from the cluster (files go directly to diamond to a specific case),
all your interactions on the cluster are logged - you can view those logs or upload them to a case.

## Things not allowed in this remote tunnel:
any port redirection (this includes aegis, prism, custom ports, anything)
uploading files to the clusters
copying any files to or from the new cot servers (cot01/ cot02) using scp or sftp
normal shell (for example /bin/bash) access

[IDF Processes & Operations | remote tunnel - how to]
## How does it work?:
User connects with SSH to the below servers using their AD credentials (firstname.lastname / AD password):
cot01.corp.nutanix.com
cot02.corp.nutanix.com
If you do not have access please contact your manager to add you to the correct AD group.
Connecting or searching tunnels to clusters can be done based on:
an exact cluster id
a salesforce case number
a partial cluster name
a partial customer name
Last two will work only if the result returns a unique open remote tunnel. Examples below and once connected using help tun_connect or help tun_search commands.
This version also gives you a possibility to use SSH keys on a per cluster basis. You can add the keys using the sshkey commands (check help sshkey for more information).
All commands are documented, if the help description is not good enough I will work on making it more clear. Drop me an email at: marekl@nutanix.com

## Other limitations:
Users will get into a limited shell (no bash full access allowed).
File downloading from the cluster copies down a *single* file at a time, use tar on the cluster to copy a whole directory structure.

## Reporting issues, asking for help:
Try build-in help system first, good starting point is: help howtouse
Ask on slack channel #remote_tunnel
For bugs or feature requests please open a JIRA using project SRE and component "Nutanix Remote"

## Easy collaboration between multiple engineers on customer cluster with none default password set for “nutanix” user.
1. sshkey_gen <cluster_id> --> this creates a private/public key pair for just this cluster
2. You get the public key to the customer via ncli / prism lockdown mode or
2a. If you can connect to the cluster using your own ssh key you can use the ncli command:
ncli cluster add-public-key name=ntnx_support_key \
file-path=/path/to/the/public_ssh_key.txt
3. you do sshkey_share and everyone else can use it (everyone having tunnel access like Engineering)
4. You can look at your private and public key with sshkey_view <cluster_id>, sshkey_view_pub <cluster_id>

[Root Cause Analyses | 4.6 Data Sync Issue]
4.6 Data Sync Issue
Suresh Sivaprakasam
Problem
1) Cluster storage widget would turn randomly turn red which means
cluster storage was 95%+ and turn off within few mins whereas real
cluster storage usage was averaging around 30%(quite far from 95%).
2) Cluster IOPs for two clusters was always 0.
3) Cluster avg latency for two clusters was always 0.
Root Cause
Two of the clusters had last stats update ~10mins and ~6 mins
behind. Due to this when we ask for latest values, we always look back
30 * 10 = 300secs or 5mins, we don't find anything whereas other
clusters didn't have this issue.
Root Cause 1) The storage usage_bytes and capacity_bytes were empty
which treated by Prism as -1, resulting in computation -1/-1 * 100 =
100% cluster usage J
Root Cause 2, 3) controller_num_iops is derived which looks at
controller_num_io, same issue nothing found in last 5mins hence
displayed 0. Same with controller_avg_io_latency.
Shrivatsan found data sync wasn't the problem, the two clusters were 8
mins behind with a 90s delay ~10mins and same with other cluster,
setting NTP synchronize fixed it.
Painpoints
1. We didn't bundle insights_rpc_tool in 4.6, we can't do anything
without this, I had to manually copy to remote tunnel cluster and
from there to PC VM.
2. We need to enable remote tunnel support to PC. Filed ENG-52321
3. We need to enable port forwarding of PC ports 9440, 2027, 2040
etc. Filed ENG-52321

[Root Cause Analyses | IDF registering too many watches in zookeeper]
IDF registering too many watches in zookeeper
June 2020

## Background:
Recently, we got an ONCALL (ONCALL-8955) where we noticed the zeus client of IDF was not able to talk to the Zookeeper server for a long time (8 hours). More details can be found in this document: https://docs.google.com/document/d/1VYN1ut6t_X7ExeIxLcIIYzEV25XRvYqlvbPj48vpaVg/edit#
We have seen similar issues before:
https://jira.nutanix.com/browse/ENG-300973
https://jira.nutanix.com/browse/ENG-239248
In those cases, Zookeeper team noticed that IDF might be registering a huge number (e.g. half a million) of watches in ZK, which cause the unresponsiveness of ZK. Though the problem has been solved from ZK client side by introducing a more efficient processing, we haven’t root caused why IDF registered so many watches in ZK.

[Root Cause Analyses | IDF registering too many watches in zookeeper]
## Action Items: To get to the bottom of the issue, we will need help from our QA team to keep an eye on this. Following are methods to keep track of the number of watches registered in ZK: Quote from https://zookeeper.apache.org/doc/r3.3.2/zookeeperAdmin.html: wchs New in 3.3.0: Lists brief information on watches for the server. wchc New in 3.3.0: Lists detailed information on watches for the server, by session. This outputs a list of sessions(connections) with associated watches (paths). Note, depending on the number of watches this operation may be expensive (ie impact server performance), use it carefully. wchp New in 3.3.0: Lists detailed information on watches for the server, by path. This outputs a list of paths (znodes) with associated sessions. Note, depending on the number of watches this operation may be expensive (ie impact server performance), use it carefully. So we can run following to get the number of watches: echo wchs | nc zk1 9876 9876 is the port used by Zookeeper. Repeat this for zk2 and zk3 if there are 3 ZK instances. We will get something as following: nutanix@NTNX-10-46-50-161-A-PCVM:~$ echo wchs | nc zk1 9876 75 connections watching 237 paths Total watches:361 We can probably have a script or something to capture this (similar to what we’ve done for the PC scale project, monitoring some metrics). [Root Cause Analyses | RCA for ENG-150969]
Problem reported in ENG-150969 was that IDF was in a crash loop while trying to reproduce oncall-3464. The reason for the crash was the memory used by insights server exceeded the RSS limit of 6 GB. The VM had 42k share_dir_metadata entities, that used about 100 MB of memory. We were running afs222 that was built on top of AOS 5.1.2 build on the VMs. The following data was collected from the cluster when the problem happened: 1500 GetEntitiesWithMetrics RPCs for share_dir_metadata consumed about 2.5 GB of memory in about ~3.30 minutes. This roughly translates to 7 RPCs per second. Verified that the # of query constructors match # of destructors. So, doesn't look like we are holding references to the query objects. The stack trace confirmed that the query ret protobuf destructors are being called as well: #6 0xf0cf8b in nutanix::insights::interface::EntityWithMetric::~EntityWithMetric() at ??:? #7 0xf0d405 in nutanix::insights::interface::QueryGroupResult::~QueryGroupResult() at Changed to opt build from release, but the same memory bloat was observed. When insights server’s memory started increasing steady, we noticed that IDF was constantly pounded with queries and was using all the 12 cores -- the VMs had 12 vcpus and 32 GB of memory, out of which 6 GB was allocated to insights server. Made changes to the query code to return from Execute function without any processing and see if the memory still increases. This was done to confirm if there were other RPCs that were

[Root Cause Analyses | RCA for ENG-150969]
server. Made changes to the query code to return from Execute function without any processing and see if the memory still increases. This was done to confirm if there were other RPCs that were responsible for the memory bloat (leak). The memory utilized by IDF remained constant (740 MB) after this change. Made changes to the query code to not return the query response (the query was processed and the response was build, but just that we cleared the response at the end). This was put under a gflag so that we could enable/disable this back and forth. When the memory was increasing, I enabled the gflag and I noticed that the memory used by IDF started going down slowly. After a few seconds, the memory used by IDF reached a constant value (740 MB). [RPC Behaviour & API Documentation | Stats Vs Attributes Persisted as Time Series]
## Stats:
Time-series data registered with is_attribute: false
Populated using PutMetricData RPC
Well tested with lots of features (complete support for different down sampling
operators and down sampling interval, etc.)
Fetching the latest data point in the latest query (query without start time and end time specified) may not always return a data point. The value is only returned if the data was populated within the last 10 (default, can be modified in query) samples for that metric. The start time is determined by the sampling interval of metric (now time - 10*sampling_interval).
No restriction in populating past or future data.

[RPC Behaviour & API Documentation | Stats Vs Attributes Persisted as Time Series]
## Attributes persisted as time series: Attribute data registered with is_attribute: true and persist_attribute_as_time_series: true. These attributes behave both as attributes as well as stats. Populated using UpdateEntity RPC (unless the entity type is a dimension fact table) Restriction in populating past or future data as the update will go via UpdateEntity RPC. Populating data with past timestamp_usecs beyond 6 months in the past and future timestamps beyond 5 mins from current time is not allowed. In a latest query (without time range), the latest populated value will be returned irrespective of when it was populated along with the exact timestamp with which it was populated. In a time range query, the values will be returned which were populated in the specified time range. If no ds interval is specified, the values will be returned with the exact timestamps with which they were populated. If the ds interval is specified, the query will return data in buckets aligned by the ds interval. Hourly retention and raw retention flags can be specified in the arg similar to how it’s done for stats and the same will be used for TTL calculation. The TTL calculation logic is exactly the same as it is for stats. bucketize_timestamps_in_tsdb field can only be set to false for such metrics.
